notes.title: Model evaluation and validation
notes.desc: Cross-validation schemes and nested CV, the confusion matrix and choosing a threshold, ROC and AUC built by hand and the tiny slice that matters at low capacity, PR and average precision, log loss, Brier and calibration, ranking and regression metrics, and comparing models honestly.

chunks.x: Model evaluation and validation · Deepam Minda

Validation must copy deployment. Stratified k-fold for independent rows, grouped folds when new customers or documents arrive, forward-in-time splits with a gap for anything temporal. A score you tuned on is optimistic: on pure-noise labels the best of 60 settings scored 0.58 accuracy in CV, while nested CV said 0.505, close to the true 0.50.

A classifier is judged three ways: its ranking (AUC, average precision), its decisions at a threshold (precision, recall, F1, cost), and its probabilities (log loss, Brier, calibration). The threshold comes from costs or capacity: with calibrated probabilities, flag when p gt C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) . Youden's J and F1 answer different questions and can be far from the cost optimum.

AUC is the chance a random positive outscores a random negative (the Mann–Whitney statistic). It ignores calibration and averages over every threshold. When a team can review only 1% of cases, only the leftmost 1% of the ROC curve matters, under 1% of the area: two models with AUC 0.95 caught 231 and 362 of 500 frauds there.

Precision–recall and average precision show what a reviewer sees. A random model's AP equals the prevalence, so AP moves with the base rate. 300 false alarms pushed above every fraud cut AP from 0.30 to 0.12 while ROC-AUC fell by 0.003.

Probabilities need proper scores and calibration. Log loss and Brier are minimized only by the true probabilities; Brier = reliability − resolution + uncertainty. Fix calibration on held-out data with Platt, temperature or isotonic scaling, and undo class reweighting by rescaling the odds by the ratio of real to training base-rate odds.

The metric decides what the model predicts: RMSE the mean, MAE the median, pinball loss a quantile, MAPE something biased low. Ranking uses P@k, R@k, MRR, MAP and nDCG per query. Compare models on the same rows: a paired bootstrap, McNemar, or a corrected t-test for CV folds, because fold scores aren't independent.

A model is only useful on data it hasn't seen. Its generalization error is the expected error on new cases drawn from the population it will serve. The training error underestimates it, because the model has partly fitted the noise in those particular rows: a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier gets every training row right and can be useless on new ones. So every honest estimate comes from rows that played no part in any decision about the model.

Three jobs. Training data fits the parameters and every preprocessing statistic; validation data (a held-out set or CV folds) chooses everything else, including the threshold and the calibration map; the test set is looked at once, after everything is frozen, since every look that leads to a change makes its score optimistic (honest splits, leakage types).

The test set should look like deployment: the most recent period, the same population, the same unit (customer, document, store). For time-ordered problems that means an out-of-time test with a gap, and its size is set by the number of positives, not rows (out of time, holdout size). Adversarial validation checks that test rows look like training rows (data-preparation note).
Refit, then don't touch. After choosing everything, it's common to refit on training plus validation data before the final test. Nothing changes after the test score is seen.
Offline is still a proxy. The last word is online: shadow mode, then an A/B test (shadow mode, A/B testing).
A metric means little until it's compared with the simplest thing that could work. Each metric has a natural do-nothing baseline:
Always predict the majority class
1 - pi ( pi = share of positives): 99.5% at 0.5% positives
Random or constant scores
Predict the base rate for everyone
The label entropy; pi(1 - pi)
The standard deviation of y ; R² = 0
Naive (tomorrow = today) or seasonal naive (= same day last week)
MASE ≈ 1 (exactly 1 in-sample)
Today's system, rule or model
The bar that decides whether to ship
The last row matters most. If a hand-written rule gets 90% of the gain, the model has to justify its cost; how to stage those baselines in a project is in the lifecycle note.

Say it in an interview: “I estimate generalization only on data that played no part in any decision. Validation chooses, the test set confirms once, and the split copies how the model will meet new data. Every metric gets its baseline next to it: a 99% accuracy means nothing if 99% of cases are negative.”

One held-out split gives one noisy number, and wastes the held-out rows for training. Cross-validation rotates which part is held out: split the data into k folds, train on k - 1 of them, score on the one left out, repeat k times, and average. Every row is used for validation exactly once.

What the average estimates. Not the score of the final model trained on all the data, but the expected score of the procedure “fit this model on (k - 1)/k of a dataset like this one”. Training on less data usually scores slightly worse, so k-fold CV is a little pessimistic, more so for small k .
The one rule that picks the scheme: each fold must imitate how the model will meet new data. Ask what's new at prediction time: new rows from the same mix, new customers, or the future.

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: Shuffle, then split into k equal folds, unless order carries meaning (time; see below).

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: k = 5 or 10 is the usual compromise. Smaller k trains each model on less data (more pessimistic) and is cheaper; larger k costs more fits.

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: Leave-one-out ( k = n ) is nearly unbiased but needs n fits, can't be stratified, and its estimate can be highly variable because the n training sets are almost identical. A metric like AUC can't be computed on a one-row fold; you'd have to pool the predictions.

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: Pooling vs averaging. AUC computed on the pooled out-of-fold predictions mixes scores from k different models, whose scales can differ; averaging the per-fold AUCs doesn't. They usually agree closely; when they don't, the fold models disagree about the score scale, which also matters if you'll pick one threshold.

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: Repeated k-fold reruns CV with different shuffles and averages, which removes the luck of one particular partition (how noisy a CV estimate is, below).

chunks.h: k-fold, and the choice of k
chunks.x: Bagged models get a nearly free validation estimate from the rows each tree didn't see (out-of-bag, in the random-forests note).

Each fold keeps the class proportions of the whole dataset. With rare positives, plain random folds can be badly uneven: with 1,000 rows, 20 positives and 5 shuffled folds, the ideal is 4 positives per fold, but in 32% of random shuffles some fold gets 0 or 1 positive (and in 41% some fold gets 7 or more). A fold with one positive gives a recall of 0 or 1 and an AUC that's pure noise. Stratification gives exactly 4, 4, 4, 4, 4. Use it by default for classification; for regression you can stratify on bins of y .

All rows of one group (a customer, patient, store, device, document, or vendor's invoice template) go into the same fold. Needed whenever deployment means new groups: if one customer's rows sit on both sides, the model can score well by recognizing the customer rather than by learning anything that transfers.
In numbers. 200 customers with 10 rows each; each customer has a hidden risk level and three fixed attributes that identify them but say nothing about that risk. A random forest:
Random 5-fold (a customer's rows on both sides)
Group 5-fold (by customer)
Truth: 2,000 brand-new customers

The random split rewarded memorizing each customer's attributes, which carry their hidden risk only for customers already seen. Grouped folds remove most of that inflation. If deployment means the same groups later in time (forecasting known stores), split by time instead. StratifiedGroupKFold does both stratification and grouping.
For anything ordered in time and predicted forward, always train on the past and validate on the future. With 12 months, three folds of two test months, and a one-month gap:
Rolling window (5 months): train

Expanding (scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit) uses all history; rolling (max_train_size) keeps a fixed-length recent window, for when old data is stale or the process drifts. Comparing the two tells you whether old data still helps.

The gap drops the rows between training and test. Use one when the label covers a horizon (default within 12 months, sales over the next 7 days: the last training labels are only known during the test period), when features use lags or rolling windows that would straddle the boundary, or when production has a real delay between the data and the prediction. Make it as long as that horizon or delay.

Why not shuffled folds: they train on the future to predict the past and turn forecasting into interpolation between neighbouring time points, so the score is optimistic (figure and leakage details in the data-preparation note).

Purging and embargo (from finance): when history is too short for forward-only folds and the relationship is assumed stable, train on blocks both before and after the test block, but purge training rows whose label windows overlap the test period and add an embargo, dropping rows just after the test block too, since their lagged features still carry test-period information. If you're simulating real forecasting, use forward splits.

chunks.h: How noisy is a CV estimate?
chunks.x: One dataset of 300 rows, a logistic regression, stratified 5-fold CV:

chunks.h: How noisy is a CV estimate?
chunks.x: The five fold scores were 0.783, 0.633, 0.667, 0.717 and 0.783: a spread of 15 points between folds, standard deviation 0.068.

chunks.h: How noisy is a CV estimate?
chunks.x: The partition alone moves the average: reshuffling the same rows 50 times gave CV accuracies from 0.687 to 0.743 (standard deviation 0.011). Picking between two models that differ by less than this on one shuffle is picking a seed. Repeated CV averages it away.

chunks.h: How noisy is a CV estimate?
chunks.x: The naive standard error, fold standard deviation / sqrt k , treats the folds as independent. They aren't: training sets overlap, and all folds come from one dataset. Over 300 fresh datasets the CV estimate's real standard deviation was 0.029; the naive formula averaged 0.024, about 17% too small. There's no unbiased estimator of the variance of k-fold CV (Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004), so treat fold spreads as a rough guide and compare models with paired methods (section 10).

Why tuning on the CV score is optimistic. Try 60 hyperparameter settings, each scored by CV, and report the best. Each score is truth plus noise, and taking the maximum picks the setting whose noise happened to be most favourable: the winner's curse. Measured: 100 rows, 20 features, labels that are pure coin flips (so every model's true accuracy is 0.50), a k-nearest-neighbours grid of 60 settings, repeated on 40 datasets:
Best inner CV score of the 60 settings
Eight points of “accuracy” on pure noise, from selection alone. The more settings tried and the smaller the data, the bigger the bias.

The fix: two loops. The outer loop estimates the score: split into k_out folds and hold each out once. The inner loop runs entirely inside each outer training part: a full CV search over the grid that picks the best setting, which is then refitted on the whole outer training part and scored once on the outer test fold. The outer test fold never influences any choice.
Nested CV. Each outer fold's test part (orange) is touched once; all tuning happens on the inner folds (purple validation parts) inside the outer training part.

What its score means: the expected performance of the whole procedure, “search this grid with inner CV, then fit”. It does not pick a hyperparameter setting; different outer folds may choose different ones (and if they disagree wildly, the choice is unstable).
The final model: run the inner search once on all the data, and report the nested score as its expected performance.

Cost: k_out times k_in times (grid size) fits: 5 × 4 × 60 = 1,200 for the design in the figure with a 60-setting grid. With plenty of data, a single train / validation / test split does the same job far more cheaply: the test set plays the outer loop.

Say it in an interview: “The folds should copy deployment: stratified for rare classes, grouped when new customers arrive, forward in time with a gap as long as the label horizon. And the score I tuned on is optimistic, because I kept the best of many noisy estimates; on pure-noise labels the best of 60 settings showed 58% accuracy. Nested CV, or an untouched test set, gives the honest number.”
A classifier gives each case a score. Three families of metric judge three different things, and most confusion in evaluation comes from reading one family as if it were another:
The ranking: are positives scored above negatives?
ROC-AUC, average precision, precision@k
The decisions at one cut-off
Precision, recall, F1, cost
The probabilities: does 0.3 mean 30%?
Log loss, Brier, calibration

It costs little on the ROC curve and a lot at the top of the ranking, and it will dominate the log loss. Sections 03 to 07 work each metric on these eight rows first, then on larger examples.

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: TPR, FNR, FPR and specificity each divide by a true class count, so they describe how the model treats positives and negatives separately. Change how many positives there are and, as long as each class's scores look the same, these don't move. Precision, NPV and accuracy mix the two classes, so they move with the prevalence pi , the share of positives. Precision written in terms of the other rates:

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: precision = fracTPRcdotpiTPRcdotpi + FPRcdot(1 - pi)

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: In words: of everything flagged, the true flags are the share of positives times the share of them caught; the false flags are the share of negatives times the share of them wrongly caught. Keep TPR = 1.00 and FPR = 0.25 from the eight rows, but move to a fraud stream where pi = 0.5\% : precision falls from 0.80 to 0.005/(0.005 + 0.25 times 0.995) = 0.02 . The same model now raises 50 alarms per real fraud.

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: “TPR and FPR don't depend on prevalence” holds only under pure label shift: the base rate changes but each class's score distribution doesn't. A new population usually changes the case mix too (a spectrum shift: more borderline positives, different kinds of negatives), and then TPR, FPR and AUC move as well.

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: In the fraud stream used later in this note (0.5% fraud), flagging nothing scores 99.5% accuracy and catches nothing. Accuracy is a fair summary only when the classes are roughly balanced and both errors cost about the same. Two single numbers that don't reward the do-nothing model:

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: Balanced accuracy, the mean of recall and specificity. A constant prediction scores 0.5. On the eight rows at t = 0.55 : (1.00 + 0.75)/2 = 0.875 .

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), the correlation between predicted and true labels, from −1 to 1, with 0 for guessing. It uses all four cells, so it's high only when both classes are handled well. On the eight rows: 0.775.

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: MCC = fracTPcdot TN - FPcdot FNsqrt(TP + FP)(TP + FN)(TN + FP)(TN + FN)

chunks.h: The running example: eight scored cases
chunks.x: In words: the cross-product of right minus wrong cells, scaled by the four row and column totals. When the denominator is 0 (a constant predictor), libraries return 0. Cohen's kappa, accuracy corrected for the agreement two raters would reach by chance, is a related idea (0.75 on the eight rows), mostly used for agreement between annotators.
When positives are rare and you care about them, the two numbers that matter are precision and recall. F1 combines them with a harmonic mean:
beginaligned F_1 &= frac2PRP + R = frac2\,TP2\,TP + FP + FN \\ F_beta &= frac(1 + beta^2)\,PRbeta^2 P + R endaligned
In words: F_1 = TP/big(TP + tfrac12(FP + FN)big) , true positives divided by true positives plus the average of the two error counts. F_beta treats recall as beta times as important as precision.

Why harmonic: it's dominated by the smaller of the two, so you can't score well by maxing one. Flagging a single sure case gives P = 1 , R = 0.01 : F1 is 0.0198, where the arithmetic mean would say 0.505.
What it ignores: true negatives. That suits rare-positive retrieval, but swapping which class is “positive” changes F1.
beta in numbers: with P = 0.4 and R = 0.8 , F1 = 0.533, F_2 = 0.667 (recall-heavy: screening, where a miss is worse) and F_0.5 = 0.444 (precision-heavy: auto-actions, where a false alarm is worse).
It isn't a cost. It has no knob for “a missed fraud costs 50 false alarms”. If you know the costs, minimize the expected cost (below).
With more than two classes, compute precision, recall and F1 per class (that class against the rest), then average. A three-class example, rows are the truth:

Macro: the plain mean of the per-class F1s, (0.890 + 0.718 + 0.400)/3 = 0.669 . Every class counts equally, so the rare class C, which the model mostly misses, drags it down. Use it when every class matters.

Micro: pool TP, FP and FN over classes, then compute once: 0.82. In single-label multi-class, every wrong prediction is one FP (for the predicted class) and one FN (for the true class), so micro precision = micro recall = micro F1 = accuracy (82 of 100). The common classes dominate.
Weighted: per-class F1 weighted by class size: 0.807. Close to micro; it hides the weak rare class too.

Beyond thresholds: top- k accuracy counts a case as right when the true class is among the k highest-scored ones; multi-class log loss is -frac1nsum_i log hat p_i, y_i , the mean surprise at the true class.
Multi-label (several labels per row): micro pools every label decision, macro averages per label, and “samples” averages F1 per row.
Report the per-class table alongside any average; the average alone hides that class C's recall is 0.30.

The threshold is a business decision made on validation data, after the model is trained. 0.5 has no special status: it's right only when the probabilities are calibrated and both errors cost the same. Sweeping the eight rows from the top (the last column, Youden's J = TPR − FPR, is explained below):

Precision zigzags as you go down (1.00, 0.50, 0.67…) because each negative knocks it down and each positive lifts it. On these balanced rows the F1 and Youden criteria agree. On imbalanced data they don't, and neither is what a business usually wants. The candidates:

F1-optimal: the cut with the highest F1. A neat fact: with calibrated probabilities, the F1-optimal threshold is half the best achievable F1 (exactly in the population, approximately on a finite sample; Lipton and colleagues, 2014). The fraud screen below confirms it: best F1 0.348, threshold 0.174.
Youden's J = TPR − FPR, the height of the ROC curve above the diagonal. It treats a missed positive and a false alarm as equally bad per class, which ignores how many of each there are.
Cost-based: minimize the expected cost. This is the principled one.

A constraint: recall at least 95% (medical screening), precision at least 90% (automatic actions), or capacity: the review team can check 1,000 cases a day, so flag the top 1,000. That last one is precision@k (section 08).

The cost-based threshold, derived. A case has calibrated probability p of being positive. Flagging it costs C_FP if it's negative; not flagging costs C_FN if it's positive. Correct decisions cost nothing here.
Expected cost of flagging: (1 - p)\,C_FP .
Expected cost of not flagging: p\,C_FN .
Flag when the first is smaller: (1 - p)\,C_FP lt p\,C_FN , i.e. when p gt C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) .
beginaligned t^* &= fracC_FPC_FP + C_FN \\ t^*_general &= fracC_FP - C_TN(C_FP - C_TN) + (C_FN - C_TP) endaligned

In words: the threshold is the false alarm's share of the total cost of the two mistakes; the general form measures each mistake against the cost of getting that case right. If a missed fraud costs 50 and a false alarm 1, t^* = 1/51 approx 0.02 : flag anything with even a 2% chance. Watch which costs are real: if every flag costs a 5-unit review including flags on real fraud, and a miss costs 100, then C_TP = C_FP = 5 , C_TN = 0 , C_FN = 100 , and t^* = 5/100 = 0.05 , not 5/105 . The applied version, a lender's break-even default probability with money on both sides, is in the project-lifecycl
The formula needs calibrated probabilities (section 07). With uncalibrated scores, sweep thresholds on validation data and pick the lowest total cost, C_FPcdot FP + C_FNcdot FN .

The same answer on the ROC curve. Moving the threshold slightly trades a little TPR for a little FPR. The expected cost is flat where those trades balance, which happens where the ROC curve's slope is
slope^* = frac1 - pipicdotfracC_FPC_FN

In words: the cost-optimal point is where one more unit of FPR buys exactly enough TPR to pay for it, and both the base rate and the cost ratio set that exchange rate. Youden's J picks the point of slope 1, so it is cost-optimal only if a miss costs (1 - pi)/pi times a false alarm: 1 times at 50% prevalence, 199 times at 0.5%. That's why Youden flags far too much on rare-event problems.

The fraud screen. The rest of the note uses one imbalanced problem: 100,000 transactions a day, 0.5% fraud (500 frauds, 99,500 legitimate), a model with AUC 0.95 (scores: legitimate mathcal N(0, 1) , fraud mathcal N(2.326, 1) , and probabilities that are the exact posteriors, so perfectly calibrated; counts below are exact expectations), and a review team that can check 1,000 cases a day. A miss costs 50, a false alarm 1 (a review that finds fraud pays for itself). Five ways to set the threshold:

Each rule answers a different question. Youden's slope-1 point is the cost optimum only for a 199:1 cost ratio; F1 quietly assumes a miss and a false alarm cost the same; the cost rule needs the true cost ratio and calibrated probabilities; capacity is the binding constraint in most real review queues (the cost optimum wants 4,285 reviews a day, four times what the team can do). Whatever the rule, choose it on validation data, confirm it on the test set, and monitor the flag rate in production: when prevalence or the score distribution shifts, the same threshold flags a different number of cas

Say it in an interview: “The threshold comes from the decision, not the model. With calibrated probabilities I'd flag when p exceeds C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) ; if there's a review capacity, it's precision at that k. Youden's J is the cost optimum only when a miss costs (1-pi)/pi false alarms, so on a 0.5% problem it flags twelve times what a team can review. F1 is a reasonable default only when I don't know the costs.”

The threshold table above has one row per cut-off. The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) draws all of them at once: TPR on the vertical axis against FPR on the horizontal, as the threshold slides from above the top score (nothing flagged, the point (0, 0)) to below the bottom one (everything flagged, (1, 1)). The area under it, AUC, is one threshold-free number for the ranking.
Walk down the ranking. Each positive you pass raises TPR by 1/n_+ ; each negative raises FPR by 1/n_- . With four of each, every step is a quarter:

The ROC curve of the eight cases is a staircase. Slice the area under it into one column per negative: each column's height is the share of positives ranked above that negative. B, the hard negative, has only A above it, so its column is short.
A perfect ranking goes straight up to (0, 1) and then right: AUC 1. A random one hugs the diagonal: AUC 0.5. Here the area is 1/16 + 3 times 4/16 = 13/16 = 0.8125 .

chunks.h: AUC is a probability: pairs won
chunks.x: Look at what the columns measure. Each column is 1/n_- wide and as tall as the share of positives above that negative, so its area is (positives above it) / (n_+ n_-) . Adding the columns counts every (positive, negative) pair in which the positive is ranked higher:

chunks.h: AUC is a probability: pairs won
chunks.x: beginaligned AUC &= P(s_+ gt s_-) + tfrac12\,P(s_+ = s_-) \\ &= frac\#\pairs the positive wins\ + tfrac12\,\#\ties\n_+\,n_- endaligned

chunks.h: AUC is a probability: pairs won
chunks.x: In words: pick one positive and one negative at random; AUC is the chance the positive gets the higher score, with ties counting half. On the eight rows: A beats all four negatives (4); C, D and E each beat F, G and H but lose to B (3 each). That's 13 of 16 pairs, 0.8125, the same as the area.

chunks.h: AUC is a probability: pairs won
chunks.x: It's the Mann–Whitney U statistic. U , the number of pairs the positives win, is the statistic of the rank-sum test (Mann–Whitney), so AUC = U/(n_+ n_-) . That gives a way to compute it from ranks alone, without building the curve. Rank all scores from smallest (1) to largest, giving tied scores their average rank, and add up the positives' ranks W_+ :

chunks.h: AUC is a probability: pairs won
AUC is a probability: pairs won
chunks.x: In words: a positive with overall rank r that is the j -th smallest positive has r - 1 cases below it, j - 1 of them positives, so it beats r - j negatives. Summing r - j over positives gives W_+ - (1 + 2 + dots + n_+) . Here the ranks are H 1, G 2, F 3, E 4, D 5, C 6, B 7, A 8, so W_+ = 8 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 23 and AUC = (23 - 10)/16 = 0.8125 . This is the O(n log n) way to compute AUC: one sort.

Suppose E (positive) and F (negative) both scored 0.50. The pair (E, F) is now a tie and counts half: 12.5/16 = 0.781 . On the curve, the tied group moves up and right at the same time, a diagonal segment from (.25, .75) to (.50, 1), and the trapezoid under a diagonal is exactly the half credit.

Emitting one ROC point per row instead of per distinct score. Then tied rows are processed in whatever order the sort left them, and the AUC changes with that order: E-then-F gives 0.8125, F-then-E gives 0.75. Group tied scores and move once per group. Ties are common with rounded scores, tree models (one score per leaf) and isotonic calibration.

The actual score values. Only the order matters, so any strictly increasing transform leaves AUC unchanged. Cube the eight scores: still 0.8125. Halve the probabilities: still 0.8125, while the log loss worsens from 0.540 to 0.656 and the Brier score from 0.176 to 0.244. So AUC says nothing about calibration. A model can have a great AUC and probabilities that are off by a factor of two.

Prevalence (under pure label shift): TPR and FPR each condition on the true class, so the curve doesn't move when the base rate does. Useful for comparing rankings across populations; useless for telling you what precision you'll get.
Which thresholds you'll use. AUC averages the ranking quality over every cut-off, including ones nobody will ever operate at. The next two subsections show why that matters.
Below 0.5 means the ranking is inverted: flip the scores and you get 1 - AUC . Exactly 0.5 can still hide signal that isn't monotone (positives at both extremes).

chunks.h: Why AUC looks fine when precision is terrible
chunks.x: The fraud screen's model has AUC 0.95, which sounds excellent. Yet at Youden's threshold it flags 12,617 cases a day for 439 frauds, a precision of 3.5%, and even the top 1,000 are 77% false alarms. Two reasons the ROC view hides this:

chunks.h: Why AUC looks fine when precision is terrible
chunks.x: FPR divides by the huge negative count. 769 false alarms in the top 1,000 is an FPR of only 769/99,500 = 0.77\% . On a ROC plot that point sits a hair from the left edge and looks superb.

chunks.h: Why AUC looks fine when precision is terrible
chunks.x: Most pairs are easy. AUC counts all 500 times 99,500 approx 50 million (fraud, legitimate) pairs equally. Almost all of the legitimate transactions are obviously legitimate and sit far below every fraud; those pairs are won for free and fill up the AUC. The operational question, whether frauds beat the few hundred most suspicious-looking legitimate transactions, is decided by a tiny fraction of the pairs.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: The setting. 100,000 transactions a day, 500 of them fraud, and a team that can review 1,000. Whatever threshold you pick, you can't flag more than 1,000 cases, so you can't produce more than 1,000 false positives. Out of 99,500 legitimate transactions, that caps the false positive rate at

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: FPR_max = frac1,00099,500 approx 1.0\%

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: In words: every threshold you could ever use lives in the leftmost 1% of the ROC plot's width. The other 99% of the curve describes thresholds that would flag more cases than the team can touch. That strip from FPR 0 to 1% is the tiny slice.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: Two different 1%s meet here. The team reviews 1% of all transactions (1,000 of 100,000), and that caps the false positive rate, which counts only the legitimate ones, at 1,000/99,500. The real operating point sits a little further left, because some of the 1,000 flags are frauds: model A's top 1,000 hold 769 false alarms, an FPR of 0.77% (the circles in the figure below).

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: How little of the AUC lives there. The slice is 0.01 wide and at most 1 tall, so at most 0.01 of area can come from it. Model A's curve gives 0.00375 there: 0.4% of its AUC of 0.95. The other 0.946 is earned at false positive rates you will never operate at. So AUC is almost entirely a measure of how frauds rank against legitimate transactions the team will never look at.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: Two models, same AUC, different slice. Model B also has AUC 0.95, but its fraud scores are more spread out ( mathcal N(3.678, 2^2) ): some frauds are blatant, some subtle. The true positive rate each model reaches at a given false positive rate:

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: B is far better inside the slice and slightly worse far outside it; the curves cross and the areas come out equal. At the team's 1,000 reviews a day:

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: Left: on the whole axis, the two curves are nearly indistinguishable and their AUCs are equal. Right: the leftmost 1% of the axis, stretched to full width. This is where every usable threshold lives, and here B catches 131 more frauds a day.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: Partial AUC is the area under the ROC curve over only the FPR range you can operate in, here [0, 0.01] :

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: beginaligned pAUC &= int_0^0.01 TPR(f)\,df \\ fracpAUC0.01 &= average recall across the slice endaligned

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: In words: TPR(f) is the height of the ROC curve at false positive rate f . Integrate it only where you'll work, then divide by the slice width to get a number between 0 and 1: the average share of positives caught over the usable thresholds. A gets 0.375, B 0.692. scikit-learn's roc_auc_score(y, s, max_fpr=0.01) reports a rescaled version (the McClish correction, tfrac12big[1 + (pAUC - f_0^2/2)/(f_0 - f_0^2/2)big] with f_0 = 0.01 : f_0^2/2 is the area the diagonal gets in the slice, f_0 the area a perfect model gets) in which a random model scores 0.5 and a perfect one 1: 0.686 for A and 0.845

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: The same thing in pairs. pAUC / 0.01 is the chance that a random fraud outscores a random legitimate transaction drawn from the 1% most suspicious-looking legitimate ones (about 995 a day). Full AUC draws that legitimate transaction from all 99,500, most of them easy wins. The slice average (0.375 for A) is below A's recall in the top 1,000 (0.46) because it averages the curve's height across the whole slice, including the stricter thresholds at its left end.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: Choosing the slice: from capacity (as here), or from a tolerable false-alarm rate. Simpler alternatives that answer the same question: TPR at a fixed FPR, recall@k or precision@k at the real k.

chunks.h: The tiny slice that matters: partial AUC
chunks.x: The general lesson: a metric should measure the model where the decision is made. AUC is right when you need the whole ranking (the order of a credit book, comparing rankings across populations); when you act on a small top slice, measure the slice.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: Gini = 2\,AUC - 1 , rescaling AUC so a random ranking scores 0 and a perfect one 1. Eight rows: 0.625; fraud models: 0.90. It's the area between the curve and the diagonal, doubled (and also called Somers' D). Credit scorecards report Gini by convention. It has nothing to do with the Gini impurity used to split trees.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: KS (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) = the largest gap between the cumulative score distributions of positives and negatives, which is max_t (TPR - FPR) : the best Youden's J. Eight rows: 0.75, at the top-five cut. It summarizes one point of the curve, where AUC summarizes all of it.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: Lift@k = precision@k / prevalence: how many times better than random the top k is. Fraud screen, model A's top 1,000: 0.231/0.005 = 46times . The cumulative gains curve plots recall against the share of all cases flagged; at low prevalence it nearly coincides with the ROC curve.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: How these feed a lending decision is in the lifecycle note's offline-metric section.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: Survival models use the same pairs-won idea: Harrell's C-index is the share of comparable pairs whose predicted risks are ordered like their observed event times, with censoring deciding which pairs count.

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: More than two classes: one-vs-rest AUC (each class against the rest, then a macro or prevalence-weighted mean), or one-vs-one (Hand and Till's average over every pair of classes, less sensitive to imbalance).

chunks.h: Gini and KS: AUC in credit clothing
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “AUC is the chance a random positive outscores a random negative, which is the Mann–Whitney U divided by the number of pairs. It depends only on the order, so it ignores calibration and, under pure label shift, prevalence. Its weakness is that it averages over every threshold. If a team can act on 1% of cases, only FPR from 0 to about 1% matters, which is under 1% of the area; two models with AUC 0.95 caught 231 and 362 of 500 frauds there. So I'd report partial AUC or precision and recall at the real k.”

The precision–recall (PR) curve plots precision against recall as the threshold slides. Where ROC asks “what share of negatives did I disturb?”, PR asks “what share of my flags were real?”, which is the question a reviewer, a user or an alert queue experiences. The eight rows' points come straight from the sweep table: (0.25, 1.00), (0.25, 0.50), (0.50, 0.67), (0.75, 0.75), (1.00, 0.80), then down to (1.00, 0.50).

The baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5. A random ranking has precision pi at every recall, a flat line. Here that's 0.5; in the fraud screen it's 0.005. So an AP of 0.30 is worse than random at pi = 0.5 and strong (60 times random) at pi = 0.005 . Always quote AP next to the prevalence.
It isn't monotone. Precision rises with each positive and falls with each negative, so the curve zigzags.
The usual summary is average precision (AP), a step sum: each rise in recall is weighted by the precision at that point.
beginaligned AP &= sum_k (R_k - R_k-1)\,P_k \\ &= frac1n_+sum_positives i precision at the rank of i endaligned

In words: recall only rises when you pass a positive, by 1/n_+ each time, so AP is the average, over the positives, of the precision you have when you reach each one. Eight rows: the positives sit at ranks 1, 3, 4 and 5, where precision is 1, 2/3, 3/4 and 4/5, so AP = (1 + 0.667 + 0.75 + 0.8)/4 = 0.804 . Compare AUC 0.8125: B's position at rank 2 costs AP more, because AP cares most about the top.

AP is not the trapezoid under the PR curve. Joining PR points with straight lines invents operating points no threshold can achieve: between two real points, precision doesn't change linearly with recall (Davis and Goadrich, 2006). On the eight rows the trapezoid gives 0.767, the step sum 0.804. Which one is larger depends on the zigzag; here the trapezoid is lower because it averages each step's precision with the dip before it. When someone quotes “PR-AUC”, ask which one; scikit-learn's average_precision_score is the step sum.

Interpolated AP (older information-retrieval and object-detection benchmarks) first replaces each precision by the best precision at any recall at least as high, which smooths the zigzag and gives slightly higher numbers.

chunks.h: PR moves with prevalence; ROC doesn't
chunks.x: Model A from the fraud screen, the same score distributions, evaluated at three base rates:

chunks.h: PR moves with prevalence; ROC doesn't
chunks.x: Nothing about the model changed; only how many negatives each positive competes with. That's a feature (AP tells you what a reviewer will experience at this base rate) and a limit (AP from a 5% test set says nothing about a 0.5% deployment). Never compare APs across datasets with different prevalence, and never compute them on a resampled test set.

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: A feature bug makes 300 legitimate transactions a day (0.3% of them, say, one merchant's refunds) score above every fraud. Everything else is unchanged.

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: Precision in the top 1,000

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: After: 300 legitimate cases on top

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: Why AUC hardly notices: AUC is the average, over negatives, of the share of frauds ranked above each one. Each of the 300 used to sit below about 95% of the frauds and now sits above all of them, so its share drops from about 0.95 to 0. But each negative carries only 1/99,500 of the average: 300 times 0.95/99,500 = 0.0029 .

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: Why AP collapses: AP averages the precision at each fraud's rank, and every fraud now sits below 300 false alarms. The first few frauds, which used to arrive with precision near 1, now arrive with precision near 0.

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: What the team sees: the first 300 alerts every morning are all false. Reviewers stop trusting the queue long before the precision in the top 1,000 (down 3 points) looks alarming.

chunks.h: Worked example: ROC-AUC barely moves, AP collapses
chunks.x: The same pattern separates models A and B from the last section: equal ROC-AUC (0.95), but AP 0.302 for A and 0.688 for B, because B's advantage is at the top.
PR curve, AP, precision@k
Positives are rare and they're what you act on (fraud, alerts, retrieval); false positives cost per item, not per rate; comparing models at one fixed prevalence
Both classes matter; you need the whole ordering (a credit book); comparing rankings across populations whose base rates differ
Partial AUC, recall at fixed FPR
You'll operate at a known low false-alarm rate
Precision and recall at the threshold, cost
The threshold is already set; this is what the business will see

One theorem ties the two views together: on the same test set, a curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space (Davis and Goadrich). But when curves cross, the model with the higher AUC need not have the higher AP, as A and B show.

Object detection's mAP is the same AP: sort detections by confidence, count a detection as a true positive if its box overlaps an unmatched true box by at least 0.5 IoU (intersection over union), compute AP per class, then average over classes. COCO's headline number also averages over IoU thresholds 0.50 to 0.95, which rewards tight boxes.

Say it in an interview: “For rare positives I'd report average precision with the prevalence next to it, since a random model's AP equals the base rate. AP weights the top of the ranking: 300 false alarms pushed above every fraud cut AP from 0.30 to 0.12 while ROC-AUC fell by 0.003. I'd use the step-sum AP, not a trapezoid, and never compare APs across different base rates.”

chunks.h: Scoring probabilities: log loss and Brier
chunks.x: Ranking metrics can't tell 0.9 from 0.6 as long as the order holds. When the number itself is used (an expected-cost threshold, a price, a risk estimate shown to someone, a confidence that routes a case to a human), judge the probabilities directly, case by case.
LogLoss = -frac1nsum_i big[y_i log hat p_i + (1 - y_i)log(1 - hat p_i)big]

In words: the average surprise, -log of the probability the model gave to what actually happened. It's the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model, the same function as the training loss of logistic regression and most neural classifiers; where it comes from and its gradient are in the loss-functions note. Per row on the eight cases (natural log):
Probability given to the truth

The mean log loss is 0.540, and B alone contributes 44% of the total. Against what baseline? Predicting the base rate for everyone scores the entropy of the labels, -pilogpi - (1 - pi)log(1 - pi) : log 2 = 0.693 at 50% prevalence, but only 0.031 at 0.5%. So a log loss of 0.03 on a fraud problem is not good; it's the do-nothing score.

Unbounded: a probability of 0.01 on something that happened costs 4.6; exactly 0 costs infinity. Libraries clip predictions to [varepsilon, 1 - varepsilon] . One confidently wrong case can dominate a comparison.
Use it when confident errors are truly costly, for choosing among probability models, and as the early-stopping metric when you need probabilities.
Brier = frac1nsum_i (hat p_i - y_i)^2

In words: the mean squared error of the probabilities against the 0/1 outcomes, between 0 and 1. Eight rows: 0.176. The base-rate predictor scores pi(1 - pi) : 0.25 here, 0.005 at 0.5% prevalence. The Brier skill score 1 - Brier/pi(1 - pi) is the share of that baseline's error removed: 0.295 here. On rare events, quote the skill score; a raw Brier of 0.0045 at 0.5% fraud removes only 10% of the do-nothing error.

Log loss or Brier? Both reward the right things. Log loss punishes confident mistakes without limit (B: 1.90 against Brier's 0.72) and is more sensitive among tiny probabilities, which matters for rare events. Brier is bounded and more forgiving of label noise. Report one of them, with its baseline.

chunks.h: Why these two: proper scoring rules
chunks.x: A proper scoring rule is one where, if the true chance is p , your expected score is best when you report exactly p . Then no model can gain by shading its probabilities. Suppose the true chance is 0.3 and the model reports q :

chunks.h: Why these two: proper scoring rules
chunks.x: Brier and log loss are both lowest at the truth: they are strictly proper. Absolute error lvert hat p - yrvert is lowest at q = 0 : it rewards rounding every probability to 0 or 1, so it's improper and never a probability metric. Accuracy and F1 only see which side of a threshold a probability falls (improper at best), and AUC isn't a per-case score at all: it sees only the order.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: Group the cases by their forecast value (bins k , n_k cases each, forecast f_k , observed rate bar o_k , overall rate bar o ). The Brier score splits into three parts:

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: beginaligned Brier &= REL - RES + UNC \\ REL &= frac1nsum_k n_k (f_k - bar o_k)^2 \\ RES &= frac1nsum_k n_k (bar o_k - bar o)^2 \\ UNC &= bar o\,(1 - bar o) endaligned

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: In words: reliability (lower is better) is the calibration error, how far each forecast sits from what happened when it was issued; resolution (higher is better) is how much the groups' outcomes differ from the overall rate, i.e. how well the model separates cases; uncertainty is how hard the problem is, fixed by the base rate, and no model can change it. The split is exact when all cases in a bin share one forecast value (as in the example below); with binned continuous scores, two small within-bin terms are left over, so the parts add up only approximately.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: By hand. A model gives 20 cases only two scores: 0.2 to ten of them (3 turn out positive) and 0.8 to the other ten (6 positive). Overall rate 9/20 = 0.45.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: Brier = 0.025 - 0.0225 + 0.2475 = 0.25 , matching the direct average of squared errors.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: Read it: the model does separate cases (resolution 0.0225), but it's overconfident (0.2 and 0.8 where 0.3 and 0.6 happened), and that costs more than the separation earns, so it scores worse than predicting 0.45 for everyone (0.2475). Replace its two outputs with 0.3 and 0.6, which changes no ranking, and REL drops to 0: Brier = 0.2475 - 0.0225 = 0.225 . That is exactly what recalibration does (next section): it removes the reliability term and keeps the resolution.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: With continuous scores, the decomposition depends on the bins. If every case gets its own bin, each observed rate is 0 or 1, the resolution equals the uncertainty, and the whole Brier score shows up as “reliability”. Bin coarsely enough that each bin's observed rate means something.

chunks.h: The Brier decomposition: reliability, resolution, uncertainty
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “When probabilities are used, I'd judge them with a proper score, log loss or Brier, which are minimized only by the true probabilities, and quote the skill against predicting the base rate, because on rare events the raw numbers are tiny. Brier splits into reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty: calibration error, separation, and the problem's difficulty. Recalibration removes the first without touching the second.”
A model is calibrated if, among the cases it gives probability q , a share q turn out positive, for every q :
P(y = 1 mid hat p = q) = q

In words: “30%” means 30%. Calibration and ranking are separate properties: the base-rate predictor is perfectly calibrated and ranks nothing (AUC 0.5); a model with AUC 0.95 can have every probability off by a factor of two. Calibration matters whenever the number is used: expected-cost thresholds (section 03), pricing, expected loss (a lender's version is in the lifecycle note), combining models, comparing scores across segments, and deciding when a model's own confidence is high enough to act without a human.

Bin the predictions, and in each bin plot the mean predicted probability against the observed positive rate. A calibrated model lies on the diagonal. The example: a simulated model on 20,000 held-out cases whose log-odds are exactly twice the true log-odds, the classic overconfident shape (base rate 15.5%):

Reliability diagram of the overconfident model (orange), and the same model after Platt scaling fitted on a separate 20,000-case calibration set (blue). Bins with fewer than ten cases are left out. Recalibration moves the points onto the diagonal and leaves the ranking alone.
Above the diagonal: the model's probabilities there are too low (0.022 predicted, 10.5% happened). Below: too high (0.851 predicted, 65% happened).
Overconfident = flatter than the diagonal (low predictions too low, high ones too high). Underconfident = steeper (squeezed towards the middle).
Calibration-in-the-large: the mean prediction against the base rate. Here 6.8% against 15.5%, so the model also understates risk on average.

Calibration slope: refit y on the model's log-odds with a logistic regression; a slope below 1 means overconfident (typical of overfitting), above 1 underconfident. Here it's about 0.5 (Platt's fit below: 0.495).

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: ECE = sum_b fracn_bn\,biglvert bar o_b - bar p_b bigrvert

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: In words: the expected calibration error is the case-weighted average gap between the observed rate and the mean prediction in each bin, the average vertical distance from the diagonal. For the overconfident model: 0.089. Four pitfalls:

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: It's biased upwards by noise, more so with more bins. A perfectly calibrated model on 1,000 cases scores ECE 0.022 with 10 bins and 0.046 with 50 (averaged over 200 simulated test sets, with scores spread like the example above), purely from sampling noise in each bin. On 10,000 cases: 0.007 and 0.014. Compare ECEs only with the same bins and the same test size.

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: A useless model can score 0. Predicting the base rate for everyone puts every case in one bin whose mean prediction equals its observed rate: ECE 0, AUC 0.5. ECE measures reliability only, never resolution.

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: Equal-width bins can be nearly empty. Above, 82% of cases fall in the first bin and the top bin has 13 cases. Equal-mass (quantile) bins give every bin the same count; show the counts either way.

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: Multi-class “top-label” ECE checks only the confidence of the predicted class, not the rest of the probability vector.

chunks.h: ECE, and why not to trust it alone
chunks.x: So report ECE (or just the diagram) next to a proper score, log loss or Brier, never alone.

All three learn a monotone map from the model's score to a probability, fitted on held-out data the model wasn't trained on (training-set predictions are overconfident, especially for trees and boosting), and never on the test set. With little data, cross-fit: train the model on k - 1 folds, fit the calibrator on the remaining fold, repeat (scikit-learn's CalibratedClassifierCV).
beginaligned Platt: hat p &= sigma(a\,s + b) \\ Temperature: hat p &= softmax(z / T) \\ Isotonic: hat p &= m(s), \ m non-decreasing endaligned

In words: Platt fits a two-parameter logistic regression with the model's score s (or its log-odds) as the only input; temperature scaling divides a network's logits z by one learned number T , the same for every class; isotonic regression fits any non-decreasing step function.
Fitted on the overconfident model

Platt and temperature recover the factor of two almost exactly, because the distortion was a pure scaling of the log-odds, which is the shape they assume. They're strictly increasing, so AUC is untouched. Isotonic assumes no shape, so it can fix any monotone distortion, but it needs more data and its flat steps create ties, which nudge AUC (here down by 0.0015). With only 200 calibration cases, isotonic overfits: test log loss 0.425 against Platt's 0.379.
Sigmoid-shaped distortion: SVMs, boosted trees, over- or under-confident models
Neural networks, multi-class; keeps the argmax and the ranking
Large (roughly a thousand or more)
Any monotone distortion, when there's enough data

Isotonic by hand: pool adjacent violators (PAV). Sort the eight cases by score, lowest first, and read their labels: H 0, G 0, F 0, E 1, D 1, C 1, B 0, A 1. The fitted values must never decrease. Go left to right, and whenever a new value is below the block before it, merge them into one block holding their average; keep merging backwards while the order is still violated.
H, G, F: 0, 0, 0. E, D, C: 1, 1, 1. Fine so far.
B is 0, below the block of 1s. Merge B with C: (1 + 0)/2 = 0.5. Still below D's 1: merge, (1 + 1 + 0)/3 = 0.67. Still below E's 1: merge, 3/4 = 0.75. Now above F's 0: stop.
A is 1, above 0.75. Fine.
Result: H, G, F → 0; E, D, C, B → 0.75; A → 1. Each block's value is its observed positive rate, which is why isotonic fits are calibrated on the data they were fitted to.

Scoring a calibrator on the rows it was fitted to. In-sample, the isotonic fit above turns B's three lost pairs into ties, so AUC “rises” from 0.8125 to 0.906 and the Brier score “improves” from 0.176 to 0.094. None of that is real. Fit on one held-out set, evaluate on another.

chunks.x: Close, if the model is roughly right

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Its loss is log loss, and with an intercept its average prediction on the training data equals the base rate. Strong regularization shrinks it towards underconfidence.

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: It multiplies evidence from correlated features as if independent, counting the same signal several times.

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Small and pure leaves say 0% or 100%, and leaves are chosen because they look extreme (details).

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Squeezed towards the middle

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Averaging many trees' votes rarely reaches unanimity, so cases whose true chance is near 0 or 1 get predictions pulled towards the middle (details).

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: SVM, boosted stumps (exponential loss)

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Sigmoid-shaped, pushed away from 0 and 1

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: They maximize margins, not likelihood; their scores aren't probabilities at all (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005).

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Gradient boosting with log loss

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Usually close; can drift overconfident with many rounds

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: It minimizes log loss, but late trees fit noise in the training set.

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Large capacity keeps lowering training log loss by growing the logits after the labels are already fitted (Guo and colleagues, 2017). Label smoothing counteracts it (loss-functions note).

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Anything trained with class weights, resampling or focal loss

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: Inflated or distorted on purpose

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: The training base rate or loss isn't the real one; see the next subsection.

chunks.h: Which models come out miscalibrated, and why
chunks.x: And anything, once the world shifts: calibration usually breaks before the ranking does, so recalibrating on recent data is a cheaper, more frequent fix than retraining (drift in the lifecycle note).

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: Train on data whose positive share pi_s differs from the real one pi (by undersampling negatives, oversampling positives, or weighting them), and the model learns the training odds. If only the base rate differs (each class's features look the same), the fix is to rescale the odds:

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: beginaligned odds_true &= odds_model times fracpi/(1 - pi)pi_s/(1 - pi_s) \\ hat p &= fracodds_true1 + odds_true endaligned

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: In words: multiply the model's odds by the ratio of the real base-rate odds to the training base-rate odds. A model trained on a 50/50 sample and deployed where 1% are positive: its 0.5 means 1%, its 0.9 means 8.3%, and it takes 0.99 to mean 50%. Undersampling negatives at rate q is the special case logit hat p = logit hat p_s + log q in the data-preparation note; class weight w on positives acts like q = 1/w .

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: The same formula handles a deployment shift in the base rate (fraud rises from 0.5% to 1%), with pi_s the training rate and pi the new one, under the same assumption that only the mix changed.

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: It changes no ranking, so AUC is untouched; precision, log loss and every cost threshold do change.

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: When the assumption fails (the kinds of fraud change, not just their number), refit a calibrator on recent labelled data instead.

chunks.h: Class weights, undersampling and the prior-shift correction
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Calibrated means 30% happens 30% of the time. I'd check it with a reliability diagram and a proper score, not ECE alone, since ECE depends on the bins and is zero for the base-rate predictor. To fix it I'd fit Platt or temperature scaling on held-out data when the distortion is a simple scaling, isotonic when there's lots of data; they keep the ranking. If I'd undersampled or weighted classes, I'd first rescale the odds by the ratio of the real to the training base-rate odds.”

Search, recommendations, retrieval for a language model, and review queues all return an ordered list per query (a search, a user, a question, a day's queue). Each item has a relevance label, binary (relevant or not) or graded (0 to 3, say). A ranking metric scores one list; the reported number is its average over queries.

The worked example. One query returns five documents. The corpus holds four relevant documents for it: grades 3, 2, 2 and 1. The system retrieved three of them; the fourth (grade 2) is missing from its list.
beginaligned P@k &= frac\#relevant in the top kk \\ R@k &= frac\#relevant in the top k\#relevant in total endaligned

In words: precision@k is the share of the shown slots that are useful; recall@k is the share of everything useful that got shown. Here P@3 = 2/3 and R@3 = 2/4 = 0.5. Hit rate@k is 1 if at least one relevant item is in the top k , else 0; averaged over queries, it's the share of queries with something useful shown. When each query has exactly one relevant item (one gold passage), recall@k and hit rate@k are the same number. Neither cares about the order within the top k .
MRR = frac1lvert Qrvertsum_q in Q frac1rank of the first relevant item for q

In words: for each query, 1 over the position of the first useful result (0 if there is none), averaged over queries. Here the first relevant item is at rank 2: reciprocal rank 0.5. Across three queries whose first hits are at ranks 2, 1 and nowhere: (0.5 + 1 + 0)/3 = 0.5 . It suits tasks where one good answer ends the search: a navigational query, a question with one right passage. It ignores everything after the first hit.
The same AP as section 05, per query: the mean of the precision at the rank of each relevant item, over all relevant items, counting a relevant item that was never retrieved as precision 0:
AP = frac14Big(tfrac12 + tfrac23 + tfrac35 + 0Big) = frac1.7674 = 0.442

In words: relevant items arrive at ranks 2, 3 and 5, with precision 1/2, 2/3 and 3/5 at those points, and the fourth relevant document never arrives. MAP is AP averaged over queries. It rewards putting every relevant item high, with binary labels.
Dividing by the number of relevant items retrieved (3) instead of the number that exist (4) gives 0.589 and hides the miss. Libraries and papers differ; check which denominator a quoted MAP uses.

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: When relevance is graded and position matters (users look at the top few), discounted cumulative gain adds each item's gain, discounted by how far down it sits:

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: beginaligned DCG@k &= sum_i=1^k frac2^rel_i - 1log_2(i + 1) \\ nDCG@k &= fracDCG@kIDCG@k endaligned

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: In words: a grade-3 item is worth 2^3 - 1 = 7 , a grade-2 item 3, a grade-1 item 1; the item at position i is divided by log_2(i + 1) (1 at the top, 1.585 at position 2, 2 at position 3). IDCG is the DCG of the best possible ordering of all the relevant items, so nDCG runs from 0 to 1. By hand, k = 3 :

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: nDCG@3 = 5.393 / 10.393 = 0.519. The grade-3 document at position 3 instead of 1 is the main loss.

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: Two gain conventions. Some libraries, scikit-learn's included, use the grade itself as the gain (linear) instead of 2^rel - 1 : here that gives 0.525. They agree for binary labels; for graded ones, state which you used.

chunks.h: nDCG: graded relevance with a position discount
chunks.x: Where IDCG comes from. It should be the ideal ordering of every known relevant item, including ones the system failed to retrieve. Computing it only from the returned list stops penalizing misses: 0.574 here with 2^rel - 1 gains. scikit-learn's ndcg_score builds IDCG from whatever labels you pass and uses linear gains, so on the returned list it gives 0.580; pass the missed documents too (with the lowest scores) to get 0.525.

Match k to the product: how many results fit on a phone screen, how many passages fit the prompt.

chunks.h: Which ranking metric for which product
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “For retrieval feeding an LLM I'd track recall@k at the k actually put in the prompt, because a passage that isn't retrieved can't be used, and MRR if one passage answers the question. For graded search results, nDCG@10, computed per query with the ideal ordering over all known relevant documents. Here a grade-3 document at position 3 instead of 1 gives nDCG@3 of 0.52.”
Five demand forecasts, used for every number below:

beginaligned MAE &= frac1nsum_i lvert y_i - hat y_irvert = frac555 = 11 \\ RMSE &= sqrtfrac1nsum_i (y_i - hat y_i)^2 = sqrtfrac7255 = 12.04 \\ WAPE &= fracsum_i lvert y_i - hat y_irvertsum_i lvert y_irvert = frac55260 = 21.2\% endaligned

In words: MAE is the typical miss in units; RMSE squares before averaging, so big misses weigh more, and is also in units; WAPE (weighted absolute percentage error) is total miss over total volume, which equals MAE divided by the mean actual. MAPE, the mean of the last column, is undefined because of item 5; over the first four it's 37.3%, and the 10-unit item supplies two thirds of that.

chunks.h: The metric decides what the model predicts
chunks.x: Each metric is minimized by a different summary of the outcome's distribution, so choosing the metric chooses what the model will learn to output. One product's demand over five days was 10, 20, 30, 40 and 400 (one bulk order). If you could forecast one constant number, which would each metric pick?

chunks.h: The metric decides what the model predicts
chunks.x: A median weighted by 1/y : pulled to small values

chunks.h: The metric decides what the model predicts
chunks.x: So the question is never “which metric is best” but “what number does the decision need?” Total revenue across many items needs the mean (errors add up), a typical-case estimate the median, a stocking level that rarely runs out a high quantile. Train with the matching loss too (why MSE fits the mean and MAE the median); a model trained on MSE and judged on MAE is optimizing one summary and graded on another.

RMSE punishes large errors more than proportionally: one 20-unit miss counts as much as four 10-unit misses. Use it when a big miss really is disproportionately bad, and when the mean is what you need.
MAE is robust to outliers and easy to explain: “off by 11 units on average”.

Their ratio is a diagnostic: MAE le RMSE le sqrt n\,MAE . Equal means every error has the same size; a ratio far above 1 means a few large errors dominate. Here 12.04/11 = 1.09: errors are similar in size.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: MAPE = frac100\%nsum_i leftlvert fracy_i - hat y_iy_i rightrvert

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: In words: the average error as a share of the actual. It's scale-free and easy for a business audience, which is why it's popular. Its problems:

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: Zeros and near-zeros. At y = 0 it's undefined (item 5); near zero it explodes. Intermittent demand, with many zero days, breaks it.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: Small actuals dominate. A 10-unit miss on a 10-unit item counts 100%; the same miss on an 80-unit item 12.5%. Item 4 alone contributes 25 of the 37.3 points.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: It biases forecasts low. For a known actual it's just absolute error divided by that actual, symmetric around it (for an actual of 100, forecasts of 50 and 150 both cost 50%). But you forecast before the actual is known, and each possible outcome's miss is divided by that outcome: if demand turns out low, the miss is a big percentage; if high, a small one. So the forecast that minimizes expected MAPE is a median weighting each outcome by 1/y , pulled towards small values. In ratio terms: forecasting double the actual costs 100%, half of it only 50%.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: The bias in numbers. Demand of 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 is perfectly symmetric: mean and median are both 60. The constant with the lowest MAPE is 40 (MAPE 48.7%, against 63% at 60). A model tuned on MAPE will under-forecast systematically, and in inventory that means stock-outs.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: sMAPE (symmetric MAPE) divides by the average of actual and forecast: 2lvert y - hat yrvert/(lvert yrvert + lvert hat yrvert) . It's bounded (0 to 200%), but it's 200% whenever exactly one of the two is zero, whatever the size of the miss (item 5: a 5-unit miss scores 200%, pulling the five-item sMAPE to 63.8%). And it isn't symmetric either: for an actual of 100, forecasting 50 costs 66.7% but 150 costs 40%, so now under-forecasts are punished more. Definitions vary between papers, so always write the formula.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: WAPE = MAE / mean actual (21.2% here). Volume-weighted, fine with zeros (unless everything is zero), and what most demand-planning teams report for aggregated demand.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: MASE (mean absolute scaled error): MAE divided by the in-sample MAE of a naive forecast (tomorrow = today, or = the same day last week). Below 1 beats the naive forecast. Comparable across series of different scales, and fine with zeros unless the training series is constant.

chunks.h: MAPE, and why forecasters distrust it
chunks.x: RMSLE, the RMSE of log(1 + y) : measures relative error, for positive targets spanning orders of magnitude.
beginaligned R^2 &= 1 - fracsum_i (y_i - hat y_i)^2sum_i (y_i - bar y)^2 \\ R^2_adj &= 1 - (1 - R^2)\,fracn - 1n - p - 1 endaligned

In words: R² is the share of the variance around the mean that the model removes, i.e. MSE measured against the “always predict the mean” baseline. Five forecasts: 1 - 725/9,880 = 0.927 . Adjusted R² charges for the number of features p : with n = 50 and p = 10 , an R² of 0.40 adjusts to 0.25.
It can be negative on test data: worse than predicting the test mean. In training, with an intercept, it can't.
It depends on the test set's spread. The same model and the same errors give a higher R² on a more varied test set, so don't compare R² across datasets.
Adjusted R² is an in-sample correction for linear models. For held-out data, just report test R² or RMSE: the held-out score is already honest.
rho_tau(e) = maxbig(tau\,e,\ (tau - 1)\,ebig), quad e = y - hat y

In words: an under-forecast ( e gt 0 ) costs tau per unit and an over-forecast 1 - tau per unit. At tau = 0.9 , an actual of 100: forecasting 80 costs 0.9 times 20 = 18 , forecasting 120 costs 0.1 times 20 = 2 . Running out is nine times as costly as overstocking, so the forecast settles at the 90th percentile. At tau = 0.5 it's half the absolute error. A pair of quantile forecasts (0.05 and 0.95) makes a 90% prediction interval; check it by coverage: about 90% of actuals should fall inside, and the interval should be as narrow as possible while they do. Conformal prediction is the standard wa
Backtest from many origins: roll the forecast origin forward (the time-series splits in section 02) and average, so one unusual period doesn't decide.
Report error by horizon: error grows with how far ahead you forecast; one average over days 1 to 28 hides that day 1 is fine and day 28 is poor. Report the horizon the decision uses.
Compare with naive and seasonal-naive at every horizon. Many “models” don't beat last week's value; MASE builds that comparison in.
Intervals for the metric need a block bootstrap (resample whole weeks), because forecast errors are correlated in time.
Big misses disproportionately bad; totals matter

Say it in an interview: “The metric decides what the model predicts: RMSE pulls towards the mean, MAE the median, pinball loss a quantile. MAPE breaks at zero, lets small items dominate and biases forecasts low: on demand of 20 to 100, the MAPE-best constant is 40 where the mean is 60. For aggregated demand I'd report WAPE, MASE across series, and pinball loss with coverage if stock levels are the decision.”
“B scores 0.822 and A 0.805” is not yet a finding. Every metric is an estimate from a finite test set; the question is whether the gap is bigger than the noise, measured the right way.
A rate on independent rows has standard error sqrta(1 - a)/n . Accuracy 0.90 on 1,000 rows: 0.0095, so a 95% interval of about ±1.9 points. A “0.5-point gain” judged against that alone is noise.
The effective n is the relevant denominator, not the test-set size: predicted positives for precision, actual positives for recall. With 20 positives, recall moves in steps of 5 points.

Small counts need the Wilson interval. Recall of 20/20 gives a standard error of 0 by the formula above, so a useless interval [1, 1]. Wilson gives [0.84, 1.00]. For 18/20 the textbook (Wald) interval runs above 1, to 1.03; Wilson gives [0.70, 0.97].

AUC's noise is set by the rarer class. With 300 positives, AUC near 0.8 has a standard error of about 0.013 in the bootstrap below and about 0.016 by Hanley and McNeil's formula (it depends on the score distributions), so roughly ±0.025 to ±0.03; the lifecycle note sizes a test set this way (holdout size).
Correlated rows shrink n . Ten rows from one customer are closer to one row than to ten.

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: For metrics with no simple formula (AUC, AP, F1, WAPE), resample the test rows with replacement, recompute the metric each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. How the bootstrap works and where it fails is in the hypothesis-testing note; what's specific to model evaluation:

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: Stratify by class (resample positives and negatives separately) when positives are rare, or some resamples have none and AUC is undefined.

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: Resample the independent unit: whole customers or documents (a cluster bootstrap), whole weeks for time series (a block bootstrap).

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: Pair the comparison. To compare two models, resample the same row indices for both and record the difference each time.

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: Why pairing matters, in numbers. Two models scored on one test set of 10,000 rows (300 positives). They share most of their inputs, so their scores correlate at 0.87 and they tend to get the same rows wrong.

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: 95% interval (2,000 stratified resamples, one seed)

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: B − A, unpaired (the two SEs combined as if independent)

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: The separate intervals overlap heavily, which tempts a “no difference” verdict. But most of each model's uncertainty comes from which rows happened to be in the test set, and that luck is shared: a resample full of hard cases hurts both. Pairing cancels the shared part, and the gap's standard error drops from 0.018 to 0.0075. B wins in 99% of the resamples.

chunks.h: Bootstrap intervals, and why to pair them
chunks.x: DeLong's test is the classical closed-form alternative for two correlated AUCs on the same rows; the paired bootstrap does the same job for any metric.

chunks.h: McNemar's test: two classifiers, one test set
chunks.x: For accuracy-type comparisons, tabulate the rows by whether each model got them right:

chunks.h: McNemar's test: two classifiers, one test set
chunks.x: A is right on 850 of 1,000 rows, B on 870. Rows both models get right or both get wrong say nothing about which is better; only the 100 rows where they disagree do. If the models were equally good, each disagreement would be a coin flip, so b would be about half of b + c :

chunks.h: McNemar's test: two classifiers, one test set
chunks.x: chi^2 = frac(lvert b - crvert - 1)^2b + c = frac19^2100 = 3.61

chunks.h: McNemar's test: two classifiers, one test set
chunks.x: In words: how far the split of disagreements is from 50/50, in chi-square units with one degree of freedom (the −1 is a continuity correction). p = 0.057 : a 2-point accuracy gap that is not quite significant at 5%. The exact version is a binomial test of 40 out of 100 against ½ ( p = 0.057 too); use it when b + c is below about 25.

The tempting test: run 10-fold CV for both models, take the 10 per-fold differences, and do a paired t-test. The problem is that fold scores aren't independent: any two training sets share 8/9 of their rows, and every fold comes from the same dataset, so the folds' differences move together. The t-test's S^2/J then understates the variance of the mean difference. Nadeau and Bengio's corrected resampled t-test inflates it:
beginaligned Var(bar d) &approx S^2Big(frac1J + fracn_testn_trainBig) \\ t &= fracbar dsqrtVar(bar d), quad J - 1 degrees of freedom endaligned

In words: J is the number of train/test results, S^2 the variance of the J differences, and the extra term accounts for the overlap between training sets. For one run of 10-fold, 1/10 + 1/9 = 0.211 instead of 0.1: the variance doubles and t shrinks by 1.45.
Worked: B beats A by 0.6 points on average over 10 folds, with a standard deviation of 0.8 points across folds. Naive: t = 2.37 , p = 0.042 , “significant”. Corrected: t = 1.63 , p = 0.137 , not.

How wrong the naive test is, simulated. Two logistic regressions with equally informative feature sets (so neither is better), compared on 300 datasets of 200 rows. Share of comparisons declared significant at 5%:
10-fold CV, once ( J = 10 )
10-fold CV repeated 10 times ( J = 100 )

Repeating CV adds more results, but not more independent data: with J = 100 the naive test divides the variance by 100 and declares most ties “significant”. The correction tracks the nominal 5% there; on a single 10-fold run it's conservative. Two habits help as much as any test: look at the per-fold differences (B winning on 10 of 10 folds is strong evidence; 6 of 10 is not), and confirm on a held-out test set with a paired bootstrap.

The best of many looks lucky. Comparing 20 models or 20 segments and reporting the winner is a multiple-comparisons problem (corrections in the hypothesis-testing note); the winner's score is optimistic for the same reason tuning on CV is (section 02).

Simpson's paradox: a metric can be better overall and worse in every segment when the segment mix differs between the two numbers compared (last month's model on last month's data against this month's). Two models scored on the same rows with a row-averaged metric can't reverse this way.

Slices and fairness: report the key metric per segment with its interval; an average can hide a segment where the model fails. Fairness checks compare error rates across groups: equal opportunity asks for equal TPR, equalized odds for equal TPR and FPR, demographic parity for equal flag rates. When base rates differ between groups, calibration within each group and equal error rates can't all hold at once (unless the model is perfect).
Practical significance: a real 0.003 AUC gain may not be worth a more complex model. Translate the gain into the business unit (frauds caught at capacity, rupees) before deciding.

Say it in an interview: “I'd compare on the same rows, paired. A paired bootstrap of the AUC difference cut the standard error from 0.018 to 0.0075 in one example, because both models share the test set's luck. For accuracy, McNemar on the disagreements. For CV, fold scores are correlated, so a naive t-test on 10-by-10 CV called 57% of equal models different; the Nadeau–Bengio correction adds n_test/n_train to the variance factor.”

A held-out score says how good a model is; these two curves say why it isn't better, and so what to do next. The idea behind both is the split of error into bias (the model is too simple for the pattern), variance (it changes too much with the training sample) and irreducible noise; the decomposition itself is derived in the linear and logistic regression note.

chunks.h: Learning curves: will more data help?
chunks.x: Plot training and validation scores against the number of training rows. The example: a nonlinear problem (the label depends on a product of two features) where even a perfect model is right only 76% of the time, because of label noise. 5-fold CV accuracy:
