Good at topic and paraphrase; weak at negation, numbers, exact IDs, long texts. Cosines aren't probabilities. Pool and prefix exactly as trained (E5: “query: ”/“passage: ”). Hard negatives from BM25 or the model, filtered for false negatives by a cross-encoder. tau approx 0.01–0.05 . Matryoshka: truncate, then re-normalize. Choose on your own labelled queries; MTEB's retrieval column only shortlists. A new model means re-embedding everything.
Bi, cross, late interaction
beginaligned FLOPs per pass &approx 2 times params times tokens \\ s_ColBERT(q, d) &= sum_i max_j q_i^top d_j endaligned

Cross-encoding 1M docs of 256 tokens: 46 PFLOP per query; bi-encoder: about 4.3 GFLOP; ratio about 10^7 . Rerank top 100: 4.6 TFLOP. ColBERT: 25.6 KB per 100-token passage in fp16. Retrieve 100–1,000 → rerank 50–100 → keep 5–10; the reranker can't recover retrieval misses.

beginaligned cos(a, b) &= fraca^top blVert a rVert lVert b rVert \\ lVert a - b rVert^2 &= 2 - 2cos(a, b) quad (unit vectors) \\ x' &= big(x, sqrtR^2 - lVert x rVert^2big),\ q' = (q, 0) quad (MIPS to L2) endaligned

Normalize ⇒ dot, cosine and L2 rank alike. Unnormalized dot favours long vectors. Use the model's training similarity. Anisotropy: shared offset inflates all cosines; hubness: some docs retrieved for everything.
beginaligned memory &= N d times bytes per number \\ recall@k &= fraclvert ANN_k cap Exact_k rvertk endaligned
10M × 768 float32: 30.72 GB, 15.36 GFLOP per query, about 0.3 s at 100 GB/s (memory-bound). Families: trees, LSH, IVF, quantization, graphs.
beginaligned P(ell ge L) &= M^-L, qquad m_L = 1/ln M \\ bytes per vector &approx 4d + 8M endaligned

Greedy in upper layers, beam of efSearch in layer 0. M: recall vs memory; efConstruction: build quality vs time (saturates); efSearch: recall vs latency per query. Measured (M = 16): ef 10 → 0.863, 40 → 0.976, 320 → 0.997. Deletes are tombstones; filters break the walk.
beginaligned distances &approx n_list + n_probe N / n_list, qquad n_list^* = sqrtn_probe N \\ lVert q - x rVert^2 &approx sum_j=1^m T_j[code_j(x)] endaligned

FAISS: n_list approx 4sqrt N–16sqrt N . 10M, 16,384 lists, nprobe 32: 35,915 distances (278× fewer). PQ 768-d, m = 96 : 3,072 → 96 bytes; 10M: 0.96 GB. Rerank the top 100 with full vectors. IVF-PQ codes the residual; reranking can't fix IVF misses. int8: 4×, ~lossless; binary: 32×, Hamming, rescore. LSH bit agreement: 1 - theta/pi .
RRF(d) = sum_r frac160 + rank_r(d)

BM25 for IDs and rare terms, dense for paraphrase. Don't add raw scores; min-max stretches small gaps. Help-centre example: d6 0.03252, d3 0.03202, d2 0.03200, d5 0.01587. At k = 60 , rank 1 is worth 1.15× rank 10. SPLADE: learned sparse terms with expansion, in an inverted index.
Vector databases and evaluation

Post-filter survivors approx K' s ; at 1% and K' = 100 : one on average, none 37% of the time. Pre-filter + exact for small allowed sets; filter inside the walk for broad ones. Shards: scatter–gather, latency of the slowest. pgvector: fine to a few million vectors; post-filters by default (ef_search 40), iterative scans from 0.8.0. Evaluate quality against labels (recall@k at the depth passed on, MRR, nDCG) and the index against brute force. Margin on a 0.8 hit rate: ±0.11 (50 queries), ±0.055 (200), ±0.025 (1,000).

notes.title: Linear and logistic regression
notes.desc: Least squares by hand and as a projection, what each assumption protects, standard errors and reading coefficients, ridge, lasso and elastic net, the bias–variance decomposition, and logistic regression from log-odds to Newton's method, separation and rare events.

sections.t: Least squares, by hand and as a projection
Why the intercept and centering matter
What breaks when each one fails
Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
Inference: standard errors, tests and what a coefficient means
The F-test: several coefficients at once
Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
Ridge: add λ to every curvature
Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
The MAP view in two sentences
Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
How regularization, flexibility and data move the terms
Newton's method and IRLS, one step by hand
Perfect separation: weights run to infinity
Generalized linear models in one page
When linear models beat trees, and when they don't

chunks.x: Linear and logistic regression · Deepam Minda

Ordinary least squares (OLS) picks the line with the smallest sum of squared misses. Setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations X^top Xhatbeta = X^top y . Geometrically, OLS drops a perpendicular from y onto the space of all possible predictions, so the residuals are at right angles to every feature column, and with an intercept they sum to zero. Five salaries give hat y = 1.8 + 1.2 times years .

Each assumption protects something different. Unbiased coefficients need nothing important left out that moves with the features (exogeneity). Valid standard errors also need independent rows and constant noise variance, or else robust or clustered standard errors. Normal errors only make small-sample tests exact. Most failures break the standard errors; omitted variables break the coefficients themselves.

A coefficient is the change in the prediction per unit of one feature with the others held fixed. Its standard error hatsigmasqrt[(X^top X)^-1]_jj shrinks with more rows, less noise and more spread in the feature, and grows with collinearity by sqrtVIF . It's an association; it's causal only when nothing is confounding it.

Ridge adds lambda to every curvature of the loss bowl: it shrinks the poorly determined directions most, never to exactly zero, and splits weight between correlated features. Lasso's pull towards zero has constant strength, so weak coefficients land exactly on zero (the soft threshold); it tends to keep one of a correlated pair. Standardize first; choose lambda by cross-validation.

Expected squared test error = noise + bias² + variance. Flexibility trades bias for variance, regularization trades variance for bias, and more data cuts variance for free. For one ridge coefficient the best penalty is exactly sigma^2/beta^2 : shrink hardest when the signal is weak.

Logistic regression is a linear model for the log-odds. Log loss is the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood, its gradient is X^top(p - y) , and it's convex but has no closed form, so Newton's method (IRLS) finishes in a handful of steps. e^beta is an odds ratio. Perfect separation sends the weights to infinity, which a penalty fixes; keeping only a fraction q of the negatives raises only the intercept, by log(1/q) .

chunks.h: Least squares, by hand and as a projection
chunks.x: Linear regression predicts a number as a constant plus a weighted sum of the features. Stack the n rows into a matrix X whose first column is all ones (that column carries the constant, the intercept), and the model for every row at once is:

chunks.h: Least squares, by hand and as a projection
chunks.x: beginaligned y_i &= beta_0 + beta_1 x_i1 + dots + beta_p x_ip + varepsilon_i \\ y &= Xbeta + varepsilon endaligned

chunks.h: Least squares, by hand and as a projection
chunks.x: In words: X is n times k with k = p + 1 columns, beta holds one weight per column, and varepsilon (the noise or error) is everything about y that the features don't explain. The prediction drops the noise: hat y = Xhatbeta .

chunks.h: Least squares, by hand and as a projection
chunks.x: “Linear” means linear in the weights, not in the inputs. Adding x^2 , log x or x_1 x_2 as extra columns is still linear regression, because the prediction is still a weighted sum of columns. What can't be written this way is a weight inside a function, like e^beta x or a threshold learned from the data.
Five people, their years of experience x and their salary y in lakh a year. Small enough that every number below can be redone with a pen.
C earns less than B despite more experience: the noise. The question is which straight line to draw through these points, and how far to trust its slope.

For a candidate line, each person's residual is the miss e_i = y_i - hat y_i . Ordinary least squares (OLS) picks the line with the smallest residual sum of squares, RSS = sum_i e_i^2 . Squaring counts misses in either direction, punishes big misses most, makes the loss smooth enough to solve exactly, and makes the best prediction the conditional mean of y . Under Gaussian noise it is also the maximum-likelihood fit (loss functions derives that).

First, the intercept. For any slope b , the best intercept makes the residuals average zero (its derivative is -2sum_i e_i ), which puts the line through the point of means (bar x, bar y) = (3, 5.4) . That leaves one number to choose. Write S_xx = sum_i (x_i - bar x)^2 , S_xy = sum_i (x_i - bar x)(y_i - bar y) and S_yy = sum_i (y_i - bar y)^2 :
Then try slopes. With the line through the means, each residual is (y_i - bar y) - b(x_i - bar x) , so RSS(b) = S_yy - 2bS_xy + b^2 S_xx = 17.2 - 24b + 10b^2 :
A parabola in b , lowest where its slope -24 + 20b is zero: b = 1.2 . In general:
beginaligned hatbeta_1 &= fracS_xyS_xx = frac1210 = 1.2 \\ hatbeta_0 &= bar y - hatbeta_1 bar x = 5.4 - 1.2 times 3 = 1.8 endaligned

In words: the slope is how much x and y move together, divided by how much x moves on its own. That's cov(x, y)/var(x) , or equivalently the correlation times s_y/s_x . Each extra year goes with 1.2 lakh more; the line predicts 1.8 lakh at zero years.
With several features the same idea needs matrices. The steps, each one short:
Write the loss. L(beta) = lVert y - Xbeta rVert^2 = (y - Xbeta)^top (y - Xbeta) , the RSS as a dot product.
Expand. L = y^top y - 2beta^top X^top y + beta^top X^top Xbeta . The two cross terms are equal scalars, so they combine.
Differentiate. nabla_beta(a^topbeta) = a , and nabla_beta(beta^top Abeta) = 2Abeta for a symmetric A such as X^top X . So nabla L = -2X^top y + 2X^top Xbeta = -2X^top(y - Xbeta) .
Set it to zero and divide by -2 : X^top(y - Xhatbeta) = 0 .
Rearrange: X^top Xhatbeta = X^top y , the normal equations. If X^top X can be inverted, hatbeta = (X^top X)^-1X^top y .

Check it's a minimum. The second derivative (the Hessian) is 2X^top X , and for any direction v , v^top X^top X v = lVert Xv rVert^2 ge 0 . The loss is a bowl that never curves down (convex), so the flat point is the global bottom. It's the only bottom when no column is a weighted sum of the others (full column rank).
beginaligned nabla L &= -2X^top (y - Xbeta) \\ X^top Xhatbeta &= X^top y \\ hatbeta &= (X^top X)^-1X^top y endaligned

In words: entry j of the gradient is feature column j dotted with the residuals. At the bottom every one of those dot products is zero: no feature lines up with what's left over. If one did, moving its weight would lower the loss.
By hand on the five salaries. With columns (ones, years), X^top X holds n, sum x, sum x^2 and X^top y holds sum y, sum xy :

beginaligned X^top X &= beginbmatrix 5 & 15 \\ 15 & 55 endbmatrix, quad X^top y = beginbmatrix 27 \\ 93 endbmatrix \\ (X^top X)^-1 &= frac15 cdot 55 - 15^2beginbmatrix 55 & -15 \\ -15 & 5 endbmatrix = frac150beginbmatrix 55 & -15 \\ -15 & 5 endbmatrix \\ hatbeta &= frac150beginbmatrix 55 cdot 27 - 15 cdot 93 \\ -15 cdot 27 + 5 cdot 93 endbmatrix = frac150beginbmatrix 90 \\ 60 endbmatrix = beginbmatrix 1.8 \\ 1.2 endbmatrix endaligned
In words: a 2×2 inverse swaps the diagonal, negates the off-diagonal and divides by the determinant. Same line as before.

When X^top X can't be inverted (it's singular): some column is an exact combination of others. A duplicated column, the same quantity in two units, all one-hot dummies plus an intercept (the dummy trap), or more features than rows ( p ge n ). Then infinitely many beta give the same, equally good predictions; only the coefficients are undetermined. np.linalg.lstsq returns the one with the smallest length (the minimum-norm solution), and ridge (section 04) makes the answer unique again.

“Compute (X^top X)^-1 and multiply.” Never in code: solving the system (np.linalg.solve) is cheaper and more accurate than inverting, and lstsq (SVD) or QR are safer still, because they work on X directly and never form X^top X . Forming it squares the condition number (the ratio of the matrix's largest to smallest stretch, which sets how much rounding error gets amplified; section below).

Stop thinking of five points on a plot. Think of the five salaries as one point y in five-dimensional space, one axis per person. Every choice of beta gives another point Xbeta , and all of them together form a flat surface through the origin: the set of all weighted sums of the columns, called the column space of X . Here it's a 2-D plane inside 5-D space, spanned by the ones column and the years column.
OLS picks the point on that plane closest to y . The closest point is found by dropping a perpendicular, like a plumb line: the orthogonal projection.
OLS as a projection. The residual e meets the plane at a right angle, so it's orthogonal to every column of X : that statement, X^top e = 0 , is the normal equations.
beginaligned hat y &= Xhatbeta = X(X^top X)^-1X^top y = Hy \\ H &= X(X^top X)^-1X^top, quad H^2 = H \\ X^top e &= X^top (y - hat y) = 0 endaligned

In words: the hat matrix H “puts the hat on y ”. Applying it twice changes nothing ( H^2 = H ), because a point already on the plane projects to itself. The residual is perpendicular to every column, which is exactly the normal equations again.

Check on the example. With residuals (0, 0.8, -1.4, 0.4, 0.2) : against the ones column, sum_i e_i = 0 ; against the years column, sum_i x_i e_i = 0 + 1.6 - 4.2 + 1.6 + 1.0 = 0 . Everything below follows from this right angle:
With an intercept, residuals sum to zero, so the average prediction equals bar y and the line passes through the point of means.

Pythagoras splits the variation. e is also perpendicular to hat y - bar y , so the total sum of squares TSS = sum_i (y_i - bar y)^2 splits into explained ( ESS ) and residual parts: 17.2 = 14.4 + 2.8 . That split is why in-sample R^2 with an intercept lies between 0 and 1 (section 03).

Leverage. The diagonal entry h_ii of H says how strongly row i 's own y pulls its own fitted value. With one feature h_ii = tfrac1n + (x_i - bar x)^2/S_xx , so here it's 0.2 + 4/10 = 0.6 at the ends and (0.6, 0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.6) in all: the end points (1 and 5 years) pull hardest, the middle one least. The leverages sum to k = 2 , so they average k/n . Leverage depends only on X .
Degrees of freedom. The residual is forced into the n - k = 3 dimensions perpendicular to the plane. That's why the noise variance is estimated by dividing RSS by n - k , not n (section 03).
No distribution was needed. The projection is pure geometry. Probability enters only when asking how much hatbeta would move with fresh noise.

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Dropping the intercept forces the line through the origin. On the salaries that gives slope sum xy / sum x^2 = 93/55 = 1.69 instead of 1.2, and residuals that sum to 1.64 instead of 0. Unless the true line really passes through (0, 0) , the slope is biased, and R^2 measured against bar y is no longer guaranteed to lie in [0, 1] . Keep the intercept unless theory says it must be zero.

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Centering means subtracting the mean from each feature, here x - bar x = (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2) . The fitted line is the same; what changes:

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: The intercept becomes bar y . X^top X turns into diag(5, 10) : the off-diagonal sum x is now zero, so intercept and slope separate. The intercept is 5.4, the salary at average experience, and the slope stays 1.2. Their estimates also become uncorrelated (the raw covariance of −0.28 drops to 0).

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Interpretation. The raw intercept is the prediction at x = 0 . For years of experience that's a fresher, fine. For flat size it's a flat of 0 m²: an extrapolation nobody should read.

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Conditioning. The curvatures of the loss bowl (for the tfrac12n -scaled squared error used in the next section) are the eigenvalues of X^top X/n : 11.83 and 0.169 raw (a ratio, the condition number, of 70), 2 and 1 centred (ratio 2). Gradient descent's speed depends on that ratio (next section).

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Polynomials and interactions. For positive x , the columns x and x^2 are almost collinear; centering first removes most of that. With an interaction x_1 x_2 , centering makes beta_1 the effect of x_1 at the average x_2 rather than at x_2 = 0 .

chunks.h: Why the intercept and centering matter
chunks.x: Penalties. Ridge and lasso must not shrink the intercept, or every prediction gets pulled towards 0. The standard recipe: centre X and y , fit the penalized slopes, then set hatbeta_0 = bar y - bar x^tophatbeta .
Gradient descent walks downhill instead of solving in one shot. For the loss frac12nlVert y - Xbeta rVert^2 (the frac12 cancels the 2, the frac1n averages):
beta leftarrow beta - eta\,frac1nX^top (Xbeta - y)
In words: Xbeta - y is each row's miss, X^top lines the misses up with each feature, and eta (the learning rate) sets the step size.
Worked, on centred years, eta = 0.5 , starting at zero:
Gradient (intercept, slope)

The slope lands on 1.2 in one step: its curvature is S_xx/n = 2 , and eta = 0.5 is exactly one over it, so that step is the exact jump to the bottom along that direction. The intercept's curvature is 1, so each step halves its distance to 5.4. On the raw years the curvatures are 11.83 and 0.169: any eta above 2/11.83 = 0.169 diverges along the steep direction, and a step that small crawls along the shallow one. At each design's best fixed rate (1/6 raw, 2/3 centred) it takes 264 steps to get every coefficient within 0.001 of the answer on raw years, against 8 centred (13 at the eta = 0.5 used
Normal equations (Cholesky on X^top X )
Fastest direct method; forming X^top X squares the condition number (8.4 → 70 here), so correlated features lose digits
Stable; the usual default in statistics software
SVD (lstsq): X = UDV^top , rotations and stretches
O(np^2) , larger constant
Most stable; handles rank deficiency and returns the minimum-norm answer
Needs scaling and a learning rate; steps grow with the condition number
Streams data; scales to huge n
Solve directly when p is up to a few thousand and the data fits in memory: exact, no learning rate, no convergence check.
Iterate when n is huge or streaming, when p is huge and sparse (text, hashed IDs), or when there's no closed form at all, as for logistic regression and lasso.

Say it in an interview: “OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals. Setting the gradient -2X^top(y - Xbeta) to zero gives the normal equations X^top Xbeta = X^top y , unique when X has full column rank. Geometrically it projects y onto the column space, so the residuals are orthogonal to every feature and, with an intercept, sum to zero. In code I'd use lstsq or QR, never an explicit inverse, and gradient descent only for huge or streaming data, after scaling.”

The projection needs no assumptions: it always finds the best-fitting line. The assumptions are about something else: whether the coefficients mean what you want them to mean, and whether their standard errors are honest. Substitute y = Xbeta + varepsilon into the OLS formula and the whole story is in one line:
beginaligned hatbeta &= (X^top X)^-1X^top (Xbeta + varepsilon) \\ &= beta + (X^top X)^-1X^topvarepsilon endaligned

In words: the estimate is the truth plus a weighted mix of the noise. If the noise averages to zero whatever the features are, the mix averages to zero and hatbeta is right on average. How much the mix wobbles depends on the noise's variance and correlations. Each assumption below controls one of those two things.
Linearity (correct functional form): the average of y given the features really is Xbeta for some beta . Curves and interactions have to be in the columns.

Exogeneity: E[varepsilon mid X] = 0 . Nothing left in the noise moves with the features: no omitted variable that is correlated with a feature and affects y , no feedback from y to x , no measurement error in x .
Independence: the rows' errors are uncorrelated. Broken by repeated measurements of one user, by time order, by geography.
Constant variance (homoscedasticity): Var(varepsilon_i mid X) = sigma^2 for every row. Its failure is heteroscedasticity: say, expensive flats are noisier than cheap ones.
Normal errors: varepsilon sim mathcal N(0, sigma^2 I) . The least important.
No perfect collinearity: no column is an exact combination of others, so X^top X is invertible and hatbeta is unique.

The Gauss–Markov theorem. Under 1–4 and 6 (no normality needed), OLS is BLUE: the best (lowest-variance) linear unbiased estimator. 1, 2 and 6 give unbiasedness (take the expectation of the line above); 3 and 4 make the noise's covariance sigma^2 I . With A = (X^top X)^-1X^top , the rule for a linear map of random noise, Var(Avarepsilon) = AVar(varepsilon)A^top , gives
Var(hatbeta mid X) = (X^top X)^-1X^top(sigma^2 I)X(X^top X)^-1 = sigma^2(X^top X)^-1

In words: the coefficient cloud's spread is the noise variance times the inverse of the bowl's shape. The catch is the word unbiased: ridge is biased on purpose and can beat OLS on total error (section 05).

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: The key split: does the failure bias the coefficients, or only the standard errors?

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: The best straight-line approximation, not the true effect; predictions systematically off in places

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Misleading, since the model is wrong

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Transforms, polynomials or splines, interactions; or a tree model

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Exogeneity (omitted confounder, reverse causality, error in x )

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Biased, and more data doesn't fix it

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Tests and intervals can be precise but centred on the wrong value

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Measure the confounder; experiment; instrumental variables; fixed effects (a dummy per unit, which absorbs anything constant about that unit)

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Usually too small: p-values too optimistic

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Clustered or time-series (HAC) standard errors; mixed models (a random offset per group)

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Unbiased, but no longer the lowest-variance option

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Robust (HC) standard errors; weighted least squares; log y

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Fine for large n (the CLT); small-sample t and F tests, and prediction intervals, are off

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Bootstrap; transform y ; more data

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Not unique (predictions still are)

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Drop or combine columns; ridge

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: For prediction you mainly need the right shape and a relationship that still holds where the model is used, both checked on held-out data. A biased-but-stable coefficient can still predict well.

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: For explanation (what does a feature do? is it significant?) exogeneity is the one that matters most, and it's the one the data can't check for you.

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Normality and the prediction interval. The CLT makes hatbeta approximately normal because it averages many noise draws. A prediction interval is about one new noise draw, with no averaging, so skewed noise makes it wrong however large n is.

chunks.h: What breaks when each one fails
chunks.x: Measurement error in a feature biases its slope towards zero (attenuation): the noisy x spreads out the points horizontally, flattening the line. Measurement error in y only adds noise.
If the model is right, the residuals look like shapeless noise. Any visible pattern says which assumption is failing.
Residuals against fitted values. A curve means the shape is wrong (add terms or transform). A funnel means the noise grows with the level of y (robust standard errors, a log target, or weights).
Missed nonlinearity or interaction
Residuals vs fitted (or sqrtlvert standardized e rvert vs fitted, the scale-location plot)
Residuals vs each feature
That feature needs a transform or spline
Q–Q plot (sorted residuals vs normal quantiles)
Low end below the line, high end above (an S)
Heavy tails: Huber or a robust loss (the opposite S means light tails)
Skew: transform y or a GLM
Residuals vs time, order or group
Runs, waves, group offsets
Dependence between rows (Durbin–Watson far from 2)
Leverage vs standardized residual (Cook's distance)
A point with high leverage and a big residual

Leverage (the h_ii from the projection) flags unusual feature values; above about 2k/n is worth a look. Cook's distance measures how much all predictions move if that row is dropped. A high-leverage point that sits on the line is harmless, even helpful; one that sits off it pulls the whole line towards itself.

Standardized (internally studentized) residuals, e_i/(hatsigmasqrt1 - h_ii) , put all residuals on one scale. High-leverage points have deceptively small raw residuals because they drag the fit towards themselves; dividing by sqrt1 - h_ii undoes that. The externally studentized version (what statsmodels and R usually mean by “studentized”) also re-estimates hatsigma without row i , so an outlier can't inflate its own yardstick.
Heavy tails or gross outliers in y call for a robust loss (Huber, absolute error) rather than deleting rows; those losses, and quantile regression for predicting a percentile, are in loss functions.
Plot validation residuals too. Training residuals look better than the truth, especially with many features.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Transform the target when the noise is multiplicative: prices, incomes, durations. log y turns “±10%” noise into constant-variance noise and often straightens curves too (Box–Cox picks the power by likelihood; see data preparation). It changes what the coefficients mean (section 03).

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Robust (sandwich) standard errors keep the OLS coefficients and fix only the uncertainty. The general variance has the noise covariance Omega in the middle; the classic formula assumes Omega = sigma^2 I , and the robust one estimates each row's variance from its own squared residual:

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: beginaligned Var(hatbeta) &= (X^top X)^-1\,X^top Omega X\,(X^top X)^-1 \\ widehatVar_HC0 &= (X^top X)^-1Big(sum_i e_i^2\, x_i x_i^topBig)(X^top X)^-1 endaligned

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: In words: the two (X^top X)^-1 are the bread, the middle is the meat. HC0 puts each row's e_i^2 in the meat. HC1 multiplies by n/(n - k) ; HC3 uses e_i^2/(1 - h_ii)^2 , which corrects for high-leverage rows hiding their own noise and is the safer choice in small samples.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: When does heteroscedasticity actually break the classic standard error? When the noise variance is large exactly where (x - bar x)^2 is large, since those rows dominate the slope. Simulated with 100 rows, true slope 2, noise spread proportional to x , refitted 4,000 times:

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: 95% CI coverage, classic vs HC3

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: x skewed (log-normal, like incomes)

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: With skewed x , the few large- x rows are both the noisiest and the most influential, so the classic SE is a third too small and a “95%” interval covers the truth only 82% of the time. HC3 is right in both designs, which is why robust SEs are a cheap default.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Weighted least squares (WLS) goes further when the variance pattern is known: weight each squared residual by 1/sigma_i^2 , so noisy rows count less. That restores the lowest-variance estimator: in the two designs above, weights 1/x^2 roughly halve the slope's spread, from about 0.10 to 0.05 (uniform) and from about 0.15 to 0.09 (skewed). Robust SEs fix the honesty of the uncertainty; WLS also shrinks it.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Clustered standard errors. When rows come in groups (orders per customer, students per school, users per city) and the errors within a group are correlated, the effective sample size is closer to the number of groups than the number of rows. The cluster-robust estimator sums x_i e_i within each cluster before squaring, so correlated errors inside a cluster add up instead of cancelling. For a feature that's constant within clusters of size m , the variance is inflated by about the design effect 1 + (m - 1)rho , with rho the within-cluster correlation of the errors.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Simulated: 50 cities × 20 users, a feature set per city, within-city error correlation 0.2. Design effect 1 + 19 times 0.2 = 4.8 , so the naive SE should be sqrt4.8 = 2.2 times too small:

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: True spread over 3,000 refits

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: A drill that shows the trap: paste every salary row in twice. The coefficients stay (1.8, 1.2), but the slope's SE falls from 0.306 to 0.187, t rises from 3.93 to 6.41 and p from 0.029 to 0.0002. No information was added; the default formula just assumed ten independent people. Correlated rows are a milder version of the same false precision.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Cluster at the level where errors are correlated (or where treatment was assigned), and have enough clusters: with fewer than a few dozen, cluster-robust SEs are themselves too small; a wild cluster bootstrap helps.

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Time series: HAC (Newey–West) standard errors allow correlation between nearby rows. The same logic applies to A/B tests analysed per session when users were randomized (hypothesis testing).

chunks.h: Fixes: transforms, robust and clustered standard errors
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Unbiased coefficients need exogeneity: nothing omitted that's correlated with the features and affects y . Independence and constant variance are about the standard errors: when they fail, the coefficients are still unbiased but the classic SEs are wrong, so I use robust HC3 SEs, cluster at the level of the correlated rows, or model the variance with weights or a log target. Normality only matters for small-sample tests and prediction intervals. I check all of it with residual-vs-fitted, Q–Q and leverage plots.”

chunks.h: Inference: standard errors, tests and what a coefficient means
chunks.x: The fitted slope 1.2 came from one noisy sample of five people. Collect five new people with the same experience levels and the slope would come out different. Inference asks how different, and whether the slope could plausibly be zero.
From section 02, Var(hatbeta) = sigma^2(X^top X)^-1 . The true noise variance sigma^2 is unknown, so estimate it from the residuals:

beginaligned hatsigma^2 &= fracRSSn - k = frac2.85 - 2 = 0.933 \\ SE(hatbeta_j) &= hatsigmasqrtbig[(X^top X)^-1big]_jj \\ SE(hatbeta_1) &= sqrt0.933 times tfrac550 = 0.306, quad SE(hatbeta_0) = sqrt0.933 times tfrac5550 = 1.013 endaligned
In words: the standard error (SE) is how much the coefficient would typically wobble across repeated samples. The diagonal of (X^top X)^-1 is read off the 2×2 inverse from section 01.

Why divide by n - k , not n . The line was bent towards these very points using k numbers, so the residuals come out smaller than the true errors. The residual vector lives in only n - k dimensions (the projection), and dividing by n - k makes hatsigma^2 unbiased. The maximum-likelihood estimate RSS /n = 0.56 runs low, for the same reason the sample variance divides by n - 1 .
With one feature the formula is Var(hatbeta_1) = sigma^2/S_xx : 0.933/10 = 0.0933 , the same. Points spread far apart along x pin the slope like a long lever; bunched points let it tilt.

What makes an SE small: less noise ( sigma^2 ), more spread in the feature ( S_xx ), more rows ( S_xx grows with n , so SE falls like 1/sqrt n ), and little overlap with the other features (the VIF, below).

To test “no effect” for one coefficient, divide the estimate by its SE: how many wobbles from zero it sits. Because hatsigma is estimated, the ratio follows a t distribution with n - k degrees of freedom (exactly, under normal errors; approximately otherwise), not a normal. The logic of the test and the p-value is the same as in hypothesis testing.

beginaligned t &= frachatbeta_1 - 0SE(hatbeta_1) = frac1.20.306 = 3.93 \\ p &= P(lvert T_3 rvert ge 3.93) = 0.029 \\ CI_95 &= hatbeta_1 pm t_3,\,0.975SE = 1.2 pm 3.182 times 0.306 = [0.23,\ 2.17] endaligned

In words: if experience truly had no effect, a slope this many SEs from zero would turn up in about 3% of samples, so it's significant at 5%. The interval is wide, though: anything from 0.23 to 2.17 lakh a year fits the data. With 3 degrees of freedom the critical value is 3.18, not 1.96; by about 30 degrees of freedom it's close to 2.04, and then 1.96.
The intercept: t = 1.8/1.013 = 1.78 , p = 0.17 : five people can't pin down a fresher's salary.
The test is conditional on the other features: “no effect of x_j holding the others fixed”. Drop or add a correlated feature and the question changes.
Interval and test agree: the 95% interval excludes 0 exactly when the two-sided test rejects at 5% (duality).
With huge data almost every coefficient is “significant”, because the SE shrinks like 1/sqrt n . Read the size and the interval, not the p-value.

chunks.h: The F-test: several coefficients at once
chunks.x: To test whether a group of q coefficients is zero (all dummies of one category, a feature and its square, two collinear twins), fit the model with and without them and compare how much the RSS rises per dropped coefficient, relative to the noise level:

chunks.h: The F-test: several coefficients at once
chunks.x: beginaligned F &= frac(RSS_restricted - RSS_full)/qRSS_full/(n - k) \\ F_salary &= frac(17.2 - 2.8)/12.8/3 = 15.43 endaligned

chunks.h: The F-test: several coefficients at once
chunks.x: In words: the restricted model here is “intercept only”, whose RSS is the TSS, 17.2. Dropping the slope would add 14.4 of squared error, 15.4 times the noise per degree of freedom; under F_1,3 that has p = 0.029 . With one coefficient, F = t^2 ( 3.93^2 = 15.43 ) and the tests are identical. With several, the F-test can reject even when no individual t-test does: the typical picture with collinear features (below), where each coefficient alone is uncertain but, given enough rows, the pair together is clearly significant.
beginaligned R^2 &= 1 - fracRSSTSS = 1 - frac2.817.2 = 0.837 \\ bar R^2 &= 1 - (1 - R^2)fracn - 1n - p - 1 = 1 - 0.163 times frac43 = 0.783 endaligned

In words: R^2 is the share of the variation in y the model explains, compared with always predicting bar y . In-sample with an intercept it equals corr(y, hat y)^2 . Adjusted R^2 charges for each of the p features (not counting the intercept).

Training R^2 never falls when a feature is added, even pure noise: the projection onto a bigger space can only get closer to y . Adjusted R^2 rises only if the new feature's lvert t rvert gt 1 , a much lower bar than significance. For choosing models, use held-out error.
On test data R^2 can be negative: the model's squared error is larger than that of always predicting the test set's own mean. As a metric it belongs with the other regression metrics (evaluation).

Low R^2 isn't automatically bad (behavioural targets are noisy but a real effect can still be estimated precisely), and high R^2 doesn't mean the model is right (a curve fitted by a line can have R^2 = 0.9 and systematic residuals).

Choosing which features to keep. Stepwise selection by p-values (add or drop one feature at a time while it's “significant”) is a classic interview trap: it runs many tests, so the surviving p-values and intervals are too optimistic, and with correlated features the chosen set is unstable. In-sample criteria such as AIC and BIC charge per parameter and are better (they're likelihood-based; see likelihood, MLE and MAP), but the direct measurement is held-out error, and lasso does selection and fitting in one step (section 04; other selection methods in data preparation).
Confidence interval vs prediction interval. At a new point x_0 , “the average salary of people with x_0 years” and “this one person's salary” are different questions:
beginaligned Var(mean at x_0) &= sigma^2\, x_0^top (X^top X)^-1x_0 = sigma^2Big(frac1n + frac(x_0 - bar x)^2S_xxBig) \\ Var(new y at x_0) &= sigma^2Big(1 + x_0^top (X^top X)^-1x_0Big) endaligned

In words: the mean's uncertainty comes only from the wobbling line and grows as x_0 moves away from bar x . A new person adds their own noise, the “1”, which no amount of data removes. At 3 years the prediction is 5.4 with a 95% CI of ±1.37 and a prediction interval of ±3.37; at 6 years (outside the data) it's 9.0, CI [5.78, 12.22], PI [4.54, 13.46].
The core sentence: hatbeta_j is the expected change in y for a one-unit increase in x_j , with the other features held fixed. The units matter, and transforms change the sentence:
beta = 1.2 : +1 year → +1.2 lakh
+1 in x → times e^beta , about +100beta\% when small
+1% in x → about +beta/100 in y
+1% in x → about +beta\% in y : an elasticity
Dummy d (one level dropped)
The difference from the reference level
“Mumbai vs the dropped city, same everything else”
Interaction beta_1 x_1 + beta_12x_1x_2
The effect of x_1 is beta_1 + beta_12x_2 : it depends on x_2
0.5 + 0.2 times rooms : 0.7, 0.9, 1.1 for 1, 2, 3 rooms

Size isn't importance. A coefficient per rupee and one per crore aren't comparable. Standardized coefficients (per standard deviation) are, and even then only if the features aren't strongly correlated.
You can't hold x^2 fixed while moving x . With a squared term the effect of x is beta_1 + 2beta_2 x , different at every x .

Back-transforming a log model: e^widehatlog y estimates the median of y , not the mean, so it runs low. Multiply by e^hatsigma^2/2 if the log-scale noise is normal (1.133 for hatsigma = 0.5 ), or by the average of e^e_i over the training residuals (Duan's smearing).

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: When features overlap, only the part of x_j that the other features can't predict helps pin down beta_j . So the one-feature variance sigma^2/sum_i (x_ij - bar x_j)^2 gets multiplied by the variance inflation factor VIF_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2) , where R_j^2 is how well the other features predict x_j (the formula, VIF and condition-number detection, and the remedies are in data preparation). The SE widens by sqrtVIF : R_j^2 = 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.99 give VIF 2, 5, 10, 100 and SEs 1.4, 2.2, 3.2 and 10 times wider.

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: Worked: experience recorded twice. Add a second column, experience from the HR system, equal to the first plus small recording differences (0.1, -0.1, 0, 0.1, -0.1) ; correlation 0.998.

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: The VIF is 268, and sqrt268 = 16.4 is roughly the SE jump (0.31 → 6.0). Neither column looks significant, the HR column even has the wrong sign, yet experience obviously matters. Redrawing the noise 5,000 times (truth: 1.2 on the first column, 0 on the copy, sigma = 1 ) shows what's going on:

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: each coefficient wobbles with spread about 5.2, and the first comes out negative in about 40% of samples;

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: the two estimates move against each other (correlation −0.998), so their sum wobbles by only 0.33, about the same as the single-column slope (0.31).

chunks.h: Multicollinearity: what it does to the variance
chunks.x: The data pins down the combined effect, not how to split it. So predictions for people who follow the usual pattern (both columns agree) are fine; a row that breaks the pattern (the two records disagree) gets a wild prediction. What collinearity hurts: individual coefficients, their SEs and signs, and interpretation. What it doesn't: predictions where the correlation holds, and the joint F-test. Ridge's mechanism for taming it is in section 04.
Suppose the truth involves two features but you regress on only one. Write the left-out x_2 as whatever x_1 predicts of it plus a leftover u that is uncorrelated with x_1 , and substitute:

beginaligned y &= beta_0 + beta_1 x_1 + beta_2 x_2 + varepsilon \\ x_2 &= delta_0 + delta x_1 + u \\ y &= (beta_0 + beta_2delta_0) + (beta_1 + beta_2delta)\,x_1 + (beta_2 u + varepsilon) \\ E[tildebeta_1] &= beta_1 + beta_2\,delta endaligned

In words: the short regression's slope tildebeta_1 picks up the real effect of x_1 plus the effect of x_2 times how much x_2 tags along with x_1 ( delta , the slope of x_2 on x_1 ). The new error term is uncorrelated with x_1 , so this is exactly what the short regression estimates.
Sign of the bias = sign( beta_2 ) × sign(correlation of x_1 and x_2 ). No bias if beta_2 = 0 (the left-out variable doesn't matter) or delta = 0 (it's uncorrelated with x_1 ).
More data doesn't shrink it. The short regression converges, precisely, to the wrong number.
Worked: wage on education, leaving out ability. Six people; the data were generated with 1.0 per year of education and 4.0 per ability point, plus a little noise:
Full model: 0.873 per year of education, 4.292 per ability point.
Ability on education: delta = 0.341 (abler people study longer here; correlation 0.92).
Short model (education only): 2.336 per year, and exactly 0.873 + 4.292 times 0.341 = 2.336 . In-sample the identity holds to the last digit.

Leaving out ability more than doubles the apparent return to education. This is also why a coefficient's sign can flip when you add a feature: the two models answer different questions (“education, with ability as it usually comes” vs “education at fixed ability”).

A regression coefficient is a conditional association. It equals the causal effect of x_j only if exogeneity holds for x_j : conditional on the included features, nothing else that drives y moves with x_j . That fails when there's
an omitted confounder (ability, above);
reverse causality (police numbers and crime, ad spend and sales: y drives x );
sample selection (only approved loans have a repayment label, and approval depended on signals that also predict repayment);

a bad control: adjusting for a mediator (the path through which x acts) removes part of the effect you want, and adjusting for a collider (a common consequence of x and y ) creates a fake association;
measurement error in x , which attenuates the slope towards zero.

The fixes are design, not more rows: randomize (A/B tests), or use a quasi-experiment such as difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity or matching (when you can't A/B test), or an instrumental variable (something that moves x but affects y only through x ), or fixed effects (a dummy per person or store, which removes every confounder that is constant within it). For pure prediction none of this matters: a confounded feature still predicts, as long as the confounding pattern holds where the model is used.

Say it in an interview: “The SE is hatsigmasqrt[(X^top X)^-1]_jj with hatsigma^2 = RSS/(n-k) ; t = hatbeta/SE on n - k degrees of freedom, and an F-test for groups of coefficients. A coefficient is the change in y per unit of x_j holding the others fixed; collinearity inflates its variance by the VIF without hurting predictions; leaving out a correlated driver biases it by beta_2delta , and more data won't fix that. It's causal only if nothing confounds it, which the regression itself can't check.”

OLS is unbiased, but with correlated features or many features per row its coefficients wobble wildly (the twins above: spread 5.2 for a true effect of about 1.2). Regularization adds a penalty on the size of the weights, accepting a little bias for a large cut in variance. The intercept is never penalized: centre X and y (or leave the ones column out of the penalty), fit the slopes, then recover hatbeta_0 = bar y - bar x^tophatbeta .

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: beginaligned L(beta) &= lVert y - Xbeta rVert^2 + lambdalVertbetarVert_2^2 \\ nabla L &= -2X^top (y - Xbeta) + 2lambdabeta = 0 \\ hatbeta_ridge &= (X^top X + lambda I)^-1X^top y endaligned

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: In words: the penalty lambdasum_jbeta_j^2 is itself a round bowl centred at zero. Adding it adds lambda to the diagonal of X^top X , that is, lambda of extra curvature in every direction. lambda = 0 is OLS; lambda to infty sends every slope to zero and predicts bar y .

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: Always solvable. For any direction v ne 0 , v^top(X^top X + lambda I)v = lVert Xv rVert^2 + lambdalVert v rVert^2 gt 0 , so the matrix is invertible even with duplicated columns or p gt n . That was the original motivation (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970). When p gg n the same answer can be computed as X^top(XX^top + lambda I)^-1y , an n times n solve instead of p times p ; swapping XX^top for a matrix of kernel similarities turns this into kernel ridge regression.

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: One feature, by hand. With centred data the formula becomes hatbeta = S_xy/(S_xx + lambda) = 12/(10 + lambda) on the salaries:

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: Intercept bar y - 3hatbeta

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: The slope is multiplied by S_xx/(S_xx + lambda) : it shrinks smoothly and only reaches zero in the limit. The intercept slides towards bar y = 5.4 because the line keeps passing through the point of means.

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: Shrinkage along principal directions. With several correlated features, rotate to the axes along which the centred data cloud is long or thin: the eigenvectors v_j of X^top X , whose eigenvalues d_j^2 are the squared spreads along them. Along a long axis the data pins the coefficients down well; along a thin one it barely does, which is exactly where OLS wobbles. Ridge keeps a fixed fraction of OLS along each axis:

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: beginaligned v_j^tophatbeta_ridge &= fracd_j^2d_j^2 + lambda\; v_j^tophatbeta_OLS \\ Xhatbeta_ridge &= sum_j u_j\, fracd_j^2d_j^2 + lambda\, u_j^top y, quad u_j = Xv_j/d_j endaligned

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: In words: the coefficient vector's component along axis j is OLS's component times d_j^2/(d_j^2 + lambda) . That's almost 1 for a long axis ( d_j^2 gg lambda ) and almost 0 for a thin one ( d_j^2 ll lambda ). The second line says the same for the predictions: u_j is axis j seen in the n -dimensional space of rows (the singular value decomposition, SVD, X = UDV^top packs the u_j , d_j and v_j together). The sum of the fractions is the effective degrees of freedom: the number of slopes for OLS, falling to 0 as lambda grows.

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: Worked: the experience twins from section 03. The centred cloud is long along “both columns up together” ( d^2 = 19.6 ) and razor-thin along “one up, the other down” ( d^2 = 0.018 ). With lambda = 1 :

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: the long axis keeps 19.6/20.6 = 95\% : its component of the coefficient vector goes from 0.854 (OLS) to 0.813;

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: the thin axis keeps 0.018/1.018 = 1.8\% : its component, the wild 3.17 that produced 2.83 vs −1.67, drops to 0.057;

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: back in the original coordinates the coefficients are 0.62 and 0.53 (both positive, sum 1.15); with lambda = 10 , 0.41 and 0.39. The effective degrees of freedom at lambda = 1 are 0.95 + 0.02 = 0.97 , down from 2.

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: With an exact duplicate column, ridge gives each copy 12/(20 + lambda) : 0.571 each at lambda = 1 . Splitting a total w as w/2 + w/2 minimizes a^2 + b^2 subject to a + b = w , so ridge always shares equally between identical columns.

chunks.h: Ridge: add λ to every curvature
chunks.x: “Ridge removes useless features.” It never sets a coefficient to exactly zero: the factor d_j^2/(d_j^2 + lambda) is positive for every finite lambda . Ridge shrinks; only an L1 penalty selects.

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: L(beta) = tfrac12lVert y - Xbeta rVert^2 + lambdalVertbetarVert_1 = tfrac12lVert y - Xbeta rVert^2 + lambdasum_j lvertbeta_jrvert

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: In words: the same fit term, with the sum of absolute values as the penalty. (Conventions differ: ridge above uses the full RSS, lasso here half of it, as glmnet does; this makes the one-feature formulas clean, and the comparisons below are about shapes, not equal penalty strengths.) Three ways to see why it produces exact zeros.

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: 1. The push towards zero. The slope of ridge's penalty is 2lambdabeta_j : it fades as beta_j shrinks, so it never quite gets there. The slope of lambdalvertbeta_jrvert is pmlambda , the same size however small beta_j is. The data's pull on beta_j at zero is x_j^top r , the feature's alignment with the current residual. If that pull is weaker than lambda , lvert x_j^top r rvert le lambda , the coefficient stays at exactly zero (the formal statement uses the subgradient of lvertcdotrvert , which is any value in [-1, 1] at 0).

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: 2. The one-feature solution is a soft threshold. For beta gt 0 the derivative is -(S_xy - beta S_xx) + lambda , zero at beta = (S_xy - lambda)/S_xx , which is only valid if S_xy gt lambda ; the negative side mirrors it; otherwise the minimum sits at the kink, beta = 0 :

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: beginaligned hatbeta_lasso &= fracS(S_xy,\ lambda)S_xx \\ S(z, lambda) &= sign(z)\,max(lvert z rvert - lambda,\ 0) endaligned

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: In words: the soft-threshold S moves z towards zero by lambda , and anything within lambda of zero becomes exactly zero. On the salaries ( S_xy = 12 , S_xx = 10 ), next to ridge's 12/(10 + lambda) :

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: Lasso subtracts a fixed amount and clips at zero; ridge divides and never arrives. (With uncorrelated, unit-length features this is exact for every coefficient: ridge scales each OLS weight by 1/(1 + lambda) , lasso soft-thresholds it, and best-subset selection hard-thresholds it, keeping big weights untouched.)

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: 3. The corner geometry. Penalizing is equivalent to fitting under a budget, sum_jbeta_j^2 le t for ridge or sum_jlvertbeta_jrvert le t for lasso (a bigger lambda is a smaller t ). Grow the elliptical contours of the squared error outwards from the OLS answer until one touches the budget region:

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: The same error contours, two budgets. The circle has no corners, so the first touch is at an ordinary point with both weights non-zero. The diamond's corners sit on the axes and stick out towards the contours, so the first touch is usually a corner, where one weight is exactly zero. In more dimensions the L1 ball has even more corners and edges, so many weights are zero at once.

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: Coordinate descent, by hand. Lasso has no closed form with several features, but each coefficient on its own is a one-feature lasso. So cycle through them: take feature j out of the fit, compute its pull on what's left (the partial residual), soft-threshold, put it back. Add a second feature to the salaries: job switches (4, 1, 3, 0, 2) , centred (2, -1, 1, -2, 0) , with x_2^top x_2 = 10 . OLS gives 1.0 per year and −0.4 per switch. With lambda = 3 , starting at zero:

chunks.x: Switches = S(rho_2, 3)/10

chunks.x: Each pull is the feature's dot product with the residual after the other feature's current part is removed: in sweep 1, rho_1 = x_1^top y_c = 12 and then rho_2 = x_2^top(y_c - 0.9\,x_1) = -9 + 4.5 = -4.5 . The two features are correlated (−0.5), so each update shifts the other's pull and it takes a few sweeps to settle. Along the whole lasso path:

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: Why switches drops out at exactly lambda = 6 : with switches at zero, years alone has slope (12 - lambda)/10 , and the pull on switches is lvert -9 + 5 times (12 - lambda)/10 rvert = 3 + 0.5lambda . It stays at zero while that's at most lambda , that is, for lambda ge 6 . The path is made of straight pieces that bend where a feature enters or leaves, which is why solvers trace it cheaply with warm starts (each lambda starts from the previous answer) and why LARS (least angle regression, which moves the coefficients along the path one breakpoint at a time) can compute it exactly.

chunks.x: It shrinks the survivors too (years: 0.6 at lambda = 6 against 1.2 alone). Refitting OLS on the selected features (relaxed or post-lasso) removes that bias.

chunks.h: Lasso: why some coefficients land exactly on zero
chunks.x: Selection isn't discovery. With correlated features the chosen set changes from sample to sample, and p-values computed after selecting are too optimistic.
How does each penalty split credit between near-copies?
Ridge shares: a^2 + b^2 is smallest at an equal split.

Lasso doesn't care: for same-sign weights lvert a rvert + lvert b rvert = lvert a + b rvert , so every split costs the same penalty, and the solver typically puts everything on one copy. With the exact duplicate of years at lambda = 1 , lasso gives (1.1, 0) and ridge (0.57, 0.57).

Elastic net mixes the two: lambdabig(alphalVertbetarVert_1 + tfrac1 - alpha2lVertbetarVert_2^2big) . The L1 part still zeroes useless features; the L2 part makes correlated ones enter together with similar weights (the grouping effect), and lets it keep more than n features. On the duplicate ( lambda = 1 , alpha = 0.5 ): (0.56, 0.56).
Instability, measured. Two twin features (correlation 0.99, true combined effect 2), one other real feature, 200 rows, refitted on 300 bootstrap resamples:

Lasso's combined effect is stable; how it divides it between the twins isn't. Use ridge when you expect many small correlated effects, lasso when you expect a few real ones and want a sparse model, elastic net when you want sparsity but features come in correlated groups (text, engineered features).

OLS doesn't care about units: rescale a feature by 12 and its coefficient divides by 12, predictions unchanged. A penalty does care, because it charges the coefficient's size, and the size depends on the units. Experience in months instead of years:
Months (converted back to per year)

In months, S_xx is 144 times bigger, so the same lambda is tiny next to it and barely shrinks. The units decided the answer. Standardizing (mean 0, standard deviation 1) makes the same effect cost the same penalty whatever the units (the same effect with two features). Fit the scaler on the training fold only, inside a pipeline (data preparation); for one-hot columns, keep all levels under a penalty (why).

Training error always prefers lambda = 0 . So try a log-spaced grid, score each value by K-fold cross-validated error with the scaler refitted inside every fold, and take the best, or the one-standard-error rule: the largest lambda whose error is within one standard error of the best, a simpler model you can't tell apart from it. Simulated: 100 rows, 3 real features and 30 junk ones, noise standard deviation 2, lasso, 5 folds:

OLS on all 33 features scores 6.92; OLS on just the 3 true ones, 3.94. Lasso at its best gets close to knowing the truth (4.10) while keeping all 3 real features and 5 junk ones with small weights (the one-SE choice keeps 3 junk): CV picks a good predictor, not the true feature set. Too little penalty lets junk in, too much starves the real features: a U in lambda , the bias–variance trade of section 05.
Fold design follows the data: time-ordered folds for time series, grouped folds when rows share a user, and nested CV or a held-out test set when the final score must be honest (evaluation).
Cheap paths: lasso and elastic net along the path with warm starts (glmnet, LassoCV); ridge with a leave-one-out shortcut that needs no refitting, e_i/(1 - h_ii) from the ridge hat matrix (RidgeCV).

chunks.h: The MAP view in two sentences
chunks.x: With Gaussian noise of variance sigma^2 , putting a Gaussian prior beta_j sim mathcal N(0, tau^2) on each weight and taking the most probable weights given the data (the MAP estimate) gives exactly ridge with lambda = sigma^2/tau^2 : a tighter prior is a bigger penalty. A Laplace prior, sharply peaked at zero, gives lasso; the derivation and the wider picture are in likelihood, MLE and MAP.

chunks.h: The MAP view in two sentences
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Ridge adds lambda to every eigenvalue of X^top X , so the solution (X^top X + lambda I)^-1X^top y always exists; it shrinks each principal direction by d^2/(d^2 + lambda) , crushing the poorly determined ones that collinearity creates, and never reaches zero. Lasso's penalty pushes with constant force lambda , so any coefficient whose pull lvert x_j^top r rvert is below lambda sits at exactly zero; the one-feature solution is the soft threshold, and coordinate descent repeats it. Ridge shares weight between correlated features, lasso picks one, elastic net keeps the gr

Regularization kept promising “a little bias for a lot less variance”. This section makes that exact: the expected test error of any model under squared loss splits into three parts that can be computed separately.

Setup. Data come from y = f(x) + varepsilon with E[varepsilon] = 0 and Var(varepsilon) = sigma^2 . A training set D is drawn and a model hat f_D fitted on it. Fix a test point x ; its test label has fresh noise, independent of D . Write bar f(x) = E_D[hat f_D(x)] for the average prediction over all the training sets you could have drawn.
Add and subtract f and bar f : y - hat f_D = (y - f) + (f - bar f) + (bar f - hat f_D) . The three pieces are the noise varepsilon , the bias, and this training set's fluctuation.
Square and take the expectation over training sets and test noise. Three squares and three cross terms.

The cross terms vanish. E[varepsilon(f - bar f)] = 0 because f - bar f is a fixed number and E[varepsilon] = 0 . E[varepsilon(bar f - hat f_D)] = E[varepsilon]\,E[bar f - hat f_D] = 0 because the test noise is independent of D . E[(f - bar f)(bar f - hat f_D)] = (f - bar f)\,E_D[bar f - hat f_D] = 0 by the definition of bar f .
What's left is three squares:
beginaligned Ebig[(y - hat f_D(x))^2big] &= sigma^2 + big(f(x) - bar f(x)big)^2 + E_Dbig[(hat f_D(x) - bar f(x))^2big] \\ &= noise + bias^2 + variance endaligned

In words: noise is the floor no model can beat. Bias is how far the average model is from the truth: a model too stiff to bend the right way is wrong the same way every time. Variance is how much the model changes from one training set to another: a flexible model bends to each sample's noise. Average over test points for the overall error.
Only squared error splits this cleanly. For 0–1 loss or log loss there are decompositions, but the parts don't simply add.
It's a statement about a procedure over many training sets. One fitted model doesn't “have” a variance you can read off; you estimate it by refitting (bootstrap, CV) or by simulation, as below.

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: Take the salary design ( S_xx = 10 ) and suppose the truth is a slope beta = 1.2 with noise variance sigma^2 = 1 . The ridge slope is hatbeta_lambda = x_c^top y/(S_xx + lambda) , linear in the noise, so its mean and variance can be written down:

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: beginaligned E[hatbeta_lambda] &= fracS_xxS_xx + lambda\,beta, qquad bias = -fraclambdaS_xx + lambda\,beta \\ Var(hatbeta_lambda) &= fracsigma^2 S_xx(S_xx + lambda)^2 \\ MSE(lambda) &= fracbeta^2lambda^2 + sigma^2 S_xx(S_xx + lambda)^2 endaligned

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: In words: lambda pulls the average estimate towards zero by the factor S_xx/(S_xx + lambda) (bias), and the same factor squared shrinks the variance.

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: The best lambda , derived. Differentiate the MSE: the numerator of the derivative is proportional to beta^2lambda S_xx - sigma^2 S_xx , zero at

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: beginaligned lambda^* &= fracsigma^2beta^2 = frac11.44 = 0.694 \\ MSE(lambda^*) &= fracsigma^2S_xx + lambda^* = frac110.694 = 0.0935 endaligned

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: In words: shrink in proportion to noise over signal. A refit on 50,000 simulated samples gives 0.0933 at lambda = 0.694 , matching. Three lessons from one line of algebra:

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: Some lambda gt 0 always beats OLS. The derivative at lambda = 0 is -2sigma^2/S_xx^2 lt 0 , so a little shrinkage always helps. (Hoerl and Kennard proved the same for the whole coefficient vector.)

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: Weak signals gain most. With beta = 0.3 instead: lambda^* = 11.1 and MSE 0.047, half of OLS's 0.1. With a strong signal the gain is small (6.5% above).

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: The best lambda depends on the unknown beta and sigma , which is why it's estimated by cross-validation. And sigma^2/beta^2 is the MAP penalty sigma^2/tau^2 with the prior's scale tau set to the true effect size: the prior is right when it matches the signal.

chunks.h: Exact numbers: ridge on the five salaries
chunks.x: The same lambda^* also minimizes the prediction error at every x_0 : with centred data the intercept is bar y whatever lambda is, so the error of the predicted mean is sigma^2/n + (x_0 - bar x)^2\,MSE(hatbeta_lambda) (add sigma^2 for a new label), and only the second term depends on lambda .

A curved truth, f(x) = sin(4x + 1) on [-1, 1] , 15 evenly spaced training points, noise sigma = 0.3 (so sigma^2 = 0.09 ). Fit polynomials of rising degree (extra columns x, x^2, dots : still linear regression), redraw the noise 1,000 times, and measure bias² and variance averaged over 101 test points:

Bias² falls as the model gets more flexible, variance rises, and their sum plus the noise floor is a U. Degree 1 is too stiff (wrong the same way every time); degree 12 is right on average but wiggles its own way on every sample, worst near the ends.
Measured directly, with fresh noisy test labels, degree 5's test error is 0.1255 against 0.1256 from noise + bias² + variance: the decomposition is an identity, not an approximation.
