chunks.x: Likelihood, MLE and MAP · Deepam Minda

Probability and likelihood are the same formula, p(data mid theta) , read two ways. Fix theta and vary the data: probabilities, which sum to 1 over the possible outcomes. Fix the data you saw and vary theta : the likelihood, a score for each theta that only means something in ratios and doesn't integrate to 1 (for 7 heads in 10 it integrates to 1/11).

Maximum likelihood (MLE) picks the theta that makes the observed data most probable. Maximize the log: same answer, sums instead of products, no underflow. A coin gives k/n ; a Gaussian gives the sample mean and the variance divided by n , which on average comes out at only (n-1)/n of the true variance, because the mean was fitted to the same points. Least squares and log loss are MLE under Gaussian and Bernoulli noise.

Near its peak the log-likelihood is a parabola, and its curvature is the Fisher information I . The standard error is 1/sqrtI : sqrtp(1-p)/n for a coin. MLE is invariant to reparameterization at any n ; it is also consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, but those three are large-sample promises: 3 heads in 3 tosses gives hat p = 1 , and separable classes send logistic weights to infinity.

Bayes' rule for parameters: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The evidence p(data) doesn't depend on theta , so MAP, the posterior's peak, ignores it. With a Beta(alpha, beta) prior a coin's MAP is (k + alpha - 1)/(n + alpha + beta - 2) : the prior acts as extra imaginary tosses, and its pull fades as n grows.

Regularization is a prior. A Gaussian prior mathcal N(0, tau^2) on the weights gives L2 with lambda = sigma^2/tau^2 ; a Laplace prior gives L1. A tighter prior is a bigger lambda . Ridge, lasso, weight decay, Laplace smoothing and smoothed target encoding are all MAP estimates or posterior means.

Conjugate priors make updating arithmetic, Beta(2, 2) plus 7 heads and 3 tails is Beta(9, 5) , and a full posterior gives more than its peak: a mean, credible intervals, and predictions that average over uncertainty. After 3 heads in 3, the next toss is a head with probability 0.8, not 1. Unlike MLE, MAP moves when you reparameterize.
Everything in this note grows from one formula. Toss a coin n = 10 times. Its chance of heads, theta , is unknown. The number of heads k follows the binomial distribution:
p(k mid theta) = binomnk\,theta^k\,(1 - theta)^n - k
In words: any particular sequence with k heads has probability theta^k(1-theta)^n-k , and binomnk counts how many such sequences there are.

The running example. You toss the coin and see 7 heads in 10. The same formula answers two different questions: “if the coin were fair, how likely is this outcome?” (a probability) and “having seen 7 heads, which values of theta explain it well?” (a likelihood).
Fill in p(k mid theta) for every outcome k and three coins:
Read down a column: probability. theta is fixed and the outcome varies. The 11 numbers are the probabilities of the 11 possible results, so each column sums to 1.

Read across the observed row: likelihood. The data are fixed at k = 7 and theta varies. The numbers 0.009, 0.117, 0.267 say how probable the data you actually saw would be under each coin. They compare coins; nothing requires them to sum to anything.
L(theta) = p(observed data mid theta), as a function of theta

In words: the likelihood of a parameter value is the probability (or density) the model with that value assigns to the data you observed. Some books write L(theta mid x) ; the bar there doesn't mean conditioning on x in the probability sense, it only marks that x is held fixed.
Across more values of theta , for the observed 7 heads:

The likelihood for the observed 7 heads in 10. Each point is one entry of the observed row of the table. The peak at 0.7 is the maximum likelihood estimate (section 02). The shaded area is 1/11, which is why the curve is not a probability distribution over theta .

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: It doesn't integrate to 1. The area under the curve is int_0^1 binom107theta^7(1-theta)^3\,dtheta = 1/11 . (For a binomial count it's always 1/(n+1) .) A probability distribution over theta would have area 1.

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: Each value is a probability of the same event under a different model. 0.267 is P(7 heads mid theta = 0.7) , not P(theta = 0.7 mid 7 heads) . Turning it into a statement about theta needs a prior and Bayes' rule (section 04).

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: With continuous data it can exceed 1. The likelihood is then a product of densities, and a density can be bigger than 1: a Gaussian with sigma = 0.1 has density 3.99 at its centre.

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: Only ratios carry meaning. L(0.7)/L(0.5) = 2.28 : the observed data are 2.28 times as probable under theta = 0.7 as under a fair coin. Factors that don't involve theta , like binom107 , cancel in every ratio and every maximization, so they're routinely dropped. Recording the exact sequence of tosses instead of the count changes the likelihood only by that constant, so it leads to the same conclusions about theta .

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: “ theta = 0.7 has likelihood 0.267, so there's a 26.7% chance the coin's bias is 0.7.” No: if the bias were 0.7, the data would have probability 0.267. A probability for theta is a posterior, and needs a prior.

chunks.h: Why the likelihood is not a probability of theta
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Probability and likelihood use the same function p(x mid theta) . Probability fixes theta and asks how likely different data are, so it sums to 1 over the data. Likelihood fixes the data I observed and asks how well each theta explains them: it's a function of theta , it doesn't integrate to 1, and only ratios matter. For 7 heads in 10, theta = 0.7 has likelihood 0.267 and theta = 0.5 has 0.117, so the data favour 0.7 by a factor of 2.3.”

Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) turns the likelihood into an estimator: pick the parameter value under which the observed data are most probable. With n observations that are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), the probability of all of them is the product of each one's probability:
beginaligned hattheta_MLE &= argmax_theta prod_i=1^n p(x_i mid theta) \\ &= argmax_theta sum_i=1^n log p(x_i mid theta) \\ &= argmin_theta sum_i=1^n -log p(x_i mid theta) endaligned

In words: multiply the probabilities of the data points, take the log so the product becomes a sum, and find the theta with the largest sum. The last line, minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), is how the same thing is written as a loss to minimize. Write ell(theta) = log L(theta) for the log-likelihood.
Same answer. The log is strictly increasing, so whatever theta maximizes L also maximizes log L .
Products become sums. The derivative of a sum is a sum of per-example derivatives, which is what lets SGD estimate it from a mini-batch.
No underflow. The probability of one exact sequence of tosses shrinks exponentially with n . At 70% heads:
Product of probabilities, in float64
0 (the true value is about 10^-2653 )
Float64 can't represent anything positive below about 5 times 10^-324 , so the product becomes exactly 0 and every theta looks equally bad. The log is an ordinary number at any n .
Common densities become simple. The Gaussian and Bernoulli are exponentials of simple expressions, so their logs are a square or a linear term, which is easy to differentiate.
Drop the constant binomnk , take the log, set the derivative to zero:
beginaligned ell(theta) &= klogtheta + (n - k)log(1 - theta) \\ fracdelldtheta &= fracktheta - fracn - k1 - theta = 0 \\ k(1 - theta) &= (n - k)\,theta \\ hattheta &= frackn endaligned
In words: each head pushes the slope up by 1/theta , each tail pushes it down by 1/(1-theta) , and the top is where the pushes balance. That happens exactly at the observed share of heads.
The slope has a name, the score. At theta = 0.5 it is 7/0.5 - 3/0.5 = 8 , positive, so raise theta . At 0.8 it is 8.75 - 15 = -6.25 , so lower it. At 0.7 it is 10 - 10 = 0 .
It's a maximum, and the only one. ell''(theta) = -k/theta^2 - (n - k)/(1 - theta)^2 is negative everywhere, so ell is concave: one peak, no other flat points.
The answer everyone guesses, 0.7, now has a reason: it's the theta that makes what you saw most probable.
Five measurements, x = 3, 5, 6, 8, 8 , assumed drawn independently from mathcal N(mu, sigma^2) . The log of the product of Gaussian densities is:
ell(mu, sigma^2) = -fracn2log(2pisigma^2) - frac12sigma^2sum_i=1^n(x_i - mu)^2
In words: a penalty for a wide bell (the first term), plus a penalty for points far from the centre, measured in units of the variance.
Set each partial derivative to zero. The mean's solution doesn't depend on sigma , so find it first and plug it into the variance's equation:

beginaligned fracpartial ellpartial mu &= frac1sigma^2sum_i (x_i - mu) = 0 \\ hatmu &= bar x \\ fracpartial ellpartial sigma^2 &= -fracn2sigma^2 + frac12sigma^4sum_i (x_i - hatmu)^2 = 0 \\ hatsigma^2 &= frac1nsum_i (x_i - bar x)^2 endaligned
In words: the MLE of the mean is the sample mean, and the MLE of the variance is the average squared distance from it, dividing by n .

With the numbers: bar x = 30/5 = 6 . The deviations are −3, −1, 0, 2, 2, their squares 9, 1, 0, 4, 4, summing to 18. So hatsigma^2 = 18/5 = 3.6 . The familiar sample variance divides by n - 1 instead: s^2 = 18/4 = 4.5 . Which one is “right” is the next question.

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: The question: averaged over many samples, does hatsigma^2 land on the true sigma^2 ? Simulate it: draw 5 points from mathcal N(6, 4) a million times and compute both estimates each time. The MLE averages 3.20; dividing by n - 1 averages 4.00. The MLE is low by the factor (n-1)/n = 0.8 .

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: Why: hatsigma^2 measures the spread around bar x , not around the true mu , and bar x was computed from these very points, so it sits closer to them than mu does. In fact bar x is the point that makes the sum of squared distances as small as possible. With the five points, if the true mean were 5:

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: beginaligned textstylesum (x_i - 5)^2 &= 4 + 0 + 1 + 9 + 9 = 23 \\ textstylesum (x_i - 6)^2 &= 9 + 1 + 0 + 4 + 4 = 18 \\ 23 - 18 &= 5 = n\,(bar x - mu)^2 = 5 times 1^2 endaligned

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: In words: measuring from the fitted centre always gives a smaller sum of squares than measuring from the true centre, and the shortfall is exactly n(bar x - mu)^2 . That identity holds for any data and any mu :

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: beginaligned sum_i (x_i - bar x)^2 &= sum_i (x_i - mu)^2 - n(bar x - mu)^2 \\ mathbb EBig[sum_i (x_i - bar x)^2Big] &= nsigma^2 - n cdot fracsigma^2n = (n - 1)\,sigma^2 endaligned

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: In words: on average each (x_i - mu)^2 is sigma^2 , so the first sum averages nsigma^2 ; bar x - mu has variance sigma^2/n (the variance of a mean), so the correction averages one sigma^2 . Fitting the mean costs exactly one sigma^2 of the sum of squares, so divide by n - 1 to get sigma^2 back on average. The simulation agrees: sums of squares averaged 20.0 around mu and 16.0 around bar x . This is Bessel's correction; the usual phrase is “one degree of freedom is used up by the mean”: the deviations from bar x must sum to 0, so only n - 1 of them are free. (The same intuition, checked by list

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: mathbb E[hatsigma^2_MLE]/sigma^2

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: The bias vanishes as n grows: the MLE is biased but consistent.

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: Unbiased isn't automatically better. Judge an estimator by its mean squared error, MSE = variance + bias^2 . For n = 5 and sigma^2 = 4 :

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: Divide the sum of squares by

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: A larger divisor shrinks the estimate, adding bias but cutting variance by more. For Gaussian data, dividing by n + 1 gives the smallest MSE. This is the bias–variance trade-off (linear-logistic-regression) in its smallest form. Two related facts: s = sqrts^2 is biased low even with n - 1 (it averages 1.88 for a true sigma of 2 at n = 5 ), because a square root is concave; and in regression the same story gives RSS/n for the MLE of the noise variance and RSS/(n - p) for the unbiased one, with p fitted coefficients (linear-logistic-regression).

chunks.h: Why the variance MLE is biased, and why n - 1 fixes it
chunks.x: “The MLE is unbiased.” Often it isn't, and that's fine: its guarantees (section 03) are about large samples. Bias is a small-sample property, and a little of it can buy a lower error.

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: The same recipe (take the log, differentiate, set to zero) covers the other distributions interviewers like to ask about.

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: Poisson counts, such as calls per minute, with p(x mid lambda) = lambda^x e^-lambda/x! :

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: beginaligned ell(lambda) &= Big(sum_i x_iBig)loglambda - nlambda - sum_i log x_i! \\ fracdelldlambda &= fracsum_i x_ilambda - n = 0 \;Rightarrow\; hatlambda = bar x endaligned

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: In words: the MLE of a Poisson rate is the average count. Its Fisher information (next section) is n/lambda , so SE = sqrthatlambda/n . For counts 3, 5, 4: hatlambda = 4 and SE = sqrt4/3 = 1.15 .

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: Exponential waiting times, p(x mid lambda) = lambda e^-lambda x : ell = nloglambda - lambdasum x_i , so hatlambda = n/sum x_i = 1/bar x . Waits of 2, 1 and 3 minutes give a rate of 0.5 per minute, and by invariance (section 03) a mean wait of 2. The rate's MLE is biased high at small n : with 3 waits and a true rate of 0.5 it averages 0.75.

chunks.h: Three more drills: Poisson, exponential, uniform
chunks.x: Uniform on [0, theta] : L(theta) = theta^-n if theta is at least every observation, and 0 otherwise. That only falls as theta grows, so the maximum sits at the edge of the allowed region, hattheta = max_i x_i : 3 for the data 2, 1, 3. No derivative is zero there, so “set the derivative to zero” finds nothing. The estimate is always below the truth (on average ntheta/(n+1) , so 3 when theta = 4 and n = 3 ).

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: Both maximize a conditional likelihood, p(y mid x, w) : the inputs are treated as fixed, and only the targets are modelled.

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: Linear regression. Assume each target is a linear function plus Gaussian noise, y_i = w^top x_i + varepsilon_i with varepsilon_i sim mathcal N(0, sigma^2) . The NLL is the Gaussian's, with w^top x_i as the mean:

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: beginaligned -ell(w) &= frac12sigma^2sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 + fracn2log(2pisigma^2) \\ hat w_MLE &= argmin_w sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 endaligned

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: In words: with sigma fixed, only the sum of squared residuals depends on w , so maximizing the Gaussian likelihood is exactly least squares. Swap the noise model and the loss changes with it: Laplace noise gives absolute error, Bernoulli gives log loss, categorical gives cross-entropy. That family, and what each loss makes the model predict, is derived in loss functions; how OLS is solved is in linear and logistic regression.

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: Logistic regression. Each label is a coin toss with its own heads probability, y_i sim Bernoulli(p_i) with p_i = sigma(w^top x_i) . The coin's log-likelihood, summed over rows, is minus the log loss:

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: beginaligned -ell(w) &= -sum_i big[y_i log p_i + (1 - y_i)log(1 - p_i)big] \\ nabla_w(-ell) &= sum_i (p_i - y_i)\,x_i = X^top(p - y) endaligned

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: In words: minimizing log loss is maximizing the Bernoulli likelihood. Setting the gradient to zero has no closed-form solution, because p is a non-linear function of w , but the NLL is convex, so any minimum that gradient descent or Newton's method (called IRLS here) finds is the global one. It's unique when the columns of X are linearly independent, and finite only if the classes aren't perfectly separable (section 03). Details are in linear and logistic regression. Training a neural network with cross-entropy is the same thing with a learned f(x) in place of w^top x (loss functions); average

chunks.h: Linear and logistic regression are MLE
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “MLE picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable. I maximize the log-likelihood: same argmax, a sum over i.i.d. examples instead of a product, and no underflow. For a coin the score equation gives k/n . For a Gaussian it gives the sample mean and the variance with divisor n , whose average is only (n-1)/n of the true variance because the mean was fitted to the same data; n - 1 corrects it, though the MLE has lower MSE. Least squares and log loss are just Gaussian and Bernoulli MLE.”
The first three hold as n grows, under regularity conditions listed below the table. Invariance holds exactly, at any n .
hattheta converges to the true theta
7/10, 70/100 and 700/1000 all say 0.7, and the wobble around the truth shrinks
hattheta approx mathcal Nbig(theta, 1/I(theta)big) : a bell around the truth whose width is set by the Fisher information I(theta) of the whole sample (next subsection)
Standard errors 0.145, 0.046, 0.0145
No unbiased estimator has variance below 1/I(theta) (the Cramér–Rao bound); the MLE reaches it in the limit
k/n reaches it exactly, at every n
The MLE of g(theta) is g(hattheta) : exact at every n , no conditions needed
Odds 0.7/0.3 = 2.33 , log-odds 0.85; for a Gaussian, hatsigma = sqrthatsigma^2

The regularity conditions, informally: the model is identifiable (different theta give different distributions), the true value is inside the parameter space rather than on its edge, the set of possible data values doesn't depend on theta , the likelihood is smooth, and the number of parameters stays fixed as n grows. The textbook counter-example: for Uniform(0, theta) the MLE is the largest observation, which is always below theta and isn't normally distributed at any n .

If the model is wrong (it almost always is), the MLE still converges, to the member of the family closest to the truth in KL divergence. The standard errors from the next section then need a correction, the “sandwich” or robust standard errors.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: The question: how sure can you be that theta is near 0.7? Look at the shape of the log-likelihood around its peak. A sharp peak means only a narrow range of theta explains the data well; a flat one means many values fit almost as well. The sharpness is the curvature, the second derivative.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: The log-likelihood relative to its peak. With ten times the data the curve is ten times as curved, so the range of plausible theta is sqrt10 approx 3.2 times narrower. The bars under the axis mark where each curve stays within 1.92 of its peak (the dashed line): the 95% likelihood-ratio intervals.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: beginaligned I(theta) &= -\,mathbb EBig[fracpartial^2 ellpartial theta^2Big] = mathbb EBig[Big(fracpartial ellpartial thetaBig)^2Big] \\ Var(hattheta) &approx frac1I(theta) \\ SE(hattheta) &approx frac1sqrtI(hattheta) endaligned

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: In words: the Fisher information is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood, how sharply it bends at theta , averaged over datasets the model could generate. Equivalently it's the variance of the score (the slope), because the score averages zero at the true theta . More information means a sharper peak and a smaller standard error. Here ell is the log-likelihood of the whole sample, so I is the information in all n points; the information in one point is written I_1 below. The observed information J(hattheta) = -ell''(hattheta) is the curvature of your own dataset's curve at its peak; so

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Deriving it for a coin. One toss x in \0, 1\ has log p(x mid theta) = xlogtheta + (1 - x)log(1 - theta) :

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: beginaligned fracpartial^2partialtheta^2log p(x mid theta) &= -fracxtheta^2 - frac1 - x(1 - theta)^2 \\ I_1(theta) &= fracthetatheta^2 + frac1 - theta(1 - theta)^2 = frac1theta(1 - theta) \\ I_n(theta) &= fracntheta(1 - theta) \\ SE(hattheta) &= sqrtfrachattheta(1 - hattheta)n endaligned

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: In words: take minus the second derivative, average it using mathbb E[x] = theta , and multiply by n because independent tosses add their information. One over the square root is the standard error. Per toss, a coin near 0 or 1 carries the most information: its outcomes vary least, so each toss pins theta down more tightly.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Information n/[hattheta(1 - hattheta)]

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Wald 95% interval hattheta pm 1.96\,SE

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Check with the observed information: 7/0.7^2 + 3/0.3^2 = 14.29 + 33.33 = 47.62 , the same as the expected information at hattheta (they coincide for the coin, not in general). Simulating many 10-toss experiments with theta = 0.7 gives a standard deviation of hattheta of 0.1449, matching.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Check the score form: at theta = 0.7 a head has score 1/0.7 = 1.43 and a tail -1/0.3 = -3.33 . Their average is 0.7 times 1.43 - 0.3 times 3.33 = 0 and their variance is 0.7 times 1.43^2 + 0.3 times 3.33^2 = 4.76 = 1/0.21 .

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: It's the A/B-test standard error. sqrtp(1 - p)/n is exactly the SE of a conversion rate in hypothesis testing. There it's the variance of an average of 0/1 values, with the central limit theorem supplying the bell shape; here it comes from the curvature. For the coin the two routes agree.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: The SE of a transformed estimate (the delta method). Invariance gives the estimate g(hattheta) ; its SE is about lvert g'(hattheta) rvert times SE(hattheta) . For the log-odds, g'(theta) = 1/[theta(1 - theta)] = 4.76 at 0.7, so the log-odds 0.85 has SE 4.76 times 0.145 = 0.69 .

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Many parameters: I becomes a matrix, the expected Hessian of the NLL, and Cov(hattheta) approx I^-1 . The square roots of its diagonal are the coefficient standard errors a regression summary prints; for logistic regression I = X^top W X with W = diagbig(p_i(1 - p_i)big) (linear-logistic-regression). It's the same Hessian Newton's method uses to take its steps.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Wald vs likelihood-ratio intervals. The Wald interval uses only the curvature at the peak, so it assumes the curve is a parabola. For 7 of 10 the curve is lopsided near 1, and the Wald upper end of 0.984 is too high. The likelihood-ratio interval uses the real curve: keep every theta whose log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the peak. Why 1.92: when theta_0 is the true value, twice the drop, 2[ell(hattheta) - ell(theta_0)] , approximately follows a chi^2 distribution with 1 degree of freedom (Wilks' theorem), whose 95% point is 3.84. That gives [0.39, 0.92] for 7 of 10 and [0.61, 0.78] for 70 of

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: The likelihood-ratio test uses the same fact. Is the coin fair? Twice the drop from the peak to 0.5 is 2ln 2.28 = 1.65 , below 3.84, so a fair coin isn't rejected ( p = 0.20 ); with 70 of 100 it's 16.5 ( p = 0.00005 ). For nested models in general, 2(ell_big - ell_small) is approximately chi^2 with one degree of freedom per extra parameter; in regression output this is the drop in deviance.

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Comparing models. Training likelihood always rises when parameters are added, so on its own it always picks the bigger model. Information criteria charge for each of the d parameters (lower is better): AIC = 2d - 2hatell and BIC = dln n - 2hatell . For 7 of 10, the fair coin ( d = 0 , hatell = -6.93 ) scores 13.86 on both; the free coin ( d = 1 , hatell = -6.11 ) scores 14.22 and 14.52, so both prefer the fair coin. For 70 of 100 both prefer the free one (AIC 124.2 against 138.6). AIC estimates out-of-sample log-likelihood; BIC approximates the evidence of section 04, and its penalty grows wit

chunks.h: Fisher information and the standard error of an MLE
chunks.x: Writing the standard error as p(1 - p)/sqrt n . The square root covers the whole variance: sqrtp(1 - p)/n . And Fisher information grows with n (it adds over independent data), while the standard error shrinks like 1/sqrt n .

Little data, extreme outcomes. 3 heads in 3 tosses gives hattheta = 1 : the model now says a tail is impossible. The standard-error formula returns sqrt1 times 0/3 = 0 , total certainty, and the first tail costs an infinite log loss. Zero counts do the same in Naive Bayes, where a word never seen with a class gets probability 0 and vetoes that class (classical NLP).

Separation. If some combination of features splits the classes perfectly, logistic regression's likelihood keeps rising as the weights grow, so no finite MLE exists. On four points x = -2, -1, 1, 2 with labels 0, 0, 1, 1, gradient descent on the NLL (learning rate 0.5, intercept included) gives a weight of 3.4 after 100 steps, 5.5 after 1,000, 7.8 after 10,000 and 10.1 after 100,000, still climbing while the loss creeps towards 0 (linear-logistic-regression).

Too many parameters for the data. The MLE fits noise as eagerly as signal. A degree-4 polynomial goes exactly through 5 points: zero residuals, an estimated noise variance of 0, an infinite likelihood. A Gaussian mixture can park one component on a single point and shrink its variance to 0, again with infinite likelihood (unsupervised learning). A full covariance matrix in d dimensions estimated from n le d points is singular.
The wrong noise model. The MLE is only as good as the assumed distribution: Gaussian noise when the real noise has heavy tails lets a few outliers drag the fit (loss functions).
The first three have one cure: add information that isn't in the data, which is what a prior does. That's MAP, section 05.

Say it in an interview: “The MLE is invariant to reparameterization at any n . Under regularity conditions it's also consistent, asymptotically normal with variance one over the Fisher information, and efficient, because it reaches the Cramér–Rao bound. Fisher information is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood; for a coin it's n/[p(1-p)] , so the SE is sqrtp(1-p)/n . Those are large-sample promises: with 3 heads in 3 the MLE says p = 1 , separable data send logistic weights to infinity, and many parameters fit noise. A prior fixes all three.”

MLE treats theta as a fixed unknown and asks which value explains the data best. The Bayesian view treats theta as uncertain, with a distribution of its own, and uses Bayes' rule to update that distribution with the data. (Bayes' rule for events belongs to a planned probability note; here it's applied to parameters.)
beginaligned p(theta mid D) &= fracp(D mid theta)\,p(theta)p(D) \\ p(D) &= int p(D mid theta)\,p(theta)\,dtheta endaligned

In words: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. The prior p(theta) is what you believed before the data, the likelihood is how well each theta explains the data, and the posterior is the updated belief. The evidence or marginal likelihood p(D) is the probability of the data averaged over the prior: one number, the same for every theta .
Worked, with a flat prior p(theta) = 1 on [0, 1] and 7 heads in 10:
beginaligned p(D) &= int_0^1 120\,theta^7(1 - theta)^3\,dtheta = frac111 \\ p(theta mid D) &= 11 times 120\,theta^7(1 - theta)^3 = 1320\,theta^7(1 - theta)^3 endaligned

In words: the evidence is the area under the likelihood curve from section 01, and dividing by it rescales the curve to area 1. The result is the Beta(8, 4) distribution, whose normalizing constant is indeed 1320. With a flat prior the posterior has the likelihood's shape, peak at 0.7 included.
Why MAP can ignore the evidence. p(D) doesn't depend on theta , so dividing by it can't move the peak. For finding the most probable theta it's enough that posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
When the evidence matters:
For the full posterior. Means, intervals and predictions need a distribution with area 1.

For comparing models. The evidence scores a whole model by how well it predicted the data, averaging over its prior. A fair-coin model ( theta = 0.5 exactly) gives the data probability p(D) = 0.117 ; the flexible flat-prior model gives 1/11 = 0.091 . Their ratio, the Bayes factor, is 1.29 in favour of the fair coin, even though theta = 0.7 fits better. The flexible model spread its prior over many values of theta that predict 7 of 10 badly, and pays for it. That built-in Occam's razor is why approximations of the evidence, such as BIC (section 03), are used to choose model size.
“The posterior is the normalized likelihood.” Only with a flat prior, and “flat” depends on how the parameter is written: flat in theta is not flat in the log-odds (section 08).

Say it in an interview: “posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The evidence p(D) normalizes it and doesn't depend on theta , so it drops out of any argmax. I need it only to get a proper posterior, for intervals and predictions, or to compare models, where it automatically penalizes flexible ones.”
Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation returns the peak of the posterior:

beginaligned hattheta_MAP &= argmax_theta\ p(theta mid D) \\ &= argmax_theta\ big[log p(D mid theta) + log p(theta)big] \\ &= argmin_theta\ big[underbrace-log p(D mid theta)_data loss (NLL)\ underbrace-\ log p(theta)_penaltybig] endaligned

In words: maximize the log-likelihood plus the log-prior. As a loss, that's the usual NLL plus a penalty, minus the log-prior, that charges for parameter values the prior finds implausible. With a flat prior the penalty is a constant and MAP equals MLE.

chunks.h: The coin with a Beta prior
chunks.x: The natural prior for a probability is the Beta distribution, Beta(alpha, beta) , with density proportional to theta^alpha - 1(1 - theta)^beta - 1 on [0, 1] . Its mean is alpha/(alpha + beta) and, for alpha, beta gt 1 , its peak is at (alpha - 1)/(alpha + beta - 2) . Beta(1, 1) is flat; Beta(2, 2) is a gentle hump at 0.5; Beta(5, 5) says “probably close to fair” more firmly.

chunks.h: The coin with a Beta prior
chunks.x: beginaligned log p(theta mid D) &= (k + alpha - 1)logtheta \\ &quad + (n - k + beta - 1)log(1 - theta) + const \\ fracddtheta: quad 0 &= frack + alpha - 1theta - fracn - k + beta - 11 - theta \\ hattheta_MAP &= frack + alpha - 1n + alpha + beta - 2 endaligned

chunks.h: The coin with a Beta prior
chunks.x: In words: the log-prior has the same shape as a coin's log-likelihood, so it simply adds to the head and tail counts. The derivative is the coin MLE's, with k + alpha - 1 heads out of n + alpha + beta - 2 tosses.

chunks.h: The coin with a Beta prior
chunks.x: Multiply the prior by the likelihood and renormalize. The posterior sits between them, closer to whichever is sharper, and is narrower than either: it combines two sources of information.

Imaginary tosses. For the MAP, Beta(alpha, beta) acts like alpha - 1 heads and beta - 1 tails seen before the experiment. Beta(5, 5) is 4 imaginary heads and 4 imaginary tails, so 7 of 10 becomes 11 of 18. The posterior mean uses alpha and beta themselves, (k + alpha)/(n + alpha + beta) (section 08).

A weighted average. The MAP is a blend of the MLE and the prior's peak, weighted by real against imaginary tosses: with Beta(5, 5) , the data get weight 10/18 = 0.556 , so 0.556 times 0.7 + 0.444 times 0.5 = 0.611 . Pulling an estimate towards a prior value like this is called shrinkage. Smoothed target encoding is the same blend, with the overall mean counting as m extra rows (data preparation).

Choosing the prior's strength is choosing how many tosses of evidence your belief is worth. Past experiments can set it (estimating the prior from data is called empirical Bayes); otherwise cross-validation can.

chunks.h: MAP becomes MLE as the data grow
chunks.x: Keep the share of heads at 70% and add tosses:

chunks.h: MAP becomes MLE as the data grow
chunks.x: The prior is a fixed number of imaginary tosses; the real ones keep coming. In log terms, the log-prior is one term while the log-likelihood has n , so the data eventually swamp any prior, and a stronger prior just takes longer. The exception is a prior that gives some region zero probability: no amount of data can move the posterior there.

chunks.h: MAP becomes MLE as the data grow
chunks.x: “MAP is the Bayesian answer.” It uses a prior but returns a single point, exactly like MLE, and discards the posterior's spread. Think of it as regularized MLE. What a full posterior adds is in section 08.

chunks.h: MAP becomes MLE as the data grow
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “MAP maximizes likelihood times prior: log-likelihood plus log-prior, or NLL plus a penalty. For a coin with a Beta(alpha, beta) prior it's (k + alpha - 1)/(n + alpha + beta - 2) , so the prior adds alpha - 1 imaginary heads and beta - 1 tails. With 3 heads in 3 and a Beta(2, 2) prior that's 0.8 instead of 1. The prior's weight is fixed while the likelihood grows with n , so MAP tends to the MLE.”

The version of the last section interviewers ask for: a regularization penalty is minus a log-prior, so a regularized fit is a MAP estimate. The setup is linear regression with Gaussian noise, y_i = w^top x_i + varepsilon_i , varepsilon_i sim mathcal N(0, sigma^2) , plus a prior on each weight.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: Put an independent zero-mean Gaussian prior on each weight, w_j sim mathcal N(0, tau^2) : “weights are probably small, and large ones are increasingly implausible”. Step by step:

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: The log-prior. -log p(w) = sum_j w_j^2/(2tau^2) + const .

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: The negative log-posterior is minus the log-likelihood plus minus the log-prior, up to constants.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: Multiply by 2sigma^2 . Scaling by a positive constant doesn't move the minimum.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: beginaligned -log p(w mid D) &= frac12sigma^2sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 \\ &quad + frac12tau^2sum_j w_j^2 + const \\ hat w_MAP &= argmin_w\ sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 \\ &qquadqquad + fracsigma^2tau^2lVert w rVert_2^2 \\ lambda &= fracsigma^2tau^2 endaligned

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: In words: ridge regression is the MAP estimate under a zero-mean Gaussian prior, and its lambda is the noise variance divided by the prior variance. A tight prior (small tau^2 ) or noisy data (large sigma^2 ) means a strong penalty; a flat prior ( tau^2 to infty ) gives lambda = 0 , plain least squares.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: Worked, one weight and no intercept. x = 1, 2, 3, 4 , y = 1, 3, 2, 5 , sigma^2 = 1 . Then sum xy = 33 and sum x^2 = 30 . The MLE is 33/30 = 1.1 , and setting the derivative of the penalized loss to zero gives hat w = sum xy/(sum x^2 + lambda) :

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: hat w_MAP = 33/(30 + lambda)

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: The weight shrinks smoothly towards 0 as the prior tightens, but never reaches it. With many features the closed form is hat w = (X^top X + lambda I)^-1X^top y ; how ridge behaves (shrinkage per direction, collinearity, choosing lambda ) is in linear and logistic regression.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: Logistic regression has no sigma : the objective is the log loss plus lVert w rVert^2/(2tau^2) . scikit-learn's LogisticRegression minimizes tfrac12lVert w rVert^2 + C sum log loss ; dividing by C shows that C is the prior variance tau^2 . A numerical MAP fit and scikit-learn give the same coefficients.

chunks.h: A Gaussian prior gives L2 (ridge, weight decay)
chunks.x: Weight decay in a neural network is the same prior. With plain SGD, the step w leftarrow w - eta(nabla NLL + lambda w) = (1 - etalambda)\,w - etanablaNLL shrinks every weight by a constant factor each step, hence the name. With Adam, adding lambda w to the gradient is not the same as decaying the weights. The L2 version still has the MAP as its fixed point, but along the way Adam divides its pull by each weight's gradient scale, so weights with large gradients are barely regularized. AdamW applies the decay to the weights directly (deep learning basics): it regularizes more evenly in practice,
Now give each weight a Laplace prior, p(w_j) = frac12bexp(-lvert w_j rvert/b) : a sharp peak at 0 with exponential tails (variance 2b^2 ). The same three steps:

beginaligned -log p(w mid D) &= frac12sigma^2sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 \\ &quad + frac1bsum_j lvert w_j rvert + const \\ hat w_MAP &= argmin_w\ sum_i big(y_i - w^top x_ibig)^2 \\ &qquadqquad + frac2sigma^2blVert w rVert_1 \\ lambda &= frac2sigma^2b endaligned
In words: lasso is the MAP estimate under a Laplace prior, with lambda again growing as the prior narrows.
Worked, same data. For w gt 0 the derivative of sum (y - wx)^2 + lambda w is -2(33 - 30w) + lambda , so hat w = (33 - lambda/2)/30 , and once lambda/2 ge 33 the best value is exactly 0:

The weight drops to exactly zero once lambda ge 66 , that is b le 0.030 . The reason is the shape of the prior at 0. Compare slopes at w = 0 . The data's loss sum(y - wx)^2 has slope -2sum xy = -66 there, pulling w up. The L2 penalty's slope, 2lambda w , is 0 at w = 0 , so it can never cancel that pull: it shrinks the weight but never all the way. The Laplace prior has a kink at 0, so the L1 penalty adds a slope of +lambda for any w gt 0 , however small. Once lambda ge 66 , the total slope is zero or positive everywhere to the right of 0, and w = 0 is the minimum. The geometry (a diamond-shape

“A Laplace prior makes weights exactly zero.” Only its peak does. In the example with b = 0.025 , the posterior mode is exactly 0, but the posterior mean is 0.075 and the posterior gives 88% probability to w gt 0 . Lasso's sparsity comes from taking the mode of a kinked distribution, not from believing the weight is zero. Bayesian models that really want “exactly zero or not” use spike-and-slab priors; the horseshoe is a continuous cousin that shrinks small weights hard without making them exactly zero.

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: Scale the features first. mathcal N(0, tau^2 I) puts the same belief on every weight, which only makes sense if the features are on comparable scales; otherwise the penalty hits each feature according to its units.

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: Don't penalize the intercept. It gets a flat prior. Penalizing it would pull every prediction towards 0 instead of towards the average target. (scikit-learn's default solver leaves it unpenalized; its liblinear solver penalizes it.)

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: The same prior has different lambda 's in different libraries. With a summed loss the prior's weight is fixed and the data swamp it as n grows (MAP → MLE). Libraries that average the loss over rows rescale lambda : scikit-learn's Lasso minimizes RSS/(2n) + alphalVert w rVert_1 , so alpha = sigma^2/(nb) , while Ridge minimizes RSS + alphalVert w rVert_2^2 , so alpha = sigma^2/tau^2 . Both were checked numerically against a direct MAP fit.

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: Choosing lambda is choosing a prior. Cross-validation picks it empirically; empirical Bayes picks the tau^2 that maximizes the evidence.

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: A prior needn't be centred on 0. mathcal N(w_0, tau^2) penalizes lVert w - w_0 rVert^2 : shrink towards a previous model's weights, for example to keep a fine-tuned model close to its pretrained starting point.

chunks.h: What the correspondence tells you in practice
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “A Gaussian prior mathcal N(0, tau^2) on the weights adds lVert w rVert^2/(2tau^2) to the negative log-likelihood; multiplying through by 2sigma^2 gives ridge with lambda = sigma^2/tau^2 . A Laplace prior adds lVert w rVert_1/b , which is lasso with lambda = 2sigma^2/b . A tighter prior means a bigger lambda . L1 gives exact zeros because the MAP is the mode of a prior with a kink at 0; the posterior mean under the same prior isn't sparse.”

A prior is conjugate to a likelihood when the posterior lands in the same family as the prior. Then updating never needs an integral: you just change the prior's parameters, usually by adding counts or sums from the data.

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: beginaligned p(theta mid D) &propto underbracetheta^alpha - 1(1 - theta)^beta - 1_prior cdot underbracetheta^k(1 - theta)^n - k_likelihood \\ &= theta^alpha + k - 1(1 - theta)^beta + n - k - 1 \\ theta mid D &sim Beta(alpha + k,\ beta + n - k) endaligned

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: In words: the prior and the likelihood are both powers of theta and 1 - theta , so multiplying them adds the exponents. The result is again a Beta, with the heads added to alpha and the tails to beta .

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: Worked, step by step, starting from Beta(2, 2) :

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: Order and batching don't matter. Updating once with 8 heads in 15 tosses also gives Beta(10, 9) , and so does updating one toss at a time. Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: The interval narrows as evidence accumulates, from 0.81 wide to 0.48 to 0.43.

chunks.h: Beta–Binomial: add heads to alpha , tails to beta
chunks.x: Bayesian A/B testing is two of these, one per arm, compared by sampling from both posteriors (hypothesis testing).

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: For the mean mu of Gaussian data with a known noise variance sigma^2 , a Gaussian prior mu sim mathcal N(mu_0, tau_0^2) gives a Gaussian posterior. With n points of mean bar x :

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: beginaligned frac1tau_n^2 &= frac1tau_0^2 + fracnsigma^2 \\ mu_n &= tau_n^2Big(fracmu_0tau_0^2 + fracn\,bar xsigma^2Big) endaligned

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: In words: precisions add (precision is one over variance: the prior's plus the data's), and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean. The prior is worth n_0 = sigma^2/tau_0^2 observations sitting at mu_0 . And n/sigma^2 is exactly the Fisher information about mu in the data, so “precisions add” says: posterior information = prior information + Fisher information.

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: Worked, with the five measurements from section 02 ( bar x = 6 , n = 5 ), a known sigma^2 = 4 and a prior mathcal N(5, 1) :

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: Precision: 1/1 + 5/4 = 2.25 , so the posterior variance is 0.444 (standard deviation 0.667).

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: Mean: (5/1 + 5 times 6/4)/2.25 = 12.5/2.25 = 5.556 . The same thing as pseudo-observations: the prior is worth 4/1 = 4 points at 5, so (4 times 5 + 5 times 6)/9 = 5.556 .

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: 95% credible interval: 5.556 pm 1.96 times 0.667 = [4.25, 6.86] . The MLE alone would be 6 pm 1.96 times 0.894 , with SE = sqrt4/5 = 0.894 .

chunks.h: Gaussian–Gaussian, and the other common pairs
chunks.x: More data: with 50 points of the same mean, the data's weight rises from 0.56 to 0.93 and the posterior mean to 5.93.

chunks.x: For example, a Gamma(2, 1) prior on a Poisson rate, with counts 3, 5, 4 over three periods, becomes Gamma(14, 4) , with mean 3.5 events per period.
Closed form. The posterior, its mean, its intervals and its predictions all have formulas: no integrals, no sampling.
Streaming updates. Keep two numbers per item (per ad, per arm, per merchant) and add counts as data arrive. Thompson sampling in bandits does exactly this.
Readable priors. A conjugate prior is pseudo-data, so you can say “this prior is worth 20 users”, and defend it.

The limit: conjugacy is a convenience, not a reason to believe a prior; choose the prior for its content. Most models, logistic regression and neural networks included, have no conjugate prior, so their posteriors need sampling (MCMC), variational inference or the Laplace approximation (section 08).

Say it in an interview: “A conjugate prior keeps the posterior in the prior's family, so updating is arithmetic: Beta(alpha, beta) plus k successes in n becomes Beta(alpha + k, beta + n - k) . Beta(2, 2) with 7 of 10 gives Beta(9, 5) , mean 0.64. For a Gaussian mean with known variance, precisions add and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average. It matters because it's closed-form and streams; without conjugacy you need sampling or an approximation.”

MAP keeps one point of the posterior. A full Bayesian analysis keeps the whole distribution, and the difference shows up in five places. The running example: a flat prior and 7 heads in 10, so the posterior is Beta(8, 4) .

Beta(8, 4) has mode 0.700 (here MAP equals MLE, because the prior is flat), median 0.676 and mean 0.667. Each is the best single summary under a different cost of being wrong: the mean minimizes the expected squared error, the median the expected absolute error, the mode the 0–1 loss (in the limit). They differ when the posterior is skewed, which happens with little data or near 0 and 1, and merge as n grows.
Wald, hattheta pm 1.96\,SE
Confidence; from the curvature at the peak
Confidence; inverts the score test (a test built on the score, the slope from section 02, at the null value)
Confidence; guaranteed at least 95% coverage, so wide
Credible; 2.5% of posterior probability on each side
Posterior, highest density
Credible; the shortest interval holding 95%
A 95% credible interval means what people want an interval to mean: given the prior and the data, theta lies inside with probability 0.95.

A 95% confidence interval is a property of the procedure: in repeated experiments, 95% of intervals built this way contain the true theta . Any single interval either does or doesn't (hypothesis testing).

The numbers often nearly agree. With a flat prior and moderate n , the credible interval is close to the better confidence intervals (here Wilson). They part company with small n , near 0 or 1, or with an informative prior.

The question: what's the probability that the next toss is a head? The plug-in answer uses one estimate, p(x_new mid hattheta) . The Bayesian answer averages the prediction over every theta , weighted by the posterior:
beginaligned p(x_new mid D) &= int p(x_new mid theta)\,p(theta mid D)\,dtheta \\ P(head mid D) &= mathbb E[theta mid D] = frack + alphan + alpha + beta endaligned

In words: the predictive probability of a head is the posterior mean of theta . With a flat prior that's (k + 1)/(n + 2) , Laplace's rule of succession, which is “add one imaginary head and one imaginary tail”.
Posterior predictive (flat prior)
After 7 of 10: next toss a head?
After 7 of 10: next two both heads?
mathbb E[theta^2] = frac8 times 912 times 13 = 0.462
After 3 of 3: next toss a head?
After 3 of 3: log loss if a tail comes

The plug-in treats hattheta as if it were known exactly. The predictive carries the uncertainty about theta into the prediction, which matters most when data are scarce and when predictions compound over several steps. That's why Bayesian predictions are less overconfident. Deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout are often described as rough approximations to this averaging for neural networks.

chunks.h: MAP depends on how you write the parameter; MLE doesn't
chunks.x: Same flat prior on theta , same 7 of 10, so the MAP is 0.7. Now estimate the log-odds z = logfractheta1 - theta instead, as logistic regression does. The belief is unchanged, but a density changes when you change variables: it gets multiplied by lvert dtheta/dz rvert = theta(1 - theta) , so a prior that's flat in theta isn't flat in z :

chunks.h: MAP depends on how you write the parameter; MLE doesn't
chunks.x: beginaligned p(z mid D) &propto theta^7(1 - theta)^3 cdot theta(1 - theta) = theta^8(1 - theta)^4 \\ peak at theta &= frac812 = 0.667 endaligned

chunks.h: MAP depends on how you write the parameter; MLE doesn't
chunks.x: In words: the same belief and the same data give a MAP of 0.700 in one coordinate system and 0.667 in another. The likelihood is a function, not a density, so it has no such factor: maximizing over z gives hat z = log(7/3) = 0.847 , which maps back to theta = 0.7 . That is the MLE's invariance from section 03.

chunks.h: MAP depends on how you write the parameter; MLE doesn't
chunks.x: The posterior median is invariant too, since quantiles survive any increasing transform (the median of z is 0.736, the log-odds of 0.676). The posterior mean isn't: mathbb E[z] = 0.760 , while the log-odds of mathbb E[theta] = 0.667 is 0.693. So a MAP estimate is a property of the belief plus a coordinate system, another reason to see it as regularized MLE rather than as a Bayesian summary.

chunks.h: MAP depends on how you write the parameter; MLE doesn't
chunks.x: Which prior is “flat”? The example shows that “uninformative” depends on the coordinates. The Jeffreys prior, proportional to sqrtI(theta) , is the standard answer: choose it in theta or in the log-odds and you get the same belief. For a coin it's sqrt1/[theta(1 - theta)] , the Beta(tfrac12, tfrac12) distribution; with 7 of 10 its posterior is Beta(7.5, 3.5) , mean 0.682. It settles which prior to call flat; the MAP still moves between coordinate systems.
When the posterior has no closed form, approximate it with a Gaussian centred at the MAP, with variance from the curvature there:
beginaligned p(theta mid D) &approx mathcal Nbig(hattheta_MAP,\ H^-1big) \\ H &= -fracpartial^2partialtheta^2log p(theta mid D)\,Big|_hattheta_MAP endaligned

In words: near its peak the log-posterior is roughly a parabola (a second-order Taylor expansion), and the exponential of a parabola is a Gaussian. Its variance is one over the curvature, the same idea as the Fisher standard error.

On Beta(8, 4) : peak 0.7, curvature 47.6, so a standard deviation of 0.145, against the true 0.131. The Gaussian also puts 1.9% of its probability above theta = 1 , which is impossible, because the true posterior is skewed against the boundary. With 70 of 100 the two standard deviations are 0.0458 and 0.0453: nearly exact.
With a flat prior H is the observed Fisher information, so the Laplace interval is the Wald interval.
Uses: Bayesian logistic regression, approximating the evidence (BIC is a cruder version of it), and cheap uncertainty for neural networks by fitting a Laplace approximation to the last layer.

Say it in an interview: “MAP keeps the peak. The full posterior also gives the mean, credible intervals with the probability reading people want, and a predictive distribution that averages over theta : after 3 heads in 3, the plug-in says the next toss is a head with probability 1, the flat-prior predictive says 0.8. MAP also isn't invariant to reparameterization, because a density picks up a Jacobian; the MLE is. When there's no closed form, the Laplace approximation fits a Gaussian at the MAP with the inverse Hessian as its covariance.”

chunks.h: Hidden data: EM as maximum likelihood
chunks.x: Sometimes part of each data point is never observed: which cluster a point came from, which of two coins was tossed. The likelihood then has to sum over the hidden values z :

chunks.h: Hidden data: EM as maximum likelihood
chunks.x: ell(theta) = sum_i=1^n log sum_z p(x_i, z mid theta)

chunks.h: Hidden data: EM as maximum likelihood
chunks.x: In words: each point's probability is the total over every way the hidden part could have been. The log of a sum doesn't split into simple terms, so there's usually no closed-form MLE.

chunks.h: Hidden data: EM as maximum likelihood
chunks.x: The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm alternates two easy steps. The E-step uses the current theta to compute each point's posterior over z , a soft assignment (the “responsibilities”). The M-step then does ordinary MLE as if those soft assignments had been observed: weighted counts, weighted means, weighted variances. Each round never lowers the likelihood, and the loop converges to a local maximum (strictly, a stationary point of the likelihood), so the starting point matters and restarts help. Adding a log-prior to the M-step turns the same loop into a MAP search, which also stops a m

chunks.h: Hidden data: EM as maximum likelihood
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “EM is maximum likelihood when some variables are hidden. The E-step fills them in with their posterior under the current parameters, the M-step does weighted MLE as if they were observed, and the likelihood never decreases, but it only finds a local optimum.”

Add a prior and the penalty follows: Gaussian gives L2 and weight decay, Laplace gives L1. Smoothing tricks like add-one counts and smoothed target encoding are posterior means with Dirichlet or Beta priors. Label smoothing is the odd one out: it regularizes the outputs, not the weights.”
Python-flavoured and short enough to write from memory. Each was run as real code on the note's examples; the results are in the → comments.
Numerical MLE by gradient ascent on the log-likelihood

def gaussian_mle(x, lr=0.1, steps=2000): mu, s = 0.0, 0.0 # s = log sigma keeps sigma > 0 n = len(x) for _ in range(steps): var = exp(2 * s) r = x - mu g_mu = sum(r) / var # d loglik / d mu g_s = sum(r**2) / var - n # d loglik / d s mu += lr * g_mu / n # ascent: + gradient s += lr * g_s / n return mu, exp(2 * s) # x = [3, 5, 6, 8, 8] → mu 6.000, var 3.600 (divides by n) # log-likelihood at the optimum: -10.297

Optimizing logsigma rather than sigma keeps the variance positive without constraints, the same trick a network uses when it predicts a variance. Gradient ascent on ell is gradient descent on the NLL.

class BetaBinomial: def __init__(self, a=1.0, b=1.0): # Beta(1,1) = flat self.a, self.b = a, b def update(self, heads, n): self.a += heads self.b += n - heads def mean(self): # = P(next is a head) return self.a / (self.a + self.b) def mode(self): # = MAP, for a, b > 1 return (self.a - 1) / (self.a + self.b - 2) def interval(self, mass=0.95): lo = (1 - mass) / 2 return beta_ppf([lo, 1 - lo], self.a, self.b) # BetaBinomial(2, 2), update(7, 10) → Beta(9, 5): # mean 0.643, mode 0.667, interval [0.386, 0.861] # then update(1, 5) → Beta(10, 9): mean 0.526, # mode 0.529; one toss at a time gives the

def map_logreg(X, y, tau2=None, lr=0.5, steps=1000): n, d = X.shape w, b = zeros(d), 0.0 for _ in range(steps): p = sigmoid(X @ w + b) g_w = X.T @ (p - y) # gradient of the NLL g_b = sum(p - y) if tau2 is not None: g_w += w / tau2 # prior N(0, tau2) w -= lr * g_w / n # bias: flat prior b -= lr * g_b / n return w, b # X = [[-2], [-1], [1], [2]], y = [0, 0, 1, 1]: # tau2=None (MLE): w 3.4, 5.5, 7.8, 10.1 after # 1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5 steps: never converges # tau2=1 (MAP): w 1.007 from 100 steps on # tau2 = 0.1, 1, 10, 100 → w 0.24, 1.01, 2.28, 3.95

The prior term w/tau^2 is the derivative of lVert w rVert^2/(2tau^2) . It's what gives the separable data a finite answer: the NLL keeps falling as w grows, but the penalty eventually rises faster. In scikit-learn terms this is LogisticRegression(C=tau2).
