Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own: the short answer, the mechanism, the why, then the likely follow-up. Questions 4, 5, 10, 11, 16, 22 and 23 are hand drills; do them with a pen.
1What's the difference between probability and likelihood?
The same function p(x mid theta) , read two ways: probability fixes theta and varies the data; likelihood fixes the observed data and varies theta .
Probability: for a fair coin and 10 tosses, P(7 heads) = 0.117 , and the probabilities of all 11 outcomes sum to 1.
Likelihood: having seen 7 heads, L(0.5) = 0.117 , L(0.7) = 0.267 , L(0.3) = 0.009 . It scores how well each theta explains what happened.
Not a distribution over theta : it doesn't integrate to 1 (here 1/11), so only ratios matter: the data favour 0.7 over 0.5 by 2.28 to 1.
Its use: maximize it (MLE), or multiply it by a prior to get a posterior (Bayes).
Follow-up: “so is L(0.7) = 0.267 the probability that theta = 0.7 ?” No; that needs a prior. (01)
2Is the likelihood a probability distribution over the parameters? Can it be bigger than 1?

It doesn't integrate to 1 over theta : for 7 heads in 10, int_0^1 120\,theta^7(1-theta)^3\,dtheta = 1/11 . Each value is the probability of the same data under a different model, not of different theta 's.
It can exceed 1 for continuous data, where it's a product of densities: a Gaussian with sigma = 0.1 has density 3.99 at its centre.
Making it a distribution over theta takes a prior and normalizing by the evidence: with a flat prior, the 7-of-10 likelihood becomes Beta(8, 4) .
3Why do we maximize the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?
Same maximizer, much easier to work with.
Same answer: log is strictly increasing, so the argmax doesn't move.
Sums, not products: i.i.d. data give a product; the log makes it a sum of per-example terms, so derivatives are sums and SGD can use mini-batches.

Numerics: 10,000 tosses at 70% heads have sequence probability around 10^-2653 , which is 0 in float64 (the smallest positive value is about 5 times 10^-324 ). The log-likelihood is −6,108.6, a normal number.
Algebra: Gaussian and Bernoulli densities are exponentials, so their logs are squares and linear terms.
Follow-up: minimizing the negative log-likelihood is how this appears as a loss. (02)
4Hand drill: derive the MLE of a coin's heads probability. What is it for 7 heads in 10?
Log-likelihood (dropping the constant binomnk ): ell(theta) = klogtheta + (n-k)log(1-theta) .
Derivative: k/theta - (n-k)/(1-theta) = 0 , so k(1-theta) = (n-k)theta and theta = k/n .
Check it's a maximum: ell'' = -k/theta^2 - (n-k)/(1-theta)^2 lt 0 everywhere, so ell is concave.
Numbers: the slope (score) is +8 at 0.5, 0 at 0.7, -6.25 at 0.8.

Follow-up: its standard error is sqrt0.7 times 0.3/10 = 0.145 (question 10). The same recipe gives the other classics: Poisson counts 3, 5, 4 → hatlambda = bar x = 4 (SE sqrt4/3 = 1.15 ); exponential waits 2, 1, 3 → rate 1/bar x = 0.5 ; Uniform (0, theta) → hattheta = max x_i = 3 , found at the edge of the allowed region, not by a zero derivative. (02, 02)
5Hand drill: derive the MLE of a Gaussian's mean and variance, and apply it to 3, 5, 6, 8, 8.
hatmu = bar x = 6 and hatsigma^2 = frac1nsum(x_i - bar x)^2 = 3.6 .
Log-likelihood: ell = -frac n2log(2pisigma^2) - frac12sigma^2sum(x_i - mu)^2 .
Mean: partialell/partialmu = sum(x_i - mu)/sigma^2 = 0 gives bar x , whatever sigma is.
Variance: partialell/partialsigma^2 = -n/(2sigma^2) + sum(x_i - bar x)^2/(2sigma^4) = 0 gives the average squared deviation.
Numbers: deviations −3, −1, 0, 2, 2; squares sum to 18; 18/5 = 3.6 . The unbiased version is 18/4 = 4.5 . By invariance hatsigma = sqrt3.6 = 1.90 .
Follow-up: why does it divide by n and is that a problem? Question 6. (02)
6Why is the MLE of the variance biased? Why does dividing by n − 1 fix it?

Because it measures spread around bar x , which was fitted to the same points and so sits closer to them than the true mean does. On average it comes out low by exactly one sigma^2 in the sum of squares.
The identity: sum(x_i - bar x)^2 = sum(x_i - mu)^2 - n(bar x - mu)^2 .
Take expectations: nsigma^2 - n cdot sigma^2/n = (n - 1)sigma^2 , since bar x has variance sigma^2/n . So mathbb E[hatsigma^2_MLE] = fracn-1nsigma^2 , and dividing by n - 1 instead is unbiased.
Numbers: for 3, 5, 6, 8, 8, the squares around 6 sum to 18 but around 5 to 23, and 23 - 18 = 5(6-5)^2 . Simulating samples of 5 from mathcal N(6, 4) : the MLE averages 3.20, the n - 1 version 4.00.
Degrees of freedom: the deviations from bar x sum to 0, so only n - 1 are free.
It fades: the ratio is 0.8 at n = 5 , 0.99 at n = 100 : biased but consistent.

Follow-up: “so is unbiased better?” Not necessarily: error is variance plus bias squared. For n = 5 , sigma^2 = 4 , dividing by 4 (unbiased) has MSE 8.00, by 5 (the MLE) 5.76, by 6 only 5.33. Ridge and lasso are deliberately biased for the same reason. And s = sqrts^2 is biased low anyway (1.88 on average for a true sigma of 2). (02)
7Show that least squares is maximum likelihood. What's the assumption, and what if it's wrong?
Least squares is the MLE when the targets are the model's prediction plus independent Gaussian noise of constant variance.
Model: y_i = w^top x_i + varepsilon_i , varepsilon_i sim mathcal N(0, sigma^2) .
NLL: frac12sigma^2sum(y_i - w^top x_i)^2 + frac n2log(2pisigma^2) . Only the sum of squares depends on w , so the MLE of w minimizes it. The MLE of sigma^2 is RSS/n (unbiased: RSS/(n - p) ).
Other noise, other loss: Laplace noise gives absolute error (the median), Bernoulli gives log loss.

If the noise has heavy tails, least squares still estimates the conditional mean (and is the best linear unbiased estimator if the errors are uncorrelated with constant variance), but outliers drag it and its small-sample intervals become unreliable; with infinite-variance noise, such as Cauchy, even large samples don't save it. A heavier-tailed likelihood (Laplace, Huber, Student-t) is more robust.
Full family: loss functions. (02)
8Logistic regression as MLE: what's the likelihood, why is there no closed form, and is the optimum unique?
Each label is a Bernoulli with p_i = sigma(w^top x_i) ; the NLL is the log loss; it's convex but non-linear in w , so it's solved iteratively.
NLL: -sum[y_ilog p_i + (1 - y_i)log(1 - p_i)] , gradient X^top(p - y) .
No closed form: setting X^top(p - y) = 0 can't be solved for w algebraically because p is a sigmoid of w .

The optimum: the NLL is convex (its Hessian X^top W X with W = diag(p_i(1 - p_i)) is positive semi-definite), so any minimum gradient descent or Newton's method (IRLS) finds is global. It's unique when X has full column rank, and finite only if the classes aren't separable.
When it doesn't: perfectly separable data (question 13).
Follow-up: the same Hessian, inverted, gives the coefficients' standard errors. (02, linear-logistic-regression)
9What are the main properties of the MLE? When do they fail?
Invariant at any n ; and for large n , under regularity conditions, consistent, asymptotically normal with variance 1/I(theta) , and efficient.
Consistent: converges to the true value.
Asymptotically normal: hattheta approx mathcal N(theta, 1/I(theta)) , which gives standard errors and intervals.
Efficient: reaches the Cramér–Rao bound, the lowest variance any unbiased estimator can have.
Invariant: the MLE of g(theta) is g(hattheta) , exactly and at any n ; the odds' MLE for 7 of 10 is 0.7/0.3 = 2.33 .

Failures: small samples (it can be biased, like the variance, or extreme, like hat p = 1 ); the truth on the boundary or a support that depends on theta (Uniform(0, θ)); parameters growing with n ; a misspecified model, where it converges to the KL-closest wrong model and needs robust standard errors.
10Hand drill: what is Fisher information? Use it to get the standard error of a coin's MLE for 7 of 10 and 70 of 100.
The expected curvature of the log-likelihood, I(theta) = -mathbb E[ell''(theta)] ; the MLE's variance is about 1/I . For a coin I = n/[theta(1-theta)] , so SE = sqrthattheta(1-hattheta)/n .
One toss: partial^2/partialtheta^2[xlogtheta + (1-x)log(1-theta)] = -x/theta^2 - (1-x)/(1-theta)^2 . Average with mathbb E[x] = theta : 1/theta + 1/(1-theta) = 1/[theta(1-theta)] . Multiply by n .
70 of 100: I = 476 , SE = 0.046 , interval [0.610, 0.790]. Ten times the data, ten times the information, sqrt10 times smaller SE.
Intuition: a sharp peak means few theta explain the data well. Equivalently, I is the variance of the score.
Same as the A/B formula sqrtp(1-p)/n , there the variance of an average of 0/1 values.
Follow-up: observed information -ell''(hattheta) is what software uses; with many parameters, invert the information matrix. (03)
11Hand drill: how do you compare two models by their likelihoods? Is the running example's coin fair?
Not by raw training likelihood, which always prefers the bigger model. Use a likelihood-ratio test for nested models, or an information criterion that charges for parameters.

Likelihood-ratio test: for nested models, 2(ell_big - ell_small) is approximately chi^2 with one degree of freedom per extra parameter (Wilks' theorem). Fair vs free coin, 7 of 10: ell = -6.931 vs -6.109 , so 2 times 0.823 = 1.65 lt 3.84 and p = 0.20 : fair isn't rejected. With 70 of 100 it's 16.5, p = 0.00005 .

AIC = 2d - 2hatell and BIC = dln n - 2hatell for d parameters; lower is better. 7 of 10: fair scores 13.86 on both, free 14.22 (AIC) and 14.52 (BIC), so both prefer fair. 70 of 100: free wins (AIC 124.2 vs 138.6).

Where they come from: AIC estimates out-of-sample log-likelihood; BIC approximates the log evidence, so it leans the same way as the Bayes factor of 1.29 for the fair coin. BIC's penalty grows with n , so it picks smaller models.
The same 3.84 gives the likelihood-ratio interval: every theta whose log-likelihood is within 1.92 of the peak, [0.39, 0.92] here.
12When does maximum likelihood go wrong? Give concrete examples.
When the data are too few or too clean for the model's flexibility: it trusts the sample completely.
Extreme small samples: 3 heads in 3 gives hat p = 1 , an SE of 0, and infinite log loss on the first tail. Zero word counts veto a class in Naive Bayes.
Separation: logistic weights grow without bound.

Too many parameters: a degree-4 polynomial through 5 points has zero residuals; a mixture component can collapse onto one point with infinite likelihood; covariance estimates are singular when n le d .
Wrong noise model: Gaussian likelihood with outliers.
The fix for the first three: a prior (MAP or a full posterior), or equivalently regularization.
13Your logistic regression's coefficients keep growing and the solver warns it didn't converge. What's happening?
Probably (quasi-)perfect separation: some feature or combination splits the classes, so the likelihood keeps increasing as the weights grow and there is no finite MLE.
Mechanism: on separable data every point can be pushed further to its correct side by scaling w up, which sends each p_i towards its label and the NLL towards 0.
Numbers: on x = -2, -1, 1, 2 , labels 0, 0, 1, 1, the weight is 3.4, 5.5, 7.8, 10.1 after 10^2 to 10^5 steps; the NLL at w = 10 is 0.0001.
Fixes: an L2 prior (with tau^2 = 1 , w settles at 1.007), Firth's correction (MAP with the Jeffreys prior), or removing a leaky feature (a separating feature is often leakage).
Symptoms: huge coefficients and standard errors, predicted probabilities of exactly 0 and 1.
(03, linear-logistic-regression)
14Write Bayes' rule for parameters. What's the evidence, why can MAP ignore it, and when can't you?
p(theta mid D) = p(D mid theta)\,p(theta)/p(D) : posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.
Evidence: p(D) = int p(D mid theta)p(theta)\,dtheta , the probability of the data averaged over the prior. With a flat prior and 7 of 10 it's 1/11, and the posterior is Beta(8, 4) .
MAP ignores it: it doesn't depend on theta , so it can't move the argmax.

You need it to normalize the posterior (for means, intervals, predictions) and to compare models: a fair-coin model gives 7 of 10 probability 0.117, the flat-prior model 0.091, a Bayes factor of 1.29 for the simpler model. The evidence penalizes flexibility automatically.
15MLE vs MAP: what's the difference, and when does it matter?

MLE treats theta as a fixed unknown and maximizes the likelihood. MAP gives theta a prior and maximizes likelihood × prior, which is MLE plus a penalty equal to minus the log-prior. Both return a single point.
With a flat prior they're equal.
It matters with little data: 3 heads in 3 gives an MLE of 1.0; MAP with a Beta(2, 2) prior gives 0.8.
It fades with lots of data: at 700 of 1,000 the Beta(5, 5) MAP is 0.698 against an MLE of 0.700.

When to prefer MAP (or the posterior mean): small counts and new items, such as a new ad's click rate after a handful of impressions, with a Beta prior estimated from past ads (empirical Bayes); and whenever the MLE degenerates (separation, zero counts, more parameters than data).
The risk: a strong, wrong prior biases MAP until the data swamp it, and forever if it gives the truth zero probability.
In ML terms: unregularized training is MLE; L2 or weight decay is MAP with a Gaussian prior; L1 is MAP with a Laplace prior.
Neither is fully Bayesian: both discard the posterior's spread. MAP also moves when you reparameterize, while the MLE doesn't.
16Hand drill: MAP of a coin's bias with a Beta(2, 2) prior, for 7 of 10 and for 3 of 3. And with Beta(5, 5)?
hattheta_MAP = (k + alpha - 1)/(n + alpha + beta - 2) .
Derivation: log-posterior (k + alpha - 1)logtheta + (n - k + beta - 1)log(1-theta) ; set the derivative to zero, exactly as for the MLE.
As a blend: with Beta(5, 5) the data's weight is 10/18 , so 0.556 times 0.7 + 0.444 times 0.5 = 0.611 .
17How does a prior act like pseudo-counts, and what happens to MAP as n grows?

A Beta(alpha, beta) prior adds alpha - 1 imaginary heads and beta - 1 imaginary tails to the MAP ( alpha and beta to the posterior mean). The real data grow while the imaginary ones don't, so MAP → MLE.
In log terms: one log-prior term against n log-likelihood terms.
Same idea elsewhere: smoothed target encoding (the overall mean counts as m rows), add-one smoothing, Bayesian A/B priors “worth 1,000 users”.
Exception: zero prior probability on a region can never be overturned.
18Derive L2 regularization from a Gaussian prior. What is λ in terms of the prior?
A mathcal N(0, tau^2) prior on each weight gives ridge with lambda = sigma^2/tau^2 .
Log-prior: -log p(w) = sum_j w_j^2/(2tau^2) + const .
Negative log-posterior: frac12sigma^2sum(y_i - w^top x_i)^2 + frac12tau^2lVert wrVert^2 + const .
Multiply by 2sigma^2 : sum(y_i - w^top x_i)^2 + (sigma^2/tau^2)lVert wrVert^2 . Tight prior or noisy data → big lambda ; flat prior → OLS.
Numbers: one weight with sum xy = 33 , sum x^2 = 30 , sigma^2 = 1 : tau^2 = 0.1 gives lambda = 10 and hat w = 33/40 = 0.825 instead of 1.1.
Logistic regression: NLL + lVert wrVert^2/(2tau^2) ; scikit-learn's C is exactly tau^2 .
Follow-up: don't penalize the intercept (flat prior), and standardize features so one prior fits all weights. (06)
19Derive L1 from a Laplace prior. Why does it give exact zeros? Is the Bayesian posterior sparse?
A Laplace prior propto exp(-lvert w_jrvert/b) adds lVert wrVert_1/b to the NLL; times 2sigma^2 , that's lasso with lambda = 2sigma^2/b . Only the MAP is sparse.

Why zeros: the prior has a kink at 0, so the L1 penalty adds a slope of lambda however small the weight; if the data's slope at 0 (here -2sum xy = -66 ) is weaker than that, the optimum is exactly 0. The L2 penalty's slope 2lambda w vanishes at 0, so it never gets there.
Numbers: one weight, hat w = (33 - lambda/2)/30 : b = 0.1 ( lambda = 20 ) gives 0.767; b = 0.025 ( lambda = 80 ) gives exactly 0.
Posterior not sparse: with b = 0.025 the posterior mode is 0 but its mean is 0.075, and P(w gt 0) = 0.88 . Sparsity is a property of taking the peak.
Follow-up: elastic net = Gaussian × Laplace prior. Mechanics: linear-logistic-regression. (06)
20Is weight decay the same as L2 regularization?
For plain SGD, yes. For Adam, no: the training paths differ, and AdamW's decoupled decay works better in practice.

SGD: w leftarrow w - eta(nablaNLL + lambda w) = (1 - etalambda)w - etanablaNLL : adding the L2 gradient is the same as shrinking the weights by a constant factor each step. Both are a Gaussian prior, i.e. MAP.

Adam + L2: the loss is still NLL + tfraclambda2lVert w rVert^2 , so its fixed point is the Gaussian-prior MAP. But on the way, the L2 gradient lambda w is divided by Adam's per-weight scale, so weights with a large gradient history are barely regularized.

AdamW: applies the decay to the weights directly, outside the adaptive step, so every weight decays at the same rate. It regularizes more evenly, but its loss has no penalty term, so it isn't exactly any fixed Gaussian prior.
(06, deep-learning-basics)
21What is a conjugate prior? Give examples, and say why it matters.
A prior whose posterior stays in the same family for a given likelihood, so updating is just changing parameters.
Beta–Binomial: Beta(alpha, beta) to Beta(alpha + k, beta + n - k) .
Dirichlet–multinomial: add counts per category. Gamma–Poisson: Gamma(a + sum x_i, b + n) .
Gaussian–Gaussian (known variance): precisions add, the mean is precision-weighted.
Why it matters: closed-form posteriors, means, intervals and predictions; streaming updates (Thompson sampling keeps two numbers per arm); priors readable as pseudo-data.
Limit: most models (logistic regression, neural nets) have none; use MCMC, variational inference or the Laplace approximation.
22Hand drill: prior Beta(2, 2). You see 7 heads in 10, then 1 head in 5 more. What's the posterior, its mean and its mode after each step?
Beta(9, 5) , then Beta(10, 9) .
Check: one update with 8 heads in 15 gives the same Beta(10, 9) ; order doesn't matter.
Next-toss probability is the posterior mean: 0.526.
23Hand drill: a mean has prior N(5, 1). You observe 5 points with mean 6 and known noise variance 4. What's the posterior?
Precision: 1/1 + 5/4 = 2.25 ; variance 1/2.25 = 0.444 , standard deviation 0.667.
Mean: (5 times 1 + 6 times 1.25)/2.25 = 12.5/2.25 = 5.556 , a precision-weighted average.
As pseudo-data: the prior is worth sigma^2/tau_0^2 = 4 points at 5: (4 times 5 + 5 times 6)/9 = 5.556 .
Compare: the MLE is 6 with SE sqrt4/5 = 0.894 ; the posterior is pulled towards 5 and is narrower.
24What does a full posterior give you that a MAP estimate doesn't?
Uncertainty, and predictions that account for it.
Other summaries: the mean and median, which can differ from the mode: Beta(8, 4) has mode 0.700, median 0.676, mean 0.667.
Credible intervals with a direct probability reading.

The posterior predictive: average the prediction over theta . After 3 heads in 3, plugging in the MLE says the next toss is a head with probability 1 (infinite log loss on a tail); the flat-prior predictive says 4/5 = 0.8 . After 7 of 10, two more heads: plug-in 0.49, predictive 0.462.
Invariance: the posterior itself doesn't depend on how you write theta ; its MAP does.
Cost: integrals, which conjugacy, sampling or approximations handle.
25What's the difference between a credible interval and a confidence interval?
A credible interval is a probability statement about theta given the data and prior; a confidence interval is a statement about the procedure's long-run coverage.
Credible, 95%: P(theta in [a, b] mid D) = 0.95 . For 7 of 10 with a flat prior: [0.390, 0.891] equal-tailed, [0.412, 0.907] highest-density.
Confidence, 95%: 95% of intervals built this way contain the true theta ; this one does or doesn't. For 7 of 10: Wald [0.416, 0.984], Wilson [0.397, 0.892], Clopper–Pearson [0.348, 0.933].
In practice: with a flat prior and moderate n they nearly agree (Wilson vs credible here); they differ with small n , near 0 or 1, or with an informative prior.
26Is the MAP estimate invariant to reparameterization? Show with an example.
No. A density picks up a Jacobian factor when you change variables, which moves its peak. The MLE is invariant because the likelihood is a function, not a density.
Example: flat prior on theta , 7 of 10: MAP in theta is 0.7.
In log-odds z : the flat prior becomes p(z) propto theta(1 - theta) , so the posterior is propto theta^8(1-theta)^4 , with its peak at theta = 8/12 = 0.667 .
MLE in z : hat z = log(7/3) = 0.847 , which is theta = 0.7 again.
Posterior median is invariant; the posterior mean isn't.
Follow-up: this is why MAP is best seen as regularized MLE rather than a Bayesian summary. (08)
27What is the Laplace approximation, and where is it used?
Approximating the posterior by a Gaussian centred at the MAP, with covariance equal to the inverse Hessian of the negative log-posterior there.
Why it works: a second-order Taylor expansion of the log-posterior is a parabola, and exp of a parabola is a Gaussian.
Example: Beta(8, 4) : mode 0.7, curvature 47.6, so sd 0.145 against a true 0.131; it even puts 1.9% of its mass above 1. With 70 of 100: 0.0458 vs 0.0453, nearly exact.
Uses: Bayesian logistic regression, approximating the evidence (BIC), last-layer uncertainty in neural networks.
Limits: poor for skewed or multi-modal posteriors and near boundaries.
28What is EM, and why is it needed?
An algorithm for maximum likelihood when some variables are hidden, such as cluster labels.
The problem: ell(theta) = sum_ilogsum_z p(x_i, z mid theta) ; the log of a sum has no closed-form maximizer.
E-step: with the current theta , compute each point's posterior over z (soft assignments).
M-step: ordinary MLE with those weights (weighted counts, means, variances).

Guarantees: the likelihood never decreases; it converges to a local maximum (strictly, a stationary point), so use several starts. A prior in the M-step gives MAP-EM and prevents collapsed components.
k-means is EM for Gaussian mixtures in the limit of hard assignments and equal spherical variances shrinking to 0.
(09, unsupervised-learning)
29Which everyday ML techniques are secretly MLE or MAP?
Most losses are negative log-likelihoods, and most penalties and smoothing tricks are log-priors or posterior means.
MLE: MSE (Gaussian), MAE (Laplace), log loss (Bernoulli), cross-entropy (categorical), language-model training (next-token categorical).
MAP: ridge and weight decay (Gaussian prior), lasso (Laplace), elastic net (both).
Posterior means: add- alpha smoothing in Naive Bayes ( Dirichlet(alpha) prior; as a MAP it's Dirichlet(alpha + 1) ), smoothed target encoding (a prior worth m rows).
Not a weight prior: label smoothing is (1 - varepsilon) × NLL + varepsilon × cross-entropy to uniform, a pull on the outputs.
EM: Gaussian mixtures, k-means.
30Write pseudocode to fit a model by numerical maximum likelihood, and to turn it into MAP logistic regression.
Gradient ascent on the log-likelihood (or descent on the NLL); for MAP, add the log-prior's gradient.
Gaussian MLE: parameters mu and s = logsigma ; gradients sum r/sigma^2 and sum r^2/sigma^2 - n with r = x - mu ; step uphill. On 3, 5, 6, 8, 8 it reaches mu = 6 , sigma^2 = 3.6 .
Logistic MLE: p = sigma(Xw + b) ; gradient of the NLL X^top(p - y) ; step downhill.
MAP: add w/tau^2 to the weight gradient (Gaussian prior), not to the bias. On separable data this turns a diverging weight into 1.007 for tau^2 = 1 .
Details: optimize logsigma so the variance stays positive; average gradients over n ; stop when the gradient is near 0.
beginaligned L(theta) &= p(observed data mid theta) \\ ell(theta) &= log L(theta) = sum_i log p(x_i mid theta) endaligned
Same formula as a probability, read with the data fixed. Doesn't integrate to 1 over theta (7 of 10: 1/11); only ratios matter. 7 of 10: L(0.5) = 0.117 , L(0.7) = 0.267 .
beginaligned hattheta_coin &= k/n \\ hatlambda_Poisson &= bar x \\ hatmu &= bar x \\ hatsigma^2_MLE &= tfrac1ntextstylesum(x_i - bar x)^2 \\ mathbb E[hatsigma^2_MLE] &= tfracn-1n\,sigma^2 endaligned

3, 5, 6, 8, 8: mean 6, MLE variance 3.6, unbiased 4.5. Exponential rate 1/bar x ; Uniform (0, theta) : max x_i . Gaussian noise → MSE; Laplace → MAE; Bernoulli → log loss; categorical → cross-entropy. Logistic: gradient X^top(p - y) , convex, no closed form.

beginaligned I(theta) &= -mathbb E[ell''(theta)] = Var(ell'(theta)) \\ Var(hattheta) &approx 1/I(theta) \\ I_coin &= fracntheta(1 - theta) \\ SE_coin &= sqrthattheta(1 - hattheta)/n \\ AIC &= 2d - 2hatell \\ BIC &= dln n - 2hatell endaligned

7 of 10: SE 0.145, Wald [0.416, 0.984]; 70 of 100: SE 0.046. LR interval: ell within 1.92 of its peak; LR test: 2(ell_big - ell_small) approx chi^2 (7 of 10 vs fair: 1.65, p = 0.20 ). Delta method: SE(g(hattheta)) approx lvert g'(hattheta)rvert\,SE(hattheta) . MLE: invariant at any n ; consistent, asymptotically normal, efficient (Cramér–Rao) for large n . Fails on 3 of 3, separation, too many parameters.

beginaligned p(theta mid D) &= fracp(D mid theta)\,p(theta)p(D) \\ hattheta_MAP &= argmax_theta\,big[log p(D mid theta) + log p(theta)big] \\ hattheta_MAP, coin &= frack + alpha - 1n + alpha + beta - 2 endaligned
Evidence drops out of the argmax; needed for normalizing and model comparison. Beta(2, 2) : 7 of 10 → 0.667, 3 of 3 → 0.8. MAP → MLE as n grows.
beginaligned hat w_mathcal N(0, tau^2) &= argmin_w\ RSS + tfracsigma^2tau^2lVert w rVert_2^2 \\ hat w_Laplace(0, b) &= argmin_w\ RSS + tfrac2sigma^2blVert w rVert_1 endaligned

Tighter prior = bigger lambda . scikit-learn: logistic C = tau^2 ; Ridge alpha = sigma^2/tau^2 ; Lasso alpha = sigma^2/(nb) . Only the MAP of a Laplace prior is sparse. Weight decay = L2 for SGD; under Adam they differ, and AdamW's decoupled decay isn't exactly a prior.
beginaligned theta mid D &sim Beta(alpha + k,\ beta + n - k) \\ tfrac1tau_n^2 &= tfrac1tau_0^2 + tfracnsigma^2 \\ mu_n &= tau_n^2Big(tfracmu_0tau_0^2 + tfracnbar xsigma^2Big) endaligned
Beta(2, 2) + 7 of 10 = Beta(9, 5) , mean 0.643. Dirichlet–multinomial adds counts; Gamma–Poisson: Gamma(a + sum x, b + n) .
beginaligned P(head mid D) &= mathbb E[theta mid D] = frack + alphan + alpha + beta \\ p(theta mid D) &approx mathcal Nbig(hattheta_MAP,\ H^-1big) endaligned

3 of 3, flat prior: predictive 0.8, not 1. Beta(8, 4) : mode 0.700, median 0.676, mean 0.667. MAP isn't invariant to reparameterization (7 of 10 in log-odds: 0.667); MLE is. EM = MLE with hidden variables, local optima.

chunks.x: Voice agents: speech recognition, synthesis and the real-time stack · Deepam Minda

A voice agent is a real-time loop: take audio in, decide when the caller has finished, understand, reply, speak, and keep listening in case they interrupt. Most production agents are a cascade (speech recognition → LLM → speech synthesis) that streams at every stage. Speech-to-speech models do it all in one network over audio tokens: faster and more natural, but harder to control, debug and use with tools.

Speech recognition (ASR) is an alignment problem: about 100 feature frames a second have to become two or three words a second, and nobody labelled which frame belongs to which word. CTC adds a blank symbol and sums over every alignment. A transducer (RNN-T) adds a small language model and streams naturally. An attention encoder–decoder such as Whisper is very accurate but works on 30-second windows, so it doesn't stream as built.

Word error rate is (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference words. Normalise both texts before scoring. WER can exceed 100%, and it weights every word the same, so a 5% WER can still get the phone number wrong. Track entity accuracy alongside it.

Turn-taking is the hardest part of the experience. Every millisecond of the silence threshold is added to every reply, but a short one cuts people off mid-number. Semantic turn detectors shorten the wait when a turn is clearly complete. Barge-in needs echo cancellation, an instant flush of queued audio, and trimming the LLM's history to what the caller actually heard.

Speech synthesis (TTS): text normalisation → phonemes → mel spectrogram → waveform, or one end-to-end model, or a language model over codec tokens. Stream it phrase by phrase. Score it with MOS (whose confidence intervals are wider than they look), re-transcription WER, speaker similarity and time to first audio.

A common goal is roughly 1 second from the caller's last word to the agent's first (a rule of thumb). The end-of-turn wait and the LLM's time to first token dominate. Stream everything, start the LLM early, co-locate services, and fill unavoidable silence. Test with simulated callers and recorded-call regressions. Cost per minute is telephony + ASR + TTS + LLM, and the LLM part grows with call length.

Before any model, the agent has a stream of numbers. How those numbers were produced (how often the sound was measured, how precisely, and over what band of frequencies) decides what a recogniser can possibly hear. Phone audio is much poorer than what most open models were trained on, and many voice-agent bugs start here.

The running example. A caller rings an order-support line from a mobile phone and says “cancel order four seven two nine”. The audio reaches the agent as an 8 kHz telephone stream. The note follows this call through recognition, scoring, turn-taking, the reply, its latency and its cost.

A microphone turns air pressure into a voltage, and an analogue-to-digital converter measures it f_s times a second: the sampling rate. A sampled signal can only represent frequencies up to half the sampling rate, the Nyquist frequency f_s/2 . Anything above it must be filtered out before sampling, or it folds back as false low frequencies (aliasing).
4 kHz (phone band is about 300–3,400 Hz)
The phone network (PSTN), most telephony APIs
“Wideband” speech; the input rate of most ASR models (Whisper expects 16 kHz)
Common TTS output rate and neural audio codecs
Music, studio recordings, WebRTC's Opus codec at full band

Vowels carry most of their energy below 4 kHz, which is why phone calls are intelligible at all. But fricatives such as “s”, “f” and “sh” live largely above 4 kHz, so on a phone line “six” and “fix”, or “sun” and “fun”, lose much of what tells them apart. That loss is permanent: resampling 8 kHz audio up to 16 kHz adds samples but cannot create the missing 4–8 kHz band.
Bit depth is how precisely each sample is stored. 16-bit linear PCM has 65,536 levels and about 96 dB of dynamic range (6 dB per bit). Bitrates follow directly:
beginaligned bitrate &= f_s times bits per sample times channels \\ 16,000 times 16 times 1 &= 256 kbit/s = 32 kB/s \\ 8,000 times 8 times 1 &= 64 kbit/s endaligned
In words: one minute of 16 kHz, 16-bit mono audio is 1.92 MB. The phone network carries 8 kHz audio at only 8 bits per sample, 64 kbit/s, and gets away with it by spacing the 256 levels unevenly.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: With 8 evenly spaced bits, a quiet sound (a soft consonant, a distant speaker) would use only a handful of levels and be buried in rounding noise, while loud vowels would waste precision. Hearing is roughly logarithmic, so the phone network (the G.711 standard) compresses each sample logarithmically before rounding it to 8 bits, and expands it again at the other end. This is called companding. The μ-law version, with mu = 255 and x scaled to [−1, 1], is:

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: F(x) = sgn(x)\,fracln(1 + mu lvert x rvert)ln(1 + mu)

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: In words: small amplitudes are stretched and large ones squeezed, so every loudness level gets about the same relative precision.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: Sample, as a share of full scale

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: Level out of 127 (linear 8-bit)

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: A sample at 1% of full scale gets 29 of the 127 positive levels under μ-law and about one level under linear 8-bit coding. Near that amplitude, one μ-law step is about 6% of the value; a linear 8-bit step would be 79% of it. Near half scale the μ-law step is about 4.5%, so the relative error stays roughly constant across loudness, which is what the ear cares about.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: Who uses which: μ-law in North America and Japan, A-law ( A = 87.6 , the same idea) in Europe and most other regions. Many cloud telephony APIs hand you 8 kHz μ-law regardless; Twilio's Media Streams, for example, send base64-encoded 8 kHz μ-law over a WebSocket. Others send 8 kHz 16-bit linear PCM, so always check the format; decoding with the wrong one produces noise, not an error.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: In the real codec the curve is approximated by eight straight segments per sign, which gives 8 bits roughly the useful range of 13–14 linear bits.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: Packets: phone audio usually travels in 20 ms packets: 160 samples, which at one byte per μ-law sample is 160 bytes.

chunks.h: μ-law and A-law: 8 bits that sound like more
chunks.x: In the pipeline: decode μ-law to linear PCM, resample to the ASR model's rate (with a proper filter), and on the way out downsample the TTS audio to 8 kHz and encode it back to μ-law.

Speech changes constantly, but over about 20–30 ms the shape of the mouth and throat barely moves, so a short slice of audio has a stable frequency content. Speech features are therefore computed on short overlapping windows that slide along by a hop (or stride). The standard choice is a 25 ms window with a 10 ms hop. At 16 kHz:
beginaligned W &= 0.025 times 16,000 = 400 samples \\ H &= 0.010 times 16,000 = 160 samples \\ frames &= 1 + Biglfloor fracN - WH Bigrfloor endaligned

In words: frames come every hop, so there are 100 a second. For one second of audio ( N = 16,000 ) the formula gives 98 frames; libraries that pad half a window at each end (“centred” frames) give 1 + N/H = 101 . Whisper's 30-second window has 480,000 samples and, after it drops the last padded frame, 3,000 frames.

Each window is multiplied by a taper (usually a Hann window, which fades the edges to zero so the cut-off ends don't smear energy across frequencies), and a fast Fourier transform turns it into frequencies. With an FFT of size 400, there are 400/2 + 1 = 201 frequency bins spaced 16,000/400 = 40 Hz apart. Squaring the magnitudes gives the power at each frequency, and stacking frames side by side gives the spectrogram: time on one axis, frequency on the other.
201 linearly spaced bins are not how hearing works, and they carry detail ASR doesn't need. Two changes fix that.

The mel scale. Perceived pitch is roughly linear in frequency below about 1 kHz and roughly logarithmic above it: 100 Hz to 200 Hz sounds like a big step, 7,000 Hz to 7,100 Hz like nothing. One common formula is m = 2595 log_10(1 + f/700) : 1,000 Hz is 1,000 mel, 4,000 Hz is 2,146 mel, and 8,000 Hz is only 2,840 mel. The spectrogram is pooled through about 80 triangular filters spaced evenly in mel, so they are narrow at low frequencies (about 45–100 Hz wide below 1 kHz) and wide at high ones (500–600 Hz, 13–15 FFT bins, at the top).

The log. Loudness is perceived roughly logarithmically, and quiet consonants are thousands of times weaker than vowels; the log compresses that range so both matter. It also turns multiplicative effects such as a microphone's or phone line's frequency response into additive offsets, which per-utterance mean normalisation can subtract.

What this keeps is the spectral envelope, the broad peaks (formants) that mark which vowel or consonant is being said; what it blurs is the fine comb of pitch harmonics, which mostly says who is speaking and with what intonation. The result for a 30-second Whisper window is a matrix of 80 mel bands × 3,000 frames (128 bands in Whisper large-v3): 240,000 numbers instead of 480,000 samples, and far more learnable ones.
MFCCs are a further step: a cosine transform of the log-mel bands that decorrelates them, which suited older Gaussian-mixture models. Neural models take log-mel directly.
Raw waveform models such as wav2vec 2.0 learn their own front end with convolutions over the samples (one vector per 20 ms), and are then fine-tuned for ASR.

chunks.h: Phone audio into a 16 kHz model
chunks.x: Spread 80 mel filters over 0–8 kHz and 18 or 19 of them sit above 4 kHz, depending on the mel formula. Feed upsampled phone audio to a model trained on 16 kHz recordings and almost a quarter of its input features are empty: the model is seeing a kind of input it rarely saw in training. Add μ-law coding noise, packet loss, cheap handsets and speakerphones, and WER on calls is typically much worse than on clean benchmarks.

chunks.h: Phone audio into a 16 kHz model
chunks.x: Train on what you'll serve: fine-tune on real call audio (how, in section 03), or on wideband data passed through the same path (downsample to 8 kHz, μ-law encode and decode, upsample).

chunks.h: Phone audio into a 16 kHz model
chunks.x: Or use a telephony model that takes 8 kHz input directly (25 ms windows are 200 samples, 10 ms hops 80 samples).

chunks.h: Phone audio into a 16 kHz model
chunks.x: Evaluate on your channel: a model's LibriSpeech WER says little about 8 kHz Hinglish calls from moving vehicles.

chunks.h: Phone audio into a 16 kHz model
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Phone audio is 8 kHz, 8-bit μ-law or A-law: 64 kbit/s, nothing above 4 kHz. ASR models usually want 16 kHz log-mel features, 25 ms windows every 10 ms, so 100 frames a second and 80 mel bands. Mel spacing matches how pitch is heard, and the log compresses loudness and turns channel effects into offsets. Upsampling phone audio doesn't bring back the high band, so I'd fine-tune or evaluate on real 8 kHz audio.”

There are two ways to turn a caller's audio into a spoken reply. The cascade puts text in the middle and uses three specialised models. Speech-to-speech models keep everything as audio tokens inside one network. The choice shapes latency, control, cost and how you debug.

The cascade passes text between three specialised models, with an orchestrator around them deciding turns and handling interruptions. A speech-to-speech model replaces the middle with one network over discrete audio tokens.

Audio arrives over the phone network or WebRTC. A voice activity detector (VAD) and a turn detector decide when the caller has finished (sections 05 and 06). A streaming ASR model has been transcribing all along and emits its final transcript. The LLM, with the conversation history and tools, generates a reply token by token; the orchestrator cuts the reply into phrases and sends each to a streaming TTS model as soon as it is complete, and audio chunks go back to the caller as they're synthesised. Nothing waits for a whole output, which is how the cascade gets close to one second.

What text in the middle buys: every turn is logged and inspectable; you can apply guardrails, redact, rewrite numbers for speech, and use any LLM with mature tool calling; each part can be measured on its own (WER, time to first token, time to first audio) and swapped for a better vendor or a language-specific model.

What it loses: everything that isn't words. Tone, hesitation, emphasis, anger, laughter and who is speaking are discarded by ASR, and the TTS has to guess the right tone from text alone. Latencies add up across stages, and ASR errors flow straight into the LLM, which sees “cancel the order for seven nine”.

A speech-to-speech model takes audio in and produces audio out with one network. The trick that makes this a language-modelling problem is the neural audio codec, which turns a waveform into a short sequence of discrete tokens and back.
Encode: a convolutional encoder turns the waveform into one vector per frame (for example every 80 ms).

Quantise in layers (residual vector quantisation, RVQ): replace the vector by the nearest entry of codebook 1; quantise what's left over (the residual) with codebook 2; and so on for Q codebooks. Each frame becomes Q integers: the first codebook captures the coarse content, later ones add detail.

Model: a transformer predicts the next audio tokens (and usually text tokens) given everything so far, exactly like a text LLM predicts words. With Q tokens per frame, the tokens are either flattened into one sequence ( Q times longer), interleaved with a delay pattern, or, as in Moshi, split between two transformers: a large one that takes one step per 80 ms frame and a small “depth” transformer that predicts that frame's 8 codebook tokens one after another.
Decode: the codec decoder turns the predicted tokens back into a waveform.
Token arithmetic. Mimi, the codec behind the Moshi model, encodes 24 kHz audio at 12.5 frames a second with 8 codebooks of 2,048 entries (11 bits each):
beginaligned tokens per second &= 12.5 times 8 = 100 \\ bitrate &= 12.5 times 8 times 11 = 1,100 bit/s endaligned

In words: about 1.1 kbit/s, roughly 350 times smaller than raw 24 kHz 16-bit audio (384 kbit/s). EnCodec at 6 kbit/s uses 75 frames a second × 8 codebooks, so 600 tokens a second. Compare text: at about 150 words a minute and roughly 1.3 tokens per word, the same speech is only about 3 text tokens a second. Audio is some 30 times more tokens than its transcript (how many positions the main transformer actually steps through depends on the design above: 12.5 a second in Moshi), which is why speech LLMs need low frame-rate codecs, and why their context fills and their cost per minute rises quick

Full duplex. Moshi models two audio streams at once, the user's and its own, plus a stream of text tokens aligned with its own speech (an “inner monologue” that improves what it says). At every 80 ms step it predicts its next tokens while still taking in the user's, so it can speak and listen at the same time, backchannel (“mm-hmm”) and be interrupted without a separate turn-taking module. Its authors report 160 ms theoretical and about 200 ms practical latency.

In between. Hosted realtime speech APIs from the major LLM providers expose speech-to-speech models with tool calling. A “half-cascade” takes audio into a speech-aware LLM but produces text, then uses a separate TTS: it hears tone and hesitation but keeps text-level control of the output.

When to choose which. Task-oriented agents for support, sales or healthcare, where entities must be exact, tools drive the outcome, transcripts must be audited, and Indian languages and code-switching matter, are mostly cascades today. Open-ended conversation, companionship and language practice, where naturalness and latency dominate, suit speech-to-speech. Many teams prototype on a realtime API and move hot paths to a cascade when they need control, or the reverse when naturalness is the bottleneck.

“Speech-to-speech is strictly better because it's lower latency.” Latency is one axis. The questions that decide production systems are usually whether the order number was captured exactly, whether the right tool was called once, whether the call can be audited, and whether the model handles the callers' languages. Say which of these your use case cares about before picking.

Say it in an interview: “A cascade is streaming ASR, an LLM and streaming TTS with an orchestrator for turn-taking and barge-in. Text in the middle gives control, tools, logs and per-stage metrics, at the cost of latency and lost tone. Speech-to-speech models run one transformer over codec tokens, about 100 audio tokens a second for a codec like Mimi, so they're faster and more natural but harder to steer and debug. For a support agent that must capture order numbers and call tools, I'd start with a cascade.”

Automatic speech recognition (ASR, also called speech-to-text or STT) maps a sequence of audio features to a sequence of text tokens. This section builds the three model families from the one problem they all solve, then covers what a voice agent needs around them: streaming, vocabulary biasing, number formatting, code-switching and diarization.

Say “cancel order four seven two nine” takes 2 seconds. That is 200 feature frames (50 after the encoder's first layers merge every 4 frames into one, the usual 4× subsampling; see Conformer below) for 6 words or 32 characters. Training data is audio plus its transcript, with no timestamps: nobody marked which frames are the “f” of “four”. People also speak at different speeds, stretch vowels and pause. So the model has to learn the alignment at the same time as the labels.

The old way: hidden Markov models with Gaussian mixtures, a pronunciation dictionary, a separately trained language model, and frame-level labels bootstrapped by forced alignment (lining up a known transcript with the audio to get each sound's timing). Many parts, each trained separately.

End-to-end models learn the alignment implicitly and output characters or subword tokens directly. There are three ways to do it: CTC, transducers and attention encoder–decoders. Most modern systems use the same kind of encoder (a Conformer or transformer over log-mel frames) and differ in the output layer and loss.

Output units: characters (small vocabulary, long outputs), or subword tokens from BPE or SentencePiece, typically a few hundred to a few thousand for CTC and transducer models and about 50,000 byte-level BPE tokens for Whisper.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Connectionist temporal classification (Graves et al., 2006) keeps the model simple: the encoder emits, for every frame, a probability over the vocabulary plus one extra symbol, the blank (written _ here), meaning “nothing new at this frame”. A sequence of one symbol per frame is an alignment (or path). To read text off a path, apply the collapse rule: first merge consecutive repeats, then delete blanks.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Path (one symbol per frame)

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: The second row shows why the blank exists: without a blank between them, the two l's merge into one. A double letter needs a blank in between. Blanks also let the model say nothing during silence and between sounds, so most frames end up as blank: CTC outputs are “peaky”, a short spike per token in a sea of blanks.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: The probability of a transcript is the sum over every path that collapses to it, and each path's probability is the product of its per-frame probabilities:

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: beginaligned P(y mid x) &= sum_a \,in\, mathcalB^-1(y) \ prod_t=1^T p_t(a_t mid x) \\ mathcalL_CTC &= -ln P(y mid x) endaligned

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: In words: mathcalB is the collapse rule, so mathcalB^-1(y) is every path that reads as y . Training raises the total probability of all of them, without ever choosing one; the model is free to put the spikes wherever it likes.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Worked by hand. Three frames, a vocabulary of just “a” and blank, and per-frame probabilities of “a” of 0.6, 0.7 and 0.2. All eight paths:

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Six paths read as “a”, so P(a) = 0.868 and the loss is -ln 0.868 = 0.142 . The only way to get “aa” is a _ a, with the blank between. The three labellings' probabilities sum to 1.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: The forward algorithm. Enumerating paths explodes: for 100 frames and a 10-token transcript with no repeated neighbours there are binom11020 approx 4.4 times 10^21 alignments. Paths share prefixes, though, so dynamic programming works. Write the target, a transcript of L tokens, with blanks around and between its tokens, z = (\_, y_1, \_, y_2, dots, \_) , which has 2L + 1 states, and let alpha_t(s) be the total probability of all path prefixes that are at state s after frame t :

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: alpha_t(s) = Big(alpha_t-1(s) + alpha_t-1(s-1) + mathbb1[skip allowed]\ alpha_t-1(s-2)Big)\ p_t(z_s)

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: In words: you reach state s by staying (a repeat), by stepping from the previous state, or by jumping over a blank, which is allowed only when z_s is a real token different from z_s-2 (jumping between two identical tokens would merge them). P(y mid x) is the sum of the last two states at the last frame: ending on the final token or the final blank. For the example, with states (_, a, _):

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: 0.164 + 0.704 = 0.868 , the same as the enumeration, in O(T cdot L) work instead of exponential. A backward pass gives the gradients; in practice you call a library's CTC loss. Real implementations work in log space (log-sum-exp), because products of hundreds of probabilities underflow.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Decoding. Greedy decoding takes the most likely symbol at each frame and collapses: here a, a, _ → “a”. Prefix beam search keeps the best few partial transcripts, merging paths that collapse to the same prefix, and is where an external language model and hotword boosts plug in (below).

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: The best path is not the best transcript. Two frames, each with P(a) = 0.4 : greedy decoding picks blank twice and outputs nothing (path probability 0.36), but “a” is reached by three paths (a_, _a, aa) totalling 0.64. Greedy is usually close enough because CTC outputs are so peaky, but prefix beam search, which adds up all the paths that share a prefix, is what searches (approximately) for the transcript with the highest P(y mid x) .

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: CTC's key assumption: conditional independence. Each frame's output depends on the audio but not on the other outputs. The model can't learn “after ‘order’, ‘four’ is more likely than ‘for’” inside the output layer; whatever context it uses must come through the encoder's view of the audio. So CTC models benefit a lot from an external language model, and their mistakes look like spelling (“four” → “for”). The other properties follow from the design:

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Monotonic and length-limited: the output length, plus one blank for each pair of repeated neighbours, can't exceed the number of frames (fine at 25 frames a second after subsampling).

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Fast: one parallel pass and a collapse, no autoregressive loop, so very cheap at inference.

chunks.h: CTC: a blank symbol and a sum over alignments
chunks.x: Streams naturally if the encoder only looks at past and current audio: each frame's output can be read as soon as it's computed.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The RNN-Transducer (RNN-T, Graves 2012) removes the independence assumption while keeping streaming. It has three parts:

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The encoder turns audio frames into vectors e_t , as before.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The prediction network reads the tokens emitted so far (not the audio) and produces a state g_u . It is effectively a small language model over the output.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The joint network combines one encoder frame and one prediction state into a distribution over the vocabulary plus blank.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: beginaligned h_t,u &= tanhbig(W_e\, e_t + W_g\, g_ubig) \\ P(k mid t, u) &= softmaxbig(W_o\, h_t,ubig)_k endaligned

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: In words: at frame t , having emitted u tokens, the model either emits a token k (then u advances, the prediction network updates, and it may emit again from the same frame) or emits blank, which means “move to the next frame”. Unlike CTC, several tokens can come out of one frame, and each choice depends on what was already emitted.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: Training sums over every path through a T times (U+1) lattice of (frame, tokens emitted so far) positions, again by dynamic programming (below).

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: Why it's the streaming default: decoding moves left to right, frame by frame, and emits tokens as soon as the encoder has seen enough audio. With a streaming encoder (below), this is the standard design for on-device and real-time production ASR.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The cost is training memory. The joint network's output is a 4-D tensor, batch × T × (U+1) × (vocabulary + 1). For 10 s of audio at 40 ms frames ( T = 250 ), a 60-token transcript and a 1,024-token vocabulary, that's 250 times 61 times 1,025 approx 15.6 million logits, 62.5 MB in 32-bit floats for one utterance and 2 GB for a batch of 32. Pruned and fused transducer losses exist to avoid materialising all of it.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: Variants: the token-and-duration transducer (TDT) also predicts how many frames to skip after each emission, which speeds up decoding.

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: The forward recursion. Let alpha(t, u) be the probability of having emitted the first u tokens of the transcript by frame t . Write varnothing(t, u) for the joint network's blank probability at (t, u) , and y(t, u) for its probability of the next correct token y_u+1 :

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: beginaligned alpha(t, u) &= alpha(t-1, u)\,varnothing(t-1, u) + alpha(t, u-1)\,y(t, u-1) \\ P(y mid x) &= alpha(T, U)\,varnothing(T, U) endaligned

chunks.h: RNN-Transducer: adding a language model inside
chunks.x: In words: you reach (t, u) either by a blank at the previous frame (move to the next frame) or by emitting token u without moving frame, starting from alpha(1, 0) = 1 ; every path ends with a final blank. With 3 frames and a one-token transcript there are 3 paths: emit the token at frame 1, 2 or 3, with blanks everywhere else.

The third family treats ASR like translation: a transformer encoder reads all the audio frames, and an autoregressive decoder generates the transcript one token at a time, attending to the encoder output through cross-attention (the mechanism is in the transformers note). The decoder is a full language model conditioned on the audio, so these models are usually the most accurate and handle punctuation, casing and written-form numbers naturally. Whisper is the best-known example.
Input: 16 kHz audio cut into 30-second windows, as log-mel features (80 bands, 128 in large-v3) with 25 ms windows and a 10 ms hop: 80 × 3,000 per window.
Encoder: two 1-D convolutions (kernel 3, GELU), the second with stride 2, so 3,000 frames become 1,500 positions of 20 ms each; sinusoidal positions; then transformer blocks.
Decoder: a transformer with learned positions that writes byte-level BPE tokens.

Multitask through special tokens: the decoder's prompt says what to do, for example <|startoftranscript|> <|hi|> <|transcribe|> <|notimestamps|>: language (or let the model predict it), transcribe or translate into English, with or without timestamp tokens. Previous text can be put before it as a prompt, which carries context and spellings across windows.

Training: 680,000 hours of weakly supervised audio with internet transcripts in the original release (later versions used more), which is why it is robust to accents and noise, and also why it sometimes writes text that is not in the audio.
Sizes: from tiny (39M parameters) to large (1,550M); “turbo” (809M) is large-v3 with the decoder cut from 32 layers to 4, much faster with a small accuracy loss.
Why vanilla Whisper doesn't stream.
Fixed 30-second input. A 2-second utterance is padded to 30 seconds, and the encoder does the full 30 seconds of work.
Whole-window attention. The encoder attends in both directions over the window and the decoder starts only after the encoder is done, so nothing can be emitted until the audio has ended.
Unstable on partial audio. It was trained on complete segments; transcribe a growing buffer every half second and the last words keep changing.
Hallucination on silence and noise. Given no speech, it can repeat phrases or produce subtitle-style text, so it must be gated by a VAD.

Workarounds exist: re-transcribe a growing buffer and commit only the prefix that two consecutive runs agree on (the LocalAgreement policy of the whisper_streaming project), or cut utterances with a VAD and transcribe each one after the caller stops. Both cost latency: the first repeats work and commits words late, the second adds the whole transcription time after the end of every turn. That's why live agents usually run streaming CTC or transducer models, and use Whisper-style models for offline transcription, analytics and labelling.

Most current ASR encoders are Conformers (Gulati et al., 2020): transformer blocks with a convolution module added, because speech needs both kinds of context. Self-attention captures long-range context (the sentence, the topic); convolution captures local patterns over tens of milliseconds (the transitions between sounds).

Each block runs, in order: a half-step feed-forward layer; multi-head self-attention with relative positions; a convolution module (pointwise convolution with a gated linear unit, a depthwise convolution, batch norm, Swish, another pointwise convolution); a second half-step feed-forward layer; and a final layer norm. The two half-step feed-forward layers sandwiching the middle are called the “macaron” layout.

A convolutional front end first subsamples the 10 ms frames by 4× (40 ms per position); FastConformer variants subsample 8× (80 ms), which cuts the quadratic attention cost by about 4×. The paper reported 2.1% / 4.3% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean / test-other without a language model. The same encoder can feed a CTC head, a transducer, an attention decoder, or a CTC and an attention head trained together.

Transcribed speech is expensive, and for most Indian languages there is little of it, while untranscribed audio is plentiful. Self-supervised models pretrain the encoder on raw audio alone, the way BERT pretrains on unlabelled text, and are then fine-tuned for ASR with a CTC head on a small labelled set.

wav2vec 2.0 (Baevski et al., 2020): a convolutional encoder turns the waveform into a latent vector every 20 ms, and spans of these are masked before a transformer builds context over them. At each masked position the model must pick the true latent (in a quantised form learned at the same time) out of distractors taken from other positions: a contrastive loss. Its authors report 4.8% / 8.2% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean / test-other after pretraining on 53,000 hours of unlabelled audio and fine-tuning on just ten minutes of labels (1.8% / 3.3% with all 960 labelled hours).

HuBERT (Hsu et al., 2021): cluster frames offline with k-means (on MFCCs at first) so every frame gets a pseudo-label, then train BERT-style to predict the cluster IDs of masked frames; re-cluster on the model's own features and train again. It works because the clusters are consistent, even though they aren't phonemes.

Why it matters for agents: multilingual versions pretrained on many languages are the usual starting point for low-resource and Indic ASR, and the same encoders give features for speaker verification, emotion and turn detection.

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: A streaming recogniser sends two kinds of result while the caller speaks:

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: Partial (interim) hypotheses every 100–300 ms or so. They change as more audio arrives: “can sell” becomes “cancel order” once the next word gives context. Useful for live captions, for starting the LLM early, and for spotting the caller starting to speak over the agent.

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: Final hypotheses, committed when the recogniser decides a segment is over (often on its own silence detection). They won't change. Tool arguments and the LLM's real input should come from finals.

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: How the encoder streams. Full self-attention needs the future, so streaming encoders use chunked attention: audio is processed in chunks, and each frame attends to its own chunk plus a cache of past chunks, and possibly a small right-context lookahead. The chunk size sets a floor on latency, because a word spoken at a random point in a chunk waits for the chunk to close:

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: Average wait for the chunk to close

chunks.h: Streaming ASR: partials, finals and chunks
chunks.x: Add any lookahead and the compute time on top. Smaller chunks mean less future context and usually a higher WER, so streaming models are typically somewhat less accurate than the same model run on whole utterances. Models trained with randomly varied chunk sizes can run at several latency settings.
Voice agents live or die on words the recogniser rarely saw in training: customers' names, product and plan names, medicine names, Indian place names, order IDs. Two tools help.
Shallow fusion with a language model. During beam search, add a text language model's opinion to the acoustic score:
score(y) = log P_ASR(y mid x) + lambda log P_LM(y) + beta lvert y rvert

In words: lambda sets how much to trust the language model, and the length bonus beta per token stops it from favouring short outputs (every extra token lowers log P_LM ). Both are tuned on a development set. A small n-gram model (see the n-gram language model section) trained on your own call transcripts is the classic choice for CTC beam search.

Contextual biasing (hotwords, keyword boosting, custom vocabulary). Give the recogniser a list of phrases to favour, and during beam search add a bonus to any hypothesis that is partway through one of them (the list is stored as a prefix tree, so partial matches can be tracked; the bonus is taken back if the phrase isn't completed). Hosted APIs expose this as keywords, phrase hints or custom vocabulary with boost weights; with Whisper, you put the terms in the prompt.
Make it per call: the caller's name and their open order IDs from the CRM are the most valuable list you have.

Don't over-boost: too much bonus makes the recogniser hear the boosted words everywhere (false insertions). Measure both recall of the boosted terms and WER on everything else, on test sets with and without the terms.
After recognition: match entities against the database with fuzzy or phonetic matching (an order ID one digit off, a name spelled differently), and confirm with the caller.
When hints aren't enough: fine-tune on in-domain audio.

Many recognisers, especially CTC and transducer models trained on normalised text, output the spoken form: “cancel order four seven two nine and refund twenty five hundred rupees”. Downstream code needs the written form: order 4729, ₹2,500. Converting is inverse text normalisation (ITN), done with hand-written grammars compiled to weighted finite-state transducers, or with a neural or LLM rewriter.
Categories: cardinals, ordinals, money, dates, times, phone numbers, emails (“ravi at gmail dot com”), units.

Ambiguity needs context: “one oh one” could be the number 101 or the code 1-0-1; “four seven two nine” is an identifier, written 4729 with no thousands separator, while “four thousand seven hundred twenty nine” is the quantity 4,729.
Indian numbers: lakh and crore grouping (“do lakh” = 2,00,000), and Hindi fractions such as “dhai sau” (250) or “saade teen” (3.5).
Where it matters: tool arguments (send 4729 to the order API), WER scoring (both sides must use the same form, section 04), and display. LLMs read either form fine.
Its mirror image, text normalisation for TTS, is in section 07.

Code-switching is changing language mid-conversation or mid-sentence, as in Hinglish: “mera order cancel karna hai, number hai four seven two nine”. It is the norm in many Indian support calls, and it breaks several assumptions:
One language per utterance: language ID at the start of a segment, or a language chosen up front, can't follow a sentence that switches twice.

Script: the same speech can be written with Hindi words in Devanagari and English in Latin, all romanised, or with English words transliterated into Devanagari (ऑर्डर for “order”). If references and model outputs use different conventions, WER counts script choices as errors.
Numbers in either language: “chaar saat do nau” and “four seven two nine” are the same order.
Data: mixed speech is scarcer than either language alone.

What helps: models trained on code-mixed audio with a shared vocabulary over both scripts (Indic-specialised ASR models exist for this; detecting the language first and routing to a per-language model works for monolingual callers but not for mid-sentence switches), a fixed output convention, and scoring after transliterating reference and hypothesis into one script. Report errors on the English and Hindi parts separately, since one can hide the other.

Accents and channel noise. Measure WER per accent or region, per handset type and per noise level, not just overall. Train with augmentation: noise added at signal-to-noise ratios from about 0 to 20 dB, room reverberation (convolving with room impulse responses), speed perturbation (0.9×, 1.0×, 1.1×), simulated 8 kHz telephony, and SpecAugment, which masks random bands of frequencies and spans of time in the features. A noise-suppression front end makes audio nicer for humans but can add artifacts that raise WER, so test it rather than assume it helps.

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: When biasing and normalisation aren't enough, adapt the model to your channel, accents and vocabulary.

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: Collect consented call audio, ideally the caller's channel on its own, cut into utterances with the VAD.

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: Transcribe cheaply: pseudo-label with the largest model you have, then have people correct a subset, prioritising entity-heavy and low-confidence utterances. Write transcription guidelines first: how to write numbers, which script to use for code-switched words, what to do with fillers and noise.

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: Split honestly: by caller and by call, never by utterance, or the same voices land in both train and test (see honest splits).

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: Train gently: start from a pretrained checkpoint with a low learning rate; freeze the lower layers or train small adapters (LoRA); mix in general-domain data so the model doesn't forget everything else; add phone-channel and noise augmentation.

chunks.h: Fine-tuning ASR on your own calls
chunks.x: Evaluate and ship carefully: WER and entity accuracy per slice against the current model on the same held-out calls, then run the new model in shadow mode on live traffic before switching (see shadow mode).

In a live two-party call the agent knows which audio is its own, so the real-time loop doesn't need diarization. It matters for mono recordings (QA, analytics, mining old human-agent calls for training data) and for calls with more than one person on the caller's side.
Embed: cut speech into short overlapping windows (around 1–2 s) and compute a speaker embedding for each (x-vector or ECAPA-TDNN style networks trained for speaker verification).
Cluster the embeddings (agglomerative or spectral clustering; the number of speakers is often unknown, so a distance threshold or the eigenvalue gap decides it).

Resegment boundaries and handle overlapping speech, which clustering alone can't. End-to-end neural diarization predicts per-frame activity for each speaker directly and handles overlap; pyannote is the common open-source toolkit.

The metric is the diarization error rate: (false-alarm speech + missed speech + speech attributed to the wrong speaker) ÷ total speech time. The cheapest fix of all: when you control the telephony, record each party on its own channel, and diarization becomes trivial.

Say it in an interview: “ASR has to align about 100 frames a second to a few words a second without labelled timing. CTC adds a blank, collapses repeats and sums over all alignments with a forward algorithm, but assumes outputs are independent given the audio. A transducer adds a prediction network over previous tokens and a joint network, which makes it the usual streaming model. Whisper is an encoder–decoder on 30-second windows: very accurate, but it needs the whole window, so it doesn't stream as built. For an agent I'd add per-call hotword biasing, inverse text normalisation for numbers,

chunks.h: Measuring ASR: WER and what it misses
chunks.x: Word error rate counts the fewest word edits that turn the recogniser's output (the hypothesis) into the correct transcript (the reference): substitutions S (wrong word), deletions D (missed word) and insertions I (extra word), divided by the number of reference words N:

chunks.h: Measuring ASR: WER and what it misses
chunks.x: In words: errors per reference word. Lower is better. Because errors can outnumber the words, 1 − WER isn't an accuracy and can go negative.

chunks.h: WER by hand: the edit-distance table
chunks.x: Reference: “cancel order four seven two nine” (N = 6). Hypothesis: “cancel the order for seven nine”. Fill a table where cell (i, j) is the fewest edits that turn the first j hypothesis words into the first i reference words:
