Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own: the short answer, the mechanism, the why, then the trade-off or the likely follow-up. Questions 4, 7, 9, 21, 22, 24 and 30 are hand drills; do them with a pen.
1Walk me through what happens in the second after the caller stops speaking.

The audio reaches the server, the system decides the turn is over, the transcript is finalised, the LLM starts its reply, the first phrase goes to TTS, and the first audio travels back: about 1 s when everything streams.
0–100 ms, inbound: the last audio crosses the phone network and the provider's media stream (8 kHz μ-law, 20 ms packets).
~100–400 ms, end of turn: the VAD sees silence; after a short pause a turn detector (text or audio model) judges the turn complete. VAD alone would wait a fixed 500–800 ms.
~50 ms, final transcript: the streaming recogniser has been decoding all along and commits the final.
~300 ms, LLM first token (prompt cached), then ~80 ms until the first phrase ends at a punctuation mark.
~120 ms, TTS first audio, then ~100 ms outbound transport and jitter buffer: about 1,050 ms in total.
Meanwhile: the VAD keeps listening for barge-in, and every stage is timestamped.
Follow-up: starting the LLM speculatively on the partial transcript overlaps it with the end-of-turn wait, saving ~150 ms. (09)
2Cascade or speech-to-speech for a customer-support agent? Why?
Usually a cascade: support calls need exact entities, reliable tool calls, auditable transcripts and coverage of the callers' languages, and text in the middle gives all four.
Cascade gains: inspect and guard the text, normalise numbers, use the best tool-calling LLM, pick Indic-specialised ASR and TTS, and measure each stage (WER, time to first token, MOS).
Cascade losses: tone and emotion are discarded at ASR, latencies add up, ASR errors flow into the LLM.
Speech-to-speech gains: one model over codec tokens: lower latency (a few hundred ms), hears tone, full-duplex models handle overlap and backchannels natively.
Speech-to-speech losses: harder to steer and debug, weaker on complex tool chains, many audio tokens per second, one vendor.
Follow-up: for companionship or language practice, where naturalness dominates, I'd lean speech-to-speech. A half-cascade (audio-in LLM, text out, separate TTS) is a middle ground. (02)

The encoder outputs a distribution over tokens plus a blank at every frame; a path collapses to text by merging repeats then deleting blanks; the loss is minus the log of the total probability of all paths that collapse to the transcript, computed by dynamic programming.
Why the blank: it lets frames emit nothing (silence, between sounds) and separates double letters: “ll” needs “l _ l”.

The forward algorithm: interleave blanks into the label (2L + 1 states); at each frame a state is reached by staying, stepping, or skipping a blank between different tokens. Cost O(T cdot L) instead of an exponential number of paths.
Conditional independence: each frame's output depends only on the audio, so there's no language model inside; external LMs help and errors look like spelling (“for” for “four”).
Properties: monotonic, output no longer than the frames, peaky (mostly blanks), fast one-pass decoding, streams with a causal encoder.
Follow-up: the transducer fixes the independence assumption with a prediction network. (03)
4Drill: collapse “h h _ e e _ l l _ l o o” and “h h e e l l l l l o o”. Then, with three frames and P(a) = 0.6, 0.7, 0.2 (else blank), find P(“a”), P(“aa”) and the greedy output.
“hello” and “helo”; P(“a”) = 0.868, P(“aa”) = 0.036, greedy gives “a”.
Collapse: merge repeats first (h _ e _ l _ l o), then drop blanks: hello. Without a blank between the l's they merge: helo.
P(“aa”): only a_a: 0.6 × 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.036. Empty: ___ = 0.096. The three sum to 1.
Greedy: argmax per frame is a, a, _ → “a”.
Follow-up: greedy can be wrong: two frames with P(a) = 0.4 each give greedy “” (0.36), but P(“a”) = 0.64. Prefix beam search sums paths. (03)
5Compare CTC, RNN-T and attention encoder–decoder models. Which would you use for streaming, and why?
A transducer (RNN-T) for streaming: monotonic, frame-synchronous decoding like CTC, but conditioned on previous outputs.
CTC: per-frame outputs, sum over alignments, outputs independent given audio. Cheapest, streams, needs an external LM for the best accuracy.

RNN-T: encoder + prediction network (an LM over emitted tokens) + joint network; blank means “next frame”, and several tokens can come from one frame. Streams naturally; the training cost is the T × U × V joint tensor (15.6M logits for 10 s of audio, 60 tokens, 1,024-token vocabulary).
Attention encoder–decoder (Whisper): a full autoregressive decoder with cross-attention; most accurate and formats text well, but needs the whole input and can hallucinate.
Shared part: all three usually sit on a Conformer or transformer encoder; streaming comes from chunked attention in the encoder.
Follow-up: chunk size sets a latency floor: a 320 ms chunk adds 160 ms on average. (03)
6Why isn't Whisper a streaming model? How would you use it in a live agent?
It encodes fixed 30-second windows with attention over the whole window, and decodes only after the encoder has seen everything; so it can't emit words while the caller is still talking.
Fixed input: short audio is padded to 30 s (3,000 log-mel frames → 1,500 encoder positions); a 2 s turn costs a 30 s encode.
Unstable partials: trained on complete segments, so the last words change as audio grows.
Hallucination: on silence or noise it can invent or repeat text; gate it with a VAD.

Workarounds: transcribe each VAD-cut utterance after the caller stops (adds the whole transcription time to every turn); or re-decode a growing buffer and commit the prefix two runs agree on (LocalAgreement), which repeats compute and commits late.
Follow-up: for live turns I'd use a streaming transducer or CTC model, and keep Whisper-class models for offline transcripts, QA and labelling. (03)
7Drill: 16 kHz audio, 25 ms windows, 10 ms hop. Samples per window and hop? Frames per second? Frames in 1 s? Feature shape for Whisper's 30 s with 80 mels? Encoder length? And at 8 kHz?
400 and 160 samples; 100 frames a second; 98 frames in 1 s without padding (101 centred); 80 × 3,000; 1,500 encoder positions of 20 ms; at 8 kHz, 200 and 80 samples.
Frames: 1 + lfloor (16,000 - 400)/160 rfloor = 98 ; with half-window padding 1 + 16,000/160 = 101 .
30 s: 480,000 samples → 3,000 frames (Whisper drops the last padded one) → 80 × 3,000 = 240,000 numbers.
Encoder: the second convolution has stride 2 → 1,500 positions, 20 ms each.
FFT: size 400 gives 201 bins, 40 Hz apart.
Bitrates: 16 kHz × 16 bit = 256 kbit/s; phone audio 8 kHz × 8-bit μ-law = 64 kbit/s.
8Why log-mel features? What goes wrong when phone audio meets a model trained on 16 kHz audio?

Mel spacing matches how pitch is perceived and keeps the spectral envelope while dropping detail; the log compresses loudness and turns channel effects into offsets. Phone audio has nothing above 4 kHz, so about a quarter of a 16 kHz model's mel bands are empty.
Mel: roughly linear below 1 kHz, logarithmic above (1,000 Hz = 1,000 mel, 8,000 Hz = 2,840 mel); 80 triangular filters, narrow at low frequencies and wide at high ones.
Log: quiet consonants and loud vowels both register; a microphone's or line's frequency response becomes an additive offset that mean normalisation removes.
Phone audio: 18–19 of 80 filters over 0–8 kHz sit above 4 kHz and are empty after upsampling; fricatives (“s”, “f”) lose cues; μ-law noise and packet loss add more.
Fixes: fine-tune on real 8 kHz calls or wideband data passed through a simulated phone channel; or use an 8 kHz model; always evaluate on your channel.
9Drill: reference “cancel order four seven two nine”, hypothesis “cancel the order for seven nine”. Compute WER by hand. Can WER exceed 100%, and why normalise first?
3 edits over 6 reference words: WER = 50% (S = 1, D = 1, I = 1). WER can exceed 100% because insertions are unbounded, and unnormalised formatting differences count as errors.
Recurrence: d_i,j = min(d_i-1,j-1 + [r_i ne h_j],\ d_i-1,j + 1,\ d_i,j-1 + 1) , first row and first column 0 to 6; the bottom-right cell is 3.
Backtrace: cancel = cancel; insert “the”; order = order; four → for (substitution); seven = seven; delete “two”; nine = nine. So (1 + 1 + 1)/6 = 0.5 .
Over 100%: “no” vs “uh no no thanks” is 3 insertions over 1 word, 300%; typical when a model hallucinates on silence or noise.

Normalisation: “cancel order 4729” vs “cancel order four seven two nine” scores 1 substitution + 3 insertions over 3 words, 133%, for a perfect transcript. Use one normaliser for both sides and report it.
Corpus WER: total edits over total words, not the average of utterance WERs, which over-weights short utterances (27.5% vs 7.1% in the note's example).
Follow-up: the order number 4729 is lost entirely, which a 50% WER doesn't tell you; entity accuracy does. (04, 04, 04)
10Why does WER understate errors on phone numbers? What would you measure instead?
WER weights every word equally, but a phone number is only useful if every digit is right: one wrong digit in a 20-word sentence is 5% WER and a 100% failed callback.
Compounding: with per-digit accuracy p , a 10-digit number is right with probability p^10 : 95% → 59.9%, 98% → 81.7%, 99% → 90.4%.
Meaning flips: “I do not want to cancel” → “I do want to cancel” is one deletion (16.7% WER) and the opposite instruction.
Measure: exact-match rate per entity type (phone, order ID, amount, date, name), keyword recall and precision, slot accuracy and task success.
Design around it: read entities back in groups, offer keypad entry, validate against known data (the caller's open orders).
11A vendor's ASR reports 6% WER on a benchmark, but on your calls the agent keeps failing. How do you debug?
Measure on your own audio and your own success criteria: the benchmark differs from your calls in channel, speakers, language mix, vocabulary and what counts as an error.
Build a test set of real (consented, redacted) calls with careful transcripts, and compute WER with one normaliser, plus entity exact-match.
Slice: 8 kHz vs app audio, accent or region, noise level, Hinglish vs monolingual, digits, names. One slice usually explains most failures.
Check the plumbing: sample rate and μ-law decoding (a wrong rate or codec ruins everything quietly), resampling filters, clipping, VAD cutting word edges.
Check turn-taking: “ASR failures” are often cut-off turns (the endpointer fired mid-number) or barge-ins on echo.
Then fix: hotword biasing, ITN rules, a domain LM, a different or fine-tuned model, keypad fallback for digits.
12The recogniser keeps getting customer names and product names wrong. What do you do?
Bias recognition towards the expected words, per call, then correct and confirm downstream.

Contextual biasing: pass a phrase list (the caller's name, their order IDs, the product catalogue) as hotwords; beam search adds a bonus to hypotheses partway through a listed phrase (a prefix tree), or with Whisper put terms in the prompt.
Language model fusion: log P_ASR + lambda log P_LM + beta lvert yrvert with an LM trained on your transcripts.
Downstream: fuzzy or phonetic matching against the database, LLM correction given the candidate list, read-back confirmation.
Risk: over-boosting creates false insertions; measure boosted-term recall and general WER, on sets with and without the terms.
If still bad: fine-tune on in-domain audio.
13What's hard about Hinglish (code-switched) speech recognition, and how do you evaluate it fairly?
Language changes mid-sentence, the same speech can be written in several scripts, numbers come in either language, and mixed training data is scarce.
Language ID per utterance can't follow “mera order cancel karna hai”.
Script ambiguity: Devanagari, romanised, or English words transliterated (ऑर्डर); mismatched conventions inflate WER without any recognition error.
Numbers: “chaar saat do nau” and “four seven two nine” must both become 4729; Indian grouping and fractions (“dhai sau” = 250) in ITN.
Models: trained on code-mixed audio with a shared vocabulary over both scripts.

Little labelled data: start from a self-supervised multilingual encoder (wav2vec 2.0 or HuBERT style) and fine-tune with CTC; wav2vec 2.0 reached 4.8% / 8.2% WER on LibriSpeech with ten minutes of labels.
Evaluation: transliterate reference and hypothesis to one script before scoring; consider CER; report errors on the Hindi and English parts separately; entity accuracy on numbers.
14How does a VAD work? Which settings matter?
It scores each 10–30 ms frame as speech or not, then smooths the scores into segments; the smoothing settings decide the behaviour.
Energy VAD: frame energy in dB vs an adaptive noise floor (+ zero-crossing rate); free, but fooled by TV, traffic, breath and quiet callers.
Model VADs: WebRTC VAD (GMM over band energies, aggressiveness 0–3), Silero (small neural net, 32 ms chunks at 16 kHz, a probability per chunk).

Settings: hysteresis (start above 0.5, stop below 0.35), minimum speech duration (ignore clicks), hangover or minimum silence (bridges pauses; this is the endpointing wait), padding (keep word edges).
Example: speech 100–400 and 520–800 ms with a 300 ms hangover is one turn, declared over at 1,100 ms; with 100 ms it's two turns.
15How would you choose the endpointing silence threshold?
It's a trade between latency and cutting callers off, and the right value depends on what the caller is doing, so I'd make it adaptive rather than pick one number.
The cost: the whole threshold is added to every reply's latency.

The risk: callers pause mid-turn. In an illustrative model (1.5 pauses per turn, median 300 ms), 300 ms cuts off 53% of ordinary turns, 800 ms 7%, 1,200 ms 2%; for digit dictation (3 pauses, median 500 ms) 800 ms still cuts off 48%.
Formula: P(cut) = 1 - e^-lambda P(pause ge T) for a Poisson number of pauses.
Better: context-dependent waits (longer after asking for a number), a turn detector, keypad for long numbers, and merging a resumed turn with the cut-off one.
Tune on data: measure cut-off rate (callers talking over a reply within a second) against latency on real calls.
16How do you detect the end of a turn better than with silence alone?
Predict whether the turn is complete from the words, the intonation and the dialogue context, and wait short when it is, long when it isn't.
Signals: syntactic and semantic completeness (“I want to cancel my order.” vs “my number is nine eight seven…”), falling pitch and final lengthening vs filled pauses, what the agent just asked for.
Models: text-based turn detectors (a small LM on the transcript, e.g. LiveKit's), audio-based ones (e.g. Pipecat's Smart Turn on the waveform), or the LLM emitting a “wait” token.
Policy: on ~200 ms of VAD silence, run the model; reply if confident, otherwise keep waiting with a maximum timeout.
Why it wins: it lowers latency and cut-offs together, which a fixed threshold can't.
Follow-up: evaluate it per language on real calls: false end-of-turn (cut-offs) vs late responses. (06)
17How do you handle barge-in, and why does it fail without echo cancellation?

Confirm it's a real interruption (not a backchannel or noise), stop audio everywhere, cancel generation, and trim the agent's message to what the caller heard. Without echo cancellation the agent hears its own voice and interrupts itself.

Detect: VAD on the echo-cancelled caller channel during playback, plus a minimum duration, a word or two of ASR, or an interruption classifier. Backchannels (“mm-hmm”, “haan”) are short, from a known list and not followed by more speech: keep talking through them.
Stop: flush the orchestrator queue, the TTS stream, the provider's buffer (e.g. Twilio's clear) and the client's jitter buffer; TTS runs ahead of playback, so seconds may be queued.
Cancel: LLM and TTS; side-effecting tools need idempotency, not blind cancellation.

Trim the history: from playback marks and TTS word timestamps; interrupted at 2.4 s, it keeps “Your refund of two thousand rupees”, marked interrupted. Use the played position, not bytes sent; otherwise the LLM thinks the caller heard “five to seven working days”.

Echo: the agent's audio leaks back (speakerphone, line echo), so the VAD fires on it or ASR transcribes it as the caller. Acoustic echo cancellation learns the echo path from the reference signal (the audio that was played) with an adaptive filter such as NLMS and subtracts the predicted echo; double-talk detection freezes learning while both speak. Best on the device (WebRTC includes it); fallbacks are higher barge-in thresholds during playback or ignoring transcripts that match the agent's own recent words.
18What audio arrives from a phone call, and when would you use WebRTC, WebSockets, SIP or DTMF?
Phone calls arrive as 8 kHz, 8-bit G.711 (μ-law or A-law) in 20 ms packets; WebRTC is for apps, WebSockets for server-to-server streams, SIP for the phone network, and DTMF for keypad input.
Phone path: PSTN → telephony provider → SIP trunk (RTP audio) or the provider's media-stream WebSocket (base64 μ-law) → decode, resample to 16 kHz for ASR; TTS back down to 8 kHz μ-law.
WebRTC: UDP, Opus, jitter buffer, on-device echo cancellation; best for browser and mobile agents and lossy networks.
WebSocket: TCP and simple, but head-of-line blocking causes latency spikes on lossy links; fine between data-centre services.
SIP: call setup and control: INVITE, BYE, REFER for transfers.
DTMF: two tones per key (“5” = 770 + 1,336 Hz), as events or in-band (Goertzel); exact and private for PINs and long numbers.
19Walk through a TTS pipeline. Where do FastSpeech 2, HiFi-GAN, VITS and VALL-E fit?

Text normalisation → grapheme-to-phoneme → acoustic model (text to mel spectrogram) → vocoder (mel to waveform); VITS merges the last two stages, and codec language models replace them with token prediction.
TN and G2P: “₹2,500” → “two thousand five hundred rupees”, order 4729 → “four seven two nine”; lexicon plus neural G2P; heteronyms and names are the failures.

FastSpeech 2: non-autoregressive; predicts each phoneme's duration, pitch and energy; the length regulator repeats phoneme vectors (durations 3, 5, 2, 4, 3, 6 → 23 frames ≈ 267 ms); parallel, robust, controllable. Tacotron 2 was autoregressive with attention, which can skip or repeat words.
HiFi-GAN: a GAN vocoder upsampling mel frames to samples, with multi-period and multi-scale discriminators; far faster than real time.
VITS: end to end (VAE + flow + adversarial training, alignment learned during training, stochastic durations).
VALL-E: language modelling over codec tokens, conditioned on a 3-second prompt; zero-shot cloning, but can hallucinate.
20How does streaming TTS work in an agent, and what is the trade-off in chunk size?

Cut the LLM's token stream into phrases at punctuation, synthesise each as soon as it's complete, and stream audio chunks while the next phrase is generated; smaller chunks are faster but sound worse.

Why: waiting for a 60-token reply at 100 tokens/s costs 600 ms after the first token; the first 8-token phrase is ready in 80 ms. Non-streaming synthesis of 18 s of audio at RTF 0.05 is 900 ms before any sound.
The cost: the TTS doesn't see what comes next: questions get the wrong intonation, every chunk falls like a sentence end, joins can be audible.
Mitigations: a short first phrase, sentence-sized later ones; APIs that take incremental text with a context id and keep prosody across chunks.
Also needed: word timestamps from the TTS, so barge-in can trim to what was heard.
21How do you evaluate a TTS voice? Drill: ten ratings 4, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 4. Give the MOS with a 95% interval.
MOS 4.00, 95% interval [3.52, 4.48]; and for real decisions, comparative tests plus automatic checks.
Drill: mean 4.00; standard deviation 0.667; standard error 0.667/sqrt10 = 0.211 ; t with 9 degrees of freedom is 2.262; half-width 0.48.
Correlated ratings: with 20 listeners × 10 sentences, the naive interval (±0.10) is about 2.5× too narrow; bootstrapping listeners and sentences gives ±0.25 in the note's simulation.
Sensitivity: CMOS or AB preference for comparing two voices; MUSHRA for ranking several close ones; 4.1 vs 4.2 at sd 0.9 needs about 1,300 independent ratings per system.
Automatic: re-transcription WER/CER (skipped words, wrong numbers), speaker-embedding similarity for cloned voices, automatic MOS predictors for regressions, time to first audio p50/p95 under load.

22Drill: inbound 100 ms, silence threshold 800, batch ASR 400, LLM first token 500 then 50 tokens at 60/s before TTS starts, TTS 500 for the whole reply, outbound 100. Total? And with streaming: turn detector 300, ASR final 50, first token 300, first phrase 8 tokens at 100/s, TTS first audio 120?
3,233 ms naive; 1,050 ms streaming.
Speculative start: begin the LLM after 200 ms of silence on the partial transcript: about 900 ms.
Percentiles: don't add per-stage p95s. In the note's simulation the sum of stage p95s is 1,887 ms but the p95 of the total is 1,500 ms, and the LLM's first token causes 77% of the variance.
23Your agent's p50 voice-to-voice latency is 1.4 s. How would you cut 300 ms?
Measure the per-stage breakdown on real turns first, then attack the biggest items, which are usually the end-of-turn wait and the LLM's first token.
End of turn: replace a fixed 800 ms silence threshold with a turn detector (300 ms on complete turns): up to ~500 ms on its own.
Overlap: start the LLM speculatively on the partial transcript during the wait (~150 ms).
LLM first token: prompt caching, a shorter prompt, a faster model for routine turns, provisioned capacity (also cuts the p95).
Network: co-locate media, ASR, LLM and TTS near the callers; warm connections. A cross-continent round trip per hop is often 150–250 ms.
TTS: stream it, a short first phrase, cached audio for fixed phrases.
Follow-up: fillers reduce perceived latency only; check cut-off rate and task success after any endpointing change. (09)
24Drill: a codec runs at 12.5 frames a second with 8 codebooks of 2,048 entries. Tokens per second, bitrate, and how does that compare with text?
100 tokens a second and 1.1 kbit/s, about 30 times as many tokens as the transcript of the same speech.
Tokens: 12.5 × 8 = 100 per second; 2,048 entries is 11 bits, so 100 × 11 = 1,100 bit/s (Mimi, used by Moshi).
Compression: raw 24 kHz 16-bit audio is 384 kbit/s, about 350× more.
Text: 150 words a minute at ~1.3 tokens a word is ~3.3 tokens a second.

Why it matters: context length and cost grow with audio tokens; a 5-minute call is 30,000 tokens per stream, or 3,750 steps of Moshi's main transformer (12.5 a second; a small depth transformer predicts each step's 8 codebook tokens). EnCodec at 6 kbit/s (75 Hz × 8) is 600 tokens a second, hence the push to low frame rates.
RVQ: each codebook quantises the residual left by the previous ones, coarse to fine.
25How would you serve 1,000 concurrent calls?
Treat calls as long-lived stateful sessions, size GPU capacity from throughput at a safe utilisation, batch across calls, and keep warm capacity in each region.
Sessions: each call stays on one worker for its whole life; scale on concurrent calls, not requests per second; drain workers on deploys instead of dropping calls.

Capacity (illustrative): a GPU running streaming ASR at RTFx 50 serves about 50 streams in principle; at 60–70% utilisation plan for 30–35, so about 30 GPUs for ASR at 1,000 calls. Repeat for TTS and any self-hosted LLM, or check vendors' concurrency quotas.
Batching: chunks from many calls in one forward pass, with the batching delay capped at a few tens of milliseconds so latency holds.
Bursts: warm pools with models loaded; at capacity, queue new calls or play a busy message rather than degrading every live call.
Regions: near callers and the telephony provider, for latency and data residency, with failover.
26How is prompting a voice agent different from prompting a chat agent?
The output is heard once, in real time, through TTS, and the input is a noisy transcript; the prompt has to account for both.

Output: short sentences, one question per turn, no markdown, lists, emojis or URLs; numbers in spoken form (“four seven two nine”, “two thousand five hundred rupees”); answer first, short first sentence for latency.
Input: say it's a speech transcript with possible misrecognitions; clarify instead of guessing; never act on one hearing of a critical entity.
Confirmation: read entities back in groups; confirm before irreversible actions.
Language: match the caller's language mix and register.
Voice situations: silence, noise, repeated failures (offer keypad or a human), interruptions.
Follow-up: keep state such as collected and confirmed slots in the orchestrator, not just the transcript. (10)
27A tool call takes 3 seconds in the middle of a call. What should the agent do?
Never leave dead air: say what it's doing before the call, give a short update if it runs long, and make the call safe to retry.
Before: have the LLM emit “Let me check that order for you.” before the tool call, or have the orchestrator play a filler if no result arrives within about a second.
During: a brief update every few seconds on long operations; keep listening for barge-in.
Correctness: arguments from confirmed, normalised entities (4729); idempotency keys so a retry or a barge-in can't cancel or charge twice; timeouts with a spoken fallback.
Speed: run independent tools in parallel; prefetch likely data (the caller's orders) when the call starts.
28What privacy and compliance issues does a voice agent for support or healthcare calls in India raise?
Consent and AI disclosure, personal and health data copied into recordings, transcripts, prompts and vendors' systems, payment data, data residency, and the rules for outbound calling.
Disclosure: say the call is recorded and that the caller is talking to an automated agent; log it.
Data: redact personal data from transcripts and logs, set retention periods, restrict access to recordings; treat health data as sensitive.
Payments: card numbers by keypad, masked in recordings and transcripts, never in the LLM's context (smaller PCI DSS scope).

India: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 for consent and use of personal data; sector rules that keep some data in the country (payment data under RBI rules); TRAI's commercial-communication rules for outbound calls (140-series numbers and the do-not-disturb registry for promotional calls, 1600-series for regulated financial entities' service calls).
Vendors and voices: where audio and text are processed and kept, and whether they're used for training; clone voices only with consent.
29How do you evaluate a voice bot before launch, and monitor it after?

Before: simulated callers over the real channel plus a regression set of recorded calls, scored on both component and conversation metrics. After: per-turn latency, turn-taking health, understanding and outcomes, with humans listening to samples.

Simulated callers: an LLM with a goal, hidden facts and a persona; TTS in varied voices; degraded to 8 kHz μ-law with noise; called over the real transport; scored by deterministic checks (tool called once with order_id 4729) and an LLM judge.
Recorded calls: re-run ASR and turn detection on stored audio; conversations diverge after the first different reply, so replay only up to there or seed a simulated caller from the call.
Component metrics: WER and entity accuracy, cut-offs and false barge-ins, TTS checks, latency p50/p95.
Conversation metrics: task success, containment, transfers.
In production: “hello?” rate, talk-over rate, repeats, early hang-ups, tool errors, drift in vocabulary and callers; vendor health with fallbacks.

30Drill: telephony $0.010/min, ASR $0.008/min, TTS $30 per million characters at 360 characters a minute, and an LLM at 4 turns a minute with a 2,000-token prompt, history growing 100 tokens a turn, 20 output tokens a turn. Cost per minute of a 5-minute call with a model at $2.50 in and $10 out per million? What happens at 20 minutes?
About $0.059 a minute, of which the LLM is $0.030; at 20 minutes the LLM part roughly doubles per minute, to $0.060.
LLM input, 20 turns: sum_k=0^19(2,000 + 100k) = 59,000 tokens; output 400. Cost: 59,000 × $2.50/1M + 400 × $10/1M = $0.1515 per call, $0.0303 a minute.
20 minutes: 80 turns, 476,000 input tokens (23,800 a minute vs 11,800), because each turn resends the whole history: $0.060 a minute for the LLM.
Levers: prefix caching at 10% of the input price brings the 5-minute LLM cost to $0.0055 a minute; trimming or summarising history; a small model ($0.0018 a minute at $0.15/$0.60).

Turn detectors (text or audio) wait short on complete turns. Barge-in: confirm, flush all buffers, cancel, trim history to what was played. AEC or the agent interrupts itself.
beginaligned CI &= bar r pm t_0.975,\,n-1\, s/sqrt n \\ n_per system &approx 16sigma^2/delta^2 endaligned

TN → G2P → acoustic model (FastSpeech 2: durations, length regulator) → vocoder (HiFi-GAN); VITS end to end; VALL-E codec LM, 3 s cloning. Stream by phrase; word timestamps. Ten ratings: 4.00 ± 0.48. Bootstrap listeners and sentences (±0.25 vs naive ±0.10). CMOS, MUSHRA, re-transcription WER, speaker similarity, MOS predictors, TTFA p95.
beginaligned naive &= 100 + 800 + 400 + 1,333 + 500 + 100 = 3,233 ms \\ tuned &= 100 + 300 + 50 + 300 + 80 + 120 + 100 = 1,050 ms \\ LLM input &= sum_k=0^n-1(prompt + k times per turn) endaligned

Goal about 1 s (rule of thumb). p95 of a sum is less than the sum of p95s; the LLM owns the tail. Levers: turn detector, speculative start, streaming, prompt caching, co-location, short first phrase, fillers. Cost per minute = telephony + ASR + TTS + LLM; with the assumed prices, $0.031 (small model) to $0.059 (large); the LLM part grows with call length. Scale on concurrent calls (sticky sessions, warm pools, about 60–70% utilisation). Compliance: consent and AI disclosure, redaction, cards by keypad, DPDP Act, TRAI calling rules.

notes.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
notes.desc: When RAG beats fine-tuning or long context, the pipeline from PDF to cited answer, chunking, query rewriting, reranking and MMR, evaluation, a failure-mode table for debugging, and production concerns (freshness, permissions, latency, cost).

sections.t: The original RAG model, in one paragraph
RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
The query path, stage by stage
Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
Contextual chunk headers and contextual retrieval
HyDE: search with a hypothetical answer
Decomposition for multi-part and multi-hop questions
Refusing when the context is insufficient

chunks.x: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) · Deepam Minda

RAG fixes what a model knows, not how it behaves. At question time, search your documents, put the best passages in the prompt, and have the model answer from them with citations. That handles stale knowledge, private data, provenance and per-user permissions. Fine-tuning changes behaviour and format; a long prompt works when the corpus is small and static (under about 200k tokens) and is cached.

Quality is decided upstream. Parsing and chunking decide what can ever be found. Small chunks match specific facts but lose their context; big chunks keep context but blur the embedding and cost tokens. Structure-aware chunks with heading headers, parent–child retrieval and contextual retrieval get most of both.

Retrieve wide and cheap, then rerank narrow and expensive: hybrid dense + BM25 for the top 50, a cross-encoder down to about 6, MMR so the 6 aren't copies of each other, and a score threshold so the system says “not found” instead of improvising. Filter by permissions inside the search, never after it.

Rewrite the query when it's the problem: follow-ups into standalone questions, several paraphrases, a hypothetical answer (HyDE), sub-questions for multi-part asks, routing between sources. Each one costs an LLM call, so use them where the eval shows they pay.

Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, then end to end: recall@k of the gold passage; faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and recall; correctness including refusals. To debug, find the first stage that lost the answer for each failed question and fix the biggest bucket.

In production, the generator dominates latency and cost, indexes go stale unless updates and deletes flow through, a new embedding model means re-embedding everything, retrieved text is untrusted input (prompt injection), and every query should be logged with its retrieved ids and scores so failures can be replayed.
A trained language model stores what it learned in its weights. That gives it four problems as a source of facts:
Staleness: its knowledge stops at the training cutoff. A policy revised last week doesn't exist for it.
Private data: it never saw your internal documents, tickets or contracts.
Hallucination: when it doesn't know, it still produces a fluent, confident answer (hallucination), and nothing in the output marks which parts are guesses.
No provenance: it can't point to where a fact came from, so a reader can't check it, and you can't fix one wrong fact without retraining.
Enterprise use adds a fifth: access control. Different users may see different documents, and anything in the weights is visible to everyone who can call the model.

The idea of RAG: separate knowledge from reasoning. Keep the knowledge in an index you can update, delete from and filter; for each question, search it and hand the model the relevant passages; ask it to answer from those passages only, citing them. It turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one. The paper that named it calls the weights parametric memory and the index non-parametric memory.

A policy assistant for a company's employees. The corpus is 1,200 documents (policy PDFs, FAQ pages, allowance tables in spreadsheets), about 2,500 tokens each on average, so 3.0 million tokens. Policies are revised every quarter and FAQs weekly. Some documents are restricted (the HR-only compensation guidelines). It gets about 20,000 questions a day. Five questions recur through the note:
How many weeks of parental leave do I get?
The easy case: one passage answers it
(next turn) And if I'm a contractor?
Meaningless without the previous turn
What's the hotel cap for band 3 in Mumbai?
The answer is one cell of a table; “band 3” is an exact token
Can I take parental leave during my notice period, and is unused leave paid out?
Two questions, answered in two different documents
Do we have pet insurance?
Not in the corpus: the right answer is “not covered by the policies”

chunks.h: The original RAG model, in one paragraph
chunks.x: Lewis et al. (2020) coined the term. Their retriever was DPR, a bi-encoder (question and passage embedded separately), over December 2018 Wikipedia split into 21 million 100-word passages and indexed with FAISS. The generator was BART-large (400M parameters). The model treats the retrieved passage as a hidden variable and sums over the top k (5 or 10): RAG-Sequence uses the same passage for the whole answer, RAG-Token can draw on a different one for each token. They trained it end to end, fine-tuning the query encoder and the generator while keeping the document encoder and index fixed, becaus

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: Three ways to get the policy knowledge into the answer. They change different things, so the choice follows from what's missing.

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: The arithmetic behind the cost row. Prices are illustrative, not any provider's list: $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens for the answering model, with cached input billed at a tenth of the normal price (one provider quotes cost cuts of up to 90% with prompt caching). A RAG answer reads about 3,500 tokens (a 1,000-token system prompt, six passages of about 296 tokens each with their headers, and about 700 tokens of history and question) and writes 250:

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: beginaligned cost per query &= fractokens_in times p_in + tokens_out times p_out10^6 \\ RAG &= frac3,500 times 3 + 250 times 1510^6 = \$0.01425 \\ whole corpus &= frac3,000,000 times 310^6 = \$9.00 per query, \$0.90 cached endaligned

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: In words: the bill is tokens times price, so stuffing the whole corpus multiplies the input by about 860. At 20,000 questions a day, RAG costs about $285 a day; the whole corpus, even cached, would cost $18,000 a day, and it doesn't fit anyway (3.0M tokens is 15 times a 200k window). For the 60-document travel policy alone (150k tokens), long context is plausible: $0.454 a query uncached and $0.049 cached (both including the answer), about 3.4 times a RAG query ($975 against $285 a day). Caching only holds while the prefix is byte-identical, so any edit to any of the 60 documents, or a differe

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: Fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts. A model needs many paraphrased exposures to absorb a fact, can't cite it, can't forget it on request, and the fact goes stale with the next policy revision. Practitioner reports and the studies they cite favour RAG for new knowledge. Fine-tune for behaviour: the answer format, the tone, when to refuse, domain vocabulary.

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: They combine. Fine-tune a small model to answer in the cited format and RAG the facts into it; or fine-tune the embedding model on your domain's question–passage pairs, which is often the most useful fine-tuning in a RAG system (sentence embeddings).

chunks.h: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
chunks.x: “Our documents fit in a 1M-token window, so RAG is obsolete.” Fitting isn't the bar. Every question pays to read every token, waits for the prefill, and gives the model more distractors (section 07); per-user permissions and edits break the cache. Long context wins for small, static, shared corpora; RAG wins as soon as the corpus is big, changing or permissioned.
The corpus is small and static: under about 200k tokens (roughly 500 pages), one provider's guidance is to put it all in the prompt with caching. No retrieval misses, no chunking.
The gap is behaviour, not knowledge: tone, format, classification, following a procedure. Prompt or fine-tune.
The answer is a computation over structured data: “average travel claim by band last quarter” needs SQL over the claims table, not text chunks. Give the model a query tool (tool calling).

The question is about the whole corpus: “what are the common complaints across 10,000 tickets?” Top- k retrieval sees a handful of passages; it needs map-reduce summarization or a graph approach (section 10).
The model already knows it reliably (public, stable facts) and nobody needs a citation.

Say it in an interview: “RAG separates knowledge from the model: an index I can update, delete from and permission, searched per question, with the model answering only from what it's given and citing it. I'd pick fine-tuning when what's missing is behaviour or format, and long context when the corpus is small and static enough to cache. Here the corpus is 3 million tokens, changes weekly and has restricted documents, so RAG at about 1.4 cents a query beats anything that reads the whole corpus.”

A RAG system has two halves. Indexing runs offline, whenever documents change: it turns files into searchable chunks. The query path runs for every question: it finds the right chunks and turns them into a cited answer. Most quality problems start in the first half and show up in the second.

Indexing (top) turns 1,200 documents into 14,400 searchable chunks. The query path (bottom) narrows them to 50 candidates, then to about 6 passages the model reads. Each arrow is a place where the answer can be lost.

Connectors. Pull documents from where they live (document drives, the wiki, the HR system) with their id, URL, owner, permission groups, last-modified time and version. A source nobody connected is missing content no model can fix; permissions not captured here can't be enforced later.

Parsing. Turn each file into text that keeps its structure. HTML and Markdown are easy: keep the headings. Digital PDFs have a text layer, but reading order breaks on two-column layouts, running headers and footnotes, and tables come out as a jumble of numbers. Scanned PDFs and images need OCR, which misreads exactly what matters in policies (0 and O, 1 and l, decimal points). Layout-aware parsers detect titles, paragraphs, lists and tables; vision-language models can read a page image directly, and vision retrievers such as ColPali index page images themselves, tables included. Check the pars

Cleaning. Strip boilerplate repeated on every page (headers, footers, page numbers, navigation menus), re-join words hyphenated across lines, normalize whitespace and Unicode. De-duplicate: if the same FAQ answer sits on three pages, it fills three of your six slots. Mark superseded versions instead of leaving them to compete with the current one.

Metadata. Title, heading path (“Leave policy › Parental leave › Eligibility”), document type, effective date, version and status (current or superseded), region, employee type, permission groups, source URL. Metadata drives filters (section 04), citations, freshness and routing.
Chunking. Split into retrievable pieces, each with a short header (section 03). With 256-token chunks and 32 tokens of overlap, the corpus becomes 14,400 chunks.
Embedding. Encode each chunk with its header using a bi-encoder (bi- vs cross-encoders); queries go through the same model. Store the model name and version with every vector.
Indexing. A vector index (vector databases), a keyword index for BM25 (BM25), and a store for chunk text and metadata, all keyed by the same chunk id.

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Follow Q3, “What's the hotel cap for band 3 in Mumbai?”:

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Query processing: it's the first turn, so no rewrite is needed. A filter extractor turns “band 3” and “Mumbai” into metadata hints, and the user's permission groups are attached (section 05).

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Retrieval: the dense search matches “hotel cap” to a chunk titled “Accommodation allowance per night”, a paraphrase; BM25 matches the exact tokens “band 3” and “Mumbai”. Fusing both puts the allowance table's band 3 chunk near the top of 50 candidates (section 04).

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Reranking: a cross-encoder reads the question and each candidate together and keeps the best 6, with MMR removing near-duplicates (section 06).

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Context assembly: order the 6, label them [S1]…[S6] with their headers, fit the token budget (section 07).

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Generation: the model answers from the sources, cites [S2], and says so if the sources don't cover the question.

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Post-processing: check that every citation exists and supports its sentence, attach source links, log everything (section 11).

chunks.h: The query path, stage by stage
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Offline, I parse with layout awareness, clean and de-duplicate, attach metadata including permissions and versions, chunk along the document's structure with a heading header on each chunk, embed, and build both a vector and a BM25 index. Online: rewrite the query if it depends on the conversation, hybrid-retrieve 50 candidates under a permission filter, rerank to about 6, assemble with ids, generate with citations or a refusal, verify the citations, and log the whole trace.”
Chunking decides the unit of retrieval: what one vector stands for, and what the model gets to read. Why not embed whole documents?
One vector can't represent many topics. The leave policy covers parental leave, sick leave, encashment and notice periods. A single vector for all of it matches none of them strongly (worked below).
Tokens cost money and attention. Retrieving a 30-page policy to answer one sentence pays for 30 pages and hands the model 29 pages of distractors.
Citations need a small target, and embedding models have input limits (512 tokens for BERT-based models; many newer ones take 8k).

Whole-document embedding is fine when each document is short and about one thing, such as FAQ entries or short articles. It breaks on long, multi-topic documents. The opposite failure is a chunk too small to stand alone: “It is 26 weeks for primary caregivers” is useless if the chunk doesn't say what is 26 weeks.
Every C tokens, with O tokens of overlap
Cuts mid-sentence, mid-table, mid-clause
Splits on the coarsest separator that fits (section break, blank line, sentence, word), then packs neighbours up to the limit
Still blind to meaning; headings get separated from text
Follows the parsed structure: sections, lists and tables stay whole; the heading path goes on every chunk
Policies, manuals, docs, anything with headings
Depends on good parsing; sections vary wildly in size, so very long ones still need a recursive split
Embeds sentences and cuts where similarity between neighbours drops
Text with no structure: transcripts, chat logs
An embedding per sentence at ingest; a threshold to tune; gains over recursive splitting are mixed
Indexes single sentences; returns the hit plus n neighbours each side
Precise facts in flowing text
Many tiny vectors; the window may still miss the clause's condition
Indexes small child chunks; returns their parent section
Long structured documents
Parents cost tokens; several children of one parent must be merged

The recursive splitter is the workhorse, and its pseudocode is in section 12. Two newer variants are worth one line each: late chunking runs a long-context embedding model over the whole document and pools token vectors per chunk, so every chunk vector has seen its document; proposition indexing has an LLM rewrite text into short, self-contained statements before indexing.

chunks.h: Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
chunks.x: The tension in chunk size comes from asking one unit to do two jobs: be specific enough to match a query, and complete enough for the model to answer from. Decouple them: index small units, return bigger ones.

chunks.h: Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
chunks.x: Both tricks match on a small unit, whose embedding is sharp, and hand the model a bigger unit, which has the context. Several matching children of one parent are merged into one copy of the parent.

chunks.h: Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
chunks.x: Parent–child (also called small-to-big or hierarchical retrieval): children of about 100–250 tokens are embedded; each stores its parent's id (a section of 1–2k tokens). Retrieve children, map them to parents, de-duplicate, and pass parents to the model. With 6 hits from 3 sections, the model reads 3 sections.

chunks.h: Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
chunks.x: Sentence-window: embed sentences, return each hit with its neighbours. Cheaper on tokens than parents, and good for prose without structure.

chunks.h: Small to match, big to read: parent–child and sentence windows
chunks.x: The cost: parents are big, so fewer distinct sources fit the budget. Cap the parent size, or fall back to the child plus its neighbours when the parent is huge.

chunks.h: Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
chunks.x: With fixed-size chunks, how often is the passage you need cut across two chunks? Say the answer is a span of L tokens starting at a random position, chunks are C tokens long and start every s = C - O tokens ( O is the overlap). The span sits whole inside a chunk if some chunk starts no more than C - L tokens before it: a window of C - L + 1 possible start positions. Chunk starts come every s tokens, so if that window is at least s wide, some chunk always fits; otherwise the chance it fits is the window's share of s :

chunks.h: Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
chunks.x: beginaligned P(split) &= 1 - fracC - L + 1C - O quad when O lt L - 1 \\ P(split) &= 0 quad when O ge L - 1 \\ P(split mid O = 0) &= fracL - 1C endaligned

chunks.h: Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
chunks.x: In words: without overlap, the chance of cutting the answer is roughly its length over the chunk length. An overlap at least as long as the passage you need guarantees that some chunk contains it whole. For the 60-token parental-leave eligibility clause (checked by simulation):

chunks.h: Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
chunks.x: What overlap costs: in the long run, stored and embedded tokens grow by C/(C - O) : 14% for 32 on 256, 33% for 64. Here each 2,500-token document rounds up to whole chunks, so the table's chunk counts grow by 20% and 30%. Overlapping neighbours also show up together in the top k as near-duplicates, which MMR or merging adjacent chunks handles (section 06).

chunks.h: Overlap, and the chance of cutting an answer in half
chunks.x: Structure-aware splitting needs less of it: when cuts fall between sections and paragraphs, a clause is rarely cut. The usual rule of thumb is 10–20% overlap for fixed-size or recursive chunks.

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Why big chunks match worse. Many embedding models average their token vectors (mean pooling), so a chunk's vector is roughly the average of what it talks about. Take the idealized case: a chunk that covers m unrelated topics equally, each topic a unit vector mathbf t_j at right angles to the others. The chunk's normalized vector and its similarity to a query about topic 1 are:

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: beginaligned mathbf c &= fracmathbf t_1 + dots + mathbf t_mlVert mathbf t_1 + dots + mathbf t_m rVert = frac1sqrt m sum_j=1^m mathbf t_j \\ cos(mathbf c, mathbf t_1) &= frac1sqrt m endaligned

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: In words: the sum of m perpendicular unit vectors has length sqrt m , so a perfect match on one topic is diluted to 1/sqrt m : 1.00 for one topic, 0.71 for two, 0.50 for four, 0.41 for six, 0.35 for eight. Real topics aren't perpendicular and models don't purely average, but the direction holds: a chunk about everything scores mediocre for everything, and a focused chunk on a neighbouring topic (cosine 0.6 with the query, say) outranks the six-topic chunk that actually holds the answer (0.41).

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Why small chunks answer worse. They lose their context (the heading, the subject of “it”, the exception in the next paragraph), they split clauses more often (the table above), and an answer spread over a section needs several of them.

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: What the model reads. Retrieving k = 6 chunks, as the running example does, when the answer is the 60-token clause, at $3 per million input tokens and 20,000 questions a day:

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Doubling the chunk doubles the cost of every question and halves the share of useful text. The other lever is the number of distinct sources: with a fixed budget, bigger chunks mean fewer of them, which hurts multi-part questions like Q4.

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Rule of thumb: 200–500 tokens with 10–20% overlap for prose, sections for structured documents, and parent–child when you want both.

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Decide with your eval, not the rule: try two or three sizes and compare recall@k of the gold passages and end-to-end answer quality (section 08). Label gold answers as text spans, not chunk ids, so the same labels work for every chunking.

chunks.h: Chunk size: recall, precision and context cost
chunks.x: Silent truncation. An embedding model trained on 512 tokens quietly drops everything after token 512. Feed it 1,000-token chunks and the second half of every chunk is invisible to dense search, with no error anywhere. Check the model's maximum input against your largest chunk, header included.

chunks.h: Contextual chunk headers and contextual retrieval
chunks.x: Headers. Prepend each chunk with where it came from, “Leave policy › Parental leave › Duration”, before embedding it and indexing it for BM25; when showing it to the model, add the version and effective date from the metadata. Keeping fast-changing metadata out of the embedded text means a version bump doesn't force re-embedding. It costs about 20–40 tokens per chunk and fixes the “it is 26 weeks” problem: the chunk now says what it's about, and BM25 can match the section's words.

chunks.h: Contextual chunk headers and contextual retrieval
chunks.x: Contextual retrieval (published by Anthropic in 2024) goes further: an LLM reads the whole document and the chunk and writes 50–100 tokens situating the chunk (“This chunk is from the 2026 parental leave policy; it gives the leave duration for primary and secondary caregivers…”). That text is prepended before both embedding and BM25 indexing. On their test sets, the retrieval failure rate (the share of relevant chunks that didn't make the top 20, one minus recall@20):

chunks.h: Contextual chunk headers and contextual retrieval
chunks.x: Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25

chunks.h: Contextual chunk headers and contextual retrieval
chunks.x: What it costs here. Each chunk's call sends the whole document: 14,400 calls of 2,500 + 256 + 50 tokens (document, chunk, instructions) is 40.4 million input tokens, 13.5 times the corpus. At illustrative small-model prices ($0.25 per million in, $1.25 per million out, 75 tokens out per chunk) that's about $11.45. With prompt caching, where each document is billed at 1.25× when first written to the cache and 0.1× for its other 11 reads, it's about $4.21. (The post quotes $1.02 per million document tokens for its own setup, which would be about $3 here.) It's a one-off cost, repeated only for c

Never separate table rows from their header. “3 | Tier-1 | 7,500” means nothing without “Band | City tier | Hotel cap per night (₹)”. Small tables: one chunk, serialized as Markdown. Large tables: split by groups of rows and repeat the header row in every piece.

Embed a sentence version, show the table. Row-to-text (“Band 3, tier-1 cities such as Mumbai: hotel cap ₹7,500 per night”) matches questions far better than pipes and numbers; the model can still be shown the Markdown table. The same idea generalizes as multi-vector indexing: index a summary or several questions per item, return the original.
Watch merged cells, multi-row headers and units in headers, the usual casualties of PDF table extraction.
Aggregates belong in SQL. “Which bands have a cap above ₹6,000?” over a 500-row table is a query, not a retrieval: route it to a tool.

Code: split along syntax (functions, classes) with a parser rather than by token count, keep signatures and docstrings with the body, put the file path and class name in the header, and lean on BM25 for identifiers, which dense models handle poorly.

Say it in an interview: “Chunk size trades a sharp embedding against a self-contained passage, and context cost against how many sources fit. I start with structure-aware chunks of a few hundred tokens with the heading path as a header, use parent–child when answers need whole sections, keep tables whole with their header row, and pick the size by recall@k on the eval set. Overlap at least as long as the typical answer span guarantees it isn't cut in half.”

Dense retrieval (embedding similarity, sentence embeddings) matches meaning: “hotel cap” finds “accommodation allowance”. Sparse retrieval (BM25) matches exact tokens: policy codes like HR-POL-017, “band 3”, acronyms, names, error codes, which embeddings blur. Hybrid search runs both and fuses the two rankings, usually with reciprocal rank fusion, which adds up 1/(60 + rank) across the lists (hybrid search and RRF). Hybrid is the sensible default; Q3 needs both halves. Questions in another language, or code-mixed (Hindi or Hinglish over English policies), defeat BM25, which matches tokens; a m

You may not need approximate search yet. Exact search compares the query with every vector: 14,400 chunks × 1,024 dimensions is about 15 million multiply-adds (30 MFLOP), around a millisecond multi-threaded, and the float32 vectors take 59 MB. At 100 million chunks it's 205 GFLOP per query and 410 GB of vectors, and that's where approximate indexes and compression come in (ANN, HNSW, IVF-PQ). Approximate search is one more place recall leaks, so measure its recall against exact search on a sample.

Filters narrow the search to what can be right: current versions only, the user's region, employee type, document type, effective dates. They come from the user's profile (region, band), from the query (an LLM or rules turning “band 3 in Mumbai” into structured filters, sometimes called self-querying), or from the product (this assistant only searches HR documents).

Permissions are a filter that must never fail. Every chunk carries its source document's permission groups; every query carries the user's groups; the search returns only chunks whose groups intersect. Anything that reaches the prompt can reach the answer, so “tell the model not to mention restricted content” is not access control.

Filter inside the search, not after it. Post-filtering means: retrieve the top 50, then drop what the user can't see. Suppose a contractor can see 5% of the corpus and relevance has nothing to do with permissions. Each of the 50 survives with probability f = 0.05 :
beginaligned E[visible] &= k f = 50 times 0.05 = 2.5 \\ P(none visible) &= (1 - f)^k = 0.95^50 = 0.077 \\ P(fewer than 5) &= sum_i=0^4 binom50i f^i (1-f)^50-i = 0.90 endaligned

In words: the contractor gets 2.5 results on average, fewer than 5 nine times out of ten, and nothing at all 7.7% of the time, even when the index holds plenty of chunks they're allowed to see. At f = 0.2 it's 10 on average and fewer than 5 only 1.8% of the time, so the bug hides from users with broad access. Pre-filtering (searching only the permitted subset) fixes it. Vector databases support filtered search; very selective filters can slow graph indexes or hurt their recall, and some engines switch to exact search over the filtered subset. With few large tenants, a separate index or namespa
Permissions change: sync them on events or a schedule, and make the sync lag part of your freshness monitoring.
Every cache needs the permission group in its key (section 10), or one user's cached answer leaks to another.
Test it: the eval set includes questions from restricted users whose answers live in documents they can't see; the right output is a refusal.
There are two k 's with different jobs:

Candidates for reranking, k_retrieve : 50–150. Their job is recall: the answer must be somewhere in here. They're cheap (no LLM reads them). Pick it from the recall@k curve on your eval set, where it flattens.

Passages the model reads, k_context : 3–20. Their job is precision within a token budget. More helps multi-part questions and costs tokens and attention. Pick it by end-to-end answer quality against tokens.

One published data point: in Anthropic's contextual-retrieval tests, passing 20 chunks beat 5 and 10, with 150 retrieved and reranked down to 20. Treat that as their setup, not a constant. A score threshold (section 06) makes k_context adaptive: a narrow question may need 2 passages and a broad one 10.

Large systems keep several indexes: policies, FAQs, tables behind SQL, past tickets, one per language or tenant. Separate indexes allow different chunking, embedding models and filters per type. A router (rules, a small classifier, or an LLM choosing among described tools) sends each question to one or several. The catches:
Scores aren't comparable across indexes, so merge with rank fusion or rerank all candidates together with one cross-encoder.
A routing mistake is a silent retrieval miss. Log the router's decision, evaluate it as a classifier on labelled questions, and search everything when it's unsure.

Say it in an interview: “Hybrid retrieval by default, because embeddings miss exact identifiers and BM25 misses paraphrases. Permissions are a pre-filter inside the search: post-filtering a top 50 for a user who can see 5% of the corpus leaves 2.5 results on average and none about 8% of the time. I retrieve 50 or more for recall, pass about 6 for precision, and choose both numbers from the eval set.”

Retrieval compares the query with the documents, and the query is often the weak side: short, vague, dependent on the conversation, or several questions at once, while the documents are written in policy language. Query rewriting changes the query before search. Every technique below costs at least one LLM call, so each must earn its latency.

Q2, “And if I'm a contractor?”, embedded on its own, is about contractors in general; nothing in it says parental leave. The fix is to condense the conversation into a standalone query with a small, fast model: last few turns plus the new message in, “How many weeks of parental leave do contractors get?” out. This is the retrieval version of what dialogue systems call state tracking (dialogue state tracking).
What goes wrong: the rewriter drops a constraint (“contractors” vanishes), invents one, or drags in the old topic after the user changed subject.

Mitigations: skip the rewrite on the first turn; retrieve with both the original and the rewritten query and fuse; log every rewrite next to the original; put multi-turn conversations in the eval set.

Ask an LLM for 3–5 paraphrases of the question (“contractor parental leave entitlement”, “do non-employees get paid parental leave”), retrieve for each in parallel, and fuse the lists with rank fusion; this combination is sometimes called RAG-Fusion. It raises recall when the user's words don't match the documents'. It costs one LLM call and n searches, adds more candidates for the reranker to sort, and can drift if a paraphrase changes the meaning.

chunks.h: HyDE: search with a hypothetical answer
chunks.x: Questions and answers look different: “how long is parental leave?” is short and interrogative; the policy says “Primary caregivers are entitled to 26 weeks…”. HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings, Gao et al. 2022) has an LLM write a plausible answer passage first, embeds that, and searches with it. Answer-shaped text lands nearer answer-shaped chunks, even if its details are wrong; the real chunks found are what the final answer uses.

chunks.h: HyDE: search with a hypothetical answer
chunks.x: Where it helps: dense retrieval with no domain-tuned model and a strong style gap between questions and documents.

chunks.h: HyDE: search with a hypothetical answer
chunks.x: Where it hurts: the hypothetical answer carries the model's prior. For private policies it invents generic specifics (“12 weeks, as is common”) that can steer the search toward the wrong section. It adds a generation of about 100–200 tokens before retrieval can even start (2–3 seconds at the 60 tokens a second section 11 assumes for a large model, under a second with a small fast one), and it does nothing for exact-token matching.

chunks.h: HyDE: search with a hypothetical answer
chunks.x: The alternative: embedding models trained on question–passage pairs (often with separate query and passage prefixes) already close much of the gap.

chunks.h: Decomposition for multi-part and multi-hop questions
chunks.x: Q4 asks two things that live in two documents. A single embedding of the whole question lands between them and may retrieve neither well. Decompose it: “Can parental leave be taken during the notice period?” and “Is unused leave paid out at exit?”, retrieve for each, then answer with both sets of passages.

chunks.h: Decomposition for multi-part and multi-hop questions
chunks.x: Independent parts run in parallel: one LLM call to split, then concurrent searches.

chunks.h: Decomposition for multi-part and multi-hop questions
chunks.x: Dependent parts (multi-hop) run in sequence: “What's the hotel cap for my manager's band?” needs the manager's band before it can look up the cap. Each hop adds a retrieval and usually an LLM call, and errors compound: a wrong first hop guarantees a wrong answer. An agent loop generalizes this (section 10).

Ask a more general question alongside the specific one (Zheng et al. 2023): for “Can I take parental leave during my notice period?”, also retrieve for “What are the rules on taking leave during a notice period?”. The general passage often states the principle the specific case follows, when no passage mentions the exact combination.

Before searching, decide whether to search: small talk needs no retrieval, a data question goes to SQL, an out-of-scope question gets a polite refusal, a policy question goes to the policy index with filters extracted from the text. A classifier costs milliseconds; an LLM router costs a call.
Latencies are rough rules of thumb for hosted models, not measurements; they depend on model size, output length and load.
