Retry transient errors only; idempotency keys. Timeouts at every level. Step limit 2–3× a typical run; block the third identical call. Checkpoint every step. Approvals by risk. 10-step run: 113,500 input + 3,000 output ≈ $0.39 at $3/$15; with a warm prefix cache ≈ $0.12. About 6.4 s a step. Prefix cache: stable content first, append only. Trace every model and tool call.
beginaligned pass@k &= 1 - binomn-ck Big/ binomnk \\ pass^k &= binomck Big/ binomnk \\ SE &= sqrtp(1-p)/n endaligned

Outcome (final state) → trajectory (in-order key calls, argument rules) → tool-call accuracy → efficiency → safety. 6 of 8: pass^1 0.75, pass^4 0.214. 100 tasks at 70%: ±9 points; 70 → 73 is noise. Simulated users with hidden goals, seeded sandboxes, several runs, regression suite on every change.

notes.title: Dialogue systems and how to measure them
notes.desc: How task bots understand a turn, track state, choose the next action and hand off to people; flows vs LLM agents vs hybrids; and the metrics bot teams live by (task success, containment, FCR, CSAT) and how each gets gamed.

sections.t: Understanding a turn: intents and slots
Deep dive: BIO tags and subword tokens
Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
Dialogue policy: deciding what to do next
Grounding in business data and knowledge
The system prompt of a support bot
Authenticating the user inside a conversation
What the bot saves, and why containment overstates it
Metrics that pull against each other
Beyond support: sales and healthcare bots
Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization

chunks.x: Dialogue systems and how to measure them · Deepam Minda

A task bot fills a frame and then acts on it. The classic pipeline splits the job into understanding (NLU), state tracking (DST), deciding the next action (policy) and wording it (NLG). An LLM agent does all four in one model. Bots in regulated domains are mostly hybrids: the LLM works out what the user means, and code decides what the bot is allowed to do.

NLU is intent classification plus slot filling. Slots are tagged as spans with BIO labels and then normalized (“dedh lakh” → 1,50,000; “kal” → tomorrow or yesterday, depending on the tense). A closed-set classifier always picks some intent, so out-of-scope requests need a threshold, chosen on real out-of-scope traffic. Slot F1 counts whole spans, so a boundary error costs a false positive and a false negative.

The dialogue state is cumulative, and corrections overwrite it. Joint goal accuracy asks whether every slot is right at a turn; slot accuracy averages over slots and is inflated by the many empty ones. One published tracker scores 48.6% on the first and 96.9% on the second, on the same data.

The policy picks the next action from the state. Confirm explicitly when the chance of a misunderstanding times the cost of acting on it is high, and implicitly when it's low. Reprompt with more help each time, disambiguate when two intents are close, and know when to hand off.

Containment counts a user who gave up as a win. Pair it with resolution: resolved containment, first-contact resolution, repeat contacts. Segment by intent, because a change in the intent mix can move the overall rate while every intent gets worse. CSAT only hears from the people who reached the survey.

Evaluate before launch with conversation test sets, LLM-simulated users, scripted regression suites and judged transcripts. A/B test with the user, not the conversation, as the unit. Then mine the logs: cluster the utterances the bot failed on, sort the failures into a taxonomy, and fix in order of volume × failure rate × the share you can actually fix.
A conversational system is a program that talks with a person over several turns, in text or speech. Three kinds differ in what “working” means:
Complete a task by collecting details and calling a backend
Schedule a repayment, book an appointment, block a card
The task is done correctly: a promise is recorded, a booking exists
Question answering / knowledge
Answer questions from documents and data
“What's the foreclosure charge?”, “Is this test covered?”
The answer is correct, grounded in the source, and complete
Keep a pleasant conversation going
Companion apps, small talk
Engagement and human ratings; there's no task
A real support bot mixes the first two and has to deal politely with the third. This note is about task-oriented bots and the knowledge answers they give along the way.

The running example. A consumer lender runs a repayment bot on WhatsApp chat and outbound voice calls. Its intents are check_due, pay_now, promise_to_pay (the customer commits to paying a set amount on a set date), payment_not_reflected (“paid, but it still shows pending”), loan_closure and agent (asks for a person). The customer in the worked dialogue owes an EMI of ₹12,400 that was due on 5 October, and today is Tuesday 13 October 2026.
Before LLMs, a task bot was a chain of separate models and rules, each with a narrow job. The names are still the vocabulary of the field, and an LLM bot still has to do each job somewhere:

The modular pipeline. Chat bots skip ASR and TTS. Each arrow carries a structured message: text, an intent with slots and a confidence, the state, a system action (“dialogue act”), text again. An LLM agent collapses the dashed box into one model that reads the conversation and calls tools; a hybrid keeps the policy box in code.
ASR turns speech into text, and TTS turns text back into speech. Both live in the voice agents note.
NLU (natural language understanding) reads one user turn and outputs an intent (what the user wants done), slots (the details: date, amount, mode) and a confidence. Section 02.
DST (dialogue state tracking) merges that turn into the state: everything the user has asked for so far, as slot–value pairs. Section 03.
The policy looks at the state and picks the next system action: ask for a missing slot, confirm a value, call a backend, answer, hand off. Section 04.
NLG (natural language generation) turns the action into words. Section 05.

Dialogue acts are the small vocabulary these parts use to talk to each other: the user can inform (“on Friday”), request (“how much is due?”), affirm, deny; the system can request(amount), confirm(date = Fri 16 Oct), inform(due = 12,400), offer. They matter because one string means different things after different questions. “Haan” (yes) after “Will you pay the full ₹12,400?” fills the amount slot; after “Shall I send the link?” it approves an action.

An LLM agent replaces the dashed box with one model, a system prompt and a set of tools. Each turn it reads the conversation so far, decides whether to call a tool (get_dues, schedule_promise) and writes the reply. The mechanics of tool calling and the reason-then-act loop live in the agents note. The parts haven't disappeared: the model still has to classify the intent, track the state and choose an action. They're now implicit, which makes them harder to test one by one.

A flow (or state machine) is a graph of steps written by the team: verify identity, read the disclosure, collect date, amount and mode, confirm, call the backend. A hybrid keeps that graph and lets an LLM do the language-heavy steps inside it: extract slots from a messy code-switched sentence, classify a free-text complaint, answer a policy question from documents with retrieval, phrase a reply, write the handoff summary. The other way round also counts as a hybrid: an LLM agent in charge, whose tools refuse to run unless code-checked preconditions hold.
Total: every path is written down
Low: behaviour emerges from the prompt
High on the steps that matter
Easy: disclosures are fixed text, steps can't be skipped
Hard to guarantee; needs guardrails and audits
Fixed steps for disclosures, identity and money
Coverage (off-script turns, long tail)
Poor: anything unplanned hits a fallback
Good: copes with digressions, corrections, mixed languages
Good inside the steps that use the LLM
Cost and latency per turn
Highest: long prompts, several calls per turn
High: the failing step is visible
Low: one opaque decision per turn
The step is visible; the LLM part inside it isn't
High: every path by hand, NLU training data
Low to start, high to make reliable
Edit the flow; behaviour changes only there
Edit the prompt; anything may change, so rerun every test
Local edits, plus tests for the LLM steps

Why regulated domains end up hybrid. Lending, insurance and healthcare have steps that must happen exactly: identify the person before discussing the debt, read a mandated disclosure verbatim, never move money without explicit confirmation, keep an audit trail. A prompt can make these likely but can't guarantee them, and “usually” isn't enough for a regulator. Meanwhile users speak in ways no hand-built NLU anticipated, which is exactly what LLMs are good at. So the split follows the risk: the LLM decides what the user means; code decides what the bot may do.

“We use an LLM agent, so we don't have NLU or state tracking.” You do; they're inside the prompt. When the bot schedules the wrong date, you still need to know whether it misheard (ASR), misunderstood (NLU), lost a correction (state) or chose badly (policy). That's why LLM bots log a structured state every turn and get evaluated part by part.

Say it in an interview: “For a lending support bot I'd build a hybrid: a flow owns identity checks, disclosures and anything that moves money, and an LLM handles understanding, slot extraction from code-switched speech, knowledge answers and phrasing. It keeps compliance deterministic while getting the coverage of an LLM, and when something fails I can see which step did it.”

chunks.h: Understanding a turn: intents and slots
chunks.x: NLU turns one user utterance into a structured guess: an intent, a set of slots and a confidence. For “main next Friday ko 5000 UPI se bhar dunga” (“I'll pay 5000 by UPI next Friday”) the output is promise_to_pay with date = “next Friday”, amount = “5000”, mode = “UPI”. Two separate problems hide in that: which intent (a classification problem) and which words are the details (a sequence labelling problem), followed by a third, what those words mean as values (normalization).
Intent classification is text classification: one label per utterance from a fixed list. The usual options, from cheapest to most flexible:
TF-IDF + logistic regression (classical text classifiers)
Dozens to hundreds per intent
Baseline; stable vocabulary; English-only or one script
Fine-tuned encoder (BERT, or a multilingual one such as MuRIL for Indian languages), the [CLS] vector into a softmax (how)
Rule of thumb: tens to a hundred per intent
Milliseconds on a CPU or small GPU
The production workhorse when the intent list is stable
Sentence embeddings + nearest examples or class centroids (embeddings)
Few-shot start; adding an intent means adding examples, no retraining
LLM with intent names, descriptions and a few examples in the prompt
Highest; hundreds of milliseconds
Long or changing intent lists, messy code-switched input, or when the LLM is already in the turn

Designing the intent list is half the work. An intent should correspond to a different next action, not just a different topic. “What's my EMI?” and “EMI kitna hai?” are one intent. “I can't pay this month” and “I'll pay on Friday” may be one intent (promise_to_pay) if the flow is the same, or two if one of them routes to a hardship team. Intents that lead to the same action but are kept separate only create confusions that cost nothing to merge. Real users also send two intents in one turn (“pay my EMI and tell me the closure amount”), so either allow multi-label output or handle one and queu

A classifier trained on six intents will assign every utterance to one of the six, including “what's the weather in Pune”. Its softmax probabilities sum to 1 over the known intents, so “none of these” isn't an option unless you build it in. And a high softmax score isn't evidence that the input is in scope: calibration is measured on data like the training data, and on inputs unlike it models are often confidently wrong. The ways to build it in:
Threshold the top probability: act only if the highest intent probability is at least t ; otherwise treat the turn as out of scope (or ask again).
Train an explicit out-of-scope class on real out-of-scope utterances from logs. Works for the kinds of out-of-scope you've seen, not for new ones.
Distance in embedding space: reject if the utterance is far from every intent's examples or centroid.
Ask an LLM with a “none of the above” option and descriptions of what the bot does and doesn't handle.
Worked example: choosing the threshold. Twelve held-out utterances: nine in scope and three out of scope, with the classifier's top intent and its probability.
paisa kat gaya par EMI pending dikha raha (money was debited but the EMI shows pending)
what's the weather in Pune
increase my credit card limit

Accept a prediction when its probability is at least t . Two numbers matter: in-scope accuracy (in-scope utterances accepted and classified correctly, out of 9; a rejection counts as an error) and out-of-scope recall (out-of-scope utterances rejected, out of 3).

In words: raising t trades in-scope accuracy for out-of-scope recall. Without a threshold the bot would treat “increase my credit card limit” as a loan closure, which is the expensive mistake. At 0.65 it catches all three out-of-scope requests and gives up two in-scope ones; above that it only loses more good turns.

Pick t from what each mistake costs, on a validation set that contains real out-of-scope traffic from logs, not invented examples: acting on a wrong intent (a wrong backend action, a confused user) against saying “sorry, I didn't get that” to a user the bot could have served. That's the general recipe for choosing a threshold; from business costs is the applied version.
Rejection isn't the end of the turn. A rejected turn gets a reprompt or a menu of what the bot can do (section 04), so a false reject costs a turn, not the conversation.

The benchmark result to quote: on CLINC150 (150 intents plus out-of-scope queries), classifiers did well in scope but struggled to recognise out-of-scope queries. Out-of-scope recall is the number to watch.

Row 9 is an in-scope utterance the classifier got wrong. At t = 0.6 it's rejected, and in-scope accuracy counts that as an error, but for the user it's an improvement: “sorry, could you say that differently?” beats being told the amount due when they're reporting a missing payment. Count “wrong intent acted on” separately; it's the error that hurts.

Slots are spans of the utterance: “next Friday” is a date, “5,000 rupees” is an amount. Finding them is sequence labelling: one tag per token. The standard scheme is BIO: B-x marks the first token of a slot of type x, I-x a token inside it, O a token outside any slot.
The same request, code-switched (“main … bhar dunga” is “I will pay”, “ko” marks the day, “se” means “by”):

Why B and I, not just “date”: with one tag per type, two slots of the same type side by side merge into one. ASR output has no commas, so “friday monday dono din” (“both days, Friday and Monday”) has two date tokens in a row: tagged date date it reads as one two-word date; tagged B-date B-date it's two dates. Adjacent same-type slots are rare, so plain per-type tags often score almost as well; B is cheap insurance.
The model: an encoder produces one vector per token, and a linear layer gives each token a softmax over the tags (the token-tagging head in BERT, end to end). Trained with cross-entropy per token.

Invalid sequences: a per-token softmax can output O I-date, which BIO forbids. A CRF (conditional random field) layer on top scores whole tag sequences: per-token scores plus a learned score for each tag-to-tag transition. It's trained on the log-likelihood of the whole gold sequence (the forward algorithm sums over all possible sequences) and decodes with Viterbi, the best-scoring sequence. It learns very low scores for transitions like O → I-date, so they rarely survive; to rule them out completely, set those transitions to −∞ at decoding (constrained decoding), which also works on a plain s

With an LLM there are no tags: you ask for "date": "next Friday", "amount": "5000", "mode": "UPI" as structured output. You lose the span positions (useful for highlighting and debugging), and evaluation becomes value matching after normalization rather than span matching.

chunks.h: Deep dive: BIO tags and subword tokens
chunks.x: Encoders split words into subword pieces: “Friday” may stay whole, but “dunga” might become “dun” + “##ga”, and “12,400” several pieces. The labels are per word, so they have to be aligned with the pieces.

chunks.h: Deep dive: BIO tags and subword tokens
chunks.x: Training: give each word's label to its first piece and mark the other pieces “ignore” (label −100 in PyTorch's cross-entropy), so each word counts once in the loss. The alternative, copying the label to every piece (turning a B into I for the later pieces), weights long words more.

chunks.h: Deep dive: BIO tags and subword tokens
chunks.x: Inference: read the prediction at each word's first piece, then rebuild spans from the word-level tags.

chunks.h: Deep dive: BIO tags and subword tokens
chunks.x: Why it matters here: Romanized Hindi is rare in most pretraining data, so its words break into many short pieces, and an amount like “1,50,000” in Indian digit grouping breaks differently from “150,000”. Check that the span reconstruction handles both before trusting the slot F1.

A tagged span is still text. The backend needs a date, an integer amount, a valid phone number. Normalization maps the span to a canonical value, relative to a reference date and the user's time zone. With today as Tuesday 13 October 2026:
“kal dunga” (I'll give it kal)
“kal” is both tomorrow and yesterday in Hindi; the tense decides
“kal pay kiya tha” (I paid kal)
Day after tomorrow (or before yesterday, by tense)
Genuinely ambiguous on a Tuesday: confirm it
5 October has passed, so the next one (23 days out, so it then fails a 10-day promise window)
May fall on a weekend or holiday when payments don't settle
“5k”, “paanch hazaar”, “five thousand”
Three languages for one number
“dedh” = one and a half; lakh = 100,000; Indian digit grouping
“dhai hazaar”, “do hazaar”
“dhai” = two and a half; “do” = two, not the English verb
“nine eight double four five triple zero one two”
“double”, “triple”; then check 10 digits starting 6–9. On voice the ASR may already have turned the words into digits (ASR)
Strip the country code or trunk 0 before validating

Do it in deterministic code, not in the LLM. Date arithmetic, lakh conversions and digit counting are where LLMs slip, and they're easy to unit test in code. Let the model extract the raw span (“Friday”); let a parser turn it into 16 October.

Then validate against business rules: the amount is between a minimum and the amount due; a promise date is within the window policy allows; the phone number is the registered one. A valid-looking but disallowed value (“end of month”, 18 days away when the policy allows 10) goes back to the user with the allowed range.
When it's ambiguous, ask. “This Friday the 16th, or the 23rd?” costs one turn; scheduling the wrong date costs a broken promise and a follow-up call.

Intent and slots inform each other: “5000” is an amount in a payment request but could be part of a loan number in a closure request. A joint model shares one encoder between two heads, the [CLS] vector into an intent softmax and every token vector into a tag softmax, and trains on the sum of the two cross-entropy losses. One forward pass serves both tasks, and the shared encoder learns features useful to both. JointBERT reported about 97.5% intent accuracy and 96.1 slot F1 on ATIS, and 98.6% and 97.0 on SNIPS; sentence-level accuracy (intent and every slot right) was lower, 88.2% and 92.8%, w
Intents: accuracy hides the rare ones. A test set of 100 utterances has 70 check_due, 20 pay_now and 10 fraud_report. A model that never predicts fraud_report (it calls those check_due) scores:
0 (never predicted; 0 by convention)
Accuracy 0.90; macro F1 0.644; weighted F1 0.853

In words: 90% accuracy, and every fraud report goes to the wrong place. Macro F1 (the plain average over intents) exposes it; weighted F1 mostly doesn't. Report macro F1 and the recall of each high-stakes intent, and read the confusion matrix to see which intents get mixed up (precision, recall and the confusion matrix).
Slots: score spans, not tokens. A predicted slot counts as correct only if its type and both boundaries match a gold slot exactly (the CoNLL convention). Four test utterances:
I'll pay 5,000 rupees next Friday through UPI
amount, date “next Friday”, mode
amount, date “Friday”, mode
2 right; the date's boundary is wrong: 1 FP + 1 FN
main next Friday ko 5000 UPI se bhar dunga
2 right; mode missed: 1 FN
paid 3000 yesterday by card
loan_id “3000”, date, mode
2 right; wrong type: 1 FP + 1 FN
11 gold spans, 10 predicted spans, 8 correct:
beginaligned P &= fraccorrect spanspredicted spans = frac810 = 0.800 \\ R &= fraccorrect spansgold spans = frac811 = 0.727 \\ F_1 &= frac2PRP + R = 0.762 endaligned

In words: of the slots the model found, 80% were exactly right; of the slots that were there, it found 73%. The same predictions score 23 of 27 tokens right (85.2% token accuracy), because most tokens are O and easy. Only 1 of the 4 utterances has every slot right.

A boundary error is punished twice. Predicting “Friday” instead of “next Friday” adds a wrong span (FP) and misses the right one (FN). Some teams also report a lenient score that credits overlaps, which is fine as a diagnostic, but quote the strict one. And for the business, the slot that matters is the normalized value: “Friday” and “next Friday” may resolve to the same date, or to dates a week apart.

In Indian markets users mix languages within a sentence (“UPI se. Actually Friday kar do”), write Hindi in Latin script with no fixed spelling (nahi, nahin, nai; kal, kaal), and switch scripts between messages. On voice, the text NLU sees is an ASR transcript: no punctuation or casing, disfluencies (“woh… matlab… five, no, six thousand”), and errors that land on exactly the words that matter: fifteen and fifty, a Hindi “do” (two) heard as the English word.

Train and test on what the model will really see. A model trained on clean typed English and served ASR transcripts of code-switched speech has a training–serving skew. Collect real transcripts, label them, and keep them in the test set.
Normalize the surface first: transliterate or standardize spellings, map number words in every language to digits, strip fillers. It shrinks the vocabulary the model must learn.

Use models that have seen the languages: multilingual encoders pretrained on Indian languages (MuRIL, which also saw transliterated text; IndicBERT), or an LLM, which handles code-switching far better than a classifier trained on a few hundred examples.
Use the ASR's uncertainty: pass the confidence of the slot words, or the n-best list, to the policy, so a low-confidence amount gets confirmed (section 04).

Measure the errors that matter: overall word error rate weights “uh” and “₹5,000” equally. Track the error rate on the key slots (amounts, dates, names) and the intent accuracy on ASR output, end to end.

Say it in an interview: “NLU is intent classification plus slot filling. I'd tag slots with BIO, normalize them in code against a reference date, and validate them against business rules. For out-of-scope I'd threshold the confidence, picking the threshold on real out-of-scope traffic by what a wrong action costs against a reprompt. I'd report macro F1 with recall on high-stakes intents, and strict span F1 for slots, measured on ASR transcripts of code-switched speech rather than clean text.”

NLU reads one turn. A task needs everything the user has said so far, with later statements overriding earlier ones. Dialogue state tracking maintains that: the dialogue state is the frame, one value or “none” per slot, plus the active intent, updated every turn. (Strictly, a belief state is a probability distribution over possible states; most trackers keep only the top value per slot.)

Why not just use the latest turn's slots? Because details arrive spread over turns, users correct themselves, “haan” means nothing without the question it answers, and references like “same as last time” point back. The tracker's job is the running total.

The promise_to_pay frame has four slots: date, amount, mode (how they'll pay) and channel (where to send the payment link). The bot has just said the ₹12,400 EMI is overdue and asked if the customer can pay today.
“Abhi nahi ho payega, Thursday ko kar dunga.” (Can't right now, I'll do it Thursday.)
Bot: “Will you pay the full ₹12,400 on Thursday?”“Nahi, abhi sirf 5000.” (No, only 5000 for now.)
Bot: “How will you pay: UPI, card or net banking?”“UPI se. Actually Friday kar do, salary Friday ko aati hai.” (By UPI. Actually make it Friday, my salary comes on Friday.)
Bot: “So ₹5,000 by UPI on Friday 16 October. Shall I send the payment link?”“Haan, WhatsApp pe bhej do.” (Yes, send it on WhatsApp.)
What happened at each turn, as operations on the frame:
Add. “Thursday” is normalized against today (Tuesday) to 15 October. The other slots stay empty; nothing is guessed.

Add, after a “no”. “Nahi” denies the offered default (the full ₹12,400), and “sirf 5000” fills the amount. A tracker that had filled amount = 12,400 from the bot's opening message would now overwrite it.

Add and overwrite in one turn. The user answers the question (mode) and, unasked, changes the date. “Actually” is a correction cue; the later value wins. A frame lets the user fill or change any slot in any order, which is what makes mixed initiative possible (section 04).
Confirm and add. “Haan” affirms the three values the bot read back, so they're marked confirmed, and “WhatsApp” fills the channel. Now the policy can call the backend.

The full set of update operations is small: add a value, overwrite it (a correction), delete it (“not Thursday” clears the date and the bot asks again), keep it (carry over, the default), and confirm it. Changing a confirmed value un-confirms it.

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Evaluate a tracker by comparing its state with the gold state after every user turn. Two metrics, which tell very different stories:

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: beginaligned JGA &= frac1Tsum_t=1^T 1big[hat s_t = s_tbig] \\ slot accuracy &= frac1T Ssum_t=1^Tsum_j=1^S 1big[hat s_t,j = s_t,jbig] endaligned

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: In words: joint goal accuracy is the share of turns where the predicted state matches the gold state on every slot (a turn with one wrong slot scores 0). Slot accuracy is the share of (turn, slot) pairs that match, empty slots included. T is the number of turns and S the number of slots.

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Two trackers on the dialogue above (4 turns × 4 slots):

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Misses the correction at turn 3 and keeps Thursday

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Copies ₹12,400 from the bot's opening message into the amount at turn 1

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Errors carry. Tracker A made one mistake, at turn 3, but the state is cumulative, so it stays wrong at turn 4 too and costs two turns of JGA. Tracker B's mistake was fixed by the user's next answer. The longer the conversation after an uncaught error, the more it costs.

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Slot accuracy is inflated by empty slots. Real schemas have many slots, most of them empty in any one conversation. With 30 slots of which 4 are filled, a tracker that predicts “none” for everything scores 26/30 = 86.7% slot accuracy and 0% JGA. One wrong slot in a turn still scores 29/30 = 96.7%.

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: The published contrast: TRADE, a tracker over 30 domain–slot pairs in MultiWOZ, reported 48.62% joint goal accuracy and 96.92% slot accuracy on the same predictions. Lead with JGA, and add F1 over the slots that are filled.

chunks.h: Joint goal accuracy and slot accuracy
chunks.x: Offline DST evaluation replays a logged conversation, so the bot's side is fixed. In production a wrong state changes what the bot says next (it confirms Thursday, the user has to object, the conversation goes somewhere the log never went). Offline JGA therefore understates what a tracking error costs live; end-to-end task success catches it.
Before LLMs, trackers predicted each slot's value from the dialogue history in one of three ways:
Pick from a list: for slots with a small set of values (mode: UPI, card, net banking), classify over the candidates. Accurate, but it can't produce a value that isn't on the list.
Extract a span: for open values (names, times), point to the start and end of the value in the conversation, like extractive question answering. It can only return words that were said.

Generate: write the value token by token, copying words from the dialogue when useful. TRADE works this way: for every domain–slot pair, a small slot gate first decides none (not mentioned), dontcare or generate, and only then is a value generated. LLM trackers are the same idea at scale.

dontcare is a value, not an absence. “Jo bhi ho, koi bhi mode” (any mode is fine) fills mode = dontcare: the user has answered, so the bot must not ask again, and the backend may choose. Treating it as empty makes the bot repeat a question the user already answered.

With an LLM the tracker becomes a prompt: the slot schema (names, descriptions, allowed values), the current state, the last few turns, and an instruction to output the updated state as JSON (structured output). Describing slots in natural language is what lets one model track new slots without retraining, the idea the Schema-Guided Dialogue dataset was built to test.

Predict the change, not the whole state, when you can: the model outputs "date": "Friday" and code merges it. Asking for the full state each turn lets the model silently drop or alter slots it wasn't asked about.
Raw values out, normalization in code. The model returns “Friday”; the parser makes it 16 October. Validate types and allowed values; on a failure, re-ask the model or ask the user.

Typical failures: filling a slot the user never gave (tracker B copied ₹12,400 from the bot's own message), keeping a value after the user changed topic, missing a correction buried mid-sentence, and losing early details in long conversations (keep the state in code, not only in the context; see agent memory).
Evaluate it the same way: replay logged conversations, compute JGA and per-slot F1, and keep the failures as regression cases.

The customer who promised ₹5,000 on the outbound call may message on WhatsApp the next day. The bot should open with “Your ₹5,000 payment for Friday is noted. Shall I resend the link?”, not “How can I help you?”.
Key the state on the authenticated customer, not the session or phone line, and reveal it only after authentication in the new channel (section 06).
Give slots an expiry. A promise date that has passed, or a half-finished flow from three weeks ago, should be dropped or confirmed again, not silently reused.
Store the structured state plus a short summary, with the channel and time of each update, so a later conversation (or a human agent) can see what was agreed and where.

Say it in an interview: “The state is the running frame of slot values. Each turn adds, overwrites, deletes or confirms values, and corrections overwrite. I'd evaluate with joint goal accuracy, because slot accuracy is inflated by empty slots: one published tracker scored 49% joint and 97% slot accuracy. With an LLM I'd have it output state changes as structured JSON, normalize and validate in code, and watch for invented values.”

chunks.h: Dialogue policy: deciding what to do next
chunks.x: The dialogue policy maps the current state (plus the latest NLU result and any backend facts) to the next system action. The action set is small and the same in every bot: request a missing slot, confirm a value, inform (answer), offer options, call a backend tool, reprompt after a failure, hand off, end. In the running dialogue the policy chose: request amount, request mode, confirm all three values, then call schedule_promise.

Most production policies are hand-written. For a form-like task the rule is: if a required slot is empty, request it; once all are filled, confirm; once confirmed, call the backend. Branches handle the rest (amount below the minimum, a promise date outside the window, a customer who says they already paid). A frame-based flow asks in a fixed order but accepts any slot at any time, so a user who says everything in one breath skips the questions.

Flows are predictable, auditable and cheap, and they fail at the edges: every situation the designer didn't write down ends in a fallback. They also grow without limit, as each newly discovered edge case becomes another branch.

Treat the next action as a label and learn it: the features are the state and recent history, the label is what a good agent did next, and the training data comes from human-agent conversations or Wizard-of-Oz collections (a person secretly plays the bot). Transformer policies over the dialogue history, such as Rasa's TED policy, work this way. Two weaknesses: the model imitates the agents' habits, good and bad, and the states the bot reaches after its own mistakes never appear in the human logs, so it hasn't learned what to do there. That second one is the standard weakness of behaviour cloni

Dialogue is a sequence of decisions with a payoff at the end, which is the setting of reinforcement learning: the state is the dialogue state, an action is a system act, and the reward is a bonus for task success minus a cost per turn. With +20 for success and −1 per turn, finishing in 5 turns earns 15 and in 8 turns 12, so the policy learns to be brief, while failing after 3 turns earns only −3. That exposes the classic flaw: a hard case that would succeed in 25 turns earns −5, worse than giving up early, so without a failure penalty (say −10, making early surrender −13) the policy learns to

In an LLM agent, the model chooses the next action itself, by calling a tool or replying. That covers any situation language can describe, and it needs guardrails in code, because the model will sometimes choose an action it shouldn't:
An allow-list of actions per stage: before authentication only FAQ answers and handoff are available; account tools aren't even offered to the model.
Preconditions in the tool, not the prompt: schedule_promise refuses unless the state holds confirmed date, amount and mode, and the amount and date pass validation.
Hard limits: a maximum number of turns and tool calls; forbidden topics and phrases checked on the output (guardrails).
Before acting on what it understood, the bot can check it.
Explicit confirmation asks a yes/no question: “You'll pay ₹5,000 on Friday the 16th, right?” Safe, and always costs a turn.
Implicit confirmation echoes the value inside the next question: “Okay, Friday the 16th. How will you pay?” Free when it's right; when it's wrong, the user has to notice and object, and some won't.

Which to use is an expected-cost question. Let p be the chance the understood value is wrong, q the chance a user notices a wrong implicit echo and corrects it (one extra turn), and C the cost of acting on a wrong value, in turn-equivalents (a broken promise, a follow-up call):
beginaligned explicit &= 1 + p \\ implicit &= pbig(q cdot 1 + (1 - q)\,Cbig) \\ none &= p\,C \\ p^* &= frac1q + (1 - q)\,C - 1 endaligned

In words: explicit always costs the question, plus a fix when wrong. Implicit costs nothing when right; when wrong, it costs a correction if the user notices and the full damage if not. Explicit wins once the error rate passes p^* , found by setting the first two equal. The model assumes users always catch a wrong explicit read-back; in practice some say “yes” anyway, especially to long read-backs on voice, which is one more reason to keep read-backs short.

With q = 0.7 : for a slot whose error costs 20 turn-equivalents, implicit is cheaper until p^* = 1/5.7 = 0.175 . For an action that costs 200 (moving money, an irreversible booking), p^* = 1/59.7 = 0.017 : confirm explicitly almost always. That's the reasoning behind common practice:
Confidence bands: high NLU or ASR confidence on a value → implicit; middle → explicit; low → re-ask. The cut-offs come from the error rate observed in each confidence band, not from a guess.
One explicit confirmation before the irreversible step, reading back all the values at once (“₹5,000 by UPI on Friday the 16th?”): one turn instead of three, at the point where C is largest.
Confirm values, not intents. “You want to make a promise to pay, is that right?” wastes a turn; the read-back of the values confirms the intent too.

Two failure events need different handling: no-match (the user said something the bot couldn't use) and no-input (silence on voice, or no reply on chat). The pattern is an escalating ladder, with a counter per slot and one per conversation:
Rephrase briefly: “Sorry, which day will you pay?” Never repeat the identical prompt; if it didn't work once, it won't work twice.
Add help: say what kind of answer works. “You can say a day, like Friday, or a date, like the 20th.”
Constrain: offer choices, buttons on chat or keypad options on voice (“press 1 for this week, 2 for next week”).
Hand off (section 07), or offer a callback.

Two more rules. Keep what was understood: if the amount came through and the date didn't, ask only for the date. And when a backend call fails, say so plainly and offer an alternative; don't make the user retry something they did right.

When the top two intents are close, a guess is a coin flip. If “I want to do the EMI thing” gives pay_now 0.46 and check_due 0.41 (a margin of 0.05), ask a choice question that names both: “Do you want to pay now, or check how much is due?” It costs one turn, and a wrong guess costs more (a payment flow started for someone who wanted information, then a correction). The trigger is a small margin between the top two, a different test from the out-of-scope threshold on the top one. The same applies to entities: a customer with two loans gets “the bike loan or the phone loan?”, not the first loan

Initiative is who steers. In system initiative the bot asks and the user answers (classic IVR menus); robust, rigid. In user initiative the user asks and the bot answers (an FAQ bot). In mixed initiative either can take over: the user gives three slots at once, changes a value unasked, or breaks off mid-flow with “wait, what's the closure amount?”. The frame handles over-answering and corrections. Digressions need a stack: answer the side question, then return to the interrupted task (“…and for Friday's payment, how will you pay?”). LLMs handle mixed initiative naturally; flows have to be buil

Say it in an interview: “The policy maps state to the next act. In production it's mostly flows, with an LLM choosing inside guardrails enforced in code. I confirm explicitly when the error probability times the cost of acting on a wrong value is high, which for money movement is almost always, and implicitly otherwise. Reprompts escalate from rephrasing to examples to choices to handoff, and a small top-two margin triggers a disambiguation question.”
The policy outputs an act, such as confirm(amount=5000, date=2026-10-16, mode=UPI). Generation turns it into words in the right language, length and tone.
One reviewed sentence per act, with slots filled in: “So that's ₹amount by mode on day, date. Shall I send the payment link?”
The model phrases the act from the act, the state and a style guide
Exact, compliant, cheap, translatable once and reviewed
Natural, varied, handles off-script turns, mirrors the user's language mix
Robotic, repetitive, breaks on unplanned situations
Can change a number, add a promise, drift in tone, cost latency
Disclosures, amounts and dates before an action, legal text
Small talk, explanations, empathy, rephrasing after failures

chunks.h: Grounding in business data and knowledge
chunks.x: Facts come from tools, never from the model. The amount due, dates and charges are fetched and passed in; the model only phrases them.

chunks.h: Grounding in business data and knowledge
chunks.x: Check the output against the facts. A cheap deterministic check: every number and date in the reply must appear in the act or tool result. If “₹5,000” went in and “₹5,500” came out, fall back to the template. This catches the most damaging generation error in money conversations.

chunks.h: Grounding in business data and knowledge
chunks.x: Knowledge answers (“what are the foreclosure charges?”) come from retrieved documents (retrieval-augmented generation, with its failure modes). When retrieval finds nothing relevant, the bot should say it doesn't know and offer a person, not improvise a policy.
Persona and tone: a name, a register (the respectful “aap” form in Hindi), how much warmth, what it never says (no blame, no shaming, no jokes about money owed).

Voice is different from chat: one or two short sentences per turn, the question at the end, no lists or links, numbers written the way they should be spoken (“twelve thousand four hundred rupees”), since a long turn invites interruptions (see TTS and turn-taking).

Compliance phrases are templates, never paraphrased: that this is an automated call, that it's recorded, who is calling and why. Some rules constrain the conversation itself: in India, regulator instructions since 2022 bar recovery calls before 8 a.m. and after 7 p.m. and prohibit threatening or humiliating language, and a healthcare bot must not diagnose and must route emergencies at once. Check transcripts for the mandatory phrases and for banned ones automatically.

Mirror the user: answer in the language and script they use, including a Hindi–English mix if that's how they write. Replying in formal Devanagari Hindi to a user who writes casual Romanized Hindi mixed with English sounds odd and is harder for them to read.
Translate critical templates once, with human review, rather than letting a model translate disclosures or amounts on the fly; machine translation is often weakest on negation and numbers.
Format for the locale: ₹1,50,000 in Indian grouping, dates as people say them, and amounts spoken in the user's language.

Say it in an interview: “Templates for anything compliance-bound or about to trigger an action, LLM generation for the rest, and the LLM only phrases facts that came from tools. A deterministic check that every number in the reply appears in the tool output catches the worst failures. On voice, short turns, the question last, and amounts spelled for speech.”
Most new bots put an LLM at the centre. What decides whether it's safe to ship is the scaffolding around it.

chunks.h: The system prompt of a support bot
chunks.x: A system prompt is a specification. A workable skeleton for the repayment bot:

chunks.h: The system prompt of a support bot
chunks.x: # Role and scope You are the repayment assistant of a consumer lender. You help customers check dues, pay, schedule a payment, and report payments that haven't shown up. Anything else: offer to connect them to a person. # Facts Use only amounts, dates and charges returned by tools. If a tool didn't return it, you don't know it. # Rules - Never offer waivers, discounts or extensions. - Before schedule_promise, read back amount, date and mode, and get a clear yes. - If the customer asks for a person, is distressed, or mentions fraud, call handoff with a summary. - Never threaten, shame or pressu

chunks.h: The system prompt of a support bot
chunks.x: Rules in the prompt are requests, not guarantees. Every rule that matters also lives in code: the tool checks for the confirmation, the output filter checks for banned phrases.

chunks.h: The system prompt of a support bot
chunks.x: The prompt is code: versioned, reviewed, and run against the regression suite (section 09) on every change, because a one-line edit can change behaviour anywhere.

Long conversations outgrow the context, and long contexts get followed less reliably. Keep three things: the structured state in code (the source of truth for slots and what's been done), a running summary of older turns, and the last few turns verbatim. The mechanics are in agent memory. What's specific to dialogue: a summary is lossy and can be wrong, so facts the bot will act on (amounts, dates, consent) are read from the structured state, never from the summary.
The bot acts through tools such as get_dues(), create_payment_link(amount), schedule_promise(date, amount, mode) and handoff(reason, summary) (mechanics in tool calling). For account actions:
The customer ID comes from the authenticated session, never from an argument the model fills. Otherwise “check the dues on loan 4471” is a data leak waiting for someone to try it.
Validate every argument in code (types, ranges, the policy window) and return a clear error the model can relay.
Make money actions idempotent: pass an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout doesn't create two payment links or two promises.
Log every call with its arguments, result and the turn that triggered it; this is the audit trail and the raw material for evaluation.

The characteristic failure of an LLM support bot is not a wrong fact about the world but a made-up policy or promise: “yes, the late fee can be waived”, “you can pay in three instalments”. In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), a British Columbia tribunal found the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation: its website chatbot wrongly said a bereavement fare could be claimed after travel, and the airline was ordered to pay the fare difference as damages. Its argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own words was rejected. Defences: ground answers in retrieved policy text, refuse when t

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: Identification is who the user claims to be; authentication is proof. The factors available in a conversation, roughly from weakest to strongest:

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: The channel identity: the WhatsApp number or caller ID matches the registered number. Useful as a first signal; caller ID can be spoofed.

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: Knowledge questions: date of birth, the last four digits of the loan account. Weak against anyone who knows the customer or has seen a statement.

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: A one-time password sent to the registered mobile: the common standard for account actions.

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: Voice biometrics: convenient, but now threatened by cloned voices; use as one factor among several.

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: Match the factor to the risk (step-up authentication): general questions need none, reading out the amount due needs a basic check, and changing the registered phone number needs an OTP and often a person. The authentication state lives in code and the tools check it; the model never decides that a user is verified. On outbound collection calls there's a step before all this: confirm you're speaking to the right person (“Am I speaking with Rahul Sharma?”) before mentioning the debt, because disclosing it to a family member or colleague is a serious violation. Mask account numbers in replies an

chunks.h: Authenticating the user inside a conversation
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “The prompt states the scope and rules, but every rule that matters is enforced in code: the customer ID comes from the authenticated session, tools validate their arguments and refuse without confirmation, money actions are idempotent, and outputs are checked against tool results. The real risk is the bot inventing a policy, so answers are grounded in retrieved policy text and commitments only happen through tools.”

A handoff (escalation, transfer) moves the conversation to a human agent. Too early and the bot saves nothing; too late and the customer arrives angry, having repeated themselves three times. The decision has to be explicit, logged with a reason, and measured.
“Mujhe kisi insaan se baat karni hai” (I want to talk to a person)
Two consecutive no-matches; the same slot asked three times; a reprompt ladder exhausted
The bot can't parse the date after three tries
Low confidence on something important
Confidence below threshold on a high-cost action
An ambiguous request to close the loan
Negative sentiment after a few turns, repeated words, all-caps, swearing
“I've told you THREE times”
Fraud, a death in the family, harassment complaints, legal threats, medical emergencies
“Someone took a loan in my name”
Beyond the bot's authority
A request only a person may grant
A fee waiver, a restructuring request
Two wrong OTPs (route to a secure process, not just a queue)
Many turns without a slot filled or a task done
A long, circular conversation

Honour explicit requests quickly. One acceptable pattern: if the task is nearly done, offer both in one turn (“I can send the link right now, or connect you to someone. Which would you like?”), and transfer on the second ask. Making people fight their way to a human is the most common way bots inflate containment (section 08), and it shows up in complaints.
High-stakes intents skip the bot's attempts entirely. A fraud report shouldn't go through a reprompt ladder.
Check that someone is there. Outside agent hours or with a long queue, offer a callback with the context saved instead of a transfer into a 20-minute wait.

A cold transfer drops the customer into a queue and the agent starts from nothing: “How can I help you?”, and the customer repeats everything. A warm transfer hands over the context before the agent speaks (on voice, sometimes with a brief introduction), so the agent opens with “I see your payment from the 9th isn't showing; let me check that.” What to pass:
Sets the agent's first move (a frustrated customer vs a fraud report)
No re-asking for what's known
Authentication status and method
Whether the agent must verify again (by policy)
“Payment link sent at 10:42”, “promise recorded for Fri 16 Oct”
Read in five seconds; generated from the state and transcript
Sentiment and language preference
Tone, and which agent pool (a Tamil speaker, a senior agent)
For the details the summary dropped
The escalation rate alone says nothing about whether escalations were right. Review samples and track:
Avoidable escalations: of a reviewed sample of handoffs, how many the bot could have handled. If 50 of 200 were avoidable, 25% of escalations are waste, and their reasons point at what to fix.

Missed escalations: of a reviewed sample of contained conversations, how many should have gone to a person (a fraud mention the bot ignored, a customer looping until they left). If 30 of 300 should have, 10% of “contained” conversations were failures that containment counted as wins.
Time to handoff: turns before the transfer. Long times on conversations that were always going to escalate mean the bot is wasting the customer's patience.
Re-ask rate: how often the agent asks for something the bot already had. That measures the handoff context.
After the handoff: agent handle time (warm transfers should shorten it), resolution, CSAT, and the agents' own rating of the summaries.
The logic itself is short; see the handoff function in the pseudocode (section 12).

Say it in an interview: “Escalate on an explicit request, repeated failure, frustration, high-stakes intents, anything beyond the bot's authority, or authentication trouble, with high-stakes intents going straight to a person. Transfer warm, with the reason, slots, auth status, actions taken and a short summary, so nobody repeats themselves. Then measure avoidable and missed escalations from reviewed samples, not just the rate.”

These are the numbers conversational AI teams report every week, set targets on, and get paid against. Each one is a ratio, and almost every argument about a bot's performance turns out to be about a numerator, a denominator or a time window. The first question to ask about any of them is “out of what, and over how long?”. Vendors define them differently: one platform's documentation, for example, counts a session as resolved when the user answers “yes” to “did that answer your question?” or doesn't answer at all.

Ten conversations from eight customers over four days. For escalated conversations, “task done” means the human agent resolved it. A repeat contact is the same customer contacting again about the same intent within 7 days.

Two repeats hide in it: U3 came back (c7) after the first escalation didn't fix the missing payment, and U5 came back (c9) after the bot's answer about loan closure didn't help. That gives 8 distinct issues (customer + intent) in 10 conversations.

Where the ten conversations ended. Containment counts every conversation that didn't reach a person, including the three conversations in orange that solved nothing. Resolved containment counts only the green leaf.

The three that cause the most confusion, written out:

beginaligned containment &= frac\#\,conversations not transferred\#\,conversations = frac710 \\ resolved containment &= frac\#\,(not transferred wedge task done wedge no repeat in 7 days)\#\,conversations = frac410 \\ FCR &= frac\#\,issues resolved at the first contact, no repeat in 7 days\#\,issues = frac48 endaligned

In words: containment asks only whether a person got involved. Resolved containment also asks whether the problem was solved and stayed solved. FCR is per issue, not per conversation, and gives no credit when an issue needed a second contact, however it was eventually resolved. It counts an issue as resolved at first contact whoever resolved it within that contact, the bot or the agent it was transferred to; in the toy log all four happen to be bot-resolved, which is why its numerator equals resolved containment's.

Task success needs a definition of “done” you can check. Best: an end state in a system of record (the promise exists in the database, the payment arrived), which is how τ-bench scores agents. Next best: an explicit confirmation from the user, or a labelled review. Weakest: the bot reached its last step.

Containment and deflection are different things. Containment is measured inside the bot's logs. Deflection is measured at the contact-centre level: contacts resolved through self-service that would otherwise have reached an agent. It's best estimated against a holdout or a baseline of agent volume, and every organization defines it a little differently, so ask how.

Abandonment needs care. c6 left after one fallback, but if the bot had shown the amount due in its first message and the customer then left, that's a silent success. Separate “left before the answer” from “left after it”, and use repeat contacts to tell which.

FCR depends on the window: 7 days is a common choice; a longer window catches more repeats and lowers FCR. Repeats through other channels (the customer phones the branch) only count if you join the logs by customer.

chunks.h: What the bot saves, and why containment overstates it
chunks.x: The business case for a support bot is usually a cost model. Suppose 100,000 contacts a month, a human contact costing ₹60 and a bot conversation ₹8 (both assumptions; one vendor's guidance quotes roughly $5–10 per human-handled contact against about $0.50 per resolved bot session). Every contact starts with the bot; the escalated 30% go to a person, and of the 30% contained but unresolved, half come back to a person within the week:

chunks.h: What the bot saves, and why containment overstates it
chunks.x: beginaligned savings &= Nbig(c_h - c_b - c_h\,(e + r\,u)big) \\ &= 100,000 times big(60 - 8 - 60 times (0.30 + 0.5 times 0.30)big) \\ &= 100,000 times 25 = 25 lakh rupees a month endaligned

chunks.h: What the bot saves, and why containment overstates it
chunks.x: In words: each of the N contacts saves the human cost c_h , minus the bot's cost c_b , minus the human cost again for the share that still reaches a person: e escalated, plus the fraction r of the unresolved-contained share u that comes back. Without the bot the month costs ₹60 lakh; with it, ₹8 lakh for the bot and ₹27 lakh for 45,000 human contacts, ₹35 lakh in all, a 42% saving. Counting containment alone (only the 30% escalated reach a person) gives ₹34 lakh, overstating the saving by ₹9 lakh, or 36%. Two more effects push the same way: the contacts that do reach people are the hard ones,

CSAT asks one question after the conversation (“How satisfied were you?”, 1 to 5). NPS asks how likely the customer is to recommend the company, so it measures the relationship more than the conversation and moves slowly. Both are biased in ways that matter for bots:

Survivorship: a survey shown at the end of the conversation never reaches customers who abandon (and if it's shown only at the end of the bot flow, transferred customers miss it too). In the toy log the survey ran at the end of every finished conversation, bot or human: both transferred customers who answered had finished, and neither abandoner answered.
Non-response: response rates are low, and those who answer skew to the very pleased and the very annoyed. A CSAT built from a small, self-selected group can move without anything changing.
Attribution: customers rate the outcome, not the bot. “You can't waive my fee” gets a 1 even when the bot did exactly the right thing.
Timing: asked before the payment link has been tried, the answer can't reflect whether it worked.
Small numbers per segment: 40 responses for one intent give an interval of roughly ±15 points; don't rank intents on that (intervals are in hypothesis testing).

Fixes: sample the survey across all outcomes, including by SMS after abandoned and transferred conversations; read it alongside behavioural measures (repeat contacts, complaints); and add an LLM-judged satisfaction score on every transcript, calibrated against the survey answers where both exist (LLM-as-judge).
Containment is cheap to raise without helping anyone, which is why it can't be the only target:
hide or remove the “talk to an agent” option, or require several asks before a transfer;
loop on reprompts until the customer gives up (abandonment counts as contained);
end the conversation after any answer, relevant or not, and call it resolved;
tell people to call back later, or to visit a branch;
count “no reply to the satisfaction question” as success.
The toy log, gamed. Version B removes the agent option. The three conversations that escalated now loop (four more turns, two more fallbacks each) and end in abandonment. Recomputing:
Issues eventually resolved
Average user turns; fallback rate
CSAT, end-of-conversation survey
CSAT, SMS survey reaching everyone

In words: containment hits 100% while the share of customers whose problem got fixed falls from 75% to 50%, because the two that a person used to fix now go nowhere. The end-of-conversation CSAT even rises, since the unhappy customers no longer reach the survey; surveyed by SMS, the three trapped customers answer 1 and pull top-2-box down to 3/6 = 50%. Resolved containment doesn't move, and the people who got stuck reappear as abandonment, extra fallbacks and, outside the bot's logs, calls to the branch.

chunks.h: Metrics that pull against each other
chunks.x: The standard answer is a small metric tree: one decision metric that already includes resolution (resolved containment, or issues resolved per customer at a given cost), and guardrails that must not get worse (CSAT sampled across all outcomes, complaints, compliance violations, missed escalations). This is the same structure as an experiment's decision metric and guardrails.

Leading (same day, per turn, plenty of data): fallback rate, the confidence distribution, the out-of-scope rate, drop-off at each step of a flow, handoff reasons, sentiment, and on voice latency and barge-ins. Good for monitoring and alerts (online monitoring), and the first to move after a release.

Lagging (days to weeks, sparse): repeat contacts (needs the 7-day window to close), CSAT, promises kept and amounts collected, complaints, churn. These are what the business cares about, so they make the decisions; leading indicators tell you early that something is off.

For a voice bot add the telephony layer: whether calls connect, whether the right person answered (right-party contact), call drops, response latency and interruptions (latency, turn-taking), and key-slot recognition errors. Then the same outcome metrics as chat.

chunks.h: Beyond support: sales and healthcare bots
chunks.x: Sales and lead qualification: the outcome is commercial, so lead the tree with qualified-lead rate, meetings booked or conversion per conversation, and revenue per conversation, with opt-out, complaint and consent violations (calling people who didn't agree to be contacted) as guardrails. Containment matters less; a good sales bot hands warm leads to people.

chunks.h: Beyond support: sales and healthcare bots
chunks.x: Healthcare: appointment bots track bookings completed and the show rate (fewer no-shows); triage and symptom bots have a hard safety guardrail, the recall on red-flag symptoms (chest pain, breathing difficulty, suicidal thoughts) that must go to a person or emergency services at once, measured on a labelled red-flag test set, with a target close to 100%. A missed red flag outweighs any amount of containment.

Intents differ hugely in difficulty: checking a due amount is easy to contain, a missing payment rarely is. So the overall rate depends on the mix, and the mix moves for reasons unrelated to the bot. In the toy log, containment by intent ranges from 100% (check_due, pay_now, promise_to_pay) to 0% (payment_not_reflected). A worked example of what that does over time:
Month 1: volume, containment
Month 2: volume, containment

In words: overall containment rose 9.5 points while every intent got worse, because a reminder SMS campaign tripled the easy “how much do I owe?” traffic. Reweighting month 2's rates to month 1's mix gives

In words: weight each intent's new rate by its old share of traffic. On a fixed mix the bot went from 56.7% to 53.7%, down 3 points. This is Simpson's paradox in a dashboard. Report every outcome metric per intent, and mix-adjusted overall; segment by channel, language, new against repeat customers, and time of day (agent availability changes how often escalation is even possible).

“Containment went up 10 points after the release, so the release worked.” First check the intent mix, the channel mix and the hours of operation. Then check resolved containment and repeat contacts. Only a randomized comparison (section 09) settles whether the release caused it.

Say it in an interview: “I'd never report containment alone: it counts customers who gave up as wins. I'd lead with resolved containment or first-contact resolution, which require the problem to be solved with no repeat contact within 7 days, guarded by CSAT sampled across all outcomes, complaints and missed escalations. Everything per intent, because a shift in the intent mix moves the overall rate without the bot changing.”

A conversation isn't one prediction but a sequence of them, where each depends on the last. Evaluation therefore works at three levels: components (intent, slots, state, scored on labelled turns), whole conversations (was the task done, was policy followed) and live outcomes (the metrics in section 08).

Build them from real conversations: transcripts of human agents and of earlier bot versions, which carry the real language mix, ASR noise and odd requests. Invented test sentences are cleaner than reality, so they overstate quality.
Stratify: enough examples of every intent (the rare and high-stakes ones over-sampled), plus out-of-scope, code-switched, noisy and adversarial cases.
Split by customer and by time, so the same customer's near-identical messages don't sit on both sides (honest splits).
Label per turn (intent, slots, state) for component metrics, and per conversation (goal, final state, policy violations) for end-to-end ones.

Logged conversations can't test a new bot, because its replies would differ from those in the log and the customer's next turn would no longer fit. A user simulator fixes that: an LLM plays the customer, live, against the bot. Each simulated conversation gets:
A persona: language and script (Romanized Hindi mixed with English), patience, literacy, mood, how much they volunteer.
A goal with private facts: “you can pay ₹5,000 on Friday, not the full amount; your salary comes on Friday”. The bot must draw these out.
Behaviour rules: correct yourself once, answer a different question than the one asked, ask for a person if the bot fails twice.
A stopping rule, and scoring by end state (did the right promise land in the database?) plus a judge for the policy rules.

Run every scenario several times, because both sides are random, and report pass^k , the chance that all k runs of a task succeed (the metric and its estimate are in evaluating agents). A bot serving thousands of customers a day needs the high- k number, not the average: at 80% success per run, independent runs give pass^8 = 0.8^8 = 0.17 .

Simulated users are too easy. They're articulate, cooperative, say everything at once, rarely code-switch the way real users do, and if they come from the same model family as the bot, they share its blind spots. Calibrate the simulator against real logs (turns per conversation, fallback rate, intent mix, how often people correct themselves) before trusting its numbers, and treat simulation as a regression and stress test, not a launch estimate.

A regression suite is a set of fixed conversations with assertions: after turn 3 the state holds date = Fri 16 Oct; schedule_promise is called once, with amount 5000; the disclosure appears in turn 1; no forbidden phrase appears anywhere; a fraud mention triggers a handoff within one turn. Run it on every change of prompt, model, flow or tool. Every production failure that gets fixed becomes a new case. With an LLM in the loop, run the generation steps at temperature 0, which reduces but doesn't remove run-to-run variation, and repeat each case several times and assert on the pass rate (decodi

For what assertions can't check, use an LLM judge. The general method (writing the rubric, the judge's known biases, validating it against human labels) is in LLM-as-judge. What's specific to conversations:

Judge the whole conversation, with its tool calls and their results, not single replies. Most dialogue failures (a lost correction, a skipped read-back, a missed escalation) only show across turns. Give the judge the transcript, the tool calls and results, the state log and the relevant policy text.

A conversation-level rubric of narrow pass/fail questions: was the customer's goal met (checked against the final state where possible); does every amount and date the bot said match a tool result; was an explicit read-back confirmed before the action; were the mandatory disclosures made; was the customer pressured or misled; should the conversation have been escalated, and was it; were turns wasted re-asking known details.

Validate it per language and channel. A judge that agrees with people on English chat may not on code-switched voice transcripts full of ASR errors, so check agreement on each (validating the judge). Its taste for longer, more detailed answers (judge biases) is a defect on voice, where a good turn is one or two short sentences: put the length budget in the rubric.
Keep people in the loop: a stratified sample reviewed every week, over-weighted towards escalations, abandoned conversations and transcripts where the judge was unsure.

Why not BLEU or ROUGE? A good reply has many forms (“Friday works, I've noted it” and “Done, ₹5,000 on the 16th” are both right), so overlap with one reference reply says little; Liu et al. (2016) found such metrics barely track human judgements of dialogue replies (reference-based metrics). Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text, not whether the task got done.

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: The final test is a randomized experiment (A/B testing end to end), with three dialogue-specific choices.

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: Randomize customers, not conversations. Repeat contacts and FCR span conversations: if a customer's first conversation is with version A and the repeat with B, which version caused the repeat? A customer who switches between versions also gets an inconsistent experience, and a bad experience in B changes how they contact you next time (straight to a human), which then shows up in A's numbers. Assign by a hash of the customer ID and analyse per customer, or correct the standard errors for per-conversation metrics (unit of randomization and analysis).

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: Watch for interference through the agent queue. Both arms share the same human agents. If B escalates more, queues get longer for A's customers too, so A's CSAT and abandonment get worse and the gap between arms understates B's harm (interference). Cap the treatment share, or watch queue times per arm.

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: Choose the metrics and the duration up front: decide on resolved containment or issues resolved per customer, with CSAT (sampled across all outcomes), complaints and compliance violations as guardrails. Lagging metrics need their window to close: keep measuring repeat contacts for 7 days after the last customer enters.

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: Before the A/B test, run the new version in shadow mode (it decides, but the old version answers) to compare their NLU and policy decisions on live traffic at no risk. And to measure deflection honestly, keep a small holdout of customers who never see the bot.

chunks.h: Online: A/B tests and the unit of randomization
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Before launch: component metrics on real labelled transcripts, an LLM-simulated user with personas and private goals, scored on the final database state and with pass^k for reliability, a regression suite on every prompt change, and a calibrated judge plus human review. After launch: an A/B test randomized by customer, not conversation, because repeat contacts cross conversations, watching for interference through the shared agent queue.”
After launch, most of the work is reading what went wrong and fixing it in the right order.

Log every turn as a structured record: the utterance (and ASR confidence on voice), the NLU output with confidence, the state before and after, the action, tool calls and their results, the latency, and the final outcome of the conversation. Then the questions become queries: where in the promise flow do people drop out? Which turns precede escalations? Which intents have the most fallbacks this week?
The utterances the bot couldn't handle (fallbacks, out-of-scope rejections, escalations with reason “other”) are where missing intents hide. To find them:
Embed each utterance with a multilingual sentence encoder (sentence embeddings).
Cluster: k-means when you can guess roughly how many groups to expect (k-means); a density method such as DBSCAN or HDBSCAN when you can't, and to leave the one-off noise unclustered (DBSCAN).
Name the clusters by reading samples, or have an LLM propose a name and description for each that a person checks.
Size and decide: a large, coherent cluster (“asking for an NOC after closing the loan”) becomes a new intent or a knowledge article; a small one waits.

Embeddings can cluster by surface form instead of meaning: the Devanagari, Romanized and English versions of one request land in three clusters, and every cluster of short messages (“hello”, “?”) looks coherent. Normalize scripts first or use an encoder trained on code-switched text, and judge clusters by reading them, not only by a cluster-quality score.

Read a sample of failed conversations and label each with the first thing that went wrong (the method, from reading traces to a taxonomy, is in error analysis). For a dialogue system the categories map onto the pipeline, which also tells you who fixes what:
“fifteen” heard as “fifty”
ASR tuning, confirmation of amounts
A missing payment classified as a balance query
Training data, intent design
“next Friday” resolved to the wrong week
Parser, a disambiguation question
Tracker, prompt, regression cases
No path for a partial payment
Engineering, a graceful fallback
No document on foreclosure charges
Wrong number in the reply, wrong tone
Not a bot failure; needs a clean handoff path
Label where it helps most: send turns near the confidence threshold and low-confidence turns to annotators first (active learning); they teach the model more per label than random turns.

Check that people agree: have two annotators label the same sample of intents and failure categories and measure agreement beyond chance (Cohen's kappa, worked in validating a judge). Low agreement means the intent definitions or the taxonomy are ambiguous, and no model will do better than its labels.
A fix is worth roughly the number of failures it removes. Multiply each intent's volume by its failure rate to get failures, then by the share of those failures the bot team can actually fix:

In words: the worst failure rate (foreclosure charges, 80%) ranks third, because few people ask. The most failures (missing payments, 560) ranks fourth, because most of them need the payments system fixed, not the bot; that's a ticket for another team. A moderate failure rate on a high-volume intent (promises, 25% of 2,000) is the best use of the next sprint. Weight by the cost of each failure (an escalation's cost, the risk) when they differ a lot.

Say it in an interview: “I log every turn with its NLU output, state, action and outcome. Fallbacks and escalations get embedded and clustered to find missing intents, failed conversations get labelled with the first thing that broke, and fixes are ranked by volume times failure rate times the share we can actually fix.”

LLM agent evaluation, simulated users, pass^k

Code-switching and script: Hindi–English mixing within sentences, Romanized Hindi with free spelling, Devanagari from some users, and other languages (Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Marathi, Kannada) mixed with English the same way. Test sets need all of these in their real proportions.
Numbers: lakh and crore, Indian digit grouping, number words in several languages, “dedh” and “dhai”, and amounts spoken partly in each language. They need their own parser and their own tests.
Speech recognition: accents, background noise and low-bandwidth phone lines raise error rates, most of all on names and numbers (ASR).
Lower-resource languages get noticeably worse NLU and ASR than Hindi or English; an English test score says nothing about them, so report each language separately.

Token cost: many general-purpose LLM tokenizers split Indic scripts into far more tokens per word than English, which raises cost and latency per turn. Measure it on your own traffic before choosing a model or a script for prompts.
Register: respectful forms of address (“aap”, “ji”), and a tone that fits the region and the situation; a collections bot that sounds rude in Hindi does more damage than one that sounds stiff.

Say it in an interview: “The public benchmarks are cleaner than real traffic: ATIS and SNIPS are saturated, CLINC150 is the one for out-of-scope, MultiWOZ for state tracking, τ-bench for LLM agents with simulated users. For Indian markets I'd build my own test sets with real code-switched, Romanized and ASR-noisy utterances, report each language separately, and give numbers and dates their own parsers.”

Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), appendix “Frame-Based Dialogue Systems” (PDF). The textbook account of frames, dialogue acts, state tracking, policy, generation and evaluation; read it first for the classic vocabulary. The chapter “Conversation and its Structure” on the book's site covers how human conversation works (turns, grounding, initiative).

Larson et al. (2019), “An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction” (arXiv). The CLINC150 paper: why out-of-scope needs its own evaluation, and how threshold and extra-class approaches compare. Read before answering an out-of-scope question.
Chen, Zhuo and Wang (2019), “BERT for Joint Intent Classification and Slot Filling” (arXiv). A short paper showing the joint model with two heads; the reference point for encoder-based NLU.

Budzianowski et al. (2018), “MultiWOZ” (arXiv), and Wu et al. (2019), “Transferable Multi-Domain State Generator” (TRADE) (arXiv). The multi-domain dataset behind most state-tracking results, and a tracker paper that reports joint and slot accuracy side by side.

Rastogi et al. (2020), “Towards Scalable Multi-domain Conversational Agents: The Schema-Guided Dialogue Dataset” (arXiv). Slots and intents described in natural language so one model can handle new services; the bridge from classic DST to how LLM trackers are prompted.

Liu et al. (2016), “How NOT To Evaluate Your Dialogue System” (arXiv). Shows that word-overlap metrics borrowed from translation barely track human judgements of dialogue replies; the reference for why dialogue is evaluated by task success, judges and people.

Yao et al. (2024), “τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains” (arXiv). Simulated users, scoring by final database state, and pass^k; read before designing a pre-launch evaluation for an LLM support agent.

Microsoft Copilot Studio documentation, “Deflection overview” (Microsoft Learn). One vendor's exact definitions of engaged sessions, resolution, escalation and abandon rates, and of deflection; useful for seeing how much a definition decides the number.

1What kinds of conversational systems are there, and what is the classic task-bot pipeline?

Task-oriented bots complete tasks, knowledge bots answer questions from documents, open-domain bots chat. The classic task bot is NLU → state tracking → policy → NLG, with ASR and TTS around it on voice.
Task success differs by kind: a correct backend action for task bots, a grounded correct answer for knowledge bots, engagement and ratings for open-domain ones. Support bots mix the first two.
NLU: one turn → intent, slots, confidence. DST: merges the turn into the running frame of slot values. Policy: state → next act (ask, confirm, call a tool, answer, hand off). NLG: act → words.
Dialogue acts (inform, request, confirm, affirm, deny) are the interface between the parts, and the reason “yes” can't be understood without the question before it.
Follow-up: an LLM agent does the four middle parts in one model, but they still exist implicitly and still need evaluating one by one. (01)
