chunks.x: The delta-method SE was 1.38× the naive one, and matched the real spread of the estimate across simulations. That ratio is close to the square root of the design effect:

chunks.h: 2. Unit of randomization and unit of analysis
chunks.x: In words: m is the number of observations per cluster (page views per user), and the intra-class correlation (ICC) is the share of the variance that comes from differences between clusters: here, the variance of users' own click rates divided by bar p(1 - bar p) . In the simulation, users' rates spread like a Beta(1, 9) distribution around 10%, with variance 0.0082, so ICC = 0.0082/0.09 ≈ 0.09. With m = 10 , DE approx 1.82 and sqrtDE approx 1.35 : 20,000 page views carry the information of about 11,000 independent ones. The simulated 1.38 is a little higher because users have different numbers
Assignment must be random with respect to everything about the user, stable (the same user always gets the same arm), and independent across experiments. The standard way:
bucket = hash(experiment salt + user id) bmod 1000

In words: a good hash function (MD5, SHA, MurmurHash) scrambles its input, so buckets look uniformly random and unrelated to anything about the user. Buckets 0–499 might be control and 500–999 treatment. The same user and salt always give the same bucket, so no lookup table is needed and the experience is consistent across visits.

Why the salt: each experiment gets its own salt, so a user's bucket in one experiment says nothing about their bucket in another. Without it, the same half of users would be in treatment in every experiment, and effects (and any damage) from one test would carry into the next.

Why not “last digit of the phone number” or “user id mod 2”: these aren't random with respect to users. Numbering often depends on when or where someone signed up (older accounts, a region, a carrier, a database shard). And the split is identical in every experiment, so the same people always get the new thing, and novelty, fatigue and earlier treatments pile up on one half. It can also be predicted or gamed.

Many experiments at once: with independent salts, each experiment's arms are balanced across every other experiment's arms, so other tests' effects average out instead of biasing this one. Genuine interactions (two changes to the same page that clash) are rarer than people fear; check for them by comparing one test's effect within each arm of the other, and put experiments that truly conflict in mutually exclusive layers.
Check it: the split should pass a sample-ratio test (step 5), and pre-experiment metrics should be balanced between arms.
Give both arms the identical experience and run the full pipeline. Nothing should be found, so:

About 5% of A/A tests should be significant at 5%, and their p-values should be uniform. Run many (or replay one metric over many historical random splits) and look at the histogram: a pile-up near 0 means the variance is underestimated.

What they catch: wrong standard errors (the 16% above), broken assignment or sample ratio mismatch, logging that differs by arm, bot filtering applied unevenly, metric definitions that silently depend on the arm.
What they can't catch: problems that only appear with a real treatment, such as interference or a treatment that changes who gets logged.

If the design is 50/50, the observed split should be close to 50/50. A significant deviation means something is removing or adding users differently by arm, and the arms are no longer comparable. Test it with a chi-square goodness of fit. With 200,000 users, observed 100,800 in control and 99,200 in treatment:
beginaligned E &= 100,000 per arm \\ chi^2 &= frac800^2100,000 + frac800^2100,000 = 12.8 \\ p &= P(chi^2_1 ge 12.8) = 0.00035 endaligned

In words: a split of 50.4% to 49.6% looks harmless, but with 200,000 users it would happen by chance about 3 times in 10,000. The same 50.4% with only 2,000 users (1,008 vs 992) gives p = 0.72 : the check gets sharper with scale, which is exactly when small biases matter.
Threshold: teams usually alert at p lt 0.001 , because the check runs on every experiment every day and false alarms are costly.

Common causes: the treatment crashes or loads slower, so fewer users reach the logging point; bot filtering that reacts to the treatment; a redirect in one arm; eligibility decided after assignment using something the treatment affects; ramping the split up mid-test; a hashing bug.
What to do: don't analyse the result. The missing users aren't random, so any difference may be selection, not the treatment. Find and fix the cause, then rerun.
For an unequal design, use the designed ratio as the expected counts: a 90/10 test that gives 90,500 and 9,500 has chi^2 = 27.8 , p approx 10^-7 .

Write the plan before launch: the hypothesis, the primary metric and guardrails, the unit, the MDE, the sample size and duration, the analysis (test, variance reduction, cap), the segments you'll look at, and the decision rule. Its purpose is to separate the analysis you planned from the ones you went looking for after seeing the data.

Duration = required users ÷ daily eligible users, rounded up to whole weeks. Behaviour differs by weekday, and a test that covers Monday to Thursday estimates a different effect. Two weeks is a common minimum.

Novelty effect: users click a new thing because it's new, and the lift decays. Primacy (change aversion): users dislike change at first, and the effect improves. Both make the first days unrepresentative.
Detecting them: plot the daily treatment effect, or compare users by first exposure date; a trend means the effect isn't settled. Effects measured on new users (who have no old habit) avoid both.
Long-term effects: keep a small long-running holdout that never gets the feature, to measure effects that take months (retention, learning).

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: Much of the variance in a metric is just “who the user is”: heavy users spend a lot in any arm. A user's behaviour before the experiment predicts that part, and because it was measured before assignment, the treatment can't have affected it. CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) subtracts the predictable part.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: Derivation. Let Y be the metric during the test and X the same user's pre-period value. Define an adjusted metric for any constant theta :

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: beginaligned Y^cv &= Y - theta\,(X - bar X) \\ Var(Y^cv) &= Var(Y) - 2theta Cov(Y, X) + theta^2 Var(X) endaligned

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: In words: this is the variance of a difference (section 01) applied to Y and theta X : scaling by theta multiplies X 's variance by theta^2 and the covariance by theta , and subtracting the constant theta bar X changes no variance. Subtracting a multiple of a correlated variable removes variance (the middle term) but adds some of X 's own (the last term). Find the best theta : the derivative with respect to theta is -2Cov(Y,X) + 2thetaVar(X) ; set it to zero.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: beginaligned theta^* &= fracCov(Y, X)Var(X) \\ Var(Y^cv) &= Var(Y) - fracCov(Y, X)^2Var(X) \\ &= Var(Y)\,big(1 - rho^2big) endaligned

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: In words: theta^* is the slope from regressing Y on X . Because the correlation is rho = Cov(Y, X)/(sigma_X sigma_Y) , the subtracted term Cov(Y, X)^2/Var(X) equals rho^2 Var(Y) . What's left is the part of Y that X can't explain: a fraction 1 - rho^2 . Users needed scale the same way.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: Why it doesn't bias the effect. The estimated effect is

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: beginaligned hatDelta^cv &= bar Y^cv_B - bar Y^cv_A \\ &= (bar Y_B - bar Y_A) - theta\,(bar X_B - bar X_A) endaligned

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: In words: X was measured before assignment, so randomization makes bar X_B - bar X_A zero on average: the adjustment removes noise, not signal. In a given sample it corrects for chance imbalance: if treatment happened to get heavier users, bar X_B gt bar X_A and the adjustment subtracts that head start. Use one theta for both arms, estimated on the pooled data. Strictly, the estimate is unbiased for a fixed theta ; estimating theta from the same data adds a bias of order 1/n , negligible at A/B-test sizes.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: By hand. Five users with pre-period X = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and test-period Y = 2, 3, 5, 5, 7. Means 3 and 4.4; Var(X) = 2 , Var(Y) = 3.04 , Cov(X, Y) = 2.4 (dividing by n ).

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: theta = 2.4/2 = 1.2 . The adjusted values keep the mean (4.4) but their variance falls from 3.04 to 0.16. Check: rho = 2.4/sqrt2 times 3.04 = 0.973 and 1 - rho^2 = 0.053 = 0.16/3.04 .

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: At realistic correlation. 10,000 users per arm, pre and post correlated at rho = 0.6 , a true effect of 0.8 on a metric with standard deviation 30, 2,000 simulated experiments:

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: Plain difference in means

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: The SE falls by sqrt1 - 0.36 = 0.80 , the estimate stays unbiased, and the same power would need 36% fewer users. The payoff by correlation: rho = 0.5 saves 25% of users, 0.7 saves 49%, 0.9 saves 81%.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: The covariate must be unaffected by the treatment: pre-period values, or attributes fixed before assignment. Using an in-experiment variable (say, sessions during the test to adjust revenue during the test) removes part of the effect itself.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: New users have no pre-period: set X to 0 (or the mean) and add a “has history” indicator; the reduction then comes only from users with history.

chunks.h: 7. CUPED: variance reduction with pre-experiment data
chunks.x: It's essentially a regression: CUPED is asymptotically the same as regressing Y on a treatment indicator and the centred X . With several covariates, or with a machine-learning prediction of Y from pre-period features as the covariate, it generalizes (regression adjustment).

If a categorical variable (platform, country, new vs returning) drives much of the variance, either randomize within each stratum so every stratum is split exactly in half (stratified randomization), or randomize normally and combine within-stratum differences weighted by stratum size afterwards (post-stratification). Both remove the between-strata variance from the comparison; post-stratification is CUPED with a categorical covariate. With a large sample, post-stratification gets nearly all the benefit and is easier to run.
The two-sample test assumes one unit's outcome depends only on its own arm (the stable unit treatment value assumption, SUTVA). It breaks whenever arms share something:

Marketplaces with shared supply. A better ranking for treatment buyers makes them book the best listings first, which leaves worse ones for control buyers. Treatment looks great partly because control got worse; launched to everyone, nobody gets the head start, and the real gain is smaller. The test overestimates.
Social and communication products. A feature that makes treatment users message more also makes their control friends reply more. Control is partly treated, so the test underestimates.
Shared budgets. Ad campaigns with one budget across arms: the arm that spends faster starves the other.
Designs that restore independence, all trading more independent units for fewer, bigger ones:

Cluster randomization: randomize whole cities, regions or graph communities, so interaction happens mostly inside a cluster. The cost is the design effect: with clusters of 100 users and an ICC of 0.01, DE = 1.99 , so 100,000 users count as about 50,000; with an ICC of 0.05 it's about 17,000. Analyse at the cluster level or with clustered SEs.

Switchback tests: one market alternates between treatment and control over time slots (say, hours of the day, randomly ordered). Everyone in a slot gets the same arm, so they can't take supply from each other. Needs slots long enough for the system to settle, short gaps (a buffer) to stop carry-over, and analysis by slot.
Budget-split and two-sided designs for ads and marketplaces: split the shared resource itself between arms.

Effects really do differ (new vs returning users, platforms). But slicing a result into many segments and reporting the ones that are significant is multiple testing in disguise. With 20 segments and no real effect anywhere, the chance that at least one shows p lt 0.05 is 1 - 0.95^20 = 64\% (40% with 10 segments, 23% with 5).
Pre-specify the few segments with a reason to differ; treat the rest as exploration that needs a new test.

Test the difference, not two p-values. “Significant on Android (p = 0.03), not on iOS (p = 0.20)” doesn't show the effect differs by platform: the difference between significant and not significant is not itself significant. Test the interaction (treatment × platform).
Correct for the number of segments (section 08), and expect segment effects to be exaggerated, since each segment has a fraction of the power.
Models of heterogeneous effects (causal forests, uplift models) are useful for targeting, but they find patterns in noise too; confirm targeting rules in a fresh test.

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Triggering and dilution. If a change only affects users who reach a certain page (say 10% of them), the other 90% add noise and no signal. Analyse only triggered users, the ones who reached the point where the arms differ. In control, log the moment a user would have seen the change (a counterfactual trigger), so both arms are filtered identically. With a share s of users triggered and per-user variance sigma^2 similar in both groups:

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: beginaligned Delta_all &= s cdot Delta_trig \\ n_all-user analysis &approx frac16\,sigma^2(s\,Delta_trig)^2 \\ n_triggered analysis &approx frac16\,sigma^2Delta_trig^2 endaligned

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: In words: averaged over everyone, the effect shrinks by the factor s , so the all-user analysis needs 1/s^2 times the users that the undiluted effect would need. The triggered analysis avoids the dilution: it needs 16sigma^2/Delta_trig^2 triggered users, and since only a share s of entrants trigger, 1/s times that many users entering the test, which is still 1/s fewer than the all-user analysis. With s = 0.1 , a per-user standard deviation of 1 and a triggered lift of 0.05: 640,000 users per arm for the all-user analysis, against 6,400 triggered users (64,000 entering) per arm, 10× fewer. To r

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Relative lifts need their own interval. Lifts are usually reported in percent, hat L = bar Y_B/bar Y_A - 1 , and the denominator is noisy too. By the delta method:

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Var(hat L) approx fracVar(bar Y_B)mu_A^2 + fracmu_B^2\,Var(bar Y_A)mu_A^4

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: In words: the first term is the noise in the treatment mean, the second the noise in the control mean that the ratio divides by. For the running example the lift is +8.0% with an SE of 4.5 points, so the 95% interval is [−0.8%, +16.8%]; working on the log of the ratio gives [−0.4%, +17.2%], and a bootstrap [−0.7%, +17.3%]. Simply dividing the absolute interval by the control rate ([−0.5%, +16.5%]) ignores the control's noise.

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Metrics conditioned on a post-treatment outcome. Spend per buyer, session length among active users and delivery time among completed orders compare different sets of people in the two arms, because the treatment changes who buys, stays or completes. If a change converts extra low spenders, spend per buyer falls even though nobody spends less (the Mann–Whitney example in section 04 is exactly this). Read such metrics as descriptions, not causal effects. Decide on metrics averaged over all randomized (or triggered) users, such as revenue per user.

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Simpson's paradox when the split changes. Ramping treatment from 1% to 50% mid-test mixes days with different baselines. Day 1: control 99,000 users at 10%, treatment 1,000 at 11%. Day 2, a weaker day: 50,000 each, at 5% and 5.5%. Treatment wins on both days, yet pooled it loses, 5.6% against 8.3%, because most of its users came on the weak day. Compare within periods and combine with fixed weights (here +0.75 points), or analyse only the period with a stable split.

chunks.h: 11. Analysis traps: triggering, relative lifts, post-treatment metrics, ramps
chunks.x: Twyman's law: any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong. A surprisingly large lift should start a hunt for bugs (sample ratio, logging, a broken control) before a celebration.

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Statistical significance says the effect is probably not zero. Practical significance asks whether it's big enough to matter, given the cost of building, maintaining and risking the change. Decide with the confidence interval against the smallest effect worth having:

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Entirely above the practical threshold

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Ship, if guardrails are fine

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Above 0, but includes values below the threshold

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Real, maybe too small to matter

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Ship if cheap and low-risk; otherwise weigh the cost

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Includes 0, narrow around 0

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Don't ship for this reason; the test was informative

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Not “no effect”: run longer, reduce variance, or decide on other grounds

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: A guardrail significantly worse

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Usually don't ship; at least escalate the trade-off

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: With enough users, a 0.01-point lift is significant and worthless. With too few, a lift worth millions isn't significant. Ship decisions also weigh reversibility, engineering and maintenance cost, and strategic fit, which the test doesn't measure.

chunks.h: 12. Reading the result: practical vs statistical significance
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “I'd fix the metric, the guardrails, the MDE and the unit first; size the test from the MDE and the metric's variance, rounded up to full weeks; assign with a salted hash; check the sample ratio and balance before reading anything; analyse at the randomization unit with CUPED; and decide from the interval against a practical threshold, not from the p-value alone.”
A 5% test is a promise about one look at one metric. Each extra look, metric, variant or segment is another chance for noise to cross the line, and the chances add up.

chunks.h: Peeking: why checking every day breaks the 5%
chunks.x: As data arrive, the z statistic of an A/A test wanders like a random walk. It is standard normal at any single, pre-chosen moment, which is why one look has a 5% false-positive rate. But the chance that the walk crosses ±1.96 at some point along the way is much larger, and stopping at the first crossing turns that chance into a reported “win”.

chunks.h: Peeking: why checking every day breaks the 5%
chunks.x: One simulated A/A test, checked 20 times. The fixed line (dashed) is crossed at look 8, so a team that peeks ships a change that does nothing; by the planned end the statistic is back near zero. O'Brien–Fleming boundaries (purple) demand overwhelming evidence early and relax to about 2.1 by the last look, keeping the overall false-positive rate at 5%.

chunks.h: Peeking: why checking every day breaks the 5%
chunks.x: How much it inflates, simulated A/A tests that stop at the first look with lvert z rvert gt 1.96 , looks equally spaced:

chunks.h: Peeking: why checking every day breaks the 5%
chunks.x: The same check with simulated users rather than an idealised random walk (10% conversion, 1,000 users per arm per day, a look every day for 14 days): 22.0% of A/A tests “won” at some point, against 5.0% looking only on day 14. With continuous monitoring and no end date, the rate climbs towards 100%, because a random walk eventually crosses any fixed line.

chunks.h: Peeking: why checking every day breaks the 5%
chunks.x: “We only stopped early because it was clearly significant.” That's exactly the rule that inflates the error. Looking is harmless; acting on a look that wasn't in the plan is the problem. Stopping early to prevent harm (a guardrail breach) is fine, because it only ever leads to not shipping.

chunks.h: Fixes: fixed horizon, alpha spending, always-valid tests
chunks.x: Fixed horizon. Compute n up front, look at the decision metric once, at the end. Dashboards can show health metrics (SRM, crashes) daily, as long as nobody makes the ship decision from them.

chunks.h: Fixes: fixed horizon, alpha spending, always-valid tests
chunks.x: Group sequential tests with alpha spending. Plan a few interim looks and spend the 5% across them, so the total chance of a false stop over all looks is 5%. Early stops happen only for huge effects, and the final test is barely stricter than a fixed design: in simulation, power fell only from 80% to 79% at the same maximum sample, and under the alternative the test stopped after 80% of the planned sample on average. chunks.h: Fixes: fixed horizon, alpha spending, always-valid tests
chunks.x: Always-valid inference (the mixture sequential probability ratio test, confidence sequences). These build intervals that hold at every moment simultaneously, so you can look continuously and stop whenever. The mixture SPRT tracks the likelihood ratio of “effect” against “no effect”, averaged over a prior on the effect size, and rejects when it exceeds 1/alpha ; under H_0 that ratio is a fair game (a martingale), and Ville's inequality bounds the chance it ever reaches 1/alpha by alpha . The price is width: at any fixed sample size they're wider than a fixed-horizon interval, so if you were goi
With m independent tests at level alpha and no real effects, the chance of at least one false positive (the family-wise error rate, FWER) is
In words: each test has a 95% chance of staying quiet, and all m must stay quiet. For 10 metrics that's 40%; for 20, 64%.
Three corrections, for m p-values sorted from smallest, p_(1) le p_(2) le dots le p_(m) :
Bonferroni: reject when p le alpha/m . Controls FWER under any dependence; simple and conservative.

Holm (step-down): compare p_(1) with alpha/m , p_(2) with alpha/(m-1) , and so on; stop at the first failure. Also controls FWER under any dependence, and always rejects at least as much as Bonferroni, so there's little reason to prefer Bonferroni, except that Bonferroni gives simple simultaneous confidence intervals (each at level 1 - alpha/m ).

Benjamini–Hochberg (step-up): find the largest k with p_(k) le (k/m)\,q and reject the k smallest. Controls the false discovery rate (FDR), the expected share of rejections that are false, at q . Valid for independent or positively correlated tests (business metrics often are, and BH is fairly robust in practice); the Benjamini–Yekutieli variant covers any dependence at a cost in power.
Worked example: ten metrics, sorted p-values, alpha = q = 0.05 . Six are below 0.05 unadjusted.

Bonferroni rejects 1, Holm 2, Benjamini–Hochberg 4. BH's step-up rule means the largest k that passes decides, even if some smaller rank had failed. The equivalent adjusted p-values: Holm's second is 9 times 0.0054 = 0.049 ; BH's fourth is 0.019 times 10/4 = 0.0475 .

Share of rejections that are false
Use FWER control (Holm) when any single false claim is costly: several variants against one control (each might ship), the guardrails, a confirmatory claim.
Use FDR control (BH) when screening many metrics or segments for leads, where a few false leads are acceptable but missing everything isn't.
Avoid needing either: one pre-registered primary metric gets the full alpha ; secondary metrics are reported as supporting or exploratory.
The Bayesian version answers the question people actually ask, “how likely is it that B is better, and by how much?”, at the price of stating a prior belief.
Give each arm's conversion rate a Beta prior. A Beta(a, b) density is proportional to p^a-1(1-p)^b-1 ; observing x conversions in n users multiplies it by the binomial likelihood p^x(1-p)^n-x :
beginaligned posterior &propto p^a-1(1-p)^b-1 cdot p^x(1-p)^n-x \\ &= p^a+x-1(1-p)^b+n-x-1 \\ p mid data &sim Beta(a + x,\ b + n - x) endaligned
In words: the prior acts like a earlier successes and b earlier failures, and the data add their own. Beta(1, 1) is flat: every rate equally likely beforehand.
The running example with flat priors: p_A sim Beta(1001, 9001) and p_B sim Beta(1081, 8921) . Drawing a few million values from each posterior (or integrating):
beginaligned P(p_B gt p_A mid data) &= 0.968 \\ mathbb Ebig[max(p_A - p_B,\ 0)big] &= 0.000054 \\ mathbb Ebig[max(p_B - p_A,\ 0)big] &= 0.0081 endaligned

In words: there's a 96.8% probability that B's true rate is higher. The expected loss of shipping B, the conversion you'd expect to give up (counting zero in the cases where B really is better), is 0.005 points; the expected loss of keeping A is 0.81 points. A common decision rule is to ship when the expected loss of shipping falls below a threshold of caring (say 0.01 points). The 95% credible interval for the difference is [−0.05, +1.65] points.

chunks.h: How it differs from a p-value
chunks.x: The question. The p-value is P(data this extreme mid H_0) ; the posterior gives P(B gt A mid data) directly, plus a full distribution for the size of the lift and losses in business units.

chunks.h: How it differs from a p-value
chunks.x: The numbers can coincide. With a flat prior and large samples, P(B gt A) approx 1 - the one-sided p-value (0.968 against 1 - 0.032 ), and the credible interval matches the confidence interval. The interpretation differs; the arithmetic often barely does.

chunks.h: How it differs from a p-value
chunks.x: Where it genuinely helps: an informative prior built from past experiments shrinks noisy estimates towards realistic effects, which is the cure for the winner's curse in section 03; and expected loss turns the result into a decision.
The prior matters when data are thin. The same data with priors centred on 10% for both arms:

A prior centred on the same rate for both arms says “differences are probably small”, so it pulls the lift towards zero. That's right if past experiments mostly produced small lifts, and wrong if it was invented. The choice must be defended, and made before the data.

Peeking still matters for decisions. The posterior is a correct summary of belief at every moment, but a decision rule applied repeatedly still has an error rate. Simulated A/A tests (10% conversion, 1,000 users per arm per day, flat priors), with the rule “ship B when P(B gt A) gt 0.95 ”:

The “Bayesians can peek” argument holds only if the prior is right and you care about posterior beliefs rather than error rates. With a flat prior when real effects are small, optional stopping produces exaggerated, often wrong wins. Expected-loss rules are more robust but not immune. And no Bayesian method fixes a sample ratio mismatch, interference, novelty or the wrong unit of analysis.

A multi-armed bandit shifts traffic towards whichever arm looks better as data arrive. Thompson sampling, for instance, sends each user to an arm with probability equal to the posterior probability that it's the best. It earns more during the experiment (less regret), which suits short-lived choices with many options: headlines, promotions, ad creative. The cost is inference: the losing arms get few users, so their estimates stay noisy, and adaptive allocation biases the plain difference in means. It also optimizes only the immediate reward, with no guardrails or long-term effects. To learn an

Sometimes randomizing is impossible (a pricing change by law applies to everyone; a city-wide launch already happened), unethical, or too slow. Observational methods then estimate what would have happened without the change. Each rests on one key assumption that the data can't fully verify, so each comes with checks that make it more credible.

Compare the change over time in the treated group with the change over the same time in an untreated group. A feature launches in city T but not city C. Weekly orders: T goes from 100 to 120, C from 80 to 90.
beginaligned DiD &= (bar Y_T,after - bar Y_T,before) - (bar Y_C,after - bar Y_C,before) \\ &= (120 - 100) - (90 - 80) = 10 endaligned

In words: T's raw jump of 20 includes whatever lifted everyone (season, marketing); C's jump of 10 estimates that common part, so 10 is attributed to the feature. Comparing the two cities after launch (120 vs 80) would say 40, mixing in their permanent difference; before vs after in T alone says 20, mixing in the trend.

Key assumption: parallel trends. Without the feature, T would have changed by the same amount as C. Checks: plot several pre-periods and confirm the groups moved together; run a placebo DiD on a fake launch date before the real one (it should find nothing); make sure nothing else changed in T at launch. Estimate it as a regression with group and period effects and their interaction, with standard errors clustered by group; that needs many groups. With a single treated city, judge significance by placebo (permutation) inference: rerun the DiD pretending each control city was the treated one, an

When one unit is treated (a single country or city) and no single control resembles it, build a weighted combination of untreated units whose pre-period path matches the treated unit's as closely as possible: perhaps 0.4 × city A + 0.35 × city B + 0.25 × city C. After launch, the gap between the treated unit and its synthetic twin is the effect.

Key assumption: the weights that reproduced the past keep reproducing the counterfactual future, with no shock hitting only the treated unit or only the donors. Checks: a close pre-period fit over a long window; placebo runs that pretend each donor was treated (the real effect should stand out from their gaps); leaving out donors one at a time.

When treatment is assigned by a cut-off on a score (credit score of 700 or above gets an offer; orders above a threshold get free delivery), units just above and just below are nearly identical except for the treatment. Fit the outcome against the score on each side and measure the jump at the cut-off.

Key assumption: everything else changes smoothly through the cut-off, so the jump is due only to the treatment; in particular, units can't precisely choose which side they land on. Checks: the density of the score should have no bunching just above the cut-off (a McCrary-style test); pre-treatment covariates should show no jump; results should hold across bandwidths. The estimate is local: it describes units near the cut-off, not everyone.

With only one series (total app orders) and a known change date, model the series before the change (trend and seasonality), project it forward, and compare with what happened. A segmented regression estimates a jump in level and a change in slope at the change point.

Key assumption: the pre-period pattern would have continued, and nothing else changed at the same time. Checks: a long pre-period with stable seasonality; placebo change points; a comparison series that shouldn't be affected (which turns it into DiD). It's the weakest design here, because any coincident event is indistinguishable from the effect.

When users chose the treatment themselves (opted into a feature, used a coupon), model each user's probability of being treated from pre-treatment features: the propensity score. Then compare treated and untreated users with similar scores, by matching, stratifying, or weighting each user by the inverse of the probability of the arm they ended up in.

Key assumption: no unmeasured confounding. Every variable that affects both the choice and the outcome is in the model. Also overlap: every kind of user has some chance of being in either group. Checks: covariate balance after matching (standardized differences near zero), the overlap of score distributions, and a sensitivity analysis asking how strong a hidden confounder would need to be to erase the effect. Motivated users who opt in are the classic hidden confounder, and no feature fully captures motivation.

An instrumental variable (something that shifts treatment but affects the outcome only through it, such as a random encouragement) is a sixth option when one exists. Whatever the method, a randomized test, even a small one or a holdout, is stronger evidence than any of them.
Python-flavoured, short enough to write from memory. Phi is the standard normal CDF and Phi_inv its inverse. Each was run as real code on the note's examples; the results are in the → comments.

def two_prop_ztest(xa, na, xb, nb, alpha=0.05): pa, pb = xa / na, xb / nb p = (xa + xb) / (na + nb) # pooled: H0 says equal se0 = sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1/na + 1/nb)) z = (pb - pa) / se0 pval = 2 * (1 - Phi(abs(z))) # two-sided se = sqrt(pa*(1-pa)/na + pb*(1-pb)/nb) # unpooled zc = Phi_inv(1 - alpha/2) # 1.96 ci = (pb - pa - zc*se, pb - pa + zc*se) return z, pval, ci # (1000, 10000, 1080, 10000) # → z 1.85, p 0.064, CI (-0.0005, 0.0165)

def n_per_arm(sigma2, delta, alpha=0.05, power=0.8): za = Phi_inv(1 - alpha/2) # 1.96 zb = Phi_inv(power) # 0.84 return ceil((za + zb)**2 * 2 * sigma2 / delta**2) def n_per_arm_props(p1, p2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8): pbar = (p1 + p2) / 2 # variance under H0 za, zb = Phi_inv(1 - alpha/2), Phi_inv(power) num = (za * sqrt(2 * pbar * (1 - pbar)) + zb * sqrt(p1*(1-p1) + p2*(1-p2)))**2 return ceil(num / (p2 - p1)**2) # n_per_arm(0.09, 0.008) → 22,075 # n_per_arm_props(0.10, 0.108) → 22,855 # for days: 2 * n / daily users, round up to weeks

def permutation_test(a, b, stat=diff_in_means, n_perm=10_000): obs = stat(b, a) pooled = concat(a, b) # one row per unit hits = 0 for _ in range(n_perm): shuffle(pooled) # relabel at random pa, pb = pooled[:len(a)], pooled[len(a):] if abs(stat(pb, pa)) >= abs(obs): hits += 1 return (hits + 1) / (n_perm + 1) # never exactly 0 # a = [3, 5, 4, 6], b = [7, 8, 6, 9] → 0.057 (exact: 4/70)
Bootstrap confidence interval

def bootstrap_ci(a, b, stat=diff_in_means, B=5000, alpha=0.05): # a, b: one row per randomization unit (user) reps = [] for _ in range(B): ra = a[randint(0, len(a), size=len(a))] # with rb = b[randint(0, len(b), size=len(b))] # replacement reps.append(stat(rb, ra)) lo, hi = percentile(reps, [100*alpha/2, 100*(1 - alpha/2)]) return stat(b, a), (lo, hi), std(reps) # est, CI, SE # running example as 0/1 rows → CI (-0.0003, 0.0163), # SE 0.0043: the same as the formula

def cuped(y, x, arm): # x: pre-period, per user theta = cov(x, y) / var(x) # pooled, both arms y_cv = y - theta * (x - mean(x)) a, b = y_cv[arm == 0], y_cv[arm == 1] diff = mean(b) - mean(a) se = sqrt(var(a)/len(a) + var(b)/len(b)) return diff, se, theta # x = [1..5], y = [2, 3, 5, 5, 7] → theta 1.2, # y_cv = [4.4, 4.2, 5.0, 3.8, 4.6], var 3.04 → 0.16

def benjamini_hochberg(p, q=0.05): m = len(p) order = argsort(p) # smallest first k_max = 0 for rank, i in enumerate(order, start=1): if p[i] <= rank / m * q: k_max = rank # largest passing rank reject = zeros(m, dtype=bool) reject[order[:k_max]] = True # all ranks up to it return reject # the ten p-values in section 08 → 4 rejections

def srm_check(n_ctrl, n_treat, share_ctrl=0.5): tot = n_ctrl + n_treat e1, e2 = tot * share_ctrl, tot * (1 - share_ctrl) chi2 = (n_ctrl - e1)**2 / e1 + (n_treat - e2)**2 / e2 return chi2, chi2_sf(chi2, df=1) # alert if p < 0.001 # (100800, 99200) → 12.8, 0.00035 def ratio_delta_var(y, x): # per-user clicks, views n = len(y) mx, my = mean(x), mean(y) R = my / mx return (var(y) - 2*R*cov(y, x) + R**2 * var(x)) \ / (n * mx**2) # SE of the CTR gap: sqrt(var_A + var_B)

Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own: the short answer, the mechanism, the why, then the trade-off or the likely follow-up. Questions 2, 9, 20, 21, 26 and 31 are hand drills; do them with a pen.
1What's the difference between a standard deviation and a standard error? Why does the SE shrink with √n and not n?
The SD measures how spread out the individual values are; the SE measures how much an estimate, such as the average, would move between reruns of the sample. For a mean, SE = sigma/sqrt n .
Example: five users spending 0, 0, 0, 0 and ₹500 have an SD of ₹200. The average of 2 random users has an SE of 141; of 100 users, 20. More users never shrink the SD; they always shrink the SE.

Why sqrt n : the sum of n independent values has variance nsigma^2 (variances of independent things add). The average divides the sum by n , which divides the variance by n^2 , leaving sigma^2/n ; the square root is sigma/sqrt n . Independent errors partly cancel, so the sum's wobble grows only like sqrt n while the sum itself grows like n .
For a rate: a 0/1 column has variance p(1-p) , so SE = sqrtp(1-p)/n : 0.003 at 10% on 10,000 users. The root covers everything; p(1-p)/sqrt n is more than 3× too small.
Which to use: tests and intervals for an average use the SE; describing how varied the users are uses the SD.
Follow-up: precision is expensive. Halving an interval's width means halving the SE, which takes 4× the users. (01)
2Drill: control converts 1,000 of 10,000 users, treatment 1,080 of 10,000. Give the SE and 95% interval for the control rate and for the gap.
Control: SE 0.003, interval 9.41% to 10.59%. Gap: 0.8 points, SE 0.43 points, interval −0.05 to +1.65 points.
Treatment: sqrt0.108 times 0.892/10,000 = 0.0031 .
Gap: sqrt0.00000900 + 0.00000963 = 0.00432 (square the unrounded SEs); margin 1.96 times 0.00432 = 0.0085 ; interval 0.008 pm 0.0085 .

Reading: the interval includes 0, so the gap isn't significant at 5% ( z = 1.85 ), but it also includes lifts worth having: the test is underpowered, not negative. The 90% interval, 0.008 pm 1.645 times 0.00432 , runs from +0.09 to +1.51 points and excludes 0.
Follow-up: the gap's margin (±0.85 points) is about sqrt 2 times one arm's (±0.59), so judging the lift against one arm's margin overstates significance. (01)
3Why do variances add when you subtract two independent estimates? And why does the z-test use a pooled SE?

The gap is off by both arms' errors, and nothing lines them up to cancel (sometimes they offset, sometimes they compound), so on average the variances add: Var(B - A) = Var(B) + Var(A) - 2Cov(A, B) , and the covariance is zero for independent arms. The pooled SE is the same formula with the single rate that H_0 assumes.
The algebra: the gap's deviation is d_B - d_A . Squaring gives d_B^2 + d_A^2 - 2d_A d_B , and the cross term averages to zero when the arms are independent.
Not the SEs: 0.0030 + 0.0031 = 0.0061 overstates the wobble; sqrt0.0030^2 + 0.0031^2 = 0.0043 is right. With equal arms the gap's SE is sqrt 2 times one arm's.

Pooled: under H_0 both arms share one rate, best estimated from everyone: 2,080/20,000 = 0.104 , giving SE_0 = sqrt0.104 times 0.896 times (1/10,000 + 1/10,000) = 0.00432 . The test is computed in the world it assumes; the interval uses each arm's own rate.

When the covariance isn't zero: the same users measured twice (paired tests) or a pre-period covariate (CUPED). Positive correlation makes the difference less noisy, which is the whole point of those designs.
4What is a z-score? A test gives z = 1.85: what does that tell you, and which critical values should you know by heart?

A z-score is a distance measured in standard deviations: (x - mu)/sigma for a value, (estimate − value under H_0 )/SE for a test statistic. A z of 1.85 puts the gap 1.85 standard errors from zero: between the 90% and 95% cut-offs, so the two-sided p-value is between 0.05 and 0.10 (it's 0.064).
Why one table works: standardizing gives any quantity mean 0 and SD 1, and by the CLT the test statistic is close to the standard normal under H_0 .
Cut-offs: 1.645 (90% in the middle, 5% beyond on each side), 1.96 (95%, 2.5% each side), 2.576 (99%, 0.5% each side). Rule of thumb: 68%, 95% and 99.7% within ±1, ±2 and ±3.
Reading 1.85: Phi(1.85) = 0.968 , so 3.2% of the bell lies beyond it on each side: two-sided p = 0.064 , one-sided 0.032.
Where the cut-offs reappear: a two-sided 5% test rejects when lvert z rvert ge 1.96 ; a 95% interval is the estimate ± 1.96 SE; the sample-size formula uses (1.96 + 0.84)^2 .
Follow-up: with a small sample and an estimated SD, the reference curve is Student's t, with wider cut-offs (2.04 at 30 degrees of freedom). (01, 04)
5What is a p-value? What is it not?
The probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
Example: 10.0% vs 10.8% conversion with 10,000 users per arm gives z = 1.85 and p = 0.064 : with no real effect, a gap this big (either way) turns up 6.4% of the time.
Not P(H_0 true) : it's computed assuming H_0 . That probability needs a prior: if 10% of tested ideas work and power is 80%, 36% of significant results are false.
Not an effect size: huge samples make trivial effects significant. Report the estimate and its interval.
Not evidence of no effect when large: p = 0.064 came with an interval from −0.05 to +1.65 points, which includes worthwhile lifts.
Under H_0 it's uniform: 5% of no-effect tests give p lt 0.05 , by design.
Follow-up: “why 0.05?” Convention. Choose alpha by the cost of a false positive against a missed effect. (02)
6The test gives p = 0.03. Is there a 97% chance the treatment works? Is there a 95% chance the true lift is inside the 95% interval?
No. 0.03 is the chance of data this extreme if the treatment did nothing, not the chance that it does nothing.

Reversing it needs Bayes' rule and a base rate. Say 10% of ideas truly work, and tests have 80% power at alpha = 0.05 . Out of 1,000 ideas: 900 duds give 45 false positives; 100 real ones give 80 true positives. So 45 of 125 “wins” (36%) are false. With 30% power it's 60%.
A single p of 0.03 is weak evidence when real effects are rare, and the effect is likely exaggerated if the test was underpowered.
What you can say: “the data would be unusual if there were no effect; the estimated lift is X with interval [L, U].”

The interval, likewise: “95%” describes the procedure: 95% of intervals built this way contain the true lift, and a given interval either does or doesn't. “95% probability the lift is in here” is the reading of a Bayesian credible interval, which with a flat prior and big samples gives nearly the same numbers.
Follow-up: a Bayesian analysis gives P(B gt A mid data) directly, but only relative to a prior (section 09). (02)
7Explain Type I and Type II errors and power. Which is worse?
Type I: declaring an effect that isn't there (rate alpha ). Type II: missing an effect that is there (rate beta ). Power = 1 - beta , the chance of detecting a real effect of a given size.
alpha is about worlds with no effect; power about worlds with one. Power isn't one number: it depends on the true effect size, which is why it's quoted at the MDE.
The trade-off: for a fixed sample, lowering alpha moves the critical value out and raises beta . Only more data, less variance or a bigger effect reduces both.

Which is worse depends on the decision. Shipping a useless but costly feature (Type I) vs missing a revenue win (Type II). For guardrails (crash rate), a missed harm is the costly error, so they often use a looser alpha or more power.
Follow-up: in A/B testing, Type II is the silent one: underpowered tests that “show nothing” kill good ideas, and the few that “win” are exaggerated (Type M). (03)
8Derive the sample size for an A/B test.
Require the distribution of z under the alternative to sit z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta standard errors from zero, then solve for n.
Two arms of n , per-user variance sigma^2 : SE = sqrt2sigma^2/n .
Under H_0 , z sim mathcal N(0, 1) ; reject beyond z_1-alpha/2 = 1.96 .
Under H_1 with true gap delta , z sim mathcal N(delta/SE, 1) .
Power approx Phi(delta/SE - z_1-alpha/2) . Setting it to 1-beta gives delta/SE = z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta .
Substitute the SE: n = (z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2 cdot 2sigma^2/delta^2 .
With 1.96 and 0.84: 2 times 2.80^2 = 15.7 , so n approx 16sigma^2/delta^2 per arm.
Intuition: the factor 2 is two noisy means; delta^2 in the denominator means halving the effect quadruples the users. For proportions, sigma^2 = p(1-p) . (03)
9Drill: baseline conversion 10%, detect +0.5 points, 5% two-sided, 80% power. How many users? And at a 5% baseline, +10% relative?
About 57,600 per arm by the rule of thumb (56,512 by the exact formula); about 30,400 per arm for the second.
First: sigma^2 = 0.1 times 0.9 = 0.09 , delta = 0.005 . 16 times 0.09 / 0.000025 = 57,600 . With 15.7 instead of 16: 56,512. Each arm's own variance: 57,763.
Second: delta = 0.05 times 0.10 = 0.005 again, but sigma^2 = 0.05 times 0.95 = 0.0475 , so 16 times 0.0475/0.000025 = 30,400 (29,826 exact). Same absolute lift, lower variance.
In relative terms: n = 16\,CV^2/r^2 with CV^2 = (1-p)/p : 16 times 19 / 0.01 = 30,400 .
To days: two arms × 57,600 = 115,200 users; at 20,000 eligible a day that's 6 days, so run a full week (two is safer).
Follow-up: the 0.8-point version needs 22,075 (formula) or 22,500 (rule); a 0.25-point lift needs about 230,000. (03, 06)
10What happens to the required sample size if you halve the MDE, want 90% power, use α = 0.01, go one-sided, halve the variance, or split 90/10?
Halve the MDE: n propto 1/delta^2 , so ×4.
One-sided 5%: (1.645 + 0.84)^2/7.85 = 0.79 , legitimate only if planned and only “better” matters.
Half the variance (CUPED at rho approx 0.71 ): ×0.5.
90/10 split: SE propto sqrt1/f + 1/(1-f) : 11.1 vs 4 for 50/50, so 2.78× the total for the same precision. The small arm is the bottleneck.
Follow-up: variance reduction is the cheapest lever because it costs no extra time. (03)
11A small test shows a big, significant lift. Why might you distrust it?
Because at low power, only estimates inflated by noise can cross the significance line: the winner's curse.

The mechanism: with 10,000 per arm on a 10% baseline, a result is significant only if the observed lift exceeds 1.96 times 0.00424 = 0.83 points. If the truth is 0.25 points, power is 9%, and the significant results overstate it by 4.1× on average (Type M); 6% of them even have the wrong sign (Type S).
The tell: a lift much bigger than past experiments in the area, from a test sized for a bigger effect, with p just under 0.05.
What to do: replicate, or extend the test; shrink the estimate towards historical effects (a Bayesian prior); plan the next launch on a conservative number.
Follow-up: “compute the observed power” doesn't help: it's a function of the p-value (p = 0.05 always gives about 50%). (03)
12One-sided or two-sided? When is one-sided acceptable?
Two-sided by default. One-sided only if chosen before the data and a result in the other direction would lead to the same action as no effect.
What it does: puts all of alpha in one tail, so the critical value drops from 1.96 to 1.645 and power rises (about 21% fewer users).
Legitimate cases: “ship only if better”; non-inferiority (“not worse by more than 0.2 points”); a guardrail tested only for harm.

Why switching after seeing the data is p-hacking: choosing the tail that matches the observed sign means you'd “find” an effect whenever lvert z rvert gt 1.645 , which happens 10% of the time under H_0 . The running example: two-sided 0.064, one-sided 0.032.
Cost: a one-sided test can't tell you the change hurt.
Follow-up: to show a change is not worse, use a non-inferiority test (one-sided, against a margin) or two one-sided tests for equivalence; a non-significant two-sided test proves nothing. (02, 02)
13t or z? And Student's t or Welch's t?

t when the spread is estimated from a small sample (at A/B-test sizes t and z coincide); and Welch rather than Student, because it doesn't assume equal variances and costs almost nothing when they are equal.

Why t: t = (bar x - mu_0)/(s/sqrt n) . When s happens to come out small, t is inflated, so its tails are heavier than a normal's. For normal data it follows Student's t with n - 1 degrees of freedom: critical values 2.571 at 5, 2.228 at 10, 2.042 at 30, 1.984 at 100. Using 1.96 with n = 5 gives 12% false positives.
Student vs Welch: Student pools both groups' variances, weighted by size; Welch uses sqrts_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 and adjusts the degrees of freedom.

What breaks: 10 users at sd 3 against 40 at sd 1. The pooled variance (2.5) is dominated by the big quiet group, so Student's SE is 0.56 instead of 0.96: 26% false positives with no true difference, against Welch's 5%. Swap which group is noisy and Student drops to 0.1% (power lost).
When variances are equal: power 33.9% (Welch) vs 34.0% (Student) in a simulation.
Don't pre-test for equal variances and then choose; the two-stage procedure has worse error rates than always using Welch.

Follow-up: t is exact only for normal data, so small, skewed samples call for a permutation or exact test. Student is fairly robust with equal group sizes, which is why the problem shows up in unbalanced rollouts. (04, 04)
14When would you use a paired test, and why is it more powerful?
When the same units are measured twice (before and after, two models on the same queries) or are naturally matched. Pairing removes the between-unit variance.
The mechanism: Var(after - before) = sigma_a^2 + sigma_b^2 - 2rhosigma_asigma_b . With high correlation, almost all the variance cancels.
Example: eight users, sessions before and after; between-user sd about 3.5, average change 1.2. Paired: SE 0.17, t = 7.0 , p = 0.0002 . Unpaired Welch on the same numbers: SE 1.81, p = 0.52 .
The non-parametric version: Wilcoxon signed-rank.
Caveat: before/after without a control group isn't an experiment: anything else that changed in between is mixed in.
Follow-up: CUPED is the A/B-test version of the same idea, using pre-period behaviour as the “before”. (04)
15What does the Mann–Whitney U test actually test? When could it mislead on revenue?

Whether a random draw from B tends to beat a random draw from A: whether P(B gt A) + tfrac12 P(B = A) differs from ½ (formally its null is identical distributions). It tests medians, or means, only if one distribution is a shifted copy of the other.
The mechanism: rank all values together; U counts the pairs B wins, ties counting half.

Where it misleads: B converts 11% vs 10%, but buyers spend 80 vs 100, so mean revenue per user is 8.8 vs 10.0: B loses money. With lognormal spend and 50,000 per arm, Welch typically says A is better ( p approx 5 times 10^-5 ) while Mann–Whitney says B is “better” ( p approx 6 times 10^-6 ); in 98% of simulated runs both were significant in opposite directions. Most pairs are zero-zero ties and B has more non-zeros.
When it's right: ordinal data (ratings), small samples, or when “does the typical user do better?” is the question.
Follow-up: for skewed revenue, keep the mean and fix the noise (capping, CUPED, more users) rather than changing the question. (04)
16What is a chi-square test? How does it relate to the two-proportion z-test, and when do you use Fisher's exact test?

It compares observed counts with the counts expected under a null: chi^2 = sum (O - E)^2/E . For a 2×2 table it equals the two-proportion z-test squared. Fisher's test replaces it when expected counts are small.
Independence: E = row total × column total / grand total; (r-1)(c-1) degrees of freedom.
Goodness of fit: E from a fixed split (a fair die, a 50/50 design); categories − 1 degrees of freedom. The SRM check is this test.
The link: the running example's 2×2 table gives chi^2 = 3.43 = 1.85^2 , same p = 0.064 .
Small counts: when expected counts fall below about 5, the approximation breaks. 9/20 vs 2/20: chi-square p = 0.013 , Yates-corrected 0.034, Fisher exact 0.031.
Follow-up: exact tests on counts are slightly conservative because the achievable p-values jump. (04)
17Bootstrap vs permutation test: what does each give, and when do you use them?
The bootstrap gives an interval (uncertainty around the data as they are); a permutation test gives a p-value (how unusual the data are when labels are shuffled).

Bootstrap: resample units with replacement, recompute the statistic, take percentiles. For medians, percentiles, ratios, anything without a formula. Fails for tiny samples, extremes like the maximum, heavy tails (it can't invent unseen whales), and dependent data resampled as independent.

Permutation: under the sharp null labels are arbitrary; shuffle them and recompute. Exact under randomization, any statistic. A = 3, 5, 4, 6 vs B = 7, 8, 6, 9: 4 of 70 splits are as extreme, p = 0.057 (a t-test claims 0.017).
Both: resample or shuffle the randomized unit (users or clusters), never individual events.
Follow-up: the permutation null is “identical distributions”, stronger than “equal means”. (04, 04)
18Revenue per user is very skewed. Why can you still use a t-test, and how big must n be?
The t-test needs the average to be normal, not the data, and the central limit theorem delivers that if n is large relative to the skew.
CLT: bar X approx mathcal N(mu, sigma^2/n) for any distribution with finite variance; the mean's skewness is gamma/sqrt n .
Rules: n ge 25gamma^2 makes the mean's skewness at most 0.2; n ge 355gamma^2 is a stricter rule for accurate tails. Conversion at 1% ( gamma approx 10 ) needs a few thousand to tens of thousands.

Evidence: a one-sample t-test on exponential data ( gamma = 2 ) at n = 30 gives 7.3% false positives, lopsided 6.6% low and 0.7% high; at 1,420 it's 4.8%. Balanced two-sample tests are more forgiving: the shared skew largely cancels in the difference.
When it fails: infinite variance (Pareto tail index below 2), or a sample too small to have seen the whales, so the SE is underestimated.
Trap: revenue per user never becomes normal; only its average does. And SE = sqrtp(1-p)/n , not p(1-p)/sqrt n . (05)
19Your revenue metric is driven by a few whales. How do you test it?
Keep the mean as the target and reduce its noise: cap at a pre-set high percentile, add CUPED, and size the test with the metric's real variance. Know what a log or trimmed mean would change.
The problem: 5% buyers with lognormal spend gives a CV of about 14; the top 1% of users bring 75% of revenue. A 10% lift needs about 296,000 users per arm.

Capping at the 99.9th percentile: mean −15%, variance −72%; power at 100,000 per arm rises from about 35% to 56%. The capped lift (8.3%) understates the true 10%, but the test of “no effect” stays valid. Fix the cap in advance.
Log transform: 18% power here, and it tests the geometric mean: for A = 1, 1, 1, 1000 vs B = 10, 10, 10, 10 the log says B wins while revenue says A wins by 25×.
Trimmed mean: trimming 10% per side removes every buyer when only 5% buy: power 0.
Mann–Whitney: tests mostly conversion here: about 5% power, no better than chance.

Follow-up: report the uncapped estimate too. Splitting revenue into conversion × spend per buyer helps explain a result, but spend per buyer compares different sets of buyers in the two arms, so it's a description, not a causal effect; revenue per randomized user stays the decision metric. (05, 07)
20Drill: 80 heads in 100 tosses. Is the coin biased? What about 60?
80: yes, overwhelmingly (z = 6, p ≈ 10⁻⁹). 60: borderline, and the exact test says not at 5%.
Setup: fair coin, X sim Bin(100, 0.5) : mean 50, sd sqrt100 times 0.25 = 5 .
80 heads: z = 30/5 = 6 , normal p approx 2 times 10^-9 ; exact binomial two-sided p approx 1.1 times 10^-9 . 95% interval for the heads rate: 0.8 pm 1.96 times 0.04 = [0.72, 0.88] .
60 heads: z = 2.0 , normal p = 0.046 ; with the continuity correction z = 1.9 , p = 0.057 ; exact p = 0.057 . The uncorrected normal is too optimistic at the boundary.
The exact rule: reject at 5% for 61+ or 39− heads; its actual false-positive rate is 3.5% because counts are whole numbers.
Follow-up: 8 of 10 heads: exact p = 0.11 , not significant (the normal approximation says 0.058; at np = 5 it's unreliable). To detect a 55% coin with 80% power: about 783 tosses. (06)
21Drill: X ~ N(10, 9) and Y ~ N(5, 16), independent. What is P(X > Y)? And do overlapping confidence intervals mean no significant difference?
P(X > Y) = Φ(1) ≈ 0.84. And no: overlapping intervals can still hide a significant difference.
Difference of normals: X - Y sim mathcal N(10 - 5,\ 9 + 16) = mathcal N(5, 25) ; variances add even when subtracting. P(X - Y gt 0) = P(Z gt -1) = 0.84 .
Shift and scale: 2X + 3 sim mathcal N(23, 36) ; the sd doubles, the variance quadruples.
Sums: four draws of mathcal N(10, 9) sum to mathcal N(40, 36) ; their mean is mathcal N(10, 2.25) .

Overlap: means 10 and 13, each SE 1. Intervals [8.04, 11.96] and [11.04, 14.96] overlap, but the difference has SE sqrt 2 = 1.41 , z = 2.12 , p = 0.034 . Non-overlap needs a gap of 3.92; significance needs only 2.77. Intervals that just touch mean p approx 0.006 .
22Design an A/B test for a new checkout flow, end to end.
Metric and guardrails, unit, MDE and sample size, assignment, checks, analysis, decision rule: all written down before launch.
Metric: primary = orders per user (or conversion); guardrails = revenue per user, payment failures, latency, refunds; trust = sample ratio.
Unit: user (consistent experience across sessions); analyse per user.
Size: MDE from the business (smallest lift worth the build); n approx 16sigma^2/delta^2 per arm with the historical variance, reduced by CUPED; duration rounded up to whole weeks.
Assignment: salted hash of user ID, 50/50; an A/A run or pre-period balance check first.
During: monitor SRM and guardrails daily, but don't decide from the primary metric until the planned end (or use alpha spending).
Analysis: Welch or z on per-user values with CUPED; delta method for ratio metrics; pre-registered segments only; Holm for several variants.
Decision: the interval against a practical threshold, guardrails fine, novelty checked (daily effect stable).
23You randomize by user but measure click-through rate per page view. What's wrong with the usual z-test, and how do you fix it?

It treats page views as independent when they're clustered within users, so the SE is too small and false positives soar. Fix it with the delta method on per-user totals, clustered standard errors, or a user-level bootstrap.
Why: some users click a lot and some never, so one user's page views are correlated. The effective sample is closer to the number of users.
How big: simulated A/A tests with 2,000 users per arm and about 10 views each: naive z 16% false positives, delta method 4.9%; the honest SE was 1.38× the naive one.
The design effect: 1 + (m-1)\,ICC = 1 + 9 times 0.09 approx 1.82 , and sqrt1.82 = 1.35 ; uneven page views per user push it to the simulated 1.38.
Delta method: Var(bar Y/bar X) approx frac1nmu_X^2(sigma_Y^2 - 2Rsigma_XY + R^2sigma_X^2) , with per-user clicks Y and views X .
Follow-up: an A/A test would have exposed it: 16% significant instead of 5%. (07)
24How do you assign users to arms? Why a salted hash, and why not user ID mod 2?
bucket = hash(experiment salt + user id) mod 1000, with ranges of buckets mapped to arms. It's random-looking, stable for each user, needs no storage, and is independent across experiments.
The hash scrambles IDs so buckets are uniform and unrelated to user traits.
The salt differs per experiment, so a user's arm in one test says nothing about their arm in another; without it the same half of users would get every new treatment.

ID mod 2 or a phone number's last digit: IDs and numbers are often assigned by signup time, region, carrier or shard, so they can correlate with behaviour; the split is the same in every experiment, so carry-over and fatigue pile onto one half; and it can be predicted or gamed.
Verify: SRM test on the split; pre-period metrics balanced.
25What is an A/A test, and what does it catch?

An experiment where both arms get the same experience. Since nothing differs, about 5% of A/A tests should be significant at 5% and their p-values should be uniform; anything else exposes a broken pipeline.

Catches: wrong standard errors (page views treated as independent: 16% significant instead of 5%), broken or biased assignment, sample ratio mismatch, logging that differs by arm, bot filtering applied unevenly, metric bugs.
How: run many, or replay historical data over many random splits, and look at the p-value histogram: flat is good, a pile-up near 0 means the variance is underestimated.
Can't catch: problems that need a real treatment, such as interference or a treatment that changes who gets logged.
26Drill: a 50/50 test has 100,800 users in control and 99,200 in treatment. Is that a problem? What do you do?
Yes: χ² = 12.8, p = 0.00035. That's a sample ratio mismatch; don't trust the result until the cause is found.
Calculation: expected 100,000 each; chi^2 = 800^2/100,000 + 800^2/100,000 = 6.4 + 6.4 = 12.8 on 1 degree of freedom, p = 0.00035 . Usual alert threshold p lt 0.001 .
Scale matters: the same 50.4% with 2,000 users (1,008 vs 992) gives p = 0.72 .
Why it matters: something removed users unevenly, and the removed users aren't random, so the arms are no longer comparable.
Usual causes: treatment crashes or loads slower before logging; bot filtering reacting to the treatment; redirects; eligibility checked after assignment; a mid-test ramp change; hashing bugs.
Follow-up: for a 90/10 design, test against 90/10: 90,500 vs 9,500 gives chi^2 = 27.8 . (07)
27Explain CUPED. Derive θ and the variance reduction. What if ρ = 0.6?

Subtract the part of the metric that pre-experiment behaviour predicts: Y^cv = Y - theta(X - bar X) with theta = Cov(Y, X)/Var(X) . Variance falls by the factor 1 - rho^2 ; the effect estimate stays unbiased.
Derivation: Var(Y^cv) = Var(Y) - 2thetaCov(Y,X) + theta^2Var(X) . Set the derivative -2Cov + 2thetaVar(X) to 0: theta^* = Cov/Var(X) . Plug in: Var(Y)(1 - rho^2) .
Unbiased: the effect becomes (bar Y_B - bar Y_A) - theta(bar X_B - bar X_A) ; X is pre-treatment, so randomization makes the second term zero on average.
rho = 0.6 : variance × 0.64, SE × 0.80, 36% fewer users for the same power. In a simulation: SE 0.424 → 0.340, power 48% → 66%, estimate unchanged.
Rules: one theta from pooled data; the covariate must be unaffected by treatment (pre-period only); new users get X = 0 plus an indicator.
Follow-up: it's essentially regression adjustment: Y on treatment and centred X . (07)
28How long should a test run? What are novelty and primacy effects?
As long as the sample size needs, rounded up to whole weeks (often at least two), and longer if the effect is still drifting.
Weeks: behaviour differs by weekday; a partial week estimates a different effect.
Novelty: users try a new thing because it's new; the lift decays.
Primacy (change aversion): users resist change at first; the effect improves over time.
Detecting them: plot the daily treatment effect, or compare cohorts by first exposure date; analyse new users, who have no old habit.
Long-term: keep a long-running holdout for effects that take months.
Follow-up: don't stop early just because it's significant (question 30), and don't extend it just because it isn't: both bias the result. (07)
29You're testing a ranking change in a two-sided marketplace. Why is a user-level A/B biased, and what would you do?
Treatment and control buyers compete for the same supply, so one arm's outcome depends on the other's treatment (SUTVA fails). Randomize at a level where they don't interact: switchbacks or clusters.

The bias: treatment buyers grab the best listings, control buyers get what's left. Treatment looks better partly because control got worse; at full launch nobody gets that head start, so the test overestimates.
Switchback: alternate a whole market between arms over random time slots; analyse by slot; leave buffers for carry-over.
Cluster (geo) randomization: whole cities per arm. Fewer units: with clusters of 100 and ICC 0.01, the design effect is 1.99, so the effective sample halves.
Social products have the opposite bias: control users are partly treated by their treated friends, so the test underestimates.
30Your PM checks the dashboard daily and wants to stop as soon as it's significant. What's the problem, and what do you propose?
Each look is another chance for noise to cross 1.96. Daily looks for 14 days turn a 5% false-positive rate into about 22%. Propose a fixed horizon, or a sequential design built for looking.

Why: z wanders like a random walk; it's standard normal at any one pre-chosen time, but the chance it crosses the line somewhere grows with every look: 14% for 5 looks, 19% for 10, 25% for 20, 37% for 100.

Group sequential (O'Brien–Fleming): for 5 looks, boundaries 4.56, 3.22, 2.63, 2.28, 2.04. Early stops only for overwhelming effects; power 79% vs 80% for the fixed design, and 20% fewer users on average when the effect is real.
Always-valid tests (mSPRT, confidence sequences): look any time, at the cost of wider intervals.
Allowed: daily monitoring of guardrails and SRM, and stopping for harm.
Follow-up: “Bayesian tests let you peek” isn't true for decisions: “ship when P(B gt A) gt 0.95 ” checked daily ships 19% of A/A tests. (08)
31Drill: ten metrics with sorted p-values 0.001, 0.0054, 0.012, 0.019, 0.030, 0.041, 0.10, 0.25, 0.60, 0.90. What survives Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg at 0.05?
Bonferroni 1, Holm 2, BH 4 (unadjusted: 6).
Bonferroni: p le 0.05/10 = 0.005 : only 0.001.
BH: thresholds 0.005k : 0.001 ≤ 0.005, 0.0054 ≤ 0.010, 0.012 ≤ 0.015, 0.019 ≤ 0.020 ✓; 0.030 > 0.025 and nothing larger passes; the largest passing rank is 4.
Why it matters: 10 independent tests at 5% with no real effects give at least one false positive 40% of the time.

Which to use: Holm (family-wise error) when any false claim is costly (variants, guardrails); BH (false discovery rate) for screening many metrics. In a simulation with 100 tests and 10 real effects, BH found 51% of them with 4.6% false discoveries; Holm 32% with 1.5%.
32The overall effect isn't significant, but it is for Android users (p = 0.03) and not for iOS (p = 0.20). What do you conclude?
Not much yet. Slicing creates multiple tests, and “significant here, not there” isn't a test of whether the effects differ.
Multiple testing: with 20 segments and no real effect anywhere, the chance at least one shows p lt 0.05 is 1 - 0.95^20 = 64\% .
Test the difference: fit treatment × platform and test the interaction. Two p-values on either side of 0.05 can come from nearly identical effects.
Power: each segment has a fraction of the users, so segment estimates are noisier and significant ones exaggerated.
What to do: treat it as a hypothesis; was the segment pre-registered with a reason? Correct for the number of segments; confirm with a new test targeted at Android.
33The result is significant but the lift is tiny. Or it isn't significant but the interval is wide. Do you ship?
Decide from the confidence interval against the smallest effect worth having (and the cost and risk of the change), not from the p-value alone.

Significant, tiny: with enough users any non-zero effect is significant. If the whole interval is below the practical threshold, the change isn't worth it on this metric; ship only if it's cheap and has other reasons.
Not significant, wide: underpowered, not “no effect”. The running example (interval −0.05 to +1.65 points) can't rule out a 16% relative lift. Extend, reduce variance, or decide on other grounds.
Not significant, narrow around 0: a real negative result; the test was informative.
Significant and above the threshold, guardrails fine: ship. A significantly worse guardrail is a trade-off to escalate.
Follow-up: reversibility, maintenance cost and strategy also enter, and the test doesn't measure them. (07)
34The feature won its A/B test, but after launch the metric barely moved. Why might that be?
Usually some mix of an exaggerated test estimate, an effect that faded, dilution, interference and a changed world; occasionally a bug.
Winner's curse: significant results from modestly powered tests overstate the effect (4.1× at 9% power), and among many tests some winners are false positives.
Novelty: part of the lift was curiosity, and it decayed after the test window.
Dilution: the test measured triggered users; across everyone the effect is the trigger share times as large.
Interference: in a marketplace the treatment arm borrowed supply from control; at full launch there's no one to borrow from.
The world changed: seasonality, a different traffic mix, other launches, a test window that wasn't representative.
Twyman's law: if the test lift looked too good, a sample-ratio, logging or metric bug may have produced it.
Follow-up: a long-running holdout measures the launched effect directly, and shrinking test estimates towards historical lifts makes forecasts honest. (03, 07)
35How does a Bayesian A/B test work? What is P(B > A), and does it let you peek?

Beta priors on each arm's rate, updated with the counts to Beta posteriors; P(B > A) and the expected loss come from comparing draws. It answers the natural question, but peeking still inflates wrong decisions.
Conjugacy: Beta(a, b) prior + x of n converting → Beta(a + x, b + n - x) .
Running example, flat priors: Beta(1001, 9001) vs Beta(1081, 8921) ; P(B gt A) = 0.968 ; expected loss of shipping B 0.005 points, of keeping A 0.81 points.
Relation to p: with flat priors and large n, P(B gt A) approx 1 - one-sided p (0.968 vs 0.032). Same arithmetic, different meaning.
Priors matter: a prior centred on 10% for both arms worth 10,000 users drops P(B gt A) to 0.907 and halves the estimated lift; defensible if built from past experiments.
Peeking: “ship when P(B gt A) gt 0.95 ” ships 5% of A/A tests checked once, 19% checked daily for 14 days.
36A feature launched in one city without an experiment. How do you estimate its effect?
Build a credible counterfactual: difference-in-differences against similar cities, or a synthetic control; check the key assumption with pre-period data and placebos.
DiD: treated city 100 → 120, control 80 → 90: effect 20 - 10 = 10 . Assumes parallel trends; check that pre-period trends match, and that a fake earlier launch date finds nothing.
Synthetic control: a weighted mix of untreated cities matching the treated one's pre-period path; placebo runs on donor cities.

Other designs by situation: regression discontinuity if a score cut-off decided who got it; interrupted time series with only one series (weakest: anything else that changed at the same time is confounded); propensity matching or weighting if users opted in (assumes no unmeasured confounding, which motivated opt-in users usually violate).
Follow-up: next time, keep a randomized holdout, even a small one. (10)

beginaligned s^2 &= frac1n-1sum (x_i - bar x)^2 \\ SE(bar x) &= sigma/sqrt n \\ SE(hat p_B - hat p_A) &= sqrtSE_A^2 + SE_B^2 \\ z &= (estimate - value under H_0)/SE \\ CI &= estimate pm z times SE endaligned

The SD describes users and doesn't shrink as you add users; the SE describes the average and falls like 1/sqrt n . Variances add for sums and differences of independent things: add variances, not SEs. A bell holds 68%, 95% and 99.7% within ±1, ±2 and ±3 SDs; cut-offs 1.645, 1.96 and 2.576 for 90%, 95% and 99%. Running example: SE_A = 0.003 , SE of the gap 0.00432, z 1.85.
Pooled two-proportion z, p-value, interval (unpooled SE):

beginaligned z &= frachat p_B - hat p_Asqrthat p(1-hat p)(1/n_A + 1/n_B) \\ p &= 2big(1 - Phi(lvert z rvert)big) \\ CI &= (hat p_B - hat p_A) pm 1.96sqrtfrachat p_A(1-hat p_A)n_A + frachat p_B(1-hat p_B)n_B endaligned

p = P(data this extreme | H_0 ), not P( H_0 | data). Interval excludes 0 ⇔ p lt 0.05 . Critical z: 1.645, 1.96, 2.576 (two-sided 10%, 5%, 1%). Running example: z 1.85, p 0.064, CI [−0.05, +1.65] points. “95%” is a property of the procedure, not of one interval. To show “not worse”: non-inferiority (one-sided bound above −margin) or TOST (90% interval inside ±margin).
beginaligned n_per arm &= frac(z_1-alpha/2 + z_1-beta)^2 cdot 2sigma^2delta^2 approx frac16\,sigma^2delta^2 \\ n_per arm &approx frac16\,CV^2r^2 \\ MDE &= 2.80sqrt2sigma^2/n endaligned
10% baseline: +0.8 points → 22,075; +0.5 → 56,512; +0.25 → 226,048 per arm. Half the MDE ×4; 90% power ×1.34; alpha = 0.01 ×1.49; one-sided ×0.79. Low power ⇒ exaggerated wins (4.1× at 9% power).

Means: Welch's t. Same units twice: paired t. Rates: two-proportion z = 2×2 chi^2 . Small counts: Fisher, exact binomial. Counts vs a split: chi^2 goodness of fit. Ranks: Mann–Whitney (tests P(B gt A) , not means). Anything, small n: permutation. Interval for anything: bootstrap over units.
beginaligned t &= fracbar x_1 - bar x_2sqrts_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2 \\ chi^2 &= sum frac(O - E)^2E endaligned
beginaligned SE(bar X) &= sigma/sqrt n \\ SE(hat p) &= sqrtp(1-p)/n \\ skew(bar X) &= gamma/sqrt n \\ SE(hat x_q) &approx sqrtq(1-q)/n\,/\,f(x_q) endaligned
n ge 25gamma^2 (strict: 355gamma^2 ). Whales: cap at a pre-set percentile, CUPED, more users. Log tests the geometric mean; trimming can delete every buyer.

beginaligned bucket &= hash(salt + id) bmod 1000 \\ SRM: chi^2 &= sum (O - E)^2/E, alert at p lt 0.001 \\ Var(bar Y/bar X) &approx fracsigma_Y^2 - 2Rsigma_XY + R^2sigma_X^2n\,mu_X^2 \\ Var(bar Y_B/bar Y_A - 1) &approx fracVar(bar Y_B)mu_A^2 + fracmu_B^2Var(bar Y_A)mu_A^4 \\ Delta_all &= s cdot Delta_trig \\ DE &= 1 + (m - 1)\,ICC \\ theta &= Cov(Y, X)/Var(X) \\ Var(Y^cv) &= (1 - rho^2)Var(Y) endaligned

Analyse at the randomization unit; trigger with a counterfactual log in control; don't decide on metrics conditioned on post-treatment outcomes. Full weeks. Watch novelty and primacy. Marketplaces and social: switchback or cluster designs. Decide on the interval vs a practical threshold.
beginaligned FWER &= 1 - (1 - alpha)^m \\ Bonferroni: p &le alpha/m \\ Holm: p_(k) &le alpha/(m - k + 1) , stop at first fail \\ BH: largest k with p_(k) &le (k/m)\,q endaligned
Peeking: 5 looks 14%, 10 looks 19%, 14 daily looks 22%. O'Brien–Fleming, 5 looks: 4.56, 3.22, 2.63, 2.28, 2.04. Holm for decisions, BH for screening.
Bayesian and observational
beginaligned p mid x &sim Beta(a + x,\ b + n - x) \\ DiD &= (T_after - T_before) - (C_after - C_before) endaligned

Running example: P(B gt A) = 0.968 . Daily checks of “ship at 0.95” ship 19% of A/A tests. DiD: parallel trends. Synthetic control: weights keep holding. RDD: no jump but the treatment. ITS: nothing else changed. Matching: no unmeasured confounding.
