chunks.x: Data preparation and feature engineering · Deepam Minda

One rule runs through everything. Anything that learns a number from the data (a median, a category's average target, a scaler's mean, a list of selected features) is fitted on the training rows only, inside each cross-validation fold. Fixes that learn nothing, such as correcting a type or a typo, can run before the split.

Before filling a blank, ask why it's blank: by pure chance (MCAR), because of other things you can see (MAR), or because of the missing value itself (MNAR). Blanks often carry signal, so keep it with a missing-indicator column or an explicit “Missing” category. Filling with the mode or median and leaving no trace is safe only when the blanks are random and few.

Encoding follows the model and the number of levels. One-hot for a few levels; out-of-fold, smoothed target encoding or count encoding for many; native categorical support in boosting libraries; embeddings in neural nets. Target encoding leaks because each row's own label sits inside its category's average.

Outliers: first decide whether a value is an error or a genuine extreme. Errors are fixed, or turned into missing values. Genuine extremes are capped or transformed, or handled by a robust loss or a tree. In fraud, the extremes are the signal.

Scaling matters for anything built on distances, penalties or gradient descent; trees ignore monotone transforms. Collinearity makes coefficients unstable but usually leaves predictions fine, and it splits a tree's feature importance between correlated features.

Split the way the model will meet new data: by time for forecasting and credit, by group when new customers arrive, stratified when a class is rare. For imbalance, move the threshold first, reweight second, resample last.

The first look is a checklist, not free browsing. Each check answers one question: what could make a model wrong, or make it look better than it is? Write the answers down; most of them decide a later step.
The unit of prediction: an application, a customer-month, a transaction. Types and shape.
It fixes how to split (rows of one customer belong together) and how to aggregate features.
Its distribution or base rate, how it's defined, when it becomes known, and how it moves over time.
It sets the metric, the need to stratify, and the prediction time, which decides what counts as leakage.
Share missing per column, columns missing together, missing rates over time, target rate when missing vs present.
It decides the imputation strategy, and shows whether blanks are a signal or a pipeline bug.
Exact copies, and the same entity or event appearing twice.
Copies on both sides of a split inflate scores.
Number of levels per categorical column, rare levels, ID-like columns.
It picks the encoding; a column with one value per row is an ID, not a feature.
Long tails, spikes at 0 or −1 or 9999 (sentinels), impossible values, constant columns.
It decides transforms, outlier handling and scaling.
A timestamp, whether feature distributions drift by month, when columns were added.
It decides a time-based split and which aggregates are legal.
Columns recorded after the prediction time (“closed date”, “collections calls”), a single feature that predicts the target almost perfectly.
They make offline scores great and production poor.

Where to look. Hygiene checks (types, duplicates, missing shares) are fine on all the data, since they learn nothing the model uses. Exploration that shapes modelling choices, such as which features look predictive or where to cap a tail, uses the training portion only; choosing features because they fit the test rows is a quiet leak.

Adversarial validation is a fast check that training and test data look alike. Label training rows 0 and test (or recent) rows 1 and train a classifier to tell them apart. An AUC near 0.5 means they look alike; a high AUC means they differ, and its top features show where: drift, a changed definition, or an ID that encodes time.
Cleaning makes each value mean what it claims to mean. Most cleaning steps are row-by-row rules that learn nothing from the data, which is why they can safely run before the split.
What: exact copies (a replayed batch, a join that fanned one row out into several) and near-copies (the same customer re-applying, a retried payment).
Why it matters: copies get extra weight, and a copy in training with its twin in validation means the model is graded on rows it memorized.

What to do: first ask whether the repeat is real; two identical purchases can both be genuine. Remove artefacts; keep genuine repeats but split by entity. Check the row count after every join, since a many-to-many join multiplies rows silently.
What: one real level written several ways: case, stray spaces, typos, synonyms (“Self-employed”, “Business owner”).
Why it matters: one level splits into several rare ones with noisy averages, and a new spelling at serving time becomes an unseen category.

What to do: trim, lower-case and normalize Unicode, then map with an explicit table. Fuzzy matching finds candidates, but a person approves the merges: “Mumbai” and “Mumba” are one place, “Austria” and “Australia” are not.
Wrong types, impossible values and units

Wrong types: numbers stored as text (“1,200”, “12k”), mixed date formats, booleans as “Y”, “yes” and 1. And the reverse: IDs and postcodes stored as numbers, so a model treats one postcode as “bigger” than another.

Sentinels: −1, 0 or 9999 meaning “unknown”. An income of 0 that means “not provided” is a blank pretending to be a value, and a linear model reads it as very low income. Convert sentinels to proper blanks.
Impossible values (an age of 230, a negative quantity, an end before a start) are errors, not outliers. Set them to missing rather than deleting the row.
Unit mismatches (rupees vs thousands, 35 vs 0.35, grams vs kilograms) show up as clusters a factor of 10, 100 or 1,000 apart. Split the distribution by source or by date to find them.

What: wrong targets: annotators disagree, a definition changed (default at 30 days past due, later 90), or a label isn't mature yet (a loan disbursed last month can't have defaulted, so it's “good” too early).
Why it matters: random noise caps the accuracy you can reach and blurs probabilities; systematic noise, like immature labels, teaches something false.
Detect: rows whose out-of-fold probability strongly disagrees with their label (the idea behind confident learning), the highest-loss rows, annotator disagreement; then review a sample by hand.

Treat: relabel or drop clear errors, set a maturity window for outcomes, and prefer training that doesn't chase every point (label smoothing, early stopping). Keep the test labels cleanest of all, or every model comparison is noisy.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Every later step asks the same question: was this fitted on data the model will legitimately have? So the split comes before any step that learns from the data.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Training set: fits the model's parameters and every preprocessing statistic.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Validation set (or cross-validation folds): chooses hyperparameters, features, thresholds and the preprocessing recipe.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Test set: touched once, at the end. Every look followed by a change turns it into a validation set, and the estimate becomes optimistic.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: The rule for preprocessing: a step that learns a number (a median, a mean and standard deviation, a category's average target, a vocabulary, a list of selected features) is fitted on training rows and applied unchanged to validation, test and production rows. Steps that learn nothing, like parsing a date, can run anywhere.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: The split must imitate how the model will meet new data. Ask: at prediction time, what's new?

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Independent rows, classification

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Each fold keeps the class ratio. With 2% positives, a random fold can get very few, and its score is noise.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Many rows per customer, store or device; new ones at deployment

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: All rows of one group stay together, so the model can't score well by recognizing the customer.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Data ordered in time; predicting forward (credit, demand, fraud)

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Time-based: expanding or rolling window, plus a final out-of-time test

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Train on the past, test on the future, as in production. Random splits leak trends and future regimes backwards.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Labels that cover a horizon (default within 12 months)

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: The last training rows' outcomes are only observed during the validation period; the gap drops them.

chunks.h: Split first: honest splits and leakage
chunks.x: Expanding-window validation. Each fold trains on everything before a cut-off, skips a gap as long as the label horizon (here, one month), and validates on the next period. The folds' scores show whether performance holds as time moves on.
Leakage is any information available in training or validation that won't be available when the model makes a real prediction. It's the most common reason for “great offline, poor in production”.

Target leakage: a feature recorded after the label, or caused by it: “number of collections calls” when predicting default, “chargeback filed” when predicting fraud. The test, per feature: is this value known, with this exact content, at the moment of prediction?
Train–test contamination: the same row, a near-copy or the same customer on both sides of the split. Oversampling or SMOTE before the split does this too.

Preprocessing fitted on all the data: a scaler, imputer, encoder, PCA or feature selection fitted before splitting. Scaling leaks a little; target encoding and feature selection leak a lot, because they use the labels.

Temporal leakage: random splits of time-ordered data, a customer's lifetime average that includes later rows, or today's value of a slowly changing table joined instead of its value at prediction time.
How it shows up: a score too good for the problem; one feature dominating importance, or predicting the target almost perfectly alone; a random split scoring far above a time-based or grouped one.

A Pipeline chains preprocessing and the model into one object, and a ColumnTransformer applies different preprocessing to different columns. Hand the whole pipeline to cross-validation and every step is refitted on each training fold, so the validation fold never touches any statistic. The same fitted object then runs in production, which removes train–serve skew (two codebases computing a feature slightly differently). A full example is in section 13.

“Scaling has no labels, so scaling everything before cross-validation is fine.” The effect is small for scaling, but the same order of steps with target encoding, feature selection or SMOTE inflates the score a lot. Put every fitted step inside the pipeline.
Filling a blank is the last step, not the first. Three questions come before any method:
Why is it missing? The mechanism decides which methods are unbiased.
Does missingness itself predict the target? If it does, it's a feature, and filling it in without a trace throws that feature away.
Will it be missing in production in the same way? The model must meet blanks at serving time exactly as it met them in training.

chunks.x: What decides whether a value is blank. The dashed box is the value itself, which you never see when it's blank. Only in MNAR does the blank depend on it.

chunks.x: A sensor drops readings at random; a batch of forms was lost in a migration.

chunks.h: Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR
chunks.x: The complete rows are a random sample, so dropping rows adds no bias; it only loses data. A mean fill keeps the mean right but still shrinks the spread and the correlations.

chunks.x: Income is blank more often for self-employed applicants, and employment type is recorded. Among the self-employed, a high earner and a low earner are equally likely to leave it blank.

chunks.h: Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR
chunks.x: The reason for the blank is a column you have. Dropping rows under-represents the self-employed, so it's biased. Imputing income from employment type and the other columns removes that bias.

chunks.h: Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR
chunks.x: MNAR, missing not at random

chunks.h: Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR
chunks.x: High earners leave income blank because it's high (privacy), or low earners because it's low. The value itself decides whether it gets reported.

chunks.h: Why values go missing: MCAR, MAR, MNAR
chunks.x: The reason is the hidden value, so no column you have can fully correct for it: two applicants who match on every observed column still differ, because the blank itself hints at the income. Imputing from other columns stays biased. The information sits in the fact of the blank, so keep it as a feature.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: One question separates them. Take two applicants who match on every column you have. If you learn that one of them left income blank, does your guess of that person's income change?

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: No: MAR. The reason for the blank is already in your data (employment type, say). Once you know it, the blank adds nothing about the income. (MCAR passes too: it's the special case where the blank doesn't depend on the observed columns either.)

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: Yes: MNAR. The blank carries information about the very value it hides. High earners hiding their salary is the classic case: a blank income means “probably high”, even among people who look identical on paper.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: In symbols, with M the “is blank” flag, x_obs the columns you can see and x_mis the hidden value:

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: beginaligned MCAR:quad P(M mid x_obs, x_mis) &= P(M) \\ MAR:quad P(M mid x_obs, x_mis) &= P(M mid x_obs) \\ MNAR:quad P(M mid x_obs, x_mis) &\ still depends on\ x_mis endaligned

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: In words: under MAR, once you know the columns you can see, the hidden value no longer changes the chance of a blank. Under MNAR it still does.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: Worked example. Eight applicants, true monthly income in ₹k. The true average is 60.

chunks.x: 30 and 120 seen (mean 75)

chunks.x: Drop the blank rows: 55, too low, because the self-employed are under-represented. Fill each blank with its group's mean (75): 60, correct

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: Under MAR, the column that explains the blanks (employment type) removes the bias completely. Under MNAR it removes none of it here (and in general it can't remove all of it): inside each group, the people who hid their income are the richer ones, and no observed column can see that. What does survive is the blank itself. An income_missing flag is 1 for exactly the two top earners, and a model can learn from it.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: The same blanks can be MAR or MNAR, depending on what you record. Say doctors are the ones who skip the income field, and among doctors, skipping has nothing to do with how much each one earns. If occupation is a column, the blanks are explained by it: MAR. Leave occupation out, and the same blanks now depend on something you can't see that's tied to income: MNAR for your dataset. So MNAR really means “depends on something unobserved that's related to the value”, and the hidden value itself is the textbook case.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: “MAR means the values are missing at random.” The name misleads: MAR blanks are not random overall (the self-employed have more of them). They're random only once you account for the observed columns. And the share that's missing says nothing about the mechanism.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: A fourth case, structural blanks: “months since last loan” for someone who has never had a loan. Nothing is unknown here; the value is undefined. Imputing a typical value would invent a loan. Use a domain rule instead: a “none” category, or a sentinel plus an indicator.

chunks.h: MAR vs MNAR: does the blank say something about its own value?
chunks.x: Why the names matter in practice. For a prediction model, the key question is whether blanks at serving time are produced the same way as in training. If they are, the blank can be used as a feature whatever the mechanism, even MNAR. For inference (estimating a coefficient, an effect, a population average) the mechanism decides whether the estimate is biased, and MNAR needs assumptions the data can't check.
Compare rows with and without the value. Look at the other columns' distributions and at the target rate in each group. If the groups differ, the data isn't MCAR.

Predict the blank. Train a classifier on the other columns to predict “is this value missing?”, scored out-of-fold. An AUC near 0.5 is consistent with MCAR. A clearly higher AUC means it isn't MCAR: the blanks depend on observed columns (MAR, or MNAR if the value itself matters too), and the classifier's top features say which. An AUC near 0.5 can't rule out MNAR. Little's MCAR test is the formal version of this check, for means.
Check whether the blank predicts the target. If rows with a blank default at twice the rate of the rest, the blank is a predictor, however it arose.

MAR vs MNAR can't be settled from the data. The difference is about values you never observe. Use domain knowledge (why would someone skip this field?), a follow-up sample where the true values are obtained, or an outside source that has them for some rows.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: A missing indicator is a 0/1 column that records whether the original value was blank, added next to the filled-in column. The model can then give blanks their own effect, and it knows which values are real and which were filled in.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: In a linear model it frees the blank rows' prediction. Fill blanks with any constant c , giving the filled column tilde x ( x where observed, c where blank), and add the indicator I :

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: beginaligned hat y &= beta_0 + beta\, tilde x + theta I \\ observed rows:quad hat y &= beta_0 + beta x \\ blank rows:quad hat y &= beta_0 + beta c + theta endaligned

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: Without the indicator, a blank row is treated as a real point at x = c , so the one fitted line has to pass near it too. If blank rows have unusual targets, they pull the line. Real rows (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) have slope 1; add two blank rows with y = 8 , filled at c = 0 , and the fitted slope becomes −1.8.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: With the indicator, a blank row's prediction beta_0 + beta c + theta is one free number, and theta sets it to the blank rows' own level (8 here). The line is then fitted to the real rows alone, so beta stays exactly 1.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: So the choice of c doesn't matter: theta absorbs it ( theta = 8 - c here). The exception is regularization: a far-off c such as −999 needs a huge theta , which the penalty shrinks, so fill with the median.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: the target rate differs between blank and non-blank rows, or MNAR is plausible;

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: you fill with a simple value for a linear model or a neural net;

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: the share missing isn't trivial (an indicator that's almost always 0 carries little).

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: Skip it, or think twice, when:

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: a boosting library handles blanks natively: it already learns where blanks go at each split;

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: the collection process will change. If the income field becomes mandatory, a model that learned “blank means risky” has a feature that no longer fires;

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: many columns go blank together (one source failed). Use one indicator per source or pattern, not one per column.

chunks.h: Missingness as a signal: the indicator column
chunks.x: Trade-off: the model now depends on how the data was collected, which is often a strong signal and always a fragile one. Monitor missing rates in production: a pipeline bug that blanks a field changes scores without any error.

Mean or median. Replace each blank with the training mean or median. It's fast, simple and stable. The median is the usual choice for skewed columns such as income, where a few huge values pull the mean. What it distorts, with a share r missing completely at random and filled with the mean ( tilde x is the filled column, z any other column):
beginaligned Var(tilde x) &approx (1 - r)\, Var(x) \\ Corr(tilde x, z) &approx sqrt1 - r\; Corr(x, z) endaligned

In words: every filled value sits exactly at the centre, so it adds nothing to the spread and nothing to any co-movement with other columns. The variance shrinks, every correlation weakens, and the histogram grows a spike at the mean.

Under MAR it's also biased: filling a self-employed applicant's income with the overall median ignores what employment type says. In a model with several correlated features, the other features absorb the missing part of x , which biases their coefficients. With an indicator, much of the damage to prediction goes away; the damage to inference doesn't. Prediction vs inference below shows why, with numbers.

A constant, plus an indicator. Fill with a fixed value. For trees, an out-of-range value such as −999 puts every blank at one end, so one split can separate them: a crude version of native handling. For linear models, an out-of-range constant without an indicator is harmful: it acts as an extreme point with high leverage and tilts the slope. With an indicator the constant doesn't matter, but only without regularization and before scaling: a −999 fill inflates a later scaler's sigma and squeezes the real values together. For linear models and neural nets, fill with the median and let the indica
kNN imputation. For a row with a blank, find the k most similar training rows, measured on the columns both have, and average their values (a majority vote for categories).
Why: it fills from rows that look alike, so it respects local structure and relationships without assuming a model.

Costs: features must be scaled first, or the largest-unit column decides who's “similar”. Every imputation searches the training set, so it's slow on big data and the training rows must be kept for serving. Distances get less meaningful as the number of columns grows.
When: small-to-medium data with a few informative numeric columns. Not for big data, many columns, or mostly categorical data.
Model-based (regression) imputation. Train a model to predict the column from the others, on rows where it's observed, and predict the blanks.
Why: under MAR it uses exactly the information that explains the blanks, so it removes the bias that mean filling leaves.

The catch: predictions sit on the regression surface with no noise, so imputed values are too regular and correlations come out too strong. Adding a random draw of the model's residual (stochastic regression imputation) fixes the spread.
When: under MAR, when the column matters to a linear model or to inference.

Never use the target as an input in a prediction pipeline: the target isn't known when a new row arrives. (In multiple imputation for inference, the reverse holds: the outcome should be in the imputation model, or the imputed values weaken its relationships.)
Iterative imputation (MICE). Model-based imputation for many columns at once, when several have blanks:
Fill every blank with a simple value (the median).
For each column with blanks in turn, fit a model predicting it from all the other columns, on the rows where it's observed, and replace its blanks with the predictions.
Cycle through the columns several times, until the imputed values stop changing much.

MICE (multiple imputation by chained equations) is the version that adds random draws at step 2 and repeats the whole process to produce several completed datasets (see multiple imputation). sklearn's IterativeImputer returns one completed dataset per run (run it several times with sample_posterior=True for multiple imputation); with random forests as the per-column model it's close to missForest. Trade-offs: it uses the joint structure of all columns and handles blanks in many columns at once, but it's slow, it assumes MAR, it can overfit, convergence isn't guaranteed, and a single determinis

Time series: forward fill and interpolation. Forward fill carries the last observed value forward; it uses only the past, so it's safe for live prediction. Add “time since last real observation”, because a value carried forward for a month isn't as trustworthy as yesterday's. Linear interpolation between neighbours uses the next value, which doesn't exist yet at prediction time: fine for cleaning a historical chart, a leak in a forecasting feature.

Domain rules. Often the best imputer is knowing the data. A blank “number of previous defaults” for a bureau record that exists means 0; a blank “spouse income” for a single applicant means “not applicable”; a blank discount means no discount. Encode these explicitly, before any statistical method.
An explicit “Missing” category: usually the best default. Treat the blank as its own level.

Why: it keeps the signal if there is one, assumes nothing about the mechanism, and works with every encoder (one-hot gives it a column, target encoding gives it its own rate, a tree can split it off).

Costs: one more level. If blanks are very rare it's a rare category with a noisy estimate (group it or smooth it). If training had no blanks but production does, “Missing” is an unseen category, so plan for it.
Mode (most frequent value): acceptable only in a narrow case.

When it's fine: the blanks are MCAR, so the blank rows are a random sample and the most common level is the best single guess; the share is small (a few percent), so the distortion is negligible; and the blank doesn't predict the target. Quick baselines and linear models where you'd rather not add a level fit this case.

What goes wrong otherwise: filled rows join the mode category, so it becomes a mixture of two populations. Its target rate, its encoding and its coefficient all drift towards the blanks' behaviour, so the biggest category's own signal gets corrupted. If the blanks were informative (MAR or MNAR), that information is erased. And if no level dominates, the mode is a poor guess: it's right only as often as its share.

A classifier-based imputer. Under MAR, predict the missing category from the other columns (employment type from income, age and region), trained on rows where it's observed and fitted on training data only. It's better than the mode when the other columns really predict the category. Costs: a model to maintain, and its hard guesses look more certain than they are; passing the predicted probabilities instead of one label keeps the uncertainty. Add an indicator if the blank itself predicts the target.
kNN. The majority category among the most similar training rows. The same trade-offs as for numbers: needs scaling, slow on big data.

XGBoost: a learned default direction. At each candidate split, the rows with a blank in that feature are tried on both sides. The split gain is computed twice, with the blanks' gradient sums G_miss, H_miss added to the left child, then to the right:
beginaligned Gain &= tfrac12Big[fracG_L^2H_L + lambda + fracG_R^2H_R + lambda \\ &qquad - frac(G_L + G_R)^2H_L + H_R + lambdaBig] - gamma endaligned
beginaligned blanks left:quad G_L &leftarrow G_L + G_miss \\ H_L &leftarrow H_L + H_miss \\ blanks right:quad G_R &leftarrow G_R + G_miss \\ H_R &leftarrow H_R + H_miss endaligned

In words: G and H are the sums of the loss's first and second derivatives over the rows in a child, lambda is the L2 penalty on leaf values, and gamma the minimum gain a split must clear. The direction with the higher gain becomes that node's default, so blanks are routed wherever they look most like the data. Only the non-missing values are sorted and scanned, which also makes this fast on sparse data. Each node learns its own direction, so a blank can mean “risky” at one node and “safe” at another.
LightGBM does the same by default (and can be told to treat zeros as missing).

CatBoost treats a numeric blank as smaller than every value by default (“Min”), so a split can always put the blanks on one side. Categorical columns need blanks turned into an explicit string such as “Missing”, which becomes its own level.
sklearn: HistGradientBoosting learns the direction like XGBoost; plain decision trees (version 1.3 on) and random forests (1.4 on) accept NaN too.
Not handled natively: linear and logistic regression, SVMs, kNN, most neural nets. They need imputation.

Should you impute before boosting? Usually not: the learned direction is at least as good as a single fill value, and it keeps the signal. The trap: if a feature had no blanks in training, there was nothing to learn from, so a blank at serving goes to an arbitrary or majority side (sklearn sends it to the child with more rows). A pipeline bug that blanks a field can silently make risky rows look safe. Monitor missing rates.

Dropping rows is acceptable when the blanks are MCAR, few, and you have data to spare. It's biased under MAR and MNAR, since the rows you keep are no longer representative. That bias is about averages and the overall population (a mean income, a default rate). For a regression's coefficients there's an exception worth knowing: if whether a row is blank depends only on the model's features (even on the missing value itself) and not on the target, the complete rows still give unbiased coefficients, just noisier ones. Dropping rows does bias them when the blanks depend on the target. And it doesn

Dropping a column is reasonable when it's mostly blank and neither its values nor its blankness predict the target. Check first: a column that's 95% blank whose presence predicts default should become an indicator, not be deleted.

Rows with a missing target can't be used for supervised training. But check why they're missing: in credit, only approved applicants have outcomes, so the training data is a selected sample (the reject-inference problem).

chunks.h: Fit imputers on the training fold only
chunks.x: Imputers learn numbers (medians, the kNN pool, per-column models), so they sit in the pipeline: refitted on each training fold, and frozen from the training fit in production. Fitting one on all rows leaks a little for a median, more for an iterative imputer, which learns relationships between columns, and seriously for anything that uses the target.

A single imputation treats filled values as if they were observed. Coefficients may be fine, but their standard errors are too small, because the uncertainty about what the blanks really were has been ignored. When you need inference (confidence intervals, p-values, effect sizes), use multiple imputation:
Create M completed datasets, each with its own random draws for the blanks (MICE with noise). M of 5 to 20 is common; use more when the share missing is large.
Fit the same model on each.
Pool the results with Rubin's rules:
beginaligned bar Q &= frac1M sum_m=1^M hat Q_m \\ bar W &= frac1M sum_m=1^M W_m \\ B &= frac1M - 1 sum_m=1^M big(hat Q_m - bar Qbig)^2 \\ T &= bar W + Big(1 + frac1MBig) B endaligned

In words: hat Q_m is the estimate from dataset m and W_m its squared standard error. The pooled estimate bar Q is their average. The total variance T adds the usual sampling variance bar W to the disagreement between imputations B , which is the uncertainty single imputation throws away. For pure prediction, multiple imputation rarely pays off; averaging predictions over the M datasets is at most a mild ensemble.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: The two goals ask different things of the filled data:

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Prediction only cares whether hat y is accurate on new rows. A coefficient can be “wrong” as long as the predictions are good.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Inference cares about the coefficients themselves (“how much does default risk rise per ₹10k of income?”) and their uncertainty: standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: A simulation. Two features x and z on the same scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1) with correlation 0.6, and y = 1 cdot x + 1 cdot z + noise , so both true coefficients are 1. Then 40% of x is blanked, the gaps are handled in each way below, and y is regressed on x and z : 1,000 rows, repeated 300 times. “CI covers” is how often the 95% confidence interval for x 's coefficient contains the true 1; it should be 95%. “Test RMSE” is the prediction error on 20,000 new rows whose blanks are made the same way; lower is better.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Case 1: blanks completely at random (MCAR).

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: No blanks at all (reference)

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: One random draw from a model predicting x from z and y (prediction plus noise), analysed as if real

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Multiple imputation, 20 draws, Rubin's rules

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Case 2: high values of x go blank more often (MNAR), 41% blank.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Multiple imputation (which assumes MAR)

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: What the numbers say, step by step:

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: A median fill biases the coefficients, and the correlated feature absorbs the missing effect. Take Case 1. In a blank row, x is a constant, so the only thing left to explain y is z . Because z moves with x (on average x = 0.6\,z ), the best slope on z in those rows is 1 + 0.6 = 1.6 : its own 1, plus 0.6 standing in for x . In the complete rows it's 1. One shared coefficient compromises at 1.31, and x 's coefficient shrinks to 0.81 to compensate. Both are wrong, and the confidence interval almost never covers the truth.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: The indicator fixes the level of the blank rows, not their slopes. It gives blank rows their own intercept theta and nothing else. Under MNAR, the blank rows' x is high on average, and that level shift is most of the extra prediction error, so the indicator takes the test RMSE from 1.20 to 1.10 (a model that also gives blank rows their own slope on z reaches 1.085). That's “much of the damage to prediction goes away”. But the slope compromise on z is still there, so the coefficients stay biased (0.88 and 1.20, covering only 54%): “the damage to inference doesn't”. With x as the only feature (t

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Under MCAR the indicator changes nothing, because blank rows aren't different on average, so there's no level to fix. Prediction was barely hurt anyway: 1.15, against 1.12 for the best a model can do with 40% of x blank (one that gives blank rows their own slope on z ).

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Even an unbiased single fill understates the uncertainty. One random draw gets the coefficients right, but the regression treats the guessed values as real data. It reports a standard error of 0.040 (its estimate of how much the coefficient would move from sample to sample), but across the 300 repeats the coefficient actually moves by 0.053. The interval is too narrow, so it covers the truth only 87% of the time. Multiple imputation adds the disagreement between draws ( B in Rubin's rules) and gets back to 94%.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Multiple imputation assumes MAR. Under MNAR it's biased too (1.07, 75% coverage). It learns how x relates to z and y from the complete rows and fills the blanks with that. But among rows with the same z and y , the blank ones have higher x (that's what MNAR means here), and nothing observed shows it. That's why MNAR calls for a sensitivity analysis, not just a better imputer: redo the estimate with the imputed values shifted up by a few plausible amounts, and check that the conclusion survives.

chunks.h: Prediction vs inference: why a fill can be fine for one and wrong for the other
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “For a prediction model, a median fill plus a missing indicator is usually fine: the indicator lets blank rows have their own level, and I judge it on validation error. If I need to interpret coefficients or report effects, a simple fill biases the coefficients of correlated features, and any single fill understates the uncertainty, so I'd use multiple imputation and pool with Rubin's rules. If the blanks might be MNAR, I'd add a sensitivity analysis.”
Few blanks, MCAR, blank doesn't predict the target
Median (numeric) or mode (categorical); dropping rows is fine if data is plentiful
The blank predicts the target, or MNAR is plausible
Keep the signal: indicator plus a simple fill, or a “Missing” category, or native handling
MAR, the feature matters, other columns predict it
Model-based or iterative imputation, plus an indicator if blanks are informative
Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost)
Leave blanks as NaN; monitor missing rates
Linear model, SVM, kNN, neural net
Median plus indicator by default; model-based if MAR and important
Structural (“not applicable”)
Domain rule: 0, a “none” level, or a sentinel plus an indicator
Time series, live prediction
Forward fill from the past, plus time since the last real value
Inference: coefficients, intervals
Multiple imputation (MICE), pooled with Rubin's rules
Column mostly blank, blank not predictive

Two things share the name. An error is a wrong value (an age of 230, an amount in the wrong unit); a genuine extreme is right but rare (a very large legitimate payment). They need opposite treatment, so first tell them apart: check domain limits, the source, and whether the rest of the row agrees.
z-score. Flag values more than about 3 standard deviations from the mean:

In words: how many standard deviations a value is from the average. It assumes a roughly normal shape, and it suffers from masking: the outliers inflate s and drag bar x towards themselves, which shrinks their own z-scores. In a sample of n points no z-score can exceed (n-1)/sqrt n , so with ten or fewer points a z above 3 is impossible, however wild the value.
Robust z-score, with the MAD. Replace the mean with the median tilde x and the standard deviation with the median absolute deviation:
beginaligned MAD &= median_i biglvert x_i - tilde x bigrvert \\ z_i^robust &= frac0.6745\,(x_i - tilde x)MAD endaligned

In words: the median and the MAD barely move when a few values are extreme, so the outliers can't hide themselves. The 0.6745 makes the score comparable to an ordinary z for normal data (the standard deviation is about 1.4826 MAD). A common flag is lvert z^robust rvert > 3.5 .
beginaligned IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ lower fence &= Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR \\ upper fence &= Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR endaligned

In words: the middle half of the data sets the scale, and anything more than one and a half middle-halves beyond it is flagged (3 IQR for “far out”). Quartiles are robust and assume no distribution, but on a right-skewed column such as income the fences flag a large part of the perfectly real long tail. Take the log first, then fence.
Multivariate methods, for points that are normal on every column but odd in combination (a large amount at 3 a.m. from a new device):

Isolation forest: random trees with random splits. An outlier sits in a sparse region, so it's isolated in few splits; the score is the average path length. Fast and scalable; its expected-outlier-share setting fixes the threshold, and it struggles when anomalies form dense clusters of their own.
Local outlier factor (LOF): compares a point's density with its neighbours', so it finds points that are odd for their region. Slow on big data and sensitive to the number of neighbours.
Residual-based: rows with large standardized residuals from a model. In linear regression also check leverage (an unusual x ) and Cook's distance (how much the fit moves without the row).
Domain rules: limits no statistic needs to find, such as non-negative quantities and dates not in the future.
What outliers do to statistics and models

Mean, standard deviation, scaling: one extreme value shifts the mean and inflates the standard deviation more, so standardization squeezes every normal value into a narrow band. Min-max is worse: one extreme sets the range.

Linear models with squared loss: a row's loss grows with its squared residual, so its pull on the fit grows with the residual, without limit. One far point can tilt the line, and a high-leverage point can rotate it. Distance methods (k-means, kNN) get pulled too.
Trees, extreme inputs: robust. Splits use only the order of values, so an extreme x just lands at one end.

Trees, extreme targets: not robust. With squared error, a leaf is a mean that one extreme target pulls, and in boosting the largest residuals dominate the gradients. Use a Huber or absolute-error loss.
Errors: fix or remove. Correct from the source if you can; otherwise set the value to missing and let the missing-value strategy handle it, rather than dropping the row.

Cap (winsorize). Clip to percentiles learned on training data, such as the 1st and 99th. The row stays with limited influence, but you lose how extreme it was; add a “was capped” flag if many rows hit the cap.
Transform. A log, Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson transform pulls in a long tail without deleting anything (section 07).
Use a robust loss or model. Huber loss is squared for small residuals and linear for large ones, so a far point pulls with constant force instead of growing force:
L_delta(r) = begincases tfrac12 r^2 & lvert r rvert le delta \\ delta big(lvert r rvert - tfrac12 deltabig) & lvert r rvert > delta endcases
In words: r is the residual and delta the point where the loss switches from squared to linear. Absolute error (which predicts the median) and quantile losses are more robust still.

Keep them when they are the signal. In fraud, anomaly detection or large insurance claims, the extremes are what the model exists to find; removing them removes the positives. And production will contain extremes anyway, so the model must behave sensibly on them.

Removing outliers from the test set. It makes the score look better while the model meets the same extremes in production. Decide the outlier rule on training data, then apply it identically everywhere, including at serving time.

Most models need numbers. An encoding decides what a model can learn from a category: whether it sees an order, how many parameters the category costs, and whether the labels were used to build it. The right choice depends on the model and on the cardinality (the number of levels).
One 0/1 column per level. No order is invented, and each level gets its own coefficient.

The dummy-variable trap. With an intercept, the K one-hot columns always sum to 1, which is exactly the intercept column. The columns are perfectly collinear, X^top X can't be inverted, and an unregularized linear model has no unique solution. Drop one level (the reference); each remaining coefficient then means “difference from the reference level”.

With regularization, keep all K . The penalty picks a unique solution and treats every level symmetrically, whereas dropping one makes the result depend on which level you dropped. Trees and neural nets don't need a level dropped either.

High cardinality hurts. Thousands of sparse columns; rare levels get noisy coefficients; memory grows. A tree can only peel off one level per split, so a high-cardinality feature's signal is spread thin across many weak columns and needs many splits to use.
Best for: a handful to a few dozen levels, in linear models and neural nets.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: The trap, in numbers. Say a city's effect on salary is Delhi 30, Mumbai 40, Bangalore 50. With an intercept and all three one-hot columns, the model is hat y = beta_0 + beta_D D + beta_M M + beta_B B , and many coefficient sets give exactly these predictions:

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Add any number to beta_0 and subtract it from every level's coefficient, and the predictions don't change. So an unregularized fit has infinitely many equally good answers ( X^top X can't be inverted). Dropping one level removes that freedom. The last row is what “drop Bangalore” gives: Bangalore's coefficient is forced to 0, so the intercept is Bangalore's level and every coefficient reads as “difference from Bangalore”.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Ridge removes the freedom by itself. Its penalty lambda sum_j beta_j^2 (the intercept isn't penalized) differs between the rows, so among all the equally good fits it takes the one with the smallest penalty: the middle row, where the level coefficients sum to zero. The intercept becomes a centre and each level a deviation from it. The answer is unique without dropping anything.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Under Ridge, dropping a level is worse, not just unnecessary. The penalty pulls every penalized coefficient towards 0. With all levels kept, they're pulled towards a shared centre, and every level is treated the same way. Drop one, and that level has no coefficient to shrink while the others are pulled relative to it, so the fit depends on which level you happened to drop. Same data (Delhi seen only twice, the other two cities ten times each), same lambda = 1 :

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Delhi's prediction (true effect 30)

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: None of these is “the” right answer. The point is that keeping every level gives one answer that doesn't hinge on an arbitrary choice.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Other penalties. Elastic net has an L2 part, so the same argument holds: keep all levels. Lasso (L1 alone) doesn't always settle on a unique answer when columns are perfectly collinear, but it still runs, and keeping all levels is common since it zeroes some out anyway.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Unregularized linear or logistic regression, when you'll read the coefficients

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Ridge, elastic net, sklearn's LogisticRegression (L2 by default)

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Trees, boosting, neural nets

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: No need (harmless either way)

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: sklearn's plain LinearRegression doesn't fail with all levels kept: its solver returns the smallest-coefficient answer (here 40 with −10, 0 and +10). The predictions are fine, but the coefficients are one arbitrary choice among many, so don't interpret them.

chunks.h: Deep dive: Dropping a level, and why regularized models don't need to
chunks.x: Say it in an interview: “Dropping a level fixes an identifiability problem: with an intercept, the K dummies are perfectly collinear. A ridge penalty already makes the solution unique, and keeping all K means the shrinkage treats every level symmetrically, instead of depending on which level I dropped.”

Truly ordered levels (education, small/medium/large, credit grades A to E): in a linear model, one slope then covers all levels, which assumes the steps between neighbours are equal. One-hot is the flexible alternative, at the cost of more parameters.
Unordered levels in a linear model: wrong. The model treats code 7 as seven times code 1, and the result depends on whatever order (often alphabetical) produced the codes.

Unordered levels in a tree: workable. A tree can cut the integer line several times, so it can still separate levels. But each cut splits a contiguous range of codes, so grouping risky levels that happen to sit far apart in the code order costs many splits. Ordering the codes by target rate fixes that, which is where target encoding comes in.
(sklearn's LabelEncoder is meant for the target; use OrdinalEncoder for features.)

Replace each level with the average target of the training rows in that level: the default rate of a postcode, the average basket value of a merchant category. For a multi-class target, use one column per class (the class's share in that level).

Why it works. It turns any number of levels into one numeric column ordered by risk. For a yes/no target, sorting the levels by their rate and trying each cut in that order is guaranteed to find the best split of the levels into two groups (Breiman's result), so one split in a tree does what one-hot needs dozens for. LightGBM's native categorical splits use the same idea, sorting levels by their gradient statistics. For a linear model, it turns a nominal column into one monotone feature.
Smoothing. A level seen 3 times has an average that is mostly noise. Shrink it towards the overall mean bar y :
beginaligned enc(c) &= fracn_c\, bar y_c + m\, bar yn_c + m \\ &= lambda_c\, bar y_c + (1 - lambda_c)\, bar y \\ lambda_c &= fracn_cn_c + m endaligned

In words: n_c is the level's row count, bar y_c its average target, and m the prior weight: the overall mean counts as m extra rows. A big level keeps essentially its own average; a tiny one is pulled to the overall mean; a level never seen gets exactly bar y . Tune m by cross-validation, or set it from the data: the noisier the target within a level, the larger m should be (the empirical-Bayes idea). sklearn's TargetEncoder by default sets m per level to the level's target variance divided by the overall target variance.

Why it leaks. Computed on the same rows the model trains on, each row's own label is inside its level's average. For a level with one row, the encoding is the label. For a level with 10 rows, a positive row raises its own encoding by a tenth.

The model learns “high encoding means positive”, which holds in training because of the row's own label and fails on new rows. Even a category with no real relationship to the target shows a strong training signal, and the effect is largest for small levels. Smoothing reduces it but doesn't remove it.

The fix: out-of-fold encoding. Split the training rows into K folds. Encode each fold's rows using averages computed from the other K - 1 folds, so no row's label touches its own encoding. Train the model on these out-of-fold encodings. For validation, test and production rows, use averages from all the training rows.
Out-of-fold target encoding. Each training row is encoded from averages that never include its own label. Test and production rows use averages from all the training rows.
Leave-one-out encoding is a trap. Excluding only the row itself sounds safe:
enc_-i = fracS_c - y_in_c - 1

Here S_c is the level's sum of targets. Within one level S_c and n_c are the same for every row, so the encoding is a decreasing function of y_i : every positive gets a slightly lower value than every negative in its level. A deep enough tree can read the label level by level. Out-of-fold encoding doesn't have this problem: rows of a level in the same fold share one value, computed without any of their labels. (A faint fold-level trace remains; smoothing and enough rows per fold make it negligible.)

It must sit inside cross-validation. If you compute the out-of-fold encodings on all the data and then run cross-validation, the validation fold's labels have already shaped the training rows' encodings. The encoder goes in the pipeline, so it's refitted on each training fold. sklearn's TargetEncoder does the out-of-fold part itself: fit_transform cross-fits, while transform on new rows uses the full training averages. Calling fit and then transform on the training rows yourself skips the cross-fitting and leaks.
Time-ordered data: encode each row from rows strictly earlier in time (an expanding average), the way the value would have been computed live.
CatBoost's ordered target statistics do the same job differently. Shuffle the training rows into a random order and encode each row from the rows before it, with a prior counted as a extra rows:
enc_i = fracS_before + a cdot priorn_before + a

Here S_before and n_before are the sum of targets and the row count of the same level among the rows earlier in the order. A row's label never enters its own encoding, and no rows are wasted. The first rows of each level get noisy encodings, so CatBoost uses several random orders. Its “ordered boosting” applies the same before-only idea to the gradients.

Trade-offs. Target encoding is compact and handles any cardinality. Its costs: the leakage risk above; noise for rare levels; drift, since a level's rate changes over time; one encoding per target (and per class); and one number per level, so any interaction between the level and other features has to be learned elsewhere.
In words: replace each level with how often it appears in the training data (its count, or its share).
Why it works: popularity is often predictive. A merchant seen millions of times is an established business; a device model seen twice is unusual, which matters in fraud.
Why it's safe: it never uses the target, so there's no target leakage, and it's one column whatever the cardinality.
When: high-cardinality features in tree models, usually next to a target encoding (how common versus how risky); unsupervised and anomaly models, which have no target.

Trade-offs: levels with equal counts become identical. Counts depend on data volume and window, so use shares or a fixed trailing window (“transactions at this merchant in the last 30 days”), computed the same way at serving. An unseen level gets 0, which is usually meaningful.
Hashing. Map each level to one of B columns with a hash function, j = h(c) bmod B , and set that column to 1.

Why: no vocabulary to store, a fixed number of columns, and new levels are handled automatically. It suits huge or open-ended vocabularies (URLs, user agents, crossed features) in sparse linear models and streaming systems.
Cost: collisions. Unrelated levels share a column, so their effects blur together. The chance that a given level shares its bucket with at least one of the other K - 1 levels is
1 - Big(1 - frac1BBig)^K - 1 approx 1 - e^-K/B

In words: to keep collisions rare you need many more buckets than levels. Hashing also can't be inverted, so it's the wrong tool when you need to interpret levels, or when the vocabulary is small enough to store.
Binary encoding writes each level's integer code in binary, one column per bit (about log_2 K columns). Compact, but each bit groups unrelated levels, so it's mostly a memory trick.

Learned embeddings. In a neural net, each level gets a dense vector trained with the task, so levels that behave alike end up close and rare levels borrow strength from similar ones; the vectors can be reused as tree features. A common size heuristic is about min(50, K/2) . Map levels below a count threshold to a shared “rare” index, which unseen levels then use. Not for small data or non-neural models, unless the vectors are pre-trained.

Group rare levels. Merge levels with fewer than some number of training rows into “Other”. It cuts noise and columns, and it gives unseen levels a natural home. The threshold is a hyperparameter, and it's learned from training data, so it belongs in the pipeline.

Plan for unseen levels at serving time, encoder by encoder: one-hot gives an all-zero row or the “Other” column; target encoding the prior; count encoding 0; embeddings the shared “unknown” index; hashing some bucket. Decide on purpose and test it: a silent mismatch between training and serving codes is a classic production bug.
Monitor the share of unseen levels. A jump means the data changed: a new product, a renamed category, a broken upstream mapping.
The default for few levels (drop one if there's no penalty)
Fine for few levels; spreads many levels thin
Only for truly ordered levels; assumes equal steps
Works even unordered, but wastes splits
Only for truly ordered levels
Target (out-of-fold, smoothed)
Good for many levels: one monotone column
Very good for many levels
Possible; embeddings usually better
Weak alone: assumes the effect is linear in popularity
Good for huge or open-ended sets of levels
As the index into an embedding table
Only as pre-trained vectors
Learned vectors as features
The default for many levels
LightGBM, CatBoost, XGBoost, sklearn's histogram boosting

Why the columns differ. A linear model gives each input column one slope, so the encoding must make the relationship linear: one-hot gives each level its own slope, target encoding makes the column monotone in risk. A tree only needs the levels to be separable by a few thresholds, so any encoding that puts similar levels next to each other works. A neural net can learn its own representation, so an embedding lets it learn which levels are alike.
beginaligned standardize:quad tilde x &= fracx - musigma \\ min-max:quad tilde x &= fracx - x_minx_max - x_min \\ robust:quad tilde x &= fracx - medianIQR endaligned
Standardizationmean 0, sd 1
The default for penalized linear models, SVMs, kNN, PCA, neural nets
Outliers inflate sigma and squeeze the normal values together
Naturally bounded features (pixels, percentages), or models that need bounded inputs
One outlier sets the range; new values can fall outside [0, 1]
Columns with outliers you want to keep
Outliers stay extreme; they just stop setting the scale
A vocabulary trap: “normalization” means min-max scaling to some people, and rescaling each row to unit length (sklearn's Normalizer) to others, so say which.
Transforms for skewed columns
Incomes, amounts, counts and durations are usually right-skewed: most values are small and a few are huge. A transform pulls the tail in.

Log (or log(1 + x) when zeros occur): turns multiplicative effects into additive ones (“10% more income” becomes a fixed step), reduces the leverage of the tail, and often makes a relationship more linear. log x needs x > 0 ; log(1 + x) allows zeros.
Box-Cox picks the power that makes the result as close to normal as possible, by maximum likelihood. It requires x > 0 :
x^(lambda) = begincases dfracx^lambda - 1lambda & lambda ne 0 \\ log x & lambda = 0 endcases
In words: lambda = 1 only shifts the values, lambda = 0.5 is a rescaled square root, and lambda = 0 is the log. The -1 and /lambda make the family join smoothly at lambda = 0 .
Yeo-Johnson extends the same idea to zero and negative values (profits, balance changes).

Quantile transform maps each value to its rank, then to a uniform or normal shape. The most robust (outliers become merely the top ranks), but it bends linear relationships, distorts distances, and clips values beyond the training range.

When transforms matter: for linear models, distance-based methods and neural nets. Trees ignore any monotone transform, since a threshold on log x is a threshold on x . Box-Cox's lambda and the quantiles are learned, so fit them on training rows.

Transforming the target is different: a model trained on log y predicts roughly the median of y , not the mean, so exponentiated predictions underestimate totals unless corrected (Duan's smearing: multiply them by the average of the exponentiated training residuals).
Which models need scaling, and why
Neural nets, anything trained by gradient descent
Mixed scales make a long, thin loss valley, so no single learning rate suits every direction.
Ridge, lasso, penalized logistic regression
The penalty treats all coefficients alike, so a feature with a small numeric range, which needs a large coefficient, is punished more for the same effect.
kNN, k-means, SVM with an RBF kernel
Distances are dominated by the feature with the largest units.
The largest-variance directions would just be the largest-unit columns.
Unregularized linear regression
Predictions don't change; coefficients rescale to match.
Decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting
A split is a threshold on one feature; any monotone rescaling gives the same partition.

chunks.h: Fit on the training data only
chunks.x: The scaler's mu and sigma (or min and max, or quantiles) are learned on training rows and frozen, the rule from section 03. At serving time there's often one row and nothing to compute statistics from. Re-fitting on test rows also hides shift: re-centring test incomes that run higher makes them look normal.

Collinearity (multicollinearity) means some features are nearly linear combinations of others: floor area and number of rooms; income and an income-derived credit limit. A total next to its parts, or all one-hot dummies next to an intercept, is perfect collinearity.
Why it hurts linear models

When two features move together, the data can't tell which one deserves the credit. The loss surface becomes a long, flat valley along “more weight on one, less on the other”, and the fitted coefficients can slide along it. For ordinary least squares:
beginaligned Var(hatbeta_j) &= fracsigma^2sum_i (x_ij - bar x_j)^2 cdot VIF_j \\ VIF_j &= frac11 - R_j^2 endaligned

In words: sigma^2 is the noise variance, and the first factor is the variance hatbeta_j would have if x_j were uncorrelated with the rest. R_j^2 is how well the other features predict feature j . Only the part of x_j the others can't predict helps pin down beta_j . The variance inflation factor (VIF) says how many times larger the coefficient's variance is than if x_j were uncorrelated with the rest; its square root is how many times wider the standard error is.
Unstable coefficients: large standard errors, big changes when a few rows change, and signs that can flip against domain sense.
Misleading tests: each feature can look insignificant alone while the pair is clearly significant together (an F-test on both shows it).
Interpretation breaks: “the effect of x_1 holding x_2 fixed” describes something the data never shows.

Predictions are usually fine while the correlation holds, because they depend on the combined effect, which the data pins down well. A new row that breaks the pattern asks about the one direction the data never covered, and its prediction swings.
Correlation matrix: quick but pairwise only; it misses a column that is the sum of three others.
VIF per feature (regress it on all the others): above 5 is worth a look, above 10 is serious.

Condition number of the standardized feature matrix (largest over smallest singular value): above about 30 is strong collinearity. Eigenvectors of the correlation matrix with near-zero eigenvalues show which columns are involved.
Do nothing if you only need predictions and the relationship is stable.
Drop one of a redundant pair, or combine them (a sum, ratio or domain index).
PCA: uncorrelated components, at the cost of interpretability.

Ridge: the penalty curves the flat valley, so the coefficients stop sliding and the twins share the weight. Lasso keeps one twin somewhat arbitrarily (unstable selection); elastic net keeps the group.
More varied data is the only fix that makes the separate effects estimable.
Trees and feature importance

Trees predict fine with correlated features, but their importance is split. Whichever twin wins a split takes its credit, so impurity importance divides the credit arbitrarily and each twin looks weaker than the signal is. Permutation importance underestimates both, because with one twin shuffled the model still has the other (and the shuffled rows are unrealistic). Random forests, which sample features per split, spread credit evenly; boosting tends to lean on one twin. Measure correlated features as a group: permute them together, or drop the group and refit.

Feature engineering hands a model a quantity it would struggle to build itself. The test of a good feature: is it known at prediction time, does it have a reason to predict the target, and would it be computed the same way in production?

Components and durations: hour, day of week, month, weekend, holiday, days to or from an event (payday, a festival, the month end); and durations up to the prediction time, such as account age or days since the last purchase, which carry far more than raw dates.
Don't use a raw timestamp as a feature: the model learns the trend in the training period and can't extrapolate it to future dates.
Cyclical encoding for features that wrap around:
beginaligned h_sin &= sin(2pi h / 24) \\ h_cos &= cos(2pi h / 24) endaligned

In words: the hour h becomes a point on a circle, so 23:00 and 00:00 are neighbours instead of 23 apart. Both coordinates are needed, because the sine alone gives the same value to two different hours (3:00 and 9:00 share a sine and differ only in the cosine). This matters for linear models, neural nets and distances; a tree can isolate a late-night window from the raw hour with two splits, so it gains less.

Statistics of an entity's history: a customer's average transaction amount, a merchant's number of distinct customers, a device's count of accounts. Often the strongest features, especially as deviations: this amount divided by the customer's usual amount.
The current row's label: “the merchant's fraud rate” over rows that include this transaction is unprotected target encoding. Compute it out-of-fold or from earlier rows only.
Future rows: a customer's average over the whole dataset includes later transactions. Compute every aggregate as of the prediction time (a point-in-time or “as-of” join).
Pooling train and test: lets test rows shape training features.
Small groups: an average over two rows is noise; smooth it towards the overall average and add the count as a feature.
Ratios, interactions and binning

Ratios such as debt-to-income or loan-to-value. A tree approximates a ratio only with a staircase of many splits, and a linear model can't form it from the raw columns (only from logs, as log a - log b ). Define the zero-denominator case, with an indicator.

Interactions (products, crossed categories): a linear model sees one only if you add it; trees find them by nesting splits, but an explicit one helps shallow trees. Let domain knowledge pick them, since all pairwise products explode the feature count.

Binning (equal-width or quantile): gives a linear model a step-shaped, non-linear effect and limits outliers' influence; credit scorecards replace each bin by its weight of evidence (the log of the bin's share of good outcomes over its share of bad ones). Costs: variation within a bin is lost and edges create jumps (splines are the smooth alternative). Fit edges on training rows. Trees don't need binning.

chunks.h: Time series: lags and rolling windows, with no future
chunks.x: Lags (yesterday's value, last week's value), rolling means and standard deviations, expanding averages, differences and exponentially weighted averages. The rule: a feature for time t may use only what was known at time t . If a source arrives two days late, the shortest usable lag is two days. The classic bug is a rolling window that includes the current row, whose target is exactly what you're predicting:

chunks.h: Time series: lags and rolling windows, with no future
chunks.x: df = df.sort_values("date") g = df.groupby("store")["sales"] df["lag_7"] = g.shift(7) # shift first, so the window ends yesterday df["mean_28"] = g.transform( lambda s: s.shift(1).rolling(28).mean())

chunks.h: Time series: lags and rolling windows, with no future
chunks.x: Centred windows (which average the past and the future around a point) are fine for smoothing a chart and always a leak in a feature.

chunks.h: Time series: lags and rolling windows, with no future
chunks.x: Cheap signals (length, word count, share of capitals or digits, keyword flags); TF-IDF with a vocabulary fitted on training text, into a sparse linear model, as a strong baseline; character n-grams for messy short strings such as merchant names; sentence embeddings from a pretrained model as dense features. Watch for text written after the event, such as resolution notes, which often contains the label.

Why select at all: with many weak features and few rows, extra features add variance; fewer features are cheaper to compute, monitor and keep correct; and there's less surface for leakage. With gradient boosting and plenty of data the accuracy gain is often small, so start by removing junk (IDs, leaky columns, constants) and keep the rest.

Filters score each feature on its own: correlation with the target, mutual information, a chi-squared or ANOVA F test, a variance threshold. Mutual information measures how much knowing X reduces the uncertainty about Y , with H the entropy (uncertainty):
I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y mid X)

It's 0 only when they're independent, so it catches non-linear relationships that correlation misses. Filters are fast, but they judge one feature at a time: they miss features that work only together, and keep two copies of one signal.

Wrappers search subsets with the model itself: recursive feature elimination (RFE) fits, drops the weakest features, refits and repeats. They see combinations, but they're expensive and overfit the selection score unless nested inside cross-validation.
Embedded methods select while training:

L1 (lasso) sets weak coefficients exactly to 0. With correlated features it keeps one more or less at random, so repeat it on bootstrap samples and keep features chosen consistently (stability selection).

Tree impurity importance is free, but it's computed on training data and favours continuous and high-cardinality features, which offer more split points to fit noise with. A random ID column can rank highly.
Permutation importance shuffles one feature in validation data and measures the drop in score. It works for any model without that bias, but correlated features hide each other's importance.

The pitfall: select inside cross-validation, not before it. Take thousands of pure-noise features and random labels, keep the few most correlated with the labels on all the rows, then cross-validate a model on them: the accuracy comes out well above chance. The selection step saw the validation labels and picked features that happen to fit them.
Selection is part of the training procedure, so it goes in the pipeline and is redone on each training fold, and the final estimate comes from data the selection never saw.

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: First ask whether it's a problem. With a proper loss (log loss) and a few hundred positives, a model ranks well despite imbalance; what changes is where the threshold belongs and which metric to read. So: threshold first, then weights, then resampling.

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: Move the threshold. With calibrated probabilities, choose it from the costs of the two mistakes, or from capacity (flag the top N a review team can handle). Flag when p > t^* :

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: t^* = fracC_FPC_FP + C_FN

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: In words: with C_FP the cost of a false alarm and C_FN the cost of a miss, the threshold is the false alarm's share of the total cost. When a miss costs far more, the threshold is low.

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: Class weights. Count each positive w times in the loss. It works with every model and discards nothing. But the model now believes positives are w times more likely in odds terms, so probabilities are inflated; at threshold 0.5 it decides about the same as the unweighted model at threshold 1/(1 + w) .

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: Undersample the majority. Keep a fraction q of negatives. Training gets much cheaper, at the cost of discarded information. Undo the probability inflation with the prior correction:

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: logit p = logit p_s + log q

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: In words: p_s is the model's probability on the resampled data; adding log q to its log-odds restores the real base rate. For class weights, use q = 1/w .

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: Oversample the minority by duplicating positives: the same effect as weights, but duplicates are easy to memorize, especially for trees.

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: SMOTE creates synthetic positives on the line between a positive and one of its positive nearest neighbours:

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: beginaligned x_new &= x_i + u\,(x_nn - x_i) \\ u &sim Uniform(0, 1) endaligned

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: Apply it only to training folds, after the split (imbalanced-learn's pipeline does this); before the split, synthetic near-copies of validation rows leak into training. Its points can be unrealistic (half-way values of integer or categorical columns, points between two separate fraud patterns), it amplifies label noise, it distorts probabilities, and with gradient boosting it rarely beats weights or a good threshold.

chunks.h: Class imbalance at the data level
chunks.x: The right metrics: not accuracy (flagging nobody scores 98% at 2% positives). Use PR-AUC (its random baseline is the positive rate), precision and recall at the operating threshold, or money saved; ROC-AUC ignores the base rate and can look excellent while precision is poor. Add log loss or a calibration plot when probabilities matter. Never resample the validation or test sets: they must reflect the real base rate.
Expected squared error on a new point splits into three parts:
beginaligned mathbb Ebig[(y - hat f(x))^2big] &= bias^2 + variance + sigma^2 \\ bias &= mathbb E[hat f(x)] - f(x) \\ variance &= Varbig(hat f(x)big) endaligned

In words: bias is how far the average model (over many training sets) is from the truth, so a model too simple for the pattern has high bias. Variance is how much the model changes from one training set to another, so a model flexible enough to fit noise has high variance. The noise can't be removed by any model.
Learning curve (both scores against training-set size): curves that meet low mean underfitting, and more data won't help; a gap that narrows as data grows means overfitting, and more data will.
Validation curve (both scores against one complexity setting, such as tree depth): pick the validation peak, or the simplest setting near it.
Training and validation both poor, small gap
Better features (ratios, aggregates, interactions); more capacity; less regularization; train longer; check for label noise
Training good, validation much worse
Overfitting (high variance)
More data; fewer or cleaner features; group rare levels and smooth encodings; stronger regularization; shallower trees, early stopping; bagging
Validation good, test or production much worse
Leakage, a shift, or overfitting the validation set through many tuning rounds
Audit features for post-prediction information; time or group split; adversarial validation; a fresh holdout and fewer tuning rounds
Repeated or grouped cross-validation; simpler model; report the spread, not just the mean

A gap isn't always overfitting. If a feature leaks only in training rows, or the validation period differs from the training period, the gap comes from the data, not the model's flexibility, and regularization won't close it.
Python-flavoured. The first block is real sklearn; the others are outlines to write out from memory.
A leakage-safe preprocessing pipeline

num = ["income", "age", "amount"] low = ["employment_type", "channel"] # few levels high = ["merchant_id"] # many levels pre = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", make_pipeline( SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), # fill + flag StandardScaler()), num), ("low", make_pipeline( SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Missing"), OneHotEncoder( handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=50)), low), # rare → 1 col ("high", TargetEncoder(), high), # cross-fitted ]) model = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)) # rows sorted by time; every step is refitted # o

Why each choice: the median resists skew and the indicator keeps the blank's signal; “Missing” is a real level; rare levels share one column, where unseen levels also go (all zeros if no level was rare). TargetEncoder cross-fits the training rows because the pipeline calls its fit_transform; calling fit then transform yourself would leak. Its internal folds are shuffled, not past-only, so for strict point-in-time encodings use an expanding mean instead. Use GroupKFold when customers repeat.
Out-of-fold target encoding
