Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: Each row of the table needs only the running count of defaults on the left (0, 1 or 3) and the node's total (4). The right side is the total minus the left. The best cut is 1.5, the split scored in section 03.

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: Why only between distinct values: a threshold can't separate two rows with the same value, so a “gap” inside a run of equal values isn't a candidate.

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: Why the midpoint: any threshold inside a gap sends the same training rows left, so the training gain can't choose among them. The midpoint hedges for unseen values that fall in the gap. (Histogram methods use bin edges instead.)

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: In NumPy, cumsum does the whole sweep at once:

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: def best_split(x, y): """Best Gini threshold for one feature, 0/1 labels.""" order = np.argsort(x) xs, ys = x[order], y[order] n = len(ys) n_l = np.arange(1, n) # rows left of each gap k_l = np.cumsum(ys)[:-1] # defaults left of it p_l = k_l / n_l p_r = (ys.sum() - k_l) / (n - n_l) kids = (n_l * 2 * p_l * (1 - p_l) + (n - n_l) * 2 * p_r * (1 - p_r)) / n kids[xs[1:] == xs[:-1]] = np.inf # not a gap i = np.argmin(kids) p = ys.mean() t = (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2 # the midpoint return t, 2 * p * (1 - p) - kids[i]

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: At the root of the credit data the four features' best cuts are:

chunks.h: Searching for the split at a node
chunks.x: late wins at 1.5, exactly sklearn's root. EMI share finds the true 0.5 but gains little here, because EMIs matter only for low incomes: it's half of an AND. Run the same search inside the left child (late ≤ 1) and income wins at 39.455, sklearn's second split.
beginaligned per feature &= O(n_t log n_t) + O(n_t) \\ per node &= O(d\, n_t log n_t) \\ per level &= O(d\, n log n) \\ per tree &= O(D\, d\, n log n) endaligned
Per feature, the sort costs O(n_t log n_t) and the sweep O(n_t) . n_t is the node's rows, D the depth. Each training row sits in exactly one node per level, so a level's nodes add up to n rows.
A balanced tree has D approx log_2 n , so about O(d\, n log^2 n) . A lopsided tree is deeper: the unconstrained tree on this data reaches depth 25.
With K classes, each row move updates K counts and each candidate is scored in O(K) .
Rescoring every threshold from scratch instead of sweeping costs O(n_t) per candidate, so O(n_t^2) per feature: 3,500 passes over the rows at the root, for the same answer.
Prediction costs O(D) per row.

Histograms: how large-data libraries skip the sort. LightGBM, XGBoost's hist method and sklearn's HistGradientBoosting cut each feature into at most about 256 quantile bins once, before training. At each node they add up the counts (or gradients) per bin in O(n_t\, d) and try only the bin edges in O(256\, d) . A sibling's histogram is the parent's minus the other child's, so only the smaller child needs a pass over its rows. The price is resolution: no threshold between two bin edges.

sklearn tries the features in a random order at every node, even when it uses all of them. When two features give exactly the same gain, the first one tried wins, so random_state can change a tree. This matters most for duplicated or perfectly correlated features (section 15). On this data, seeds 0 to 4 all give the same depth-3 tree.

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: A feature with 3,500 distinct values offers 3,499 candidate cuts; a yes/no feature offers one. Even when both are pure noise, the many-valued one has far more chances at a lucky gain. In 200 simulations with 1,000 rows, a pure-noise target with 10% positives, one continuous noise feature and one binary noise feature, the continuous one won the root 96% of the time.

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: That's how age ≤ 23.18 got into the tree:

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: The truth in that branch is flat. All 331 applicants there (2+ late payments, income over ₹40.5k) have a true chance of 28%, so every candidate cut is noise: about 330 each for income, EMI share and age, and 3 for late, some 990 in all.

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: A depth limit never refuses a split. With only max_depth=3, every impure node above depth 3 must split, even when all its candidates are noise.

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: So the luckiest cut wins. The best gains there were age 0.0095, EMI 0.0044, income 0.0027 and late 0.0009. The income ≤ 146.44 node is the same story: its truth is a flat 3% and its best gain is 0.0001.

chunks.h: Why noise splits win: more thresholds, more lottery tickets
chunks.x: Defences: leaf-size limits and pruning, which refuse or remove splits that gain too little (sections 10 and 11). Conditional-inference trees and CHAID pick the feature by a significance test first, which removes the bias towards many-valued features. The same bias inflates impurity-based importance (section 14).

A numeric feature has an order, so a split is a cut in that order. A categorical feature (state, employer type, loan purpose) has none: a split sends some subset of the categories left. With K categories there are 2^K-1 - 1 ways to split them into two non-empty groups: 127 for 8 states, about 5.6 times 10^14 for 50. Three ways to search them:
Exhaustive: try every subset. Only feasible for small K .
One-vs-rest: try the K splits that peel off one category. This is all a tree can do with one-hot columns.
Sort by the mean target: order the categories by their share of class 1 (or their mean target, for regression) and try only the K - 1 cuts in that order, as if it were a numeric feature.

Sorting is exactly optimal for a binary or regression target. For a 0/1 target with Gini or entropy (Breiman and others, 1984), and for squared error (Fisher, 1958), the best of all 2^K-1 - 1 groupings is always one of the K - 1 cuts in sorted order.

The intuition is an exchange argument: if a riskier category sat on the safe side while a safer one of the same size sat on the risky side, swapping them pushes the two sides' shares further apart while the parent's share stays put, and under a concave impurity that can only raise the gain. So the optimal groups are contiguous in the sorted order.
By hand. Categories A, B, C, D, 100 applicants each, with 5, 30, 8 and 25 defaults. Sorted by rate: A (5%), C (8%), D (25%), B (30%).
sorted cut 3, and one-vs-rest
sorted cut 1, and one-vs-rest

Three sorted cuts find the best of all seven groupings. One-vs-rest's best, B alone, gains half as much: it needs two levels of splits to build A, C vs D, B, and each level costs rows. A, B | C, D, which mixes a safe and a risky category on each side, gains almost nothing (0.00005): both sides land near the overall 17%.
More than two classes: there's no single order to sort by, and no such shortcut. Libraries fall back on heuristics: one-vs-rest, or sorting by a gradient statistic, as LightGBM does.

The catch: the sort order is learned from the labels. With many rare categories it's mostly noise, and the split overfits. LightGBM guards it with a minimum count per category (min_data_per_group) and smoothing (cat_smooth).
In sklearn's decision tree: encode first

sklearn's DecisionTreeClassifier splits only on numbers (its HistGradientBoosting models do have native categorical splits). A made-up example: 8 states whose default rates alternate low and high in code order (3%, 25%, 4%, 22%, 2%, 28%, 5%, 20%), trained on 2,000 rows and tested on 2,000:
The state's default rate (sorted)

Test AUC; the best possible is 0.718 on average (0.720 edges past it by test-set luck). Arbitrary codes invent an order that a cut can use only once. One-hot needs four levels to peel the states apart. Replacing each state by its default rate turns the sort-by-mean trick into a numeric feature, and one split gets there.

That encoding used the labels: target encoding. With 8 states of 250 rows each it's fine. With thousands of rare categories (merchant IDs, pin codes), a rate from 3 rows is mostly noise, and when it's computed on the rows the tree trains on, each row's own label leaks into its feature: brilliant in training, poor on new data. Compute it out-of-fold (each row's rate comes only from the other folds) and shrink rare categories towards the overall rate bar p :
rate_c = frack_c + m\,bar pn_c + m

A category with n_c rows and k_c positives is pulled towards bar p as if it had m extra rows at the overall rate. sklearn's TargetEncoder does both; CatBoost uses ordered target statistics. A category never seen in training gets the overall rate with a target encoder, all zeros with one-hot (handle_unknown="ignore"), and an arbitrary position with codes: decide it explicitly and test it.

For a numeric target, like the credit limit, the same machinery works with a different impurity: the node's variance, the mean squared distance from the node's mean. A leaf predicts the mean of its training targets, because the mean is the single number with the smallest squared error: the total squared error sum_i (y_i - c)^2 has slope -2sum_i (y_i - c) , which is zero exactly at c = bar y . A split's gain is the drop in size-weighted variance, the variance reduction:
gain = Var(P) - tfracn_Ln\,Var(L) - tfracn_Rn\,Var(R)
By hand. Four applicants with incomes 20, 30, 60, 90 and limits 30, 50, 110, 170 (₹k). All four: mean 90, variance 3,000.
The best cut is at ₹45k, and its leaves predict 40 and 140.
The regression sweep: running sums
A node's total squared error needs only the sum of the targets, S , and the sum of their squares:
beginaligned SSE &= sum_i (y_i - bar y)^2 = sum_i y_i^2 - fracS^2n \\ SSE_L + SSE_R &= sum_i y_i^2 - Big( tfracS_L^2n_L + tfracS_R^2n_R Big) endaligned

(Expand the square: sum y_i^2 - 2bar y sum y_i + nbar y^2 , and with bar y = S/n the last two terms combine to -S^2/n .) The sum y_i^2 is the same for every split, so the sweep just maximizes S_L^2/n_L + S_R^2/n_R , updating S_L by one addition per row. On the toy:
With sum y_i^2 = 44,400 , cut 45's children have SSE 44,400 - 42,400 = 2,000 , which is n = 4 times the weighted variance of 500 in the table.
Depth on the credit limits

The noise has spread 10, so no model can beat an RMSE of about 10; depth 8 reaches 11.3. A straight line can't get close, because the truth multiplies two features. The unlimited tree has one applicant per leaf, so each prediction carries that neighbour's noise on top of the test applicant's own, about 10sqrt 2 approx 14 .

Classification trees are regression trees in disguise. For a 0/1 label with share p , the variance is p(1 - p) and Gini is 2p(1 - p) , exactly twice as big. Every gain doubles, the same split wins, and a squared-error tree on the 0/1 label gives exactly the same predictions as the Gini tree.
The loss decides what a leaf predicts
not in sklearn's trees; use quantile boosting or quantile forests

Why the median for absolute error: nudge a guess up. Every target above it gets closer by the nudge and every target below gets further by the same amount, so the total falls while more than half the targets are above the guess. The best guess has half on each side.
Why absolute error is slower: a mean updates from running sums with one addition per row moved; a median can't, so after every move the new middle value must be found again.
Heavy-tailed targets (loan amounts): squared error lets a few huge values dominate both the splits and the leaf means. Model the log, or use absolute error.

Counts (transactions per month): Poisson deviance, 2[yln(y/mu) - (y - mu)] per row, judges a miss relative to the mean. A miss of 5 costs 7.54 on a node averaging 2 ( y = 7 ), but only 0.12 on one averaging 200 ( y = 205 ); squared error charges 25 for both, so the heavy users dominate its splits.

A whole tree is section 04 on repeat. Find the best split of all the rows; that makes two groups. Treat each group as a new, smaller dataset and do the same, until a stop rule fires or no split is possible. This is recursive partitioning (the full pseudocode is in section 16):

grow(rows): if a stop rule fires or no split is possible: return leaf(value of rows) # shares or mean feature, threshold = best split of rows left = grow(rows with feature <= threshold) right = grow(the other rows) return node(feature, threshold, left, right)
The ten applicants, down to the last leaf:

root: 10 rows, 4 defaults, Gini 0.48 best cut late ≤ 1.5, gain 0.163 left: late 0 0 0 1 1 1 | defaults 0 0 0 0 1 0 Gini 0.278. One gap to try, at 0.5: 0/3 | 1/3 → 0.5(0) + 0.5(0.444) = 0.222 gain 0.278 − 0.222 = 0.056 → split right: late 2 2 3 3 | defaults 1 1 1 0 Gini 0.375. One gap to try, at 2.5: 2/2 | 1/2 → 0.5(0) + 0.5(0.5) = 0.25 gain 0.375 − 0.25 = 0.125 → split leaves: late 0 → 0 of 3 late 1 → 1 of 3 late 2 → 2 of 2 late 3 → 1 of 2

Two leaves are still mixed, but each holds a single late value, so no threshold can separate its rows and growth stops. Rows with identical features but different labels always end in a mixed leaf, so even an unlimited tree can't always reach 100% training accuracy.

Each split is the best one right now, chosen without looking ahead and never revisited. Searching all possible trees is hopeless: building an optimal tree is NP-complete (Hyafil and Rivest, 1976, for the tree that needs the fewest questions on average; finding the smallest tree is NP-hard too), so every standard library grows trees greedily.

Where it fails: XOR. Two features on [0, 1] ; the label is 1 when exactly one of them is above 0.5. Each feature alone says nothing: split on either at 0.5 and both halves are still 50/50. A depth-2 tree would be perfect (split one feature at 0.5, then the other at 0.5 on each side), but greedy growth can't see that the first split pays off only after the second. On 1,000 rows:
the correct first split, x_1 le 0.5 , has a Gini gain of 0.000003;
with nothing useful available, the root grabs noise: it peels off the 28 rows whose second feature is below 0.039, where a chance imbalance gives a sliver of gain;
training accuracy by depth 1 to 5 is 52%, 53%, 56%, 89% and 100%: three levels are wasted before the real cuts appear;
a stop rule of “split only if the gain is at least 0.005” gives up at the root: a single leaf.

Why greedy still found the credit rule. An AND leaves a trace in each feature alone; an XOR leaves none. At the root, income's best gain was 0.009 and EMI's 0.0025: each half of “income under 40 AND EMIs over half” already separates defaulters a little by itself, so greedy picked up income one level down and EMI beneath it.

Lookahead would solve the XOR, by scoring pairs of splits together. But every candidate must then be tried with every candidate in both children, roughly (d\,n)^2 work per node instead of d\,n , so it's rarely done.

Growing deep and pruning back fixes the stop-rule failure: pruning judges whole branches, so it keeps a weak split with strong children (section 11). It won't replace a wasted noise split at the top with the right one, so the tree stays bigger than it needs to be.

Averaging many trees is cheaper still. A 200-tree random forest capped at depth 3 scores 96.9% on fresh XOR data, where one depth-3 tree scores 53%: random feature choices and resampling let some trees start with a useful cut.
A leaf's value is the single number that minimizes the training loss over the rows in it:
Classification (Gini, entropy)
The shares minimize log loss (and squared error on the 0/1 labels) over the leaf's rows
Regression, squared error
Minimizes the sum of squares
Regression, absolute error
Half the targets on each side

With sample weights every count becomes a weighted count, so the leaf holds weighted shares. For the impurities, gains and leaf values, a weight of 2 is the same as putting the row in twice (but sklearn's min_samples_leaf and min_samples_split still count rows; min_weight_fraction_leaf counts weight). (In gradient boosting a leaf holds something else, a step that lowers the ensemble's loss, but the routing is the same.)

An applicant with income ₹30k, EMIs at 60% of income, no late payments and age 35 lands in the 213-row leaf. 105 of those 213 training applicants defaulted, so the tree says 49.3%, exactly their share.

predict vs predict_proba: predict takes each leaf's majority, a 0.5 cut-off. Only the two small leaves with a default majority vote “default”, so it flags 18 of the 1,500 test applicants while 130 actually defaulted. With a 9% default rate, 0.5 is almost never the right cut-off.

Only as many scores as leaves. This tree gives 8 distinct probabilities, so its ROC curve has only 8 straight segments and an approval cut-off can only fall between leaves. Declining the two riskiest leaves turns away 1.2% of applicants; the next leaf jumps that to 6.4%. “Decline exactly the riskiest 5%” is impossible, and score deciles can't be formed.
Inside a leaf, everyone is the same. An applicant earning ₹45k and one earning ₹140k, both with no late payments, both get 2.5%.

Far outside the data, say ₹5 lakh a month with no late payments, an applicant follows the richest applicants seen into the income > 146.44 leaf: 6.7%. A tree can't say anything new beyond its data (section 13).

chunks.h: Explaining one prediction: walk the path
chunks.x: Each question on the applicant's path moves the default share of the node they're in. The steps add up exactly to the leaf's score minus the overall rate:

chunks.h: Explaining one prediction: walk the path
chunks.x: Rank only the steps that raised the risk: reason 1 is the EMI share, reason 2 is income. A counterfactual comes free: with EMIs under half of income, this applicant would be at 3.7%. This readability is a single tree's biggest selling point in lending. The catch is that the credit depends on the order the questions were asked; SHAP removes that (section 14).
A probability is calibrated if, among all applicants given 20%, about 20% default. A leaf's probability is its training share, hat p = k/n , and three things make it rough:

Small leaves are noisy. A share from n rows typically misses the truth by its standard error, sqrthat p(1 - hat p)/n . The 20-row leaf says 90%; one standard error is sqrt0.9 times 0.1/20 = 0.067 , so two (roughly a 95% range) give 77% to 100%.

Small leaves are pushed towards the extremes. That leaf's truth, 73%, sits outside even that range. It isn't bad luck: the tree chose this leaf because its share looked extreme, out of many candidate cuts, so selected leaves are biased towards 0 and 1, not just noisy.
Pure leaves say exactly 0% or 100%, the far end of the same effect, and log loss punishes a confident wrong answer without limit.
The depth-3 tree's leaves (L = late payments, inc = income in ₹k), training share against the share on fresh test data and the truth:
L≥2, inc>40, age≤23 (noise)

The big leaves are close to the truth. The small ones, and above all the two noise splits, promised shares that fresh data doesn't deliver. So a shallow tree with big leaves is roughly calibrated; a deep tree is overconfident.

Bigger leaves help, but don't fix it. With min_samples_leaf=30 the tree ranks well (test AUC 0.804) but its log loss is 0.731, against 0.216 for depth 3: 51.5% of test applicants get exactly 0% or 100%. Most applicants have a true chance of 3%, and 30 of them all repaying is common ( 0.97^30 approx 0.4 ), so many 30-row leaves are pure.
Smooth towards the base rate (an m-estimate): pretend each leaf also holds m extra rows that default at the overall rate bar p .
hat p = frack + m\,bar pn + m

With m = 10 , a pure leaf of 30 says 2.2% instead of 0%, and the min_samples_leaf=30 tree's log loss falls from 0.731 to 0.241 with the same leaves. Choose m by cross-validation; too large pulls every leaf to 8.7% and loses the spread.

Honest leaves: the shares lean to the extremes because the same rows chose the leaves and then filled them. Grow the tree on one half of the training rows and fill the leaf shares from the other half. For a min_samples_leaf=30 tree grown on half the training rows, filling the leaves from the other half and smoothing gives a log loss of 0.227, against 0.725 when it uses its own shares.

Calibrate on held-out data with Platt scaling (a logistic fit on the score) or isotonic regression (a monotone step fit). Isotonic can merge neighbouring leaves into one score but can never split one, so the tree still has at most as many scores as leaves.
Average many trees, as a random forest does: leaves that disagree average into smoother, less extreme probabilities.

class_weight="balanced" makes each class count equally in total: the training set has 3,196 payers and 304 defaulters, so each defaulter counts r = 3196/304 approx 10.5 times as much as a payer. That changes which splits win, and it multiplies every leaf's odds of default by r : a leaf with k defaulters among n rows reports p_w = rk/(rk + n - k) . The depth-3 tree's average prediction becomes 32.7% against a real 8.7%, and its log loss 0.466. Solving for k/n undoes it exactly:
p = fracp_wp_w + r\,(1 - p_w)

That brings the log loss back to 0.236 (not 0.216, because the splits stay as the weighted tree chose them). The ranking barely moves: multiplying every leaf's odds by the same r keeps the leaves in order, so only the changed splits move the AUC (0.823 here, against 0.808). Oversampling the rare class r times does the same and is undone the same way.

Three separate questions: does the model rank well (AUC), do its probabilities mean what they say (calibration, log loss), and where do you cut to approve? A tree can pass the first and fail the second.

With no stop rule (sklearn's default: max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=1), the tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure or can't be split. It then answers every training question perfectly, noise included.
On the credit data it reaches depth 25 with 327 leaves, 139 of them holding a single applicant.
Training accuracy is 100%; test accuracy is 89%, worse than the 91.3% of predicting that nobody defaults.

Test AUC is 0.623 and log loss 3.965. Every leaf is pure, so every prediction is 0% or 100%: 165 of the 1,500 test applicants got 0% and defaulted, or 100% and repaid. Each costs -ln(2.2 times 10^-16) approx 36 (sklearn clips 0 to machine precision), and 165 times 36/1500 approx 3.97 is the whole log loss.

Training AUC rises with every level; test AUC peaks at depth 3, the depth of the true rule. Depths 1–2 are too simple to express the rule: that's bias. Deep trees change a lot from one training sample to the next (section 13): that's variance. (Comparing on the test set is for teaching only; choose settings by cross-validation.)
Rules that stop growth early are pre-pruning. Each refuses a split under some condition:
the node is already this deep
Blunt: big and small branches get the same limit
either child would get fewer rows than this
Can hide a real but rare group
the node has fewer rows than this
Doesn't protect the children: 20 rows can split into 1 and 19
the tree already has this many leaves
Splits are then made best-first, anywhere in the tree
the weighted gain is below this
Kills weak splits that would have led to strong ones (XOR)
min_impurity_decrease compares against the gain scaled by the node's share of all N training rows, so a split deep in a small branch must be proportionally purer to pass:
fracN_tNBig( I_t - fracN_tLN_t\, I_L - fracN_tRN_t\, I_R Big) ge threshold
One knob at a time on the credit data:
min_impurity_decrease=0.001
min_samples_split=20 still leaves one-row leaves; min_samples_leaf=30 ranks well but has pure leaves (section 09).
max_depth when people must read the tree: 3–5 levels stay readable.
min_samples_leaf when you'll use the probabilities: it's the most direct control over leaf noise.
max_leaf_nodes caps the size but lets the tree go deep where the data supports it (LightGBM grows leaf-wise like this).
min_impurity_decrease last: it trips on XOR-like patterns.
Set together, every limit applies and whichever binds first stops that branch.

Tuning depth and leaf size together by 5-fold cross-validation on log loss picks max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=30 (test AUC 0.809, log loss 0.218): it found the true depth. When the model will score future applicants, use folds split by time: train on earlier months, validate on later ones.

Monotonic constraints. monotonic_cst forces predictions to only rise (or only fall) with a feature, for example “more late payments never lowers the risk”, which credit models often need. sklearn enforces it bluntly: at each split on a constrained feature it caps every leaf on the low side, and floors every leaf on the high side, at the midpoint of the two children's values.

Constraining late here caps the whole late ≤ 1 side at 18.2%, so the stressed applicant from section 08 drops from 49.3% to 18.2%, though late payments were never their problem, and test AUC falls to 0.791.

Grow a big tree, then cut back the branches that don't earn their keep: post-pruning. A branch is a node plus everything below it; cutting it turns the node back into a leaf. Unlike stopping early, pruning judges a whole branch, not one split, so it can keep a weak split whose children are strong.
CART gives every leaf a price alpha and, among all trees obtained by cutting branches off the big one, keeps the one with the lowest
beginaligned R_alpha(T) &= R(T) + alpha\,lvert Trvert \\ R(T) &= sum_leaves t fracn_tN\, I(t) endaligned

R(T) is the tree's training impurity (each leaf's impurity times its share of the rows) and lvert Trvert its number of leaves. alpha = 0 keeps the full tree; a large alpha leaves only the root. In sklearn it's ccp_alpha.
The weakest link. You don't have to search all subtrees. For each branch T_t under node t , ask how much training impurity it removes per extra leaf:
g(t) = fracR(t) - R(T_t)lvert T_trvert - 1

R(t) is node t 's impurity if it were a leaf, R(T_t) the total over the leaves beneath it. Once alpha passes g(t) , those leaves aren't worth their price. So cut the branch with the smallest g , recompute g for the branches above it, and repeat. That gives a short list of nested trees, each the previous one with one more branch cut, each optimal over a range of alpha . Breiman showed that for every alpha there's a unique smallest optimal subtree and that these are nested, so this list contains every tree pruning could ever pick.
By hand, on the ten-applicant tree from section 07. Each node's R is (its rows / 10) × its Gini:

leaves late 0: 0.3 × 0 = 0 late 1: 0.3 × 0.444 = 0.133 late 2: 0.2 × 0 = 0 late 3: 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1 left branch (late ≤ 1), 2 leaves as one leaf: 0.6 × 0.278 = 0.167 g = (0.167 − 0.133) / (2 − 1) = 0.033 ← weakest right branch (late ≥ 2), 2 leaves as one leaf: 0.4 × 0.375 = 0.15 g = (0.15 − 0.1) / (2 − 1) = 0.05 root, 4 leaves as one leaf: 1.0 × 0.48 = 0.48 leaves total: 0 + 0.133 + 0 + 0.1 = 0.233 g = (0.48 − 0.233) / (4 − 1) = 0.082 cut the left branch (α = 0.033), recompute the root: its leaves now 0.167 + 0.1 = 0.267 g = (0.48 − 0.267) / (3 − 1) = 0.107 the right branch (0.05) is now weakes

sklearn's cost_complexity_pruning_path returns exactly these: alpha = 0, 0.033, 0.05, 0.163. For a branch with two leaves, g(t) is just that split's gain times its share of the rows: the right branch's 0.05 is 0.4 times 0.125 .
Each nested subtree's R_alpha is a straight line in alpha : its training impurity plus alpha times its leaf count. Pruning keeps whichever line is lowest. The crossings are the weakest-link values.

On the credit data. The depth-3 tree's path cuts the two noise splits first (income ≤ 146.44 at alpha = 0.00007 , then age ≤ 23.18 at 0.00089): they bought almost nothing for their extra leaf. Then the whole late ≥ 2 branch goes at 0.00215, and only the root is left after 0.0122. The full 327-leaf tree's path has 110 values of alpha . Choosing among the 20 largest by 5-fold cross-validation on log loss picks alpha = 0.00215 and a 4-leaf tree:

From 327 leaves to 4, with no noise splits, scoring like the depth-3 tree (test AUC 0.810, log loss 0.216). It keeps all of 2+ late payments in one leaf at 30.5%, though the truth splits them (28% vs 73%): only 63 training applicants had both 2+ late payments and low income, and cross-validation judged that split not worth a leaf.
alpha must be chosen on held-out data. Training impurity always prefers more leaves, so on the training data the best alpha is always 0.
Pruning can only remove splits; it can't bring back one that growth never made. So grow the big tree with no early stopping (or very light).
Pre vs post: they differ when a weak split has strong children, as in the XOR. A gain threshold refuses the first split; pruning sees the whole branch's value and keeps it.

The scale of alpha is “impurity per leaf”, because sklearn measures R as row-share-weighted impurity. Other pruning methods: reduced-error pruning (cut while a validation set's error doesn't rise) and C4.5's pessimistic pruning (an upper confidence bound on each leaf's error).
At a split on income, a row with a blank income has no side to go to. There are four standard answers: learn a direction, surrogate splits, C4.5's fractional rows, or impute.
Learn a direction for the blanks (sklearn, XGBoost, LightGBM)

sklearn's trees accept NaN (since version 1.3). During the sweep at a node, the rows whose value is missing are set aside, and every candidate threshold is scored twice: once with all the blanks sent left, once with them sent right. The better option wins, and the node stores the direction (tree_.missing_go_to_left). It also scores one extra candidate: all blanks on one side, every present row on the other. So blanks learn their own route at every split. XGBoost's “default direction” and LightGBM work the same way.
If a feature had no blanks at that node in training, a blank at prediction time goes to the child that had more training rows. That's a silent guess, not a learned rule.
Surrogate splits (classic CART)
Choose the primary split, say income ≤ 39.46, using the rows where income is present.
For every other feature, find the split (threshold and direction) that best mimics the primary one: the one that sends the most rows the same way, measured on rows where both features are present.
Keep only surrogates that agree better than the “majority rule” (sending everyone to the primary split's bigger side), ranked by agreement.
For a row missing income, at training or prediction time, use the best surrogate whose feature is present. If all are missing, follow the majority.

Surrogates help only when features are correlated: a loan amount can stand in for income. In this dataset the features were drawn independently, so a surrogate could beat the majority rule only by chance. R's rpart does this; sklearn doesn't.
C4.5 sends a row with a blank down both branches, weighted by the share of training rows that went each way, and averages the leaves it reaches by those weights.
Impute, or encode the blank
Mean or median: simple, but the blank now looks like a typical value, so any signal in being blank is lost.
Imputation plus a “was blank” indicator column (SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True)): works with any model, and the tree can split on the indicator.
An out-of-range constant such as −999: one split can isolate the blanks, but until it does they travel with the lowest values.
Blank as its own category for categorical features.
Fit any imputation on training data only.
When a blank is information

Suppose stressed applicants often skip the income field: half of them leave it blank, against 5% of everyone else. Blank-income applicants then default 23.4% of the time, against 7.4% for the rest. Take an applicant with a blank income, EMIs at 60%, no late payments, age 35:
The blanks learned to go to the low-income side
The blank became ₹84k and looks safe
The indicator brings the signal back
A tree that never saw a blank
Sent to the bigger child: the safe side
Native handling also scores best overall here (test AUC 0.804, against 0.785 with median imputation). Why values go missing decides how safe it is to lean on the blank:
Missing completely at random: the blank tells you nothing.
Missing at random (for reasons visible in other columns): other features can stand in.

Missing not at random (because of the value itself, as here): the blank carries the most signal, and the model is most fragile when the process creating blanks changes. A pipeline bug that blanks a field would silently move applicants to whichever side blanks learned; a form that makes income mandatory removes the signal overnight. Monitor missing rates, and make serving treat blanks exactly as training did.
Almost everything here follows from one fact: a tree only ever asks “is this one value above or below a cut?”

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Standardizing, taking logs or square roots all keep the values of a feature in the same order, so the same rows fall on each side of every possible cut, and the split search sees exactly the same candidates and gains. The tree comes out the same; only the printed thresholds change units. Refitting with log income gives identical test predictions, and e^threshold of its income split is 39.455, the same cut.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: A strictly increasing transform gives the same tree. A decreasing one (multiply by −1) gives the same partitions with left and right swapped.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: One subtlety: the midpoint of a gap moves under a non-linear transform, so a new value inside that tiny gap could in principle fall the other way.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Mixing features is not free. Rotating them (PCA) or replacing income and EMI share by their sum and difference changes the tree, and can turn an axis-parallel rule into a diagonal one.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Standardizing anyway is harmless, and convenient when the same pipeline feeds a linear model.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Interactions come free, if each part helps a little

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: The truth has an AND: high EMIs matter only for low incomes. The tree found it by splitting on income, then on EMI share inside the low-income branch; a split inside a branch applies only there. Logistic regression adds one effect per feature, so it can't express the AND unless handed it: it scores a test AUC of 0.756 alone and 0.822 once given the two true rules as columns, while the tree got 0.808 on its own.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Two limits: a pure XOR defeats greedy growth (section 07), and depth caps the interaction order, since a path of depth D involves at most D features.

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: Outliers: harmless in the features, harmful in the target

chunks.h: No scaling: invariant to monotone transforms
chunks.x: An income typed with three extra zeros just moves that applicant further to the right of cuts it was already right of. But a regression tree with squared error chases a typo in the target, because one huge value drags a leaf's mean: one ₹10 crore limit in the training data changes every test prediction of a depth-3 tree, whose first two splits only wall off that row. With absolute error (leaf = median) the typo can't drag a leaf: no split chases it, and at most one leaf's median shifts by one row (here, no prediction changed at all).

Every split cuts one feature at one value, so a tree's boundaries are made of horizontal and vertical pieces. A diagonal boundary has to be built as a staircase, and every step costs leaves. Take a toy with two features where the label is “feature 2 > feature 1”:

Two trees on the diagonal toy, shaded where they predict class 1; the dashed line is the truth. Every boundary is a horizontal or vertical segment, so the diagonal is approximated by a staircase that refines only as leaves are added.
Stump on feature 2 − feature 1

The error falls only like 1/leaves. A staircase of k equal steps along the diagonal leaves small triangles on the wrong side, of total area about 1/(4k) , and each step costs about 2 leaves. Halving the error doubles the leaves.

Give the tree the combination. With the difference as a feature, one split is perfect. The credit data shows the same thing: hand the tree the EMI amount in rupees instead of the share, and “EMIs over half of income” becomes the diagonal “amount > 0.5 × income”. The depth-3 tree's test AUC drops from 0.808 to 0.789. Ratios like debt-to-income are worth building by hand, even for trees.

Smooth additive effects waste leaves too. Giving each of two features 4 steps of effect needs the 4 steps of one repeated inside each of the 4 ranges of the other, 16 leaves, where an additive model needs 4 + 4 numbers.

Oblique trees split on a weighted sum of features and draw the diagonal in one split, but finding the weights at every node is much harder than a sorted sweep and the rules are harder to read, so they're rare. Ensembles average many staircases into a smoother edge.

A leaf predicts the mean of its training targets, so a regression tree can never predict outside the range of training targets, and every input beyond the outermost cut lands in the same edge leaf. A straight line keeps going.
Predicted credit limit as income grows, for an applicant with 20% EMIs. The training incomes stop at ₹150k; beyond that, the tree is flat.
Truth, 2 times income times 0.8

No tree model extrapolates. A random forest averages flat trees and boosting adds them up, so both go flat outside the data: for incomes of 150, 200 and 300, sklearn's gradient boosting predicts 240 for all three and a 100-tree random forest 236.

Predict something that stays in range. The limit per rupee of income is about 2(1 - emi) , between 0.4 and 2 whatever the income. Model that and multiply back: the last row of the table. It even wins inside the data (test RMSE 10.4, against 11.3 for the best plain tree), because the ratio depends only on emi.
Other fixes: remove the trend first, or add a linear part (LightGBM's linear_tree fits a line inside each leaf).

Where it bites: a new segment of richer applicants, amounts that grow over time, any forecast with a trend. When incomes drift up in production, more and more applicants pile into the edge leaves; tracking each leaf's share of traffic against training is a cheap drift monitor.

chunks.h: High variance: small changes, a different tree
chunks.x: Each split wins by some margin over the runner-up, often a small one, so resampling the rows can change the winner. Every split below depends on the ones above, so one change near the top rewrites the whole branch under it. Refitting the depth-3 tree on 20 bootstrap samples of the training rows (3,500 drawn with replacement):

chunks.h: High variance: small changes, a different tree
chunks.x: The root is stable: late ≤ 1.5 wins 18 times out of 20 (income ≤ 40.5 the other 2).

chunks.h: High variance: small changes, a different tree
chunks.x: The small branch is not. Right of the root sit only about 390 applicants, and its question takes 17 different forms in 20 refits: income at 44, at 47.6, at 122.3, age at 25.1, EMI share at 0.1…

chunks.h: High variance: small changes, a different tree
chunks.x: So are the predictions. One high-risk applicant (true chance 73%) gets anything from 27% to 100%, a standard deviation of 0.23. With full-depth trees it's worse: 100% in 17 refits and 0% in 3, a standard deviation of 0.36.

chunks.h: High variance: small changes, a different tree
chunks.x: Averaging many trees fitted on bootstrap samples (bagging, random forests) cancels much of this variance. It's also a warning: before presenting one tree's rules as policy, refit on a few resamples and keep only the rules that survive.

A feature with more distinct values offers more candidate thresholds, so it wins more often by luck (section 04): a continuous noise feature beat a binary one 96% of the time. The bias lives in the split search, so it shows up wherever splits are counted, most of all in impurity importance (next section). Leaf-size limits, pruning, and significance-test trees (CHAID, conditional inference) are the defences.

sklearn's feature_importances_ is the mean decrease in impurity: for every split, take its gain weighted by the share of all training rows that reach it, add these up per feature, and scale the totals to sum to 1.
importance_j propto sum_splits t on j fracn_tN\, gain_t

Totals: emi 0.0191, late 0.0120, income 0.0099, age 0.0009, together 0.0419. Dividing by 0.0419 gives the importances emi 0.455, late 0.287, income 0.237, age 0.021. EMI share outranks late payments although late is the root: the EMI split reaches only 17% of the rows, but it turns a 20%-default group into 3.7% and 49%, a gain eight times late's. Impurity importance measures how much training impurity a feature's splits removed, not how early it was asked.

It favours many-valued features. In the unconstrained tree, age, pure noise but continuous, gets 0.205, more than twice the 0.096 of late, a real cause with only a handful of distinct values. Add a column of uniform random numbers and it gets 0.200, on a par with income (and age drops to 0.185, because the extra column changes the tree); a random yes/no column gets 0.014.
It's measured on the training data, so splits that only fit noise count as much as real ones. That's how the noise columns above earn their share in a deep tree.

Correlated features share it arbitrarily. Add an exact copy of income: predictions don't change, but income's 0.237 is split between the twins by random_state (0.036 and 0.201 with seed 0; 0.237 and 0 with seed 4). Neither number says which one “matters”.
It's relative (it sums to 1) and says nothing about direction.

Shuffle one feature's column in held-out data, which breaks its link to the target while keeping its distribution, and measure how much the model's score drops. Repeat a few times and average. On the test set, the drop in AUC (20 shuffles each):

The two answer different questions. MDI asks how much training impurity a feature's splits removed; permutation asks how much the model's held-out predictions depend on it. Shuffling income scrambles the question that 89% of rows pass through and that decides who even reaches the EMI split; shuffling EMI only reshuffles the 17% low-income branch. And on the unconstrained tree with the random column added, permutation gives the random column −0.003 and age −0.015, where MDI gave them 0.200 and 0.185.

Correlated features: shuffle one and its twin still carries the signal, so both look unimportant. Shuffling also creates impossible rows (a high income with a tiny loan amount), and the model is scored on inputs it never saw.
It measures what this model uses, not what causes the outcome. It costs one prediction pass per feature per repeat.

SHAP explains one prediction as a sum: base rate plus one contribution per feature. A feature's Shapley value is its average marginal contribution over every order in which features could be revealed, where “the prediction knowing only the features in set S ” is estimated by following the tree for features in S and averaging over both children, weighted by their training rows, for the rest. TreeSHAP computes this exactly in polynomial time, O(T L D^2) for T trees with L leaves and depth D , instead of over all 2^d subsets. For the stressed applicant from section 08:

Both add up to the prediction. The path walk gives the big jump to whichever feature was asked when it happened, EMI, because income was asked first; SHAP averages over orders and gives income the larger share, since without a low income the EMI question is never reached. Averaging lvertSHAPrvert over many rows gives a global importance with direction and per-row detail. It doesn't fix the many-valued bias, though: SHAP explains the model, so if a deep tree split on noise, SHAP credits the noise too. On the unconstrained tree with a random column, mean lvertSHAPrvert on test rows gives the ran
The follow-ups that test whether you know what happens inside the tree.

Depth 1, a stump. One split, late ≤ 1.5, and two scores, 5.9% and 30.5%: test AUC 0.653. It can't express the AND (high bias), and it combines no features, so a sum of stumps (boosting with depth 1) is an additive model with no interactions.
Unlimited depth. Splits until every leaf is pure: depth 25, 327 leaves, 100% training accuracy, test AUC 0.623, log loss 3.97, every probability 0 or 1 (section 10).

min_samples_leaf=1. That's the default, and it means the leaf-size limit is off: a split may peel off a single row. With no depth limit it gives the unlimited tree above. Raising it to 200 gave the best ranking of any single setting here (12 leaves, test AUC 0.824).

Duplicating a feature. Predictions don't change, since a split on the copy is the same split. Importance is split between the copies by random_state, which decides which copy is tried first when they tie. Correlated features do the same more softly.

Adding a noise feature with many unique values (a random number, an ID). In the depth-3 tree it can still win the nodes where the truth is flat: over 20 random columns it took the income ≤ 146.44 noise split in 10, because the real features' best gain there is only 0.0001; where real signal exists, a real feature wins. In a deep tree it wins splits in small branches, gets an impurity importance of 0.200 (on a par with income) and a permutation importance of about 0, and test performance barely moves. A yes/no noise feature gets 0.014. Many values, many lottery tickets.
Scaling a feature (standardizing, rupees to dollars): the same tree, thresholds in new units. Trees need no scaling.
A monotone transform (log, square root, rank): the same tree (log income gives identical predictions). A non-monotone one (squaring a centred feature) or mixing features (PCA) changes it.

Class imbalance, 1:100 as in fraud. The root's Gini is only 2 times 0.01 times 0.99 approx 0.02 , so every gain is tiny and a min_impurity_decrease tuned on balanced data blocks every split. A 30-row leaf of ordinary users holds no fraud about three times in four ( 0.99^30 approx 0.74 ) and says exactly 0%. predict flags almost nobody. Use leaf sizes big enough to hold some positives, class weights if needed (then correct the probabilities, section 09), and judge by precision-recall, not accuracy.
Some labels are wrong. A deep tree memorizes each wrong label as its own tiny leaf and passes the mistake on to every similar new row.
The same customers in training and test (repeat borrowers). A memorizing tree scores them well because it has seen them, so the test score is too optimistic. Split by customer, not by row.
An outlier in the target. Under squared error it moves leaf means and can capture the top splits; under absolute error it's ignored (section 13).

The full CART build for classification, with the split search, missing values, categories, prediction and pruning. Regression swaps class counts for the running sum of targets and sum_k n_k^2/n for S^2/n .

# ---- building ------------------------------------------ def build(rows, depth): node = Node(value=class_shares(y[rows])) if (depth == max_depth or len(rows) < min_samples_split or is_pure(y[rows])): return node # a leaf best = None # sklearn keeps drawing past max_features until # it has found at least one valid split for j in shuffled(features)[:max_features]: cand = (best_categorical(rows, j) if categorical(j) else best_numeric(rows, j)) if cand and (best is None or cand.gain > best.gain): best = cand if best is None: return node # no valid split w_gain = best.gain * len(rows) / N if w_ga

One detail it glosses over: when a feature has no blanks at a node in training, both directions score the same, and sklearn stores “the child with more rows” as the route for blanks at prediction time.
