Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Numbers in the answers come from the credit example above, but each answer stands on its own.
1Walk through how a tree decides its first split.
It tries every feature and every threshold on all the training rows, scores each candidate by how much it lowers the size-weighted impurity, and keeps the best one.
Measure the root: its impurity, e.g. Gini 2p(1 - p) . With 8.7% defaults that's 0.159.
For each feature, sort the rows by it. Candidate thresholds sit at the midpoints between consecutive distinct values: any threshold inside a gap sends the same rows left, so one per gap is enough.
Sweep the sorted rows once, moving them one at a time from the right side to the left and updating the class counts on each side. At each gap, score the split from the counts:
beginaligned gain &= I(P) - tfracn_Ln I(L) - tfracn_Rn I(R) \\ children &= tfracn_LnGini_L + tfracn_RnGini_R \\ &= 1 - tfrac1ntextstylesum_k big(n_Lk^2/n_L + n_Rk^2/n_Rbig) endaligned
In words: the gain is the parent's impurity minus the children's, each child weighted by its share of the rows, and the weighted Gini needs only the class counts n_Lk, n_Rk on each side.
Take the best threshold per feature, then the best feature. In the credit example, late ≤ 1.5 gains 0.012, beating income (0.009), EMI share (0.0025) and age (0.0005).

Why it's done this way: sorting lets one sweep with running counts score each candidate in O(1) , so a feature costs O(n log n) instead of O(n^2) ; the size weights stop a tiny pure child from looking excellent. Follow-up: the search is exhaustive for this one split but greedy across levels, so the best first split isn't necessarily the start of the best tree.
2Gini or entropy: what's the difference, and does it matter?

They're nearly the same curve, so they almost always choose the same split. Entropy is steeper near pure nodes, so it gives more credit for cleaning up a nearly pure node; Gini is the default because it's CART's choice and skips the log.
beginaligned Gini &= sum_k p_k (1 - p_k) \\ &= 1 - sum_k p_k^2 \\ entropy &= sum_k p_k (-log p_k) endaligned

In words: both are the expected “surprise” at a row's class. Gini uses 1 - p where entropy uses -ln p , and 1 - p is the tangent line of -ln p at p = 1 , so Gini is entropy with the log replaced by its first-order approximation.
Where they differ: rare classes. -ln p blows up near 0, so entropy rises steeply near the ends. A 2%-positive node sits at 14% of entropy's peak but only 8% of Gini's.
In practice: on real data, trees grown with each typically differ in a split or two, often noise splits. Depth and leaf size matter far more.

Trade-off: Gini is a little faster; entropy may suit very imbalanced problems slightly better. Follow-up: “the Gini” in credit scoring usually means the Gini coefficient, 2\,AUC - 1 , a ranking metric unrelated to Gini impurity.
3Hand drill: a parent has 4 positives in 10. A split sends 1 of 6 left and 3 of 4 right. Compute the Gini gain and the information gain.
Gini gain 0.163; information gain 0.256 bits.
Check with counts (5 and 1 on the left, 1 and 3 on the right):
beginaligned tfrac5^2 + 1^26 + tfrac1^2 + 3^24 &= 6.833 \\ 1 - 6.833/10 &= 0.317 endaligned

Why the two numbers differ: entropy is in bits with a peak of 1 and Gini peaks at 0.5, so gains are only comparable within one criterion; what matters is which split each ranks first. Follow-up: the gain ratio divides the information gain by the entropy of the 6/4 split sizes, 0.971, giving 0.264.
4Why weight the children by size? Why not split on misclassification error?

Without the weights, peeling off one pure row would always look great. Misclassification error is a bad criterion because it's straight-sided: a split that sharpens the class shares without flipping a majority scores exactly zero.
Size weights: a one-row child is pure (impurity 0). In a plain average it would count for half, so a useless split would beat a real one. Weighted, it counts for 1/ n .
The geometry: the parent's class share is the size-weighted average of the children's, so the children's weighted impurity is a point on the chord between their two points on the impurity curve.
beginaligned p &= tfracn_Ln p_L + tfracn_Rn p_R \\ gain &= I(p) - tfracn_Ln I(p_L) - tfracn_Rn I(p_R) \\ &ge 0 endaligned

In words: for a strictly concave impurity (Gini, entropy) the chord lies below the curve, so any change in the shares gives a positive gain (Jensen's inequality). Misclassification error, 1 - max_k p_k , is a straight line on each side of 0.5, so when both children keep the same majority the chord lies on it and the gain is 0.

Example: a root split that moves the default share from 8.7% to 5.9% and 30.5% gains 0.012 in Gini and 0.038 in entropy, and exactly 0 in misclassification error, because both sides are still mostly payers. Follow-up: misclassification error is fine for pruning and for reporting accuracy; it's only blind as a split criterion.
5How is the best threshold for a numeric feature found efficiently, and what does building a tree cost?
Sort the node's rows by the feature, then sweep the gaps between distinct values with running class counts, scoring every midpoint in one pass: O(n log n) per feature per node, dominated by the sort.
beginaligned per node &= O(d\, n_t log n_t) \\ per level &= O(d\, n log n) \\ whole tree &= O(D\, d\, n log n) endaligned

In words: n_t is the node's rows, d the features, D the depth. Each row sits in one node per level, so a level's nodes add up to n rows. A balanced tree has D approx log_2 n , about O(d\, n log^2 n) in all; prediction is O(D) .
Why only distinct values: a threshold can't separate equal values. Why midpoints: every threshold in a gap gives the same training split; the midpoint hedges for unseen values.
Why the sweep: moving one row across updates the counts in O(1) ( O(K) for K classes). Rescoring each threshold from scratch would cost O(n^2) per feature.

Trade-off: histogram methods (LightGBM, XGBoost hist) bin each feature into about 256 quantiles once, then each node adds up per-bin counts in O(n_t\, d) and tries only bin edges; a sibling's histogram is the parent's minus the other child's. Much faster, at the cost of threshold resolution.
6How do trees split categorical features?

A categorical split sends a subset of the categories left. For a binary or regression target, sorting the categories by their mean target and trying the K - 1 cuts in that order is guaranteed to find the best of all 2^K-1 - 1 subsets; otherwise use one-vs-rest or heuristics.
The search space: K categories have 2^K-1 - 1 two-group splits: 127 for 8, about 5 times 10^14 for 50. Exhaustive search is out for large K .
One-vs-rest: the K splits that peel off one category, which is all a tree can do with one-hot columns. It needs several levels to build a good grouping, and each level costs rows.

Sort by mean target: optimal for a 0/1 target with Gini or entropy (Breiman) and for squared error (Fisher). Intuition: if a riskier category sat on the safe side while a safer one of the same size sat on the risky side, swapping them pushes the two sides apart without moving the parent, which can only raise the gain of a concave impurity. So the best groups are contiguous in sorted order.
Example: four categories of 100 rows each, at 5%, 8%, 25% and 30% default. The sorted cut 5%, 8% vs 25%, 30% gains 0.0221; the best one-vs-rest split gains 0.0113.

Trade-offs: with more than two classes there's no single order, so no shortcut. The sort order is learned from the labels, so rare categories make it noisy and the split overfits (LightGBM adds minimum counts and smoothing). sklearn's DecisionTreeClassifier needs numbers: one-hot for few categories, or target encoding computed out-of-fold and shrunk towards the overall rate, (k_c + mbar p)/(n_c + m) , to avoid leaking each row's own label.
7What does a regression tree's leaf predict, how are its splits scored, and why is absolute error slower?

A leaf predicts the mean of its training targets, and a split is scored by variance reduction. With absolute error the leaf predicts the median, which can't be updated from running sums, so the sweep is slower.
beginaligned SSE &= sum_i y_i^2 - fracS^2n \\ SSE_L + SSE_R &= sum_i y_i^2 - Big(fracS_L^2n_L + fracS_R^2n_RBig) endaligned
In words: S is the sum of the targets. The total sum y_i^2 is the same for every split, so the sweep just maximizes S_L^2/n_L + S_R^2/n_R , updating S_L with one addition per row moved.
Why the mean: sum_i (y_i - c)^2 has slope -2sum_i (y_i - c) , zero at c = bar y .

Why the median for absolute error: moving the guess up helps every target above it and hurts every target below by the same amount, so the best guess has half on each side. A median can't be maintained with one addition per row, so the sweep has to keep each side's values ordered.
Classification is regression in disguise: for a 0/1 label, Gini 2p(1 - p) is exactly twice the variance p(1 - p) , so a squared-error tree on 0/1 labels is the same tree.

Follow-ups: heavy-tailed targets let a few huge values dominate the splits and leaf means, so model the log or use absolute error; counts suit Poisson deviance, which judges a miss relative to the mean.
8Why is greedy tree growth not globally optimal?
Each split is chosen as the best one now, without looking ahead and never revisited. A split that's useless alone but enables great splits below it, as in an XOR, is never chosen.

XOR: label 1 when exactly one of two features is above 0.5. Splitting either feature at 0.5 leaves both halves 50/50, so its gain is about 0, although a depth-2 tree using exactly those cuts is perfect. Greedy grabs noise instead (on 1,000 rows it needed depth 5 for what depth 2 can do), and a minimum-gain stop rule never starts at all.
Why it usually works: an AND leaves a trace in each feature alone (each half of “low income AND high EMIs” already separates defaulters a little), so greedy can follow it one feature at a time.
Why not search properly: finding the optimal tree is NP-complete (Hyafil and Rivest, 1976). One-step lookahead costs roughly (d\,n)^2 per node instead of d\,n .

Fixes: grow deep and prune (pruning judges whole branches, so it keeps a weak split with strong children), or average many randomized trees (a random forest of depth-3 trees solves the XOR that one depth-3 tree can't). Optimal-tree solvers exist for small data and shallow trees.
Growing, stopping and pruning
9A tree gets 100% training accuracy and a test log loss near 4. What happened?
It grew without limits until every leaf was pure, so it memorized the training data, noise included, and every prediction is exactly 0 or 1.

Mechanism: with sklearn's defaults (max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=1) a node splits until it's pure or its rows are identical. On 3,500 credit applicants that's depth 25 and 327 leaves, 139 of them a single row.

The log loss: a pure leaf predicts 0% or 100%. Every test row that lands in a leaf of the wrong class costs -ln(2.2 times 10^-16) approx 36 after clipping. 11% of test rows were such cases: 0.11 times 36 approx 4 .

Bias and variance: training AUC climbs with every level, while test AUC peaked at depth 3 (0.808) and fell to 0.62 at full depth. Shallow trees underfit; deep trees fit noise that changes with every sample.
Fix: limit depth or leaf size, prune, or use an ensemble, choosing the settings by cross-validation. Follow-up: a training score says nothing about a tree's quality.
10Which pre-pruning knobs exist, and what's the difference between min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf?

min_samples_split says how many rows a node needs before it may split; its children can still be tiny. min_samples_leaf guarantees every leaf has at least that many rows, which directly limits how noisy a leaf's probability can be.
max_depth: readable, but blunt: big and small branches get the same limit.
min_samples_split: a 20-row node can still split into 1 and 19. In the credit example it left one-row leaves and a log loss of 2.0.
min_samples_leaf: every split must leave enough rows on both sides. The most direct control over leaf noise.
max_leaf_nodes: grows best-first, so it goes deep only where the data supports it.
min_impurity_decrease: refuses splits whose gain, weighted by the node's share of all rows, is too small.
tfracN_tNbig(I_t - tfracN_tLN_t I_L - tfracN_tRN_t I_Rbig) ge threshold

Trade-off: every stop rule judges one split at a time, so it can refuse a weak split whose children would be strong (an XOR). Tune depth and leaf size together by cross-validation, with time-based folds when the model will score future data.
11How does cost-complexity pruning work, and how does it differ from stopping early?

Grow a full tree, then for a price alpha per leaf keep the subtree that minimizes training impurity plus alpha times its leaf count. As alpha rises, branches are cut weakest-first, giving a short nested sequence of trees; pick alpha by cross-validation.
beginaligned R_alpha(T) &= R(T) + alpha\,lvert Trvert \\ g(t) &= fracR(t) - R(T_t)lvert T_trvert - 1 endaligned

In words: R(T) is the leaves' impurity weighted by their share of rows; g(t) is how much impurity the branch under node t removes per extra leaf. The branch with the smallest g is the weakest link: once alpha passes g(t) , its leaves aren't worth their price.

The loop: cut the weakest branch, recompute g for the branches above it, repeat. Each cut gives the next tree and the alpha where it takes over. Breiman showed these optimal subtrees are nested, so this list contains every tree pruning could pick.

Example: a 4-leaf tree on ten rows (leaves with 0 of 3, 1 of 3, 2 of 2 and 1 of 2 positives) has alpha values 0.033, 0.05 and 0.163: cut the left branch, then the right, then the root split. On real data, a 327-leaf tree pruned by CV came down to 4 leaves with no noise splits.
Why alpha by CV: on training data more leaves always lowers R(T) , so the best alpha there is always 0.

Pre vs post: stopping early judges each split alone, so it refuses a weak split with strong children; pruning judges whole branches and keeps it. Pruning can only remove splits, never add one growth didn't make, and it costs growing the full tree first.
12Why are decision trees high-variance?
Splits often win by small margins, so a slightly different sample picks a different split, and every split below depends on the ones above, so one change near the top rewrites the whole branch.
Hierarchy amplifies noise: a different root threshold changes which rows reach every node below, so their splits change too.

Small branches are least stable: fewer rows, closer races. In 20 bootstrap refits of a depth-3 credit tree, the root was the same 18 times, but the question in a 390-row branch took 17 different forms.
Leaves are small averages: one applicant's predicted risk ranged from 27% to 100% across the refits (standard deviation 0.23), and 0.36 with full-depth trees, whose pure leaves flip between 0 and 1.

Fixes: bagging and random forests average many trees on resampled data, which cancels much of the variance (decorrelating them with random feature subsets helps more). Bigger leaves and shallower trees reduce it at the cost of bias. Trade-off: an average of 300 trees is no longer a readable rule list; before trusting one tree's rules, refit on resamples and keep only the rules that survive.
13How do trees handle missing values?

Four ways: learn which side blanks go at each split (sklearn ≥ 1.3, XGBoost, LightGBM), use surrogate splits (classic CART), send the row down both branches with fractional weights (C4.5), or impute first, ideally with a “was blank” indicator.

Learned direction: during the sweep, rows with a missing value are set aside, and each candidate threshold is scored twice, with the blanks sent left and sent right. The better side is stored per node. If a feature had no blanks at that node in training, a blank at prediction goes to the child with more training rows: a guess, not a learned rule.

Surrogate splits: after choosing the primary split, find for each other feature the split that best mimics it (sends the most rows the same way); keep those that beat sending everyone to the bigger side. A row missing the primary feature follows the best available surrogate. They help only when features are correlated.
Fractional rows (C4.5): send the row down both branches, weighted by the share of training rows that went each way, and average the leaves it reaches.
Imputation: mean or median makes a blank look typical and erases any signal; adding an indicator column restores it.

Why it matters: blanks are often informative (missing not at random). If risky applicants skip the income field, a native-NaN tree learns to send blanks to the risky side (40% for one such applicant), median imputation makes them look safe (7%), and a tree that never saw a blank sends them to the bigger, safer side (2.5%). Trade-off: a model that leans on blanks breaks when the process that creates them changes, so monitor missing rates and treat blanks identically in training and serving.
14Why don't trees need feature scaling?
A split only asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, so only the order of a feature's values matters, and scaling, logs and other monotone transforms keep that order.

Mechanism: after a monotone increasing transform, sorting the node's rows gives the same order, so the sweep sees the same candidate partitions with the same gains, and the same split wins at every node. Only the printed thresholds change units (a log-income tree's threshold maps back to the same ₹39.46k).
A decreasing transform gives the same partitions with left and right swapped.
Contrast: gradient descent, regularization penalties and distances (k-NN, SVMs, PCA) all depend on scale, which is why linear models and neural nets need standardizing.

Caveats: mixing features (PCA rotation, sums and differences) does change the tree. A new value inside the gap between two training values could route differently, since the midpoint moves under a non-linear transform. Standardizing anyway is harmless.
15Why can't trees extrapolate?
Every prediction is a leaf's mean of training targets, so it can't leave the training range, and every input beyond the outermost threshold lands in the same edge leaf: the prediction goes flat.
beginaligned f(x) &= c_j \ for x in R_j \\ min_i y_i le c_j &le max_i y_i endaligned
In words: the leaf value c_j is an average of training targets, so it's bounded by them, and the edge boxes R_j stretch to infinity.

Example: credit limit grows with income, and training incomes stop at ₹150k. For an applicant with 20% EMIs (truth 1.6 times income), a depth-6 tree predicts 217.6 at incomes of 150, 200 and 300, where the truth is 240, 320 and 480; a linear model keeps rising.
Ensembles too: a random forest averages flat trees and boosting adds them, so both go flat.

Fixes: model a quantity that stays in range (limit per rupee of income) and multiply back, remove the trend first, or add a linear component (LightGBM's linear_tree). Follow-up: in production this shows up as drift: new data piling into the edge leaves.
16Why do trees struggle with diagonal boundaries and smooth additive effects?
Every split is parallel to an axis, so a diagonal boundary must be built as a staircase, and every step costs leaves and data.

The staircase: for the boundary “feature 2 > feature 1”, a depth-2 tree (4 leaves) scores 86%, depth 4 (16 leaves) 94%, an unlimited tree (54 leaves) 97.7%, and logistic regression 99.85% with one line. A staircase of k steps leaves wrong-side triangles of area about 1/(4k) , so the error falls only like 1/leaves.
Additive effects: giving each of two features 4 steps of effect needs the 4 steps of one repeated inside each of the 4 ranges of the other, 16 leaves, where an additive model needs 8 numbers.

Fixes: hand the tree the combination: with the difference as a feature, a single split is perfect; ratios like debt-to-income are worth building even for trees. Oblique trees split on weighted sums but are slow and hard to read; ensembles average many staircases into a smoother edge. Follow-up: rotating the features (PCA) can turn an axis-parallel rule into a diagonal one and hurt a tree.
17A split like “age ≤ 23.18” appears deep in a small branch. Is it real? Why do such splits appear?

Probably noise. In a small branch where the truth is flat, every candidate cut is noise, a depth limit still forces a split, and the luckiest of hundreds of cuts wins; features with many distinct values hold the most lottery tickets.

Mechanism: in a 331-row branch with three continuous features there are about 990 candidate thresholds. The best of 990 random gains looks like a rule: 10 of the 18 youngest applicants happened to default.

The bias: a continuous feature offers n - 1 thresholds, a binary one 1. In 200 simulations (1,000 rows, a pure-noise target with 10% positives), a continuous noise feature beat a binary one at the root 96% of the time.

How to tell: its leaf is tiny (18 rows), it's among the first branches pruning removes, bootstrap refits rarely repeat it, and on fresh data its leaf's share collapses (55.6% in training, 12.5% on test).

Defences: min_samples_leaf, cost-complexity pruning, and significance-test trees (CHAID, conditional inference) that pick the feature by a test before searching thresholds. Follow-up: the same bias inflates impurity-based feature importance.
Importance and explanations
18How is a tree's feature importance computed, and what are its pitfalls?

sklearn's importance is the mean decrease in impurity (MDI): each split's gain weighted by the share of training rows reaching it, summed per feature and normalized to 1. It's biased towards many-valued features, computed on training data, and split arbitrarily between correlated features; permutation importance on held-out data and SHAP are the usual checks.
importance_j propto sum_splits t on j fracn_tN\, gain_t
It counts impurity removed, not order: a split deep in a 17% branch with a huge gain can outrank the root split.
Many-valued bias: in an unconstrained credit tree, pure-noise age (continuous) got 0.205 against 0.096 for late (a real cause with few values); a column of random numbers got 0.200.
Training data: splits that only fit noise count fully.
Correlated features: an exact copy of a feature takes some or all of its importance depending on random_state.

Permutation importance shuffles one column in held-out data and measures the score drop: the random column scores about 0. But with correlated features, the twin still carries the signal so both look unimportant, and shuffling creates impossible rows. SHAP (TreeSHAP, exact in polynomial time for trees) splits each prediction into additive per-feature contributions averaged over all feature orders; mean lvertSHAPrvert is a global importance, but it inherits any noise splits the model made, so it's only as clean as the tree. None of them measures causation.
19How would you explain one prediction from a tree?

Walk the row's path: each question moves the node's predicted share, and the steps add up exactly to the prediction minus the base rate. SHAP gives an order-independent version of the same decomposition.
beginaligned f(x) &= bar p + sum_path big(hat p_child - hat p_parentbig) \\ 49.3 &= 8.7 - 2.8 + 14.1 + 29.3 \ (points) endaligned

In words: everyone starts at the base rate 8.7%; “at most 1 late payment” lowers it to 5.9%, “income ≤ ₹39k” raises it to 20%, “EMIs over half” to 49.3%. The reasons to give are the steps that raised the risk, largest first; a counterfactual comes free (with EMIs under half, 3.7%).
The catch: the path walk credits whichever feature was asked when a jump happened, so it depends on the order of the questions. Here EMI gets +29.3 because income was asked first.

SHAP averages each feature's contribution over all orders, using the tree's training counts for features not yet known. For the same applicant it gives income +26.4 and EMI +17.7: without a low income, the EMI question is never reached.
Follow-up: before defending a single tree's decision to a customer, check that the rule survives refits on resampled data.
20What happens if you duplicate a feature, or add a random ID-like column?

A duplicate changes no prediction but splits the importance between the copies arbitrarily. A random many-valued column wins the splits where nothing real is left to find, rarely in a shallow tree and often in a deep one, which inflates its impurity importance while its permutation importance stays near zero.

Duplicate: a split on the copy is the same split, so the gains tie exactly. sklearn tries features in a random order per node and the first one wins, so random_state decides which copy gets the credit (0.036 and 0.201 with one seed, 0.237 and 0 with another). Correlated near-copies share it the same way, more softly.

Random column, shallow tree: it can't beat a real signal, but it competes for the noise splits. In 20 tries it took the depth-3 tree's income ≤ 146.44 split half the time, with almost no effect on test AUC.

Random column, deep tree: in small branches, where the real features are exhausted, its thousands of thresholds win by luck. Its MDI reached 0.200, on a par with income; its permutation importance was −0.003; test AUC barely moved. A random yes/no column got only 0.014.

Why it matters: a true ID column lets a deep tree memorize individuals, which looks good only if the same customers appear in training and test. Drop identifiers, limit leaf size, and judge importance on held-out data.
21Are a tree's predicted probabilities calibrated?

Only roughly, and only for big leaves. A leaf's probability is its training share k/n : noisy in small leaves, pushed towards 0 and 1 because the tree chose those leaves for looking extreme, and exactly 0 or 1 when pure. Deep trees are overconfident.
beginaligned hat p &= frackn \\ SE(hat p) &= sqrtfrachat p(1 - hat p)n endaligned
In words: a share from n rows typically misses by its standard error. A 20-row leaf at 90% has an SE of 6.7 points.

Selection bias: of hundreds of candidate cuts, the tree keeps the one whose children look most separated, so small leaves overstate how extreme they are. In the credit tree, an 18-row leaf said 55.6% and delivered 12.5% on test; a 2,436-row leaf said 2.5% and delivered 3.0%.
Pure leaves: with min_samples_leaf=30, half the test rows got exactly 0% or 100%: AUC 0.804 but log loss 0.731. Ranking and calibration are different questions.

Fixes: bigger leaves; smoothing towards the base rate, (k + mbar p)/(n + m) (log loss 0.731 → 0.241 with the same leaves); honest leaves filled from held-out rows; Platt or isotonic calibration on a held-out set; or an ensemble. Check it with a reliability curve, log loss or Brier score on held-out data.
22What does class_weight="balanced" do to a tree?

It makes each minority row count r times as much in every impurity and every leaf share. That changes which splits win and multiplies every leaf's odds by r , so the probabilities are inflated, while the ranking barely moves.
beginaligned p_w &= fracr kr k + (n - k) \\ p &= fracp_wp_w + r(1 - p_w) endaligned
In words: a leaf with k positives among n rows reports p_w under weights; solving for k/n gives the second line, which undoes it exactly. Here r is the ratio of negatives to positives in training.

Example: with 8.7% defaults, r approx 10.5 ; the balanced tree's average prediction is 32.7% and its log loss 0.466. The correction brings the log loss to 0.236, not to the unweighted tree's 0.216, because the splits stay as the weighted tree chose them.
Why the ranking barely moves: multiplying every leaf's odds by the same r keeps the leaves in order; only changed splits move the AUC.

Trade-off: weights can help a rare class win splits, but if you need probabilities, correct or recalibrate afterwards. Moving the decision threshold is often all that's needed. Oversampling behaves the same way.
23How does severe class imbalance (1:100) affect a tree?
Gains become tiny, leaves of the majority class become pure, predict flags almost nobody, and accuracy becomes meaningless.
Tiny gains: the root's Gini is 2 times 0.01 times 0.99 approx 0.02 , so every gain is small, and a min_impurity_decrease tuned on balanced data blocks every split.
Pure leaves: a 30-row leaf of ordinary users holds no positive with probability 0.99^30 approx 0.74 , so most such leaves say exactly 0%.
Majority votes: predict uses a 0.5 cut-off, and hardly any leaf has a positive majority.

What to do: use leaf sizes large enough to hold some positives, use predict_proba with a threshold chosen for the business cost, consider class weights (then correct the probabilities), smooth or calibrate the leaves, and judge by precision-recall or PR-AUC, not accuracy. Trade-off: entropy is slightly more sensitive than Gini to cleaning up rare-class pockets, but leaf size matters far more.
24Write the pseudocode for building a decision tree.
Recursive: at each node, check the stop rules, search every feature's sorted thresholds for the best gain, split, and recurse into both children.

def build(rows, depth): node = Leaf(value=class_shares(y[rows])) if depth == max_depth or is_pure(rows) \ or len(rows) < min_samples_split: return node best = None for j in features: order = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: X[r, j]) L, R = zeros(K), counts(y[order]) for i in range(len(order) - 1): L[y[order[i]]] += 1; R[y[order[i]]] -= 1 if X[order[i], j] == X[order[i + 1], j]: continue # not a gap if min(L.sum(), R.sum()) < min_samples_leaf: continue g = gini_gain(L, R) # from counts if best is None or g > best.gain: a = X[order[i], j] b = X[order[i + 1], j] best = Split(j, (a + b) / 2, g) if best

Points to say: sorting lets one sweep with running counts score each candidate in O(1) , so a node costs O(d\, n log n) ; the counts give the Gini gain directly; prediction walks one path, O(depth) . For regression, replace the class counts with running sums of y and the leaf value with the mean. Missing values add a second pass per threshold (blanks left, then right), and pruning is a separate weakest-link loop over the finished tree.
25When would you use a single tree rather than a random forest or boosting?
When the rules must be read, audited or followed by people, or as a quick baseline and leakage check. When accuracy or probabilities matter most, use an ensemble.
Single tree: a credit policy or fraud triage rule people must follow, reason codes from the path, bins for a scorecard, a first look at the data. A depth-2 tree with an AUC of 0.99 is a leak alarm.
Its weaknesses: high variance (rules change with the sample), rough probabilities, staircase boundaries, a ceiling on accuracy.

Ensembles: forests average away the variance and smooth the probabilities; boosting fixes errors step by step and usually wins on tabular data. Explain them with SHAP, and add monotonic constraints where policy demands a direction.

Trade-off: none of them extrapolates, so for trends add a linear part or model a ratio. If you need one readable tree that behaves like the ensemble, fit a shallow tree to the ensemble's predictions and check how often they disagree.

beginaligned Gini &= 1 - textstylesum_k p_k^2 \\ Gini, 2 classes &= 2p(1 - p) \\ entropy &= -textstylesum_k p_k log_2 p_k \\ misclass. &= 1 - max_k p_k \\ regression &= tfrac1ntextstylesum_i (y_i - bar y)^2 endaligned

beginaligned gain &= I(P) - tfracn_Ln I(L) - tfracn_Rn I(R) \\ Gini, kids &= 1 - tfrac1ntextstylesum_k big(n_Lk^2/n_L + n_Rk^2/n_Rbig) \\ SSE, kids &= textstylesum_i y_i^2 - big(S_L^2/n_L + S_R^2/n_Rbig) \\ SplitInfo &= -textstylesum_j tfracn_jnlog_2 tfracn_jn \\ GainRatio &= IG / SplitInfo endaligned
beginaligned per node &= O(d\, n_t log n_t) \\ per tree &= O(D\, d\, n log n) endaligned
Candidates: midpoints of the gaps between consecutive distinct values; sweep with running counts.
Categories with a binary or numeric target: sort by mean target, try K - 1 of the 2^K-1 - 1 splits.
beginaligned hat p &= k/n \\ SE &= sqrthat p(1 - hat p)/n \\ smoothed &= frack + mbar pn + m \\ undo weight r &: \ p = fracp_wp_w + r(1 - p_w) endaligned
beginaligned min decrease &le tfracN_tNbig(I_t - tfracN_tLN_t I_L - tfracN_tRN_t I_Rbig) \\ R_alpha(T) &= R(T) + alpha lvert Trvert \\ g(t) &= fracR(t) - R(T_t)lvert T_trvert - 1 endaligned
beginaligned MDI_j &propto textstylesum_t on j tfracn_tN\, gain_t \\ permutation_j &= score - score_j shuffled endaligned
Behaviour in one line each
Monotone transforms change nothing; mixing features does.
Flat beyond the training range; diagonals as staircases; smooth additive effects need many leaves.
High variance, worst in small branches; averaging fixes it.
Many-valued features win more splits by luck, and inflate MDI.
Blanks: learned direction, surrogates, or impute plus an indicator.

notes.title: Random forests and bagging
notes.desc: Why averaging decorrelated trees cuts variance: bootstrap samples, per-split feature menus, out-of-bag error, each knob's effect on bias, variance and correlation, importance traps.

chunks.x: Random forests and bagging · Deepam Minda

A full-depth tree has low bias and high variance: its leaves memorize the rows it saw. Bagging grows B trees on bootstrap samples ( n rows drawn with replacement, about 63.2% of them distinct) and averages them. Averaging keeps one tree's bias and cancels the part of the error the trees don't share.

The trees share one training set, so their errors correlate. With tree variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho , the average has variance rhosigma^2 + (1-rho)sigma^2/B . More trees remove only the second term; past a few hundred trees, only less alike trees (a smaller rho ) or steadier trees (a smaller sigma^2 , from bigger leaves) help.

A random forest makes the trees less alike by offering every split a fresh random subset of max_features features. That lowers rho but weakens each tree (raises sigma^2 ), so it pays only when rhosigma^2 falls. Rules of thumb: sqrt p for classification, p/3 for regression. Tune it.
Trees are grown deep and unpruned, because averaging fixes variance but never bias. Leaf size is the knob for smoother, better probabilities.
Each row is out of bag for about 37% of the trees. Scoring every row with only those trees gives a nearly free validation score, which breaks when rows repeat or time order matters.

Impurity importance is computed on training rows and inflates high-cardinality and noise features. Permutation importance on held-out data doesn't, but both split the credit between correlated features, and neither is causal.

Forests never overfit by adding trees, can't extrapolate, squeeze probabilities away from 0 and 1, and shrug off feature outliers. Tuned boosting usually wins on accuracy; a forest wins on small or noisy data, or when there's no time to tune.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Every number in this note comes from one synthetic dataset, so it can be checked against a known truth: 5,000 loan applicants with four features.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: income: ₹15k to ₹150k a month;

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: emi: the share of income already going to loan repayments (EMIs), 0 to 0.8;

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: late: late payments last year (mostly 0, 1 or 2);

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: age: 21 to 60, a decoy with no effect.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: The true chance of default is built from flat steps. Everyone starts at 3%. Being stressed (EMIs over half of income and income under ₹40k) adds 45 points, and two or more late payments add 25. So the truth takes only four values:

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: One fixed split keeps 3,500 rows for training (304 defaulters) and 1,500 for testing (130 defaulters). A second target, for regression, is the credit limit granted: 2 times income times (1 - emi) , plus noise with a standard deviation of 10 (₹ thousand).

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Every model is scored three ways on the test set:

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: AUC: how well it ranks defaulters above non-defaulters. Higher is better.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Log loss: how much probability went to what actually happened. Lower is better.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Gap: the mean squared difference between the predicted and the true chance, frac1n sum_i (hat p_i - p_i)^2 . 0 is perfect. It can only be measured because the truth is known, and it ignores the noisy 0/1 labels, so it's the cleanest check here.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Results are written as (AUC, log loss, gap). The truth itself scores (0.817, 0.212, 0). With only 130 test defaulters, a test AUC wobbles by about ±0.02, so a model can edge past the truth's AUC by luck. When AUC and the gap disagree, trust the gap.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: One tree memorizes; many trees disagree

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: A decision tree (CART, the standard algorithm) splits the rows with yes/no questions such as late <= 1.5. At each node it picks the question that most reduces impurity, how mixed the node's classes are. For a node where a share q of the rows defaulted, the Gini impurity is 2q(1-q) : 0 when the node is pure, largest at a 50/50 mix.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Grown to full depth, a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, so each leaf holds one or a few applicants and answers a flat 0 or 1. Grow 100 such trees, each on a random half of the training rows, and ask eight of them about one applicant from each risk level:

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Each tree is confidently wrong for many applicants, but trees grown on different rows are wrong in different places. Over all 1,500 test applicants:

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: The gap shrinks more than tenfold. In bias–variance terms, a full-depth tree has low bias: it isn't wrong in any systematic way, since it can carve out any shape. But it has high variance: its answer swings with the exact rows it saw. Averaging keeps the low bias and cancels much of the swing, the way the average of 100 people's guesses of a cow's weight beats most single guesses.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: The middle two applicants are still off by about 0.17. All 100 trees learned from the same 3,500 rows, so any quirk those rows have near an applicant is shared by every tree, and averaging can't remove it. Section 04 measures that shared part.

chunks.h: One deep tree: low bias, high variance
chunks.x: Only different data helps. Ten full-depth trees on the same rows, differing only in their random seed, disagree on just 4% of test applicants: the seed only breaks ties between equally good splits. Their misses correlate about 0.84, and their average scores AUC 0.637 against 0.623 for one tree.

There's only one training set. To fake many, draw n rows from it with replacement: each picked row goes back in the pot and can be picked again. Some rows appear twice or more, some not at all. That's a bootstrap sample.
Each draw misses a given row with chance 1 - 1/n , so all n draws miss it with chance (1 - 1/n)^n :
beginaligned P(a row is in the sample) &= 1 - Big(1 - frac1nBig)^n \\ &to 1 - frac1e \\ &approx 0.632 endaligned
In words: a bootstrap sample holds about 63% of the distinct rows, with some repeated to make up the count. The other 37% are that sample's out-of-bag rows. The limit arrives fast:
Share of distinct rows in the sample
0.632 (one real draw: 0.626)
By hand with n = 3 : each draw misses row A with chance 2/3, so
beginaligned P(all three draws miss A) &= (2/3)^3 \\ &= 8/27 \\ &approx 0.30 \\ P(A is in the sample) &= 19/27 \\ &approx 0.70 endaligned
How many times is each row drawn? A row's count is the number of hits in n draws, each with chance 1/n . For large n that's a Poisson count with mean 1:
P(drawn k times) = frace^-1k!

"Left out" and "drawn once" are equally likely. A bootstrap sample is really a random weighting of the rows, and sklearn's forests implement it exactly that way: each tree is fit on every row, with sample_weight set to the row's count.

Why with replacement: drawing all n rows without replacement just reorders the same data, so every tree would come out identical. Replacement changes both which rows a tree sees and how much each one counts.

Subsampling draws k < n rows without replacement (called pasting when used for bagging). It also makes trees differ, with no duplicates. Half-samples and bootstraps behave much alike here: gaps of 0.0058 and 0.0065.

Smaller bootstraps: a forest's max_samples draws a fraction f of n per tree, so a row is in with chance 1 - (1 - 1/n)^fn , which is about 1 - e^-f . At f = 0.3 each tree sees about 26% of the distinct rows.

Duplicated rows break the picture. Two copies of one applicant can land one in the bag and one out, so the "left-out" copy isn't really unseen. The trees vary less than they seem, and the out-of-bag score turns optimistic (section 07).
The bootstrap's day job is measuring uncertainty: resample, recompute a statistic, look at the spread. Bagging borrows the resampling to build many models instead.
idx = rng.integers(0, n, n) # n draws, with replacement len(np.unique(idx)) / n # → about 0.632 counts = np.bincount(idx, minlength=n) # weights oob = counts == 0 # out-of-bag rows
Bagging (bootstrap aggregating; Breiman, 1996) is the averaging of section 01, with bootstrap samples:
Draw a bootstrap sample of the training rows.
Grow a full-depth tree on it.
Repeat B times, and average the trees' predictions.
hat p(x) = frac1B sum_b=1^B hat p_b(x)

In words: the bagged prediction is the plain average of the B trees' predicted probabilities (for regression, of their predicted numbers). The trees never see each other, so they train in parallel. sklearn does the same in one line with BaggingClassifier; its random draws differ, so its numbers differ slightly.

Bagging with three trees and ten rows. Each tree grows on its own bootstrap sample: filled cells are in its bag (a digit means drawn that many times), empty cells are its out-of-bag rows. The forest averages the trees; in a random forest, each tree also draws m features at every split. Row 5 (dashed) was left out by trees 1 and 3, so its out-of-bag prediction averages just those two; row 9 is in every bag and gets none.

P = np.empty((B, len(X_te))) for b in range(B): r = rng.integers(0, n, n) # bootstrap t = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X[r], y[r]) P[b] = t.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] bag = P.mean(axis=0) # bagged prediction
Why one tree's log loss explodes, and what averaging fixes

A full-depth tree's leaves are pure, so it predicts exactly 0 or 1. Log loss charges -log hat p for the probability given to what happened, and sklearn clips an exact 0 to 2.2 times 10^-16 , so every confident mistake costs about 36. This tree is confidently wrong on about 13% of test applicants, and 0.13 times 36 approx 4.7 : that's the whole 4.71.

The average of 200 trees gives fractions like 37/200 instead, so most confident mistakes vanish. What's left of the bag's 0.336 comes from 5 defaulters that all 200 trees put in pure "no default" leaves, because the training data has no defaulters near them. They alone add 5 times 36 / 1500 approx 0.12 ; everyone else scores 0.216, against the truth's 0.212. Bigger leaves fix this (section 06): each tree then averages a wider neighbourhood, so it becomes rare for every tree to say exactly 0.
There are two ways to combine classifiers:
Majority vote (hard voting): each tree casts its predicted class, and the most common class wins. This was Breiman's original rule.
Probability averaging (soft voting): average the trees' leaf probabilities, then apply a threshold. sklearn's forests and BaggingClassifier do this.

With pure leaves the two carry the same information: each tree says 0 or 1, so the average is the vote share. With bigger leaves they can disagree. Say three trees report 0.45, 0.45 and 0.9 for one applicant:
beginaligned tree votes &= (0,\ 0,\ 1) \\ majority vote &= 0 \\ average &= (0.45 + 0.45 + 0.9)/3 \\ &= 0.6 endaligned

Averaging keeps how sure each tree was, so it gives a ranking (which AUC and any threshold need) and has lower variance. A vote gives only a class: with 8.7% defaulters, just 61 of 1,500 test applicants get a "default" majority from the 200 bagged trees. Averaged probabilities can still be poorly calibrated (section 11).
Averaging removes variance, never bias
Every tree is grown the same way, on an equally random sample, so all trees have the same expected prediction, and so does their average:
beginaligned mathbb E[bar f(x)] &= frac1B sum_b=1^B mathbb E[f_b(x)] \\ &= mathbb E[f_1(x)] endaligned
In words: the forest is exactly as biased as one of its trees. Averaging attacks only the spread, so a model that is wrong the same way on every sample stays wrong.

Logistic regression shows it. It is stable (its bootstrap refits barely differ), but its straight-line log-odds can't express "EMIs over half and income under ₹40k". Fit both models on the same 100 bootstrap samples and split each one's error into two parts:
the wobble: how much the refits disagree with each other (their variance). Averaging removes it.
the shared miss: how far the average refit sits from the truth. Averaging keeps it. It holds the true bias, plus quirks of this one training set that every bootstrap inherits.
Five refits for one applicant (true chance 0.03)

The wobble and shared-miss columns are averages over all 1,500 test applicants; the five refits just show one applicant's spread. The two parts add up to one refit's mean squared miss: for the tree, 0.0529 + 0.0068 approx 0.060 , the sigma^2 of section 04.

Almost all of logistic regression's error is shared miss, so bagging 50 of them changes nothing: (0.756, 0.261, 0.0105) before and after. Most of a tree's error is wobble, so bagging cuts it to about 0.007.

Why logistic regression is stable: it fits one smooth formula through all 3,500 rows. Each row pulls the coefficients only slightly, and a bootstrap's dropped and doubled rows mostly cancel out, so predictions move by about 0.01.

Why a tree is unstable: it makes hard, greedy yes/no choices. A resample that nudges the top threshold sends different rows down each branch, and every split below can change. At full depth a leaf is one or a few rows, so whether one particular defaulter made it into the sample flips the answer between 0 and 1.

So bagging helps unstable learners (deep trees, neural nets on small data) and does nothing for stable ones (linear models, k-nearest neighbours with a large k), or even slightly hurts them, since each bootstrap holds only 63% of the distinct rows.

Bagging stumps (depth-1 trees) shows the same limit from the other side. The bootstrap flips which single question wins: 160 of 200 stumps ask late <= 1.5, and 40 ask about income near ₹40k. The average mixes two one-question rules, giving four score levels instead of two, so ranking improves (AUC from 0.653 to 0.781). But the gap barely moves (0.0115 to 0.0104): no mix of one-question rules can say "EMIs high and income low". That's bias.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: If the trees' mistakes were independent, averaging 200 of them would cut the variance 200 times. They aren't: every tree grew from the same 3,500 rows. If those rows hold an unlucky cluster of defaulters somewhere, every tree sees it and errs the same way there. Averaging cancels the parts of the mistakes that differ between trees; the shared part survives.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: Let each tree's prediction at a point have variance sigma^2 , and any two trees have correlation rho . The variance of a sum is the sum of all the pairwise covariances: B terms sigma^2 (each tree with itself) and B(B-1) terms rhosigma^2 (each tree with another one):

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: beginaligned Var(bar f) &= frac1B^2 Big[ Bsigma^2 + B(B-1)rhosigma^2 Big] \\ &= rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoBsigma^2 endaligned

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: the second term is the part that differs from tree to tree, and it shrinks as trees are added;

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: the first term is the shared part, and it never shrinks. With infinitely many trees, rhosigma^2 is what's left.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: The variance of an average of B trees, in units of one tree's variance. Independent trees ( rho = 0 ) keep improving; correlated trees flatten onto a floor of rhosigma^2 . The bagged trees here have rho approx 0.1 , so 200 trees (dotted) are already on the floor.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: A check with made-up guesses, each a shared part plus its own part, scaled so that sigma^2 = 1 : at rho = 0.3 , the average of 10 guesses has variance 0.377 (the formula says 0.370), and the average of 1,000 has 0.302 (formula 0.301). The floor of 0.3 holds however many you average.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: Measured on the 200 bagged trees

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: Take each tree's miss against the true chance, applicant by applicant. One tree's mean squared miss is sigma^2 = 0.0598 , and two trees' misses correlate rho = 0.105 on average:

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: beginaligned rhosigma^2 &= 0.105 times 0.0598 \\ &approx 0.0063 \\ frac1-rhoBsigma^2 &= frac0.895 times 0.0598200 \\ &approx 0.0003 endaligned

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: The two add up to 0.0065, which is exactly the bag's real gap. The useful part is what the formula says next: the bag is already at its floor. 200 trees reach 0.0065, and infinitely many would reach 0.0063. 1,000 trees would get 0.00633: 3% better for five times the compute.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: When more trees stop paying. The part more trees can still remove, as a share of the floor, is

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: frac(1-rho)\,sigma^2 / Brho\,sigma^2 = frac1-rhorho B

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: In words: with rho = 0.1 it's 9% at 100 trees and under 1% at 1,000. Once B is well past (1-rho)/rho , decorrelation matters more than more trees. There are only two ways lower:

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: make the trees less alike (a smaller rho ): the random forest's trick, next section;

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: make each tree less wobbly (a smaller sigma^2 ), for example with bigger leaves (section 06).

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: What sigma^2 and rho really are

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: The textbook meaning: fix one applicant x . Imagine redrawing the whole training set many times and bootstrapping from each. sigma^2 is how much one tree's prediction at x varies over all that, and rho is the correlation between two trees grown from the same training set. Given the training set, the bootstrap draws are independent, so all the correlation comes from sharing it.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: What was measured here: with only one training set, the numbers above are taken across applicants (each tree's vector of misses). The same algebra holds, so the match is close to bookkeeping; the useful reading is the floor.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: What the shared part holds: full-depth trees have almost no bias, so most of it here is noise in the 3,500 training labels. A bias common to every tree also sits in the shared part, and survives any amount of averaging.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: The extremes: rho = 1 gives sigma^2 : averaging identical trees does nothing (the same-rows trees of section 01, with rho approx 0.84 , came close). rho = 0 gives sigma^2/B , which goes to 0, but that needs truly independent training sets, which you never have.

chunks.h: Why correlated trees cap the gain
chunks.x: More trees make a forest repeatable, not right. Refit with a new seed and a bigger forest changes less, because a finite average sits closer to its limit. That limit can still be biased, or overfit the training set.

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: Why are bagged trees alike? Every tree sees roughly the same data, so every tree finds the same strong splits near the top: late <= 1.5 is the root of 160 of the 200 bagged trees. The top splits shape everything below them.

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: A random forest (Breiman, 2001) adds one rule. At every split, the tree may only choose among m features drawn at random (max_features), drawn fresh for that split. Sometimes the strongest feature isn't on the menu, so the tree splits on something else and grows differently from its neighbours. A given feature is on the menu with chance m/p , for p features in all. Which feature roots each of 200 trees:

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: With 2 of 4 features on offer, late roots only 90 trees, and the rest start from income or EMIs. With 1, the roots spread evenly, even onto the decoy age. The effect on the forest (200 full-depth trees; the bagging row uses fresh random draws, so its rho is 0.104 against section 04's 0.105):

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: rho drops from 0.104 to 0.075: the trees really are less alike.

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: Each tree is about as good ( sigma^2 stays near 0.059). With 3 of the 4 features useful, any menu of 2 or more holds a useful one, and even at m = 1 , where a quarter of the splits get only age, sigma^2 barely moves.

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: So the forest's gap falls by about 28%, from 0.0065 to 0.0047: the floor rhosigma^2 coming down.

chunks.h: Random forests: a fresh feature menu at every split
chunks.x: The AUC dip is small enough to be noise at this test size; the gap doesn't depend on the noisy labels.
Training rows that reach it
Bootstrap rows that reach it, weighted by how often each was drawn
m drawn at random without replacement, fresh at this node
Every midpoint between neighbouring values
The same, for the m candidates only
Biggest weighted impurity drop
Depth or leaf-size limits, often then pruning
Until pure or a leaf-size limit; no pruning
Weighted share (bootstrap counts, class weights)
Average of B leaves' values

Two details. Features that are constant in the node don't count towards m , so sklearn keeps drawing until it has tried at least one that varies. And Extra Trees (section 09) change two rows: one uniform random cut per candidate instead of every midpoint, and, by default, all rows with no bootstrap.

Per split, not per tree. A common misconception is that each tree gets one fixed feature subset. That's an older method, the random subspace method (Ho, 1998; in sklearn, BaggingClassifier with max_features below 1), and it locks a tree out of a feature everywhere: a tree that never sees late is weak all over.
A fresh draw at every node keeps every feature available somewhere in every tree while still forcing variety at each node, most importantly at the top splits that shape the whole tree.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Neither number is derived. They're the defaults of Breiman and Cutler's original code and of R's randomForest (Breiman's 2001 paper itself tried m = 1 and lfloor log_2 p rfloor + 1 ), and The Elements of Statistical Learning repeats them, along with a minimum leaf size of 1 for classification and 5 for regression. sklearn's classifier uses sqrt p , but its regressor defaults to all features, which makes RandomForestRegressor plain bagging unless you change it. The reasoning for giving regression a bigger menu:

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Classification accuracy forgives weak trees; squared error doesn't. For accuracy, only which side of 0.5 the forest's average lands on matters, so weaker, less alike trees still land it on the right side, and decorrelation buys a lot. (The argument is about accuracy, not the quality of the probabilities.) In regression, every tree's own error feeds straight into the forest's squared error (the sigma^2 in rhosigma^2 ), so a weaker tree costs more.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Regression targets are often smooth. A tree copies a smooth surface as a staircase of many small steps, which needs useful features at split after split, so every wasted split makes the staircase coarser. Class boundaries are often a few sharp cuts, which a tree finds early.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: How fast the menu shrinks: with p = 100 , sqrt p offers 10% of the features at each split, and p/3 a third.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Measured on the credit limit, which is smooth and depends on only 2 of the 4 features (300 trees, leaves of at least 5; sigma^2 and gaps in (₹ thousand)²). Here rho and sigma^2 are averages over tree pairs and trees, so the floor matches the forest's gap only to within about ±1:

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: "sqrt" halves rho but triples sigma^2 , so the floor rises and the forest gets worse.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: 1 feature: sigma^2 is ten times bagging's, and rho even climbs back up. Trees this crude all miss the same way (too flat where the limit changes fast), and a miss shared by every tree counts as correlation.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Why sigma^2 jumps here and not for default risk: only 2 of the 4 features matter. With 2 on the menu, both are missing when the pair drawn is late, age: 1 of the 6 possible pairs. In 4 of the other 5 pairs only one of the two is offered, so the tree must cut on whichever it gets, even when the other would split better. With 1, half the splits miss them.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Default risk is different: 3 of its 4 features matter, so every pair holds a useful one.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Feature sampling helps only when rho shrinks by a bigger factor than sigma^2 grows. For default risk it did; for the credit limit it didn't. That's why max_features is the first knob to tune, not a constant.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: The bootstrap already does most of the decorrelating

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Turn off both sources of randomness (no bootstrap, all features) and every tree sees the same rows and the same features, finds the same splits, and rho = 1 . On the credit limit, all 300 trees are identical: sigma^2 = 48 , a floor of 48.3, and RMSE 11.97. From there:

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: the bootstrap alone takes rho from 1 to 0.186, and sigma^2 from 48 to 56 (each tree sees only about 63% of the rows), so the floor falls from 48.3 to 10.4;

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: feature sampling at "sqrt" then takes rho only from 0.186 to 0.088, and here pushes the floor back up to 14.7.

chunks.h: Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression
chunks.x: Default risk shows the same pattern: same-rows trees correlate about 0.84, bootstrap trees 0.104, and feature sampling gets to 0.075 at best. The bootstrap moves rho so far because small changes compound down the tree. The top income cut barely shifts, but each shift changes which rows go down each branch, and deep splits are chosen from a few dozen rows, where adding or dropping a couple changes the winner. By the leaves, two bootstrap trees look quite different.

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: Add 20 pure-noise columns, so only 3 of 24 features matter. With k useful features out of p , the chance that a split's menu holds no useful feature is

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: P(no useful feature on the menu) = binomp-km Big/ binompm

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: In words: the number of menus made only of useless features, over the number of possible menus. Here p = 24 and k = 3 (100 trees, leaves of at least 5):

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: Splits with no useful feature on offer

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: The gap is worst with 1 feature (weak trees, most splits forced onto noise), best in the middle, and worse again with all 24 (alike trees). Breiman put a bound on this for a forest classifier:

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: test error le fracbarrho\,(1 - s^2)s^2

chunks.h: Too much randomness: the strength–correlation trade-off
chunks.x: In words: barrho is the average correlation between trees, and s is the trees' strength, how far on average the right class's vote share beats the best wrong class's. Less alike trees and stronger trees both lower the bound; max_features lowers barrho but also lowers s . The bound is loose, so use it for the direction of the effect, not for numbers.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: By default a forest grows every tree to full depth: it splits until the leaves are pure (often a single row), with no depth cap and no pruning. That would be reckless for a single tree. Here it's the design:

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: A division of labour. Averaging removes variance but never bias (section 03), so each tree should bring as little bias as possible, and a full-depth tree can carve out any shape. Pruning would add bias that no amount of averaging takes back.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: Deep trees decorrelate better. Deep splits are chosen from a few rows each, so they change most from one bootstrap to the next. Shallow trees agree more (a higher rho ).

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: One less thing to tune: no pruning means no validation step to pick the pruning strength.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: Shallow trees can work when the truth is shallow. Averaging 100 depth-3 trees (each on a random half of the rows) takes the gap from 0.0047 for one tree to 0.0009, because the truth is only three questions deep. On real data you don't know how deep the truth is; a deep tree has little bias for any shape, and averaging handles its variance.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: The cost of full depth is noisy probabilities. Pure leaves answer 0 or 1, so the forest needs many trees to smooth them out, and regions with no training positives get exact zeros. A minimum leaf size makes each leaf an average over several rows: each tree is less wobbly (a smaller sigma^2 ), at the price of a little bias. With 300 trees:

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: The gap falls fourfold by a leaf size of 20, and the log loss approaches the truth's 0.212. If the probability itself drives a decision (pricing a loan, an expected loss), this is the knob.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: From 200 on the gap gets worse again, and at 500 the ranking collapses too. The stressed group has 235 training applicants, but a bootstrap holds only about 0.632 times 235 approx 150 distinct ones, and min_samples_leaf counts distinct rows, not bootstrap weights. So with leaves of 200 or more no tree can give the group a leaf of its own, and its risk is averaged with its neighbours': bias.

chunks.h: Deep, unpruned trees, and when to stop earlier
chunks.x: A depth cap, or a leaf size? Capping the depth at 5 scores (0.814, 0.216, 0.0008) and at 8 (0.832, 0.215, 0.0018), which is good here only because the truth is three questions deep. In general prefer a leaf-size limit. It adapts to the data, stopping where rows run thin and letting dense regions keep splitting, while a depth cap stops every branch at the same depth whether it holds 5 rows or 5,000.

Each tree never saw about 37% of the training rows, its out-of-bag (OOB) rows. So every training row has a set of trees that never saw it: about 110 of 300. Average only those trees' predictions and you get an honest prediction for that row, made exactly as for a new applicant. Score every row that way and you have the OOB score: a validation score with no held-out set and no refitting.
beginaligned O_i &= \\, b : row i is not in bootstrap sample b \,\ \\ hat p_OOB(x_i) &= frac1|O_i| sum_b in O_i hat p_b(x_i) \\ mathbb E\,|O_i| &approx 0.368\, B endaligned
In words: O_i is the set of trees whose bag left row i out; row i 's OOB prediction averages only those trees; on average that's 37% of them.
Step by step, on a whiteboard
Five applicants, A to E. B and E defaulted; A, C and D didn't. Three trees:
B is out of two bags, so its OOB prediction is (0.2 + 0.4)/2 = 0.3 . A gets 0.1, C 0.0 and D 0.6, from one tree each.
E is in every bag, so it gets no OOB prediction at all. A row is in all B bags with chance 0.632^B : 25% with 3 trees, 1% with 10, effectively never with 300.
Score A to D. The one defaulter, B (0.3), ranks above A (0.1) and C (0.0) but below D (0.6), so the OOB AUC is 2 wins out of 3 pairs: 0.67.

tot = np.zeros(n) # per row: sum of OOB predictions cnt = np.zeros(n) # per row: trees that left it out for t, rows in zip(rf.estimators_, rf.estimators_samples_): out = np.ones(n, bool) out[rows] = False # rows it never saw tot[out] += t.predict_proba(X[out])[:, 1] cnt[out] += 1 oob = tot / cnt # = rf.oob_decision_function_[:, 1]
Why it's almost a free validation set
Estimate (300 trees, leaves of 5)
OOB, which came with the fit
5-fold cross-validation (five refits)
100,000 fresh applicants (the real answer)
The forest's own training rows (never do this)

OOB and cross-validation agree, and OOB cost nothing. Each OOB prediction comes from trees that never saw that row, just like a held-out prediction. No refit is needed, because the bootstrap already held rows out.
Why "almost": each row is scored by only about 37% of the trees, so OOB measures a smaller forest. With few trees that's noticeably worse, and some rows get no OOB trees at all.

A small pessimism with tiny leaves. When a defaulter is out of bag, the trees predicting it were trained without its default, so its neighbourhood looks slightly safer than it is; a non-defaulter's looks slightly riskier. Within a group of look-alikes, defaulters then score a bit below non-defaulters, which costs AUC. Tiny leaves are neighbourhoods of a few rows, where one missing label matters most (Janitza and Hornung, 2018). Cross-validation has the same effect.
Even at leaf size 5, OOB trails fresh data by 0.03, and part of that may be this training sample's own luck. The pessimism shows in the trend: the shortfall shrinks as the leaves grow.

Never judge a forest on its own training rows. Each training row was in the bootstrap of about 63% of the trees, which have partly memorized it. So "train 0.97, test 0.82" says nothing on its own. The OOB score is the forest's honest training-set score.

The default oob_score_ is accuracy. It reports 0.917, but always predicting "no default" gets 0.913. Score oob_decision_function_ with AUC or log loss instead. Passing oob_score=roc_auc_score doesn't help: sklearn hands the function hard 0/1 predictions.

Repeated rows. If each applicant appears three times (three loans, one profile), a row can be out of bag while its copies are in, so the tree has effectively seen it. OOB AUC 0.993; real test AUC 0.828.

Time order and drift. A bootstrap mixes months, so March's OOB prediction comes from trees that saw April. In a simulation where the late-payment effect grows every month, a forest trained on months 0–17 looks perfectly calibrated out of bag (7.6% predicted, 7.5% actual). On months 18–23 it predicts 7.3%, and 11.3% default. OOB measures how well the forest fills gaps inside the training period, not how well it forecasts.
Too few trees. With 10 trees, about 1% of rows ( 0.632^10 ) are in every bag. sklearn warns and fills them with zeros, which corrupts the score.
Tuning on OOB, then reporting it. Out of many settings you picked the one whose OOB rows happened to suit it, so its OOB score is optimistic. Keep a final test set, or use nested cross-validation.
When customers repeat or the world drifts, validate the way you'll deploy: grouped folds for repeated customers, past-to-future splits for time.
Breiman's original importance measure reuses the OOB rows. For each tree, shuffle feature j among that tree's OOB rows and measure how much the tree's error rises; then average over the trees:
VI_j = frac1B sum_b=1^B Big[ err_bbig(OOB_b,\ x_j shuffledbig) - err_bbig(OOB_bbig) Big]

In words: every tree is scored only on rows it never saw, so a feature it used only to memorize training rows earns nothing. R's randomForest reports it (importance=TRUE, "mean decrease in accuracy"). sklearn doesn't; its permutation_importance applies the same idea to the whole forest, on any held-out set you pass (section 10). For regression forests, oob_prediction_ holds the OOB predictions and oob_score_ is their R^2 .
Read every knob through the forest's expected error at a point:
beginaligned error &= bias^2 + forest variance + noise \\ forest variance &= rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoB\,sigma^2 endaligned
In words: the forest's bias is one tree's bias (section 03), sigma^2 is one tree's variance, and rho is how alike two trees are. Each knob moves some of them:
max_features ("sqrt"; regressor 1.0), down
Up (a lot if few useful features)
min_samples_leaf (1) up, or max_depth (none) down
Second; key for probabilities
Up sharply (1 with all features)
max_samples (all rows), down
class_weight (none), "balanced"
Rarely; recalibrate after

Smoother trees agree more, which is why bigger leaves usually raise rho ; with class weights, a few heavy rows decide each leaf, which raises sigma^2 . max_features is covered in section 05, and leaf size and depth in section 06. The rest are below.
Fit 500 trees (leaves of 5) once, then score the forest made of the first k trees:

Why it can't overfit: adding a tree doesn't make any tree more complex. It only brings the average closer to its limit, the expected prediction over all possible bootstraps and feature draws, which is fixed once the data and the other settings are. So the error falls towards the floor and stays there; wiggles like 0.821 at 25 trees and 0.816 at 50 are noise.
Returns diminish like 1/B : fast over the first 10 trees, flat by about 100–200.
Probabilities need more trees than ranking. AUC settles by 25–100 trees; log loss needs about 200 to smooth out the last exact zeros.
A forest can still overfit, through tree size (leaves too small for noisy data), not tree count. More trees make it repeatable, not right.
Boosting is different: each new tree fits the previous trees' mistakes, so too many rounds do overfit and need early stopping.
warm_start=True keeps the trees already grown when you raise n_estimators and refit, so a forest can be grown in steps until the OOB score flattens.
Off, with all features: every tree is the same tree ( rho = 1 ), so the forest is one tree at many times the cost.

Off, with max_features below p : the feature draws are the only randomness. Each tree sees every row, so it's slightly stronger, but trees are more alike. Extra Trees default to this, and their random thresholds supply the missing variety.
Off means no OOB score, since no row is ever left out.

Each tree's bootstrap draws a fraction f of the n rows, so it sees about 1 - e^-f of the distinct rows: 26% at f = 0.3 , leaving 74% out of bag. The trees are smaller, weaker, less alike and faster to grow. With full-depth trees it improved the gap from 0.0052 to 0.0024 here (AUC 0.83, log loss 0.22). It's a cheap regularizer on big data, and it keeps each tree's cost fixed as the data grows. It only applies when bootstrap=True.

class_weight="balanced" weights each row of class c by n/(2 n_c) , so the two classes weigh the same in total. Here each of the 304 defaulters counts 5.76, and each of the 3,196 others 0.55. The weights act at fit time, in two places:

The splits: every candidate split is scored with weighted Gini, so the weights change which splits win. In a "balanced_subsample" forest (300 trees, leaves of 5), 13% of the trees choose a different root split than without weights, and the trees grow bigger (85,596 nodes against 79,646).
The leaf values: a leaf stores the weighted share of defaulters. A test applicant who lands there reads back that stored number; predict_proba takes no weights.
A real leaf from a weighted depth-2 tree holds 476 non-defaulters and 119 defaulters, a plain share of 0.20. It stores
beginaligned fracw_1 n_1w_1 n_1 + w_0 n_0 &= frac5.76 times 1195.76 times 119 + 0.55 times 476 \\ &approx 0.724 endaligned
In words: weighting multiplies the leaf's odds by the weight ratio w_1/w_0 approx 10.5 :
beginaligned plain odds &= 119/476 \\ &= 0.25 \\ weighted odds &= 0.25 times 10.5 \\ &approx 2.63 \\ stored probability &= 2.63/3.63 \\ &approx 0.724 endaligned
That's exactly the value the weighted log loss would choose for the leaf.

Across a whole forest ("balanced_subsample", 300 trees, leaves of 5), the ranking survives: AUC 0.823 against 0.824, and the two forests' orderings correlate 0.96. The level doesn't: the mean prediction is 0.17 against a real default rate of 0.087, and the gap rises from 0.0026 to 0.0188.

Heavier defaulters push every mixed leaf's share up together, so the leaves keep their order. The mean only doubles, rather than rising tenfold, because most leaves are pure non-default, and odds of 0 stay 0 at any weight.
Use class weights only if you'll recalibrate or need only a ranking. "balanced" computes the weights once on the whole training set; "balanced_subsample" recomputes them on each tree's bootstrap.
Other settings, and a tuning order
min_samples_split, max_leaf_nodes, min_impurity_decrease and ccp_alpha are other ways to stop trees earlier; leaf size is the most direct.
criterion (Gini, entropy or log loss) rarely changes much.

n_jobs=-1 trains and predicts trees in parallel on all cores (for a single-row prediction, starting threads can cost more than it saves), and random_state fixes the bootstraps and feature draws, so results repeat.

A tuning order that works: max_features over "sqrt", 0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 1.0, then min_samples_leaf over 1, 5, 20, 50, judged on OOB or cross-validation with the metric you actually care about. Then set n_estimators just high enough that the score stops moving. The defaults are already strong, so gains are usually modest.

Extremely randomized trees (Extra Trees; Geurts, Ernst and Wehenkel, 2006) push the randomness one step further. At each split a random forest searches every threshold of each candidate feature. Extra Trees draw one random threshold per candidate feature, uniformly between that feature's smallest and largest value in the node, and keep the best of those random cuts. sklearn's version also skips the bootstrap by default, so every tree sees every row.
The root split, with one random cut drawn on each feature and scored by Gini gain (the drop in impurity):
The searched best: late, at 1.5

Every random cut is far weaker than the searched one, so this Extra Tree's root is emi <= 0.23. Each Extra Tree is cruder: more bias. But its steps sit at random places, so averaging 300 of them blurs the steps into a gentle slope, like stacking staircases whose steps are offset. A smoother average also moves less between training sets (less variance), and with no sort-and-scan, training is faster.
Default risk: AUC, log loss, gap
Credit limit: test RMSE (noise floor 10)
Nodes in all 300 trees (default risk)
Sharp steps: a tie. Default risk is made of sharp cut-offs (income 40, EMI 0.5), which a searched split lands on exactly and random cuts only approximate.

Smooth target: Extra Trees edge ahead. The noise alone has a standard deviation of 10, so both are close to the floor and the margin is small. (Both regressors use all features by default, so this is bagged trees against Extra Trees.) A single tree tuned to depth 6 gets 12.5.
The bigger trees come from seeing every row, not from the random cuts: with the bootstrap on, Extra Trees shrink to 86,124 nodes, with the same scores.
Speed: about twice as fast on one core here. The saving grows with the rows, since a full search sorts each candidate's values at every node.

When it helps: smooth targets, noisy data where extra smoothing pays, and large data where training time matters. When it doesn't: the truth has sharp thresholds, such as policy cut-offs, that a search finds exactly. It's cheap to try both.
Two common ways to ask which features the forest relies on:

Impurity importance (MDI, mean decrease in impurity; sklearn's feature_importances_): credit every split's impurity drop to the feature it used, and add up over all splits in all trees. It comes free with the fit, but it's measured on the training rows.
Permutation importance: on held-out data, shuffle one column, which breaks its link with the target while keeping its values, and measure how much the score drops.
Impurity importance, by hand

A node with n_t rows, d of them defaulters, has Gini impurity G = 2q(1-q) , where q = d/n_t . Its total impurity is rows times Gini, which works out to 2d(n_t - d)/n_t . A split's weighted drop, as a share of all n training rows, is
Delta_t = fracn_t G_t - n_L G_L - n_R G_Rn
In words: the node's total impurity minus its two children's, over the training rows. Deep splits count little, because they hold few rows. A depth-2 tree on the 3,500 training rows:
Rows (defaulters): node → children
Total impurity: node − children

Add up per feature: late has 0.0120 and income 0.0083 + 0.0015 = 0.0098 . Scaled to sum to 1, that's late 0.55 and income 0.45. A forest does this in every tree, on that tree's bootstrap sample, scales each tree's totals to sum to 1, and averages over the trees.
Why impurity importance is biased

On the full forest (300 trees, leaves of 5) MDI gives income 0.341, emi 0.321, late 0.158 and age 0.180. The decoy age outranks late, which adds 25 points to the chance of default and makes the best first split of all. Why:
age offers a cut between every pair of neighbouring values, while late (0, 1, 2, …) offers only two or three, so in every node age holds many more lottery tickets;
