deep in a tree, a node holds a handful of training rows, and among many candidate cuts one usually separates them a little better, by chance;
MDI adds up these tiny, training-only gains over tens of thousands of deep splits.

So MDI favours features with many distinct values (continuous or high-cardinality), signal or not, and it rewards overfit splits most when the trees are deepest. Add a random applicant ID and a pure-noise column to make it obvious:
Permutation (test AUC drop)
MDI hands a third of the credit to three columns with no information. Permutation importance gives all three about zero (±0.01 is the noise level here).
Fixes for MDI exist, such as computing it on OOB rows, or forests with unbiased split selection (conditional inference forests), but the usual answer is permutation importance on held-out data.

A real application number is worse than a random ID: it usually rises with time, so it can encode when someone applied and leak information about the outcome, and then it looks important under every measure.

base = auc(y_te, rf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]) for j in range(p): Xs = X_te.copy() Xs[:, j] = rng.permutation(Xs[:, j]) # break column j p_j = rf.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1] imp[j] = base - auc(y_te, p_j) # repeat, average

On the four features, averaged over 10 shuffles: income 0.159, emi 0.093, late 0.127, age −0.002. Shuffling age costs nothing, because the forest doesn't need it for new applicants. Three choices change the answer:

Which data. On the training rows, age, the ID and the noise column each get about 0.02. The forest used them to memorize training rows, and shuffling breaks the memorized leaves, so importance on training data measures memorization too.

Which metric. With accuracy, the importances collapse: income 0.034, emi 0.026, late 0.003, age 0.003. Only 52 of the 1,500 applicants are called defaulters, and accuracy changes only when a prediction crosses 0.5. For most applicants two late payments lift the chance only to 0.28, below 0.5; only for the 11 stressed-and-late test applicants do they push it past 0.5 (from 0.48 to 0.73). So by accuracy late looks nearly useless.
Which segment. A feature can matter in one month or segment and not in another.
Correlated features split the credit
Add income2, a near-copy of income (correlation 0.997), as if reported on a second document. (The what-if in section 13 uses an exact copy.)
Drop-column (refit without it)
MDI splits income's credit between the copies (0.22 and 0.19), so each looks less important than income did alone (0.34).

Permutation is fooled worse. The trees split on both copies, so shuffling one breaks only the splits that used it; the splits on the other still work, the score drops only partly, and neither looks important (0.05 and 0.02, against 0.16 for income alone). It also scores the model on applicants who can't exist, say ₹20k on one document and ₹140k on the other.

Drop-column asks "what does this feature add, given the others?", which is the wrong question for twins: drop either one and the other takes over, so neither seems to matter. It's also noisy (every refit has its own randomness) and costs a refit per feature.

The fix is to shuffle the group together. Permuting both copies with the same row order drops AUC by 0.186: income matters after all. Conditional permutation shuffles a feature only among rows with similar values of its partners, which avoids impossible inputs, at more setup cost.
SHAP splits one prediction among the features. For applicant x :
f(x) = phi_0 + sum_j=1^p phi_j(x)

In words: phi_0 is the average prediction, and phi_j(x) is feature j 's share of how far this applicant sits from it. The shares are Shapley values from game theory: each feature's average marginal contribution over all orders in which features could be added.
TreeSHAP computes them exactly for trees, in polynomial time, and a forest's SHAP values are the average of its trees' (Shapley values are linear in the model).
Uses: per-applicant reasons (reason codes for a declined loan), and a global importance as the average of |phi_j| .

The same trap with correlated features: the default tree-path version follows the training data's correlations and can credit a feature the model barely uses; the interventional version breaks the correlations and evaluates impossible inputs, as permutation does.

Which output is explained: for a forest, TreeSHAP explains the averaged probability directly (log-odds aren't additive across averaged trees); for a booster, the raw log-odds score is the natural additive scale.
Which way does a feature push?

Importance gives a size, never a direction. Partial dependence plots the average prediction as one feature is swept across its range, with the other features kept at their observed values. ICE curves draw the same sweep for each applicant separately, so interactions show up as curves that aren't parallel. Both evaluate impossible inputs when features are correlated (sweeping income while its twin stays put). ALE (accumulated local effects) avoids that by averaging only small, local changes among similar rows.
Importance is not causation

Importance says what the model's predictions lean on, not what changing a feature would do in the world. Replace income with a phone price that tracks income but causes nothing. Its permutation importance is 0.129, close to late's, because it stands in for income.

Ask the model what happens if the 91 stressed test applicants each get a ₹150k phone, and it says their risk falls from 0.39 to 0.05. Their true risk stays 0.51, since the truth never uses the phone. The common ways this goes wrong:
A proxy: a confounder (income) drives both the feature (phone price) and the outcome.
A reversed arrow: collection calls predict default because calls follow missed payments.
Side effects: cutting an EMI by restructuring also stretches the loan's term and flags the borrower as distressed.

A causal answer needs an experiment, or a quasi-experiment such as difference-in-differences or a regression discontinuity at a score cut-off. And a single feature that dwarfs all the others is a reason to check for leakage first: something recorded after the outcome, or a proxy for the label.

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: Unroll the average. Each tree's leaf value is a (bootstrap-weighted) average of the training targets in that leaf, so the forest's prediction is a weighted average of training targets:

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: beginaligned hat f(x) &= sum_i=1^n w_i(x)\, y_i \\ w_i(x) &= frac1B sum_b=1^B fracc_bi\, mathbf 1[x_i in L_b(x)]sum_j c_bj\, mathbf 1[x_j in L_b(x)] endaligned

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: In words: L_b(x) is the leaf of tree b that x falls into, and c_bi is how many times row i was drawn into tree b 's sample. A training row gets weight when it shares a leaf with x , and more weight the more trees it shares one in. The weights are never negative and sum to 1.

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: So a forest is an adaptive nearest-neighbour method (Lin and Jeon, 2006): "near" means "lands in the same leaves", which stretches along features that don't matter and tightens along those that do. Three behaviours follow:

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: a prediction can never leave the range of the training targets (no extrapolation);

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: a probability reaches 1 only if every row with weight is a positive (the squeeze, below);

chunks.h: A forest is a weighted nearest-neighbour average
chunks.x: the share of trees in which two rows land in the same leaf is Breiman's proximity, used for clustering, outlier scores and imputing missing values.
Predict the credit limit at EMIs of 20% for incomes beyond the training range, which stops at ₹150k:

Past the data, every tree routes the applicant to its edge leaf, so the forest repeats its edge value. Any trend beyond the training range, including a time trend, is invisible. Remedies: model a ratio or a detrended target, add a linear model for the trend, or use trees with a linear model in each leaf. Boosted trees have the same limit.

Each true-risk group's average forest prediction (300 trees, leaves of 5) against its true chance. The middle groups sit on the diagonal; the riskiest, rarest group is pulled down to 0.659, and no applicant scores above 0.753.

Near the edges, variance turns into one-sided error. A probability can't go above 1 or below 0. For an applicant whose true chance is near 1, any tree that errs can only err downwards, so the average is pulled down; near 0 it's pulled up. The bootstrap and feature sampling add exactly this tree-to-tree variance, which gives random forests their typical S-shaped reliability curve: too low at the top, too high at the bottom (Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005).

Rare extreme groups share leaves with milder neighbours. Only about 22 training applicants are in the 0.73 group, so many of their leaves mix in lower-risk rows. Bigger leaves make this worse; smaller leaves make the probabilities noisy instead.

In this data, 0.73 isn't that close to 1, so the top group's shortfall likely comes mostly from the second cause. The 0.03 group stays on the line: most of its leaves are pure, so many trees agree on a near-zero answer.

Two exceptions run the other way. In a region with no training positives, every tree can say exactly 0 (the 5 defaulters of section 03). And on its own training rows a forest is overconfident, since each row sits in about 63% of the trees.

The fix is to calibrate on held-out data: Platt scaling (a sigmoid fitted to the scores) or isotonic regression (a monotone step fit, which needs more data), for example with CalibratedClassifierCV. OOB predictions can serve as the held-out scores, with the caveat that each comes from only about 37% of the trees. Boosters trained on log loss usually start out closer to calibrated.

A forest has no built-in handling of imbalance; it just sees few positives. Scale the true chance down so that about 1% default: 37 training defaulters, so each tree sees about 23 distinct ones and most leaves hold none. Four in ten test applicants get exactly 0 from every tree, and with 10 test defaulters, the test AUC wobbles by about ±0.09. The options, roughly in order:
Leave the training alone and move the threshold. Ranking is what a forest does well; choose the cut-off from the costs or from how many cases can be reviewed.
Use bigger leaves, so rare positives aren't isolated in one-row leaves and most probabilities aren't exact zeros.
Judge it properly: PR-AUC or log loss, with a confidence interval; never OOB accuracy.

Reweight or rebalance: class_weight="balanced_subsample", or a balanced random forest, where each bootstrap draws equal numbers from each class by undersampling the majority (BalancedRandomForestClassifier in imbalanced-learn). Both change the splits and inflate the probabilities (section 08), so recalibrate afterwards. Dividing a leaf's odds by w_1/w_0 undoes the weighting exactly for one tree, and only roughly for the forest's average.
Get more positives, for example from a longer time window. That beats all of the above.

Outliers in a feature barely matter. A split depends only on the order of the values, so an extreme income just sits at the end of the sorted list; it can't pull a coefficient. Any monotone transform (log, rank, scaling) leaves the searched splits unchanged. Extra Trees and Isolation Forest are different: they draw cuts uniformly over a feature's range, so a log transform does change them.

Outliers in a regression target matter locally. A leaf predicts the mean of its rows, so one huge target pulls its leaf's value in the roughly 63% of trees that drew it, and averaging with the other trees dilutes it. Clip or transform the target, or use criterion="absolute_error", which is much slower.

Label noise is tolerated well. Deep trees memorize noisy labels, but different trees memorize different subsets, and averaging washes them out. Boosting, by contrast, keeps fitting the rows it gets wrong, which are disproportionately the mislabelled ones. That's worst for AdaBoost's exponential loss; gradient boosting with log loss, shrinkage, subsampling and early stopping suffers much less.
Many noise features hurt through the menu. At "sqrt", with 3 useful features out of 24, 56% of splits have no useful feature on offer (section 05). Remove junk features, or raise max_features.

chunks.h: Missing values, scaling, categories and constraints
chunks.x: Missing values: recent scikit-learn (1.4 and later, for random forests) accepts NaN directly. At each candidate split, the tree tries sending all the missing rows left and then right, and keeps whichever gives the bigger impurity drop. At prediction, missing values follow the learned side; if a node saw no missing values for that feature in training, they go to the child that held more rows.

chunks.h: Missing values, scaling, categories and constraints
chunks.x: Older routes for missing values: impute (a median plus a "was missing" indicator, which lets the trees learn from missingness itself), CART's surrogate splits (R's rpart), or Breiman's proximity-based imputation.

chunks.h: Missing values, scaling, categories and constraints
chunks.x: No scaling needed: searched splits are unchanged by any monotone rescaling.

chunks.h: Missing values, scaling, categories and constraints
chunks.x: Categories: sklearn's forests need numbers. One-hot encoding spreads a category over many sparse columns, each rarely on the menu and each a weak split, so ordinal or target encoding often works better for trees (fit a target encoding out of fold, or it leaks). R's randomForest splits categorical factors natively.

chunks.h: Missing values, scaling, categories and constraints
chunks.x: Monotone constraints: when risk must rise with late payments, recent scikit-learn forests accept monotonic_cst (1.4 and later), which forces each tree's predictions to move one way along that feature. Boosters have the same option.

Size: a full-depth tree has at most about one leaf per distinct in-bag row, so up to about 2 times 0.632\, n nodes, and the forest multiplies that by B . Here 300 trees with leaves of 5 hold 79,646 nodes, against 15 for one depth-3 tree. The size grows with the data, because deep trees grow more leaves.
Prediction cost: each row walks B root-to-leaf paths, so about B times depth comparisons, and deep unbalanced trees can run 20–40 levels.

Training cost: per tree, roughly (features tried per split) × (rows) × (depth), plus sorting, with trees spread over cores. max_samples cuts the rows per tree, a smaller max_features cuts the features tried, and Extra Trees skip the sort.

To shrink a forest: use fewer trees (the curve is flat after 100–200), bigger leaves or a depth cap, or switch to a booster with a few hundred shallow trees. Check that the scores don't shift when you shrink it.
Deep: low bias, high variance
Shallow: high bias, low variance
In sequence; each fits the current errors (gradients), scaled by a learning rate
Bias, one small correction at a time
Never overfit; the score plateaus
Eventually overfit; needs early stopping
Defaults near-best; tune max_features and leaf size
Learning rate, rounds, depth and regularization interact
More exposed: later trees focus on rows still wrong (worst for AdaBoost)
Sequential across rounds (parallel within a tree)
Hundreds of deep trees: big, slower
Shallow trees: smaller, faster
Squeezed toward the middle
Usually closer to calibrated, with log loss
Only with row subsampling; usually a validation set

Why the split of labour. A forest starts from trees that are already flexible enough (low bias) and spends its effort removing their variance. Boosting starts from weak trees (high bias, little variance) and spends its effort removing bias. Its variance creeps up as rounds are added, which is why it needs a learning rate and early stopping.
Tuned boosting usually wins on tabular data, especially with lots of it, and gives smaller, faster models. A forest can win when:
the data is small or noisy: boosting is more exposed to label noise, while a forest averages it;
there's little time to tune: a forest's defaults are close to its best, a booster's aren't;
the validation set is too small for early stopping to pick the number of rounds reliably.

To show which cause is at work, compare the two with repeated cross-validation on the same folds (a paired comparison), and plot learning curves: if the booster pulls ahead as the data grows, small data was the reason. Adding label noise on purpose and watching which model degrades faster is another telling experiment.

It's plain bagging. Every split sees every feature, so the trees share the same strong top splits and are the most alike ( rho 0.104, against 0.075 at one feature). It's sklearn's regressor default, and the right choice when few features are useful and the target is smooth: it beat "sqrt" on the credit limit.

Each split's feature is drawn at random, and the tree only chooses the threshold. The trees are as different as they can be, and individually weak. With 3 of 4 features useful it had the best gap (0.0047). With 20 noise columns it was the worst (gap 0.0106), since 88% of splits had no useful feature on offer. On the smooth credit limit it was disastrous (RMSE 13.32 against 10.18).

A forest of stumps is an average of one-question rules: an additive model with no interactions. It ranks better than one stump (AUC from 0.65 to 0.78 when bagged), but it can never express "EMIs high and income low", and averaging can't remove that bias.

With max_features below p , the stumps are also forced onto weaker questions. In boosting, each new stump fixes what the previous ones missed, so their sum does reduce bias, but only within additive shapes: it still can't express an AND. A booster needs trees of depth 2 or more for interactions, since tree depth sets the interaction order.

In bagging it roots most trees (160 of 200 here), so the trees are alike and the other features barely shape them. With m of p features on the menu it's missing from a share 1 - m/p of menus, so other features get to root trees (it rooted 90 of 200 at m = 2 ), and the trees' mistakes differ more. Check a dominant feature for leakage before celebrating.
…you add many noise features?
More splits get no useful feature on offer (section 05), so the trees weaken and deep splits chase noise.
MDI hands the noise columns real importance; permutation importance on held-out data doesn't.
The fix: drop junk features (judged by permutation importance), or raise max_features.
…there are very few trees?
The (1-rho)sigma^2/B term is still large: 10 trees score log loss 0.479, against 0.223 for 500.
With pure leaves every prediction is a multiple of 1/B , and many positives get an exact 0 from every tree, so the log loss explodes (0.988 for 10 bagged full-depth trees).
OOB breaks: about 0.632^10 , or 1%, of the rows are in every bag and get no OOB prediction.
…two features are near-duplicates?
Accuracy barely changes: the information is still there.
The forest leans on that information more. It gets two tickets in the menu lottery. With p = 5 and m = 2 , a single feature is on a menu with chance 0.4, but at least one of two copies is:
beginaligned P(a copy is on the menu) &= 1 - binom32 Big/ binom52 \\ &= 0.7 endaligned

The importance splits. For an exact copy, the two give identical splits that tie, and the tree takes whichever copy it meets first in its random feature order. So MDI splits about evenly (0.196 and 0.199, against 0.341 for income alone), permutation gives each 0.03 against 0.16, and drop-column about 0.01 each. (Section 10's near-copy split a little less evenly.) Permute the pair as a group.
…every tree gets the same rows, and only the seed changes?

The trees differ only where the seed breaks ties between equally good splits (or, with max_features below p , in their feature draws). With all features, 10 such trees disagree on 4% of applicants and correlate 0.84, so averaging barely helps.
…the data has duplicated rows or repeated customers?
Each duplicate acts as extra weight, and an out-of-bag copy whose twin is in the bag isn't unseen: OOB says 0.993 when the real test AUC is 0.828. Deduplicate, or validate with grouped folds.

A bootstrap holds only about 150 distinct stressed applicants, and min_samples_leaf counts distinct rows, so leaves of 200 or more can't isolate the group. The gap is already worse at 200 (0.0062), and at 500 AUC falls to 0.747 and the gap rises to 0.0143. Bias wins.
…prediction must take a few milliseconds?
Use fewer trees (the curve is flat after 100–200), bigger leaves, or a booster with a few hundred shallow trees, and check that the scores don't shift.
…you need an uncertainty for one prediction?

The spread of the trees' predictions shows how much they disagree, but it isn't a calibrated interval. The trees share one training set ( rho > 0 ), so their spread understates how much a new training set would move the answer, and for a regression target it ignores the outcome's own noise. Use quantile regression forests, or conformal prediction, which sets the interval's width from the model's errors on held-out rows.
For the variance of the forest's prediction itself, the infinitesimal jackknife (Wager, Hastie and Efron, 2014) estimates it from the trees' bootstrap counts.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Trees can find odd points with no labels at all. Keep cutting a cloud of points with random cuts (a random feature, a random threshold between its min and max) until one particular point is alone.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: A point far out on its own is isolated in a few cuts; a point in the crowded middle needs many. Average the number of cuts, the path length, over many random trees: a short average path means an outlier. That's Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting and Zhou, 2008), a common first screen for odd transactions.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: In one dimension, by hand. Take payments of ₹1k, ₹2k, ₹3k, ₹4k and ₹20k. The first cut falls uniformly between 1 and 20, and it isolates ₹20k whenever it lands between 4 and 20: a chance of 16/19, about 0.84. ₹3k can never be alone after one cut, because it needs a cut on each side. Averaged over 10,000 random trees:

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Average cuts to isolate it

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: ₹20k needs one cut with chance 16/19, and about 2.1 cuts when the first cut falls below 4 (chance 3/19):

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: beginaligned mathbb E[cuts for ₹20k] &approx tfrac1619 times 1 + tfrac319 times 2.1 \\ &approx 1.17 endaligned

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: In two dimensions, the most central of 1,000 ordinary points needs about 18.5 cuts, and a planted outlier five standard deviations out needs about 4.6.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: sklearn grows each tree on a random subsample of 256 points, caps its depth at lceil log_2 256 rceil = 8 , and turns the average path into a score:

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: beginaligned s(x) &= 2^-mathbb E[h(x)] / c(psi) \\ c(psi) &= 2H(psi - 1) - frac2(psi - 1)psi endaligned

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: In words: mathbb E[h(x)] is the average path length, psi the subsample size, and H(i) approx ln i + 0.5772 . c(psi) , about 10.2 for 256 points, is the typical path length in a random tree of psi points. So s is near 1 for points isolated much faster than typical, and 0.5 or below for ordinary ones. (sklearn's score_samples returns -s , so lower means odder.)

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: When a branch stops at the depth cap with k points still together, sklearn adds c(k) to the path length, the average number of extra cuts those points would have needed, so a point in a crowded leaf still gets a long path.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: contamination only sets the flagging threshold for predict; the scores and the ranking don't change. In practice, rank by score and flag as many as you can review.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Masking: a tight cluster of anomalies, such as a fraud ring of 50 points, shields itself, since its points aren't alone. Smaller subsamples help, because each tree then holds only a few of the ring: the ring's median rank (1 = oddest) goes from 82 with every row in every tree, to 49.5 at 256, to 26.5 at 64. The opposite error, swamping, flags normal points that sit near a big group of anomalies; small subsamples help there too.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Odd isn't fraud: a large honest purchase is odd too. Use the score as a review queue, or as one feature of a supervised model once labels exist.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Features: no scaling is needed, since each cut falls within its own feature's range, but log a heavy-tailed feature like amount first: uniform cuts over a long tail mostly land in its empty stretch, so every large value looks isolated. Irrelevant features dilute the signal: with 5 noise columns added, the five planted outliers rank 2, 11, 19, 45 and 65 instead of 1 to 5.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Other tree families to recognize by name:

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Quantile regression forests keep all the training targets in each leaf, not just their mean, which gives a whole predicted distribution: quantiles and intervals.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Survival forests handle time-to-event targets with censoring ("hasn't defaulted yet").

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Causal forests estimate how much a treatment changes the outcome for each kind of person, tau(x) = mathbb E[Y(1) - Y(0) mid X = x] . "Honest" versions use separate rows to choose the splits and to estimate the effects. They still need randomized or unconfounded data.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: BART (Bayesian additive regression trees) is a sum of small trees fitted by Bayesian sampling, which gives uncertainty intervals.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: Model trees put a small linear model in each leaf: smoother fits, and a little extrapolation.

chunks.h: Isolation Forest, and other tree families
chunks.x: RuleFit turns tree paths into if-then rules and keeps a few of them with a lasso.
Training, with a fresh feature draw at every node

def fit_forest(X, y, B, m, min_leaf): n, p = X.shape forest = [] for b in range(B): c = bootstrap_counts(n) # row i drawn c[i] times rows = where(c > 0) forest.append((grow(rows, c), c)) return forest def grow(rows, c): if pure(rows) or len(rows) < 2 * min_leaf: return Leaf(weighted_class_shares(rows, c)) # m features, no replacement, fresh at EVERY node # (sklearn: constant features don't count to m) feats = sample(range(p), m) best = None for f in feats: vals = unique_sorted(X[rows, f]) for t in midpoints(vals): L = rows[X[rows, f] <= t] R = rows[X[rows, f] > t] if min(len(L), len(R)) < min_

imp is the impurity (Gini for classes, squared error for numbers) computed with the bootstrap counts as weights, and wt is a set's total weight. For Extra Trees, replace the loop over midpoints with one uniform random cut between the feature's min and max in the node, and skip the bootstrap.

def oob_predictions(forest, X): total = zeros(n) count = zeros(n) for tree, c in forest: for i in where(c == 0): # tree's OOB rows total[i] += predict_tree(tree, X[i]) count[i] += 1 ok = count > 0 # in every bag: none return total[ok] / count[ok], ok p_oob, ok = oob_predictions(forest, X) oob_score = auc(y[ok], p_oob) # not accuracy

# X, y: held-out rows; score: higher is better (AUC) def perm_importance(model, X, y, score, k=10): base = score(y, model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]) imp = zeros(X.shape[1]) for j in range(X.shape[1]): # or a group drops = [] for _ in range(k): Xs = X.copy() Xs[:, j] = shuffle(Xs[:, j]) p_s = model.predict_proba(Xs)[:, 1] drops.append(base - score(y, p_s)) imp[j] = mean(drops) return imp

Answer out loud first, then open the answer. The numbers come from the running example: 3,500 training and 1,500 test loan applicants. Default risk is the classification target (four true levels: 0.03, 0.28, 0.48 and 0.73), the credit limit is a smooth regression target, and the gap is the mean squared distance between predicted and true default probability (0 is perfect).
1Why does a random forest reduce variance, and why not bias?
Averaging B trees keeps one tree's expected prediction, and so its bias, while cancelling the part of their errors the trees don't share.
beginaligned mathbb E[bar f(x)] &= mathbb E[f_1(x)] \\ Var(bar f) &= rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoB\,sigma^2 endaligned

In words: every tree is grown the same way on an equally random sample, so they share one expected prediction, and the average of equal expectations is that same expectation. The variance falls, but only down to the shared part rhosigma^2 .

Mechanism: a full-depth tree has low bias but high variance; its leaves memorize the rows it saw. Trees on different bootstrap samples are wrong in different places, and averaging cancels those parts. Here one tree's gap of 0.066 falls to 0.006 for 100 averaged trees.

Why not bias: a mistake every tree makes survives the average. Bagging logistic regression changed nothing (gap 0.0105 before and after), and bagging stumps improved ranking but kept the gap, since no mix of one-question rules can express an AND.
Why not a full 1/B : the trees share one training set, so rho > 0 .
Follow-up: so use low-bias base learners (deep trees), and once B is large enough, lower rho (feature sampling) or sigma^2 (bigger leaves) instead of adding trees. (03, 04)
2What is a bootstrap sample, and why does it hold about 63% of the rows?
n rows drawn from the n training rows with replacement. A row is missed by all n draws with chance (1 - 1/n)^n , which tends to 1/e approx 0.368 .
beginaligned P(in the sample) &= 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n \\ &to 1 - 1/e \\ &approx 0.632 endaligned
In words: each draw misses a given row with chance 1 - 1/n , the draws are independent, so the chances multiply.
Counts: a row's count is Poisson with mean 1, so 37% of rows are left out, 37% drawn once, 18% twice, 6% three times. A bootstrap is a random reweighting, and sklearn implements it as sample weights.
Why with replacement: drawing all n rows without replacement gives every tree the same data. Replacement varies which rows a tree sees and how much each counts.
The left-out 37% are the tree's out-of-bag rows, which give the OOB score.

Follow-ups: with max_samples a fraction f , a row is in with chance about 1 - e^-f (26% at 0.3). Subsampling without replacement ( k < n rows) works about as well. Duplicate rows in the data break the "unseen" logic. (02)
3Derive the variance of an average of B correlated trees. What does it imply?
rhosigma^2 + (1-rho)sigma^2/B . More trees remove only the second term; the shared part rhosigma^2 is a floor.
beginaligned VarBig(frac1B sum_b f_bBig) &= frac1B^2 Big[ Bsigma^2 + B(B-1)rhosigma^2 Big] \\ &= rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoB\,sigma^2 endaligned
In words: the variance of a sum is the sum of all pairwise covariances: B variances sigma^2 , plus B(B-1) covariances rhosigma^2 . Dividing by B^2 gives the two terms.
The floor: as B grows, the second term vanishes. The removable part as a share of the floor is (1-rho)/(rho B) : with rho = 0.1 , 9% at 100 trees and under 1% at 1,000.

Measured: 200 bagged trees here had sigma^2 = 0.0598 and rho = 0.105 , so a floor of 0.0063 and a total of 0.0065, matching the bag's real gap. 1,000 trees would be 3% better for five times the compute.
Why rho > 0 : given the training set, bootstrap draws are independent, so all the correlation comes from sharing that training set.
Implication: past a point, decorrelation (max_features, max_samples) or steadier trees (leaf size) matter more than more trees. (04)
4Why random feature subsets, and why at every split rather than per tree?
Bagged trees all find the same strong top splits, so they're alike. A fresh random menu at every split forces different trees, which lowers rho and so the floor rhosigma^2 .

Mechanism: a feature is on a split's menu with chance m/p . Here late rooted 160 of 200 bagged trees, but only 90 with 2 of 4 features on offer; rho fell from 0.104 to 0.075 and the gap from 0.0065 to 0.0047.

Why per split: one subset per tree (the random subspace method) locks a tree out of a feature everywhere, so a tree without the key feature is weak all over. A fresh draw at every node keeps every feature available somewhere in every tree, while still forcing variety at each node, especially at the top splits that shape the rest.
Detail: features that are constant in the node don't count towards m , so sklearn keeps drawing until it has tried one that varies.
Trade-off: each tree is weaker ( sigma^2 rises), so it helps only if rho falls faster. On the smooth credit limit it didn't. (05)
5What does max_features do to bias, variance and correlation?

Fewer features on the menu lowers the trees' correlation rho , raises each tree's variance sigma^2 , and adds a little bias, a lot when useful features are rare. The forest improves only if rhosigma^2 falls.
beginaligned forest variance &= rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoB\,sigma^2 \\ P(no useful feature on the menu) &= binomp-km Big/ binompm endaligned
In words: rho and sigma^2 move in opposite directions, so what counts is their product. The second line is how often a split is forced onto useless features, with k useful features out of p .
Bias: a split forced onto a useless feature wastes rows, leaving fewer for the useful splits below, so the fit gets coarser. The forest inherits one tree's bias.
When it helps: default risk (3 of 4 features useful): rho 0.104 to 0.075 at the same sigma^2 .

When it hurts: the credit limit (2 of 4 useful, smooth): "sqrt" halves rho but triples sigma^2 , so the floor rhosigma^2 rises from 10.4 to 14.7 (₹ thousand)². With 20 noise columns, one feature per split leaves 88% of splits with nothing useful on offer.
Extremes: m = p is bagging (the most alike trees); m = 1 chooses features at random (the weakest trees).
Practice: tune it first, over "sqrt", 0.2, 0.33, 0.5, 1.0, on OOB or cross-validation. (05, strength–correlation)
6Why sqrt p for classification and p/3 for regression?
They're rules of thumb from Breiman and Cutler's code and R's randomForest, not derivations. Regression gets a bigger menu because each tree's own error counts for more.

Accuracy forgives weak trees: only which side of 0.5 the averaged probability lands on matters, so weaker, less alike trees still classify correctly, and decorrelation buys a lot. (That's about accuracy, not probability quality.)
Squared error doesn't: in regression each tree's squared error feeds straight into the forest's (the sigma^2 in rhosigma^2 ), so a weaker tree costs more.
Smooth targets need many good splits: a tree copies a smooth surface as a fine staircase, so every split forced onto a useless feature coarsens it.
Defaults differ by library: R uses sqrt p and p/3 ; sklearn's classifier uses sqrt p , but its regressor uses all features, which is plain bagging.
Evidence: on the credit limit, all features (RMSE 10.18) beat "sqrt" (10.31) and p/3 rounded down to 1 (13.32). Follow-up: the best value depends on how many features carry signal, so tune it. (05)
7Can a random forest overfit by adding more trees?
No. Adding trees moves the average towards a fixed limit, so the test error falls to a plateau and stays there. A forest overfits through tree size, not tree count.
beginaligned bar f_B(x) &= frac1B sum_b=1^B f_b(x) \\ bar f_B(x) &to mathbb E_Thetabig[f(x; Theta)big] quad as B to infty endaligned

In words: Theta is one tree's randomness (its bootstrap and feature draws). Given the data, the trees are independent draws, so their average converges to the expected tree, which more trees can't make any more complex.
Numbers: gap 0.022 with 1 tree, 0.0028 with 100, 0.0026 with 500. Log loss needs about 200 trees to settle; AUC about 25–100.
What does overfit: leaves too small for noisy data. Fix it with leaf size or depth.
A trap: train AUC 0.97 against test 0.82 isn't evidence of overfitting. Every training row sits in 63% of the trees; the OOB score is the honest training score.
Contrast: in boosting each tree fits the previous trees' errors, so too many rounds overfit, and early stopping is needed. Trade-off: cost and memory grow linearly with B . (08)
8Why are a forest's trees grown deep and unpruned?
Averaging removes variance but never bias, so each tree should bring as little bias as possible. Deep trees also differ more from one another.
Division of labour: a full-depth tree can carve out any shape (low bias); its high variance is what averaging removes. Pruning would add bias that no amount of averaging takes back.
Decorrelation: deep splits are chosen from a few rows, so they change most between bootstraps. Shallow trees agree more.
Simplicity: no pruning strength to validate.

Trade-off: pure leaves give noisy 0/1 probabilities and big models. A minimum leaf size of 5–20 smooths them (gap 0.0052 to 0.0013, log loss 0.271 to 0.218), while leaves of 200 or more turn biased (gap 0.0062 at 200, AUC 0.747 at 500): a bootstrap holds only about 150 distinct applicants of the stressed group, and the leaf-size limit counts distinct rows. Prefer a leaf-size limit to a depth cap: it stops where rows run thin and lets dense regions keep splitting. (06)
9Walk through what happens at one node of a forest tree, compared with a single tree.
The same greedy search, on different rows and a restricted menu: bootstrap-weighted rows, m features drawn fresh at that node, every threshold of those m only, and no pruning afterwards.
Rows: the bootstrap rows that reached the node, each weighted by how often it was drawn. A single tree uses the plain training rows.
Menu: draw m of the p features without replacement, fresh at this node. A single tree considers all p .
Search: for each candidate, sort the node's values and try every midpoint; score each split by the weighted impurity drop.
Choose the best split among the m . Features constant in the node don't count towards m , so sklearn draws on until one varies.
Stop only when the node is pure or a leaf-size limit is hit. No pruning; a single tree is often pruned.
Leaf value: the weighted share of each class. The forest's prediction averages the B leaves that x falls into.
gain = I(t) - fracw_Lw_t I(L) - fracw_Rw_t I(R)
In words: the node's impurity minus its children's, each weighted by its share of the node's (bootstrap-weighted) rows.
Follow-up: Extra Trees replace the threshold search with one random cut per candidate and skip the bootstrap by default. The same impurity drops, summed per feature, are MDI importance. (05)
10Majority vote or averaged probabilities?
sklearn averages the trees' probabilities (soft voting); Breiman's original forest used a majority vote. Averaging keeps each tree's confidence, so it ranks better and has lower variance.
beginaligned tree probabilities &= (0.45,\ 0.45,\ 0.9) \\ majority vote &= 0 \\ average &= 0.6 endaligned
In words: two of three trees lean "no", so the vote says 0, but the third is very sure and the average comes out above 0.5.
With pure leaves they're the same thing: each tree says 0 or 1, so the average is the vote share.
Why averaging: it gives a score to rank and threshold (AUC needs one). A vote gives only a class; only 61 of 1,500 test applicants get a "default" majority from 200 bagged trees.
Trade-off: averaged probabilities are still squeezed toward the middle, so calibrate if the probability drives a decision. (03)
11What is OOB error, how is it computed, and when does it mislead?
Each training row is predicted by only the trees whose bootstrap left it out, about 37% of them, and those predictions are scored. It's a nearly free validation score.
beginaligned O_i &= \\, b : i notin sample b \,\ \\ hat p_OOB(x_i) &= frac1|O_i| sum_b in O_i hat p_b(x_i) endaligned
In words: for row i , average only the trees that never saw it, exactly as for a new applicant; then compute any metric over all rows.
Why it works: the bootstrap already held rows out, so no refit is needed. Here OOB AUC 0.786 matched 5-fold cross-validation's 0.784.

Mildly pessimistic: each row is scored by a smaller forest (37% of the trees), and with tiny leaves an out-of-bag positive's own label is missing from its neighbourhood (0.784 OOB against 0.808 on fresh data at leaf size 1).

Misleading when: the default oob_score_ is accuracy (0.917 against a 0.913 baseline); rows repeat (0.993 OOB against 0.828 real); time order or drift matters (OOB looked calibrated while the future defaulted at 11.3% against 7.3% predicted); there are too few trees ( 0.632^B of rows get no OOB trees); or settings were tuned on it.
Follow-up: shuffling a feature within each tree's OOB rows gives Breiman's OOB permutation importance. (07)
12Which hyperparameters would you tune, in what order, and what does each do?
max_features first, then min_samples_leaf (or max_depth); set n_estimators just high enough for the score to plateau; leave the rest near their defaults.
error = bias^2 + rhosigma^2 + frac1-rhoB\,sigma^2 + noise
In words: every knob moves bias, a tree's variance sigma^2 , the correlation rho , or the number of trees B .
max_features down: rho down, sigma^2 up, bias up slightly. The strength–correlation trade-off.
min_samples_leaf up / max_depth down: sigma^2 down, bias up, rho usually up. Matters most for probabilities.
n_estimators up: only the 1/B term shrinks. Never overfits; costs time.
bootstrap off: slightly stronger but far more alike trees (identical with all features); no OOB.
max_samples down: weaker, less alike, faster trees; a cheap regularizer on big data (gap 0.0052 to 0.0024 at 0.3).
class_weight: changes splits and inflates probabilities; recalibrate after.
How: judge on OOB or cross-validation with the metric you care about. Gains over the defaults are usually modest. (08)
13Hand drill: compute a depth-2 tree's impurity importance.
For each split, take the node's total impurity minus its children's, over the n training rows; add up per feature; scale to sum to 1.
beginaligned n_t G_t &= frac2 d (n_t - d)n_t \\ Delta_t &= fracn_t G_t - n_L G_L - n_R G_Rn endaligned
In words: a node with n_t rows and d defaulters has total Gini impurity 2d(n_t - d)/n_t (its Gini times its rows), computed straight from the counts.
Root, late <= 1.5: 3,500 rows (304 defaulters) give 555.2; the children give 346.2 and 166.9. The drop is 42.1, or 0.0120 per row.
Per feature: late 0.0120, income 0.0098; scaled, late 0.55 and income 0.45.

Follow-up: a forest does this per tree on its bootstrap sample, normalizes each tree, and averages. Because the sums use training rows, chance gains at deep splits inflate continuous and noise features. (10)
14How does a random forest handle class imbalance?

Not by itself; it just sees few positives. Leave the training alone and move the threshold, use bigger leaves, and judge with PR-AUC or log loss. Class weights or balanced bootstraps change the splits but inflate the probabilities.
beginaligned w_c &= fracn2 n_c \\ weighted leaf odds &= fracw_1w_0 times plain leaf odds endaligned

In words: balanced weights make both classes weigh the same, and a leaf then stores the weighted share of positives, which multiplies its odds by the weight ratio (10.5 here: a plain 0.20 leaf stores 0.724).
The damage without care: at 1% positives, each tree sees about 23 distinct defaulters, 40% of test applicants get exactly 0 from every tree, and 10 test positives make AUC wobble by ±0.09.
What weights do: they change which splits win (weighted Gini) and what leaves store, at fit time. Ranking barely moves (AUC 0.823 against 0.824), but the mean prediction doubles (0.17 against 0.087).
Variants: "balanced" fixes weights on the whole training set, "balanced_subsample" per bootstrap; a balanced random forest undersamples the majority in each bootstrap instead.
Trade-off: reweighting can help the splits find the rare class, but recalibrate afterwards, or divide each leaf's odds by w_1/w_0 (exact per tree, approximate for the average). (11, 08)
15Why are random forest probabilities poorly calibrated?
Near 0 and 1, the trees' errors can only point inwards, so averaging them pulls predictions toward the middle. Rare extreme groups also share leaves with milder neighbours.

One-sided errors: for an applicant whose true chance is near 1, a tree that errs can only say less, never more than 1, so the average sits below the truth; near 0 it sits above. The bootstrap and feature sampling add exactly this tree-to-tree variance, which gives random forests their typical S-shaped reliability curve.
Mixed leaves: the riskiest group (true chance 0.73) has about 22 training applicants, so its leaves mix in lower-risk rows: the forest predicts 0.659 for it, and nothing above 0.753.
Exceptions: regions with no training positives get exact 0s, and on its own training rows a forest is overconfident.

Fix: calibrate on held-out (or OOB) predictions with Platt scaling or isotonic regression; use moderate leaves; avoid class weights unless you recalibrate. Follow-up: boosters trained on log loss usually start closer to calibrated. (11)
16What are the pitfalls of random forest feature importance?

Impurity importance (MDI) is computed on training rows and inflates high-cardinality and noise features. Permutation importance on held-out data fixes that, but both split credit between correlated features, and neither is causal.

MDI bias: a continuous feature offers thousands of thresholds, and deep in a tree one always separates a few training rows by chance. Here the decoy age (0.18) outranked late (0.16), and a random ID and a noise column got about 11% each; permutation gave all three about 0.
Permutation choices: on training rows it measures memorization (noise columns get 0.02); with accuracy it collapses for rare events; it can differ by segment.

Correlated features: MDI splits the credit (0.22 and 0.19 for income and its copy, against 0.34 alone); permutation makes both look unimportant (0.05 and 0.02 against 0.16), since the splits on the unshuffled twin still work; drop-column says neither matters. Permute the group together (0.186).
SHAP (TreeSHAP) gives per-prediction, additive shares, but has the same correlated-feature trouble.

Not causal: a phone price standing in for income got importance 0.129, and the model "predicted" that giving people expensive phones cuts their risk. Importance is what the model uses, not what to change.
Follow-up: one feature far above the rest is a leakage alarm before it's a finding. (10)
17Random forest or Extra Trees?
Extra Trees draw one random threshold per candidate feature instead of searching for the best, and by default skip the bootstrap: cruder trees, a smoother average, faster training.
Bias and variance: each tree is cruder (more bias), but random cut positions blur the average's steps into a slope, so it varies less between training sets.
Here: a tie on step-shaped default risk (gap 0.0026 both), a win on the smooth credit limit (RMSE 10.00 against 10.18, the noise floor being 10), and about twice as fast.
No bootstrap by default: the random thresholds supply the variety, and each tree sees every row (hence bigger trees).
Trade-off: it loses where the truth has sharp cut-offs that a search lands on exactly. It's cheap to try both. (09)
18Can a random forest extrapolate?
No. Its prediction is a weighted average of training targets, so it can never leave their range; beyond the data it repeats its edge value.
beginaligned hat f(x) &= sum_i=1^n w_i(x)\, y_i \\ w_i(x) &ge 0 \\ textstylesum_i w_i(x) &= 1 endaligned
In words: w_i(x) is the share of leaf weight row i has alongside x , averaged over trees. A weighted average with non-negative weights summing to 1 stays between the smallest and largest target.
Here: the credit limit for incomes of ₹150k, ₹300k and ₹600k (truth 240, 480, 960) is 233.7 every time.
Why it matters: time trends, growing prices or anything that drifts beyond the training range are invisible.
Fixes: model a ratio or detrended target, add a linear model for the trend, or use model trees with linear leaves. Boosted trees share the limit. (11)
19How does a forest cope with outliers, label noise and missing values?
Feature outliers barely matter, label noise is averaged away, target outliers distort only their own leaves, and recent sklearn sends missing values to a learned side at each split.

Feature outliers: a split depends only on the order of values, so an extreme value just sits at the end; any monotone transform leaves the searched splits unchanged (not Extra Trees' random cuts, which are drawn over the range).
Target outliers (regression): a leaf predicts its rows' mean, so an extreme target pulls its leaf in the 63% of trees that drew it. Clip or transform the target, or use absolute-error splitting.

Label noise: deep trees memorize noisy labels, but different trees memorize different ones, and averaging dilutes them. Boosting keeps refitting the rows it gets wrong, which are disproportionately mislabelled (worst for AdaBoost; shrinkage and early stopping limit it).

Missing values: each split tries sending missing rows left and right and keeps the better side; at prediction they follow that side (or the bigger child if none were seen in training). Alternatives: impute with a missing indicator, surrogate splits, proximity imputation.
Follow-up: many noise features do hurt, by crowding useful ones off the split menus. (11, 11)
20Random forest or gradient boosting: when does each win, and why?

A forest averages deep, independent trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees in sequence to cut bias. Tuned boosting usually wins on accuracy and model size; a forest wins on small or noisy data and when there's no time to tune.
Mechanism: forest trees are low-bias and high-variance, averaged; boosting trees are high-bias and low-variance, each fitting the current errors with a small learning rate.
More trees: a forest plateaus; boosting eventually overfits, so it needs early stopping and a validation set.
Noise: boosting is more exposed to mislabelled rows (AdaBoost most of all; shrinkage and early stopping help); a forest averages them away.
Tuning: a forest's defaults are near-best; a booster's learning rate, rounds and depth interact.
Practicalities: forests train in parallel and give an OOB score; boosters give smaller, faster models and better-calibrated probabilities. Neither extrapolates.
To tell which cause is at work: paired cross-validation on the same folds, learning curves over data size, or injected label noise. (12)
21What happens with one dominant feature, or with many noise features?
A dominant feature makes bagged trees alike, which random menus fix. Many noise features crowd useful ones off the menus, which weakens trees and inflates impurity importance.
beginaligned P(feature on a menu) &= m/p \\ P(no useful feature) &= binomp-km Big/ binompm endaligned
In words: with m of p features drawn, a given feature is offered at a share m/p of splits, and a split has nothing useful with the chance on the second line, for k useful features.
Dominant feature: it rooted 160 of 200 bagged trees, but 90 with 2 of 4 features per menu, so the others get to shape trees. Check it for leakage.
Noise features: with 3 useful out of 24, a menu of 4 has nothing useful 56% of the time, and a menu of 1 88% of the time (gap 0.0106, the worst). MDI credits the noise; permutation doesn't.
Fix: drop junk features using permutation importance, or raise max_features. (13)
22Write the pseudocode for training a forest and computing its OOB score.
For each tree: bootstrap, then grow with a fresh feature draw at every node and no pruning. Predict by averaging. For OOB, average each row over only the trees that left it out.

for b in range(B): c = bootstrap_counts(n) # weights trees[b] = grow(rows with c > 0, c) grow(node): if pure or too small: leaf(weighted shares) F = sample(features, m) # per node best split over F, all thresholds grow(left); grow(right) # no pruning for each tree b, for each i with c_b[i] == 0: total[i] += tree_b(x_i); count[i] += 1 oob = total / count # where count > 0 score = auc(y, oob)
Per node, not per tree: the feature draw sits inside grow.
Weights: bootstrap counts weight the impurity and the leaf shares.
OOB: skip rows in every bag (likely only with few trees), and score with AUC or log loss, not accuracy.
Follow-up: for Extra Trees, replace the threshold search with one random cut per feature and drop the bootstrap. (15)

beginaligned P(row in a bootstrap) &= 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n \\ &to 1 - 1/e \\ &approx 0.632 \\ P(drawn k times) &= e^-1/k! \\ P(in, drawing a fraction f) &approx 1 - e^-f \\ P(in all B bags) &= 0.632^B \\ hat p_OOB(x_i) &= mean of trees with i out of bag endaligned
beginaligned hat p(x) &= tfrac1B textstylesum_b hat p_b(x) \\ mathbb E[bar f] &= mathbb E[f_1] \\ Var(bar f) &= rhosigma^2 + (1-rho)sigma^2/B \\ removable share of floor &= (1-rho)/(rho B) endaligned
beginaligned P(feature on a menu) &= m/p \\ P(no useful feature) &= tbinomp-km big/ tbinompm \\ m &= sqrt p \ (classes), quad p/3 \ (numbers) \\ test error &le barrho\,(1 - s^2)/s^2 endaligned
Importance, weights, neighbours

beginaligned Delta_t &= (n_t G_t - n_L G_L - n_R G_R)/n \\ permutation_j &= score - score_x_j shuffled \\ f(x) &= phi_0 + textstylesum_j phi_j(x) \\ w_c &= n/(2 n_c) \\ hat f(x) &= textstylesum_i w_i(x)\, y_i \\ s(x) &= 2^-mathbb E[h(x)]/c(psi) endaligned
Same (only the 1/B term shrinks)
Bigger leaves / shallower
Next: Gradient boosting and XGBoost, the other way to combine trees.

notes.title: Gradient boosting and XGBoost
notes.desc: Trees fitted to gradients, tree by tree: g and h, XGBoost's leaf weight and gain, regularizers, missing values, split finding, LightGBM, CatBoost, tuning and monotone constraints.

sections.t: The pieces: a sum of trees, one loss
g and h: the same thing, renamed
What each regularizer does, and why it exists
Missing values: the learned default direction
CatBoost: ordered statistics, ordered boosting, symmetric trees
Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables

chunks.x: Gradient boosting and XGBoost · Deepam Minda

Boosting builds F(x) = F_0 + eta sum_m f_m(x) , one small regression tree at a time. Each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions: the residual y - F for squared error, y - p for log loss. It's gradient descent, with each step a tree.

A leaf stores a correction, not a target. For squared error the best correction is the mean residual and the best split is the biggest drop in squared error. For classification F is the log-odds, and the sigmoid is applied once, to the total.

XGBoost expands each row's loss to second order around its current prediction: slope g and bend h . Summing over a leaf gives the best leaf value w^* = -G/(H + lambda) . A split's gain is half of (left score + right score − parent score), minus gamma , where a node's score is G^2/(H + lambda) . For log loss, g = p - y and h = p(1 - p) .

lambda shrinks leaves with a small hessian sum (few rows, or rows the model is already sure about), gamma is a price per leaf, and min_child_weight is a minimum hessian per child. All three stop a leaf chasing a handful of rows.

Missing values: at every split, the missing rows' G and H are tried on the left and on the right, and the better side is stored as the default direction. If training had no missing values, that direction was never learned.

Speed comes from histograms (bin once, sum g and h per bin, get one child by subtraction) and parallel work inside each tree. LightGBM adds leaf-wise growth, GOSS and EFB; CatBoost adds ordered target statistics, ordered boosting and symmetric trees.

Boosting cuts bias and overfits as trees are added; a forest cuts variance and doesn't. Fix eta , early-stop on a validation set that looks like production, then tune depth and min_child_weight, subsampling, and the penalties.

In practice: scale_pos_weight multiplies the predicted odds (recalibrate), monotone constraints are enforced at split time with bounds on the leaf values, split-count and gain importances mislead (prefer SHAP), and a sum of trees can't extrapolate.

Six loan applicants and one feature: how many late payments they've had. The same rows carry two targets: a credit limit for regression (section 02) and whether they defaulted for classification (section 05).
Watch row 3. It defaulted with 0 late payments, just like rows 1 and 2, who didn't. No question about late payments can separate it from them, so it shows what boosting does with a row it can't fix.
Settings used throughout: learning rate eta = 0.3 (XGBoost's default), and each tree makes one split, so every tree can be worked by hand. The same steps work at any depth.
A tree is questions plus numbers

A tree asks a few yes/no questions, like “late < 1.5?”, to send each row to a leaf, and each leaf holds one number. Building a tree means choosing two things: the questions, which decide which rows end up together, and the number in each leaf. A row the tree has never seen still falls into some leaf, so the tree works on new data too.
The model is a sum of trees
F(x) = F_0 + eta\, f_1(x) + dots + eta\, f_M(x)
F_0 is the starting number, the same for everyone.
f_m(x) is the m -th tree's output: a correction to the prediction so far, not a prediction on its own.
eta is the learning rate: each correction is only partly trusted (section 02 says why).
For regression, F is the prediction itself. For classification, F is a score, the log-odds, which becomes a probability only at the very end (section 05).
One loss for the whole model

Each row gets a penalty for how wrong it is, and the penalties add up: L = sum_i ell(y_i, F_i) . For regression ell = tfrac12 (y - F)^2 , so being off by 10 costs 50; for classification it's the log loss. Everything below is chosen to make this one number smaller: the starting number, every split and every leaf.

Choosing 100 trees at once to minimize L is hopeless: there are far too many combinations. So boosting is greedy (the textbook name is forward stagewise additive modelling): keep everything built so far fixed, find the one new tree that lowers L the most, add it, freeze it, repeat. Every round solves the same problem: with the current predictions F_i fixed, find the tree f that minimizes
sum_i ellbig(y_i,\ F_i + f(x_i)big)

This is “the loss inside the tree”. It isn't Gini or entropy, which belong to a standalone classification tree; it's the model's own loss, measured after adding the new tree. And since a leaf holds a number to be added, every tree in boosting is a regression tree, even for classification.
Boosting vs a random forest
Independently, each on a bootstrap sample
One after another, each fixing the last
Shallow, typically depth 3–8
Variance: jumpy deep trees, averaged
Bias: weak trees, added up
Never hurts; validation loss goes flat
Eventually overfits; needs early stopping

In an interview: “Boosting builds an additive model, a starting value plus a sum of small trees. Each tree is a correction to the prediction so far, fitted greedily to lower one loss given everything before it. Each is a regression tree, even for classification, because its leaves hold numbers that get added to a score. A forest averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees in sequence to cut bias, which is why it can overfit as trees are added.”
The loss is tfrac12 (y - F)^2 . Every step asks one question: what makes this loss smallest?
Round 0: the starting number
Before any tree exists, which single number c should everyone get? Try a few:
Total loss tfrac12sum (y - c)^2
The bottom is at 80, the mean. In general the slope of tfrac12sum (y - c)^2 in c is sum (c - y) , which is zero at c = bar y . So F_0 = 80 for every row.
Tree 1: the number in a leaf
What's left to fix for each row is its residual, r = y - F :
Suppose a leaf holds rows 1–4. Every row in it gets the same nudge w . Which w makes these rows' loss smallest? After the nudge, the leaf's loss is
sum_leaf tfrac12big(y_i - (F_i + w)big)^2 = sum_leaf tfrac12 (r_i - w)^2
The bottom is at 15, the mean residual. Setting the slope -sum (r_i - w) to zero gives it in general:
w^* = frac1n_leaf sum_leaf r_i
Residuals aren't a trick someone made up. They fall straight out of asking which nudge makes squared error smallest.
A leaf stores a correction, not a target. Rows 1–4 have a mean limit of 95, but the leaf stores +15, because 80 + 15 = 95.
Tree 1: choosing the split

Which question should the tree ask? The one that leaves the least loss, once each side gets its best nudge. Before any split the node's best nudge is the mean residual, 0, so the loss is tfrac12sum r^2 = 1600 .

The winning 250: left residuals 20, 30, 10, 0 minus 15 are 5, 15, −5, −15, whose squares add to 500; the right residuals −30, −30 minus −30 are 0. Half of 500 is 250, and the drop is 1600 − 250 = 1350. Tree 1 is “late < 1.5? → +15, otherwise −30”: an ordinary regression tree, grown on residuals instead of on y .
A shortcut you'll see again. The drop needs only sums and counts:
beginaligned drop &= frac12 Big[ frac(sum r_L)^2n_L + frac(sum r_R)^2n_R \\ &qquad - frac(sum r)^2n Big] endaligned

For late < 1.5: ½ × [60²/4 + (−60)²/2 − 0²/6] = ½ × [900 + 1800] = 1350. It works because giving a group its mean residual removes exactly tfrac12 (sum r)^2/n of its loss: (sum)²/count is big when many rows push the same way. XGBoost's gain (section 06) is exactly this with new names.
Deeper trees repeat the search inside each child, on that child's rows only, with that child's own loss as the “before”. They stop at the maximum depth, or when no split lowers the loss.
Don't add the whole tree. Add eta times it, with eta = 0.3 : +4.5 for rows 1–4 and −9 for rows 5–6, so F becomes 84.5 (rows 1–4) and 71 (rows 5–6).

Why not the full +15 and −30? Tree 1 was fitted to these exact rows, noise included, so trusting it fully overfits. Taking 30% leaves room for later trees to correct it. The cost is more trees (section 03).

Does eta change which split wins? No. The split search pretends the full leaf value will be added; eta is applied afterwards. Adding only eta of a leaf's value removes a share 2eta - eta^2 of its full drop (expand tfrac12sum (r - eta w)^2 ). With eta = 0.3 that's 0.51 for every split: 1200 → 612, 1350 → 688.5, 540 → 275.4. Every drop shrinks by the same factor, so the order is unchanged. What eta does change is the residuals the next tree sees.
Every residual is now measured against the current prediction, r = y - F_0 - eta f_1(x) :
Tree 2 does exactly what Tree 1 did, on these residuals. The loss before any split is ½Σr² = 911.5.

The best split moved. Tree 1 pushed row 4 (limit 80) up to 84.5, so it's now over-predicted ( r = -4.5 ) and belongs with the “push down” group. Each tree sees only what's left over, so different trees cut in different places, and their sum builds a staircase.

Trap: average the residuals, not the targets. In Tree 1 you couldn't tell them apart, because every row had the same F . Now you can. On the right side of late < 0.5 (rows 4–6, with F = 84.5, 71, 71), the mean target is 60: as a nudge, that would send row 4 from 84.5 to 144.5. The mean residual is −15.5, which moves each row toward its target, leaving a loss of ½ × (11² + 5.5² + 5.5²) = 90.75.
Tree 2 is “late < 0.5? → +15.5, otherwise −15.5”. Times eta , that's ±4.65, so F becomes 89.15 (late 0), 79.85 (late 1) and 66.35 (late 2–3).
Where it ends, and predicting a new row
The six rows (dots) and the prediction after 0, 1, 2 and 50 trees. Tree 1 cuts at 1.5, tree 2 at 0.5; after 50 trees the staircase sits at the mean limit for each number of late payments.
It settles at the mean limit for each number of late payments: (100 + 110 + 90)/3 = 100, then 80, then 50. That's the best squared error can do with this one feature.
A new applicant with 2 late payments, after 2 trees: add up the start and each tree's shrunk leaf value.
beginaligned F &= 80 + 0.3 times (-30) + 0.3 times (-15.5) \\ &= 80 - 9 - 4.65 \\ &= 66.35 endaligned

With 1 late payment: 80 + 4.5 − 4.65 = 79.85. Tree 1 sends late = 1 left, but Tree 2 sends it right. For regression, the sum is the prediction. And an applicant with 10 late payments also gets 66.35: past the last split, a sum of trees is flat (section 13).
The regression loop in one box

F0 = mean(y) F = F0 for every row repeat for each tree: r = y - F # what's left per row split: biggest drop in ½Σr² # each side gets its mean r leaf value = mean r of its rows F = F + eta * (row's leaf value) predict(x) = F0 + eta * Σ (x's leaf values)

In an interview: “Start from the mean. Each round computes residuals against the current prediction and fits a small regression tree to them: the leaf value is the mean residual, the split is the biggest drop in squared error, and the tree goes in after shrinking by the learning rate. Leaves store corrections, not targets; from the second tree on, rows in a leaf have different predictions, so you average residuals, not targets.”
The slope of tfrac12 (y - F)^2 in the prediction F is F - y . So the residual is minus the slope:
beginaligned fracpartialpartial F\, tfrac12 (y - F)^2 &= F - y \\ r &= y - F \\ &= -fracpartialpartial F\, tfrac12 (y - F)^2 endaligned

Each tree in section 02 was fitted to minus the slope of every row's loss: the downhill direction for that row. Adding the tree moves every row a little way downhill. That's gradient descent, and it generalizes to any loss you can differentiate.
Gradient descent on the predictions
Treat the n training predictions as the parameters. Their loss is a function of n numbers, and plain gradient descent would update each one:
beginaligned L(F_1, dots, F_n) &= sum_i ell(y_i, F_i) \\ g_i &= fracpartial ell(y_i, F_i)partial F_i \\ F_i &leftarrow F_i - eta\, g_i endaligned

That would just memorize the training rows, and say nothing about a new x . So boosting replaces the step -g by the tree that's closest to it, which is a function of the features and therefore works for any row:
beginaligned f_m &= argmin_f in trees sum_i big(-g_i - f(x_i)big)^2 \\ F_m(x) &= F_m-1(x) + eta\, f_m(x) endaligned

In words: the tree is the best tree-shaped approximation of the negative gradient, and adding it is one gradient step taken in the space of functions. That's why it's called functional gradient descent, and why -g_i is called the pseudo-residual.
Friedman's algorithm (classic gradient boosting)
Start at the best constant: F_0 = argmin_c sum_i ell(y_i, c) .
Each round: compute the pseudo-residuals r_i = -g_i at F_m-1 .
Fit a regression tree to the r_i by squared error. This only chooses the regions (the leaves).
Re-set each leaf to the value that minimizes the real loss on that leaf's rows: c_j = argmin_c sum_i in j ellbig(y_i, F_m-1(x_i) + cbig) .
Add eta times the tree, and repeat.
y - F , capped at pmdelta
Close to a mean that ignores the extremes
One Newton step (section 05)
Log-odds of the base rate

Why step 4 matters. For absolute error the tree is fitted to signs, ±1, so its raw leaf values are at most 1 in size: useless as step sizes when the residuals are in the tens. Re-setting each leaf to its median residual makes every step the right size. For squared error the mean residual is already the best value, so step 4 changes nothing. For log loss the best value has no formula, so it takes one Newton step instead. XGBoost goes further and uses that Newton information to choose the splits too (section 06).

Why the loss matters: outliers. In a larger simulated loan book, corrupting 2% of the training limits with a +₹500k typo gave a test RMSE of 29.0 under squared error, against 10.5 under absolute error and 10.9 under Huber. Under squared error those rows have residuals near 500 and every tree chases them; under absolute error each row only says “up” or “down”.

F_0 is the best constant for the loss: the mean for squared error, the median for absolute error, and the log-odds of the base rate for log loss, where the slope sum (p - y) is zero exactly when p = bar y . A bad start isn't fatal but wastes trees: in the same simulated book (8.7% defaults), starting XGBoost at p = 0.5 needed 64 trees instead of 35 to reach the same test log loss, because the first trees spent themselves walking everyone down to 8.7%. Recent XGBoost versions estimate the start from the data for this reason.
Shrinkage: why a small learning rate generalizes better

Each tree is a greedy, noisy estimate of the downhill direction, fitted to the same rows it will be judged on. A full step bakes all of that noise in, and later trees have to spend themselves undoing it. A small step keeps only a little of each tree, so the final model is an average over many trees, each fitted to slightly different residuals: the noise in any one of them is diluted. It's the same reason a small step size makes gradient descent stable. Validation log loss on the simulated book, depth-3 trees, 400 trees each:
A large rate overshoots: best after 2 trees, and a worse best.

Small rates trade off with the number of trees: for the two small rates, eta times trees is about the same (0.03 × 91 ≈ 0.01 × 266 ≈ 2.7), because small steps walk roughly the same path in shorter strides.
A small rate forgives a bad tree count: past the best round it climbs slowly (0.233 after 400 trees at 0.01) where a large one climbs fast (0.280 at 0.1).
The cost is training and prediction time, both proportional to the number of trees.
Stochastic gradient boosting

Friedman's later variant fits each tree on a random subsample of the rows, drawn without replacement, typically 50–80% (subsample). The tree is then applied to every row, so every prediction still moves. It helps in three ways: consecutive trees can't all latch onto the same noisy rows, so they're less alike and the sum has lower variance; each tree is cheaper; and the left-out rows give a free out-of-bag estimate of each round's improvement. The cost is a little bias and noisier steps, so it usually wants a few more trees. Column subsampling (section 09) does the same with features.

In an interview: “Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space. Each round computes the negative gradient of the loss for every row at the current predictions, fits a regression tree to it by least squares, sets each leaf to the value that minimizes the real loss there, and adds a shrunk copy. For squared error the negative gradient is the residual, so ‘fit the residuals’ is a special case; for absolute error it's the sign; for log loss it's y - p . Start at the best constant, keep the learning rate small, and subsample rows to decorrelate the trees.”

For squared error the slope is F - y and the bend is always 1, which is why section 02 looked like “mean residual”. “Residual” and “row count” only mean something for squared error; “slope” and “bend” mean something for any loss with two derivatives and a bend above 0. F is a score, and the sigmoid comes last

A sum of trees can be any number, while a probability must stay in (0, 1), and probabilities can't be added (0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3). So for classification F is the log-odds, and it becomes a probability only at the very end:
beginaligned p &= sigma(F) \\ &= frac11 + e^-F \\ F &= logfracp1 - p endaligned
A tree has no sigmoid inside it. Each leaf holds a change in log-odds, like −0.3 or +0.6.
The sigmoid is applied once, to the total: p = sigma(F_0 + eta f_1 + eta f_2 + dots) .
During training the sigmoid appears only when computing g and h , always on the running total F .
ell = -big[\, y log p + (1 - y) log (1 - p) \,big]

A defaulter costs -log p and a non-defaulter -log(1 - p) : a defaulter given p = 0.9, 0.5 or 0.1 costs 0.11, 0.69 or 2.30. The best single probability for everyone is the base rate, here 3/6 = 0.5, so F_0 = log(0.5/0.5) , which is 0, and every row starts at p = 0.5 . In general F_0 = logfracbar y1 - bar y ; for a 10% default rate that's log(0.1/0.9) = -2.20 .
The slope g and the bend h
One fact does all the work: the sigmoid's slope is p(1 - p) .
beginaligned fracdsigmadF &= frace^-F(1 + e^-F)^2 \\ &= frac11 + e^-F cdot frace^-F1 + e^-F \\ &= p\,(1 - p) endaligned
The slope g , by the chain rule through p :
beginaligned y = 1:quad fracdelldF &= -frac1p cdot p(1 - p) \\ &= p - 1 \\ y = 0:quad fracdelldF &= frac11 - p cdot p(1 - p) \\ &= p \\ both:quad g &= p - y endaligned
The bend h : in g = p - y only p moves as F moves, at the sigmoid's rate, so
beginaligned h &= fracdgdF \\ &= p\,(1 - p) endaligned
g = p - y is the probability error, with a sign. Positive means p is too high, so push down. It plays the role the residual played ( y - p = -g ).
h = p(1 - p) is how much p moves when F moves by 1. It depends on how sure the model already is: 0.25 at p = 0.5 , 0.09 at 0.9, 0.0099 at 0.99.

This is the one real difference from regression: h is no longer 1. A row the model is unsure about has a large h ; a row it's sure about has h near 0. And the claim about round 0 follows: for a single constant the slope is sum (p - y) , zero at p = bar y .
Why the exact leaf value doesn't work
In section 02 each leaf's best nudge was exact. Try that here, on the split late < 1.5:
Left leaf (rows 1–4, labels 0, 0, 1, 0, all at F = 0 ): the best probability is the leaf's rate, 1/4, so the best nudge solves sigma(0 + w) = 1/4 : w = log(1/3) , about −1.10. That one works.
Right leaf (rows 5–6, both defaulted): the best probability is 1, so w = +infty . A pure leaf wants infinity.

From Tree 2 on, rows in a leaf have different F s, and the best w solves sum_i sigma(F_i + w) = sum_i y_i , which has no formula. A numerical search for every leaf of every candidate split, every round, is too slow, and each new loss would need its own solver.
The shortcut: a Newton step
Do exactly what section 04 did: the slope is G now and it flattens by H per unit, so walk G/H downhill.
beginaligned w &= -fracGH \\ &= -fracsum_i (p_i - y_i)sum_i p_i (1 - p_i) endaligned
For squared error this is exact, because the bend really is constant.

For log loss it's an approximation. As you walk, p shifts and the bend changes; we pretend it stays at today's value. That replaces each row's loss curve with a parabola with the same slope and bend at the current point: the second-order approximation, or a Newton step (step = −slope / bend). It's close enough, and the next tree corrects what's left.
On Tree 1's leaves: left, G = 1 , H = 1 , so w = -1 (exact: −1.10); right, G = -1 , H = 0.5 , so w = +2 (exact: ∞, but the shortcut gives a finite step).

Why divide by H , not by the number of rows? g is an error in probability, while F is measured in log-odds. Near p = 0.5 , one unit of log-odds moves p by about 0.25. The left leaf is 0.25 too high on average, so it needs about 0.25 / 0.25 = 1 unit down. Dividing by h converts “wrong in probability” into “how far to move in log-odds”. In regression F and y share units, so h = 1 .

The split score carries over unchanged: the same tfrac12[G_L^2/H_L + G_R^2/H_R - G^2/H] , now the loss a split removes under the parabola. It's Newton's method for logistic regression, one leaf at a time.
Every row is at p = 0.5 , so g = 0.5 - y and h = 0.25 :

Leaves: −1/1 = −1 and 1/0.5 = +2. Times eta = 0.3 : F becomes −0.3 for rows 1–4 and +0.6 for rows 5–6, so p = 0.426 and 0.646. (Added in full, the step would give 0.27 and 0.88 after one tree: very confident, on two rows.)
