chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: Where the forest sits: a random forest shares the trees' column (no preprocessing, robust to useless features, flat outside the range, TreeSHAP). It differs from boosting as in section 01: it cuts variance rather than bias, doesn't overfit with more trees, needs little tuning and trains in parallel, and usually scores a little lower once both are tuned. It's the safer choice when you can't validate carefully.

chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: Why trees win on most tables. Benchmarks on medium-sized tabular data (Grinsztajn et al., 2022) point to three reasons. Real tabular targets are irregular, full of thresholds and steps, and neural nets are biased toward smooth functions. Useless columns hurt an MLP much more than a tree, which simply never splits on them. And each column has its own meaning: trees work feature by feature, while an MLP treats the inputs as a rotatable vector and has to learn which directions matter.

chunks.h: Boosting vs random forest vs neural nets on tables
chunks.x: When neural nets win: very large data; raw images, text or audio inside the row; sequences such as transaction histories; many tasks sharing learned embeddings; end-to-end training with other modalities. Tabular foundation models trained to do in-context learning are now competitive on small tables. Ensembles of a booster and a neural net often beat either alone.

Every tree goes in at full size, noise and all. On the six rows, one tree takes the late 2–3 group from 0.5 to 0.88, on two rows, and two trees to 0.96. For log loss a full Newton step from far away also overshoots, because the parabola is only accurate near the current point: in a simulated book, one full step took a group with a real 30.5% default rate from the 8.7% base rate to 58%. Validation loss bottoms early and high ( eta = 0.5 was best after 2 trees at 0.239, against 0.232 for small rates) and then climbs fast. Given the same residuals, eta doesn't change which split wins; but a full
…the trees are very deep?

Each tree fits the current residuals almost exactly, noise included. With full-depth trees and eta = 0.1 , every round leaves 90% of each residual and the next tree refits the same pattern, so after 200 rounds the sum is about 1 - 0.9^200 approx 1 times one memorizing tree: a test RMSE of 13.5 in a simulated book, no better than a single deep tree (13.9), against 10.3 for depth-3 trees. Boosting reduces bias; a deep tree has no bias left to reduce, only variance, and adding deep trees in sequence doesn't average it away. Depth also raises the interaction order and shrinks leaves, so min_child_

Leaves become -G/H , so a leaf with a tiny hessian sum takes a huge step: 10 confident rows with one surprise default give 9.1 in log-odds instead of 0.82. Pure groups climb without limit: on the six rows the late 2–3 score reaches 17.6 after 200 trees, against 3.9 with lambda = 1 . With squared error and big leaves, lambda = 0 barely matters, since H is a row count. LightGBM's default is lambda = 0 , relying on min_child_samples instead.
…there's no early stopping?

Training loss keeps falling; validation loss is a U and climbs past the best round. In a simulated book at eta = 0.1 , the best was 15 trees (0.232), and 600 trees reached 0.301 while training loss fell to 0.044. Probabilities grow overconfident: on the six rows, 200 trees push the late 1 and late 2–3 groups to 0.000 and 1.000. A small eta makes the climb slower, not absent.
…min_child_weight is huge?

No split can give both children enough hessian, so every tree is a single leaf, w = -G/(H + lambda) : a constant shift. At the base-rate start G = 0 , so the model never moves from F_0 . On the six rows even the default of 1 does this (every cut leaves a side with H < 1 ): five trees, all single leaves of value 0, and every applicant stays at 0.5. Less extreme values bite harder as training goes on, because confident rows carry less hessian. High bias, by design.
…a feature is duplicated?

With exact search, the copy offers exactly the same gains, so ties are broken by a fixed rule and predictions don't change. Two things do change: with column subsampling, the duplicated feature is twice as likely to be offered at each tree or node, so it's effectively up-weighted; and importances. Without column subsampling every tie goes to the same copy (XGBoost prefers the lower column index), so one copy takes all the splits and the other shows zero; with column subsampling each copy wins when the other isn't offered, so the credit is split between them. Near-duplicates with a little noise
…one label is a big outlier?

For regression with squared error, that row's residual is huge and dominates G in every leaf it lands in, so every tree bends toward it; in a simulated book, a 2% share of +₹500k typos took test RMSE from about 10 to 29.0, while absolute error (10.5) and Huber (10.9) shrugged it off. For classification a flipped label caps at lvert g rvert le 1 but never goes away (section 13), so deeper trees isolate it. Use a robust loss, early stopping and bigger leaves, and look at the rows with the largest final gradients: they're often label errors.
…every feature is missing for a row?

The row follows the default direction at every split, so in each tree it lands in one fixed leaf: the end of the “all-missing” path. Its prediction is F_0 plus eta times those leaves, which isn't the base rate and isn't a considered estimate either. Each default direction was learned from rows where that one feature was missing (or not learned at all), not from rows where everything was. On the six rows, after two trees, a missing late count gets 0.374 (the low-risk value) from this note's NumPy build and 0.744 (the high-risk value) from XGBoost's default histogram method: two arbitrary defaul
…you start from 0 instead of the base rate? The first trees spend themselves walking everyone to the base rate; the end point is the same, the early rounds are wasted.
…you fit the gradient instead of the negative gradient? Every step goes uphill and training loss rises each round. It's the classic from-scratch bug; the check is that training loss falls.

…the trees are fitted in parallel on the same target? They come out nearly the same, so the sum is one tree with a bigger step. The correction only happens because tree m sees what trees 1 to m - 1 got wrong.

…the base learner is linear? A sum of linear models is one linear model, so boosting adds nothing a regularized linear fit doesn't have. Trees work because sums of steps build curves and interactions.
…a category at inference was never seen? CatBoost gives it the prior; LightGBM sends it down the “other” side of each categorical split; one-hot gives all zeros.
Generic gradient boosting (any loss)

INPUT X, y, loss, M trees, eta F0 = argmin_c Σ_i loss(y_i, c) # mean | median | log-odds of rate F[i] = F0 for every row i repeat M times: r[i] = -∂loss(y_i, F[i]) / ∂F[i] # pseudo-residuals tree = regression tree on (X, r), by squared error # picks the regions for each leaf j: c[j] = argmin_c Σ_(i in j) loss(y_i, F[i] + c) # mean / median / Newton F[i] += eta * c[leaf of row i] save (tree, c) PREDICT(x): s = F0 + eta * Σ_m c_m[leaf_m(x)] regression: return s classification: return sigmoid(s)
XGBoost: one round and one tree

each round: for every row i: g[i], h[i] = slope, bend at F[i] # squared: g = F - y, h = 1 # log loss: p = sigmoid(F) # g = p - y, h = p * (1 - p) tree = GROW(all rows, depth = 0) F[i] += eta * tree(x_i) GROW(rows, depth): G = Σ g; H = Σ h # over these rows if depth == max_depth: return LEAF(-G / (H + lam)) best = SPLIT_SEARCH(rows, G, H) if best.gain <= 0: return LEAF(-G / (H + lam)) split rows by best.f < best.cut # missing f → best.default side return NODE(best, GROW(left, depth + 1), GROW(right, depth + 1))
One split search, with the default direction

SPLIT_SEARCH(rows, G, H): best.gain = -infinity for each feature f: M = rows where f is missing Gm = Σ g over M; Hm = Σ h over M P = rows with f present, sorted by f GL = 0; HL = 0 for k = 0 .. len(P) - 2: GL += g[P[k]]; HL += h[P[k]] if f(P[k]) == f(P[k+1]): continue # no cut inside ties for side in (left, right): gl, hl = GL, HL if side == left: gl += Gm; hl += Hm gr = G - gl; hr = H - hl if min(hl, hr) < min_child_weight: continue gain = 1/2 * ( gl²/(hl + lam) + gr²/(hr + lam) - G²/(H + lam) ) - gamma if gain > best.gain: cut = (f(P[k]) + f(P[k+1])) / 2 best = (gain, f, cut, side) return be

Cost: sorting once per feature before training makes each node one linear sweep per feature; histograms replace the sorted rows by at most 256 bins. With gamma , XGBoost's exact method then prunes bottom-up any split whose gain is below gamma and whose children are both leaves.
XGBoost from scratch, in NumPy
Every piece by hand: g and h , the running-sum split search with the default direction, the gain and the leaf value. It follows the pseudocode line by line.

import numpy as np def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) def grad_hess(y, F, loss): if loss == "squared": return F - y, np.ones_like(F) p = sigmoid(F) # log loss return p - y, p * (1 - p) def score(G, H, lam): return G * G / (H + lam) def best_split(X, g, h, cfg): lam, best = cfg["lam"], None G, H = g.sum(), h.sum() for j in range(X.shape[1]): x = X[:, j] miss = np.isnan(x) Gm, Hm = g[miss].sum(), h[miss].sum() o = np.argsort(x[~miss]) xs = x[~miss][o] gs, hs = g[~miss][o], h[~miss][o] GL = HL = 0.0 for i in range(len(xs) - 1): GL, HL = GL + gs[i], HL + hs[i] if xs[i] == xs[i + 1]: conti
Check it on the six rows. The # → lines are the real outputs (NumPy 1.x printing), and they match sections 02, 05 and 08. Two-space indents keep the lines phone-width; it's ordinary Python.

late = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3.0]) X = late.reshape(-1, 1) limit = np.array([100, 110, 90, 80, 50, 50.0]) default = np.array([0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1.0]) cfg = dict(eta=0.3, max_depth=1, lam=0.0, gamma=0.0, mcw=0.0) F0, trees = fit(X, limit, "squared", 2, cfg) predict(X, F0, trees, cfg, "squared") # → [89.15 89.15 89.15 79.85 66.35 66.35] F0, trees = fit(X, default, "logloss", 2, cfg) predict(X, F0, trees, cfg, "logloss").round(3) # → [0.374 0.374 0.374 0.374 0.744 0.744] cfg1 = dict(cfg, lam=1.0) F0, trees = fit(X, default, "logloss", 3, cfg1) predict(X, F0, trees, cfg1, "logloss").round(4) # → [
Answer out loud first, then open the answer.
1How does gradient boosting work, step by step?
It builds an additive model one small regression tree at a time: each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions, and added after shrinking by the learning rate.
Start every row at the best constant F_0 : the mean for squared error, the log-odds of the base rate for log loss.
Each round, compute every row's gradient g (and, for XGBoost, the hessian h ) at its current prediction.
Grow a regression tree on them: classic GBM fits -g by least squares; XGBoost scores splits with the second-order gain.
Set each leaf to the value that lowers the loss most: the mean residual for squared error, a Newton step -G/(H + lambda) for log loss.
Update F leftarrow F + eta cdot tree(x) and repeat until validation loss stops improving.
Predict with F_0 + eta sum_m f_m(x) , passed through the sigmoid for classification.

Why it works: each tree moves every row's prediction downhill on its own loss, and because the step is a function of the features, it moves unseen rows sensibly too. On a toy where credit limits fall with late payments, tree 1 cuts at 1.5 late payments; tree 2 cuts at 0.5, because tree 1 over-pushed the one applicant with a single late payment. Follow-up: trees are built in sequence, since each needs the previous predictions; the parallelism is inside a tree. (02, 03)
2Why fit the negative gradient? Why not fit the target directly?
Adding a tree fitted to the negative gradient is one gradient-descent step on the predictions, so every round lowers the loss; for squared error the negative gradient is exactly the residual.
beginaligned L &= sum_i ell(y_i, F_i) \\ -g_i &= -fracpartial ell(y_i, F_i)partial F_i \\ f_m &= argmin_f sum_i big(-g_i - f(x_i)big)^2 endaligned
In words: the steepest way down for each row is -g_i ; the tree is the closest function of x to that direction. -g is y - F for squared error, sign(y - F) for absolute error and y - p for log loss.

Why not the target: every round would see the same labels and grow the same tree, ignoring what the model already knows. With gradients, rows that are already right have g approx 0 and barely pull on the split, so each tree works on what's still wrong. Trade-off: the gradient gives a direction, not a step size, so the leaves are re-set by a line search or Newton step. Fitting +g by mistake makes the training loss rise every round: the classic from-scratch bug. (03)
3What loss does each tree minimize? Gini, entropy? Are they classification trees?
Neither Gini nor entropy: each tree minimizes the model's own loss after the tree is added, and its leaves hold real numbers, so every tree is a regression tree, even for classification.

beginaligned &sum_i ellbig(y_i, F_i + f(x_i)big) \\ &quad approx const + sum_i big[ g_i f(x_i) + tfrac12 h_i f(x_i)^2 big] \\ &Gain = tfrac12 Big[tfracG_L^2H_L + lambda + tfracG_R^2H_R + lambda \\ &qquad - tfracG^2H + lambdaBig] - gamma endaligned

In words: XGBoost approximates the loss after the tree to second order, and the gain is how much a split lowers that approximation. Classic GBM instead grows each tree by squared error on -g and fixes the leaf values afterwards.

Why not Gini: Gini and entropy score class purity for a standalone tree whose leaves predict classes. Here a leaf is a correction added to a running log-odds score, and what matters is the ensemble's loss. Follow-up: for squared error with lambda = 0 the gain is exactly half the drop in squared error, the usual regression-tree criterion. (01, 06)
4Does each tree output a probability? Where's the sigmoid?
No: each tree outputs a change in log-odds, and the sigmoid is applied once, to the total.
p = sigmaBig(F_0 + eta sum_m f_m(x)Big)

In words: add up the start and every tree's shrunk leaf value in log-odds, then convert to a probability. During training the sigmoid appears only when computing g = p - y and h = p(1 - p) from the running total.

Why: probabilities are bounded and can't be added (0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3), while log-odds can take any value, so any sum maps back into (0, 1). Example: start at F_0 = 0 (a 50% base rate); if two trees add +0.6 and +0.465 for some applicant, F is 1.065 and p = sigma(1.065) , about 0.744. Follow-up: AdaBoost's score is half the log-odds, so its probability is sigma(2F) . (05)
5What is the initial prediction F₀, and why does it matter?
The best constant for the loss: the mean for squared error, the log-odds of the base rate for log loss.
beginaligned squared:quad textstylesum_i (c - y_i) &= 0 \\ c &= bar y \\ log loss:quad textstylesum_i (sigma(c) - y_i) &= 0 \\ c &= logfracbar y1 - bar y endaligned
In words: set the slope of the total loss in one shared constant to zero. At that start the gradients already sum to zero, sum g = 0 , so imbalance doesn't tilt the first trees.

Why it matters: start elsewhere and the first trees spend themselves walking everyone to the base rate. In a simulated book with 8.7% defaults, starting at 0.5 needed 64 trees instead of 35 for the same test log loss. Follow-up: for absolute error it's the median; XGBoost's base_score sets it, and recent versions estimate it from the data. (03)
6Derive g and h for squared error and for log loss. What changes for multiclass?
Squared error: g = F - y , h = 1 . Log loss on the raw score: g = p - y , h = p(1 - p) .

beginaligned fracdpdF &= p(1 - p) \\ fracpartial ellpartial p &= -fracyp + frac1 - y1 - p \\ &= fracp - yp(1 - p) \\ g &= fracpartial ellpartial p cdot fracdpdF \\ &= p - y \\ h &= fracdgdF \\ &= p(1 - p) endaligned
In words: the sigmoid's slope p(1 - p) cancels the denominator, leaving the probability error; differentiating p - y again leaves only the sigmoid's slope.

Why it matters: h is how much p moves per unit of log-odds, so confident rows ( p near 0 or 1) have h approx 0 and count little. Multiclass: K scores, softmax probabilities, g_k = p_k - y_k and h_k = p_k(1 - p_k) (XGBoost uses twice that), and K trees per round. Follow-up: absolute error has h = 0 almost everywhere, so the Newton leaf breaks; classic GBM uses the median residual instead, and XGBoost's absolute-error and quantile objectives grow the tree with h = 1 , then re-set each leaf by a line search, like Friedman's step 4. (05)
7Derive XGBoost's optimal leaf weight and split gain.
Expand the regularized objective to second order, group rows by leaf, and minimize each leaf's parabola: w^* = -G/(H + lambda) ; the gain is the drop in the resulting structure score.

beginaligned Omega &= gamma T + tfrac12 lambda textstylesum_j w_j^2 \\ Obj &= textstylesum_i ell(y_i, F_i + f_i) + Omega \\ &approx textstylesum_i big[g_i f_i + tfrac12 h_i f_i^2big] + Omega \\ &= textstylesum_j big[G_j w_j + tfrac12 (H_j + lambda) w_j^2big] \\ &quad + gamma T \\ w_j^* &= -fracG_jH_j + lambda \\ Obj^* &= -tfrac12 textstylesum_j fracG_j^2H_j + lambda + gamma T endaligned

In words: line 3 is the Taylor expansion, dropping the current loss, which the tree can't change; lines 4–5 use that every row in leaf j gets w_j ; line 6 sets each leaf's slope G_j + (H_j + lambda) w_j to zero; line 7 plugs it back. A split replaces one leaf by two and adds one gamma :
beginaligned Gain &= frac12 Big[fracG_L^2H_L + lambda + fracG_R^2H_R + lambda \\ &qquad - frac(G_L + G_R)^2H_L + H_R + lambdaBig] - gamma endaligned

Why it's useful: the gain needs only sums of g and h , so every cut is scored in one sweep with running sums. Check: six rows at p = 0.5 , lambda = 1 , split late < 1.5: G_L = 1 , H_L = 1 , G_R = -1 , H_R = 0.5 , so the gain is ½ × (0.5 + 0.667 − 0) = 0.583 and the leaves are −0.5 and +0.667. XGBoost's dump shows 1.167, because it drops the ½. (06)
8Why second-order? Why divide by the hessian?

A first-order approximation gives a direction but no step size; the second-order term makes each leaf a parabola whose minimum is a Newton step, and dividing by h converts an error in probability into a step in log-odds.
beginaligned ell(F + w) &approx ell(F) + g\, w + tfrac12 h\, w^2 \\ w^* &= -g / h endaligned

In words: a straight line has no bottom; a parabola does. Near p = 0.5 , one unit of log-odds moves p by about 0.25, so a leaf whose probabilities are 0.25 too high needs about one unit down: G/H = 0.25/0.25 = 1 (the exact answer on the toy was 1.10).
Rows weighted by certainty: confident rows have h approx 0 , so they barely count in H or in the choice of split.
Any loss plugs in: any twice-differentiable loss with h > 0 only needs to supply g and h ; that's how custom objectives work.

Trade-off: the parabola is accurate only near the current prediction. From far away a full Newton step overshoots (a group with a real 30.5% rate jumped from 8.7% to 58% in one full step), which is one reason for eta < 1 and for recomputing g and h every round. (05)
9What do λ, γ and min_child_weight do? Give numbers.
lambda shrinks leaf values, most where the hessian sum is small; gamma is the minimum gain a split must earn; min_child_weight is the minimum hessian sum each child must have.

lambda sits in -G/(H + lambda) and in the gain. A one-row leaf ( G = -0.5 , H = 0.25 ) goes from 2.0 to 0.4 at lambda = 1 ; a 100-row leaf goes from 2.0 to 1.92. It's lambda units of hessian saying “don't move”.

gamma is a price per leaf. XGBoost compares it with the gain without the ½: the toy split (1.167) survives gamma = 1.1 and is pruned at 1.2. The exact method grows to max_depth and prunes bottom-up, so a weak split with a strong one below it survives; the default histogram method checks gamma as it grows, so it never makes the weak split.
min_child_weight counts rows weighted by p(1 - p) . Ten rows at p = 0.01 have H = 0.099 : with one surprise default and lambda = 0 their leaf would be 9.1 in log-odds; the default of 1 refuses it.

Why they exist: a leaf with little hessian (few rows, or rows the model is already sure about) takes a big step on little evidence. Trade-off: all three raise bias and lower variance. For squared error min_child_weight is just a minimum row count; for log loss it tightens as predictions grow confident. (07)
10How does XGBoost handle missing values? What can go wrong?
Sparsity-aware split finding: at each candidate split it tries sending the missing rows left and right, and keeps the side with the higher gain as that split's default direction.
beginaligned left &= (G_L + G_M,\ H_L + H_M) \\ right &= (G_R,\ H_R) \\ or: left &= (G_L,\ H_L) \\ right &= (G_R + G_M,\ H_R + H_M) endaligned

In words: scan only present values, compute the missing rows' sums G_M and H_M once, and score each cut twice with the usual gain: once with the missing rows' sums on the left (first two lines), once on the right. On the toy, two missing defaulters at late < 1.5 score 1.083 on the right against 0.167 on the left, so missing goes with the risky group.

Why it's good: no imputation, missingness itself can carry signal, and the scan costs only the present values, so sparse data is cheap. What goes wrong: if a feature had no missing values in training, the direction is a fixed default, not learned, so values that go missing only in production all go one arbitrary way (in a simulation, AUC fell from 0.832 to 0.66); sparse matrices treat unstored zeros as missing; and CatBoost doesn't learn a direction (missing is the smallest value). Monitor missing rates between training and serving. (08)
11Exact vs approximate vs histogram split finding. Why weight quantiles by h?
Exact scores every distinct value; approximate scores candidates at h -weighted quantiles; histogram bins each feature once and scores only bin edges.
Exact: sort each feature once, then sweep with running sums G_L , H_L and G_R = G - G_L . Precise, slow on big data.
Approximate: candidate cuts at quantiles where each row weighs h_i , proposed per tree or per node; a weighted quantile sketch makes this mergeable across machines.

Histogram: about 256 quantile bins per feature, one-byte codes, one pass per node to sum g and h per bin, the larger child's histogram by subtraction. The default in XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost and sklearn's HistGB.
g\, w + tfrac12 h\, w^2 = tfrac12 h big(w + g/hbig)^2 - fracg^22h

Why h : in words, each row is a squared-error target -g/h with weight h , so unsure rows deserve finer cut points. Trade-off: binning costs a little precision: in a simulation the best income cut moved from 39.46 to 39.66 and lost 0.6% of its gain. (09)
12Learning rate vs number of trees: how do they trade off?
A smaller learning rate needs proportionally more trees and usually reaches the same or a slightly better validation loss, with a flatter minimum.

On a simulated loan book: eta = 0.1 was best at 15 trees, 0.03 at 91 and 0.01 at 266, all at a validation log loss of 0.232; for small rates eta times trees stayed about 2.7. eta = 0.5 was best after 2 trees, at a worse 0.239.

Why small helps: each tree is a greedy, noisy fit to the same rows; a small step keeps only a little of each tree's noise, so the model averages over many trees. Past the best round, a small rate also climbs slowly, so a mis-set tree count costs less. eta doesn't change which split a tree picks (every drop shrinks by the same factor 2eta - eta^2 ); it changes the residuals later trees see. Trade-off: training and prediction time grow with the number of trees. In practice: fix 0.05–0.1, early-stop, lower it at the end if you can afford it. (03)
13How do you prevent overfitting in gradient boosting?
Stop it chasing noise at two levels, the ensemble and the leaf, and check it on validation data that looks like production.
Ensemble: early stopping on the number of trees; a small learning rate; row and column subsampling, which decorrelate the trees.
Each tree: shallow depth or few leaves (lower interaction order); min_child_weight or min_child_samples; lambda , alpha and gamma .
Structure: monotone and interaction constraints remove wiggles that are usually noise.
Data: a robust loss for outlying targets, label cleaning, out-of-time validation for drifting data, and the test set used once.

Why boosting needs it: each tree fits what's left, and eventually that's noise, so training loss falls forever while validation loss is U-shaped. Follow-up: tune in order: eta with early stopping, then size, then sampling, then penalties. (12)
14Boosting vs bagging: bias and variance?
Bagging averages deep, independent trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow, dependent trees in sequence to cut bias.
VarBig(frac1B sum_b T_bBig) = rho\, sigma^2 + frac1 - rhoB\, sigma^2

In words: for a forest of B trees each with variance sigma^2 and correlation rho , more trees only shrink the second term, so adding trees never hurts. Boosting instead reduces the remaining error tree by tree; once only noise is left, more trees raise variance.

On a simulated book, boosting's validation loss was best at 15 trees (0.232) and reached 0.301 by 600, while the forest's fell steadily and flattened at 0.249. Trade-off: tuned boosting usually wins on accuracy; a forest is harder to break, parallel to train, and needs almost no tuning. (01, 14)
15Why does boosting overfit noisy labels more than a random forest?
Boosting aims each new tree at the remaining error, and a mislabelled or unpredictable row stays in the remaining error forever, so it keeps attracting splits.

On a six-row toy with one feature, a defaulter whose feature value matches two non-defaulters (so no split can separate them) has g = −0.5 at the start, −0.70 after ten trees and settles at −0.667, while a fixable row's g falls to −0.002. The unfixable row ends up with one of the largest gradients, round after round, and deeper trees will isolate it.
The forest: every tree fits the labels with each row weighted equally; a noisy row distorts a few leaves in some trees, and averaging over bootstrap trees dilutes it.
The loss matters: log loss caps each row's pull at lvert g rvert le 1 ; AdaBoost's exponential loss grows without limit, so it's more fragile; squared error lets one outlier dominate a leaf.
Guards: early stopping, min_child_weight and lambda , subsampling, a robust loss, and looking at the rows with the largest final gradients, which are often label errors. (13)
16Depth-wise vs leaf-wise tree growth?
Depth-wise splits every node level by level; leaf-wise always splits the single leaf with the largest gain, wherever it is.
Leaf-wise (LightGBM; XGBoost's lossguide) lowers training loss more for the same number of leaves, because no split is spent on a leaf with little to gain.
The risk: deep, thin branches that fit a few rows. On a simulated book, validation loss after 500 rounds was 0.243 with 4 leaves and 0.746 with 127.
Controls: num_leaves as the main knob, min_child_samples as the floor (it's what saved small data: 0.272 with one-row leaves vs 0.237 with 50-row leaves), max_depth as a cap.
Follow-up: CatBoost's symmetric trees are the opposite extreme: one question per level, fast and hard to overfit, less flexible per tree. (10)
17XGBoost vs LightGBM vs CatBoost?
All three are second-order gradient boosters; they differ in how trees grow, how splits are searched and sampled, and how categories are handled.

XGBoost: depth-wise by default, exact / approximate / histogram search, lambda = 1 by default, learned missing directions, monotone and interaction constraints, native categories (sorted by leaf weight, like LightGBM), custom objectives, a mature distributed and GPU ecosystem.
LightGBM: histograms with leaf-wise growth, GOSS and EFB; usually fastest on large data; overfits small data at default settings; categories split by sorting on G/H .
CatBoost: ordered target statistics and ordered boosting, symmetric trees, strong defaults; the best native handling of high-cardinality categoricals; slower to train, very fast to predict.

How to choose: tuned, they usually land within noise of each other, so choose by the data. Many high-cardinality categories: CatBoost (with has_time if there's a time order), or XGBoost/LightGBM with out-of-fold or time-ordered target encoding. Very large data: LightGBM or XGBoost's histogram method. The validation design matters more than the library. (10, 11)
18Why is CatBoost's target encoding special? What's prediction shift?
CatBoost encodes each row using only the rows before it in a random permutation (plus a prior), so a row's own label never enters its own encoding; naive target encoding leaks exactly that.
hat x_i = fracsum_j prec i,\ c_j = c_i y_j + a cdot prior\#\\, j prec i : c_j = c_i \,\ + a

In words: the average label of earlier rows in the same category, pulled toward the overall rate by a pseudo-rows. Naively, each row's label sits inside its category's mean: a useless 300-level pincode scored train AUC 0.779 and test 0.471, and dropped a model's test AUC from 0.809 to 0.609. Ordered statistics removed the fake signal (train AUC 0.492, model 0.812). Smoothing alone doesn't, because it keeps the order.

Prediction shift is the same leak inside boosting: each row's gradient comes from a model trained on that row, so training residuals look smaller than they would on new data. Ordered boosting computes each row's gradient from a model built only on earlier rows. Trade-off: early rows get noisy encodings (CatBoost keeps several random permutations and uses different ones for different trees, so no row is always early), a random order isn't time order, and ordered boosting costs more. Elsewhere, out-of-fold target encoding does the same job. (11)
19Feature importance: weight vs gain vs cover vs SHAP. What is TreeSHAP?

Weight counts splits, gain averages their gains, cover averages the hessian reaching them; SHAP splits each prediction into additive per-feature contributions, and mean |SHAP| is the most trustworthy of the four.
Weight favours many-valued features, noise included: a useless age feature got 29% of splits in a simulation, while a 6-valued strong feature got 5%.
Gain favours a feature used in one big early split per tree (that same strong feature: 65%), and isn't consistent: a model can rely more on a feature while its gain falls.
Cover favours splits near the root. All three are measured on training data, so they reward noise splits.
F(x) = phi_0 + sum_j phi_j(x)

TreeSHAP, in words: phi_0 is the average raw score, and each phi_j is a Shapley value, feature j 's marginal contribution averaged over all orders in which features could be revealed. TreeSHAP computes them exactly in polynomial time, by following known features' branches and averaging over unknown features' branches by the training cover. Caveats: SHAP explains the model, not causes; correlated features share credit arbitrarily; for global importance, permutation importance on held-out data is a good cross-check. (13)
20What are monotonic constraints, and how are they enforced?
They force the prediction to move only one way in a feature, with every other feature fixed, and they're enforced while each tree grows: violating splits are rejected and leaf values are bounded.
For a split on a feature constrained to increase, a candidate whose lower-value child gets the larger weight is refused.

After an accepted split with w_L le w_R , the midpoint (w_L + w_R)/2 becomes an upper bound for every leaf under the left child and a lower bound for every leaf under the right child; later splits inherit the bounds.
Leaf values are clipped into their bounds, so each tree is monotone, and a sum of monotone trees is monotone.

Why credit wants it: decline reasons must make sense (more income can't raise risk), regulators check directions, and removing wiggles usually removes overfitting. In a simulation, constraining income, EMI share and late payments removed every rise in every applicant's curve at no cost in log loss (0.222 → 0.221), though AUC fell from 0.832 to 0.811. Trade-off: a wrong constraint adds bias (forcing risk to rise with income took log loss to 0.262); it holds “others fixed”, which can differ from the raw trend; and it doesn't govern where missing values go. (13)
21Class imbalance: what does scale_pos_weight do to the model?
It multiplies every positive row's g and h by k , as if each positive appeared k times, so the model learns odds k times too high.
beginaligned k\, n_+ (p - 1) + n_-\, p &= 0 \\ fracp1 - p &= k cdot fracn_+n_- endaligned

In words: the weighted loss's best constant for a group with n_+ positives and n_- negatives has k times the true odds. With k = 50 , a true 3% risk (odds 0.031) becomes odds 1.55, about 0.61; in a simulation with 8.7% defaults the mean prediction became 0.55 and AUC fell from 0.825 to 0.794.

What to do: subtract log k from the raw score or recalibrate before using probabilities. Often you don't need it: starting at the base-rate log-odds already balances the gradients, and for a decision you can keep the plain loss and move the threshold. It can help when positives are so rare that splits on them can't clear min_child_weight; max_delta_step is the other knob there. (13)
22Are a booster's probabilities calibrated?
Often roughly, if it's trained and early-stopped on log loss; reweighting, too many rounds or a large learning rate break it, so always check.
Why it can be calibrated: log loss is a proper scoring rule: it's minimized by the true probabilities, so an honest fit is rewarded.

What breaks it: past the best round, groups get pushed toward 0 and 1 (on the toy, 200 trees put one- and two-row groups at 0.000 and 1.000); scale_pos_weight, class weights and undersampling multiply the odds; tiny leaves and large eta make extreme steps.

How to check and fix: a reliability curve on held-out, out-of-time data; Platt scaling (a logistic regression on the raw score) with little data, isotonic regression with more, fitted on data not used for training or early stopping.

Follow-up: Platt scaling is strictly increasing, so the ranking and AUC are unchanged; isotonic regression creates ties, so AUC can shift slightly. Calibration matters when the probability itself is used, for pricing or expected loss. (13)
23Can gradient boosting extrapolate? Does it need feature scaling? What about outliers?
It can't extrapolate, it doesn't need scaling, and outliers in features are harmless while outliers in the target matter under squared error.

Extrapolation: each tree is flat beyond its last split, so the sum is too. A simulated booster predicted a limit of 242.6 at incomes of 150, 300 and 600 where the truth was 240, 480 and 960. Fixes: predict a ratio that stays in range, boost the residual of a linear model, or use linear leaves.
Scaling: a split only uses the order of a feature's values, so any monotone transform gives the same splits.

Outliers: a feature outlier just sits at one end (and shares the last histogram bin). A target outlier has a huge residual that every tree chases: 2% of +₹500k typos took a simulated test RMSE from about 10 to 29.0; absolute error or Huber brought it back to 10.5 and 10.9.
Follow-up: monitor inputs that drift beyond the training range; the model will silently predict the edge value. (13)
24Gradient boosting vs random forest vs a neural net on tabular data?
Boosting is usually the most accurate on typical tables, a forest is the robust low-effort alternative, and neural nets win with very large data, unstructured inputs, sequences or multimodal setups.

Why trees win on tables: tabular targets are irregular (thresholds, steps) and nets are biased toward smooth functions; useless columns hurt an MLP but a tree just never splits on them; and columns have individual meanings that trees use one at a time, while an MLP must learn which directions matter.
Practical edges of trees: no scaling, native missing values and categories, monotone constraints, TreeSHAP, cheap training.

When nets win: raw text or images in the row, transaction sequences, huge data, shared embeddings across tasks, end-to-end training with other modalities. Tabular foundation models are now competitive on small tables.
Trade-off: boosting needs early stopping and some tuning; a forest needs almost none; ensembles of a booster and a net often beat both. (14)
25What does XGBoost add over classic gradient boosting? How can it be parallel if boosting is sequential?
Second-order split finding, regularization inside the objective, learned missing-value directions, faster split search and column subsampling; it's parallel inside each tree, not across trees.
Splits from g and h : classic GBM grows each tree by squared error on -g and adds a Newton step only in the leaves; XGBoost uses the second-order gain for both.
Regularization: lambda , alpha , gamma and min_child_weight in the objective, plus column subsampling by tree, level or node.
Missing values: a default direction learned per split.
Speed: sorted column blocks, weighted quantile sketches, histograms, GPU and distributed training.

Parallelism: each tree needs the previous predictions, so trees are sequential; but computing g and h for all rows, building histograms and scanning features all run in parallel within a tree. Follow-up: for squared error with lambda = 0 , classic GBM and XGBoost grow the same trees, since h = 1 . (06, 09)
26AdaBoost vs gradient boosting?

AdaBoost reweights rows each round and gives each weak learner a vote; it turns out to be forward stagewise modelling with the exponential loss, and gradient boosting generalizes it to any differentiable loss.
beginaligned alpha_m &= tfrac12 logfrac1 - epsilon_mepsilon_m \\ w_i &propto e^-y_i F(x_i) endaligned

In words: a learner with weighted error epsilon gets a vote alpha , and a row's weight is its current exponential loss, which is also the size of that loss's gradient (labels are ±1). So AdaBoost carries the gradient as a weight instead of fitting it as a target.

Why gradient boosting replaced it: the exponential loss grows exponentially with a confident mistake, so a mislabelled row gets an enormous weight; log loss grows only linearly there. Follow-up: AdaBoost's score is half the log-odds, so its probability is sigma(2F) .
27Hand drills: work these with a pen.
Small numbers that exercise every formula in this note.
A leaf has G = -3 , H = 2 . Its value with lambda = 1 ? With lambda = 0 ? → 3/3 = 1.0; 3/2 = 1.5.
Three non-defaulters at p = 0.5 , lambda = 1 : G , H , leaf? → g = 0.5 each, G = 1.5 ; h = 0.25 each, H = 0.75 ; w = −1.5/1.75 = −0.857, pushing their risk down.
Regression residuals 10, 20 on the left and −30 on the right, lambda = 0 : gain? → ½ × [30²/2 + 30²/1 − 0²/3] = ½ × [450 + 900] = 675.
Log loss, F_0 = 0 , eta = 0.3 . Tree 1: late < 1.5 → −1 / +2. Tree 2: late < 1.5 → −0.718 / +1.549. A new applicant with 1 late payment: p ? → F = 0.3 × (−1) + 0.3 × (−0.718) = −0.515, so p = 0.374.
Squared error, F_0 = 80 , eta = 0.3 . Tree 1: late < 1.5 → +15 / −30. Tree 2: late < 0.5 → +15.5 / −15.5. The same applicant? → 80 + 4.5 − 4.65 = 79.85 (tree 2 sends late = 1 right).
Missing rows with G_miss = -1 , H_miss = 0.5 ; present left 1, 1 and right -1, 0.5 ; lambda = 1 . Which side? → right: ½ × [1/2 + 4/2 − 1/3] = 1.083; left: ½ × [0 + 1/1.5 − 1/3] = 0.167.
True risk 10%, scale_pos_weight = 9: predicted probability? → odds 0.111 × 9 = 1, so 0.5.
Follow-up: if you can do these without notes, you can rebuild any node of any tree in this note.
28Write the pseudocode for gradient boosting and for one XGBoost split search.

Start at the best constant; each round compute g and h , grow a tree by sweeping sorted features with running sums and scoring each cut with the gain (trying missing rows on both sides), set leaves to -G/(H + lambda) , and add eta times the tree.

F = F0 for all rows repeat M times: g, h = slope, bend of loss at F tree = GROW(rows, g, h) F += eta * tree(X) # in GROW, at each node (mcw = # min_child_weight): for each feature f: Gm, Hm = sums over rows missing f GL = HL = 0 for each cut, in sorted order of f: GL += g; HL += h for side in (left, right): add (Gm, Hm) to that side's sums GR = G - GL; HR = H - HL skip if HL or HR < mcw gain = ½(GL²/(HL+λ) + GR²/(HR+λ) - G²/(H+λ)) - γ keep the best (f, cut, side) leaf value = -G / (H + λ)

Why it's shaped like this: the gain needs only sums, so one sorted sweep scores every cut; the missing rows' sums are computed once and tried on both sides. Follow-up: the cost is one linear sweep per feature per node after a single upfront sort, or a sweep over at most 256 bins with histograms. Full versions and a runnable NumPy build: section 16.
beginaligned F(x) &= F_0 + eta sum_m f_m(x) \\ F_0 &= bar y quad or quad logfracbar y1 - bar y \\ p &= sigma(F) quad (once, at the end) endaligned
beginaligned squared error:quad g &= F - y \\ h &= 1 \\ log loss:quad g &= p - y \\ h &= p(1 - p) \\ pseudo-residual:quad r &= -g endaligned

beginaligned ell(F + w) &approx ell(F) + g w + tfrac12 h w^2 \\ w^* &= -fracGH + lambda \\ Obj^* &= -frac12 sum_j fracG_j^2H_j + lambda + gamma T \\ Gain &= tfrac12 Big[tfracG_L^2H_L + lambda + tfracG_R^2H_R + lambda \\ &qquad - tfracG^2H + lambdaBig] - gamma \\ w^*_L1 &= -fracsign(G)\, (lvert G rvert - alpha)_+H + lambda endaligned
Settings in one line each
eta : shrinks every tree; smaller needs more trees, generalizes a little better.
lambda : adds to H ; shrinks small-hessian leaves. gamma : minimum gain per split (XGBoost: no ½).
min_child_weight: minimum H per child; for log loss, rows weighted by p(1 - p) .
Missing: try (G_miss, H_miss) on each side; keep the better as the default direction.
scale_pos_weight k : odds × k ; subtract log k or recalibrate.
Monotone: reject violating splits; midpoint (w_L + w_R)/2 bounds each subtree.
LightGBM: leaf-wise (num_leaves), GOSS weight (1 - a)/b , EFB, categories sorted by G/(H + s) with s = cat_smooth.
CatBoost: ordered target statistic big(sum_earlier y + a cdot priorbig)/(n_earlier + a) , ordered boosting, symmetric trees.
SHAP: F(x) = phi_0 + sum_j phi_j , in log-odds.

notes.title: The data science project lifecycle
notes.desc: From a business problem to a monitored model: framing, metrics, labels, validation, baselines, error analysis, A/B tests, deployment, monitoring and communication, on one running credit example.

sections.t: The loop, and the running example
Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
Out of time, with a gap
The untouched holdout, and how big it must be
Reason codes for a declined applicant
Why offline gains often don't transfer
Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
Cheat sheet: the lifecycle as a checklist

chunks.x: The data science project lifecycle · Deepam Minda
Start from the decision, not the model: business objective → the decision the prediction changes → the ML task. If no decision changes, there's no project.

Choose metrics in layers: a business metric, an offline metric that measures the model where the decision is made, online metrics for the experiment, and guardrails, all fixed before you look. Thresholds come from the costs of each mistake; calibration matters whenever a score is used as a probability.

The label and the split define “better”. Write the label and its window down, never count outcomes that haven't matured as negatives, and validate out of time, grouped by customer, with a holdout you touch once.
Baseline first: today's policy, then logistic regression, then gradient boosting. Most of the gain comes from labels, features and error analysis, not from tuning.

Offline wins often fail online through selection bias, proxy metrics, drift and training–serving skew. Shadow mode checks the plumbing; a randomized champion–challenger with loss caps checks the value.

After launch, watch what you can see now (data quality, input and score drift, early outcomes) while the real labels arrive. Retrain on evidence, not habit, and guard against feedback loops where the model decides which labels you get.

chunks.h: The loop, and the running example
chunks.x: A project is a loop, not a line. Each stage hands a decision to the next, and later stages keep sending you back: error analysis to the labels, a flat experiment to the metric, monitoring to retraining or to a new framing. Each box below is a section of this note.

chunks.h: The loop, and the running example
chunks.x: The lifecycle as a loop. Purple stages define the problem, blue ones build the model, green ones ship and run it. Monitoring feeds new labels back for retraining, or sends you back to framing when the business changes. Error analysis sends you back to the data far more often than to the model.

A digital lender offers small unsecured personal loans, about ₹50,000 over 12 months, applied for and decided inside its app in seconds. Today it approves with a credit-bureau score cut-off plus a few policy rules (identity verified, no serious delinquency right now). It approves 40% of applicants, and 6% of the loans it makes go bad. The business asks: can a model approve more good borrowers without raising losses?
The economics, used throughout (1 lakh = 100,000):
Interest earned, minus funding and running costs
On average ₹35,000 is still owed when a loan defaults (the exposure at default), and 80% of it is never recovered (the loss given default)
So the expected loss on a loan is the textbook product:
EL = PD times LGD times EAD

In words: the chance it defaults (PD), times the share lost if it does (LGD, here 0.8), times what's owed at that point (EAD, here ₹35,000). At 10,000 applications a month, the lender makes 4,000 loans and 240 of them default: about ₹67 lakh of each month's lending is lost to defaults over the loans' life, while the 3,760 good loans earn about ₹1.9 crore.
Framing turns a vague goal into three precise statements, in this order:
Business objective: grow lending profit, meaning more approvals at no higher loss rate.
Decision: for each application, when it's submitted, approve or decline, and at what limit.
ML task: estimate the probability of default (PD): the chance this applicant goes 90+ days past due within 12 months, using only what is known at application time.

Keep the prediction separate from the decision. The model outputs a PD; a policy turns the PD into approve, decline or a limit. The cut-off can then move when funding costs or risk appetite change, without retraining, and each part can be tested on its own. It also means the PD has to be a real probability, not just a ranking (03).
Five questions before any data work

Is ML needed at all? A model earns its place when the decision repeats often enough for small gains to add up, rules leave value on the table, labels exist or can be collected, and the pattern is stable enough to learn. Here: 10,000 decisions a month, ₹67 lakh of monthly losses and years of labelled loans, so yes. With 200 applications a month, a points scorecard or a credit officer is the better tool.
What's the baseline heuristic? Today's bureau cut-off plus rules. The project's value is the gap between the model and this policy at the same approval rate, not the gap to random guessing.

What action will the prediction drive? Approve, decline, set the limit, perhaps the price. If nothing can change (a partner fixes the policy, say), there's no project. Note too that the action creates the label: only approved loans can default (04).

What does a mistake cost? Call default the positive class. A false negative, approving someone who defaults, costs about ₹28,000. A false positive, declining someone who would have repaid, costs the ₹5,000 margin plus that customer's future business. The costs differ more than fivefold, so accuracy, which counts them equally, is the wrong yardstick.
What are the constraints?
Latency: the applicant is waiting, and the bureau call takes most of the few seconds available.
Interpretability: a declined applicant must be told the main reasons, and the credit-risk team must be able to audit the model.
Regulation and consent: only data the applicant agreed to share; no protected attributes such as religion or gender, and no obvious proxies for them.
Timing: only data that exists at the moment of decision. Anything recorded later is leakage.
Size the prize before you start

The ceiling: a perfect model at today's 40% approval rate would swap all 240 monthly defaulters for good borrowers. Each swap gains the loss avoided plus the margin earned, ₹28,000 + ₹5,000, so the ceiling is about ₹79 lakh a month.
A realistic target: swapping a quarter of them, 60 a month, is worth about ₹20 lakh a month. Set against what a model actually delivers, it later decides when to ship (13).
Write it down in a one-page framing document:
the objective, the decision, and who owns it;
the prediction target, the moment it's made, and the unit (the applicant, not each application);
the baseline, the metric and the constraints;
a success criterion, and a kill criterion such as “if the model can't beat today's policy by an agreed margin at today's approval rate on out-of-time data, we stop”.

Solving the wrong problem. Many loans that miss the very first instalment are fraud: the borrower never meant to pay. That needs identity and device signals, not credit history, and mixing the two blurs both models.
No lever: an accurate prediction that nobody can act on.
A vague prediction time. “Predict default” without “as of the application” later lets post-decision data leak in.
The wrong task type: a yes/no classifier when the decision needs a probability (pricing, limits, expected loss) or a ranking (a review queue).
What a senior person checks
“If the model were perfect, what would we do differently, and what's that worth?”
“What exactly is known at the moment of prediction?”
“What does today's policy achieve, measured the same way?”
“Who owns the decision, and have they signed off the success and kill criteria?”
Four layers, each answering a different question:
Profit per application; loss rate at the approval rate
Is the new model better on past data?
Bad rate at today's approval rate; Gini (2·AUC − 1); calibration by score band
Early delinquency of the new model's loans; approval rate
Approvals for thin-file applicants (little credit history); fairness gaps; latency; complaints; early fraud

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: The business metric is slow (defaults take a year) or can't be computed offline (you never see what declined applicants would have done). So you need an offline stand-in, and it has to pass four tests:

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: It measures where the decision is made. The lender will approve about 40%, so what matters is the ordering around that cut-off. AUC averages over every possible cut-off, including ones nobody will use. Report the bad rate among the 40% the model would approve, next to AUC. Some of those 40% were declined in the past and have no outcome, so they must be filled in (04), which is why the live test has the final word.

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: It's weighted by money when amounts vary. A model that catches many small defaults and misses the large ones wins on counts and loses on rupees. Count each default by its rupee loss (exposure × loss given default), not as 1.

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: It matches how the score is used. If only the order matters (a fixed approval rate, a review queue), ranking metrics are enough: AUC; Gini = 2\,AUC - 1 , which rescales it so random ordering scores 0 and perfect ordering 1; and KS, the largest gap between the score distributions of goods and bads. If the number itself is used (expected loss, pricing, a cut-off from the economics), add calibration.

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: It has predicted online results before. Across past model changes, did offline gains turn into live gains? If not, fix the offline metric before trusting it.

chunks.h: Choosing an offline metric that tracks the business one
chunks.x: The most faithful offline metric is a simulation of the decision itself: run the new policy over past applications and add up the profit. Its blind spot is that past outcomes exist only for approved applicants (04).
Approve when the expected gain beats the expected loss. With PD p , gain G if the loan is repaid and loss L if it isn't:
(1 - p)\,G > p\,L quadLongleftrightarrowquad p < p^* = fracGG + L

In words: approve while the chance of default is below the break-even point, where the margin on good loans exactly pays for the bad ones. Here p^* = 5,000 / 33,000 approx 15\% . It's the general rule t^* = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) with C_FP = G and C_FN = L .
With 1,000 applicants in each risk band, approving from the safest band down:

Profit peaks after band C. Approving band D still leaves the whole book profitable (the average PD of A to D is under 15%), but every band-D loan loses money. Set the cut-off where the marginal applicant breaks even, not where the average does.

Other ways the threshold gets set: a risk-appetite cap on the portfolio's bad rate (the lender may stop short of the profit maximum); capacity, where a “refer” band around the cut-off goes to manual underwriting, sized to the team; or a target approval rate. Whatever the method, choose it on validation data, confirm it on the test set, and revisit it when costs or the applicant mix change.

The limit follows the same logic. A bigger limit raises the margin on a good loan and the exposure on a bad one, and can raise the PD itself if the repayment strains the borrower's income. Offer the largest limit at which (1 - p)\,G still beats p\,L , with p , G and L all evaluated at that limit.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: A model is calibrated if, among applicants given a PD of 10%, about 10% default:

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: Pr(y = 1 mid hat p = q) = q quad for every q

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: The break-even rule uses the PD as a probability, so it needs calibration. Suppose every PD came out at half its true value. Band D would show 9%, below the 15% break-even, and be approved at a loss. AUC, Gini and KS wouldn't move, because the order is unchanged.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: Check it on out-of-time data: the predicted against the observed bad rate in each score band, the average predicted PD against the observed rate, and a proper score such as the Brier score or log loss.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: Fix it with Platt scaling (a two-parameter logistic fit to the scores) or isotonic regression (any monotone correction; needs more data), fitted on recent held-out data. Both are monotone, so the ranking barely changes (isotonic's flat steps create a few ties). If you reweighted or undersampled the classes, the probabilities are inflated by design and must be corrected before use.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: It breaks before the ranking does. A recession raises every applicant's risk: the order may hold while every PD is too low. So recalibration is a cheaper, more frequent fix than retraining.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: Metrics that must not get worse, each with a margin agreed before the test: approvals for thin-file applicants (people with little credit history, whom a bureau-heavy model can shut out), approval and error rates across groups, decision latency at the 99th percentile, the complaint rate, and the first-payment default rate (first instalment missed: an early fraud signal).

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: AUC chosen because it's the default, though the business works at one cut-off.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability
chunks.x: Accuracy on a 6% positive class: approving everyone is 94% accurate.

chunks.h: Calibration, when the score is used as a probability

For each source ask: is it available at decision time, within the latency budget? What share of applicants have it? Are we allowed to use it for lending? Will it still exist, with the same meaning, next year?

Point-in-time correctness. Each training row must see the data exactly as it was at its application timestamp: the bureau report pulled then, the app history up to then. Joining today's value of a table (current balance, current address) leaks the future into the past.
“Default” is a definition you choose, and it should match the loss the business cares about:

The event: 90+ days past due (DPD) is the usual “bad” for consumer loans. It's the standard regulatory default definition and where many regulators class a loan as non-performing. Write-offs and settlements for less than was owed count as bad too.
The window: within the first 12 months on book. Too short misses late defaults; too long makes the newest complete labels very old.
Exclusions: loans cancelled during the cooling-off period, deaths, and confirmed fraud, which belongs to a fraud model.

Indeterminates: loans that reached, say, 30–89 DPD and recovered. Scorecard practice often drops them from training to sharpen the contrast between good and bad, but they stay in evaluation (counted as goods), because they'll be scored in production. Dropping them raises the training bad rate, so calibrate on the full population.

Choosing the window. Plot vintage curves: for each monthly batch of loans, the cumulative bad rate by months on book. Pick the point where the curves flatten, so most eventual defaults have shown up. A roll-rate table (what share of loans at 30 DPD go on to 90 DPD) tells you whether an earlier, lower threshold is a good stand-in.
With a 12-month window, the newest complete labels are at least a year old. Three ways to live with that:
Never count immature loans as good. A loan paid out last month hasn't had time to default. Train and evaluate only on cohorts whose window has closed.

Early proxy labels: first-payment default (the first instalment missed) or 30+ DPD at 3 months on book. Validate each on old vintages: does it rank applicants and model versions the same way the full label does?
Use partial outcomes: a survival (time-to-default) model treats an immature loan as censored, survived so far, rather than good, so recent loans still contribute.

“The last few months look much cleaner.” If last quarter's bad rate is half the long-run rate, the borrowers didn't improve: their labels haven't arrived. Training on them teaches the model that whatever is typical of recent applicants is safe.
Outcomes exist only for approved applicants, but the model will score everyone who applies. Three consequences:
The training population (approved) is safer than the scoring population (all applicants), and the riskiest region has no labels at all, so the model extrapolates there.

If past approvals used information the model doesn't have, such as an underwriter's judgement, the approved members of a risky-looking group were the best of that group. The model then underestimates risk for the rest of it.
Gini measured on approved loans alone understates the model, because the old cut-off already removed the riskiest applicants.

Reject inference, in one line: estimating what declined applicants would have done. Best done by approving a small, capped, random slice below the cut-off; next best from their bureau outcomes at other lenders; least reliably by statistical patches (reweighting, inferred labels), which add assumptions rather than information.
Other sampling biases to name: a new acquisition channel changes who applies, and the training period may be unusual (a boom year, a lockdown).

A data contract is an agreement between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that use it: the schema, what each field means (is a null “no history” or “not fetched”?), how fresh it is, and how changes are announced and versioned. Without one, an upstream team renames a code or changes a unit, and the model quietly degrades.
Checks to automate, in training and in serving:
schema and types; one row per application;
null rates and ranges against expected bounds, including sentinel values like −999 that mean “missing”;
row counts and freshness against expected volumes;
distributions against a reference period, with the population stability index (PSI, 12);
the label rate by cohort: a sudden jump usually means a definition or pipeline change, not a change in borrowers.
A training run should stop on a failed check. Live scoring should alert and fall back.
Post-decision fields used as features: collections calls, the limit actually granted, a bureau report pulled after the application, which already shows this lender's own enquiry or even the new loan.
Fraud and credit losses mixed in one label.
One person's repeat applications in both training and test.
A feature that exists in the warehouse but can't be computed in real time.
What a senior person checks
“Show me the label definition, and the vintage curves behind the window.”
“For each feature, when is it known relative to the decision?”
“Who owns each source, and what happens when it changes?”

Inside a project, exploratory analysis has one job: confirm the data means what you think before anything is built on it. Cleaning, imputation, encoding and feature construction are covered in depth in the companion note, Data preparation and feature engineering; this section is the lifecycle view.
What to look at first, in this order:
Volumes over time: applications and approvals by month. Gaps and jumps are pipeline events or policy changes you need to know about.
The label by cohort: the bad rate by the month loans were paid out. It shows maturity, policy changes and seasonality at once.
Missingness, and what it means: “no bureau record” describes a thin-file applicant, not a data error. Keep that information as a feature rather than imputing it away.
Single-feature power: a feature that separates goods from bads almost perfectly on its own is leakage until proven otherwise.
Stability: each feature's distribution month by month. A feature that drifted a lot in the past will drift in production.
Preparation decisions that matter for the rest of the lifecycle:
every transformation (scaling, imputation, encoding, binning) is fitted on training data only, inside a pipeline, so it's refit in each fold and applied identically when serving;
aggregates such as “payments in the last 90 days” are computed as of the application timestamp;
the same feature code runs in training and in serving, or you'll meet training–serving skew (11).

Where it goes wrong: imputing with statistics from all the data, including the test period; dropping rows with missing bureau data, which silently removes thin-file applicants, the very group the business wants to grow; hours of plots that never change a decision.
What a senior person checks: “Which findings changed the label, the split or the features?” If none, the EDA was decoration.
Decide how “better” will be measured before training anything. The split defines the question the score answers, and choosing it after seeing results invites leakage and wishful thinking.

chunks.h: Out of time, with a gap
chunks.x: Why not a random split: interest rates, the economy, the marketing mix and the product all move. A random split mixes periods, so the test looks like the training data and hides that drift. If a random split scores much higher than the out-of-time one, something leaks through time or the relationship is drifting.

chunks.h: Out of time, with a gap
chunks.x: A gap, if history allows: in production, the newest data a model can learn from is at least a year older than the applicants it scores, because of the label window. Leaving a gap between the training and test periods copies that, so the test shows the decay you'll really face. In the table, the validation quarter doubles as a 3-month gap; to see the full decay, also train on months 1–9 and test on 22–24. Without a gap, expect the live model to do somewhat worse than the test says.

chunks.h: Out of time, with a gap

chunks.h: Out of time, with a gap
chunks.x: One person can apply many times. If their applications land on both sides, the model is graded partly on memory. Within the training period, split folds by customer (group k-fold), and on the test set report returning and new applicants separately.

chunks.h: The untouched holdout, and how big it must be
chunks.x: Every decision made while looking at a dataset uses it up: its score becomes optimistic. The test set is looked at once, at the end, after every choice is frozen. Its size is set by the number of bads, not rows. With 300 bads in the test set (three months of this lender's loans hold about 700), AUC has a standard error of about 0.016, so a 95% interval is about ±0.03 (±0.06 in Gini). A 0.005 AUC gain is noise. To compare two models, use a paired bootstrap on the same rows, which is much tighter than two separate intervals because the models' errors are correlated.

chunks.h: The untouched holdout, and how big it must be
chunks.x: Where it goes wrong: random splits on time-ordered data; tuning on the test set (“just one more look”); too few bads in the test to tell models apart; a validation period that's unusual, such as a festive season or a policy change.

Before a strong model, build the simplest things that could work, and evaluate them exactly as the final model will be: same test set, same operating point. Illustrative numbers:
Today's policy (the bar to beat): bureau cut-off and rules
Logistic regression, 10 binned features (what simple features carry)
Gradient boosting, 150 features (what interactions add)

At 4,000 loans a month, going from 6.0% to 5.0% is 40 fewer defaults, worth about 40 × ₹33,000 ≈ ₹13 lakh a month. One caveat a reviewer will raise: a model's top 40% includes applicants the old policy declined, who have no outcomes. Their outcomes are filled in from bureau records at other lenders or by reject inference (04), so these figures are estimates until the live test (10).
They set the bar. The project's value is the gap to today's policy, not to random.
They catch bugs and leakage. If boosting beats logistic regression by a mile, look for a leaking feature before celebrating. If nothing beats the policy, the features may carry little signal.

They price complexity. Logistic regression is easier to explain, audit and monitor. Here boosting cuts the bad rate a further 0.3 points (5.3% → 5.0%), 12 defaults or about ₹4 lakh a month: that has to be worth more than its extra cost in maintenance and explanation.
They're the fallback. A simple model or the rules can decide when the main model is down.

Then iterate, one change at a time. Log every experiment (data version, features, parameters, the score with its interval), and keep a change only if its gain beats the noise. The usual order of payoff: fix labels and leakage, add strong features, choose the model, and only then tune.
Where it goes wrong: no baseline, so a Gini of 0.56 means nothing; a straw-man baseline (untuned, missing obvious features) that flatters the new model; baselines scored on a different split.
What a senior person checks: “What's the gain over today's policy at the operating point, with an interval, and is it worth the complexity?”
Tabular data, thousands of rows or more
Mixed types, missing values and interactions out of the box; scores in milliseconds; explained with SHAP
Small data, or transparency above all
Logistic regression, or a points scorecard on binned features
Each feature's effect is a few numbers anyone can audit
Sequences of transactions
Aggregates (counts, sums, trends) fed to the booster first
A sequence model costs latency and explainability; add one only if it beats good aggregates
A pretrained encoder, its embeddings fed to the booster
Labels are scarce; reuse what's already learned

For the lender: gradient boosting with monotonic constraints, so predicted risk can never fall as missed payments rise, or as the share of income already going to loan repayments rises. They usually cost little accuracy, and they make the model stable across retrains, explainable, and defensible in a credit review.
Constraints shape the choice as much as accuracy: latency, explanation requirements, how often it must be retrained, and what the team can maintain.
For boosting, a handful of settings matter:
the learning rate and number of trees, set together through early stopping;
tree size: depth or number of leaves, and the minimum data in a leaf;
row and column subsampling;
L2 regularization on the leaf values.

Random search or Bayesian optimization over these, with log scales for the learning rate and regularization, finds good settings in a few dozen trials. A grid wastes most of its trials on settings that barely matter. Tune on the validation period, never on the test. Expect small gains: tuning rarely adds as much as a better label or one strong feature, and the best of many noisy trials is optimistic (the winner's curse), which is why the test set stays untouched.

Train with a small learning rate, score the validation set after each tree, and stop once the validation loss hasn't improved for, say, 100 trees. The number of trees becomes a fitted quantity instead of a guess, and training stops before the model starts memorizing noise. Two cautions: early-stop on validation, never on test; and when refitting on training plus validation data for the final model, reuse the tree count you found (or scale it up a little for the extra data).

Refit before shipping, or ship what you tested? Refitting on all matured data, test quarter included, buys recency, which matters when the world drifts. But the refit model is no longer the one you measured, and the calibrator and threshold were fitted on validation data it has now trained on. A common answer: refit with every setting frozen, refit the calibrator on a recent held-out slice, and check the result in shadow mode before the ramp.
Imbalance and reproducibility
A 6% bad rate isn't extreme. Train on the natural rate. If you reweight or undersample, recalibrate afterwards (03).
Every model must be rebuildable from a code commit, a data snapshot and a config: fixed seeds, pinned library versions, logged parameters. In lending you may have to explain a two-year-old decision.

Where it goes wrong: tuning before fixing the data; picking the top of a leaderboard whose differences are noise; an ensemble too slow to serve inside the latency budget; a model that's non-monotone in a way no credit officer can defend.
What a senior person checks
“What did tuning add over the defaults, and is it bigger than the noise?”
“Can we rebuild this exact model from the commit and the data snapshot?”
An aggregate metric hides where the model fails. Error analysis finds the biggest fixable failure, and it sends you back to the data far more often than to the model.

Compute the operating-point metric and the calibration for each segment that matters: bureau record or thin file, acquisition channel, loan-amount band, salaried or self-employed, new or returning, region. Report each slice's size and interval, because small slices are noisy. The typical finding is one segment, often thin-file applicants, that is much worse or badly calibrated, hidden by the average.
Sort the failures into buckets

Read the worst errors: the confident ones, such as applicants given a PD under 3% who defaulted, and high-PD applicants who repaid. Group them by cause, estimate what fixing each bucket would gain, and fix the biggest first.

Global: what drives the model. SHAP importance, the average absolute contribution of each feature, is more reliable than the trees' built-in split-gain importance, which favours features with many distinct values.

Shape: how a feature acts. A partial dependence plot shows the average predicted PD as one feature varies. Check that it moves the way the domain expects (risk rises with credit utilization). With correlated features it averages over impossible combinations, so read it with care; accumulated local effects (ALE) plots avoid this.
Local: why this applicant. SHAP splits one prediction into per-feature contributions, in log-odds for a boosted classifier, that add up to this applicant's prediction minus the average prediction.

chunks.h: Reason codes for a declined applicant
chunks.x: In many jurisdictions a lender must tell a declined applicant the main reasons. From SHAP: take the features that pushed this applicant's risk up the most, and map each to a fixed, plain-language reason, such as “recent missed payments” or “high use of existing credit limits”. Group correlated features under one reason. Good reason codes are:
