chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Selection bias. The test set holds only applicants the old policy approved. A new model differs from that policy mostly on applicants it declined, and their outcomes were never seen.

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Proxy mismatch. The offline metric (Gini) isn't the business metric (profit at the cut-off).

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Drift. By launch, the test period is months old: new channels, new rates, a different economy.

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Training–serving skew. Live features are computed differently from training features (11).

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Gains in the wrong place. Better ordering among applicants far from the cut-off changes no decision.

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Behaviour. Applicants and fraudsters react to a new policy; a looser cut-off attracts riskier applicants.

chunks.h: Why offline gains often don't transfer
chunks.x: Leakage made the offline score too good to begin with.

Line up the old and new policies at the same approval rate. Most applicants get the same decision from both. What matters are the swap-outs, approved by the old policy and declined by the new, and the swap-ins, declined by the old and approved by the new. Swap-outs have outcomes, because the old policy approved them. Swap-ins mostly don't. So the offline case for the new model rests on half the evidence, and only a live test supplies the other half.
Score live applications with the new model, keep acting on the old policy, and log both. It checks the plumbing at no risk:
latency and timeouts under real load;
feature parity: the live features against the same features recomputed offline for the same applications;
the live score distribution against the out-of-time test (a large population stability index, PSI, points to skew or drift);
the size and make-up of the swap sets.
It can't tell you whether swap-ins repay. Only approving some of them can.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: What to randomize: applicants, by a hash of the customer ID, not individual applications, so someone who reapplies stays in the same arm. Most applicants go to the current model (the champion), a small slice, say 10%, to the new one (the challenger).

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: Protection: hard policy rules apply in both arms; the challenger gets loss caps (smaller first limits for its swap-ins, a ceiling on total exposure) and a kill switch tied to the guardrails.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: Primary metric: profit per applicant, or the bad rate compared at the same approval rate, never the raw bad rate.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: Guardrails: approvals for thin-file applicants, fairness gaps, first-payment default, latency, complaints.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: Duration and power: each group needs about n approx 16\,p(1-p)/delta^2 loans (80% power, 5% significance). Comparing whole arms, seeing 30+ DPD at 3 months on book fall from 3.0% to 2.5% needs about 18,000 loans per arm: four years for a 10% challenger making 400 loans a month.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: So read the swap sets, where the gap is large. If about 15% of approvals swap, the 6.0% → 5.0% gain means swap-outs default at roughly 12% and swap-ins at roughly 5%. On the full label, about 300 swap-ins then suffice: five months of the challenger's lending at about 60 a month. Early-delinquency proxies give a first read a quarter after that; the full label takes a year.

chunks.h: Champion–challenger: the A/B test for credit
chunks.x: “The challenger's bad rate is lower, so it's better.” A model that approves fewer people almost always has a lower bad rate. Compare at the same approval rate, on profit per applicant, or on the swap sets directly: the challenger's swap-ins against the champion's swap-outs.
Check the split first. The arms' sizes must match the design (a chi-square test for sample ratio mismatch). A mismatch means assignment or logging is broken, and nothing downstream can be trusted.
Pre-register one primary metric, the guardrails with their margins, the duration and the analysis.
Don't peek. Stopping the first time p < 0.05 inflates false positives, unless a sequential test was planned.
Read an interval, not just a p-value: does its low end still beat the cost of the change?
Check consistency across months and the pre-registered segments, without hunting through dozens of segments for a winner.
Read only matured cohorts, on a proxy that has been validated against the full label.
Where it goes wrong: comparing bad rates at different approval rates; randomizing by application; reading immature cohorts; no loss caps; declaring victory on an unvalidated proxy.
What a senior person checks
“What did shadow mode show about feature parity?”
“Are we comparing at the same approval rate, or on profit?”
“Which proxy are we reading, and has it ranked models correctly before?”
The decision can wait: pre-approved offers, collections lists, nightly limit reviews
Someone is waiting: a loan application, a payment
Simple, cheap, easy to rerun and audit
Scores go stale between runs
Needs online features, low latency, high availability and a fallback
The application decision is real time. Pre-approved limits for existing customers could be batch, refreshed nightly.
Split the time the applicant waits into parts, and give each an owner. An example for a 3-second decision:
About 2 s: the biggest part, and the least controllable

Budget for the slowest 1% of requests, not the average. Decide the fallback in advance: if the bureau times out, refer the application or decide on rules alone. A timeout must never turn into a silent approval.
The model sees different numbers live than it saw in training, even though nothing is “wrong” in either place. Typical causes:
two code paths: SQL in the warehouse for training, service code for serving;
different windows for aggregates, such as “last 30 days” ending at midnight in training but at the request time live;
late-arriving data that is in the warehouse but didn't exist at decision time;
different handling of nulls, defaults or categories never seen before.
The fixes: one feature definition used by both paths; log the features at serving time and train on the logged values; parity tests in shadow mode.

A feature store keeps each feature's definition once and serves it twice: an offline store with full history and point-in-time joins for training, and an online store with the latest values at low latency for serving. It prevents skew and lets models share features. It's also infrastructure with a running cost: for a single batch model, a well-tested feature pipeline is enough.
Versioning, reproducibility and rollback
Version everything that changes a decision: code, data snapshot, feature definitions, model file, configuration, and the policy (cut-offs, limits) separately from the model.
Log every decision with the model version, the features it saw and the reason codes. Lending decisions get disputed and audited months later.
Roll out in stages (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) behind a flag, with the previous model kept running. Rollback is then a config switch, not a redeploy.
Rollback doesn't undo loans. Every loan a bad model approved stays on the book for a year, so cap exposure during the ramp.
Where it goes wrong: a feature that can't be computed in real time; no fallback; the cut-off hard-coded inside model code; nobody able to say which model made a given decision.
What a senior person checks
“What happens when the bureau times out?”
“Which model version, and which feature values, decided this application last March?”
“How fast can we roll back, and how much exposure builds up meanwhile?”
Defaults take a year to show, so monitoring is mostly about what you can see before the labels arrive. Watch in layers, fastest first:
Latency, errors, timeouts, fallback rate
Nulls, ranges, schema, freshness, volumes
PSI or KS for each feature against training
Score PSI, approval rate, average PD, mix of reason codes
First-payment default; 30+ DPD by months on book, per monthly cohort
Performance may be slipping
Gini and calibration on matured cohorts
How good the model really is
PSI = sum_i (a_i - e_i)\, lnfraca_ie_i

In words: cut the feature (or the score) into bins on the training data, usually deciles, then compare the live share a_i with the training share e_i in each bin. Two bins moving from 50/50 to 40/60 give 0.04. The usual rule of thumb: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 worth a look, above 0.25 a real shift.

KS, used here as a drift test between training and live data, compares two distributions of a continuous feature by the largest gap between their cumulative shares. On large samples its p-value flags trivial shifts, so alert on the size of the statistic, not on significance.

Drift isn't degradation. A cashback campaign can shift spending features without changing anyone's risk; a recession can leave the inputs unchanged while risk rises (concept drift). Drift says “look”; outcomes say whether the model got worse.

With delayed labels, watch the vintage curves: each monthly cohort's 30+ DPD rate by months on book. A new cohort climbing faster than older ones at the same age is the earliest real warning, months before 90+ DPD shows.
A schedule (retrain every quarter) is simple and predictable, but it can be too frequent (no new labels have matured, so you refit noise) or too late (an abrupt shift).
Triggers retrain when there's a reason: early outcomes beyond a threshold, calibration off on recent cohorts, high PSI on important features or the score, or a new product, channel or policy.

Match the cadence to how fast labels arrive and how fast the world moves. A credit model gains new full labels only as cohorts mature, so monthly monitoring, recalibration when levels drift, and a rebuild every year or two (or on a trigger) is typical. A fraud model faces adversaries and gets most labels within weeks (some chargebacks take months), so weekly to monthly retraining is common.
Never auto-deploy a retrained model. It's a challenger: compare it with the champion on the latest matured data, then shadow and ramp it like any new model.

The model decides who gets a loan, and only those people produce labels. Each retrain sees a narrower, safer population, and the model can never learn that it was wrong about the people it declined. Mitigations:
a small, capped, random exploration slice below the cut-off, which keeps labels coming where the model is least sure;
logging the probability of each decision (in the exploration slice, where approval isn't certain either way), so later training can reweight;
keeping data from before the model's own policy took over.

A second loop: actions taken because of the score, such as early collections calls to high-PD borrowers, change the outcomes, so the next model learns from treated borrowers. Record the treatment, and account for it when building labels.
Where it goes wrong: monitoring only outcomes, which arrive too late; hundreds of drift alerts nobody reads; alerts with no owner or runbook; retraining on immature or treatment-contaminated labels.
What a senior person checks
“What would tell us the model is broken before the defaults arrive?”
“Who gets alerted, and what do they do?”
“How is a retrained model validated before it replaces the champion?”
Break the project into phases that each end in a decision:
Framing document, data audit, baseline numbers
Out-of-time results against today's policy, at the operating point
Is the gain real and big enough?
Feature parity, latency, swap-set profile
The durations are illustrative. The data audit is the step most often underestimated.

Credit risk owns the policy, product owns the applicant's experience, engineering owns serving, compliance owns data use and reason codes, finance owns the P&L, and operations owns collections and fraud. Bring compliance in during framing, not at launch: a feature vetoed late costs weeks. In regulated lending, an independent model-validation team also reviews the model before it goes live; book its time early.

Updates go in business terms, with the uncertainty and the next step: “On last year's applicants, at today's approval rate, the model would have cut defaults from 6.0% to 5.0%, about ₹13 lakh a month; the live test will tighten that estimate. Next: two weeks of shadow mode.” Lead with the decision and the money; the method comes after, if they ask.

Tie every request to the objective and the date. “Can it also set the interest rate?” becomes “Yes, as phase two. Adding it now moves the launch by six weeks. Which matters more?” Keep a written backlog, so the no is a “later”, not a refusal.
A model card lets someone who wasn't there understand, use and audit the model. It records:
the purpose, intended use, and uses it's not for (pricing, say, or applicant groups it never saw);
the data sources, label definition, training and test periods, and exclusions;
performance overall and by segment, with intervals, and calibration;
fairness checks and known limitations;
the monitoring plan, retraining triggers, owner and version.
Keep a decision log next to it: what was decided, when, by whom, and why.
Estimating timelines, and when to stop

Estimate per phase, as ranges, and re-estimate at each milestone. Data access, cleaning and label work usually take longer than modelling, and integration and compliance review need calendar time you don't control.

Stop polishing when the next gain is smaller than the noise, or worth less than the delay costs. Here the first model reaches about ₹13 lakh of the ₹20 lakh target: enough to clear the kill bar, so ship it, and chase the rest through challengers. Every month of waiting forgoes that ₹13 lakh.
Stop the project when the kill criterion hits. If the out-of-time gain over today's policy can't clear the agreed bar, say so early: a clear no is a result.
Where it goes wrong: building alone and unveiling a finished model nobody asked for; vetoes discovered at launch; promising a number before the data audit; decisions that live only in someone's head.
What a senior person checks
“Can the business owner state the success and kill criteria?”
“Could an auditor who wasn't here understand the model from its card?”
“Has independent model validation signed off, and on which version?”
The same few failures account for most projects that disappoint. For each, how it shows up and how to catch and fix it:
A good model nobody uses; “defaults” that are really fraud
Ask what decision changes; separate fraud from credit
Metric away from the cut-offmetrics
Bad rate at the operating point; rupee weighting; a profit simulation
Uncalibrated scoresmetrics
The right order but the wrong cut-off; losses above plan
Predicted against actual by band; recalibrate on recent data
Too-good scores; one feature dominates; random split far above out-of-time
Point-in-time features; pipelines; single-feature checks
Immature labels counted as gooddata
Recent cohorts look safest
Maturity windows; validated proxies; survival models
Selection biasdata, online
Fine on approved applicants, poor on swap-ins
Capped random approvals; champion–challenger
Random split on time-ordered datavalidation
The offline score is never seen again
Out-of-time split with a gap
Nobody can say whether the model adds value
Today's policy and a simple model, same test, same operating point

Test well below validation
An untouched holdout; fewer tuning rounds

The live score distribution differs from the test's
Log served features; one definition; parity checks in shadow
The challenger looks safer because it approves fewer

Feature and score PSI; vintage curves; retraining triggers
Each retrain sees a narrower population
An exploration slice; logged decision probabilities

Late launches; surprised stakeholders
Phases that end in decisions; compliance in from framing
Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own.
1Walk me through a project end to end.

Tell it as a chain of decisions: the business problem and the decision it drove, how success was measured, the label and the split, the baseline, the model and why, what error analysis changed, how it went live, how it's monitored, and the result in money.
A sample answer on a lending model, in about a minute:

“A lender approved loans with a bureau-score cut-off and wanted more approvals at the same loss rate. The decision was approve or decline at application time, so I framed it as predicting 90+ days past due within 12 months, using only data known at application.

Success was profit at today's approval rate. Offline, I tracked the bad rate at that approval rate, plus calibration, because the cut-off came from the economics: break-even at about 15% PD. I trained only on matured cohorts, with an out-of-time split grouped by customer and a test quarter touched once.

Against today's policy and a logistic regression, gradient boosting with monotonic constraints cut the bad rate at the same approval rate from 6.0% to 5.0%, about ₹13 lakh a month. Error analysis showed first-instalment defaults were mostly fraud, so they moved to the fraud model.

We ran it in shadow mode to check feature parity and latency, then as a 10% challenger with loss caps, reading early delinquency. It's monitored with feature and score PSI and vintage curves, and retrained on triggers.”
What the listener is scoring: the order (the decision before the model), numbers at the operating point, one or two real trade-offs you made, something that went wrong and how you caught it.
Have one stage ready to go deep on: the label definition, the validation design or the launch.

Trade-off: breadth against depth. Give the whole skeleton in the first minute, then offer to go deeper. Running out of time before evaluation and monitoring is the common failure, and it's what interviewers remember.
Follow-up: “What would you do differently?” Have a real answer, such as bringing compliance in at framing, starting a random exploration slice from day one, or agreeing the kill criterion up front.
2When would you not use ML?

When a rule gets most of the value, when no decision would change, when there are no labels and no way to get them, when the volume is too small to repay the cost, or when the decision must follow an explicit rule set by law or policy.
A rule is the requirement: eligibility set by law (minimum age, verified identity) is a rule, not a prediction.
Too few decisions: at 200 loan applications a month, a points scorecard or a credit officer beats a model that must be built, served, monitored and maintained for as long as it runs.
No labels: if outcomes can't be observed, or arrive too late to matter, start with rules and collect labels.
No lever: if nobody can act on the prediction, accuracy is worthless.
An unstable world: if the pattern changes faster than you can relearn it.

Trade-off: rules are transparent and quick but brittle and maintained by hand; a model generalizes but costs upkeep. In practice the answer is often rules first, then a model, then both together: hard rules for what must never happen, and a model for the grey zone.

Follow-up: “When do you switch from rules to a model?” When volume and the value of better decisions justify it, labels have accumulated, and a model beats the rules by a clear margin at the operating point.
3Why start with a baseline? How do you choose between logistic regression and gradient boosting?

A baseline sets the bar and exposes bugs. Logistic regression wins when data is small or transparency is paramount; boosting wins when there's enough data and interactions matter. The gap between them tells you whether the extra complexity pays.
Baselines: today's policy (the real bar: the project's value is the gap to it), then a simple model. Score all of them on the same out-of-time test, at the same operating point.
They catch problems: a model far above logistic regression usually means a leaking feature; nothing beating the policy means weak features.

Logistic regression or a scorecard: transparent, stable across retrains, easy to monitor, familiar to auditors. It needs binning or transforms for curved effects and misses interactions unless you build them.

Gradient boosting: captures interactions (“low income is fine if it's steady”), curved effects and missing values on its own. Monotonic constraints and SHAP make it explainable enough for most credit uses.

Trade-off: accuracy against simplicity and governance cost. Decide on the money: if boosting cuts the bad rate from 5.3% to 5.0% on 4,000 loans a month, that's 12 fewer defaults, about ₹4 lakh a month, to weigh against the cost of maintaining and explaining a bigger model.

Follow-up: “Boosting beats logistic regression by 0.15 Gini. Happy?” Suspicious. Check for leakage first: single-feature power, random against out-of-time scores, and when each top feature becomes known.
4How do you choose a metric?

Start from the decision and the cost of each mistake. Pick the business metric the decision moves, an offline metric that measures the model where the decision is made, and guardrails, all fixed before looking at results.

The decision sets the metric. A fixed approval rate needs good ordering at that rate (the bad rate among approvals). A cut-off from the economics needs calibrated probabilities. A review team that handles 500 cases a day needs precision in the top 500.
Weight by money when amounts differ: missing one large default can outweigh catching ten small ones.
Imbalance: accuracy is useless at a 6% bad rate (approving everyone scores 94%), and AUC averages over cut-offs nobody uses. Prefer metrics at the operating point.
Validate the offline metric: has it predicted live results in past launches?
Guardrails, with margins: thin-file approvals, fairness gaps, latency, complaints.

Trade-off: a metric close to the business, like a profit simulation, is noisy and rests on assumptions; a clean statistical metric like AUC is stable but can move without the business moving. Report both.

Follow-up: “AUC went up but profit didn't. Why?” The gain was away from the cut-off, calibration broke so the cut-off landed in the wrong place, or the swap-ins behave worse than the approved population suggested.
5How do you set the decision threshold?
From the costs of each mistake, using calibrated probabilities: approve while the expected gain beats the expected loss. Capacity or risk appetite can override it.
With PD p , margin G on a repaid loan and loss L on a default, approve when (1 - p)\,G > p\,L , that is when p < G/(G + L) . With a ₹5,000 margin and a ₹28,000 loss, the break-even PD is about 15%.
Marginal, not average: the last applicant approved should break even. A book can be profitable overall while its riskiest approved band loses money.
Other constraints: a cap on the portfolio bad rate, a manual-review band sized to the team, a target approval rate.
Procedure: choose on validation data, confirm on the test set, revisit when costs or the applicant mix change. Without calibration, sweep thresholds on validation and add up the total cost at each.
Trade-off: the profit-maximizing cut-off against risk appetite and customer experience: a tighter cut-off is safer but turns away more good customers.

Follow-up: “Funding costs rise and the margin falls to ₹4,000.” Break-even drops to 4,000/32,000 = 12.5%, and the cut-off tightens without retraining, because the policy is kept separate from the model.
6When does calibration matter, and how do you check and fix it?

Whenever the score is used as a number rather than just an order: expected loss, pricing, limits, a cut-off from the economics, or combining models. Check predicted against observed by score band; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on recent held-out data.

Why it bites: if every PD is half its true value, a band whose true PD is 18% shows 9%, falls under a 15% break-even, and is approved at a loss. AUC, Gini and KS don't change, because the order is the same.
Check: a reliability table by decile (predicted against observed bad rate), the average PD against the observed rate, and the Brier score or log loss against a constant-rate baseline.

Fix: Platt scaling fits two parameters (good for small data and S-shaped distortion); isotonic regression fits any monotone correction (needs more data). Both keep the order. After resampling the classes, correct the probabilities for the true base rate.
What breaks it: class reweighting or resampling, a change in the overall default rate (a recession), a change in the applicant mix (a new channel), and raw boosting scores in some setups.
Trade-off: isotonic regression is flexible but can overfit small data; Platt is stable but assumes the distortion has a sigmoid shape.
Follow-up: “Ranking holds but calibration has drifted since launch. Retrain?” Usually recalibrate first: it's cheaper and the order still holds. Retrain if the ranking itself decays.
Data, labels and validation
7How do you handle label delay?
Never treat outcomes that haven't matured as negatives. Train and evaluate on matured cohorts, and act sooner with early proxy labels that have been validated against the final label.
Maturity window: read it off vintage curves, the cumulative bad rate of each monthly cohort by months on book, at the point where they flatten.
Proxies: first-payment default, or 30+ days past due at 3 months on book. Check on old cohorts that they rank applicants and model versions the same way as the full 12-month label.
Partial information: a survival model treats a young loan as censored (survived so far), not as good, so recent data still contributes.
Validation: leave a gap between training and test periods that matches the delay in production.
Monitoring: drift and vintage curves now, full metrics when cohorts mature.
Trade-off: a short window gives fresher data and faster iteration but misses late defaults, and can reward models that delay default rather than prevent it. A long window is complete but old.
Follow-up: “The last three months show half the usual bad rate. Good news?” No: their labels haven't arrived. Exclude them, or wait.
8You only see outcomes for approved loans. What does that do, and what can you do about it?

The training data is a filtered, safer population, so the model is blindest exactly where its new decisions differ: below the old cut-off. Real labels from a small, capped, random approval slice fix it; statistical reject inference only patches it.

Effects: no labels below the old cut-off, so the model extrapolates there. If underwriters used extra information, the approved applicants in risky-looking groups were unusually good, so the model underestimates risk for the rest of those groups. And Gini measured on approved loans alone understates the model.
Offline evaluation: the new model's swap-ins, approved now but declined before, have no outcomes, so the offline case rests on half the evidence.

Fixes, most trustworthy first: capped random approvals below the cut-off; a champion–challenger test; bureau outcomes of declined applicants who borrowed elsewhere; reweighting by the inverse probability of approval, or assigning inferred labels.
Trade-off: exploration costs real losses and must be capped and agreed with the risk team; without it, the model can never learn about the people it declines.
Follow-up: “Why can't reweighting alone fix it?” Applicants who were always declined have an approval probability of zero, and no weight can recover a region with no data.
9How would you design the validation for a credit model?
Out of time and grouped by customer: a later validation period for every choice, and a still later test period looked at once, ideally after a gap like the label delay.
Layout: train on applications from months 1–18, validate on 19–21, test on 22–24, all with matured labels.
Why out of time: rates, the economy and the applicant mix move. A random split mixes periods and hides that drift.
Why a gap, if history allows: a live model learns from data at least a year older than the applicants it scores. The gap copies that decay; without it, the test flatters the model a little.
Why grouped: repeat applicants on both sides let the model score on memory.
Leakage control: preprocessing, encoders and feature selection fitted inside training folds; threshold and calibration on validation.
Size: set by the number of bads. With 300 bads, AUC's 95% interval is about ±0.03, so compare models with a paired bootstrap.
Trade-off: a more recent test period is more representative but leaves less, older data for training. Walk-forward evaluation over several windows is more reliable but costs more compute.
Follow-up: “Random-split AUC is 0.80, out-of-time 0.70. What does it mean?” Leakage through time or through repeat customers, or a relationship that drifts. Find the features that drive the gap.
Experiments and production
10The model is great offline but bad in production. Why?

Either the offline estimate was wrong (leakage, a random split, selection bias, a proxy metric) or production differs from the test (drift, training–serving skew, changed behaviour). Check the cheap, mechanical causes first.
The pipeline: compare logged live features with the same features recomputed offline for the same applications. Skew and broken feeds are the most common cause and the fastest to find.
The population: PSI of the features and the score between the test set and live traffic. A new channel or campaign may have changed who applies.
The offline number: the gap between random-split and out-of-time scores, single-feature checks for leakage, whether the labels were mature.
The metric: did the offline gains sit near the cut-off, and in rupees?
Selection bias: the new model's swap-ins were never in the offline test.
Reactions: applicants or fraudsters adapting to the new policy.
Trade-off: some causes can't be told apart without labels. Skew and drift show at once; selection bias shows only through a randomized test.
Follow-up: “How would you have caught it before launch?” Shadow mode with feature-parity checks, an out-of-time test with a gap, and a small capped challenger before full rollout.
11How do you know your A/B test result is real?
Check the experiment's validity before its result, then read the result as an interval that is practically meaningful, pre-registered and consistent over time.
Validity: no sample ratio mismatch (a chi-square test of arm sizes against the design); assignment by a stable hash of the user; the same logging in both arms; no interference between them.
Pre-registration: one primary metric, guardrails with margins, the duration and the analysis, all fixed before launch.
No peeking, unless a sequential test was planned: stopping at the first p < 0.05 inflates false positives.
An interval: does its low end still clear the cost of the change, or the smallest effect worth shipping?
Consistency: the effect holds week by week (a fading effect suggests novelty) and in the pre-registered segments.
For credit: compare at the same approval rate or on profit, read only matured cohorts, on proxies validated against the final label.
Twyman's law: a surprisingly large result is usually a bug.
Trade-off: stricter significance and longer tests mean fewer false wins but slower decisions and more missed real gains.

Follow-up: “One of 20 segments is significant at p = 0.03 . Ship for that segment?” No. With 20 looks, at least one false positive is likely ( 1 - 0.95^20 approx 64\% ). Treat it as a hypothesis for the next test.
12The challenger model has a lower bad rate than the champion. Ship it?
Not yet. A stricter model always has a lower bad rate, so first check how many people each approves. Compare at the same approval rate or on profit per applicant, on matured labels.

Example: the champion approves 40% with a 6.0% bad rate; the challenger approves 32% with 5.2%. The fair comparison is the champion's bad rate among its own safest 32%, or profit per applicant in each arm.

Swap sets: the clearest read compares the challenger's swap-ins (approved only by it) with the champion's swap-outs (approved only by the champion). Score both models on every applicant, so each arm's swap sets are defined; randomization makes each arm's swap set a fair sample of the same kind of applicant.
Validity: labels matured for every cohort read, split checked, guardrails passed.
Trade-off: fewer approvals mean fewer losses but less revenue and more good customers turned away. Profit per applicant puts both on one scale.

Follow-up: “Profit per applicant is equal, but the challenger approves fewer. Which one?” That's a strategy call, not a modelling one: a growth phase favours more approvals, a cautious one favours fewer, safer loans. Put the trade-off to the business explicitly.
13What is training–serving skew, and how do you prevent it?

The model receives different feature values live than it was trained on, usually because features are computed by different code or at different times. Prevent it with one feature definition, logged serving features and parity checks.

Causes: warehouse SQL for training and service code for serving; windows that end at midnight in one and at the request time in the other; late-arriving data that's in the warehouse but wasn't there at decision time; different handling of nulls and unseen categories.
Detection: in shadow mode, compare logged live features with offline recomputations for the same applications; compare the live score distribution with the test set's.
Prevention: a shared feature definition (a feature store or a shared library); training on features logged at serving time; point-in-time joins; tests for nulls and unseen values.
Trade-off: training on logged features guarantees parity, but only for features you've been logging, which delays new features. A feature store prevents skew at the cost of infrastructure.

Follow-up: “Give an example.” “Payments from this device in the last 24 hours” computed by a nightly batch for training but by a live counter for serving: the window edges and late events differ, so the model sees different numbers.
14How do you detect drift, and what do you do about it?
Compare live distributions of the inputs and the score with training using PSI or KS, watch early outcomes by cohort, and act according to what drifted and whether performance actually fell.
PSI: bin a feature on the training data, then sum (a_i - e_i)ln(a_i/e_i) over bins, where a_i is the live share and e_i the training share. Below 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 a look, above 0.25 a real shift.
KS: the largest gap between two cumulative distributions. On big samples, alert on the statistic's size, since the p-value flags trivial shifts.

Kinds: the inputs change (covariate shift: a campaign brings new applicants); or the relationship between inputs and default changes (concept drift), either uniformly (a recession lifts every applicant's risk, so the order holds and recalibration fixes it) or by reordering (some sectors are hit harder, so retrain).
Actions: a pipeline bug, fix the data; input drift with stable outcomes, watch and check calibration in the new segment; a uniform rise in risk, recalibrate; a reordering, retrain or add features.
Trade-off: sensitive alerts catch problems early but cause alert fatigue. Alert on the score and the most important features, with thresholds tied to actions.

Follow-up: “Score PSI is 0.3 but the bad rate hasn't moved.” Either the population moved without its risk changing, or the labels simply haven't arrived. Find which features moved, and check calibration on the new segment as its cohorts mature.
When there's evidence it will help: new matured labels, measured decay, or a known change in the world. Not by habit. And a retrained model must beat the current one before it replaces it.

Triggers: early outcomes (30+ days past due by months on book) worse than past cohorts at the same age; calibration off on recent cohorts; PSI above about 0.25 on the score or key features; a new product, channel or policy.

A schedule gives a floor and predictability. Set its pace by how fast labels arrive: a credit model gains full labels slowly, so monitor monthly, recalibrate when levels drift, rebuild every year or two; a fraud model faces adversaries and faster labels, so retrain weekly to monthly.
Recalibrate or retrain: if the order holds but the levels are off (a recession lifting everyone's risk), recalibrate. If the order itself decays, retrain.
Process: train, compare with the champion on the latest matured data, shadow, then ramp.
Trade-off: frequent retraining tracks change but adds release risk and chases noise when no new labels have matured; rare retraining is stable but slow to react.
Follow-up: “What can go wrong when you retrain?” Immature labels counted as good, a feedback loop narrowing the population each time, and upstream data that changed meaning without anyone noticing.
16How do you produce reason codes for a declined applicant?

Compute each feature's contribution to this applicant's risk (SHAP for a boosted model, points for a scorecard), take the ones that raised the risk most, and map each to a fixed, plain-language reason.
SHAP: contributions in log-odds that add up to this applicant's score minus the average score, so “what pushed this person's risk up” is well defined.
A reason catalogue: each feature maps to one reason, and correlated features (several measures of utilization) share one, so the explanation doesn't split across near-duplicates.
Requirements: stable across similar applicants and across retrains; understandable and actionable; never a protected attribute or a proxy for one.
Monotonic constraints help: the reasons always point the way a credit officer expects.
Trade-off: with correlated features SHAP can split credit unpredictably, so grouping features into reasons is what makes the codes stable. A scorecard gives exact reasons but usually less accuracy.
Follow-up: “Can the applicant act on ‘high utilization’?” Usually, yes, but SHAP explains the model, not causes in the world, so never promise that changing one thing will get them approved.
17How do you explain a model to non-technical stakeholders?
Explain the decision and its effect in their terms, show it working on examples and in a simple table, be honest about uncertainty, and keep the method for when they ask.
Lead with what changes and what it's worth: “at today's approval rate, about 40 fewer defaults a month, worth around ₹13 lakh”.

A gains table: sort applicants by score into ten equal bands and show each band's default rate. “The riskiest tenth of applicants holds about a quarter of the defaults; the safest tenth almost never defaults” makes the model's value visible without the word AUC.
Examples: two real applicants, their scores, and the top reasons for each.
What drives it: the main factors in plain words, each moving in the expected direction.
Limits: where it's weaker (thin-file applicants), what could go wrong, and how you'd know.

Trade-off: simplicity against accuracy. A simplified story must not mislead: “the model learned that missed payments predict default” is fine; “missed payments cause default, so the model knows the cause” is not.
Follow-up: “Why should we trust it?” Out-of-time results against today's policy, the shadow period, a capped live test, and monitoring that would catch a problem early.
18How do you prioritize between improving the model and shipping?

Ship when the model beats the current policy by a measured, meaningful margin and the guardrails pass, then keep improving through challenger releases. Each month of delay gives up the gain already in hand.

Compare value: a month's delay forgoes the model's monthly value (say ₹13 lakh) once. Polishing pays only if its extra monthly gain, times the chance it works, summed over the model's life, beats that, and only if it couldn't ship later as a challenger anyway. Usually it can.
Shipping teaches what offline work can't: outcomes for swap-ins, real latency, real drift.
The biggest remaining gains are usually data: better labels, new sources. They take calendar time, so run them in parallel with the launch.
Don't ship if the guardrails fail, calibration is off, the gain is inside the noise, or monitoring and rollback aren't ready.
Trade-off: shipping early puts a less polished model in production and may need a second release; waiting loses value and learns less.
Follow-up: “What would make you delay a launch?” Failed feature parity in shadow mode, an unexplained gap between validation and test, missing monitoring or rollback, or an open compliance question.
19How do you scope a project, estimate its timeline, and decide when to stop?

Scope it by the decision and a measurable success criterion, split it into phases that each end in a go/no-go decision, estimate each phase as a range, re-estimate at every milestone, and agree a kill criterion up front.
Phases: framing and a data audit; a first model judged against today's policy; shadow mode; a live challenger. Each has a deliverable and a decision.
Front-load the uncertainty: data access and label quality sink more timelines than modelling does, so audit them in the first week or two.
Dependencies: compliance review, engineering capacity for serving, and data owners all need calendar time you don't control.
Stopping: stop polishing when the next gain is below the noise or worth less than the delay; stop the project when the kill criterion hits, and say so early.
Scope creep: new requests go to a written backlog, with their cost to the date made explicit.
Trade-off: a detailed upfront plan will be wrong; no plan drifts. Short phases that end in decisions balance the two.
Follow-up: “Halfway through, the business also wants a pricing model.” Offer it as phase two, and say what adding it now would do to the launch date, so they choose.
20What goes into a model card, and why bother?
Enough for someone who wasn't there to use, audit and maintain the model: its purpose and limits, data and label, performance by segment, fairness checks, monitoring and ownership.
Purpose: intended use, and uses it's not for.
Data: sources, label definition and window, training and test periods, exclusions.
Performance: overall and by segment, with intervals; calibration.
Risks: fairness checks, known limitations, segments where it's weak.
Operations: monitoring plan, retraining triggers, owner, version.

Why bother: audits and disputes months later, handovers when people leave, model-risk reviews in regulated lending, and stopping the model from being reused for things it wasn't built for. Writing it also forces you to state the limitations.
Trade-off: documentation takes time and goes stale. Keep it short, version it with the model, and generate the numbers from the training pipeline.
Follow-up: “What's the most important line?” The intended use and the uses it's not for: much of the harm models do comes from being applied where they were never validated.

notes.title: Deep learning basics
notes.desc: Forward pass and backprop in NumPy, optimizers, activations, losses, initialization, normalization, regularization, residuals, convolutions and reading loss curves.

sections.t: A neuron, a layer, a network
Adam's bias correction, step by step
The training loop, and debugging it

chunks.x: Deep learning basics · Deepam Minda
A layer is a = f(Wx + b) : a weighted sum, then a non-linearity. Without the non-linearity, any stack of layers collapses into one linear map.

The forward pass computes and stores every layer's output. The backward pass applies the chain rule from the loss backwards: delta_l = (W_l+1^top delta_l+1) odot f'(z_l) , and each weight's gradient is delta_l\, a_l-1^top .
One backward pass costs about two forward passes and gives the gradient for every weight. That's why deep learning is feasible.

Deep networks fail when gradients vanish or explode (a product of one factor per layer). The fixes are ReLU-family activations, variance-preserving initialization, normalization, residual connections and clipping.
Regularization (weight decay, dropout, early stopping, augmentation) fights overfitting; Adam(W) with a tuned learning rate and warmup is the default optimizer.
Add vectors when they're updates to the same representation (residuals, positions); concatenate when they're different sources that need their own weights.

chunks.h: A neuron, a layer, a network
chunks.x: A neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies a non-linear activation. A layer is many neurons side by side, so the weights become a matrix:

chunks.h: A neuron, a layer, a network

chunks.h: A neuron, a layer, a network
chunks.x: Why the non-linearity is essential: two linear layers make one, since W_2(W_1 x) = (W_2 W_1) x . Only the bend between layers lets depth build curved decision boundaries. With it, a single hidden layer that's wide enough can approximate any continuous function (the universal approximation theorem); depth makes that far more efficient. Why: with ReLU the network is piecewise linear, and each layer folds the pieces made by the layer before, so the number of linear pieces can grow exponentially with depth but only polynomially with width.
Run the layers in order and keep every intermediate result, because the backward pass will need them. For a two-layer classifier:
beginaligned z_1 &= W_1 x + b_1 \\ a_1 &= ReLU(z_1) \\ z_2 &= W_2 a_1 + b_2 \\ hat y &= softmax(z_2) \\ L &= -textstylesum_k y_k log hat y_k endaligned

A two-layer network. Forward (blue) computes and stores every intermediate value. Backward (orange) starts at the loss and multiplies by one local derivative per step; each weight's gradient is read off on the way.
Every operation here is simple, with a simple local derivative. That's what makes the next section work: the chain rule just multiplies local derivatives along the path.

The question backprop answers: for every weight, how much would the loss change if that weight moved a little? Define the error at layer l as the gradient at its pre-activation, delta_l = partial L / partial z_l . Everything follows from four equations:

beginaligned (1)quad delta_out &= hat y - y \\ (2)quad delta_l &= big(W_l+1^top delta_l+1big) odot f'(z_l) \\ (3)quad fracpartial Lpartial W_l &= delta_l\, a_l-1^top \\ (4)quad fracpartial Lpartial b_l &= delta_l endaligned

(1) Start at the output. For softmax with cross-entropy (or sigmoid with log loss), the gradient at the logits is prediction minus truth. For a linear output with the loss tfrac12 (hat y - y)^2 it's hat y - y too (without the ½ it's twice that).

(2) Pass the error back one layer. W_l+1^top sends each unit's error back along the same weights it used going forward (unit j collects sum_i W_ij\, delta_i ). Then multiply by the activation's slope, f'(z_l) , slot by slot, because the error has to pass back through the non-linearity. For ReLU that slope is 1 where the unit was on and 0 where it was off.
(3) Read off the weight gradient. W_l[i,j] multiplied a_l-1[j] into z_l[i] , so its gradient is delta_l[i] cdot a_l-1[j] : an outer product, the same shape as W_l .
(4) The bias gradient is just the error, since the bias is added with slope 1.
Batch version (rows = examples)
Delta_out = (hat Y - Y)/B
B times K (the 1/B is from averaging the loss)
Delta_l = (Delta_l+1 W_l+1) odot f'(Z_l)
partial L/partial W_l = Delta_l^top A_l-1
d_l times d_l-1 : the sum of every example's outer product
partial L/partial b_l = column sums of Delta_l
Forward and backward, in NumPy

# X: (B, d) Y: (B, K) one-hot; W1: (H, d) W2: (K, H) Z1 = X @ W1.T + b1 # (B, H) A1 = relu(Z1) Z2 = A1 @ W2.T + b2 # (B, K) logits P = softmax(Z2) # (B, K) loss = -(Y * log(P)).sum() / B D2 = (P - Y) / B # delta at the logits: (B, K) dW2 = D2.T @ A1 # (K, H) db2 = D2.sum(axis=0) D1 = (D2 @ W2) * (Z1 > 0) # back through W2, then ReLU's slope: (B, H) dW1 = D1.T @ X # (H, d) db1 = D1.sum(axis=0) for p, g in [(W1, dW1), (b1, db1), (W2, dW2), (b2, db2)]: p -= lr * g # one gradient-descent step
Why it's cheap, and what it costs

Reverse mode. The loss is one number and there are millions of weights. Going backward from that one number reuses every intermediate result, so one backward pass (about twice the cost of a forward pass) gives all the gradients. Nudging each weight and re-running the forward pass would cost one pass per weight. Forward-mode differentiation has the same problem: it needs one pass per input direction, while reverse mode needs one per output, and there's only one loss.

Why about twice. Going forward, each layer does one matrix multiply, W a . Going back it does two: W^top delta to pass the error on, and delta\, a^top for the weight gradient. So a full training step costs about three forward passes.
Memory. The backward pass needs every stored activation, so memory grows with depth × batch × width. Gradient checkpointing stores only some and recomputes the rest, trading compute for memory.
Gradient checking: compare with (L(w + varepsilon) - L(w - varepsilon)) / 2varepsilon on a few weights when you write a backward pass by hand.

“The gradient at a layer is the prediction minus the target.” Only at the output layer. Everywhere else, delta is the error passed back through the weights and multiplied by the activation's slope at that layer.
beginaligned SGD:quad theta &leftarrow theta - eta\, g \\ Momentum:quad u &leftarrow beta u + g \\ theta &leftarrow theta - eta\, u endaligned

beginaligned Adam:quad m &leftarrow beta_1 m + (1 - beta_1)\, g \\ v &leftarrow beta_2 v + (1 - beta_2)\, g^2 \\ hat m &= m / (1 - beta_1^t) \\ hat v &= v / (1 - beta_2^t) \\ theta &leftarrow theta - eta\, hat m / (sqrthat v + epsilon) endaligned
Mini-batch SGD: each step uses the gradient on a small batch, a noisy but cheap estimate of the full gradient. The noise even helps escape sharp minima.
Momentum keeps a decaying sum u of recent gradients (named u so it isn't confused with Adam's v ), so steps build up speed in consistent directions and zig-zags cancel out.
RMSProp divides each weight's step by a running average of its squared gradient, so rarely-updated and steep directions get sensibly sized steps.

Adam does both: m is a running average of the gradient (the direction), v of its square (the typical size), and each weight steps by eta\,hat m/sqrthat v . The hats are the bias correction, which undoes the fact that both averages start at 0. Why it's needed, why beta_2 is so close to 1, and why warmup is still needed afterwards: Adam's bias correction, step by step.

AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding lambdatheta to the gradient, where Adam's per-weight scaling would distort it. It's the default for transformers. The two update steps side by side: Adam + L2 vs AdamW.
The learning rate is the most important hyperparameter: warm it up at the start, then decay it (step, cosine).

Why warm up: at first Adam's averages hold only a few gradients, so it can't tell signal from noise and every weight takes a full step eta (details in the bias-correction walkthrough). And right after initialization the gradients are large and change fast, so a full-size step can overshoot and diverge. A short ramp from near 0 lets the network reach a calmer region where big steps are safe.
Why decay: mini-batch noise keeps the weights bouncing around a minimum by an amount that grows with the learning rate. Lowering it lets them settle.

Batch size. A mini-batch gradient averages B per-example gradients, so its variance falls as 1/B . A bigger batch can usually take a proportionally bigger learning rate (the linear scaling rule, for SGD; Adam usually needs a gentler increase): one step with a k times bigger batch and rate covers about the same ground as k small steps, as long as the gradient barely changes over them. Small-batch noise also helps generalization, by bouncing the weights out of sharp minima.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: Starting at zero makes both averages too small. Each update keeps beta of the old value and adds 1 - beta of the new gradient. Unrolled after t steps:

chunks.x: A proper average's weights sum to 1. The missing beta_1^\,t went to the starting value, 0. So m_t is the true average shrunk by 1 - beta_1^\,t , and v_t is shrunk by 1 - beta_2^\,t . With beta_1 = 0.9 the missing share dies out within a few dozen steps; with beta_2 = 0.999 it takes thousands. So v is under-estimated far more, and for far longer, than m .

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: Without correction, the steps are too big. On the very first step m_1 = (1 - beta_1)\,g and v_1 = (1 - beta_2)\,g^2 , so

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: fracm_1sqrtv_1 = frac1 - beta_1sqrt1 - beta_2\; sign(g)

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: which is about 3 with the defaults: every weight steps three times further than Adam's intended maximum. m recovers quickly, but v stays shrunk, so the oversized steps go on for a while.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: The correction divides each average by its own missing share:

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: beginaligned hat m_t &= fracm_t1 - beta_1^\,t \\ hat v_t &= fracv_t1 - beta_2^\,t endaligned

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: Each is now a proper average, with weights summing to 1. v is scaled up by more than m , but only because it was shrunk by more: the two effects cancel exactly, and neither average is distorted. On step 1 this gives hat m_1 = g and hat v_1 = g^2 , so the step is exactly pmeta , as intended.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: Why warmup is still needed. The correction removes the bias: on average hat v is right. It can't remove the noise. Early on, hat v averages only a handful of squared gradients (on step 1, a single one), so hat m/sqrthat v approx pm 1 for every weight, and a weight whose gradient is pure noise takes the same full step as one with a real signal. Later, with many samples, that noisy weight's hat m is near 0 and it barely moves. Warmup keeps eta small through this early, undiscriminating phase. RAdam builds the same idea into the optimizer.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: Why beta_1 = 0.9 and beta_2 = 0.999 . An average with factor beta remembers roughly the last 1/(1 - beta) steps.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: The right direction changes as the weights move, so the memory must be short enough to stay current but long enough to smooth out mini-batch noise. This is momentum.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: A weight's typical gradient size changes slowly, and squared gradients are very noisy, so estimating it needs many samples. v also sits in the denominator: a noisy, momentarily small v means a huge step. A long memory keeps it stable.

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: beta_2 too close to 1: when the gradient scale jumps suddenly (a loss spike, an unusual batch), v catches up too slowly, stays too small, and m/sqrt v explodes. That's why large language-model runs often use beta_2 = 0.95 (GPT-3, LLaMA).

chunks.h: Adam's bias correction, step by step
chunks.x: beta_2 as small as beta_1 : v just tracks the last few squared gradients, m/sqrt v stays near pm 1 for almost every weight, and Adam degenerates into stepping by the sign of the gradient. It loses the signal-versus-noise distinction that makes it useful.
First, where lambdatheta comes from. L2 regularization adds the squared size of the weights to the loss, and the gradient of that square is linear in theta :
beginaligned L_reg &= L + tfraclambda2lVertthetarVert^2 \\ nabla L_reg &= nabla L + lambdatheta endaligned

So a lambdatheta in an update is the squared penalty after differentiation (the tfrac12 only cancels the 2). With plain SGD it turns into theta leftarrow (1 - etalambda)\,theta - etanabla L : every weight shrinks by the same factor each step, which is what “weight decay” means, so under SGD the two names describe one update. Under Adam they differ, only in where lambdatheta enters:

beginaligned Adam + L2:quad g &= nabla L + lambdatheta \\ theta &leftarrow theta - eta\,frachat msqrthat v + epsilon \\ AdamW:quad g &= nabla L \\ theta &leftarrow theta - etaBig(frachat msqrthat v + epsilon + lambdathetaBig) endaligned

Here hat m and hat v are built from g as above. In words: with L2, the decay term goes into m and v , so it ends up divided by sqrthat v . Weights with a large gradient history are then barely decayed, and rarely-updated ones are decayed hard, which isn't what the regularizer intends. AdamW keeps the decay outside the adaptive scaling, so every weight shrinks by the same fraction etalambda per step. With plain SGD the two are identical, since there's no per-weight scaling to distort the decay. Strictly, then, AdamW is decoupled weight decay, not L2 regularization: there's no penalty term in it

m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g # running mean of gradients v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g * g # running mean of squared gradients m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t) # bias correction (m, v start at 0) v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t) w -= lr * (m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps) + wd * w) # AdamW: decay applied to w directly

Output layer for yes/no and gates. Saturates and isn't zero-centred, so it's poor in hidden layers.

Cheap and doesn't saturate for z > 0 , so the default. Units can “die” (stuck at 0, zero gradient forever).
A small slope for z < 0 keeps dead units learning.

z\,sigma(z) ; gated (xW) odot SiLU(xV)
SwiGLU is the FFN in most modern LLMs.
With cross-entropy: hat y - y

The short version. The full note, Loss functions, covers where each loss comes from, gradients, numerical stability, imbalance and calibration, ranking, contrastive and generative losses, and 20 questions.
MSE = tfrac1nsum (y - hat y)^2 qquad BCE = -[y log p + (1 - y)log(1 - p)] qquad CE = -sum_k y_k log hat y_k qquad Focal = -(1 - p_t)^gamma log p_t

Each loss is a likelihood: Gaussian noise gives MSE, Laplace noise gives MAE, Bernoulli labels give binary cross-entropy, categorical labels give cross-entropy. Huber is MSE near 0 and MAE in the tails, so it's robust to outliers.

Why cross-entropy, not MSE, for classification: with a sigmoid or softmax, MSE's gradient includes the activation's slope, which is tiny exactly when the model is confidently wrong. Cross-entropy's gradient at the logits is simply hat y - y , largest when most wrong.
beginaligned fracpartial L_CEpartial z &= hat y - y \\ fracpartial L_MSEpartial z &= (hat y - y)\,hat y(1 - hat y) endaligned
The derivation, step by step: Why not MSE for classification.
Focal loss down-weights easy, well-classified examples ( (1 - p_t)^gamma ), for heavy class imbalance. Class weights are the simpler alternative.

The backward pass multiplies the error by one factor, W^top diag(f') , per layer. Over many layers that product shrinks or grows exponentially: vanishing or exploding gradients. Early layers stop learning, or training blows up.

beginaligned delta_1 &= D_1 W_2^top\, D_2 W_3^top cdots D_L-1 W_L^top\, delta_L, qquad D_l = diagbig(f'(z_l)big) \\ lVert delta_1 rVert &le prod_l=1^L-1 big(max lvert f' rvert cdot lVert W_l+1 rVertbig)\, lVert delta_L rVert endaligned

In words: unroll backprop's equation (2) and the error at the first layer is the output error times one (slope × weights) factor per layer, where lVert W rVert is the most W can stretch a vector. If every factor is below 1, the bound forces the product to decay exponentially with depth. The bound is only a ceiling, so it can't prove explosion, but when the typical stretch is above 1 the product usually grows exponentially. Sigmoid's slope is at most 1/4, so a sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient unless its weights are large, and large weights push units into saturation, where the slope is even s

Initialization keeps the signal's size steady. Write a layer as z_l = W_l\, a_l-1 , a_l = f(z_l) . Each pre-activation is a sum of n_in terms w_j a_j , and with zero-mean weights independent of the inputs, Var(w a) = mathbbE[w^2]\,mathbbE[a^2] . So every layer multiplies the variance by the same gain r :
beginaligned Var(z_l) &= n_in\,Var(w)\,mathbbE[a_l-1^2] \\ &= n_in\,Var(w)\, c\, Var(z_l-1) \\ &= r\, Var(z_l-1) \\ Var(z_L) &= r^L\, Var(z_0) endaligned

In words: mathbbE[a^2] is the average squared input. It equals Var(a) only when the inputs average 0, and ReLU outputs don't. c is how much of the second moment the activation keeps: tfrac12 for ReLU, which zeroes half of a symmetric input, and about 1 for tanh near 0, where tanh z approx z .
Why the same variance at every layer ( r = 1 ):

Any other gain compounds. Over tens of layers r^L explodes if r is a little above 1 and vanishes if it's a little below; only r = 1 is safe at any depth. The level is 1 because the inputs are standardized to variance 1.
Forward: too large and tanh or sigmoid units saturate (slope near 0) or the numbers overflow; too small and activations collapse towards 0, so different inputs look alike deep in the network.

Backward: the error delta passes back through the same weights and picks up a similar gain per layer, and a layer's weight gradient is delta_l\, a_l-1^top . If a or delta scales like r^l , layers get gradients that differ by orders of magnitude, and no single learning rate suits them all.

Only at initialization, and on average. Training moves the weights, so normalization layers and residual connections keep the scale in check from then on. Residual streams add variance, Var(x_l+1) approx Var(x_l) + Var(F) , so deep residual nets also shrink each branch at initialization (zero-initialize its last layer, or scale it by 1/sqrtN as GPT-2 does).
Setting r = 1 gives the standard initializations:
beginaligned Xavier (tanh):quad Var(w) &= frac2n_in + n_out \\ He (ReLU):quad Var(w) &= frac2n_in endaligned

Xavier balances two needs: the forward pass sums over n_in inputs (so it wants Var(w) = 1/n_in ), and the backward pass sums over the n_out units a layer feeds (so it wants 1/n_out ). It uses one over their average, and assumes the activation has slope 1 near 0, which holds for tanh; sigmoid fits only roughly, since its slope at 0 is 1/4.

He has the extra factor 2 because ReLU zeroes the negative half of its inputs: for a pre-activation symmetric around 0, mathbbE[ReLU(z)^2] = tfrac12 Var(z) , so the next layer's mathbbE[x^2] is halved.
All-zero (or all-equal) initialization fails: every unit in a layer computes the same thing and gets the same gradient, so they stay identical forever. Random initialization breaks the symmetry.

The full toolkit against vanishing/exploding: ReLU-family activations, He/Xavier initialization, normalization layers, residual connections, gradient clipping (for exploding), and gated cells in RNNs.

Gradient clipping rescales the whole gradient when its norm goes over a threshold c : g leftarrow g cdot min(1, c / lVert g rVert) . The direction is kept. With plain SGD every step is then at most eta c ; with Adam, which divides by sqrthat v anyway, it mainly stops one spike from inflating m and v . Clipping each value separately would change the direction. It does nothing for vanishing gradients.
Standardization rescales each input feature j to mean 0 and variance 1, using statistics from the training set only:
tilde x_j = fracx_j - mu_jsigma_j
Fit mu_j, sigma_j on the training data and apply the same numbers to validation, test and production. Computing them on all the data leaks information from the test set.
Why it helps gradient descent. For a linear model with MSE, each weight's gradient scales with its feature, and the loss's curvature is set by the features' scales:
beginaligned fracpartial Lpartial w_j &= frac1Nsum_i (hat y_i - y_i)\, x_ij \\ H &= nabla^2 L = frac1N X^top X endaligned

A badly shaped bowl. A feature measured in thousands next to one measured in fractions makes the loss surface a long, thin valley: very steep along one weight, nearly flat along another. One learning rate can't suit both. Small enough not to overshoot the steep direction means crawling along the flat one, and the path zig-zags across the valley. Standardizing makes X^top X closer to a correlation matrix and the bowl rounder, so one learning rate works for every direction. (Formally, it lowers the Hessian's condition number, the ratio of its largest to smallest curvature, which sets how many st

A double mismatch per weight. A large-scale feature gets a large gradient but needs only a small weight, and a small-scale feature the reverse. Adam's per-weight scaling softens this, but it can't fix correlated or off-centre features.

Centring matters too. If a feature is always positive, every gradient on a neuron's incoming weights shares the sign of hat y - y , so they all move up or down together and the path zig-zags. It's the same argument that makes zero-centred activations preferable.

Initialization and activations assume it. Xavier and He initialization are derived for inputs with unit variance. Large raw inputs push the first layer's pre-activations far out, saturating tanh or sigmoid from the very first step.
Why it matters beyond gradient descent.

Regularization. L1 and L2 penalize every weight equally, which is only fair when features share a scale. Otherwise a small-scale feature needs a large weight and gets penalized more for the same effect.
Distances. k-NN, k-means, RBF-kernel SVMs and PCA all use distances or variances, which the largest-scale feature dominates. Unscaled PCA mostly finds “the feature with the biggest units”.

When it doesn't matter. Tree models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) split on thresholds, which no monotonic rescaling changes. Unregularized least squares gives the same predictions either way; only the coefficients rescale.

Variants. Min-max scaling to [0, 1] suits bounded inputs such as pixels, but one outlier squashes everything else. Robust scaling (median and interquartile range) resists outliers. Take a log first for heavily skewed features (incomes, counts). Images are usually divided by 255, then standardized per channel. Categorical features get embeddings or one-hot encodings instead.

BatchNorm and LayerNorm are the same idea inside the network. Each layer's input is the previous layer's output, and its scale drifts as the earlier weights change, so normalization layers standardize the activations as well, with a learned scale and shift added back.
beginaligned hat x &= fracx - musqrtsigma^2 + epsilon \\ y &= gamma\, hat x + beta endaligned
Same formula, different axis. BatchNorm computes mu, sigma down a column (one feature, all examples); LayerNorm across a row (one example, all its features).

BatchNorm (CNNs): statistics per feature over the batch. At inference there may be one example, so it uses running averages saved during training; the train/eval switch is a classic bug. It struggles with small batches (noisy statistics) and padded sequences (padding pollutes them). CNNs with tiny batches use GroupNorm instead, which normalizes groups of channels within one example.
LayerNorm (transformers, RNNs): statistics per example over its features. It doesn't depend on the batch and behaves the same in training and inference.

Why they help: they keep each layer's inputs at a steady scale, which allows bigger learning rates and smooths the loss landscape. The learned gamma, beta let the network undo the normalization if that's better.

No moving target: without them, an update to an early layer shifts the scale of everything after it. (This “internal covariate shift” was the original motivation; later work found the smoother loss surface matters more.)

Scale invariance: scaling the weights that feed a normalization layer by any c > 0 leaves its output unchanged, so only the weights' direction matters and growing weights can't blow up the activations. A step turns that direction by about (step size) ÷ (weight norm). Changing only the length doesn't change the loss, so the gradient has no component along the weights, and each step slightly lengthens them; longer weights then turn less on later steps. The effective step size steadies itself.
Out of saturation: centred, unit-scale inputs keep sigmoid and tanh units in their sloped region.

Where it sits in a transformer: pre-norm, x + F(Norm(x)) , normalizes only the branch and leaves a clean identity path through the residual stream, so it trains stably. Post-norm, Norm(x + F(x)) , the original design, puts the norm on that path and starts with large gradients near the output, so it needs warmup.
beginaligned Dropout (training):quad tilde h &= frach odot m1 - p, qquad m_i sim Bernoulli(1 - p) \\ L2:quad L_total &= L + fraclambda2lVert w rVert^2 endaligned

Weight decay (L2) shrinks weights every step, favouring simpler functions. L1 pushes weights to exactly 0 (sparsity). Why the difference: L2's pull on a weight, lambda w , fades as the weight nears 0, so weights get small but stay non-zero; L1's pull, lambda\, sign(w) , is the same size however small the weight, so whenever the data's pull on a weight is weaker than lambda , the best value is exactly 0.

Dropout zeroes each unit with probability p during training (each m_i is 1 with probability 1 - p , else 0) and scales the survivors by 1/(1-p) , so the expected activation is unchanged and nothing needs rescaling at inference, where it's off. It stops units relying on each other and acts like averaging many thinned networks.

Early stopping keeps the checkpoint with the best validation loss. Data augmentation adds realistic variations. Label smoothing softens one-hot targets so the model isn't pushed to infinite confidence.

Bias–variance: big gap between train and validation → overfitting (high variance): regularize, add data, shrink the model. Both bad → underfitting (high bias): bigger model, longer training, better features. A learning curve over training-set size shows whether more data will help: if validation is still improving as the data grows, collect more.

Double descent: for big models, the U-shaped test-error curve has a second half. Test error peaks near the size where the model can only just fit every training point, since there's essentially one way to fit them and it has to contort to fit the noise. Bigger still, many weight settings fit the data exactly, and gradient descent from a small initialization tends to find a smooth one, so test error falls again. The same peak can appear over training epochs. So for large networks, many parameters isn't by itself overfitting.
BatchNorm, LayerNorm and dropout, in code

def batchnorm(x, training): # x: (B, F) if training: mu, var = x.mean(axis=0), x.var(axis=0) # per feature, over the batch run_mu = 0.9 * run_mu + 0.1 * mu # saved for inference run_var = 0.9 * run_var + 0.1 * var else: mu, var = run_mu, run_var # inference: no batch statistics return gamma * (x - mu) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta def layernorm(x): # per example, over its features mu = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True) var = x.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True) return gamma * (x - mu) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta # same in training and inference def dropout(h, p, training): if not training: return h # off at inf
beginaligned x_l+1 &= x_l + F_l(x_l) \\ fracpartial x_l+1partial x_l &= I + fracpartial F_lpartial x_l endaligned
In words: each block adds a learned correction F_l to its input. I is the identity, the matrix that leaves a vector unchanged, so the gradient always has a path back that isn't shrunk.

The gradient gets a straight path. The identity term means the error reaches early layers even when partial F/partial x is small. That's what made 100+ layer networks trainable (ResNet, 2015). Loss-landscape plots also show skip connections make the loss surface much smoother, which makes optimization easier.

Doing nothing is easy. A block only has to learn a correction to its input; if a layer isn't useful, F to 0 leaves the input unchanged. Without the skip, it would have to learn the identity mapping, which is surprisingly hard. That's why, before ResNet, deeper plain networks had higher training error than shallower ones (the degradation problem): an optimization failure, not overfitting.
Shapes must match for the add. When a block changes the width or resolution, the skip uses a 1×1 convolution or a linear projection.
The same idea appears as the LSTM's cell update through time and as the transformer's residual stream through depth.
In words: split W = [W_1\ \ W_2] into the columns that read x and those that read y . Concatenating and then applying a linear layer is the same as projecting each input separately and adding.
Adding superimposes two vectors in one shared space and keeps the width. Concatenating keeps them side by side, so the next layer weighs each with its own columns of W .
Same weights for both: W(x + y) = Wx + Wy
Separate weights: W_1 x + W_2 y
More parameters and memory downstream
Residuals; token + position embeddings; transformer residual stream; summing a bag of embeddings
LSTM [h_t-1, x_t] ; bi-LSTM outputs; multi-head concat → W_O ; U-Net skips; DenseNet; feature fusion

Rule of thumb: add when it's an update to the same representation and you want a fixed width; concatenate when the inputs are different things the next layer should weigh separately, and you can afford the width. A sum is also order-free, which is right for sets.

The cost of adding: the two signals share coordinates, so the next layer can't pull them apart unless training learns to keep them in different directions. In high dimensions there's plenty of room for that, which is why adding token and position embeddings works.
The short version. The full note, Convolutional neural networks, covers receptive fields, architectures, how convolution is computed (im2col, FFT, Winograd), upsampling and U-Net, and 22 questions.
A convolution is one small weighted window slid across the input: local (each output sees a 3×3 patch) and shared (the same 9 weights everywhere).
beginaligned output size &= Biglfloor fracn + 2p - ks Bigrfloor + 1 \\ parameters &= k cdot k cdot C_in cdot C_out + C_out endaligned

Why not a dense layer: parameter sharing (a 3×3×64→64 conv has about 37K weights, whatever the image size) and locality (neighbouring pixels matter together). A pattern learned in one place is detected everywhere: translation equivariance. Pooling adds some invariance and shrinks the map.

The output size, term by term: padding adds p cells on each side ( n + 2p ). The window's first cell starts at 0, s , 2s , …, and the last start must be at most n + 2p - k , or the window would run off the edge. That's lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s rfloor steps after the first start, plus 1 for the first. For odd k , “same” padding p = (k - 1)/2 keeps the size at stride 1. Parameters don't depend on n , because the same filter is reused at every position.
Receptive field grows with depth, stride, pooling and dilation: early layers see edges, deep layers see objects.

1×1 convolution: a dense layer across channels at every pixel. It changes the channel count cheaply (bottlenecks) and adds a cheap extra layer, and so another activation (the 1×1 convolution itself is linear); it's the CNN version of the transformer's per-token FFN.
Tensor shape in PyTorch: B times C times H times W ; the weights are C_out times C_in times k times k .
A convolution, in code (naive loops)

# x: (C_in, H, W) w: (C_out, C_in, k, k) no padding, stride 1 for o in range(C_out): for i in range(H - k + 1): for j in range(W - k + 1): y[o, i, j] = (w[o] * x[:, i:i+k, j:j+k]).sum() + b[o] # same weights everywhere

Read a training run by plotting train and validation loss on the same axes, with the gradient norm and the learning rate underneath. Most problems have a recognisable shape:
Train keeps falling, validation falls then rises

Not learning: learning rate far off, a data bug (labels shifted by one), saturated inputs, dead units

Lower it, add warmup, use a bigger batch

Clip the gradient norm, lower the learning rate, check the inputs, use loss scaling
Long plateau, then a sudden drop
