notes.desc: RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs: gates, how gradients flow back through time, what the ablation studies found, and bidirectional and stacked models.

sections.t: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU

chunks.x: Sequence models · Deepam Minda
A plain RNN carries one vector, h , and rewrites all of it every step through the same matrix and a tanh. Old information fades, and so does the gradient that could teach it to stay.
A gate is a vector of dials between 0 and 1, recomputed every step from [h_t-1, x_t] through its own weight matrix, and multiplied slot by slot into a signal.

The LSTM keeps a notebook c that changes only by erasing ( times f ) and writing ( +\, i odot g ), and shows h = o odot tanh(c) . The GRU merges notebook and output into one h : the update gate z decides keep-versus-write, the reset gate r decides what the draft is built from.
Neither cell predicts anything by itself: a separate output layer reads h_t , hat y_t = softmax(W_y h_t + b_y) .

Backprop: on the memory path, each step back multiplies the gradient by diag(1 - h_t^2) W_h in an RNN, by f_t in an LSTM and by 1 - z_t in a GRU. Swapping a fixed matrix and slope for a learned dial is the whole fix.
In ablations, the forget gate (started near 1) matters most and the output gate least; the learning rate matters more than any architectural tweak.
beginaligned h_t &= tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_t-1 + b) \\ hat y_t &= softmax(W_y h_t + b_y) endaligned
Notation for the whole page: d = input size (e.g. the embedding size), H = hidden size, K = number of classes (or the vocabulary size V ), T = sequence length, B = batch size.
State → state (square: the state maps onto itself)
Whole sequence in / all states out
Weight gradient share delta a_t\, x_t^top
(H times 1)(1 times d) = H times d

In code everything gets a leading batch dimension, and rows are examples, so a step is h_t = tanh(x_t W_x^top + h_t-1 W_h^top + b) with x_t of shape B times d and h_t of shape B times H . PyTorch's nn.RNN(d, H, batch_first=True) takes B times T times d and returns all states as B times T times H , plus the last one as layers times B times H . Parameters: H(d + H) + H for the cell, plus KH + K for the head. PyTorch stores two bias vectors, b_ih and b_hh , so it reports H(d + H) + 2H for the cell; only their sum matters (more on this under the LSTM). None of it depends on T , because the same we

chunks.x: For text, x_t is a learned embedding, exactly as in a transformer. The text is split into tokens, each token is an id in a vocabulary of size V , and the id picks one row of an embedding table E :

chunks.x: In PyTorch that's nn.Embedding(V, d) → nn.LSTM(d, H) → nn.Linear(H, V), the same embedding layer a transformer uses.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: An embedding is the first weight matrix. With a one-hot input, W_x\,onehot(i) is just column i of W_x . The embedding table does that lookup directly, without building a V -dimensional vector, and the cell's own W_x then maps d to H .

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: No position signal. Nothing is added for position: order comes from the recurrence itself, since step t only runs after step t-1 . A transformer needs position embeddings because attention ignores order.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Vocabularies. In the LSTM era they were usually whole words (30k–100k) with an <UNK> token for unseen ones, or characters. Transformers use subwords (BPE, WordPiece), so no word is unknown.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Initialization. The table was often filled with pretrained word2vec or GloVe vectors, then frozen or fine-tuned. Those give one vector per word type (“bank” is the same in every sentence); the recurrence adds the context in h_t .

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Weight tying. A language model's output layer W_y ( V times H ) can share weights with E when H = d , or with a projection in between (Press & Wolf, 2017): fewer parameters and usually lower perplexity. GPT and BERT do the same.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Cost. V cdot d is often the largest block of parameters in a small word-level model, another reason to tie weights or use subwords.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Padding. Batches pad every sequence to one length with a pad id. padding_idx keeps that row at zero, and packing (pack_padded_sequence) stops the RNN stepping through the padding.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Before all this: how text becomes tokens, bag of words, TF-IDF, n-gram models, word2vec and GloVe are covered in depth in the Classical NLP note.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Not text? For time series or sensor data there's no vocabulary: x_t is the feature vector itself, or a linear projection of it. Only categorical features (a store id, the day of the week) get embedding tables, concatenated with the numeric ones.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: One step of a plain RNN. One vector, h , is both the memory and the output, and all of it is rewritten every step.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: The same W_x , W_h , W_y are used at every step, so the model handles any length, and a pattern learned at one position is recognized at every other. The trouble is that h does two jobs at once: it is the memory, and it is the output. And every step, all of it goes through W_h and a tanh.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Forgetting. Something seen at step k reaches step T only after T - k passes through that matrix and squash, like a photocopy of a photocopy.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: No way to leave a slot alone. Keeping a fact means W_h has to pass that slot through unchanged every step, and the tanh must not squash it. Nothing in the design makes that easy.

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: Vanishing gradients. The gradient from step T back to step k is a product of one factor per step in between:

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: fracpartial h_Tpartial h_k = prod_t=k+1^T diag\!left(1 - h_t^2right) W_h

chunks.h: Where x_t comes from: tokens to vectors
chunks.x: How much one factor can stretch a vector is at most the tanh slope (never above 1, and near 0 when a unit saturates) times the largest stretch of W_h (its largest singular value). If that's below 1, the product shrinks like a number below 1 raised to the power T - k : exponentially with distance. If W_h stretches some direction by more than 1, it can explode instead. A weight's gradient is a sum of one share per step, so the shares from distant steps are exponentially smaller than the nearby ones, and the network learns only short-range patterns. That's the same product as the forgetting, read
gate_t = sigmabig(W [h_t-1, x_t] + bbig) in (0, 1)^H
A vector of dials, one per memory slot. It's a sigmoid because it answers “how much?”: 0 blocks, 1 passes.
Used by element-wise multiplication, gate odot signal : slot j lets through the fraction gate_j .

Recomputed every step from the current input and the previous output, so how much passes depends on the data. Compare the RNN, where how much of the past carries over is fixed by W_h , the same matrix every step.
A gate is not a weight matrix. It's an activation, a vector computed fresh each step. Each gate has its own weight matrix that computes it.

Long short-term memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) gives the network a notebook, the cell state c , kept separate from what it says, h . Each step it decides what to erase, what to write, and what to read out.
The LSTM cell. The notebook c runs along the top and only ever gets multiplied by f and added to. The four blocks at the bottom all read the same thing, [h_t-1, x_t] .
In: x_t (what just happened), h_t-1 (what I said last step) and c_t-1 (my notebook). Stack the first two into u_t = [h_t-1, x_t] , then ask it four questions, each with its own weights:
f_t = sigma(W_f u_t + b_f)
Which old notes do I keep?
i_t = sigma(W_i u_t + b_i)
How much of the draft should I write?
g_t = tanh(W_g u_t + b_g)
o_t = sigma(W_o u_t + b_o)
What should I show right now?
beginaligned c_t &= f_t odot c_t-1 + i_t odot g_t \\ h_t &= o_t odot tanh(c_t) endaligned
Out: c_t goes only to the next step. h_t goes to the prediction and to the next step, inside u_t+1 . Both start at zero. And c_t-1 has no separate equation: it is this same update, one step earlier.
In code: one stacked 4H times (H + d) matrix, one multiply, split into quarters
One dial (or draft value) per slot
Same size, so odot works slot by slot
PyTorch weight_ih_l0 / weight_hh_l0
The same stacked matrix, split by input; order i, f, g, o. From layer 2 up, d becomes H ( 2H if bidirectional)
PyTorch bias_ih_l0 / bias_hh_l0
Two bias vectors; only their sum matters (see below)
nn.LSTM output, (h_n, c_n)
B times T times H , (layers times B times H) each
Bidirectional: output B times T times 2H
beginaligned \#params, textbook &= 4\,big[H(H + d) + Hbig] \\ \#params, PyTorch &= 4\,big[H(H + d) + 2Hbig] endaligned
For d = 100 and H = 128 the textbook count is 4 times (128 times 228 + 128) = 117,248 ; PyTorch reports 4H more, for its second bias vector (explained under “Parameters” below).

def lstm_step(x, h, c): # x: (d,) h, c: (H,) u = concat([h, x]) # (H + d,) z = W @ u + b # one stacked matmul: W (4H, H+d) -> (4H,) i, f, g, o = split(z, 4) # PyTorch order i, f, g, o; each (H,) i, f, o = sigmoid(i), sigmoid(f), sigmoid(o) # dials in (0, 1) g = tanh(g) # the draft, in (-1, 1) c = f * c + i * g # erase part, write part h = o * tanh(c) # read part out return h, c h, c = zeros(H), zeros(H) for t in range(T): h, c = lstm_step(x[t], h, c)

A block is anything computed from [h_t-1, x_t] through its own weight matrix: sigma or tanh of W u_t + b . The LSTM has four: f , i , g and o . The inputs and states x , h and c have no weights of their own; c_t and h_t are just multiplied and added together from the blocks. Each block holds H(H + d) + H numbers (PyTorch stores one more H of bias), which is where the parameter count comes from. (The GRU has three: z , r and its draft tilde h .)
The cell only produces the hidden state. To predict anything, put an ordinary output layer, the “head”, on top. It is not part of the cell:
hat y_t = softmax(W_y h_t + b_y), qquad W_y is K times H
Many-to-many (tag every word, flag every payment): apply the same W_y to every h_t .
Many-to-one (one label per message): apply it once, usually to the last state h_T , or to a summary of all of them (their mean, max, or an attention-weighted sum).
Use a sigmoid for a yes/no label and no activation for regression. In PyTorch, nn.LSTM returns every h_t plus the final (h_T, c_T) ; you add nn.Linear(H, K) yourself.
Per slot: keep (1) or erase (0) the old note. Fraud example: keep “new payees lately” through normal payments, and wipe it once the customer verifies with the bank.
Stuck at 1: the notebook can never be cleared, so it fills and saturates. Stuck at 0: no memory at all.
The new content: exactly a plain RNN update, tanh(W_g u_t + b_g) .
It's tanh, not sigmoid, because a write must push a slot up or down, as evidence for or against.
Is the draft worth writing? It's separate from g because what an input says and whether to record it are different questions. A routine payment has content, but nothing worth noting.
With one set of weights doing both jobs, they pull against each other. The 1997 paper called this the input weight conflict.
Which notes to expose now. It lets a fact sit silently (a password reset three steps ago) until it matters (a large transfer arrives), so stored facts don't disturb every step.
The tanh before it keeps h bounded, because c is a sum of writes and can grow.
Why does h go to the next step if the notebook c already holds everything?
h is read from the notebook. It's o odot tanh(c) , so the next step's gates do see the notebook, through this filtered readout.

Keeping two states means hiding isn't forgetting. The output gate can hide a slot from everything downstream (the prediction and the next gates) while c keeps it safe. With one vector doing both jobs, hiding a fact would erase it. That's exactly the GRU's trade-off.
c is unbounded (a sum of writes), so feeding it raw into sigmoid gates would saturate them. h is bounded.
Letting the gates read c directly was tried. These are “peephole” connections (Gers and Schmidhuber, 2000), and they gave no consistent gain.

c is one vector of H slots (often 64 to 512), each with its own dials, so it holds many facts at once: one slot counting new payees, another overwritten every step. Real slots aren't that tidy, since facts get spread across several, but the picture holds. Because f and i are separate, each slot has four moves:
replace: erase, then write
accumulate: keep and add, so it can count
wipe: clear without writing
Parameters: four blocks, each an H times (H + d) matrix plus H biases, so 4\,[H(H+d) + H] . In code they're one 4H times (H+d) matrix multiply, split into quarters (PyTorch orders them i, f, g, o).

PyTorch's second bias. nn.LSTM keeps two bias vectors per block: b_ih on the input projection and b_hh on the hidden projection, so each pre-activation is W_ih x_t + b_ih + W_hh h_t-1 + b_hh . They're always added together, so only b_ih + b_hh matters and one of them is redundant. It's there because cuDNN's formulation puts a bias on each of its two matrix multiplies, and PyTorch matches it so the fast kernel can run the same weights. Hence PyTorch's 4\,[H(H+d) + 2H] .
Not tied to T . The same weights run at every step, so the count is the same for any sequence length.

Per layer. In a stack, layer 2 reads layer 1's h , so its input size is H instead of d ( 2H if bidirectional). A bidirectional layer has two independent sets of weights, one per direction, so it doubles the count.
The gated recurrent unit (Cho et al., 2014) is a simpler LSTM. It merges the notebook and the output into one state h and uses two gates instead of three.

beginaligned z_t &= sigma(W_z [h_t-1, x_t] + b_z) \\ r_t &= sigma(W_r [h_t-1, x_t] + b_r) \\ tilde h_t &= tanhbig(W_n [\, r_t odot h_t-1,\; x_t \,] + b_nbig) \\ h_t &= (1 - z_t) odot h_t-1 + z_t odot tilde h_t endaligned
Stacked in code as 3H times (H + d) ; PyTorch order r, z, n
Everything is one H -vector per step
3[H(H + d) + H] ; PyTorch 3[H(H + d) + 2H]
25% fewer than an LSTM of the same size: 3 blocks instead of 4

PyTorch's GRU also keeps two bias vectors per block, but here the pair isn't fully redundant. Its draft is tanh(W_in x_t + b_in + r_t odot (W_hn h_t-1 + b_hn)) , so b_hn is scaled by the reset gate while b_in isn't. Only the r and z bias pairs collapse into one.

def gru_step(x, h): # z = how much to write z = sigmoid(W_z @ concat([h, x]) + b_z) r = sigmoid(W_r @ concat([h, x]) + b_r) draft = tanh(W_n @ concat([r * h, x]) + b_n) # r filters the past before the matmul return (1 - z) * h + z * draft # blend old and new
The GRU cell. One state. The reset gate decides how much of the old state the draft gets to see; the update gate slides the new state between the old state and the draft.

Update gate z : how much to write. A slider: the new state sits a fraction z of the way from the old state to the draft, so it keeps 1 - z and writes z . It does the jobs of the LSTM's forget and input gates at once, tied together: f = 1 - z , i = z .

Reset gate r : what the draft is built from. It multiplies the old state before it enters the draft's matrix. With r approx 0 the draft is built from the input alone, a fresh start (a new sentence, a new session); with r approx 1 it is a plain RNN update. It erases nothing by itself: erasing happens when z writes that draft over the old state.

No output gate. The state is always fully shown, to the output and to every gate at the next step. It can't hide a fact without forgetting it, which is the trade the LSTM avoids by keeping two states.

The cost of tying. Every write erases the same fraction, and the state is an average of old and new, so it stays within the draft's range and can't count. It wins some of this back because the draft reads the old state through r : old memory can ride inside the new write.
In the LSTM the input gate multiplies the draft, i odot g . Why does the GRU's r act on h_t-1 inside the draft instead?

Because it has a different job. “How much to write” is already done by z . If r multiplied the draft's output, it would be a second volume knob for the same thing. Acting on the draft's input gives it a new job: choosing what the draft is computed from.

It stands in for the LSTM's output gate, for the draft only. An LSTM's draft reads h_t-1 = o odot tanh(c_t-1) , a version of the memory already filtered by the output gate. A GRU's h is the raw memory, so without r every draft would be built from the entire past, relevant or not.

It sits before the matrix multiply so the past's contribution can be dropped slot by slot while the input's is kept; once W_n mixes them, they can't be pulled apart. (PyTorch applies r to W_hn h_t-1 , after the past's own multiply but still apart from the input's.)

Cho et al. (2014) found that units tracking short-range patterns lean on the reset gate and long-range ones on the update gate. A one-gate version, the minimal gated unit (Zhou et al., 2016), does about as well on several tasks, so the split helps but isn't essential.
The same jobs exist in all three cells. What changes is which piece does them.
What the output and the next step read
How much old memory to keep
How much new content to write
Which part of the memory the draft sees
Whatever last step's o let into h
What to hide from the outside

Here z means “how much to write” (as in Chung et al., 2014). The original paper and PyTorch flip it: h_t = z odot h_t-1 + (1 - z) odot tilde h_t , so their z means “keep”. PyTorch also applies r after the matrix multiply: tanh(W_in x + b_in + r odot (W_hn h + b_hn)) . Say which convention you're using.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Backprop through time asks, for every step: if this step's state had been slightly different, how much would the loss change? For an early step, the answer is carried backward one step at a time, and each step multiplies it by how strongly this step's memory depends on the previous step's. Everything that separates the three cells in training comes down to that per-step multiplier.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Two kinds of gradient come out of the walk back:

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: State gradients ( delta h , delta c ) travel backward through time, one step at a time.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Weight gradients are collected along the way. Every weight is shared across steps, so its gradient is a sum of one share per step, each share being (gradient at the output of its multiply) × (what it multiplied) ^top . An early step only adds a real share if its state gradient survived the walk.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Plain RNN: a weight matrix and a slope at every step

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: delta h_t-1 = W_h^topbig[delta h_t odot (1 - h_t^2)big] \;+\; (gradient from step t-1's own output)

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Each step back goes through the tanh's slope, 1 - h_t^2 , and then through W_h^top . Chained over many steps, that's prod diag(1 - h_t^2) W_h . If each factor shrinks the gradient, it vanishes exponentially. If W_h stretches it, it can explode. It's the same fixed matrix at every step, with no way to say “pass this through untouched”.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: LSTM: a second path with no weights on it

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: delta c_t = underbracedelta h_t odot o_t odot big(1 - tanh^2 c_tbig)_from this step's output \;+\; underbracedelta c_t+1 odot f_t+1_from the future, along the cell

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: The second term is the highway. Going back one step along the cell multiplies the gradient by f , and only f : no weight matrix and no tanh slope. With f approx 1 , it arrives almost whole. With f = 1 , the update is c_t = c_t-1 + i_t odot g_t , a residual connection through time (the 1997 paper's “constant error carousel”).

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: The gates learn from side branches. Three come from delta c_t , the output gate from delta h_t :

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: beginaligned delta f_t &= delta c_t odot c_t-1 \\ delta i_t &= delta c_t odot g_t \\ delta g_t &= delta c_t odot i_t \\ delta o_t &= delta h_t odot tanh(c_t) endaligned

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Each is multiplied by its activation's slope, then feeds its weight's gradient and, through those weights, delta h_t-1 . These side paths do go through matrices, so they can still explode, which is why LSTMs are still clipped.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Memory and gradient fade together. Unrolled, the cell is a sum of every past write, faded by the forget gates since: c_t = sum_k big(prod_j>k f_jbig) odot i_k odot g_k . The gradient back to each write is that same product, so the cell keeps a fact exactly as long as it can learn from it. Start the forget bias at 1, so f approx 0.73 . At 0, f approx 0.5 halves memory and gradient every step, like a plain RNN. Not 10, though: there f sits a hair below 1, where the sigmoid is flat, so the side branch that trains the gate carries almost no gradient and the gate can barely learn to forget.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: GRU: the blend is the highway

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: delta h_t-1 = delta h_t odot (1 - z_t) \;+\; (paths through z_t,\ r_t and tilde h_t)

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: The direct term comes from the (1 - z) odot h_t-1 half of the blend, so it's multiplied only by 1 - z , a gate value, just like the LSTM's f . While the GRU keeps ( z approx 0 ), the gradient passes back almost whole. When it writes ( z approx 1 ), the direct path is cut, and what comes back has to go through the draft ( r odot h_t-1 inside tilde h ). That path runs through W_n and a tanh slope, like a plain RNN.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: The direct path back through time. In a plain RNN each step multiplies by a weight matrix and a tanh slope, so the signal thins out. In an LSTM's cell and a GRU's state, each step multiplies only by a gate value, f or 1 - z ; when those are near 1 the signal arrives almost whole.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: That's the whole fix in one line: replace a fixed matrix times a slope with a learned dial. Attention goes one step further and removes the walk altogether, because every token connects to every other in one step (see Transformers).

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: “The forget gate is a sigmoid, whose slope is at most 0.25. Doesn't the gradient vanish through it?” No. Along the cell, the gradient is multiplied by the gate's value f , not its slope. The slope only appears on the side branch that trains the gate's own weights.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: In practice: clipping and truncated BPTT

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Clip by norm, not by value. Clipping by norm rescales the whole gradient when its length passes a threshold tau , so the direction stays the same and only the step shrinks. Clipping by value caps each component on its own, which tilts the direction toward the small components. An exploding gradient usually comes from a steep cliff in the loss: its direction is still useful, it's just far too long (Pascanu et al., 2013). Neither version helps a vanishing gradient, since both only shrink.

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: beginaligned by norm:quad g &leftarrow g cdot min\!big(1,\ tau / lVert g rVertbig) \\ by value:quad g_j &leftarrow max(-tau, min(tau, g_j)) endaligned

chunks.h: How the gradient flows: RNN → LSTM → GRU
chunks.x: Truncated BPTT. Full BPTT stores every step's activations, so memory grows with the sequence length, and a stream that never ends can't be backpropagated at all. Instead, process it in chunks of k steps: carry the state forward from chunk to chunk, but detach it at each boundary (both h and c in an LSTM), so gradients stop there. The price is that the gradient can't teach dependencies longer than k steps, so pick k at least as long as the ones you care about.

Most of this comes from two big ablation studies: Greff et al. (2015, “LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey”, 8 variants on speech, handwriting and music) and Jozefowicz et al. (2015, over 10,000 architectures searched).
Original LSTM, no forget gate
On long continuous streams the cell grows without limit. The forget gate was added to fix this. Gers et al., 2000
The biggest drop of any change, on every task. Greff 2015
Remove the tanh on the cell output
Also a large drop: h becomes unbounded. Greff 2015
Remove the input gate, the output gate or the candidate's tanh
Worse on speech and handwriting, no effect on music. Greff 2015
No significant change. Greff 2015
Couple the gates, i = 1 − f
No significant change on benchmarks Greff 2015, but the cell can no longer count (shown for the GRU, whose gates are tied the same way) Weiss et al., 2018
Closes the gap between the LSTM and the GRU. Jozefowicz 2015
Rank the gates by importance
Forget gate crucial, input gate important, output gate the least important. Jozefowicz 2015
Comparable, and both far better than a tanh RNN Chung 2014. The GRU won on most tasks except language modelling Jozefowicz 2015.
Keep only the forget gate
Competitive on several benchmarks. van der Westhuizen & Lasenby, 2018
The forget gate, started near 1, is the heart of it. The output gate matters least, which is why the GRU can drop it.
Greff also found the learning rate mattered more than any architectural variant, and the hyperparameters barely interact. Tune the learning rate first.

A neat theory result (Tallec and Ollivier, 2018): gates fall out of asking a recurrent model to be robust to time being stretched or squeezed. That suggests setting the forget bias from the dependency lengths you expect (“chrono” initialization).
very short context, teaching
long dependencies, counting, lots of data; the safe default
less data, shorter sequences, tight latency; a fast baseline
GRU for tight latency and memory: 3 weight blocks instead of 4, so 25% fewer parameters and 25% fewer multiplies per step.
GRU for less data: fewer parameters leave less room to overfit. The effect is modest, so confirm it on validation.

GRU for shorter sequences: there's no separate cell, so retention rests on the update gate alone, and that same gate also decides writing. Keeping a slot means not writing to it, and every write erases part of what's stored, so over many writes old facts erode; short sequences rarely hit that limit. There's also no output gate to protect a hidden memory, so a fact can't be hidden without being erased, though ablations rate the output gate as the least important, so that costs less.
LSTM for long dependencies and counting: separate forget and input gates can keep and add at once, so a slot can hold a fact or a running count for a long time while other slots are rewritten.
LSTM with lots of data: at the same hidden size, its fourth block is extra capacity, which pays off once there's enough data to fit it.
LSTM as the safe default: it's the best-studied cell with a known training recipe (forget bias 1, clipping), and Greff et al. found no variant that reliably beat it.
Plain RNN only for very short context: its memory and its gradient fade exponentially with distance.

What the comparisons found: no consistent winner. Chung et al. (2014) found the two gated cells comparable; Jozefowicz et al. (2015) found the GRU ahead on most tasks except language modelling, until a forget bias of 1 closed the gap; Greff et al. (2015) found the learning rate was the most important hyperparameter, while most variants changed little. So in practice, try both: the gap between them is usually smaller than the effect of features and tuning.

Against transformers, RNNs lose because they run step by step (no parallel training across time), squeeze the past into a fixed-size state, and need n steps to connect token 1 to token n . Attention keeps every past state and connects any two in one step, at a cost that grows as n^2 . RNNs still win for streaming with constant work per event, such as per-transaction scoring or on-device models, because a new event only updates a fixed-size state, while a transformer has to attend over every past event and its cache keeps growing.
Run two LSTMs over the sequence: one left to right, one right to left. At each position, join their states, so every position sees its whole context:
beginaligned overrightarrowh_t &= LSTM(x_t, overrightarrowh_t-1) \\ overleftarrowh_t &= LSTM(x_t, overleftarrowh_t+1) \\ h_t &= [overrightarrowh_t ;\, overleftarrowh_t] endaligned

Built for tagging and for labelling finished sequences. Examples: named-entity tags, part-of-speech tags, or one codon per amino acid. A stacked bi-LSTM is a common baseline for exactly that. Each output sees both sides of its position.
Costs: twice the parameters and compute, and the output size doubles to 2H .

Not for generation or live scoring. The backward half has already read the future. For a per-step prediction made in real time, that's leakage: offline metrics look great, and production can't supply the future.
Many-to-one with a bi-LSTM: join the forward pass's last state with the backward pass's first state (each has read the whole sequence), or pool over all positions.
Its successors: ELMo (2018) used stacked bi-LSTM language models as contextual word embeddings. BERT then replaced the LSTMs with a bidirectional transformer.

Layer 2 reads layer 1's sequence of h 's as its inputs. Two to four layers is typical; more rarely helps, because each layer adds another set of weights and another non-linear step between input and output at every time step, so deep stacks get harder to train and the gains flatten out.

Put dropout between layers, not on the step-to-step connection. Fresh noise on h_t-1 to h_t at every step corrupts the memory. If you want it there, use the same mask at every step (“variational” dropout).
Residual connections between layers help deep stacks; Google's 2016 translation system used 8 LSTM layers with residuals.
The last state, or a pool of all states
A fraud score per session; a label per message
Tagging; a codon per amino acid; flag each payment
Encode everything, then decode
Translation; forecast the next 7 days
One input, a sequence out

Teacher forcing: while training a generator, feed it the true previous token, not its own guess. It converges faster and more stably, because each step learns from a correct prefix and one early mistake can't derail the rest. But at inference it meets its own mistakes for the first time (“exposure bias”): one wrong token puts it in a state it never trained on, and errors compound. Scheduled sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) gradually feeds the model its own predictions during training; beam search at inference softens an early slip.
Variable lengths: pad to the longest, then mask or pack (pack_padded_sequence) and read each sequence's true last state. Without that, padding steps keep changing the state.
Checklist, with the reason for each:
forget bias 1, so the cell starts out remembering;
clipping by norm (1–5), since the weight paths can still explode;
Adam with a tuned learning rate, the setting that matters most;
standardized inputs, so the gates don't start saturated;
truncated BPTT for long streams, so memory stays bounded (detach both h and c ).
Answer out loud first, then open the answer. Each answer stands on its own: the one-line answer first, then how it works, then why.
1Why do plain RNNs struggle with long sequences?

The same matrix and squash are applied to the whole memory at every step, so old information, and the gradient that could teach the network to keep it, shrink (or blow up) exponentially with distance.
All of h is rewritten every step, and going back from step T to step k multiplies one Jacobian per step in between (the matrix of how each slot of a state depends on each slot of the one before):
beginaligned h_t &= tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_t-1 + b) \\ fracpartial h_Tpartial h_k &= prod_t=k+1^T diag(1 - h_t^2)\, W_h endaligned

Why it vanishes. One factor can stretch a vector by at most the tanh slope (never above 1, near 0 when a unit saturates) times the largest stretch of W_h (its largest singular value). If that's below 1, the product shrinks like a number below 1 raised to the power T - k .
Why it can explode. If W_h stretches some direction by more than 1 and the units aren't saturated, the same power can grow instead.
Why that stops learning. A weight's gradient is a sum of one share per step, and shares from distant steps are exponentially smaller, so only short-range patterns get learned.
Why forgetting is the same thing. Information from step k reaches step T through the same chain, so it fades the same way.
Fixes: clipping shrinks an exploding gradient but can't enlarge a vanishing one; that needs gates (LSTM, GRU) or attention.
2Walk me through an LSTM step. What does each gate do?
Each step erases part of the cell, writes a gated draft into it, and reads a filtered view of it out as h .
Stack u_t = [h_t-1, x_t] and compute four blocks, each with its own weights, then update the cell and the output:

beginaligned f_t &= sigma(W_f u_t + b_f) \\ i_t &= sigma(W_i u_t + b_i) \\ g_t &= tanh(W_g u_t + b_g) \\ o_t &= sigma(W_o u_t + b_o) \\ c_t &= f_t odot c_t-1 + i_t odot g_t \\ h_t &= o_t odot tanh(c_t) endaligned
Forget f : which old notes to keep, slot by slot.
Candidate g : the draft of new content, exactly a plain RNN update.
Input i : how much of the draft to write. It's separate from g because what an input says and whether it's worth recording are different questions.
Output o : which notes to show now, to the prediction and to the next step's gates.

Why these activations. The gates are sigmoids because each is a per-slot fraction in (0, 1) . The draft is tanh because a write must push a slot up or down. The tanh on c keeps h bounded, since c is a sum of writes and can grow. All four read [h_t-1, x_t] because whether to keep or write depends on both what just arrived and the context so far.
Likely follow-up: “Why does this help the gradient?” One step back along c multiplies only by f_t , with no weight matrix, so where f approx 1 the gradient survives.
3Cell state vs hidden state: why keep both?
c is the memory and h is what the cell shows. Keeping them apart lets the LSTM hide a fact without forgetting it, keeps the gates' inputs bounded, and leaves a weight-free gradient path.
beginaligned c_t &= f_t odot c_t-1 + i_t odot g_t \\ h_t &= o_t odot tanh(c_t) endaligned
Hide without forgetting. o_t can zero a slot in h , so neither the prediction nor the next gates see it, while c keeps it for later. With one state, as in the GRU, hiding a fact means overwriting it.
Bounded inputs for the gates. c is a running sum of writes, so it's unbounded; fed raw into the next step's sigmoids, it would saturate them. h lies in (-1, 1) .
A clean gradient path. c is only multiplied by f and added to, so the gradient along it meets no weight matrix. h goes through all four weight blocks at the next step.

How much it matters: in ablations the output gate is the least important gate (Jozefowicz 2015), and the GRU does without the split at little cost. Letting the gates read c directly (peepholes) gave no consistent gain.
4How does the LSTM fix vanishing gradients? Can it still vanish or explode?
It adds a memory path whose per-step gradient multiplier is a learned gate value, f_t , instead of a weight matrix times a tanh slope.
On the direct path along the cell, one step back is just:
fracpartial c_tpartial c_t-1 = diag(f_t)

Why that helps. No W_h and no tanh slope sit on this path. Where the network learns f approx 1 , the gradient arrives almost whole: a residual connection through time, the 1997 paper's “constant error carousel”.
Why it's controllable. f is recomputed every step from the data, per slot, so a slot can hold for a long stretch and then reset. A fixed W_h can't do that.
It can still vanish. Over a gap of T - k steps the factor is a product of f 's. Below 1 it still decays, just far more slowly and under the model's control.
It can still explode. h_t-1 feeds every gate and the draft through weight matrices. Those side paths behave like an RNN's, so LSTMs are still clipped.

Likely follow-up: “The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so doesn't the gradient vanish through f ?” No. Along the cell it's multiplied by the gate's value; the slope only appears on the side branch that trains the gate's own weights.
5Why initialize the forget-gate bias to 1? Why not 10?
At 1 the cell starts out remembering, so long-range gradients exist from the start; at 10 the gate is saturated and can't learn to forget.
At initialization the weights are small, so f approx sigma(b_f) , and the cell path multiplies both memory and gradient by f every step.
Bias 0: f approx 0.5 , so memory and gradient halve every step, much like a plain RNN. Long-range dependencies send almost no gradient back, so the model never discovers it should keep them.
Bias 1: f approx 0.73 . The cell leans toward keeping, gradients reach further back, and the gate is still in the sigmoid's responsive range, so it can learn to move either way.

Bias 10: f is a hair below 1, where the sigmoid is flat. Its slope is almost zero, so the gradient into the gate's weights vanishes and it can barely learn to forget. The cell then piles up writes until tanh(c) saturates.
Evidence: Jozefowicz et al. (2015) found this one change closes the LSTM–GRU gap.

In practice: Keras does it by default; PyTorch doesn't. PyTorch's forget slice is [H:2H] (order i, f, g, o). b_ih and b_hh are added together, so set it in one of them only; both would give an effective bias of 2.
6Why separate forget and input gates instead of i = 1 − f?
Separate gates let a slot keep and write at the same time, which is what lets an LSTM accumulate and count. Tied gates force every write to erase.
With separate gates each slot has four moves: keep ( f = 1, i = 0 ), replace ( 0, 1 ), accumulate ( 1, 1 ) and wipe ( 0, 0 ). Tie them and the update becomes a weighted average of old and new:
c_t = f_t odot c_t-1 + (1 - f_t) odot g_t
Every write erases. Writing a fraction 1 - f of the draft costs exactly that fraction of the old memory, so remembering and writing compete.

It can't count. An average of values in (-1, 1) stays in (-1, 1) , so the cell can't grow with the number of events. Weiss et al. (2018) showed the LSTM can count and the GRU, whose gates are tied, can't.
The gradient pays too. The cell path's multiplier is f = 1 - i , so each strong write also cuts the gradient flowing back past it.

The other side: coupled gates (CIFG in Greff 2015, and the GRU) do about as well on standard benchmarks, which rarely need counting. Separate gates matter when the task accumulates evidence over time, such as counting events in a session.
7Write the GRU and compare it with the LSTM.
The GRU merges the cell and the output into one state, ties forget and input into one update gate, and drops the output gate: three blocks instead of four.

beginaligned z_t &= sigma(W_z[h_t-1, x_t] + b_z) \\ r_t &= sigma(W_r[h_t-1, x_t] + b_r) \\ tilde h_t &= tanh(W_n[r_t odot h_t-1, x_t] + b_n) \\ h_t &= (1 - z_t) odot h_t-1 + z_t odot tilde h_t endaligned
In words: z slides the state between its old value and the draft, and r decides how much of the past the draft is built from.
Tied gates: z plays the LSTM's input gate, and 1 - z its forget gate. Every write erases the same fraction, and the state stays within the draft's range, so it can't count.
No output gate: the whole state is always shown, so it can't hide a fact without overwriting it.
Gradient: one step back along the blend multiplies by 1 - z_t , the GRU's version of the LSTM's f_t .
Cost: 3 weight blocks instead of 4, so 25% fewer parameters and multiplies per step.

Convention trap: the original paper and PyTorch write h_t = z odot h_t-1 + (1 - z) odot tilde h_t , so their z means “keep”, and PyTorch applies r after the hidden matrix multiply. Say which one you're using.
8What does the reset gate do that the update gate doesn't?
The update gate decides how much of the state to replace; the reset gate decides what the replacement is built from.
beginaligned tilde h_t &= tanh(W_n[r_t odot h_t-1, x_t] + b_n) \\ h_t &= (1 - z_t) odot h_t-1 + z_t odot tilde h_t endaligned
r approx 0 : the draft ignores the past and is built from x_t alone, a fresh start (a new sentence, a new session). Then z decides whether to write it over the old state.
r approx 1 : the draft is a plain RNN update from the whole past.

Why z alone isn't enough. Without r , every draft is computed from the entire old state, so z could only blend the old state with something that already contains it. There'd be no way to build new content that isn't coloured by irrelevant history.
Why r doesn't erase. It only filters the draft's input. Nothing leaves the state until z writes the draft over it.

Evidence: Cho et al. (2014) saw units that track short-range patterns lean on r , and long-range ones on z . The minimal gated unit (Zhou et al., 2016) uses one gate for both jobs and does about as well on several tasks, so a separate reset gate helps but isn't essential.
9Which LSTM gate matters most? What happens if you remove each one?
The forget gate matters most and the output gate least. Each removal hurts in proportion to the job it leaves undone (Greff 2015; Jozefowicz 2015 ranks forget, then input, then output):
Forget gate: the biggest drop, on every task. The cell can only add, so it can't reset at boundaries, it grows on long streams, and tanh(c) saturates. That's why it was added in 2000.
Tanh on the cell output: also a large drop. h = o odot c becomes unbounded, so the next step's gates saturate and activations can blow up.
Input gate: every draft is added in full on top of what's stored, so routine inputs keep corrupting stored facts. Worse on speech and handwriting.
Output gate: the whole cell is always shown, as in a GRU, so stored facts disturb every step. Also worse on speech and handwriting, though Jozefowicz ranks it the least important gate.
Candidate's tanh: writes become unbounded too. It hurt on some tasks.
Peepholes, or coupling i = 1 - f : no significant change on benchmarks.

Why the forget gate ranks first: it sets both how long memory lasts and how far the gradient reaches, the two things a plain RNN lacks. Greff also found the learning rate was the most important hyperparameter, while most variants changed little.
10Hypothetical: swap the sigmoid gates for ReLU, tanh, or hard 0/1 switches?
Each one breaks something a gate needs: a value between 0 and 1, the meaning “how much”, or a gradient.

ReLU: unbounded above, so a forget value above 1 multiplies the memory by more than 1 every step, and c and its gradient explode. Below zero it outputs exactly 0 with zero slope, so a gate that closes can get stuck closed.
Tanh: range (-1, 1) . A negative gate flips a slot's sign every step, so the memory oscillates and “how much to keep” loses its meaning. Rescaled to (1 + tanh)/2 , it's just a sigmoid again.

Hard 0/1: a step function's slope is 0 almost everywhere, so no gradient reaches the gate's weights and they never learn when to open. Workarounds exist (a straight-through estimator, or a piecewise-linear “hard sigmoid” with a slope in the middle), but they approximate the smooth gate.
Why the sigmoid fits: it's bounded in (0, 1) , so it reads as a fraction; it's smooth with a non-zero slope everywhere, so training can move it; and it starts mid-range, with room to open or close.
11Hypothetical: what if f = 1 and i = 1 at every step?
The cell becomes a pure running sum of drafts: it never forgets, grows without limit, and saturates its own readout.
beginaligned c_t &= c_t-1 + g_t \\ &= sum_k le t g_k endaligned
Why it grows. Nothing ever scales c back, so it's a sum of t drafts, and its size can keep growing with the length of the stream.
Why h stops responding. h = o odot tanh(c) , and once |c| is large, tanh(c) is stuck near pm 1 . New inputs barely change the output.

Why learning stalls. The gradient from each output into the cell carries the factor 1 - tanh^2(c_t) , near zero when saturated. The cell path itself multiplies by exactly 1, a perfect carousel, but almost nothing gets onto it.
Why it can't reset. With f = 1 , facts from a previous sentence or session stay forever and pollute the next.
History: this is close to the original 1997 LSTM, which had no forget gate. Gers et al. (2000) added one because the cell failed on long continuous streams in exactly this way.
12Parameter count for an LSTM and a GRU?
Count weight blocks: an LSTM has 4, a GRU 3 (so 25% fewer), a plain RNN 1. PyTorch stores one extra bias vector per block.
One block maps the H + d numbers of [h_t-1, x_t] to H outputs: H(d + H) weights plus H biases. So:
beginaligned LSTM, textbook &= 4\,[H(d + H) + H] \\ LSTM, PyTorch &= 4\,[H(d + H) + 2H] \\ GRU, textbook &= 3\,[H(d + H) + H] \\ GRU, PyTorch &= 3\,[H(d + H) + 2H] endaligned

PyTorch's second bias. nn.LSTM and nn.GRU keep b_ih on the input projection and b_hh on the hidden one. In an LSTM each pre-activation is W_ihx_t + b_ih + W_hhh_t-1 + b_hh , so only the sum b_ih + b_hh matters: the second vector is redundant, kept to match cuDNN's formulation.

The GRU is not fully redundant. Its candidate is tanh(W_inx_t + b_in + r_t odot (W_hnh_t-1 + b_hn)) , so b_hn sits inside the reset gate's product while b_in doesn't. Only the r and z pairs collapse to one.
Independent of T : the same weights run at every step.
Per layer: in a stack, layer 2 reads layer 1's states, so its input size is H , or 2H if bidirectional. A bidirectional layer has two sets of weights, so it doubles the count.
A plain RNN is one block, H(d + H) + H (PyTorch adds H ). An output head over K classes adds KH + K , and an embedding table for a vocabulary of V tokens adds Vd .
13LSTM or GRU, and why did transformers replace both?
Neither wins consistently, so try both. Lean GRU for small data, shorter sequences or tight latency; lean LSTM for long dependencies, counting, or plenty of data.
GRU is cheaper per step. 3 weight blocks instead of 4, so 25% fewer parameters and multiplies: lower latency and memory.
GRU can suit small data. Fewer parameters leave less room to overfit, though the effect is modest.

GRU is weaker over long spans. With no separate cell, retention rests on the update gate alone, and that gate also decides writing: keeping a slot means not writing to it, and every write erases part of it, so old facts erode. And with no output gate to protect a hidden memory, it can't hide a fact without erasing it (ablations rate this as minor).
LSTM can hold and count. Separate forget and input gates keep and add at once, so a slot holds a fact or a count while others are rewritten.

Evidence: Chung et al. (2014) found them comparable; Jozefowicz et al. (2015) found the GRU ahead except on language modelling, until a forget bias of 1 closed the gap; Greff et al. (2015) found no variant reliably beat the standard LSTM.

Why transformers replaced both: attention trains all positions in parallel, links any two tokens in one step and keeps every past token, at n^2 cost. RNNs still suit streaming, with constant work per event.
14Is the LSTM's h_t the prediction? How do you get an output?
No. h_t is the hidden state; a separate output layer, the head, turns it into a prediction.
hat y_t = softmax(W_y h_t + b_y), qquad W_y is K times H

Why a separate head. h_t holds H numbers in (-1, 1) chosen to be useful memory, not K probabilities that sum to 1. The head maps the state to the task's outputs, so the same cell serves any task by changing only the head.
Many-to-many (tag every token, flag every payment): apply the same head at every step and add up the per-step losses.

Many-to-one (one label per message): apply it once, to h_T or to a pool of all the h_t . Pooling (mean, max or attention weights) helps on long inputs, because h_T is dominated by the most recent steps.
Activation by task: softmax for one of K classes, sigmoid for yes/no or multi-label, none for regression.
In PyTorch: nn.LSTM returns every h_t ( B times T times H ) plus the final (h_T, c_T) ; you add nn.Linear(H, K). With padded batches, read each sequence's true last state, not the padding's.
15Why does the GRU's reset gate act on h_t-1 inside the draft, when the LSTM's input gate multiplies the draft's output?
Because the GRU's update gate already does the input gate's job, so r gets a different one: choosing what the draft is computed from.
beginaligned LSTM write &= i_t odot g_t \\ GRU draft &= tanh(W_n[r_t odot h_t-1, x_t] + b_n) endaligned
Not a second volume knob. “How much to write” is z , in h_t = (1 - z_t) odot h_t-1 + z_t odot tilde h_t . An r on the draft's output would duplicate it.

A stand-in for the output gate, for the draft only. An LSTM's draft reads h_t-1 = o odot tanh(c_t-1) , memory already filtered by o . A GRU's h is the raw memory, so without r every draft would be built from all of the past, relevant or not.
Why before the matrix multiply. Once W_n mixes h_t-1 and x_t , their contributions can't be pulled apart. Filtering h_t-1 first drops the past slot by slot while keeping the input.

PyTorch's variant computes tanh(W_inx_t + b_in + r_t odot (W_hnh_t-1 + b_hn)) : r acts after the hidden multiply but still apart from the input's. It's faster, because W_hnh_t-1 can run in the same multiply as the other gates' hidden projections, and the accuracy difference is usually small.
16Compare how the gradient flows back through time in an RNN, an LSTM and a GRU.
On the memory path, one step back multiplies the gradient by a fixed matrix and a slope in an RNN, but only by a learned gate value in an LSTM ( f_t ) or a GRU ( 1 - z_t ).

beginaligned RNN:quad delta h_t-1 &= W_h^topbig[delta h_t odot (1 - h_t^2)big] + dots \\ LSTM:quad delta c_t-1 &= delta c_t odot f_t + dots \\ GRU:quad delta h_t-1 &= delta h_t odot (1 - z_t) + dots endaligned
Here delta x means the gradient of the loss with respect to x . The “ dots ” are the other routes: the step's own output and, in the gated cells, the paths through the gates and the draft.
RNN: the same W_h and a tanh slope at every step, so over many steps the product vanishes or explodes exponentially, and nothing in the model can stop it.

LSTM and GRU: no weight matrix and no slope on the direct path. The multiplier is per slot and per step, and the network can hold it near 1 where memory is needed: a near-identity highway, like a residual connection through time.
What still goes through weights: the gates and the draft read h_t-1 through matrices, so those side paths can still explode. Clip by norm.
GRU detail: when it writes ( z approx 1 ), the direct path is cut, and the gradient has to go back through the draft, which behaves like an RNN step.
Likely follow-up: attention removes the walk altogether, since any two tokens are one step apart.
17What is truncated backprop through time, and what does it cost you?
Backpropagate through only the last k steps of a long sequence, while still carrying the state forward through all of it.

Split the stream into chunks of k steps. Run each chunk forward from the previous chunk's final state, backprop and update within the chunk, then detach the state: keep its values, but cut the graph, so the next chunk's gradients stop at the boundary.

h, c = zeros(H), zeros(H) for chunk, target in chunks(stream, k): h, c = h.detach(), c.detach() # keep values, cut the graph out, (h, c) = lstm(chunk, (h, c)) # forward k steps loss(head(out), target).backward(); clip(); step()
Why truncate. Full BPTT stores every step's activations, so memory grows with sequence length, and you get one update per whole sequence. A stream that never ends can't be backpropagated at all.
Why detach. Without it the graph would chain back through every earlier chunk, and memory would grow just as before. In an LSTM, detach both h and c .

The cost. The gradient can't teach dependencies longer than k steps. The state still carries information further, but only what was stored for shorter-range reasons. Pick k at least as long as the dependencies you care about.
18Gradient clipping: by norm or by value? Why?
By norm: it shrinks an oversized gradient without changing its direction, while clipping by value changes the direction.
beginaligned by norm:quad g &leftarrow g cdot min\!big(1,\ tau / lVert g rVertbig) \\ by value:quad g_j &leftarrow max(-tau, min(tau, g_j)) endaligned

By norm looks at the whole gradient vector, usually the global norm over all parameters. If it's longer than tau , it's scaled down to length tau . Every component shrinks by the same factor, so the step points the same way, just shorter.
By value caps each component separately. Big components are cut and small ones aren't, so the direction tilts toward the small ones.

Why direction matters. An exploding gradient in an RNN usually comes from a steep cliff in the loss surface. Its direction is still informative, it's just far too long, and a full step would throw the weights off the cliff (Pascanu et al., 2013).
What clipping can't do: it only shrinks, so it does nothing for vanishing gradients.
Choosing tau : log the gradient norm and set tau a little above its typical value, so only spikes get clipped. Common choices are 1–5 for RNNs and 1.0 for transformers.
19What is teacher forcing, and what is exposure bias?

Teacher forcing trains a sequence generator on the true previous token instead of its own guess. Exposure bias is the mismatch this creates at inference, when the model has to condition on its own outputs.
beginaligned training:quad s_t &= LSTM_dec(y_t-1,\ s_t-1) \\ inference:quad s_t &= LSTM_dec(hat y_t-1,\ s_t-1) endaligned
In words: s_t is the decoder's state; in training its input is the true previous token y_t-1 , at inference the model's own guess hat y_t-1 .

Why teacher forcing. Each step's loss is computed on a correct prefix, so one early mistake doesn't derail the rest, and gradients stay stable. In a transformer it's also what makes training parallel: every input is known, so all positions run at once under a causal mask.

Why exposure bias hurts. The model never saw its own errors in training. One wrong token at inference puts it in a state it never learned from, the next guess is worse, and errors compound over long outputs.

Fixes: scheduled sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) gradually swaps true inputs for the model's own predictions during training; sequence-level training scores whole generated outputs with a metric (via REINFORCE); and beam search at inference reduces the damage of one early slip.
Trade-off: scheduled sampling breaks a transformer's parallel training, so large language models mostly accept the bias and lean on scale and decoding instead.
20When can't you use a bidirectional LSTM?
Whenever the prediction at step t has to be made before the future arrives: generation, forecasting, and live per-event scoring.
h_t = [overrightarrowh_t ;\, overleftarrowh_t], qquad overleftarrowh_t has read x_t, dots, x_T

Why it leaks. The backward pass starts at the end of the sequence, so overleftarrowh_t already contains everything after t . For a fraud score per payment, that means using payments that hadn't happened yet: offline metrics look great, and production can't supply the future.
Why it can't generate. Producing token t+1 needs a state that depends only on tokens up to t . The backward half would need the very tokens it's trying to produce.
Where it shines: labelling a finished sequence, such as tagging, named entities, one codon per amino acid, or one label for a whole message. Every position benefits from both sides.
Costs: twice the parameters and compute, an output of size 2H , and no output until the whole sequence has arrived.
Many-to-one with a bi-LSTM: join the forward pass's last state with the backward pass's first state, since each has read the whole sequence, or pool over all positions.
beginaligned h_t &= tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_t-1 + b) \\ fracpartial h_Tpartial h_k &= prod diag(1 - h_t^2) W_h endaligned
LSTM, with u_t = [h_t-1, x_t]
beginaligned f, i, o &= sigma(W_f,i,o\, u_t + b) \\ g &= tanh(W_g u_t + b_g) endaligned
beginaligned c_t &= f odot c_t-1 + i odot g \\ h_t &= o odot tanh(c_t) \\ fracpartial c_tpartial c_t-1 &= diag(f_t) endaligned
beginaligned z, r &= sigma(W_z,r [h_t-1, x_t] + b) \\ tilde h_t &= tanh(W_n [r odot h_t-1, x_t] + b_n) endaligned
h_t = (1 - z) odot h_t-1 + z odot tilde h_t

sections.t: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
Training and using BERT, end to end

chunks.x: Transformers · Deepam Minda
Seq2seq squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed vector. Attention let the decoder look back at every encoder state. The transformer dropped recurrence and kept only attention.
Each token reads every other token directly, softmax(QK^top/sqrtd_k)\,V . Training runs in parallel and any two tokens are one step apart, at a cost that grows as n^2 .
Each block adds two things to a residual stream: attention, which moves information between tokens, and an MLP, which processes it within each token.
BERT (encoder-only) is pretrained to fill in masked tokens and suits classification and tagging. GPT (decoder-only) is pretrained to predict the next token under a causal mask and suits generation.

To adapt a pretrained model: a frozen backbone with a linear probe when labelled data is small, fine-tuning when there's more data or a domain shift, LoRA when memory is tight or many tasks share one base.
The field moved from LSTMs to transformers in three steps, each fixing the last one's bottleneck.
1. Seq2seq: encode, then decode (Sutskever, Vinyals and Le, 2014)
An LSTM encoder reads the source sentence. Its last state is handed to an LSTM decoder, which writes the output one token at a time, each output becoming the next input:
beginaligned h_j &= LSTM_enc(x_j, h_j-1) \\ c &= h_T endaligned
beginaligned s_0 &= c \\ s_t &= LSTM_dec(y_t-1, s_t-1) \\ p(y_t mid y_<t, x) &= softmax(W s_t) \\ L &= -sum_t log p(y_t mid y_<t, x) endaligned

Seq2seq. Everything the decoder learns about the source arrives through one fixed-size vector (green), whether the sentence has 4 words or 40, so quality fell on long sentences. During training the decoder's inputs are the true previous words (teacher forcing).
2. Attention: let the decoder look back (Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, 2014)
Keep every encoder state. At each decoder step, score each one against the decoder's current state, softmax the scores into weights, and read their weighted sum, the context:
beginaligned e_tj &= v^top tanh(W s_t-1 + U h_j) && additive (Bahdanau) \\ e_tj &= s_t-1^top h_j && dot product (Luong's version) endaligned
beginaligned alpha_tj &= fracexp(e_tj)sum_k exp(e_tk) \\ c_t &= sum_j alpha_tj h_j \\ s_t &= LSTM_dec([y_t-1;\, c_t],\ s_t-1) endaligned
Encoder states H_enc = [h_1; dots; h_T_x]
One row per source word, all kept
Additive score: W,\ U,\ v
a times H,\ a times H,\ a
a is a small attention size; e_tj is one number
Scores e_t , weights alpha_t
One per source word; alpha_t sums to 1
Context c_t = alpha_t^top H_enc
(1 times T_x)(T_x times H) = H
A weighted average of the rows
Decoder input [y_t-1; c_t]
Previous word's embedding plus context
Logits over the target vocabulary
One attention step, in code

# enc: (T_x, H) every encoder state; s: (H,) decoder state scores = v @ tanh(W @ s[:, None] + U @ enc.T) # (T_x,) additive score per source word alpha = softmax(scores) # (T_x,) sums to 1 context = alpha @ enc # (H,) weighted average of encoder states s = lstm_dec(concat([embed(y_prev), context]), s) y_hat = softmax(W_out @ s + b_out) # next-word probabilities

One decoder step with attention. The weights say how relevant each source word is right now (here, the second). Every source word is one step from every output word, so nothing has to survive a long chain, and the bottleneck is gone.
3. The transformer: attention without recurrence (Vaswani et al., 2017)

If attention gives the direct path, drop the recurrence altogether: let every position attend to every other position, in every layer, all at once (“Attention Is All You Need”). BERT (encoder-only) and GPT (decoder-only) followed in 2018, and modern LLMs descend from GPT.
How positions are processed
Path from token 1 to token n
Cost per layer for n tokens
n sequential steps of about H^2
About n^2 d for attention, plus n d^2 for the MLP
One more token at inference
Constant work: update the state
Grows with n : attend to every past token

The last row is why recurrent models still win for streaming with constant memory, and why recent state-space models such as Mamba try to get both: a fixed-size, RNN-like state with parallel training.

Each token starts as an embedding (a learned vector per token) plus a position signal. A stack of identical blocks then updates every token's vector, and each block does two things: attention moves information between tokens, and a small MLP processes it within each token.
Self-attention: a soft lookup
beginaligned Q &= XW_Q \\ K &= XW_K \\ V &= XW_V \\ Attention(Q, K, V) &= softmax\!Big(fracQK^topsqrtd_kBig) V endaligned

Scaled dot-product attention, for all tokens at once. Row i of the score matrix is how relevant every token is to token i . The softmax turns each row into weights, and each output row is that weighted mix of the value vectors.
Every token makes three vectors: a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain, as an advertisement?) and a value (what do I hand over if picked?).
Score = query · key. Row i of QK^top says how relevant each token j is to token i . The softmax turns each row into weights that are positive and add up to 1.

Output = weighted average of values. Token i 's new vector is a mix of every token's value, weighted by relevance. All tokens do this at once, as two matrix multiplies, which is why it trains in parallel.

Why three separate projections? What a token looks for and what it advertises differ (a verb looks for its subject; the subject doesn't look for the verb the same way), so the scores can be asymmetric. And what gets copied (the value) needn't be what was matched on (the key).

A dot product of two random d_k -dimensional vectors with independent, zero-mean, unit-variance entries has variance d_k : it's a sum of d_k independent products, each with variance 1, and variances add. With d_k = 64 the scores spread over tens, the softmax goes nearly one-hot, and its gradient goes to almost zero: the same saturation problem as a tanh stuck at ±1. Dividing by sqrtd_k , the standard deviation, brings the variance back to about 1. Dividing by d_k would overshoot, shrinking the scores toward 0 so every row would start out nearly uniform.
beginaligned head_i &= Attentionbig(XW_Q^(i),\, XW_K^(i),\, XW_V^(i)big) \\ MultiHead(X) &= [head_1; dots; head_h]\, W_O endaligned

Instead of one attention over the full width d , run h heads in parallel, each with its own W_Q, W_K, W_V of width d/h , then concatenate their outputs and mix them with W_O . One softmax can only focus on one pattern per token, since its output is a single weighted average, and averaging two different relations blurs both; several heads can track several (a syntactic link, a coreference, a neighbouring word) at once. It costs about the same as one full-width head, because h heads of width d/h add up to the same d times d projections and the same n^2 d of score work.
Where word order comes from
Attention treats its input as a set: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle the same way. So position has to be added.
Sinusoidal (the original paper): fixed sine and cosine vectors of different frequencies added to the embeddings. They work for any length and change smoothly with position.
Learned (BERT, GPT-2): one trained vector per position. Simple, but capped at the longest length seen in training.

RoPE (most modern LLMs, e.g. Llama): rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, so q_i cdot k_j depends only on the offset i - j . Relative position is built into the score itself.
beginaligned PE_(pos,\,2i) &= sin\!big(pos / 10000^2i/dbig) \\ PE_(pos,\,2i+1) &= cos\!big(pos / 10000^2i/dbig) endaligned
Each dimension pair is a sine wave of a different wavelength, so every position gets a unique pattern, and a fixed offset is a fixed rotation of it. That makes relative positions easy to read off.
beginaligned x &leftarrow x + MultiHead(LN(x)) \\ x &leftarrow x + FFN(LN(x)) \\ FFN(x) &= W_2\,GELU(W_1 x) endaligned

A pre-LN transformer block. Attention gathers information from other tokens; the FFN processes it inside each token. The residual stream is a straight line, so the gradient has an untouched path through every layer, just like the LSTM's cell does through time.

The FFN is a two-layer MLP applied to each token separately, usually 4× wider than d . Attention gathers; the FFN thinks. Most of a transformer's parameters, and much of its stored knowledge, live here.

Residual connections make each sublayer add to the stream instead of replacing it, so the gradient has a straight path through every layer. It's the same trick as the LSTM's c_t = c_t-1 + dots , applied across depth instead of time.

LayerNorm, not BatchNorm. LayerNorm normalizes each token's vector on its own, so it doesn't care about batch size, sequence length or padding, and it behaves the same in training and at inference. BatchNorm would average across a batch of padded, variable-length sequences, so each token's output would depend on what else is in the batch, and the running averages it uses at inference may not match the sequences seen then.

Pre-LN vs post-LN. The original transformer put LayerNorm after each residual add (post-LN) and needed a learning-rate warmup to train. Putting it inside the branch (pre-LN, above) keeps the residual path clean and trains more stably, so most modern models use pre-LN.
For one sequence of n tokens, model width d , h heads with d_k = d_v = d/h , and FFN width d_ff = 4d . A batch adds a leading B everywhere.
Look up one row per token
One row per token; the residual stream keeps this shape all the way through
W_Q, W_K, W_V (all heads)
In code: B times n times d → reshape → B times h times n times d_k
Scores QK^top , weights A
B times h times n times n : the memory that grows as n^2
Mixes the heads; output n times d
Hidden activations n times 4d
Normalizes each row (token) over its d features
Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder
Logits n times V ; often tied to E^top
2 times n times d per layer
Grows by 2d numbers per layer for every generated token
Parameters per block: 4d^2 ( W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O ) +\ 8d^2 (FFN) approx 12 d^2 , plus small bias and LayerNorm terms.
The transformer in pseudocode

def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None): # Q: (n, d_k) K: (m, d_k) V: (m, d_v) scores = Q @ K.T / sqrt(d_k) # (n, m): how relevant each key is to each query if mask is not None: scores = where(mask, scores, -inf) # blocked pairs get weight 0 A = softmax(scores, axis=-1) # each row sums to 1 return A @ V # (n, d_v): weighted mix of values def multi_head(X, mask=None): # X: (n, d) Q, K, V = X @ W_Q, X @ W_K, X @ W_V # each (n, d) Q, K, V = split_heads(Q, K, V, h) # each (h, n, d/h) heads = [attention(Q[i], K[i], V[i], mask) for i in range(h)] return concat(heads, axis=-1) @ W_O # (n, d) def block(X, m

Before the softmax, blocked scores are set to -infty , so they get weight 0. A padding mask blocks pad tokens. A causal mask blocks the future: token i may only attend to tokens j le i . That's what lets a decoder train on every position of a sequence at once without peeking at the answer.
A causal mask on five tokens. Each row is one token's attention: it may look at itself and everything before it, never after.

The original transformer (encoder–decoder). The encoder lets every source token see every other. The decoder's masked self-attention sees only earlier target tokens; its cross-attention takes queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder's outputs (green). BERT keeps only the left tower, GPT only the right one without cross-attention.
CrossAttn(S, H) = softmax\!Big(frac(S W_Q)(H W_K)^topsqrtd_kBig)\, H W_V qquad S = decoder states,\ H = encoder outputs
Bidirectional: sees both sides
Classification, embeddings, tagging
Encoder bidirectional; decoder causal, plus cross-attention (queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder)
Map one sequence to another
Translation, summarization
The original transformer, T5
Attention builds an n times n score matrix per head: about n^2 d time and n^2 memory per layer. The FFN costs about n d^2 . Short sequences are dominated by the FFN, long ones by attention.

Training processes all positions at once. Generation is still one token at a time; the KV cache stores every past token's keys and values, so each new token's attention costs about n d per layer instead of recomputing everything (its own projections and FFN add about d^2 ).
Parameters per block: 4d^2 for W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O , plus 8d^2 for the FFN with a 4× hidden width, so about 12 d^2 .
Decoding: greedy, beam search, sampling
A decoder outputs a probability for every possible next token; something still has to pick one.
Greedy: take the most likely token at each step. Fast, but short-sighted: the best whole sequence may start with a token that wasn't the single best first step, and greedy can't go back.

Beam search: keep the w best partial sequences by total log-probability ( w is the beam width). Each step, extend each by every token and keep the best w again, at about w times the cost of greedy. Log-probabilities are negative and add up, so each extra token lowers the score and the search is biased toward ending early; dividing by a length penalty such as t^alpha corrects for that.

Sampling: draw from the distribution. A temperature tau divides the logits first (below 1 sharpens, above 1 flattens); top- k keeps only the k likeliest tokens; top- p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set whose probabilities add up to at least p .

Beam search suits tasks with one right answer: translation, summarization, speech recognition. For open-ended text the single most probable continuation is often bland and repetitive (Holtzman et al., 2019), so chat models sample instead.
The “take a piece out, what happens?” questions. Each answer follows from what the piece is for.
Scores grow with d_k , the softmax saturates to near one-hot, gradients through it vanish, and training gets unstable.
Drop positional encodings
The model sees a bag of tokens: “dog bites man” = “man bites dog”. (A causal decoder can still infer some order from how much it is allowed to see.)
Drop residual connections
Every gradient has to pass through every sublayer, so deep stacks train badly, much like a plain deep network without skip connections.
BatchNorm instead of LayerNorm

Statistics get mixed across padded sequences and examples, so outputs depend on the rest of the batch; they're noisy with small batches; and the running averages used at inference may not match the sequences seen then. In a causal decoder, statistics over positions would also leak the future.
Drop the causal mask in a decoder
In training each position can see the token it is supposed to predict, so the loss collapses. At generation the future isn't there, so it fails.
One head instead of many (same width)
Each token gets one attention pattern instead of several, so it can't track several relations at once. Quality drops; cost is about the same.
Each layer can only take weighted averages of value vectors, with no per-token computation. Capacity drops sharply.
Drop the softmax (linear attention)
Weights are no longer positive and normalized. With kernel tricks it can run in O(n) , but quality is usually lower.
Tie queries and keys ( W_Q = W_K )
Scores become symmetric, and each token tends to score itself highest, so it over-attends to itself.
Replace attention with an LSTM layer
Back to sequential processing: you lose the parallel training and the one-step path between tokens.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: The modern recipe: pretrain a transformer on a huge unlabelled corpus with a self-supervised objective, then adapt it to a small labelled task. The two classic objectives produce the two classic shapes.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: BERT reads the whole sentence at once and is trained to recover hidden tokens; its [CLS] output feeds a classifier. GPT reads left to right under a causal mask and predicts the next token at every position, so every position is a training example. The small grids show which tokens each one may attend to.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: beginaligned L_BERT &= -sum_i in mathcalM log pbig(x_i mid x_setminus mathcalMbig) \\ L_GPT &= -sum_t log p(x_t mid x_<t) \\ p(x) &= prod_t p(x_t mid x_<t) endaligned

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Here mathcalM is the set of masked positions and x_setminus mathcalM is everything else. BERT learns from about 15% of the tokens per sentence, while GPT learns from every one.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Checking BERT-base: 12 d^2 = 12 times 768^2 approx 7.1M per block, × 12 blocks ≈ 85M, plus embeddings 30,522 times 768 approx 23M ≈ 110M.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: How small a linear probe is: a linear head on a frozen 1024-d encoder for 61 classes is 1024 times 61 + 61 = 62,525 parameters. That's the entire trainable model; the encoder, often hundreds of millions of parameters, stays frozen.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: BERT: fill in the blanks (encoder-only)

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Masked language modelling. Pick 15% of the tokens. Of those, replace 80% with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and leave 10% unchanged. Predict the original token at those positions only, with cross-entropy over the vocabulary. Why 15%: fewer gives little training signal per sequence, and more leaves too little context to predict from. It's a choice rather than a tuned optimum; later work found about 40% works as well or better for large models (Wettig et al., 2023).

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Why 80/10/10? It fixes two problems you'd get if every chosen position showed [MASK]:

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: A train/test mismatch. The loss would only ever ask about [MASK] positions, so the model would have no reason to build careful vectors for the ordinary words it sees. But BERT is mostly used as an encoder for classification, tagging, QA and embeddings, and there the input never contains [MASK]: every token is a real word. (You can put [MASK] in at inference for fill-in-the-blank; that is the one exception.)

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: The random 10% (“the cat sat on the banana”, predict “mat”) means no visible word can be blindly trusted, since any might be a planted fake. The model has to check every token against its context.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: The unchanged 10% (the true word shown, still predicted) stops the opposite habit of ignoring what it sees: the visible word is usually right, so use it, but verify it. These positions also look exactly like real inputs.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Because the random and unchanged cases look like ordinary words, the model can't tell which tokens are being tested, so it keeps a good contextual vector for all of them. Overall that's 12% of tokens masked, 1.5% randomized and 1.5% left as-is. The exact split was chosen by ablation in the BERT paper.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Input format: [CLS] tokens [SEP], with token, position and segment embeddings added together. The final [CLS] vector feeds classification heads, and each token's final vector feeds tagging heads.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Next-sentence prediction was a second objective in the original BERT. RoBERTa dropped it, trained longer and re-drew the mask every epoch (“dynamic masking”), and did better.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Why bidirectional suits understanding: each token sees both sides, which is what tagging and classification need. It can't generate text left to right naturally.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: Domain BERTs: the same recipe on other “languages”. ProtBert is BERT trained with masked LM on protein sequences, with amino acids as tokens.

chunks.h: Pretrained language models: BERT, GPT and fine-tuning
chunks.x: def mlm_example(tokens): labels = [IGNORE] * len(tokens) # no loss at unmasked positions for i in sample_positions(tokens, frac=0.15): labels[i] = tokens[i] # predict the original token here r = random() if r < 0.8: tokens[i] = MASK_ID # 80%: [MASK] elif r < 0.9: tokens[i] = random_token() # 10%: a random token # else: 10%: leave it unchanged return tokens, labels logits = bert(tokens) # (n, V), bidirectional: no causal mask loss = cross_entropy(logits, labels, ignore_index=IGNORE)

chunks.x: Here h_i is the encoder's final vector at position i , g is a small dense + GELU + LayerNorm head, and E is the token-embedding matrix reused as the output layer (one logit per vocabulary word). The original BERT added next-sentence prediction, a binary cross-entropy on the [CLS] vector, so L = L_MLM + L_NSP ; RoBERTa later dropped it.
